en: Preface:

Now, the Vinaya is the lifeblood of the True Dharma. This is because when the precepts are pure and the Sangha is authentic, the karma of both natural and proscribed offenses remains unstained and unrestrained.
Thus, the Way is propagated and virtue is perfected; the teachings of both expedient means and ultimate reality are successfully expounded and elevated, benefiting oneself and others alike.
They cross the ocean of suffering to reach the other shore. They carry on the legacy of their predecessors and initiate the future, sustaining the life of wisdom to revitalize the profound Way.
Therefore it is said: "When the Vinaya endures, the True Dharma endures. Otherwise, the five perversions would go unchecked and the eight impurities would be pursued as one's own nature;
the venerable title of the Sangha-treasure would be diminished, and the pure virtue of the field of merit would be lost. Above, there would be no model; below, there would be no standard. Even if...
To gather a multitude and rectify one’s followers while they all belong to the faction of the Dharma-demons and outsiders—how could one wish for the True Dharma to abide long in such circumstances?

(The Master) remained secluded in a remote and desolate corner; his learning was modest compared to the sages of old, yet he falsely inherited the final charge of his predecessors and strove mightily to plant the banner of the precepts.

Reflecting that the ocean of the Vinaya is vast and deep, making it difficult for students to fathom, he has therefore searched for the essential points of the various sections to clearly elucidate the principles of restraint and observance.
This work is a great achievement. Although it does not exhaustively explore the source, it is hoped that it will serve as a convenient reference.

It is my earnest wish that all virtuous colleagues will strictly observe the seven groups of precepts to guard against transgressions and revere the four reliances to advance upon the Path with contentment.

Thus, in this world of five turbidities, the fragrance of the precepts shall pervade the great earth, and the Dharma-rain of the six harmonies shall bestow abundant blessings upon humanity. This is what is meant by "the Vinaya abides."
If the world abides in the True Dharma, is it not likewise so?

The division of the Vinaya into various schools originated from differing tenets. For a wise person who propagates the great model, it is logically appropriate to harmonize and integrate them.
According to the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Śāriputra asked: "How is it that the Tathāgata’s True Dharma has become so fragmented in such a short time?

Now that its original flavor has been lost, how should one uphold it? (The phrase "in a short time" refers to the three or four hundred years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. The Buddha said: "Mahā..."
In the *Saṃghāṭa*, its flavor is pure and correct; in the other schools, it is as if nectar has been added.
When the gods drink it, they drink only the nectar and discard the water. When humans drink it, they take both the water and the nectar together;
thus, at times it cures illness, and at times it causes disease. It is the same for those who recite it: those with great wisdom can extract [the essence].
It can be relinquished; yet foolish people are unable to discern it. (Text) Thus we know that the divisions of the various schools arise from differing views.
As for the principles of acceptance and rejection, they are prophesied by the holy words [of the Buddha].

Therefore, although this compilation takes the Dharmaguptaka school as its primary tenet, whatever illuminating insights are found in other schools have all been adopted. This is also the method of Nanshan.
The Vinaya-pitaka masters have compiled this as the ultimate synthesis of the tradition. Question:

Since it is said that the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Mo-xun Seng-qi) is pure and correct in its flavor, why do you not follow it, but instead follow the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Si-fen)? Is this not like drinking nectar mixed with water? Answer:
Regarding the forty fascicles of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* contained within this canon, the masters of antiquity all judged them to be an abridged version; therefore...
It is not that which we take as our primary authority, for its text is brief and its meaning incomplete, and furthermore, it does not accord with the number of two hundred and fifty precepts.
As for those who now take the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) of Tanwude as their authority, it is because this was the tradition followed by the holy masters of Nanshan;
because it has been widely propagated since the Tang dynasty; and because the characteristics of the two hundred and fifty precepts are fully complete within it.
Since the *Khandakas* are systematic and free from disorder, I now take them as my primary authority; what cause for doubt could there be?
The Vinaya regulations are rigorous and detailed, and the translated text is so repetitive that beginners, upon reading it, cannot help but sigh at its vastness.
To facilitate easy consultation, I have now abridged the essential passages; however, regarding the underlying principles, there has been neither addition nor subtraction.
The precepts were established based on specific events; they arose only when there was a cause. Therefore, beneath each article, the circumstances of the offense are first presented.
One must understand that within a sandalwood forest, there is never a common tree; how could there be ordinary beings at the assembly on Vulture Peak?

These were all manifestations of great skillful means to secretly protect the ranks of the Sangha. By requesting the Buddha to establish the precepts, they assisted in spreading the Dharma transformation. Those who read this should...
One should give rise to reverence and faith; be careful not to look down upon it and incur the reproach of arrogance. Therefore, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* states:
"If an elder hears of this impure conduct, be careful not to be startled or find it strange. Why?
Because the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us, spoke these harsh words for the sake of establishing the precepts. If he had not spoken of them, how could we know of the *pārājika* offense?"
[If one laughs] with the teeth exposed, it is a *pārājika*, a *sthūlātyaya*, or a *duṣkṛta*. If a Dharma master is lecturing for others, you must be careful not to laugh with your teeth bared;
if anyone laughs, they shall be expelled. Why is this? The Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, has spoken these words from his golden mouth.
You should listen with a sense of shame and remorse; why do you laugh?

The translations produced by various schools differ in their phonetic renderings, yet their meanings are truly without distinction. Because the languages of the Five Indies vary, some terms carry greater weight while others are more abbreviated;
thus, all follow the ancient precedents. These notes are either appended beneath the text or added at the end of the fascicle, so as to spare the reader the labor of searching for them.

Regarding the characteristics of the five categories of precepts, each has its own fundamental nature, its consequential flow, its natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), its proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*), and the afflictions from which they arise.
"Natural" refers to that which is inherently sinful by its very nature; "proscribed" refers to that which becomes an offense only because of a specific regulation.

Furthermore, natural offenses occur solely within a defiled state of mind, whereas proscribed offenses may occur in both defiled and non-defiled states of mind. Only the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* elucidates these fundamental natures and their consequential flows with such excellence.

Observing the Vinaya, one determines whether an action is of the nature of a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited by prohibition). According to the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*, the underlying afflictions (*kleśa*) are identified.

Now, regarding each precept, whether [an affliction] is present or absent shall entirely follow the scriptural records; there shall be no private additions whatsoever. If one infers according to the underlying meaning, other cases may likewise be understood by analogy.
Under each precept, there are approximately eight sections: first, the origin of the enactment of the precept; second, an exegesis of the text according to the Vinaya;

third, the determination of the gravity of the offense; fourth, the extension of the regulation to other groups; fifth, the provision of exceptions according to specific circumstances; sixth, the collation and extraction from various recensions.
Seventh, citations from sūtras and śāstras; eighth, supplementary investigations based on contextual matters. However, the presence or absence of these eight sections is not fixed;
one shall see this for oneself upon encountering the text. As for the main body of the precepts, all lines are indented at the top; all other material is set down by one character.
If one uses a text from the same section, it should simply be indicated by the word "Vinaya" followed by the ordinal number of the division (e.g., "the third division") and so forth.
If one uses a text from another section, its specific title must be separately indicated to identify it, as this facilitates the examination of the library cases.
The Vinaya comprises two modes of observance: abstention (*saṃvara*) and performance (*kriyā*). Abstention primarily clarifies the principles of what is permitted and what is prohibited;

performance, however, encompasses the regulations for the recitation of the precepts. There exists a compilation based on a separate version of the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts) translated by Buddhayaśas.

This [previous] work used a separate compilation and did not distinguish between the broad categories of *śīla* (precepts) and their observance (*pravṛtti*) or non-observance (*nivṛtti*). This present collection, however, focuses exclusively on investigating the single gate of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and upholding the precepts (*dhāraṇa*).

Therefore, it clarifies only the characteristics of the two hundred and fifty precepts. Consequently, the *poṣadha* verses and the rituals for the proclamation of purity (*jñapti-karman*) and so forth are not recorded at the beginning of this volume.
As for the practices of active observance, they shall naturally be recorded and explained within the section on the ritual of reciting the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara-vyākhyāna*). In this way, one may...
There is no admixture of what is to be practiced and what is to be abandoned.

While the Sūtras encompass various teachings, the Vinaya is exclusively the Buddha’s own ordinance. Even those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment downward are not yet capable of it, let alone the lesser sages who would dare to compose words therein.
This is truly because the Tathāgata’s practice and fruition are perfectly complete, having exhausted the light and heavy [karmic offenses] of all sentient beings.
The nature of karma is such that the *vinaya* was established solely by the Buddha; all others of lower status may only rely upon and follow it.

It differs from the sūtras and śāstras, which permit the acceptance of other teachings. Therefore, I revere this [vinaya] and dare not engage in arbitrary interpretation. The explanations of meanings and the presentation of matters are all in accordance with the texts of the *vinaya-piṭaka*.
Whether a matter is subject to heavy punishment or light dispensation, one must entirely abide by what was spoken from the Golden Mouth.

The essential teachings of the Sūtras benefit sentient beings, universally reaching all realms of existence. Whether in the heavens or dragon palaces, whether dwelling in the Jeta Grove or on Vulture Peak,
whether in the residences of kings and ministers, or amidst wilds, forests, and springs— these appear solely in accordance with the faculties and conditions of beings.
In matters of conversion and guidance, there is never any exclusion or restriction for those who come to listen. The Vinaya, however, is not thus;
if an offense occurs elsewhere, it must be formally established as a precept within the Saṃgha. Even when a nun commits a transgression, the regulation likewise relies upon the Saṃgha.
First, this causes all bhikṣus to feel shame and reverence, thereby carefully guarding against non-action (akriyā). Second, it serves as a barrier to prevent outsiders from giving rise to slander.

Fearing that [such knowledge] might lead to disrespect toward the monastic community, the Vinaya was established as an internal regulation of the Buddha, to be observed exclusively by the great monks (bhikṣus).
It is like a king’s secret treasury, which is not permitted for outside ministers to know. Even if laypeople or śrāmaṇeras were to examine it first, [it would remain restricted].

Later, when he wished to ascend the platform for ordination, he was not permitted to receive full precepts because he had committed the offense of "staying like a thief" (*steyāśana*). This is called a "grave obstacle.
Thus, the preface to the *Śīla-hetupratyaya-sūtra* states: "In India, those who uphold the Vinaya do not allow their texts to be viewed by everyone indiscriminately;

only those who are firm and clear-minded practitioners of the twelve dharmas may open the sealed bindings to transmit them to one another. Yaśas saw this entrustment and received these instructions with great earnestness.
Zhuǎn! It is said, "One may cause people to follow [the Way], but one cannot cause them to know it. These words are most urgent, for they stem from [the Buddha] himself.
(Text) Lately, when lectures on the Abhidharma and Vinaya have been held, both laypeople and śrāmaṇeras have been indiscriminately permitted to sit and listen.

While this may be called the "gift of Dharma," it is in fact a violation of the law. To thus insult and disregard the solemn regulations—how can such a crime escape punishment? It is my hope that all who...
If those who inherit the teacher’s lineage or occupy the position of senior elder (sthavira) should see laypeople or śrāmaṇeras perusing the Vinaya collections or this compilation,
they ought to instruct them with compassionate words so that they shall not continue to read them. This will bring benefit to both oneself and others, and the path of the Dharma may flourish.

The virtue of the precepts is inconceivable; its merit surpasses all other practices. It takes the initial cause and the ultimate fruit as its foundational basis, and the pure land and its joyful retribution as its root.
For those lost on perilous paths, it serves as an excellent guide; for those seeking rescue from the sea of suffering, it serves as a vessel.
Thus, it is that which the worthy and sages cultivate and the Buddhas realize, extending even to the temporary joys of humans and devas, and [protects against] evil...

The Path is eternally detached; nothing transcends the precepts. Therefore, from the Deer Park until the Śāla trees, throughout the five periods of teaching, our Śākyamuni World-Honored One extensively praised the Dharma of the precepts within the Great Canon of the Tripitaka. It is not only this one Buddha who esteemed the Vinaya;
indeed, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods who appear to benefit sentient beings and preach the Dharma likewise do so.

However, if one practices apart from the precepts while hoping to transcend the three realms, it is like desiring to walk without feet, wishing to fly without wings, or seeking to cross a river without a boat;
how could such a thing ever be achieved?
There are three kinds of precepts. Fruit and cause mutually establish one another; their acquisition is discussed differently, yet in terms of function, they are common to all.

These are: first, the *pratimokṣa* precept, which is the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*). Second, the dhyāna precept, which is the precept concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*).
Concentration is quiescent gathering; at the time of entering meditative concentration, the three karmas naturally become disciplined and wholesome, and no evils arise. Third...

Uncontaminated precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are precisely the precepts concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahagata-śīla*). The Path is that which enables thorough penetration; once true realization has arisen, one naturally refrains from transgression.
This is like the field of a first-stage fruit (*srotāpanna*), where insects remain four inches away [from the plow]; this is the power of the precepts concomitant with the Path.

Since these two types of precept-dharma are superior functions of the mind capable of giving rise to the precepts, and since the Path-concentration (*mārga-samādhi*) and the restraint (*saṃvara*) arise simultaneously, they are termed "concomitant."
Now, the Piṭaka of Vinaya primarily elucidates discipline (vinaya-saṃvara), yet it also encompasses meditative concentration (samādhi) and the Path (mārga).

Since the virtues of meditative concentration and wisdom arise from maintaining pure ethical conduct, discipline serves as the cause, while concentration and the Path constitute the fruit. This occurs through the power of dhyāna and the outflow-free state (anāsrava).

When natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and proscribed precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*) are both rendered completely pure, then the *vimukti* (liberation) is the fruit, while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*) serve as the conditions.
Therefore, within the Vinaya, it is required that the bhikṣus increase their mind and wisdom. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"This *pratimokṣa* precept exists when a Buddha appears in the world, but does not exist when a Buddha does not appear; however, the dhyāna and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precepts [exist regardless]."
The Pratimokṣa precepts exist at all times and are obtained through instruction; the dhyāna and anāsrava precepts are not obtained through instruction.

Furthermore, the Pratimokṣa precepts exist only among the disciples of the Buddha, whereas both the dhyāna precepts and the anāsrava precepts are possessed by both Buddhists and non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Indeed, it is these who are able to sustain the Buddha-dharma; with the seven assemblies existing in the world, the fruits of the paths of the three vehicles continue in succession.
It is uninterrupted; it takes the prātimokṣa as its very foundation. The meditative and the outflow-free precepts are not so.
Therefore, among the three types of precepts, it is the most excellent.

One who upholds the Vinaya must know the gravity of offenses and what is permitted or prohibited, and must resolve doubts and regrets; only then can the True Dharma be made to abide long and remain uninterrupted.

Thus, the Fourth Part states: "There are five qualities that constitute being one who upholds the Vinaya: first, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense;

third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is grave; fifth, extensively reciting the precepts of both divisions. Furthermore, there are another five qualities, four of which are as follows: [text continues].

First: five methods for the extensive recitation of the Vinaya. Furthermore, there are five dharmas; four are as before, and the fifth refers to abiding in the Vinaya without wavering. Again, there are five dharmas;

Regarding the first point, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching, there are both general and specific aspects. As for the general aspect, it means that the Tathāgata appeared in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal event (*ekamahākaruṇāhetu-pratyaya*).

Specifically, regarding this Vinaya alone, there are ten further meanings that serve as the causes for the arising of the teaching: first, to gather the Saṃgha; second, to cause the Saṃgha to rejoice;
third, to cause the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness; fourth, to cause those who have not yet had faith to believe; fifth, those who have already... [text continues].
First, it causes faith to increase; second, it brings those who are difficult to tame into submissiveness; third, it grants peace and happiness to those with a sense of shame and remorse;
fourth, it cuts off outflows (*āsrava*) in the present; fifth, it cuts off outflows in the future; sixth, it ensures that the True Dharma endures for a long time.
First, regarding "embracing the Saṃgha": this refers to those among the various classes of people in the world—whether men or women—who possess profound faith;

having entered into the True Dharma and developed deep reverence and trust, they delight in becoming bhikṣus so as to constitute the Saṃgha, thereby enabling them to attain the fruit of the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Second, causing the Saṃgha to rejoice (the *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "for the sake of the Saṃgha’s supreme excellence"):

this means that once one has entered into the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, one recognizes the venerability of the Saṃgha, strengthens one's resolve for the Path, takes delight in upholding the precepts, and purifies mundane sentiments;
because it is able to cause wholesome dharmas to increase and become most preeminent.

Third, regarding "causing the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness": this means that by relying on the purity of the prohibitive precepts for one’s livelihood, cultivating oneself through the three types of wisdom, and remaining untainted by the five kinds of wrong livelihood, one repays the debt of the faithful offerings with the seven kinds of spiritual wealth. Thus, one’s virtuous deeds gradually increase, and one does not fall away because of those offerings.

Fourth, causing those who have not yet developed faith to do so. This means that by maintaining the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*) and being pure in both nature and observance, and by maintaining a dignified and disciplined demeanor in the four modes of conduct (*iryāpatha*), one refrains from engaging in derision.
Thus, one causes those who have not yet developed faith to know how to take refuge in the Buddha-way, and brings about the arising of correct faith in those with wrong views.
Regarding "causing those who have already attained faith to increase": this refers to the purification of the code of discipline (*vinaya*) and the exemplary nature of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Just as one who benefits through teaching and possesses a compassionate majesty worthy of reverence can cause others to remain long within the Buddha-dharma, they inspire veneration and following, thereby further increasing pure faith.
Regarding the sixth point, "those who are difficult to discipline are made disciplined" (the *Vinayasamgraha* states: this is for the purpose of subduing wicked persons).
This refers to a certain class of bhikṣus in name only, as well as another class who, despite possessing faith, have powerful afflictions and karmic habits.
Now, by means of admonition and discipline according to the gravity of their transgressions, they are subdued so that they may recognize their own faults and accord with the Sangha.

Regarding the seventh point, "those with a sense of shame and remorse obtain peace and happiness": this refers to the pure discipline that tames those who are difficult to tame and brings them to contentment.

Those who delight in the precepts and possess a sense of shame and remorse—monks who share a single boundary (*sīmā*) and the six harmonies—experience no disturbance in body or mind; because they attain such serenity, they advance upon the Path.
Regarding the eighth [category], the abandonment of present outflows (*āsrava*): this refers to the fact that all evil actions that give rise to karma are moistened by rebirth.

Now, through the functional power of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) as a preventive measure, one is able to oppose their active manifestation and dry up the seeds of karma, so that afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise;

Ninth, regarding the severance of future outflows (*āsrava*): this refers to the arising of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), whereby the mind is free from defilement, the seeds of the outflows are forever severed, one no longer undergoes future existence, and the fruit of the Sangha Jewel is realized.
Tenth, regarding causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time: this means ensuring that the lineage of the pure Jewel of the Sangha continues without interruption;
by proclaiming the Dharma according to the teachings, extensively benefiting humans and devas, and instructing one another in succession, the True Dharma is thereby enabled to abide for a long time.
Regarding the ten meanings explained above according to the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, these constitute the causes for the establishment of the retreat (*varṣā*) in this teaching.
The Sarvāstivādins state: "The Tathāgata established the precepts based on these ten meanings in order to accord with these ten benefits and merits, and to attain these ten benefits and merits.

It states that śrāvakas of fixed nature and icchantikas devoid of Buddha-nature shall all eventually attain Buddhahood; only then does it exhaustively present the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna, which is termed "Final" because it accords with the true principle and is also called "Real.

Although it explains the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it also ultimately converges upon their true nature (*dharmatā*). This is the ultimate point of the Mahāyāna and is called the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*).
Fourth is the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*). This teaching clarifies that the non-arising of even a single thought is itself called Buddhahood;

it does not teach according to the gradual progression of stages and positions, and is therefore termed "Sudden. Within it, the characteristics of phenomena are not explained, but only the true nature is clarified. All...
There is that which is merely conceptual construction; the entire dharma-realm is solely beyond words—this is called the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao).

Fifth is the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao). What is taught in this teaching is solely the inexhaustible dharma-realm, wherein the ocean of nature is perfectly interfused and the atoms of lands are without obstruction;

Because they are shrouded [by ignorance], they consequently give rise to greed, hatred, and false views, becoming entangled by the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
They are swept away and submerged in the four currents, rising and sinking through the nine stages. Thus, the six consciousnesses and the three poisons constitute the root of defilement.

Third, divining good and bad fortune through physiognomy:

this refers to those bhikṣus who study heterodox arts, practice divination regarding life spans and the interpretation of physical features, and discourse upon auspicious and inauspicious signs. And...

Seeking gain and offerings: fourth, manifesting majesty with loud voices; that is to say, various bhikṣus speak loudly and in high tones, falsely assuming an air of dignified deportment to inspire awe and respect in others, thereby seeking gain and offerings. Fifth, speaking of the gains one has obtained to stir the hearts of people;
that is to say, various bhikṣus, having obtained gain in that place, speak of it here; or having obtained gain here, [speak of it] there.
To speak in such a way as to move the hearts of others for the sake of seeking gain and offerings—these five kinds of conduct cause one’s livelihood to be wrong.

Regarding the eighth impurity, the acquisition of fields and houses: it is said that a bhikṣu should dwell in dependence upon the Saṅgha and diligently cultivate the supramundane, pure, and unconditioned Path.
If one privately acquires fields and houses in order to provide for oneself, this is improper.
1. Purity. 2. Planting roots and sprouts. A bhikṣu should diligently cultivate the work of the Path and not give rise to greedy attachment toward worldly matters of livelihood.
If, for his own sake rather than for the sake of the community, he privately plants fields and gardens, it will internally obstruct his spiritual practice;
this is impurity. 3. Hoarding grain and millet. This means that a bhikṣu should sustain his body by means of alms-gathering.
To maintain a pure livelihood: if one does not do so for the sake of the community, but instead privately hoards grain, millet, rice, and wheat, this is considered impure.
Fourth, regarding the keeping of slaves and servants: a bhikṣu should dwell in a secluded and quiet place, cultivating and restraining his mind.
Practicing the conduct of peace and happiness, if one does not do so for the sake of the community but instead keeps slaves and servants to employ in labor, this is impure.
Fifth, keeping herds of livestock: this means that a bhikṣu should maintain the prohibitive precepts and, with a compassionate heart, refrain from killing;
if he keeps cattle, horses, or other species that breed, it defiles his pure conduct (brahmacarya), and this is impure. Sixth, hoarding...

Regarding the accumulation of gold, silver, coins, and treasures: it is said that a bhikṣu should regard purity and elegance as supreme, finding contentment in poverty and delighting in the Way, possessing no superfluous belongings.

If one greedily accumulates worldly gold, silver, wealth, and other such assets, seeking profit for livelihood and calculating income and expenditure, this deviates from the practice of the Way and is considered impure. Seventh, the accumulation of ivory in seven treasuries.
As for objects such as carved and engraved items: a bhikṣu should uphold the Buddha’s precepts and aspire to frugality and simplicity.
He should not harbor greedy attachment toward various playthings or luxuries; wearing coarse cloth and sitting on grass mats, he should always maintain contentment.
To crave rare, ornate objects of the world is considered impure. Eighth, he should not hoard copper or iron cauldrons and pots to cook his own food.

This means that when a bhikṣu dwells among the community, he should eat together with the community, or else subsist on almsfood while exerting himself in the holy life to accomplish the work of the Path.
If, however, he hoards up cauldrons and pots for his own cooking and eats apart from the community, [he acts improperly].
This is what is called impurity.
"Xun" (殉) is pronounced like "jun" (旬); it means to follow.

Regarding the pure virtue of the field of merit, the first arousal of the mind involves departing from the secular world; that is to say, a person who has left the household life arouses a courageous and resolute mind.
To transcend the mundane world, practice the Bodhi of the Buddha, and be able to cherish and wear the wondrous Way, thereby becoming a field of merit for the world—this is the first pure virtue.

Second, to destroy one's physical beauty: this means that those who have left the home life shave off their hair and beards, abandon their [worldly] marks of excellence, cast off the dusty garments of the secular world, and don the Dharma robes of the Tathāgata, thus being fully endowed with the qualities of a Buddha.
Maintaining dignified deportment and serving as a field of merit for the world—this is the second pure virtue. Third, to forever sever ties of kinship and affection:
this refers to leaving home to join the Buddha, cutting off the feelings of parental love, and single-mindedly and diligently practicing the Way.
This is to repay the virtue of one’s parents who gave birth and raised them; furthermore, it enables one to become a field of merit for the world.

This is the third pure virtue. Fourth is the relinquishing of body and life: this refers to those who have left the household life and are able to cast aside their physical existence without any attachment or regret, devoting themselves single-mindedly to seeking realization of the Buddha-way; furthermore, they are able to serve as a field of merit for the world. This is...
The fourth is pure virtue. The fifth is the aspiration for the Mahāyāna. This means that those who have left the household life constantly maintain a mind intent on saving all beings;
they single-mindedly and diligently seek the Dharma of the Mahāyāna to deliver all sentient beings and serve as a field of merit for the world. This is the fifth pure virtue.
The *kai* (model) tree grows upon the tomb of the Duke of Zhou; its leaves are green in spring, red in summer, white in autumn, and black in winter—thus it attains correctness through its color.
The *kai* tree grows upon the tomb of Confucius; its remaining branches are sparse yet unbending—thus it attains rectitude through its substance.
These two characters derive their meaning from these qualities: "correctness" (*zheng*) and "rectitude" (*zhi*). May they be so.
As for the rule of the Dharma:
this fragrant grass, O bhikṣus, grows in the Snowy Mountains and possesses five virtues, by which it serves as a metaphor for the bhikṣu.
First, its nature is supple and soft; this serves as a metaphor for the bhikṣu’s ability to subdue the coarseness of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Second, the spreading of trailing vines on all sides; this is a metaphor for how bhikṣus transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings in an unceasing succession.
Third, the fragrance being heard from afar; this is a metaphor for how the bhikṣu’s virtuous conduct and precepts are so fragrant that they are renowned among the masses.
Fourth, the ability to heal pain; this is a metaphor for how the bhikṣu can sever the painful afflictions of the poisons of the defilements (*kleśa*). Fifth, not turning one's back...
"Sunlight" is used as a metaphor for a bhikṣu’s right view and reflection, which always turn toward the sun of the Buddha and never turn away from it.

Regarding the general principles of the scriptures, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are three types of teachings: first, those spoken by the Buddha, meaning what was proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata.
Second, the teachings of the disciples, which refers to the various śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who speak by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power and empowerment.

Third, the teachings of the sages, which refers to the great sages within the Buddha’s assembly who entered the Path under the Buddha, vowed to propagate the Buddha’s transformation, and proclaimed the True Dharma.
Fourth, the teachings of the devas, which refers to how Śakra, every time he is in the Hall of Good Dharma, [speaks for them].

The devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven expound the Prajñāpāramitā, as do the five types of emanated beings; that is to say, the noble ones of the Three Vehicles manifest transformations according to the capacities of sentient beings.
For example, Rāhula manifested as a Cakravartin King to deliver an elderly woman to the east of the city;
he first praised the causes and conditions for the fruits of merit, and subsequently taught the wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
"Those equal to or below the Perfectly Awakened One" refers to Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), such as the present Bodhisattva Maitreya.

From the perspective of those on the lower stages, although they are equal to the Buddha, because they have not yet exhausted even a single most subtle grade of ignorance, they are still called Bodhisattvas. The term "below" indicates the nine stages of the lower levels.
"Xian" (賢).
"Cuo" (措) is pronounced with the fourth tone; it means to place or settle. This is the essential outline.
The twelve factors of the Dharma are the twelve ascetic practices (*dhūta*). They are also called *dhuta*;
this is translated as "shaking off," "cultivating and purifying," or "winnowing. As for the twelve factors: first, dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
1. Always begging for food; 2. Begging for food in successive order; 3. Practicing the rule of eating one meal a day; 4. Moderating the quantity of food; 5.
Not drinking fruit juice or honey syrup after midday; 6. Wearing rag-robes; 7. Possessing only three robes; 8.
Dwelling among burial mounds; 9. Staying at the foot of a tree; 10. Sitting in the open air; 11. Sitting only and not lying down.
*Jianteng* (緘縢): The upper character is pronounced *jiān*; the lower character is pronounced *téng*. It refers to a cord or binding. Specifically, it denotes the cords used to bind a chest.
The phrase "a person may be made to follow [the Way] but not made to know it" originates from the *Lunyu* (Analects).

It is being used here figuratively to mean that a person who has newly received the precepts may only be made to practice according to the Vinaya, but cannot yet be made to peruse the Vinaya-piṭaka to gain understanding.
Regarding the origins from which the precepts were established: the group of six bhikṣus and their like were all manifestations of great spiritual power (mahā-upāya).

They intentionally displayed the conditions for transgression for the sake of the degenerate age, out of sincere concern that the ignorant might fail to understand and instead take these events as literal facts, thereby falling into laxity and self-indulgence.
Teachers who expound the teachings through the study of meaning (yixue) have deeply entered the ocean of doctrine; hence they are called "masters of the study of meaning.
Regarding the phrase "perilous paths," "perilous" refers to danger and obstruction, while "paths" refers to roads; this is a metaphor for the three miserable realms (trividha-durgati).
The Deer Park (Mṛgadāva) is located more than ten *li* from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
This was the dwelling place where the Tathāgata and Devadatta were both formerly deer kings; each presided over a herd of more than five hundred deer.
At that time, while the king was hunting in the plains and marshes, the Bodhisattva deer king went before him and said: "Great King, as you hunt across the central plains, [you must] release..."
"Flaming arrows fly. All of us, your followers, have our lives hanging by this very morning; before long, we shall be stinking corpses, with nothing left to eat.
We wish to take turns each day to provide a deer, so that Your Majesty may have a meal of fresh meat and we may prolong our lives for a few more days."
The king approved of these words and turned his carriage back. As the two herds took turns offering up their lives, there was a pregnant doe in Deva’s herd whose turn had come to die.
She said to her leader, "Though my body deserves death, my offspring has not yet reached its turn.
The deer king replied angrily, "Who does not cherish their own life? The doe sighed, "My lord is unkind; I shall die without..."

The time had come. He then went to appeal for help to the Bodhisattva Deer King. The King said, "How tragic is the heart of a compassionate mother; her thoughts reach even to that which has not yet taken form.
I shall now take your place. He then proceeded to the king's gate. The king asked for the reason, and the deer related the situation in detail.
Upon hearing this, the king sighed and said, "I am a human being with the body of a deer, while you are a deer with the heart of a human. Thereupon, he released all the deer.
No longer did they lose their lives; thus, that grove became a refuge for deer and was consequently named the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva). The *heqù* tree is also called the Crane Grove (*Hālindā*).
When the Tathāgata appeared in the world to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings, his work of transformation and his karmic conditions were completed.
Between the twin śāla trees, on the fifteenth day of the second month, he entered parinirvāṇa. Both trees turned entirely white, like the color of cranes;
therefore, they are called the Crane Trees (Krauñcavana).
*Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "Individual Liberation. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Regarding 'individual liberation' (*prātimokṣa*):

because one relies upon the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and practices according to its instructions, one gradually eliminates the nine grades of afflictions—ranging from the lowest of the low to the highest of the high—and because one never regresses, one attains liberation from all afflictions; thus it is called 'individual liberation. Furthermore..."
The afflictions of both the seeing and cultivation stages are numerous in their various types; the ability to abandon them individually is called *prātimokṣa*.
Because sentient beings are swept away by delusions throughout the three realms, they first seek the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* as the primary cause for liberation.
Furthermore, it is said that it "conforms to liberation. This is a designation established based on its fruit, for it conforms to both conditioned and unconditioned fruits.
Furthermore, it is said that it "guarantees liberation," meaning that when one's precepts are pure and one possesses wisdom, the Tathāgata guarantees that one will certainly realize nirvāṇa.
The first is Madhyamaka and the second is Yogācāra. Madhyamaka is the school of Nāgārjuna, which the world calls the Dharma-nature (Faxing) school.
Yogācāra is the school of Dharmapāla, which the world calls the Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang) school. It is named Yogācāra because it takes the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* as its fundamental authority;
this term translates as "correspondence" (*xiāngyìng*).
"Idle entanglement" means that which is cluttered; "entanglement" means that which is not untied.
The "leather air-bag that does not leak" is a vessel for crossing the ocean. Long ago, there was a merchant who carried such a bag across the sea.
A rākṣasa in the ocean begged him for his air-filled life-sack. The man would not give it to him. He then begged for half of it, but was still not granted permission.
When he begged for even a single thread, the request was still not fulfilled. Why? Because his life depended upon the sack; if the life-sack were to burst, [his life would end].
Then one will ultimately be unable to reach the shore of the ocean. This serves as a metaphor for a person who upholds the precepts and desires to cross the bitter sea of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Even if they encounter a *rākṣasa* of craving and attachment who offers to grant a single wish, it will ultimately not be granted. Why? Because their life depends upon the precepts.
If the precepts are broken, one will drown in the bitter sea of birth and death, with no time of escape in sight. Therefore, one must protect them.
The precepts are such as these.
Do not treat even a minor transgression lightly, for it may result in the final exhortation at the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
He commanded all bhikṣus to take the precepts as their teacher and to abide by the precepts; thus, it is called the "final exhortation. If one disregards even subtle faults and...
To be unrestrained and dissolute is to violate the Bequeathed Teaching and not to be a disciple of the Buddha; therefore, it is said, "Do not treat them lightly.
I have briefly presented one corner, for it is said that objects have four corners: by presenting one corner, one may infer the other three.
*Māyī* is fully rendered as *Mātṛkā*, which translates as "Mother of Wisdom" (*jñānamātṛ*), because it is capable of generating wisdom.
Fascicle One:
The Jewel of the Sangha refers to the fruit of Arhatship, which is the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
The three types of wisdom are self-cultivating; "cultivating" (*shu*) means goodness, harmony, and pure clarity. As for the three types of wisdom: first is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
This arises from hearing the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); because of this hearing, one is able to generate untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-ārya-prajñā*).
Second is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which arises from being able to contemplate the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, as well as from [relying on] a spiritual friend.
The meanings of the Dharma as heard are all capable of giving rise to untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-ārya-prajñā*). Third is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*):
having already heard the Dharma and contemplated its significance, one should then practice accordingly; through this cultivation, one is able to give rise to untainted noble wisdom.
The seven kinds of wealth of the Dharma refer to the seven types of supramundane Dharma-wealth, beginning with faith.
If all sentient beings practice these seven dharmas, they will be sustained and perfected into the fruit of the Way; therefore, they are called "wealth. First is the wealth of faith:
this means that faith enables one to decisively receive and uphold the True Dharma as the provisions for the Buddha-way. Second is the wealth of vigor: this means...
Being unable yet to perceive the truth of the ultimate reality, one single-mindedly and diligently seeks the supramundane path as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood.

Third is the wealth of the precepts (*śīla-dhana*); it means regarding the precepts as the root of liberation, capable of restraining and preventing the evils and transgressions of body, speech, and mind, thereby serving as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood.
Fourth is the wealth of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya-dhana*). "Shame" (*hrī*) refers to feeling shame before the heavens. "Remorse" (*apatrāpya*)...

This refers to one who possesses a sense of shame. It means that once one is capable of both *hrī* (self-respect) and *apatrāpya* (shame before others), one will not commit various evil karmas, thereby establishing the foundation for attaining Buddhahood.

Fifth is the wealth of hearing (*śruta-dhana*). Hearing is the foremost of the three types of wisdom; through hearing, one is necessarily able to reflect (*cintā*), and through reflection, one is necessarily able to practice (*bhāvanā*).
If one can hear the Buddha’s voice and teachings, one will develop wondrous understanding and practice according to what has been taught, thereby making it the provision for attaining Buddhahood.

Sixth is the relinquishing of wealth; "relinquishing" means giving. That is to say, if one can exercise a mind of equanimity, free from thoughts of hatred or attachment, and bestow one's body, life, and material possessions upon those who seek them, without any stinginess, this serves as the provision for attaining Buddhahood.

The seventh is the wealth of concentration and wisdom. Concentration and wisdom are precisely *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Concentration gathers the mind so that it does not scatter and ceases all deluded thoughts;
wisdom illuminates and comprehends all phenomena and destroys all false views, serving as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood.
Regarding "not falling away because of giving," the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one does not practice seated meditation or recitation, but instead manages affairs for the Three Jewels;
or if one does not maintain the precepts yet accepts the faithful offerings of others, then one falls away because of giving."
The *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "As for 'existence' (*bhava*), it refers to karma that causes the continuity and rebirth of future lives;

this is the meaning of 'existence. As for 'outflows' (*āsrava*), it has the sense of causing one to dwell and remain; that is, it causes sentient beings to dwell and remain within the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "There are two kinds of phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*): first, the cause; second, the fruit."
That which is the fruit of outflows (*sāsrava*) is called suffering (*duḥkha*); that which is the cause of outflows is called the origin (*samudaya*).
*Ting* (with the second tone) refers to a small boat; those exceeding two hundred *hu* in capacity are called *ting*. These boats are small and long.
*Bo* (舶) is pronounced *bai*. It refers to a large ship on the ocean.

The ten *śaya* (使) are: first, the *śaya* of greed; second, the *śaya* of anger; third, the *śaya* of delusion; fourth, the *śaya* of pride; fifth, the *śaya* of doubt; sixth, the *śaya* of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);

seventh, the *śaya* of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); eighth, the *śaya* of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); ninth, the *śaya* of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and tenth, the *śaya* of clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

These ten are all called "messengers" (*dūta*), meaning they are able to drive and employ the mind and consciousness of the practitioner, causing them to transmigrate through the birth and death of the three realms.

Among the four floods (*ogha*), the first is the flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*), which refers to the afflictions of view within the three realms; that is, when the mental faculty (*manas*) encounters mental objects (*dharmāḥ*), [it gives rise to these].

This refers to the view of discrimination (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*). Second is the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), which refers to the afflictions of volition (*cetanā-kleśa*) in the desire realm. Because the five faculties crave the five sense objects, they are termed "afflictions of volition";
these consist of greed, hatred, and pride. Third is the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*); because cause and effect do not perish, it is called existence.

These are the afflictions of volition (*vitarka*) within the realms of form and formlessness; specifically, they consist of greed (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*). Fourth is the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*):
because there is no clear understanding, it is called ignorance, which refers to the delusion (*moha*) among the afflictions of volition within the three realms.
These four are all termed "outflows" (*āsrava*) because sentient beings are caused to flow and wander by these three types of delusion, drifting through the three realms and unable to return.
Regarding the other shore of nirvāṇa:
the nine stages are, first, the stage of mixed habitation with the five destinies; second, the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion; third, the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration;
fourth, the stage of sublime bliss free from joy; fifth, the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness; and sixth, the sphere of infinite space.

The stages are: first, the stage of the desire realm; second, the stage of the form realm; third, the stage of the formless realm; fourth, the stage of infinite space; fifth, the stage of infinite consciousness; sixth, the stage of nothingness; seventh, the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Birth-emptiness is also called person-emptiness, which is identical to self-emptiness.

This means that ordinary beings falsely conceptualize the five aggregates as a self, arbitrarily establishing a sovereign controller, thereby giving rise to afflictions and creating various karmas. It is for the sake of destroying this misconception that the Buddha [taught this].

It is taught that the five aggregates are without self; the followers of the Two Vehicles realize this and enter into the principle of non-self, which is called the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the two types of self-clinging: first is innate self-clinging (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*), which refers to the forceful establishment of a sovereign and the false attachment to it as a self within the phenomena of the five aggregates and so forth;
this arises simultaneously with the body and is thus called innate self-clinging. Second is conceptual self-clinging (*vikalpita-ātma-grāha*).

Self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) refers to the conceptualization of a self within those phenomena conceived as "I," giving rise to attachment regarding such things as "I can perform virtuous deeds" or "I can perform non-virtuous deeds.
This is called conceptual self-grasping (*vikalpa-ātma-grāha*).
*Śikṣā* is translated here as "learning" (*xué*).
The character *liè* (躐) has the level tone (*líán*, entering tone); it means to step over or leap across. The Confucians say, "In learning, one does not leap over stages.

Just as a person’s primary ancestor is the one conceived in the womb—the first to receive the physical form—after which the various faculties gradually develop, it is for this reason that [the term] is so called.
The "Ancestor" (Bizu) refers to the progenitor. Since Upāli compiled the Vinaya in eighty recitations (*aṣṭaka-śata-khaṇḍa*), he is the progenitor of all the schools;
thus he is called the "Ancestor. The character *réng* (芿) is pronounced *chéng*.
When old grass is not mowed down and new grass grows again, it is called *réng*.
The five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are: first, the single foot that does not tread upon the ground; this means the body is able to fly, traversing space as if it were solid earth.

Second, knowing the minds and lifespans of others; this means being able to know the thoughts of other people—whether they perform good or evil deeds—and where they will be reborn, in a favorable or unfavorable state.
Third, the eyes that turn back a thousand *li*; this means [seeing] all classes of sentient beings throughout the world, whether beautiful or ugly, [and their cities...]
Regarding houses, mountain crags, and trees, when he turns his eyes, there is no distance near or far; he can see them all.
At the four calls of his name, they arrive immediately—referring to the voices of men and women throughout the world, as well as elephants, horses, and all things great and small.
There is nothing he cannot hear. If anyone calls his name, whether from afar or nearby, he arrives immediately.
Five-stone walls do not obstruct him; that is to say, as he moves to and fro throughout the world, mountains, rivers, and stone walls present no hindrance.
The character *yì* (裔) is pronounced like *yè*. It means "descendant.

Among the Nine Schools, the first is the Confucian School (*rú-liú*). They trace their lineage back to Yao and Shun and take Wen and Wu as their model for governance; they revere Zhongni (Confucius) as their master.

This school originally emerged from the Minister of Instruction (*sī-tú*). The second is the Daoist School (*dào-liú*). They discard ritual and music, abandon benevolence and righteousness, and rely solely on purity and emptiness.
The third is the flow of Yin and Yang, which originated from the Grand Historian (Shiguan); it reverently accords with the Great Heaven and calculates the movements of the sun and moon.
The fourth is the flow of Law, which originated from the Office of Xi and He; it relies on trust, rewards, and punishments to assist the ritual system.
The fifth is the flow of Titles, which originated from the Office of Justice; as the offices held by officials differ, the rituals also vary accordingly. These [five flows] emerged from...

1. The Ritual Officials (*lìguān*). The sixth is the Stream of the Mo-ists (*liú-mò*). This promotes the principle of universal love (*jiān'ài*) and issues from the office of the *qīngmiào* (Pure Temple).

2. The seventh is the Stream of the纵横 (*zōnghéng*, Vertical and Horizontal Strategists). It speaks of acting according to the exigencies of the moment and accepting mandates rather than fixed formulas; it issues from the office of the *xíng rén* (Diplomatic Officers). 3. The eighth is the Miscellaneous Stream (*zá liú*).

It combines Confucianism and Mohism, and unites the schools of Names (*míng*) and Law (*fǎ*); it issues from the office of the *yì guān* (Deliberative Officials). 4. The ninth is the Agricultural Stream (*nóng liú*).
The *Liu* (Annals) disseminates the hundred grains and encourages agriculture and sericulture; it originates from the offices of the Ministers of Agriculture and Millet.
It is the essential compendium of the imperial gates.
Attached herein is a brief biography of the translator.
The Master Buddhayaśas was a native of Kaśmīra and was of Brahmin descent. He entered the monastic order at the age of thirteen.
Once, while traveling through a vast wilderness with his teacher, they encountered a tiger. His teacher wished to flee and avoid it, but the Master said, "This tiger is already satiated;
it will certainly not harm us. Shortly thereafter, the tiger departed. As they proceeded further, there were indeed traces of its feeding left behind. His...
The Master kept this in mind with particular regard. At the age of fifteen, he could recite twenty to thirty thousand words of scripture daily.

An arhat, who esteemed his intelligence, would constantly beg for food to provide for him. He followed his maternal uncle to study the treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and all worldly arts and techniques;
there was nothing in which he was not thoroughly proficient. Later, he received the offerings of the Crown Prince of the kingdom of Śākala, who treated him with great honor and generosity. Thereupon—

He took his leave and traveled east to Kucha to seek out Kumārajīva. It was because Kumārajīva had previously studied under the Master in the kingdom of Kashgar, where the Master held him in high esteem.
At that time, the Master had been captured by Fu Jian and detained as a prisoner in Guzang. He sent a messenger to summon the Master, but the Master was detained by the people of the country;
though he wished to depart, he could not succeed. Consequently, he commanded his disciples to fetch pure water and recite mantras over it.
He washed his feet with medicinal water and set out under the cover of night. After traveling several hundred *li*, at dawn he asked his disciples, "What did you perceive?
They replied, "We heard only the sound of a violent wind. The people of the country pursued him but could not catch up. Just as they reached Guzang, Kumārajīva had already entered Chang'an.
Chang'an was ruled by Yao Xing, the lord of the Qin; upon hearing the Master’s name, Yao Xing immediately prepared grand ceremonies for his reception.
He was invited [to the capital]. The Master did not accept, saying with a smile: "Once the imperial decree has been issued, one ought indeed to set out at once.

However, since the patron treats scholars so generously, if it were as Kumārajīva saw it, I would not dare to accept the command. This was because Yao Xing had previously pressured Kumārajīva with his concubines.
When the envoy returned and reported this, Yao Xing sighed in admiration of his prudence and sent messengers again with earnest entreaties; only then did the Master finally consent.
Upon arriving in Chang’an, Daoxing went out in person to welcome him and invited him to the Xiaoyao Garden.

Thereupon, he and Kumārajīva translated the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the *Dīrgha-āgama*, and other scriptures. The Master’s appearance was dignified and elegant, yet his beard was red;
he was especially proficient in the *Vibhāṣā*. People of the time called him "The Red-bearded Vibhāṣā. Having served as [Kumārajīva's]...
He was also called Mahāvibhāṣā. Later, he returned to his native country, and it was not known where he ended his life. (Yìng [pronounced yìn;
refers to a woman sent to accompany a bride upon her marriage; all such escorts are termed yìng].)

Master Zhu Fonian was a native of Liangzhou. He entered the monastic order in his youth; his resolve and practice were pure and firm. Outwardly harmonious and inwardly luminous, he possessed a remarkably swift discernment.
From an early age, he delighted in traveling to various regions, thoroughly mastering local customs. There was no aspect of Chinese or Sanskrit phonology and semantics that he did not master.
Thus, although his reputation for scholastic expertise in the Abhidharma was lacking, his fame for extensive learning was very prominent. During the Jianyuan era of the Fu clan...
In his later years, he entered Chang’an and, together with Saṃghavarman, Dharmaratna, and others, translated various scriptures.
He resolved doubts regarding characters, phonetics, and meanings; since the time of An Shigao and Zhi Qian, none had surpassed him.

Thus, during the two reigns of Yao Xing and Yao Fu, he was the preeminent master among translators. The renowned and virtuous of Guanzhong all praised and esteemed him. Later, he again produced [translations] on his own initiative.
He had begun to edit and finalize such scriptures as the *Bodhisattvālaṃkāra*, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃyojana-cchedana*, and the *Yao tai zhong yin deng jing*.
His work was largely incomplete when he suddenly fell ill and passed away in Chang’an.
The Compendium of the Vinaya: On Restraint and Maintenance, Volume Two, compiled by the Vinaya-dhara Śramaṇa Duti of Baohua Mountain in Jinling. Section Seven:
The Detailed Explanation of the Characteristics of the Precepts. As for this, the first five sections are expositions of the doctrinal meanings; the sixth section is...
Analysis of the Title: Since the titles concerning the teachings and their meanings have already been clarified, one should now correctly explain the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*).
Generally, all *śrāmaṇeras* who receive and uphold the ten precepts do so as the foundation for the full set of precepts (*upasampadā*).

When they have ascended the altar for the higher ordination, the emphasis lies on the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations), which brings forth the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*). Subsequently, the characteristics of the precepts are explained for them, in order to protect [them].
Regarding its essence: I shall now explain the characteristics of the precepts to clarify their observance. First, I will set forth the essence of non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
As for "non-informative," Master Tiantai said: "The essence of the precepts is simply non-arising; if it arises, it is the insubstantial non-informative *rūpa* (form) of the nature."
Master Pan’s commentary states: "This essence of the precepts may not arise at all; yet if it does arise, it is the entirety of the nature (xing).

Thus, nature and cultivation mutually accomplish one another. There must necessarily be unmanifested form (avijñapti-rūpa). Once the unmanifested has been produced, it spontaneously ceases evil and spontaneously performs good.
After it has been produced once, it does not require further production; hence it is called 'unmanifested' (wu zuo). (Text) It is said that the unmanifested is unmanifested form.

Regarding this: among the eleven types of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), each has both a conventional and an ultimate aspect. Within the category of matter included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), only matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) is called ultimate matter;

manifest and unmanifest matter (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) are both called conventional matter. The two types of ethical discipline (*śīla*), wholesome and unwholesome, each have both manifest and unmanifest forms.
Manifest matter is termed "action" (*kṛti*), while unmanifest matter is termed "non-action" (*akṛti*). For now, I shall explain wholesome discipline.
Kneeling with one knee raised in diligent application is called the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*). Reciting the request for ordination three times is called the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).

The harmonious assembly of the Saṃgha gathering together at the site of ordination (*sīmā*) is also called the bodily intimation. The formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is also called the vocal intimation.

Through these ritual acts, one receives the pure essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*), attains the nature of a bhikṣu, and becomes an object of perception for the mental faculty, functioning spontaneously.
One constantly attains the two wholesome states of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insightful conduct); therefore, it is said that once performed, there is no need for repetition.
This is called "unconditioned manifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*). This unconditioned precept-body is attained at the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*.
One attains the abstention from sexual misconduct toward all males and females, and the abstention from theft toward all sentient and insentient beings.
Regarding form: one attains the quality of non-killing toward all sentient beings; one attains the quality of non-deception toward all sentient beings;

and so on, up to attaining the quality of not digging the earth in all lands, the quality of not destroying grasses and trees in all vegetation, and the quality of not drinking alcohol in regard to all intoxicants. Such are the two hundred and fifty rules of training.

Each and every one of these individually pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, the *Sūtra on the Merit of Leaving Home* clarifies that the merit of observing the precepts for a single day and night is inexhaustible.
This is precisely because this wondrously wholesome discipline (*śīla*) universally takes the *dharmadhātu* as its object.

Thus, the unconditioned essence of the precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīlaskandha*) is form belonging to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*); it is untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*), whereas the five [aggregates] with outflows are...
The physical body of the aggregates (*skandha*) serves as the basis; the body of untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla-skandha*) serves as the basis.
The tainted physical body is born from the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood; it is a derivative form (*upādāya-rūpa*) belonging to the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*).

The untainted body of precepts is obtained through the ritual procedure (*karma*) of the three masters and seven witnesses; it is a derivative form belonging to the sense-base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). For this reason, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is called "one who gives birth by power."

It is precisely because it can give rise to the aggregate of precepts (*śīlaskandha*) that it receives its name. Once this aggregate of precepts is attained, one becomes equal to the Jewel of the Sangha;

one is able to cause devas and nāgas to pay reverent homage and spirits and ghosts to receive it with respect. In recent times, however, those who transmit and receive [the precepts] have become confused regarding their essential nature and remain ignorant of it.
If appearances are obscured and one lacks clear understanding, how can one hope to establish a firm foundation for the Way and maintain the pure brilliance of the *brahmacarya*?
Therefore, I shall first set forth the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*), so that the act of bestowing and receiving them may not be in vain, and they may be protected and kept pure.
Next, the correct explanation of the characteristics of the precepts follows the Vinaya in dividing them into eight categories: first, the *pārājika* rules;
second, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules; third, the *aniyata* rules; fourth, the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules; fifth, the *pāyattika* rules.
Six *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas; seven *śaikṣa* dharmas; eight *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* dharmas. Regarding the first, the *pārājika* dharmas, there are four rules in total.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The meaning of *pārājika* is 'extreme evil,' which means that there is no [recovery] beyond it."
Matters more serious than this are explained collectively by way of three meanings: first, retrogression and extinction, because by violating this precept one has no share in the fruits of the Path;

second, non-cohabitation, for not only does one lose the fruits of the Path, but one is also unable to dwell within the two types of Saṃgha—namely, those engaged in the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and those performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*); third, falling, for after casting off this body, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
Because of hell. The Vinaya states:
"One who commits a *pārājika* offense is like a person whose head has been severed; they can never return to life.
It is like cutting the heart of a *tāla* tree; it will never grow again. It is like a needle with a broken eye; it is no longer fit for use."
It is like a great rock split into two parts; it can never be joined back together again. (Tāla—here translated as "shore-form"—is straight and tall; its leaves are large enough to write upon.)
If the heartwood of this tree is cut, it immediately withers and dies, never to sprout again.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "A *pārājika* offense is an extremely grave transgression; it is utterly loathsome, contemptible, and undesirable.
If a bhikṣu commits even one such offense, he is immediately no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya; he has fallen away."
The nature of a bhikṣu is contrary to the nature of nirvāṇa; he falls and collapses, is overcome by others, and cannot be rescued.
Like the head of a tāla tree that has been cut off, it will not grow again; it can no longer flourish, increase, or expand.
Therefore, it is called a *pārājika*.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Pārājika" means "extremely evil" and carries the sense of "defeat by another. At the very moment it is committed, one is defeated by fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*).
Having gone forth and received full ordination (*upasampadā*) for the purpose of eliminating afflictions (*kleśa*), one is now, having broken the prohibitions, instead brought low.
Furthermore, because it can harm wholesome qualities and cause them to perish, and moreover, because it can give rise to evil—

Because one has committed a transgression leading to a [lower] rebirth, it is called a *pārājika*. Furthermore, having been attacked and defeated by an army of non-Dharma, the son of the Dharma King suffers defeat at the hands of another;
since he has lost what is most honorable, it is called "defeat" (*parā-jita*). (Regarding the term *upasaṃpadā*: "round" [*saṃpada*] refers to *nirvāṇa*;
by receiving the bhikṣu precepts, one is able to draw near to *nirvāṇa*, and thus it is called "ordination" [*upasaṃpadā*].)
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Pārājika" means falling into an undesirable state. It is like two people fighting, where one wins and the other loses.
One who commits this offense is not permitted to perform repentance; they will ultimately and eternally fall into the state of defeat.
Furthermore, it is like a parched grain seed: although planted in fertile soil and diligently watered, it will not produce sprouts or fruit.
So too is one who violates the precepts; despite diligent application of effort, they can ultimately never produce the sprouts or fruit of the Path.

The *Buddhabhāṣita-laghugurukarmapātayantika-sūtra* states: "One who commits a *pārājika* offense falls into hell for a lifespan equal to sixteen thousand years of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven (according to the *Śāstra*, one thousand six hundred years among humans constitutes one day and night for that heaven).

By human reckoning, this amounts to nine million two hundred and ten million six hundred thousand years. (Note: This number of years is certainly a translation error, as clarified in the *Yinyi*). This hell...

The Plow is the Hell of Blazing Heat. This refers to when the hell-wardens place sinners within an iron city, where fires blaze and cause them to wither and rot, burning and scorching sentient beings.
This is merely named for its intervals; as for the sins of slandering the Triple Gem, the five heinous crimes, and so forth—
Their lifespan shall be one great kalpa, and they shall fall into the Avīci Hell of Eightfold Torment.

First, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct: "Sexual misconduct" refers to defiled, lewd, and loathsome acts that are unfitting; it is termed non-celibacy (*abrahmacarya*) and is also called [unrighteous conduct].

Regarding pure conduct: according to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, this is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Even for one who has not received the Buddha’s precepts, it is sinful by the very nature of worldly law;
however, violating the Buddha’s precepts is grave, whereas violating national prohibitions is light. As for the light offenses:

the state law prescribes execution for those who commit rape, flogging for those who commit adultery through mutual consent, and caning for lewd men. As for the grave offenses: the Buddha’s regulations do not distinguish between men and women, etc. [One].

If one engages in sexual intercourse with a mind of desire, one will fall into the three miserable realms, enduring extreme suffering for the duration of an eon; this is not like secular punishment and cannot be adequately described.

If a bhikṣu, while sharing the same precepts as other bhikṣus, does not return his precepts, nor does he relinquish them when his vows have become weak, and commits an impurity without repentance—[he has fallen].
[Engaging in] sexual intercourse, even with an animal—this bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense and shall not co-reside [with the Saṃgha].

The Origin Story: Generally, the mind turns according to its objects; precepts are established based on specific matters. If the object is illusory and the mind is empty, then emotional attachments are forgotten and the underlying principle is revealed.
Therefore, the formulation of the five categories of precepts all arises from the existence of outflows (*āsrava*). Thus, the Great Sage, riding upon...
At that time, he established a training rule (*śikṣāpada*). Thus, the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "When there were no [monks] with outflows (*āsrava*), the Tathāgata formulated the precepts.
Beings then conceived thoughts of slander, saying: 'How is it that the Śramaṇa Gautama is like his śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are of noble lineage or former royalty?
Having renounced wealth, palaces, wives, children, and retinues, they do not spare even their own bodies or lives.'"
"All these people are contented and have no further desires. Why, Gautama, do you instead bind them with the *prātimokṣa*?
Thus you speak because you, Gautama, are not yet skilled at discerning worldly people. If precepts were established, worldly people would likewise not give rise to a heart of reverence.
It is like a physician who is not yet skilled in treating illnesses; when he first sees a person..."
When a boil was about to form but had not yet fully developed, he would suddenly burst it open. Once burst, blood flowed out and he suffered great agony.
When medicine was applied, the wound would immediately heal. The physician said to him, "I have treated your illness; you must give me my fee.
The patient replied, "This foolish physician—if it were my own illness, I might allow you to treat it. As for me, originally..."
"I am not ill. You have forcibly torn my flesh to make blood flow, causing me great agony, yet you instead blame me for being straightforward;
is this not deception? The śrāvaka disciples are also like this: if they first establish precepts and then give rise to slander.
"I am personally without fault; yet you have forcibly established this precept. For this reason, the Tathāgata does not establish a precept beforehand.
If there were those with outflows (*sāsrava*), it would be at that time that the Tathāgata would establish a precept for his disciples.

(Text) For this reason, beneath each precept, the *nidāna* (circumstantial origin) is first presented. Furthermore, after a precept has been established, there may be another *nidāna* that leads to an additional regulation.

There are also cases where precepts were established based on specific circumstances; thus, within the Five Groups of Offenses (*pañcāpattinikāya*), there are differences in how certain rules were formulated.
This present precept against sexual misconduct has three stages of formulation. The Vinaya states:

When the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, who possessed firm faith, left the household life to follow the Path. At that time, grain was expensive and difficult to obtain through alms-seeking.
Alms-food was difficult to obtain. Sūtiputra took several bhikṣus and went to the village of Kalandaka to beg for food.

When his mother heard that her son had returned, she went to him to urge him to abandon the path and return home. Although she pleaded with him twice and thrice, he would not consent. She then instructed her daughter-in-law to settle her son so that the lineage might not be severed;
she then seized her daughter-in-law by the arm and led her into the garden, where they committed the three acts of impurity. At that time, Sūtiputra...
After Naṭaputra had committed an impure act, he was constantly filled with grief and anxiety. His fellow students, having learned the reason for this, reported it in full to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked him, saying: "What you have done is wrong."
"It is not proper conduct; it is not that of a śramaṇa; it is not pure practice; it is not the practice of conformity; it is something one ought not to do.
You, Sudinna, how could you, within this pure Dharma leading even to the extinction of craving and nirvāṇa, engage in impure sexual intercourse with a former wife?
[The Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus: 'It would be better for a man to insert his male organ into the mouth of a venomous snake than to hold..."
It enters into the female organ. Why is this? Because one does not fall into the evil realms on account of this condition.
If one commits an offense against a woman, at the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into the three evil realms. Why is this?

For I have taught through countless skillful means the Dharma for severing desire, severing the perception of desire, extinguishing thoughts of desire, dispersing the fever of desire, and transcending the fetters of craving. I speak thus of desire.
It is like fire; like a torch of grass; also like the fruit of a tree; furthermore, like a loan; like a dry bone;
also like a piece of meat; like what is seen in a dream; like treading upon the edge of a blade; like a new earthen vessel filled with water placed in the sun;
like the head of a venomous snake; like a whirling wheel-blade; like being upon a sharp stake; like being pierced by a sharp halberd. It is most [painful].
It is loathsome. Having rebuked him, the Buddha established a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering ten points of significance:
first, to maintain the integrity of the Saṃgha; second, to bring joy to the Saṃgha; third, to bring peace and happiness to the Saṃgha; fourth, to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed.

1. To cause those who have already gained faith to increase it; 2. To bring those who are difficult to tame into submissiveness; 3. To enable those with a sense of shame and remorse to attain peace and happiness;
4. To sever the outflows (*āsrava*) of the present; 5. To sever the outflows of the future; 6. To ensure that the True Dharma (*saddharma*) endures for a long time.
The one who recites the precepts should speak thus: "If a bhikṣu commits an impure act, engaging in sexual intercourse, that bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
This is the original formulation. Having thus established the rule, [the Buddha said:]...
