At that time, there was a Vatsiputra bhikṣu who, being distressed and finding no joy in the pure life, returned home and engaged in unchaste conduct with his former wife.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha assembled the Saṃgha and rebuked him, saying: "You foolish man!
You have committed a pārājika offense and are no longer to live in communion. If any other bhikṣu finds no joy in the pure life, he is permitted to relinquish the precepts and return."

If one who has left the household life wishes to return to the household life, yet desires to practice the pure conduct within the Buddha-dharma, they should be ordained, allowed to leave the household life again, and receive the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇa-śīla*).
It was for this reason that the rule against ordaining those who have previously broken their vows and failed to repent was further established.
This is the second regulation. Subsequently, there was another bhikṣu who lived by alms-gathering, dwelling in a forest grove, where he associated with a female macaque.
He engaged in unchaste conduct. When a monk on patrol saw this, he informed the Buddha. As previously described, the assembly was convened and he was rebuked;
subsequently, the rule concerning "cohabiting with animals" was established. This is the third formal prohibition (*pratikṣepa*).

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it was five years after the Buddha’s enlightenment, during the twelfth day of the fifth half-month of winter, after the midday meal, due to [the incident involving] Sudinna.

The Master [Guṇabhadra] established this precept against sexual misconduct (according to the Western Regions, the year is divided into three seasons: from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month is the spring season;

from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month is the summer season; from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month is the winter season. Each season lasts four months, and every four months consists of eight half-months.

According to the current system, this corresponds precisely to the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Due to delusion, it arises from the affliction of desire and sexual misconduct..."

Therefore, this training rule was established. Since all afflictions arise based on the non-awakening of ignorance (*avidyā*), and ignorance is itself delusion (*moha*), it is for this reason that in each and every precept the Buddha does not fail to reprove [the offender], saying, "What you have done is the deed of a deluded person.
Thus, delusion is truly the root source of violating the precepts. Furthermore, when the precepts are formulated, they must necessarily...
Regarding the requirement to assemble the Saṃgha, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, there are five reasons: first, the Buddha does not act arbitrarily on his own initiative;

second, the Buddha does not assemble the assembly to deliberate upon the gravity of an offense before enacting a precept, but rather brings about harmony with the assembly so that the offender’s mind may be subdued;
third, just as a king who governs a nation, though he possesses sovereign power, must consult with [his ministers] regarding all state affairs...
When various loyal ministers deliberate upon matters, the state is able to endure for a long time. It is the same with the King of the Dharma (the Buddha):

although he possesses sovereignty over the Dharma, for the sake of upholding the Buddha-Dharma, whenever there is a matter concerning the Dharma, he assembles the community so that all may know it; thus, the Dharma is able to endure for a long time.
Fourth, this is to solemnize present and future disciples: regarding all monastic affairs, whether one has power or lacks power, it is essential [to consult the assembly].
One must consult the assembly for what is appropriate; one may not act alone or independently. This is the natural law of all Buddhas; it is not the practice of a single Buddha alone.

Furthermore, once the Sangha has been assembled, the Buddha, though already knowing the matter, asks intentionally. He asks at the proper time and with full knowledge. There are two reasons why he asks with knowledge:

first, because it is the constant law of the Buddhas; second, because there is nothing the Buddha does not know. His purpose is to cause the person before him to acknowledge their fault, thereby following the principle of self-accusation.
Regarding the method of treatment: Third, it is for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings. There is nothing the Buddha does not know and nothing he does not see.

If one were not to inquire, and the person before him were to speak of their own transgressions based on their own knowledge and vision, then sentient beings would constantly harbor fear and dread, unable to find peace within themselves;
this would not be the method for assembling the assembly to bring peace to sentient beings. Fourth, if one were to examine the minds of others with hostility, it would not be [the correct method].
Regarding the physical bearing of the Great Man and Holy Lord, when he inquires at the appropriate time, he does so specifically within the assembly of bhikṣus;

he does not inquire before śrāmaṇeras or white-robed laypeople. This is for one reason: that the present is the time for establishing the precepts (*śīla*). Furthermore, it is said: "All wholesome dharmas are not called 'establishments' (*saṃvara*);

why then do you speak only of 'establishing the precepts'? Nevertheless, the precepts are the root of all myriad virtues; it is simply because they are established [at this time] that they are so designated.
Precepts are that which bind together all wholesome dharmas.

Explanation of the meaning: The text is divided into three sections. "If a bhikṣu" refers generally to one who has received and maintains the full precepts (the following cases are to be understood accordingly).
From "together with the bhikṣus" onwards, the specific matters of the offense are clearly explained. From "this bhikṣu" onwards, the conclusion of the offense is established.

Regarding the offenses committed (*āpatti*): (According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the meaning of "bhikṣu" contains three aspects. First, the sense of destroying evil (*pāpa-nāśana*). This refers to when one first receives the precepts; through the three *karmavācanās*, one gives rise to the wholesome discipline (*kuśala-saṃvara*) and destroys the unwholesome discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*), and thus is called a "destroyer of evil.

If considered comprehensively in terms of practice and understanding: through the precepts, one guards against physical transgressions; through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one eliminates mental distraction; and through wisdom (*prajñā*), one realizes that perceptions are empty, thereby being able to destroy the evils of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Second, the sense of terrifying Māra (*mārasya trāsa*). Since he can destroy evil, Māra thinks:

"This person will not only leave my realm, but may even transmit the lamp of the Dharma and convert my followers, leaving my palaces empty," and thus gives rise to alarm and fear. Generally speaking, the three types of Māras are also terrified. Third, the sense of a mendicant (*bhikṣu*). "Bhikṣu" is [derived from] begging...)

"Begging" is its name; "Sage" (*śramaṇa*) is a term for one who is pure and refined. Those who have left the household life must internally cultivate the virtue of purity and refinement. They must distance themselves from the four wrong livelihoods and abide in a pure way of life to benefit sentient beings.

By shattering the mind of arrogance and maintaining humility and self-effacement, they seek the necessities of life to perfect their virtue of purity and refinement. The Vinaya clarifies eight kinds of *bhikṣus*: 1.

The *bhikṣu* in name only (referring to worldly people who have been given the title "bhikṣu," or those of the bhikṣu lineage who do not belong to the community of the monastic dharma). 2. The *bhikṣu* in appearance (referring to someone who has shaved off their hair and beard but has not received the Buddha’s...).

Those who observe the precepts and whose physical appearance resembles that of the monastic community—though *śrāmaṇeras* have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), they are nonetheless included among the number of *bhikṣus*—are therefore called "semblances" (the assembly of those who do not follow the Dharma).

Those who call themselves *bhikṣus* (meaning those who shave their hair and beards, don the *kāṣāya*, and remain within the monastic community while declaring, "I am a *bhikṣu*") are termed "thieving dwellers" (*cora-vāsika*). Furthermore, this includes *bhikṣus* who have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*) and no longer dwell in common with the Sangha, yet still claim to be *bhikṣus*.

The "Welcome, *Bhikṣu*" (meaning: when a layperson endowed with faith comes before the Buddha desiring to seek renunciation, and the Buddha perceives that their faculties and nature are mature and fit for deliverance, he then calls out, "Welcome, *bhikṣu*; rejoice freely within my Dharma").

"One may cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) and attain the exhaustion of the source of suffering. Before the Buddha had finished speaking, his hair and beard fell away naturally, and he was fully endowed with robes and bowl, like a bhikṣu of a hundred years' seniority. His deportment was dignified and orderly, and he attained full ordination (upasampadā), just as the great disciples such as Kauṇḍinya did.

A *piṇḍapātika* bhikṣu (a "begging" bhikṣu) is one who does not accept invitations to meals, but throughout his life subsists on alms-food for the sake of sustaining his body; this is called a *piṇḍapātika* bhikṣu. A *khaṇḍika-cīvara-dhara* bhikṣu (one who wears cut-and-sewn robes) is one for whom the price of a robe is high;

once the bhikṣu has obtained it, he cuts and sews it, thereby destroying its value. He stitches it together with needle and thread, ruining its fineness and softness. He uses tree bark, ruining its original color, so that it becomes an old garment. This is [the practice of] being able to...
"One who wears these robes" refers to a *bhikṣu* who wears the *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (the robe of cut-and-sewn patches).

A "bhikṣu who has destroyed the fetters" (*prahīṇa-saṃyojana*)—where all afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "fetters" because they bind sentient beings and drive them to wander through the three realms—if such a person, whether having left the household life at twenty years of age or less than that, is able to destroy and sever these afflictions and realize *arhatship*, they are said to have obtained full ordination (*upasampadā*).

A "bhikṣu who has attained the status [of ordination] through the formal procedure of the fourfold motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karma*) according to the Dharma"—that is to say, there is a son of good family who seeks full ordination; at...

Regarding the three preceptors and seven monks: first, one requests [ordination]; then, the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) is performed for him. When this is accomplished according to the Dharma, brought to its ultimate fulfillment, and the nature of a bhikṣu is established, it is called "receiving the full ordination through the ritual of one motion and three proclamations, accomplished according to the Dharma, and obtaining the status of a bhikṣu.

Among these, if a bhikṣu has received the full ordination through the ritual of one motion and three proclamations, accomplished according to the Dharma, and obtained the status of a bhikṣu within the Dharma, this is defined as the meaning of "bhikṣu" (referring here to the current formulation of the *Prātimokṣa* as the ritual of one motion and three proclamations).

Regarding the *karmavācanā*: because he is a bhikṣu who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the formal procedure of the fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), his "coming forth" (*svāgata*) destroys the fetters (*saṃyojana*). He possesses spontaneous precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*) and is forever free from the faults and afflictions of violating prohibitions. His defilements (*kleśa*) are exhausted and the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established.

As for the three previous types [of assemblies], they share the same name but are assemblies that do not accord with the Dharma; therefore, they are not included within the scope of these prohibitions. Regarding all subsequent precepts where it says "if a bhikṣu," the meaning should be understood according to this principle. As for "together with bhikṣus":

it means as other bhikṣus who have received full ordination through the fourfold proclamation and have duly accomplished the rite, thereby attaining the status and dwelling in the dharmas of a bhikṣu.
This is the meaning of being "together with the bhikṣus. What is meant by "identical precepts" (*samāna-śīla*)?

After I have established the precepts for my disciples, they would rather die than violate them. Within this community, one shares with other bhikṣus: identical precepts (the essence of the precept is non-dual), identical precepts (the characteristics of the precept are without distinction), and equal precepts (the practice of the precept is entirely equal).

This is called "identical precepts. (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If there is one who has previously received full ordination, even if it has been a hundred years since, the matters he should study are the same as those of a newly ordained [bhikṣu].")

The recipients [of the precepts] are equal and without distinction. If one newly receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), the matters that ought to be studied are no different from those of one who has been fully ordained for a hundred years. That is to say, regarding the training rules of the *śīla*, the observance of what is to be maintained and what is to be transgressed, and the ritual procedures—all these are attained as being identical.

Therefore, they are called "common precepts" (*sādhāraṇa-śīla*) and "shared precepts. What is the returning of the precepts? Returning the precepts means relinquishing the precepts. As the Vinaya states:

"If a bhikṣu does not delight in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), desires to return to the household life, grows weary of the bhikṣu-dharma, and constantly harbors a sense of shame and remorse..."

Delighting in the life of a householder, or delighting in the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), or thinking of śrāmaṇeras, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), or the disciples of non-Buddhists, as well as those who are not śramaṇas and not sons of the Śākya, they speak these words: "I renounce the Buddha; I renounce the Dharma;
I renounce the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; I renounce my preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and teacher (*ācārya*); I renounce my fellow preceptors and fellow teachers. (Regarding "fellow preceptors":...)

That is to say, that bhikṣu—whether it be his own upādhyāya, or one who received the precepts under the same teacher, or one of the same seniority (the same applies to an ācārya)—abandons the holy life, abandons the Vinaya, and abandons the training.
He adopts the way of a householder, saying: "I am a *kappiya-kāraka* (purifier); I am an *upāsaka*; I am a *śrāmaṇera*;
I am a follower of an external path; I am a disciple of an external path; I am neither a śramaṇa nor a member of the Śākya clan."
"Son, if you again speak such words as, 'I shall stop; I have no need for the Buddha. What benefit does the Buddha bring me?

and thus depart from the presence of the Buddha—and if this applies likewise even to the matters of training—and if you further speak other words that disparage the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, even the matters of training, and instead praise domestic affairs, down to saying, 'He is not a śramaṇa, he is not a son of the Śākya,' by..."
If one speaks in such a manner, speaking clearly and distinctly, this is called "renouncing the precepts. If one does not speak such clear words, this is called "not returning the precepts.
If one renounces the precepts while insane, renounces the precepts with a deranged mind, or renounces the precepts due to excruciating pain, [it is not a valid renunciation].

If one renounces the precepts in jest or laughter, it does not constitute a renunciation of the precepts. Furthermore, if one renounces the precepts before someone who is insane, mentally deranged, afflicted by intense pain, mute, or deaf;

or before a person from the Central Land (Madhyadeśa) in the presence of a person from a Borderland (Pratyantajanapada), or a person from a Borderland in the presence of a person from the Central Land;
or if one renounces the precepts before a deva, nāga, yakṣa, or rākṣasa, or before a sleeping person, a dead person, or an unconscious person—it is not a valid renunciation. If...
If one does not speak; or if one speaks but the person before them does not understand—in such cases as these, it is not termed "abandoning the precepts.

Regarding "the weakening of the precepts," the Vinaya states: if a bhikṣu is sorrowful and finds no joy in the holy life (brahmacarya), desiring to return home, loathing the dharma of a bhikṣu, having his mind set on the household life, and even wishing to perform the practices of those who are neither śramaṇas nor sons of the Śākya, he then acts accordingly.
To say: "I recall my parents, brothers, sisters, wife, children, villages, towns, fields, gardens, and bathing pools;

I wish to abandon the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, even the training rules; I wish to take up the affairs of a householder, even the ways of those who are neither śramaṇas nor sons of the Śākya"—this is called "weakness in morality" (*śīla-kaśāya*). To not feel remorse for this (regarding the Tathāgata’s disciplinary law) [is the second offense].

Lacking the power to maintain it, one harbors sorrow within but does not express regret; this is what is meant by "not repenting for oneself. If one should think in this way: "I wish to abandon the precepts," [one should reflect further].

One then abandons the precepts; this is called abandoning the precepts while they are weakened. As for "one who practices impure conduct": this refers to sexual desire (*dharma*). [The Vinaya-saṃgraha says:

"Conduct" refers to the Noble Path, and "purity" refers to Nirvāṇa. It is only through the Eightfold Noble Path that one can realize and attain them. To engage in impure conduct is to directly contradict that path. "Down to animals" means...
This refers to a place where sexual intercourse can be performed. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "When one has sexual union with a woman, the fulfillment of desire is complete;

when one has sexual union with a female animal, the passion for pleasure is slight. Therefore, it says 'down to animals and the three evil realms. Since these are the lowest of the five destinies, it says 'down to animals' [as the limit]").
What is meant by *pārājika*? It is like severing a person's head; they cannot rise again. A bhikṣu is also like this: one who commits this offense no longer becomes [a bhikṣu].
“Monk,” [this] is called a *pārājika* (the detailed explanation follows as before). What is meant by “not living in communion”? There are two forms of communal living:
performing the same formal ritual (*kamma*) and reciting the same code of precepts (*prātimokṣa*). Since one is not permitted to abide in these two matters, it is called “not living in communion.”

The Definition of the Offense: Regarding those who commit this offense, it refers to performing the act of impurity in three places—the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth—with respect to a human female, a non-human female, or an animal female;
or with respect to a human male, a non-human male, or an animal male;
or with respect to a human hermaphrodite, a non-human hermaphrodite, or an animal hermaphrodite.
If, with respect to a human hermaphrodite, a non-human hermaphrodite, or an animal hermaphrodite;

or with respect to a human male, a non-human male, or an animal male—one engages in unchaste conduct at two locations, namely the anus and the mouth—if such a bhikṣu possesses a lustful mind and the act is first fully entered, it is a *pārājika*;
if he employs the preparatory means but does not fully enter, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

[The Buddha] prohibited it. If one engages in sexual intercourse with a person who is a fit object for such an act— whether there is an obstruction, whether there is an obstruction on both sides, whether there is an obstruction on one side and not on the other,
or whether there is no obstruction on either side (an obstruction meaning that one enters while the organ is wrapped in an object)— in all these cases, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, approaches a sleeping woman, or a corpse that is not yet decomposed or mostly undecomposed,
and inserts [the organ] into the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth— even if only slightly inserted— he incurs a pārājika offense.
It is the same for the wives of non-humans, and even for male animals.

If an enemy forcibly seizes a bhikṣu, whether it be himself (meaning he causes another to commit sexual misconduct with him) or another person (meaning another comes to commit sexual misconduct with him), and if at any one of the three stages—the initial entry, during the entry, or upon exiting—he gives rise to a mind that experiences pleasure, he immediately incurs a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding "experiencing pleasure": it is like obtaining food when hungry, or obtaining drink when thirsty. Regarding "not experiencing pleasure": it is like a pure and refined person having various corpses bound to his body.
If [the semen] is discharged upon the neck,
or between the bones, or upon a half-decomposed corpse, or into a hole in the ground, or into a hole in packed mud, or into the mouth of a *kuṇḍikā* (here translated as "vessel"),
all such acts of impure conduct constitute a *sthūlātyaya*. (*Kuṇḍikā* is here translated as "bottle").
If one perceives what is the Path as the Path, perceives what is the Path with doubt, or perceives what is the Path as not the Path, in all such cases it is a *pārājika*.

If one perceives what is not the Path as the Path, or perceives what is not the Path with doubt, in all such cases it is a *sthūlātyaya*. (That which is "not the Path" refers to everything except the three [proper] paths;
it includes the armpits, the space between the thighs, a water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*), a lump of clay, the ground, empty space, and so forth.)
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to engage in impure conduct: if he carries out the instruction, it is a sthūlātyaya; if he does not carry out the instruction, it is a duṣkṛta.
According to the underlying principle, for one to commit this offense and incur the full gravity of the sin, four conditions must be fulfilled:
first, the presence of a lustful mind; second, a complete object; third, entry into the path; and fourth, the experience of pleasure. If [any of these are absent], it is not so.
[Included]. As there are allowances in the Vinaya, regarding the *sthūlātyaya*:
according to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, "sthūla" means "great," and "atyaya" means "obstruction. It obstructs the path to goodness and leads subsequently to falling into the evil realms.
Its essence is base and defiled; as for establishing its name based on this unwholesome essence, it is because it can bring about the first [offense].

This is due to the offenses of these two categories. According to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) is explained as "coarse" (*sthūla*), while *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibitory offense) is "transgression" (*sāvadya*).
There are two kinds of "coarse": first, the preliminary stage (*prayoga*) of a heavy offense; second, that which can sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

As for "transgression," it refers to acting without relying on the precepts established by the Buddha; hence it is called a transgression. Furthermore, within this, there is a division into those arising from [other offenses] and those that are independent.
Regarding the "Independent [Offenses]" (*mūlaka*), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If a heavy offense arises from the first category (*pārājika*), it should be confessed before the entire Saṃgha.

If a light offense arises from the first category, or a heavy offense arises from the second category (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), it should be confessed before a community of four bhikṣus outside the boundary (*sīmā*).

If a light offense arises from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it should be confessed before a single bhikṣu. For now, we shall discuss these based on their origin; such are the three grades of independent offenses.
The Method for Confession is explained in detail within the *Zuochi* (Making and Maintaining). The Sūtra states:

"If one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense, one will fall into the *naraka* hell for a lifespan equivalent to four thousand years in Tuṣita Heaven. (In human reckoning, four hundred years constitute one day and night in that heaven;
thus, it is five hundred and seventy-six million years by human calculation. This *naraka* is the Raurava Hell," which refers to the prison...
He finally seizes the offender and hurls him into an iron cauldron; because he wails and screams loudly, this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one opens the section on groups, it is listed separately as the third, as in the *Pratideśanīya* chapter, wherein it subsumes the preceding two cases.
Furthermore, for *bhikṣuṇīs*, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense (this is a shared regulation and a training rule common to those in the same study).

For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense resulting in expulsion (*niḥsaraṇa*). (Regarding the four fundamental grave offenses—sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying—if those belonging to the three minor groups commit them, although they do not incur the formal name of a *pārājika*, their expulsion already carries the sense of being cast out.

They may not engage in the same activities or studies as other pure *śrāmaṇeras*. Nor may they stay together with the *bhikṣus* for two or three nights, as pure *śrāmaṇeras* may. Although it is called a *duṣkṛta*...)

[This constitutes] a *pārājika* offense (and it is truly not subject to confession). If a bhikṣuṇī instructs a bhikṣu to engage in unchaste conduct (*aśubha-karma*), if she carries out the instruction, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;

if she does not carry it out, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī instructs a bhikṣu, whether he carries out the instruction or not, the instructor incurs a *duṣkṛta* in all cases.
Exemptions from offense: If one is asleep and lacks awareness; if one does not experience pleasure; if there is no intention for sexual misconduct at all;
or if it was before the precept had been established; or if one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain (*Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* states:).

Seeing fire, they grasp it as if it were no different from gold; seeing excrement, they grasp it as if it were no different from sandalwood. This is called being possessed by a deluded, deranged mind, entangled in painful affliction. Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: There are five characteristics of a madman:

one becomes mad because all one's kinsmen have died; one becomes mad because all one's wealth has been lost; one becomes mad because all one's fields, property, and subjects have been lost; one becomes mad because the four great elements (mahābhūta) are in disorder; or one becomes mad due to the retribution of past karma. There are five causes and conditions that cause the mind to become distracted:

the mind becomes distracted because one is struck by a non-human spirit (*amanuṣya*); the mind becomes distracted because a non-human spirit causes it to be so; the mind becomes distracted because a non-human spirit consumes the essence of the heart; the mind becomes distracted because the four great elements are in disorder; or [the mind becomes distracted] due to past...

Because of worldly karmic retribution, the mind becomes distracted. There are five kinds of illnesses that destroy the mind: either the mind is destroyed by an illness arising from wind (*vāta*), or by an illness arising from heat (*pitta*), or by an illness arising from cold (*ślesman*), or by an illness arising from the simultaneous outbreak of all three (*sannipāta*), or by an illness arising from seasonal miasma (*kāla-doṣa*).

Even if one’s mind is thus impaired by such madness, distraction, or illness, if a bhikṣu consciously commits sexual intercourse, he incurs a *pārājika* offense; if he does not know it himself, he does not commit an offense.
Regarding the following precepts, there are likewise three cases where one does not commit an offense due to illness; this may be understood by analogy and need not be explained further.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one says to the five groups of monastics or to laypeople, 'I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha,' or 'I renounce communal residence,' and so forth, all such instances are termed 'renouncing the precepts' (*śīla-tyāga*). It further states:

"If one says, 'I renounce the Buddhas of the past and future,' 'I renounce the [teachings] of the past and future,' 'I renounce the Saṃghas of the past and future,' or 'I renounce many bhikṣus,' none of these are termed 'renouncing the precepts.'"
One incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one says, "I renounce past and future dharmas," or "I renounce this sutra and treatise," this is called renouncing the precepts.
Furthermore, since even non-Buddhists each claim to possess the Buddha-dharma, if one truly intends to renounce the Buddha-dharma, [one must state so explicitly].
If one says, "I renounce the Buddha of the non-Buddhists," or "I renounce the dharma of the non-Buddhists," this is not called renouncing the precepts; one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says, "I renounce [the training] regarding past and future many bhikṣus," or "I renounce one bhikṣu," it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If one says, "I renounce [the training] regarding one bhikṣu of the past or future," it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*). If one says, "I renounce my preceptor (*ācārya*)," it is not [renouncing the precepts].

This is called "renouncing the precepts" and incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. (The *Mūla-vinaya* states that renouncing one's *ācārya* also constitutes renunciation; this is because at the time of originally receiving the precepts, the quorum of ten monks was not met, and thus the precepts were not obtained.

If one wishes to return the precepts, it suffices to renounce even one person from among those ten. Here, however, it is stated that only by renouncing the *upādhyāya* does renunciation become complete; this is because when the precepts were originally obtained, the body of the precepts (*śīla-kāya*) arose in dependence upon the *upādhyāya*.

Thus, it is a renunciation of the very source from which they originated. One must know that the *upādhyāya* comes first; in such cases, one should follow the *Mahāsāṃghika* rule. If the *upādhyāya* is in a distant land or a different region, one should rely on one’s own local community (*nikāya*). Although the methods differ in these two cases, the permissions and prohibitions vary according to the circumstances. If...

He forms this thought: "It would be better for me to abandon the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha and become a follower of an external path. While this thought has not yet been finalized through speech, he speaks of it to others;
this is called "weakness of the precepts" (*śīla-kaśāya*). If one speaks of such an act of weakness of the precepts, for every utterance there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Furthermore, he forms this thought and speaks these words: "It is better that I abandon the Buddha," and so on, up to "I practice..."
If one says, "As a layperson, I am superior," this is called the matter of weakness regarding the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-kaśāya*).

For every such utterance, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one says, 'I shall practice the rituals of non-Buddhists,' for every such utterance there is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one says, 'I shall practice the rituals of a layperson (*avadātavasana*),' it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is not called abandoning the precepts (*śikṣā-pratyākhyāna*). If one speaks with the mouth...
"I renounce the precepts. This is called "renouncing the precepts.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "When receiving the precepts, three masters and seven monks are required. Yet, if one renounces the precepts before only a single person, it is because one seeks a superior dharma;
thus, the renunciation of the precepts requires many conditions and much effort, just as when [one receives them]."

It falls from a great height; therefore, it need not be much. Furthermore, receiving the precepts is like acquiring wealth and treasures, while abandoning the precepts is like losing wealth and treasures.
It is like entering the sea to gather jewels: after countless expedients, one finally obtains them;
yet when the time comes to lose them, they are scattered and destroyed in an instant by thieves, robbers, water, or fire. Abandoning the precepts is likewise.

Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse—whether obtained by purchase, obtained by hire, obtained through affection or obligation, obtained through an acquaintance, obtained through dalliance, obtained for the sake of experimentation, or obtained from one who has no prior experience—if he engages in intercourse with any such person, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu, with a defiled mind, desires to look at a woman, he incurs a *duṣkṛta*."
In the Vinaya, there is repentance through mental resolve. If one sees with the eyes or hears a sound, one commits a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If there is physical contact, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Even if [the organ] enters as little as a sesame seed, it is a *pārājika*.
If the body is large and enters [the opening] but does not touch its edges, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If the woman’s body is split into two parts...
If one commits sexual intercourse with a person of the two-fold [gender], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one binds [the partner] together to commit sexual intercourse, it is a *pārājika*.
If, with a lustful mind, one follows behind a woman, for every step there is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If, with a lustful mind, one speaks across a wall to a woman, for every word there is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse, whether by external means with internal emission of impurity, or by internal means with external emission of impurity, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The preparatory offense (*pṛyogika-sthūlātyaya*) may be either light or heavy.

A light sthūlātyaya occurs when one intends to commit a grave act of sexual misconduct (meaning the affliction of desire has arisen with great intensity), but stops and sits back down; this is a light sthūlātyaya.

Furthermore, setting out toward a woman and turning back before making physical contact, or making contact but failing to emit semen, or even kissing and embracing—all these constitute light sthūlātyaya."
If the male organ has entered the female organ but semen has not been emitted, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*. If semen is emitted, one incurs a heavy *sthūlātyaya*.
If the male organ touches the female organ up to the point of half the glans (*ardhapuṭa*), regardless of whether semen is emitted or not, it is entirely a heavy *sthūlātyaya*.
This applies even in the case of a living woman or a dead woman, or when engaging in sexual intercourse in improper places such as under the armpits or between the thighs.

If one commits sexual intercourse with a heavy *sthūlātyaya* offense involving a living girl or a dead girl, or with one that has been destroyed, fallen, or eaten by insects, one incurs a heavy *sthūlātyaya* offense in each case.
If one intends to commit sexual intercourse with a non-human male, an animal male, or a *paṇḍaka*, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The same applies to the gravity [of the offenses].

This precept is equally established in the Mahāyāna. Although the Mahāyāna permits repentance—as in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*—one must perceive auspicious signs, or encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others who expound the profound Dharma for them, so that they may suddenly give rise to the Great Resolve (*mahācitta*), as in the case of Jìngyè.

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* serves as a barrier [to such transgressions]. However, one who possesses great shame and remorse, gives rise to great wearying detachment (*saṃvega*), refrains entirely from concealment, and sincerely repents—only such a person may undertake this matter. This is essentially similar to the method for monks here to train in repentance.
If one lacks a sense of dread and a resolute mind, how could it be permitted—even if one belongs to the Mahāyāna?
One should immediately perform repentance. As for the principle that "one may act upon seeing the opportunity," this refers only to lay bodhisattvas and not to bhikṣus.
The Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra contains explicit clarifications on this; please examine it carefully.

as for those of the lowest grade, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "It would be better to cast this body into a great pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of knives than ever to violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman. Fourth, because those harmed by venomous snakes are permitted to participate in the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*) for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and may attend all formal monastic procedures (*karmavācanā*) as part of the group of fourteen, whereas those harmed by women do not share these privileges with the Saṃgha.

Appendix for Examination: The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, having committed a pārājika offense, has no intention whatsoever to conceal it, they shall perform repentance according to the Dharma.

"Having committed a grave offense, one should be expelled (parivāsa). The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: 'From this point forward, after the formal ritual (karmavācanā), this bhikṣu shall be called a pure upholder of the precepts.
