The Third Precept on Killing:
To kill is to lose one's own fundamental compassion and to sever the life-root of another; it is the most evil and depraved of deeds. This is its intrinsic nature.

Regarding sin: even if one has not received the Buddha’s precepts, according to the laws of the world, there is naturally sin; by national statute, one who kills must necessarily repay with their own life.

If one violates the Buddha’s precepts, one will certainly fall into the suffering of the three evil realms for long kalpas; whether on land or in the midst of the sea, one cannot escape it and shall not avoid receiving retribution.
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being with his own hand; or provides a weapon to another; or praises death, saying "it would be well"; or encourages death, saying "Alas, man!

What is the use of this wretched life? It is better to die than to live," and with such thoughts and reflections employs various means to praise death and encourage death—it is an offense of pārājika for that bhikṣu, and he is not to live in communion.
The Origin: While the Buddha was traveling by the Monkey River in Vaiśālī, he taught the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) within the lecture hall and praised this meditation on impurity.
He further extolled the contemplation of impurity (the meditation on impurity is also known as the nine perceptions;

when these nine methods of contemplating impurity are fully mastered and the mind is no longer distracted, if one attains the perfection of *samādhi*, sensual desire will naturally be eradicated, delusions and karma will be extinguished, and the fruit of the Path will be realized). Although these nine perceptions are merely conceptualized for the purpose of cultivation, they are nonetheless effective when applied.

This is a great matter. It is like a corpse in the great ocean: a drowning person who clings to it will immediately cross over. 1. The Contemplation of Bloatedness (*ādhmātaka-saṃjñā*): This refers to the practitioner’s mental visualization of a corpse becoming bloated, like a leather bag filled with wind, its appearance changed from its original state. This is the contemplation of bloatedness. 2. The Contemplation of Lividness (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*):

Having already contemplated the bloated corpse, one further contemplates how, blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, the skin and flesh become yellowish-red and mottled with dark blue-black lividity. This is the contemplation of lividness. 3. The Contemplation of Putrefaction (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*):

Having already contemplated the livid corpse, one further contemplates how, transformed by the wind and sun, the skin and flesh crack and fall apart, the body breaks into six parts, the internal organs rot, and foul stench flows forth. This is the contemplation of putrefaction. 4. The Contemplation of Blood-Smearedness (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*)... [text continues]

The visualization of the pervasive coating of blood: Having already contemplated the state of decay, one further contemplates the corpse from head to foot, with pus and blood overflowing from the entire body and smeared over it in filth. This is the visualization of the pervasive coating of blood. Next is the visualization of the fivefold putrefaction: having already contemplated the pervasive coating, [one proceeds as follows].

Furthermore, one contemplates the nine orifices of the corpse, from which pus and worms flow out; the skin and flesh decay and rot, lying in disarray upon the ground, with the stench increasing ever more. This is the perception of putrefaction (*pūyabhijñā*). Sixth is the perception of being devoured by worms (*kṛmibhakṣaṇasaṃjñā*):

Having already contemplated the putrefaction, one further contemplates the corpse being gnawed by maggots and insects, and being mangled, bitten, and stripped by birds and beasts. This is the perception of being devoured by worms. Seventh is the perception of dispersion (*vidhvaṃsana-saṃjñā*):

Having already contemplated the devouring by worms, one further contemplates the corpse being eaten by birds and beasts, torn apart and scattered, with tendons severed, bones separated, and head and feet strewn across one another. This is the perception of dispersion. Eighth is the perception of bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*): Having already contemplated the dispersion, one further contemplates the corpse’s skeletal frame exposed, where skin and flesh have been entirely consumed, leaving only the white bones strewn in disarray.

Like a conch shell, like a white jade disk—this is the contemplation of bones. Ninth is the contemplation of burning. Having already contemplated the bones, one further contemplates a corpse being burned by fire, cracking and bursting with smoke and stench; the white bones burn along with it. When the fuel is exhausted and the fire extinguished, it becomes identical to ash and dust.

This is called the "perception of burning. Having heard this, the bhikṣu practiced the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) and became weary of his body and life; he sought a blade, intending to commit suicide.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Mūlika-nandī, who had gone forth from the Śramaṇa caste (the term "Śramaṇa-caste" refers to his clan).
Holding a sharp sword in his hand, he entered the Vāruṇārāma park. A certain bhikṣu said to him, "Venerable sir, take my life;
I shall give you my robes and bowl. He accepted the employment and took his life. He then went to the river to wash the blade, whereupon remorse immediately arose within him.
At that time, a heavenly Māra stood in the water and exhorted and praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have now attained a great [merit]."
Regarding his merit: at that time, when Du-bu-du (Anupama) saw that his remorse had been extinguished, he entered the park again and killed sixty bhikṣus;
the corpses lay scattered in a chaotic heap within the enclosure. The householder was shocked, astonished, and felt revulsion.
At that time, the Buddha observed that the assembly was diminished. Knowing the reason, he asked intentionally. Ānanda reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha—
He then assembled the multitude and addressed the bhikṣus: "There is the Ānāpāna-samādhi (the meditation on mindfulness of breathing), which is tranquil and blissful;
it can immediately extinguish all unwholesome dharmas and ensure they never arise again. (Ānāpāna is translated here as 'sending away what comes' and 'sending away what goes';

it refers to the Dharma-gate of the Sixteen Special Victories. The *Fajie Cidi Chumen* states: first, knowing the inhalation; second, knowing the exhalation; third, knowing the length or shortness of the breath; fourth, knowing the breath pervading the body; fifth, eliminating all bodily formations—these belong to the foundation of mindfulness of the body; sixth, observing sensations...")"

1. Joy; 2. Suffering; 3. Happiness; 4. Unhappiness; 5. Mental formations; 6. Perception of form; 7. Perception of pleasure; 8. Perception of various mental activities—these three belong to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*). 9. The mind produces joy; 10. The mind produces concentration; 11. The mind produces liberation—these three belong to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).

12. Contemplating impermanence; 13. Contemplating emergence and dispersal; 14. Contemplating dispassion; 15. Contemplating cessation; 16. Contemplating relinquishment—these five together belong to the contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*). Furthermore, knowing the inhalation and knowing the exhalation is correctly based upon the breath as the gateway.

When one attains the coarse and subtle abidings (*sthiti*) as well as the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), one knows [the breath] to be long or short. Upon entering the stage of "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya-bhūmi*), one knows it to pervade the entire body. Attaining the first dhyāna, one eliminates bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) and experiences the feelings of joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*), as well as all mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*).

Attaining the second dhyāna, the mind produces joy and achieves internal composure. Attaining the third dhyāna, the mind achieves liberation. Attaining the fourth dhyāna, one contemplates impermanence (*anityatā*). Attaining the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one contemplates emergence and dispersion.

Attaining the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), one contemplates detachment from desire (*vairāgya*). At the stage of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one is able to contemplate cessation (*nirodha*). At the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one contemplates relinquishment (*upekṣā*). Although these share the same dwelling with the fundamental four dhyānas and four concentrations, there are distinct practitioners who, at each successive stage, cultivate contemplation and achieve clear realization.

Thus, within each stage [of the path], no more perversions arise; the mind is not defiled or attached. According to the convergence of causes and conditions, one immediately, upon that very stage, gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom and realizes the fruits of the Three Vehicles.
Having spoken this samādhi, he assembled the bhikṣus and established the precepts based on ten points of meaning. In all cases of killing, it arises from delusion;
being unable to endure a situation, one harbors hatred within and severs the life-root of another. Thus, this training rule was enacted.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: In the sixth year after the Buddha attained enlightenment, on the ninth day of the third half-month of winter, before the morning meal, he established this precept for the sake of Mūlika Nandika (according to this calculation, it corresponds precisely to the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month).

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: The Tathāgata, observing with his divine eye, saw that in the past there were five hundred hunters who entered an araṇya together to kill herds of deer, making this their livelihood.
They fell into the three evil realms and underwent various sufferings. After a long time, they emerged from them;
possessing a slight residue of merit from the past, they were born among humans and left the household life to practice the Way. Due to their past calamities...
It was not yet over. Within half a month, they continued to slaughter one another; even the Buddhas could not save them.

Among these five hundred people, there were four noble ones who had attained the fruits of the path; for them, birth and death had a limit, though some remainder remained. As for ordinary people, their cycle of rebirth is without end.
For this reason, I taught them the contemplation of impurity. I did not originally teach death, but only how to be born in the heavens. However—

They can be rescued and protected through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). For this reason, after teaching them the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), he entered a quiet chamber for half a month, permitting only one person to bring him food. He did not allow others to say such things as:

"The Buddha is omniscient (*sarvajña*), yet he could not prevent his disciples from killing one another; because the World-Honored One has entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), no one was able to go [to them]."
This is merely what was said. The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* asks:
"The Buddha possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajña*). For what reason did he instruct the bhikṣus in such a way as to cause them to undergo such decline and affliction?
If he did not know [the consequences], he would not be called 'all-knowing. The answer is: "The Buddha is all-equal."
The Teaching. At that time, it was not only these sixty people who received the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). The Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is without partiality;

however, the benefits received vary, being more or less according to the capacity of each. The Buddha deeply knows the beginning, middle, and end of the faculties and karma of sentient beings, and that through the causal conditions of this very dharma, they will surely attain great benefit later on.
These sixty bhikṣus had previously received the meditation on impurity under Kāśyapa Buddha.
Regarding the Dharma: he was unable to practice it exclusively and frequently committed evil deeds. At the end of his life, he entered hell.

Now that a Buddha has appeared in the world, his retribution for sins has ended and he has been reborn among humans, though he has fallen into a lowly and base family. Having left home to enter the Path, because of his past conditions, he is destined to receive this Dharma.
Once his life there has ended, he will be reborn in the heavens; subsequently, descending from the heavens, he will listen to the Dharma from the Buddha.
They attain the fruit of the path. By these causes and conditions, the Buddha is without partiality.
*Explanation of the Meaning:* The text is divided into two sections. From "With one's own hand, taking the life of a human being" onwards, it correctly clarifies the matter of the offense.
From "That bhikṣu... onwards, it establishes the nature of the committed offense. The Vinaya states: "A human being" refers from the initial consciousness up to the final...

Consciousness. And it cuts off its life-force. (This consciousness is the eighth, the *ālaya-vijñāna*. It is called the "store-consciousness" because there is no phenomenon it does not contain and no object it does not encompass.

It is also called the "consciousness of the sustaining function" because it can sustain all seeds of good and evil. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "When this consciousness first enters the womb at the time of conception, like a magnet attracting iron, it is called the 'initial consciousness.

Even until the moment of death, as the sensation of cold gradually arises, only this consciousness is able to maintain the body. If this consciousness abandons the body, the four great elements disperse; this is called the 'consciousness of the end of life. This is what is meant by the one who goes before and comes after acting as the master. This is called the 'final consciousness. Furthermore—)

All sentient beings possess the three factors of sensation (*vedanā*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which are linked together in an uninterrupted succession; this is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Now, to cause those [factors] so that the physical form and mind no longer continue in succession is called the severance of life.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Among humans, there are the three refuges, the five precepts, and the *prātimokṣa* discipline. Furthermore, the four fruits of the śramaṇa are mostly attained among humans. One attains Buddhahood and Pratyekabuddhahood only among humans, because it is there that the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is achieved. For this reason, one incurs the offense of *pārājika* by harming a human being, whereas one does not incur it in other realms.

Furthermore, the character "then" (*zé*) should be connected to what follows; the exhortation to "admire" (*tàn*) is precisely the mind that performs the action, demonstrating that it was not an error. "Ho! (*duō*) is an exhortation used to alert [the listener], indicating that they should know it is a man.
Regarding the words "summoning" (the call). As for "killing": if one kills oneself, it means killing by means of one's own hand, or with a potsherd, stone, sword, staff, or other objects.
If one causes another to kill, it means that at the time of killing, one personally supervises the act, such as throwing the victim into water or fire.
If one pushes [the victim] from the top of a mountain to the valley floor; or causes a wild beast to devour them; or causes a snake to bite them;

or employs various other means to kill; or dispatches a messenger to kill—meaning a bhikṣu dispatches a messenger to take the life of such-and-such a person, and that messenger goes and takes it as instructed;
or regarding the messenger who goes and returns—the bhikṣu dispatches a messenger to take the life of such-and-such a person, and [the messenger] goes according to the instruction.
Intending to kill, but failing to do so, he returns; then, following his previous instructions, he goes again to kill.

Or, if he sends repeatedly to kill—meaning a bhikṣu dispatches a messenger saying, "Go and take such-and-such a person's life," and subsequently dispatches messengers up to four or five times, and that messenger then goes and kills.
Or, if he dispatches messengers in succession to kill—meaning a bhikṣu dispatches a messenger saying, "You must cut off..."
"Kill such-and-such a person. That messenger, in turn, dispatches another messenger—whether it be a hundred or a thousand—who goes to take his life.
Or, if he seeks a man to kill, thinking, "Who among these knows of such a person who can wield a blade and possesses the skillful means?"
Having practiced for a long time, he is not terrified and is capable of not retreating when he can take the life of such-and-such a person. That messenger then goes and takes his life.
If one instructs someone to seek out a man to kill, it is also as in the instruction given above regarding seeking out a person.

If one seeks out a man with a sword to kill, this means personally seeking who is brave and capable of wielding a sword to take the life of such-and-such a person; that person then goes and kills him.
If one instructs someone to seek out a person with a sword to kill [another], it is as explained above regarding instructing another to seek [a killer].

Or if one manifests signs through the body—that is, by making bodily gestures to cause death—such as causing [the victim] to fall into water or fire, to fall from a mountain peak into a valley, to be trampled by an elephant, or to be devoured or stung by wild beasts and venomous snakes; because of these manifestations of the body, the person kills themselves. Or if [it is done] through speech...

This refers to praising death within the context of formal prohibitions—that is, exhorting death by saying it is a pleasant thing to die. Or one might say: "The evil you have committed is devoid of benevolence;
harboring a poisonous mind, you have not performed any virtuous deeds. You have failed to provide protection for your own life and thus must undergo retribution;

it would be better for you to die than to endure so much. (This is exhorting death because the evil karma one has created is so great. Furthermore, if one speaks these words: "You have not committed violent evils... and so forth.
Be compassionate. Do not harbor malice. You have performed many virtuous deeds; you have cultivated merit; you have provided protection.
Though you have been born into this life of manifold sufferings, upon death you shall be reborn in heaven.

Because of these words, he then took his own life (this is an instance of performing many meritorious acts and exhorting one toward death). It is the same when bodily or verbal signs are manifested, or when a letter is sent.
"Kill. This refers to writing a letter stating, "Whatever good or evil you have done," and so forth, as explained extensively above.
Regarding killing by dispatching a messenger via letter, it is also as described above. As for "by a pitfall," this means knowing with certainty the path by which the person will inevitably travel;
one should then dig a deep pit along that path and place fire within it, or a blade, or a venomous snake.
A sharp stake: if one coats it with poison and drives it [into the ground], causing [the victim] to fall into a pit and die;
or if it is leaning against something—meaning knowing that the person will certainly lean against that spot—whether it be a tree, a wall, or a fence, and if one sets fire to the outside of it.
Whether by means of a blade, a stake, a venomous snake, or a poisoned needle; or by using a mechanical device to cause them to fall into these and die;
or by administering medicine—specifically, knowing that a person is ill, giving them the wrong medicine, or mixing it with poison, or giving various medicines in excessive doses to cause death;
or by setting up lethal implements—specifically, first knowing that the person has from the outset been weary of their own life and body.
Despising this body, he immediately takes up a blade, poison, a rope, or some other means of death and places them before him;
if he uses any one of these objects to commit suicide (this refers to the "holding a blade for another" mentioned in the *Zhengzhi* [Correct Regulation]).

Regarding the determination of the offense: herein, one who commits suicide in this manner, or even provides the means for death, as well as those who employ other expedients to kill another person such that they die, all incur a *pārājika* offense. If the expedients were employed but the person did not die, all incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If among the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, ghosts, spirits, or animals, there are those who understand human speech and are capable of changing their form,
and one employs skillful means to seek to kill or cause them to die, it is all *sthūlātyaya*; if one employs skillful means but they do not die, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If one kills an animal that is unable to transform its form, it is a *pāyattika*. If one employs a means [to kill] but it does not die, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If it is actually a human being and one perceives it as such and kills it, it is a *pārājika*. If it is a human being but one kills it while doubting its identity, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If it is a non-human being and one perceives it as such; or if it is a non-human being and one perceives it as a human being;
or if it is a non-human being and one doubts its identity—in all these cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The fourth section states: If many bhikṣus send one person to take another’s life, all are guilty of *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu uses incantations on medicine, flower garlands, incense, or clothing to cause death, it is entirely *pārājika*.
If he employs skillful means to cause an abortion, it is *pārājika*. If the mother dies but the child lives, there is no offense; however, he merely incurs [the aforementioned penalty].
Thullaccaya (if the murderous intent was not directed at the mother, but originally at her child; if the child survives, it is Thullaccaya, and if the mother dies, there is no offense).
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, a human being; second, the perception that it is a human being;
third, the intent to kill; and fourth, the severing of life. If even one of these conditions is lacking, the Vinaya provides an exemption.
The rules for Bhikṣuṇīs regarding the pārājika offenses are governed by the same regulations (as for the bhikṣus; they study the same precepts).
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense resulting in expulsion. This is defined as an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if one throws a weapon, a staff, a tile, or a stone and it accidentally strikes and kills another;
if, while engaged in construction work such as building a house, one accidentally causes a person to die by falling bricks, stones, timber, rafters, or pillars;

or if, when supporting a seriously ill person to rise or to lie down, or during bathing, or during the administration of medicine, or when moving from a cool place to a warm place, or from a warm place to a cool place, [an accident occurs].
Entering or leaving a room, going toward or returning from the latrine, or dying while entirely free of an evil mind;
as well as when the precepts have not yet been established, or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense suffering—these constitute no offense.

Regarding the section on "Appropriation," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: To treat a "sensitive area" (*kāma-sthāna*) with a knife constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. (A "sensitive area" refers to the space four finger-widths on either side of the anus.
If a bhikṣu is walking along a path and a person who harbors prior resentment approaches to ask for directions, he thinks:
"Now I have this man; I shall show him the way so that he dies, ensuring not a single one survives. He then points out the way.
Regarding evil paths: if one points out an evil path—such as the perils of kings, or lions, tigers, and venomous stinging insects—at the time of pointing it out, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if they experience suffering and pain, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if they die, it is a *pārājika*.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: After entering the mother’s womb, forty-nine days are designated as the stage of being "like a human" (*manuṣya-pratirūpaka*). Beyond this period, one is fully designated as a "human.

Whether it be one who kills a being like a human or a full human, in all cases it constitutes a *pārājika* offense. (Regarding "one like a human": this refers to the initial acquisition of the two faculties upon taking conception in the mother’s womb;

at the moment of first entering the conditions, the union of the parents' vital essences and one's own consciousness within the womb results in the acquisition of the two faculties of body and life. After seven weeks have passed, the six sense-faculties are complete, and the physical form of a human is formed; hence it is called "one like a human"). If [one acts]...
If one writes an order for someone to kill, each word constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. When the letter reaches the recipient and they die as a result, it is a *pārājika*.
If one gives instructions for killing using indirect or figurative speech, and the person dies because of that, it is a *pārājika*.
Generally, at the moment the murderous intent arises, it is a *duṣkṛta*; when the preparatory means are employed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; and when the person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
There were two bhikṣus who harbored mutual resentment. Later, while traveling together on a road, they struck one another, and one of them died.

The Buddha said, "Since there was no intent to kill, this does not constitute a grave offense. Striking a bhikṣu with anger constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. From now on, I do not permit mutual resentment.

If one travels on a road with someone who has not yet repented [of such resentment] and commits an offense, it is a *dukkaṭa*. [This also applies to] intending to kill that person but killing by mistake."
This constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one constructs a pit, a trap, a snare, or a net for the sake of another person, and that person dies because of it, it is a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, but later die because of it, it is also a *pārājika*. If they do not die because of it later, it is a *sthūlātyaya*."
If one digs a pit for a non-human being and that non-human being dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a human or an animal dies, it is all a *duṣkṛta* (this offense is established because of the murderous intent; since the initial thought was not directed toward a human or an animal, the penalty is light). If one digs a pit for an animal and that animal dies, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a human or a non-human being dies, it is all a *duṣkṛta* (this *duṣkṛta* offense is incurred because of the murderous intent used to dig the pit, even though the intended victim was not [the one who died]).
[It is] obtained through humans and non-humans. If one does not intend a single specific case, but acts so that all those who come into existence die:
if a human dies, it is a *pārājika*; if a non-human dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if an animal dies, it is a *pāyattika*.
If no one dies at all, there is one *sthūlātyaya* and two *duṣkṛta*s. To sever one's own genitals is a *sthūlātyaya*; to sever one's own finger is a *duṣkṛta*.
Dukkata for killing a transformed being (nirmāṇa-pudgala). Thullaccaya for striking a person with the intent to kill but not causing death.
Thullaccaya for abandoning a patient who has been ill for a long time out of a sense of weariness, thereby causing them to die. Thullaccaya for intentionally providing [harmful] medicine or food.

If one causes death by means of ordinary clothing, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one causes death by lancing an unripe boil, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one causes death by lancing a ripe boil, there is no offense.
The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one intends to kill an ordinary person but mistakenly kills an Arhat; or if one intends to kill an Arhat but mistakenly kills [an ordinary person]..."

If an ordinary person intends to kill his father but kills his mother by mistake, or intends to kill his mother but kills his father by mistake, in both cases it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

This is because, regarding the two precepts of killing and stealing, the gravity of the offense is determined by the state of mind (*citta*) rather than the gravity of the physical act. Since the intended victim has not yet been killed, this is classified as a preparatory offense (*prayoga*).

However, as for the one who was killed by mistake, since there was no actual intent to kill them, a grave offense is not incurred. If, after having already performed the preparatory act for killing the mother, the person dies first and the mother dies later...
If one commits a grave offense (*stūlātyaya*) by first dying oneself and subsequently causing the mother to die; the same applies if the father is an Arhat.

The *Vinayaviniścayasaṃgraha* states: "If one employs a means to cause another to be killed, but later gives rise to a mind of regret and does not desire their death, even though the person dies, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya*.
Or, if during a cold night in the open air, one causes a man or woman to freeze to death..."
If a person is male, and the caregiver perceives him as being alive, and because of this perception causes his death, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If a monk caring for a patient becomes weary or gives rise to an evil thought, hoping for the patient's property, or utters words of anger such as, "Let him die," [it is likewise an offense].
I cannot look [upon it], for by doing so one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) regarding the deceased.
Furthermore, if there are foods currently available that are suitable or unsuitable for consumption, the person tending to the sick also incurs a grave offense.

Seeing another bhikṣu who is ill and about to die, if one does not repair one's own robes and bowl, thinking, "When he passes away, all his robes and requisites shall rightfully belong to me"—[this too constitutes an offense].

This is the intention of a caṇḍāla; [if one acts thus], one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (dharmātikrama). If one performs surgery with a knife due to haste of speech, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If no physician can be found and one performs surgery, there is no offense. If a person suffers from hemorrhoids, they should not be excised;
rather, they should be eliminated through the application of medicine, mantras, and skillful means. If one sees a sentient being who has been swept away by water, or...

At that time, though tormented by thirst, he did not take [the water] with his own hand nor give it to him. Seeing that he was about to die, there were other means by which he could have been saved, yet he did not rescue him.
Or, even if he did not wish for death, he maintained a state of indifference (*upekṣā-citta*). If the other person should die, in all such cases, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
A bhikṣu struck his own penis. The Buddha said: "It is only right that you strike this; why instead strike [something else]?"
Other ignorant bhikṣus incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"If one instructs a person to kill another, and that messenger further dispatches someone else, and this process continues in succession until ten people are involved, when the last person among them actually kills, all [the preceding instigators] incur the *pārājika* offense."

If a bhikṣu is well-versed in astrology, the yin-yang system, the *guīyì* (tortoise and milfoil divination), and understands the rise and fall of nations and the strategic formations of armies and cavalry,
and if, on account of that bhikṣu’s words, he leads an expedition against a foreign land, resulting in slaughter and the acquisition of wealth and treasures.
In all such cases, both the killing and the stealing constitute *pārājika* offenses.

If one intends to kill with a blade or a staff, yet the victim does not die immediately upon being struck by the staff or pierced by the blade, but is expected to die within ten days, and subsequently another person strikes them and they die immediately from that blow, the second person who struck them commits a *pārājika* offense for killing.
The first person who struck them commits a grave *sthūlātyaya* (thullaccaya) offense.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, digs the earth and makes a pit so that a certain person shall fall into it and die—he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the first moment of digging up the earth;
if the person falls into the pit and suffers, he incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgression).
[If the victim] dies, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. If another person falls into it and dies, the bhikṣu is not guilty [because when digging the pit he intended only to kill a specific individual;
however, since all who fall into the same pit are included under "unintentional injury," this is exempted]. If a pit is made for everyone and a person falls into it and dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If parents fall into it and die, it is a *pārājika* and a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). If the pit is deep...
If a person carrying provisions falls into a pit and does not die immediately, but later eats them all and is certain to die with no hope of escape,
the one who originally made the pit incurs a *pārājika* offense at the moment of the fall. If the pit was originally made with the intent to kill a person,
but that person did not come and instead someone else accidentally fell into it and died, at the time the pit was first made, the offender incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the offense: when making offerings, there may be a hostile bhikṣu sitting among the assembly who, being obscured by darkness, does not realize he has arrived.
He speaks these words: "Why does this thief [named so-and-so] not kill him?
Why does the venomous snake not bite him? Why do people not poison him? My heart takes great pleasure in that person's death. Thus he utters such a curse.
In all such cases, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. If one knows that [the person] has already left after sitting down, yet performs such a spell, one likewise incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
This precept is equally prescribed in the Mahāyāna. For a Bodhisattva, the four great vows take the liberation of sentient beings as the foremost; thus, in the Mahāyāna Prātimokṣa, killing—
Precepts come first. One should give rise to a mind of constant compassion and provide benefit and salvation through skillful means; this is not like the self-benefit of the Śrāvakas.
Therefore, one must be even more rigorous regarding transgressions and repentance as described above.

Citation: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death. If the murderous mind is not eliminated, one cannot escape the realm of dust.
Even if much wisdom and meditative concentration manifest before them, if they do not sever killing, they will inevitably fall into the path of spirits. Those of the highest grade become..."
As for the powerful ghosts, those of middle grade are the flying yakṣas.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "When a bhikṣu was extremely ill and suffering, the other bhikṣus, seeing his condition was grave, spoke with a heart of compassion, saying:
'Venerable one, venerable one! You were fully endowed with the observance of the precepts; it is only because of your fear of death that you have now [fallen ill]...'"
"It is suffering. Elder, if you die, you will certainly be reborn in heaven. When the sick bhikṣu heard these words, he thought to himself:
"All the bhikṣus praise me for being fully endowed with the observance of the precepts; I shall surely be reborn in heaven upon death. Thus, he refrained from eating and sought death.
[The one] who offered such praise incurs a *pārājika* offense. Therefore, when a wise bhikṣu goes to visit a sick person, he must be careful not to offer praise.
He dies. One may rightly say: "Venerable one, you were fully endowed with the precepts. Do not be attached to your dwelling, nor to your robes and requisites, nor to your acquaintances.
Rather, maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem and mindfulness of the impurity of the body. Be careful not to be indolent within the three realms.
According to the length of your lifespan, if this sick bhikṣu dies because of these words, it is thus due to such discourse."
Dharma. If one dies without fault, or if one preaches the contemplations on suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and impurity, and a person hears this and takes their own life, there is no offense.
This is the fourth precept concerning false speech.
As for false speech: this is a great falsehood. To claim realization when one has not realized it, or to claim attainment when one has not attained it, is a lack of sincerity in one's mental conduct.
Deceiving others out of greed for gain and offerings is the most unwholesome act among all aspects of spiritual practice. This is a fundamental transgression (prakṛti-sāvadya).

Even if one has not received the Buddha’s precepts, such fraudulent schemes to acquire wealth are sinful according to the laws of the world; however, to utter a lie while violating the Buddha’s precepts is a grave offense.
One who has realized the noble state may fall into the three evil destinies.
If a bhikṣu, while actually possessing no such knowledge, claims of himself: "I have attained the state of a superior person;
I have entered the sublime dharma of noble wisdom; I know this; I see this," and if at a later time, whether questioned or unasked, he desires to clear himself...
Because it is pure, this statement is made: "I truly did not know and did not see, yet I said I knew and I saw; this was a false, deceptive, and lying speech.
With the exception of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), such a bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
The Origin Story: This precept has two origins. At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Multi-storied Lecture Hall on the banks of the Monkey River in Vaiśālī.
At that time, grain was expensive and the people were suffering from famine; it was difficult to obtain almsfood. The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among you, those who have the same upādhyāya or the same ācārya, or who follow one another as close friends and acquaintances, each of you should together [at this Vaiśālī...]"
"Let us depart and settle for the rains retreat wherever it is appropriate. I, too, shall observe the rains retreat at this very place. Why?

Because food and drink are difficult to obtain, and I consider the exhaustion and suffering of the assembly. Then, according to the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus dispersed to various suitable locations.
Some observed the rains retreat in a monastery by the side of the Vālukā River, where they addressed the local householders as follows:
He said: "I have attained the state of a superior person (uttarimanussa-dhamma)," and he praised himself. He also said, "That certain bhikṣu has likewise attained the state of a superior person.
The lay devotees, believing his words, immediately provided him with food and drink as offerings, so that he was no longer troubled by the lack of sustenance.
When the rains retreat (varṣā) had concluded, he went to see the World-Honored One. After the Buddha had greeted him with words of comfort, he reported all these matters in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "You foolish people! Even that which is real should not be spoken of to others, let alone that which is unreal.
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: 'In the world there are two kinds of thieves: the first is one who is actually not of pure conduct.'"
They claim to practice pure conduct for the sake of food and clothing.
Though it is unreal and not their own, they deliberately make false claims among the great assembly, saying, "I have attained the qualities of a superior person.
Among these, the second type is the greatest thief. Why? Because they steal the food and drink offered by others. He rebukes them with countless skillful means.
Having done so, he assembled with the bhikṣus and established the precepts based on the ten points of meaning; this was the first enactment.
This training rule was formulated because of delusion, due to the pursuit of gain and offerings, and the affliction of seeking gain and offerings.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu of overweening pride who said to others, "I have attained the Path. At another time, he practiced with diligence... [text continues].

Being indolent, he diligently sought skillful means to realize the supreme and most excellent Dharma. Having heard the Buddha’s formulation of the precepts, he suspected that he had committed an offense and spoke of it.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: In the winter season of the sixth year after the Buddha attained enlightenment, on the thirteenth day of the fourth half-month after the meal (which corresponds precisely to the twelfth day of the tenth month), the precepts were established.
**Explanation of the Meaning:** The text is divided into four sections. The section beginning with "In reality, there is nothing known" correctly clarifies the matter of the offense committed.
The section beginning with "At another time" consists of the words for purifying oneself through confession. The phrase "Excepting overweening pride" is the provision for exemption from guilt.
The section beginning with "This bhikṣu" concludes by establishing the nature of the offense committed. The Vinaya states: "One who does not know and does not see" refers to the actual...
Having no knowledge, he makes claims for himself. He claims to possess morality, generosity, learning, wisdom, and eloquence. Regarding persons and phenomena:

"persons" refers to the aggregates (the five aggregates), the sense bases (the six bases), and the elements (the eighteen elements). Regarding superhuman states (*uttari-manussa-dhamma*): these are the various dharmas that lead to transcendence and accomplishment.

The Dharma is cultivated and expanded. Like a well-trained vehicle, it is guarded and observed;
one attains skillful equanimity and achieves certainty, becoming free from further hardship and attaining mastery.

To say "I am one of right mindfulness" means that one possesses mindfulness capable of leading others to liberation, as described above. This is what is meant by saying "I am one of right mindfulness. To say...
They maintain the precepts; they claim to have desire, claim to be heedful, and claim to be diligent, as described above.

They also claim to have attained concentration and right attainment—namely, the samādhi with directed thought and evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra*), the samādhi without directed thought but with evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra*), the samādhi without directed thought and without evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra*), and the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness (*śūnyatā-animitta-apraṇihita*) samādhis—and they become intimate with and closely associate with them.
He contemplates this concentration and enters into it correctly; the rest is as explained above. Regarding those who claim to possess the Path:

As for "familiarity" and so forth, it is as explained above. Regarding those who claim to have attained [the fruits]: they have attained the stages of stream-enterer (srotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), and non-returner (anāgāmin) on the path.
As for "familiarity," "association," and "intimacy," the rest is as explained above. Regarding those who claim the fruit: from stream-enterer up to...

If one perceives a human as a human and speaks [of them], it is the fundamental offense; if one is in doubt regarding a human, it is likewise. If one perceives a non-human as a human, or a human as a non-human, or is in doubt regarding a non-human, in all such cases it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This precept constitutes the fundamental offense only when six conditions are fully met: first, that one actually possesses no knowledge; second, that what is spoken is... [text truncated]

speaking in jest; speaking rapidly; speaking alone in a private place; speaking in a dream; or intending to say one thing but mistakenly saying another. And...

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that there are eight ways of incurring a *pārājika* offense. The first is: having previously formed this thought, "I..."

To speak based on a different view, claiming to have attained superhuman states ("different" meaning "not having seen [the truth]"). 5. To have a different perception.

1. Speaking of having attained superhuman states (claiming to have attained superhuman states when one has not). 2. Speaking of having attained superhuman states through a different kind of patience (*kṣānti*)—where "different patience" means not yet having realized [the truth]. 3.

Speaking of having attained superhuman states through a different kind of joy (*rati*)—where "different joy" refers to claiming to have attained it when one has not yet attained the true joy of the Dharma. 4. Speaking without answering according to the question.
To claim superhuman attainments (i.e., to speak of them oneself) constitutes a *pārājika* offense in all cases. It is further said:
"It would be better to eat burning stones or swallow molten copper than to consume the faithful offerings of others through falsehood. There are five great thieves in the world:
first, one who acts as the leader of a hundred or a thousand men, destroying cities and villages, harming people, and seizing their property; second, there is the wicked bhikṣu.
1. There will be bhikṣus who travel through human settlements and preach the Dharma for the sake of a wrong livelihood.

To falsely claim for oneself that one has attained superhuman states—this fifth thief is called the greatest thief among all those in the world, including gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas. Furthermore, it is said: "For the sake of gain and offerings."

To praise another’s perfection of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation while secretly using it for one's own glorification constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
To act with composed deportment— whether sitting, rising, walking, or standing— and to speak calmly for the sake of gain,

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If someone asks a bhikṣu, "Are you an arhat? and he remains silent, it constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense. He should say, "I am not an arhat."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states: "If one claims for oneself that one maintains pure precepts and that no lustful desire arises, yet this is not true, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If asked whether one has attained the fruits [of the path], and one answers, "I have attained them," while pointing with the hand, [it is a *sthūlātyaya*].
The result is a *sthūlātyaya*.

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "Saṃghāvaśeṣa" (Sengcan) means that it is like a person who has been hacked by another; because a throat remains, it is called "residual" (*avaśeṣa*).

If one obtains a pure assembly that performs the ritual for confessing and removing the offense according to the Dharma, this offense can be removed.
If a pure assembly is not available, it cannot be extinguished. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The Sūtra states: "One who commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense falls into hell for a lifespan equal to eight thousand years of the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven (where one day and night is equivalent to eight hundred human years). This *niraya* is the Hell of Screaming (*Raurava*). It is so called because the hell-wardens place the offenders within iron cauldrons, where they wail and cry out loudly.
First is the precept against intentionally discharging semen.

The Origin Story (*nidāna*): This precept was established in two stages. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

Kālodāyin’s lustful desires were so intense that his complexion grew haggard and his body became emaciated. Following his thoughts and recollections, he manipulated his organ and emitted impurity. [The monks]...
His faculties were joyful and his complexion was radiant. When the bhikṣus who were his kinsmen and friends learned of the reason for this, they reported it in full to the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the Saṃgha and rebuked Kāla:
"How can you, having gone forth within my pure Dharma, engage in such defiled conduct? You fool! You stretch out your hand to receive the faithful offerings of others, and furthermore..."

[The Buddha] established the precept by gathering with the bhikṣus for the ten points of the *Daśottara-sūtra*, from "unifying the Saṃgha" as the first point, up to the tenth point, "causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time. This was the initial enactment.
At that time, after the Buddha had established the precept, there was a certain bhikṣu who fell asleep with a distracted mind and emitted semen during a dream. Upon waking, he reflected on this.
This was reported to the Buddha as a matter of doubt. The Buddha said: "There are five faults in sleeping with a distracted mind:

first, having bad dreams; second, not being protected by the devas; third, the mind not entering into the Dharma; fourth, failing to contemplate the signs of light; and fifth, emitting semen during a dream.

There are five merits in sleeping with a well-directed mind; these are the opposites of the above and should be understood accordingly. Therefore, there is the practice of removing [the influence of] dreams."

In this case, there is no offense. This was the second formulation of the precept. Because of delusion and lack of wisdom, and based upon sexual acts and the affliction of lust, this training rule was established;
it constitutes the fundamental category of the first section concerning sexual misconduct.
Exegesis: The text is divided into three sections. First, "intentionally emitting," etc., correctly clarifies the act that constitutes the offense.

Second, "excepting in a dream" is the provision for exemption. Third, "the Saṃgha," etc., establishes the nature of the offense committed. The Vinaya states: "Intentionally" means with a deliberate mind.
Regarding "emitting semen," there are seven types. "Blue" refers to the semen of a Cakravartin King. "Yellow" refers to the [semen of a] Wheel-... [text fragmentary].
The essence of the Prince is pure. That which is red in color is the essence of one who has frequently indulged in female desire. That which is white is the essence of a person carrying heavy loads.
That which is black is the essence of the foremost minister of a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*). That which is the color of curd is the essence of a *srotāpanna*.
