If this woman perceives another woman as that [other] woman, and that other woman perceives her as this woman, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. This is because their nature is inclined toward coarse and wicked behavior."
If one speaks with a mind that is not lustful, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
This precept requires six conditions to constitute the full offense: first, there must be a lustful mind; second, the object must be a human woman;

third, there must be the perception of her as a human woman; fourth, the speech spoken must be coarse and vile; fifth, there must be the perception that the speech is coarse and vile; sixth, [the completion of the act].
The teaching and the hearing are clear and distinct. If the conditions are not fulfilled, the offense is a *prayoga* (preparatory act);
this also governs the *bhikṣuṇī*, for whom it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) [the same governance, though different training].
For the *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if one explains the nine impurities of leakage (*āsrava*) to a woman;

or if one is explaining the Vinaya and these words are mentioned in the course of the discourse; or even if spoken in a dream; or if spoken erroneously; or if it concerns a case prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the "Admonition": The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if a woman stands before a bhikṣu and asks him in reverse, saying, "Did you not act in such a manner within the three orifices?
and so on for up to a hundred words, and the bhikṣu complies with her intent.
Regarding the various expressions used: for each individual expression, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind and employing skillful means to seek pleasure in this matter, uses indirect speech;
if a woman understands this speech, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
This precept is established in common with the Mahāyāna; it may be understood according to the above.
Fourth, the precept against praising one’s own body to solicit desire:
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful desire, speaks before a woman, praising his own body, saying: "Sister, I practice the holy life (brahmacarya)."
"One who upholds the precepts and exerts diligence, cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas—such a person may offer this dharma of sexual desire to me.
Such an offering is the foremost and most supreme. This constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

The Origin: This precept was also established based on a previous incident. After the Buddha had concluded the three preceding precepts, [a monk] again engaged in praising his own body and soliciting sensual desires;
therefore, he established this precept. Due to delusion and a lack of right knowledge, and because of the affliction of lust, he formulated this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
This constitutes the first section of the chapter on the fundamental categories of sexual misconduct.
The commentary is divided into two parts: from "with a lustful mind" onwards, it correctly clarifies the act committed;
from "the Saṃgha," etc., it establishes the offense incurred. The Vinaya states: "With a lustful mind as described above, toward a woman as described above, oneself..."
As for praising one's own body: it is to praise one’s physical form as upright and handsome, and one’s complexion as excellent;

to say, "I am of the kṣatriya caste," or "I am of the householder or brāhmaṇa lineage" (the term "sister" [mahā-bhagini] is used as a form of address, though she is called "younger sister" because she was born later); and to claim, "I am a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacarya), diligently cultivating freedom from defilement and impurity."
The upholder of the precepts is neither deficient nor torn [in his observance]; he is free from outflows and undefiled. Diligently practicing wholesome dharmas, he delights in secluded places;

he goes for alms at the proper time, wears rag-robes, practices the practice of eating only leftover food, observes the practice of not eating after the meal has been set aside, and practices eating in a single sitting.
1. Eating only one meal a day; sitting in a cemetery; sitting in the open air; sitting at the foot of a tree; sitting constantly; sitting wherever one happens to be; wearing the three robes;
being skilled in chanting; being learned; being able to preach the Dharma; and practicing meditation.

Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, if a bhikṣu acts in this way, praising himself by saying, "Come and provide me with offerings," yet does not mention sexual desire, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If he mentions sexual desire while praising his own person, [it is likewise].
If [the offense] is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for each instance; if it is not clearly understood, it is all a *sthūlātyaya*.
Whether by hand gesture, letter, messenger, or by manifesting a sign to make the other understand—[if] he understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if he does not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
With the exception of the two [sexual] organs, if one further solicits offerings from other parts [of the body], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one addresses a female *rākṣasa*, a female among devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or animals who is able to transform her form, and praises her own body with clear speech, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the speech is not clear, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This applies even when addressing those who are unable to transform their forms.
If she has the form of a female animal and praises herself, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If she praises herself toward a man, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If it is a human woman and she perceives her as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If it is a human woman but she suspects it, or if it is a human woman but she perceives her as a non-human woman, or if it is a non-human woman but she perceives her as a human woman, or if she suspects it is a non-human woman—in all these cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This precept requires five conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the presence of a lustful mind; second, the object being a human woman;

third, the perception that she is a human woman; fourth, the explicit statement that sexual intercourse is the foremost and best; and fifth, the clear communication and understanding between speaker and listener.
If even one of these is lacking, it constitutes a preparatory offense (*prayoga*).
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a sthūlātyaya (grave offense); for a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise a sthūlātyaya (the same rule, different training).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta (wrongdoing). This constitutes an offense.

Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if a bhikṣu says to women, "This place is wondrous, supreme, and most excellent" (referring to the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-gate), and "This bhikṣu is diligent in observing the precepts and cultivating wholesome dharmas;
you should provide compassionate offerings through your actions of body, speech, and mind"; or if, when expounding the Vinaya, his words are merely figurative or conventional.
If spoken in a dream, if spoken erroneously, or regarding matters prior to the initial promulgation of the precepts, these do not constitute an offense against this Mahāyāna precept;
the regulations are the same as those stated above.
Citation of Scriptural Authority: The above four precepts all originated from the causal conditions initiated by the Venerable Kālodāyin.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, it asks: "If one whose lustful mind is excessive does not commit a major offense and break the precepts, why is that?
It answers: "Because this person’s faculties are mature and should attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); furthermore, he was to be converted within this city of Śrāvastī."
Within this assembly, a thousand households have been fully gathered to accomplish great benefit; yet we lack but one person. For this reason, the great undertaking cannot be performed.

Kālodāyin possesses such merit and wisdom that he shall surely attain the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya). Do not, on account of a minor circumstance, cause yourself to lose your own faith and reverence.
The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: When a bhikṣu is practicing, there are two kinds of afflictions that may arise.
Due to the loss of right mindfulness, he may recall a distant object from the past and give rise to defiled attachment, thereby committing various transgressions;

furthermore, due to an object present before him, he may give rise to defiled attachment and commit various offenses. Having understood the conditions for the arising of these offenses, he should immediately...
Regarding this matter, one should give rise to a mind of antidote to cause it to be eliminated.

If the defiled conditions are so powerful that they cannot be dispelled, one should approach a venerable elder, or one who is learned in the Tripiṭaka and possesses virtuous conduct, to request instruction and admonition, and apply mental attention to remove them.
If they still do not cease, one should diligently engage day and night in recitation, hearing, and reflection, discerning the profound meaning. In...
At the abodes of the Triple Gem, one should offer sincere worship; toward teachers and elders, one should forget one's own hardships and provide for them with all one's heart.
Whether traveling abroad, reducing one's food, dwelling in a cemetery, or living alone in an araṇya, one should practice the contemplation of impurity and so forth;
or cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, or contemplate impermanence and death, hoping thereby to eliminate the afflictions.
It ceases. If it still does not cease, one should give rise to shame and remorse, reflecting thus: "What I have done is wrong;
my precepts are not pure, yet I continue to receive the heavy gifts of others' faith and the fourfold offerings.
Furthermore, all the Buddhas, those with the divine eye, my fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life, and all the benevolent deities are all beholding me. Therefore, I ought not to do this."
Having committed various sinful karmas, you should reproach yourself as if your head were on fire. Before regret arises, confess your offenses before a pure object of refuge to purify them.
If, while practicing such remedial actions as previously described, your afflictions remain numerous and cannot be extinguished, you should carefully examine yourself;
you may then relinquish the precepts and become a layperson, ensuring that no further transgressions occur.

When receiving the offerings of others' faith, one may, through the act of consumption, further create numerous karmas of evil and wickedness, which will certainly result in the ripening of painful fruits in the future, as extensively explained in the sūtras; therefore, one should practice with great care and diligence.
The fifth precept concerning matchmaking:
If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between for either side, conveying the intentions of a man to a woman or the intentions of a woman to a man—
whether for the purpose of arranging a marriage or for illicit sexual relations— even for a mere moment, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Kāla who had formerly been a high minister to the king and was well-versed in worldly customs. He acted as a matchmaker for marriages.

When the men and women were pleased with their unions, they would offer him gifts and praise; when they were displeased, they would revile, curse, and disparage him. The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Tathāgata established this precept for the Saṃgha; it is a prohibitive offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya). Because of being shrouded by ignorance, due to base and evil matters, and because of base karmic afflictions, he formulated this training rule (śikṣāpada).
It belongs to the category of the fundamental types of sexual misconduct in the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. From "Going and coming between them" onwards, the specific acts committed are clearly explained.
From "If for the sake of accomplishing the business of marriage, etc. onwards, the offense committed is formally established. The Vinaya states:

"Going and coming" refers to one who facilitates a union that ought to be brought about (the "mediator" [媒] means to scheme; "marriage" [嫁] refers to sending a daughter back to her husband; conveying the man’s intent to the woman and the woman’s intent to the man clearly demonstrates the act of going and coming; this is called "mediating" [媒說]).
To inform them of the matter). Women have twenty kinds of protection: protection by the mother (meaning she guards and cherishes her);
protection by the father; protection by both parents; protection by the elder brother; protection by the elder sister;
protection by both elder brother and sister; or self-protection, meaning she has mastery over her own person.

As for "protection by the Dharma," this refers to practicing the holy life (brahmacarya). If there is a woman who upholds the fivefold training rules of the household life, she is protected by the Dharma as if by frost and ice.
This is called protection by Dharma. As for protection by lineage: it refers to not being given to a low-caste family;
or being protected by one's kinsmen; or voluntarily becoming a slave to others; or becoming a slave for the price of clothing;
or becoming a slave for the price of wealth, even down to the price of a single coin; or becoming a slave through joint labor. Or...
Those who have not yet become husband and wife; those rescued from being swept away by water and taken as female slaves;
those taken as female slaves because taxes were not paid; and female slaves who have been released—meaning those purchased, those born in the household, and those serving as hired laborers.
Hiring laborers for wages, such as a household servant; or a girl protected by another, receiving a flower garland as a pledge;
or obtaining a slave from a frontier region, meaning one captured through plunder—these constitute twenty types [of women]. There are likewise twenty types of men.
These include a man protected by his mother, a woman protected by her mother, and sending a bhikṣu as a messenger to say to him: "You..."
To act as my wife (meaning to be my wife for life); or to have illicit relations with me (distinguishing this from being a wife for life);

or for a brief moment (one day and night comprises thirty *kṣaṇas*); or for the duration of a single thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*) (the *Saṃghāṭī-vinaya* states that twenty thoughts constitute one blink, and twenty blinks are called one finger-snap;
this refers to the shortest possible interval of time).
**The Offense of Confession:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if a bhikṣu receives a message himself, goes in person to deliver it to the other party, and returns with a reply;
or if he receives a message himself, goes in person to deliver it to the other party, and dispatches a messenger to bring back the reply;

or if he receives a message himself, dispatches a messenger to deliver it to the other party, and returns with the reply himself; or if he receives a message himself and dispatches messengers together to deliver it [to the other party].
He dispatches a messenger to carry a reply back.
If a bhikṣu personally receives a message, writes it himself, and carries it to that person; then personally carries the reply letter back.

Or, having personally received a message and written it himself, he carries it to that person and dispatches a messenger to carry the reply letter back. Or, having personally received a message... [he dispatches a messenger... to carry the reply back.
He sends an envoy with a letter to that person; he himself carries a reply back; he receives the message himself.
He dispatches an envoy with a letter to that person; he dispatches an envoy with a reply back.
If a bhikṣu personally receives a letter, carries it to the other person, and personally carries a reply back;

or if he personally receives a letter, carries it to the other person, and dispatches a messenger to carry the reply back; or if he personally receives a letter, dispatches a messenger to carry it to the other person, and personally carries the reply back;
or if he personally receives a letter, dispatches a messenger to carry it to the other person, and dispatches a messenger to carry the reply back.
In this manner, for every instance where one acts as a matchmaker and reports the matter clearly and completely, it is declared a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for each case;
for every instance where one does not report it clearly and completely, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each case.

If a bhikṣu accepts a message and goes to that person, but does not deliver the message upon returning; or if he does not accept a message but goes to that person and delivers it upon returning—in both cases, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣu accepts a message but does not go to that person, nor deliver the message upon returning; or if he does not accept a message, yet goes to that person and... [delivers it].
If one does not report [the match], it is all *duṣkṛta*.
This applies even if one acts as a go-between for female deities, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, or animals capable of transforming their appearance, as well as for eunuchs or those with both sexual organs.
If one speaks clearly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if one speaks unclearly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one cannot transform the form of an animal to act as a matchmaker, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To act as a matchmaker for a male is a *duṣkṛta* (in this context, acting as a matchmaker for eunuchs, those with both sexual organs, or males all subsumes the matter of illicit intercourse).
If one acts as a matchmaker for those coming and going while perceiving it as matchmaking, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one suspects it is matchmaking, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If one acts as a matchmaker while perceiving it as not matchmaking, or if one perceives it as matchmaking when it is not matchmaking, or if one suspects it is not matchmaking, in all these cases it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one acts as a matchmaker for a human woman while perceiving her as a human woman, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If there is doubt regarding whether she is a human woman, or if one perceives a human woman as a non-human woman, or if one perceives a non-human woman as a human woman, or if there is doubt regarding whether she is a non-human woman—in all these cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu takes another’s letter and does not go to see it, it is a duṣkṛta. If he performs other services for a layperson, it is a duṣkṛta.
This precept requires six conditions to constitute the full offense: first, he must have received a commission from another to act as a matchmaker; second, he must personally...
1. One must have the intention of acting as a matchmaker for marriage. 2. It must involve human men and women. 3. One must perceive them as human men and women. 4.

One must communicate on their behalf in a manner that is acceptable. 5. There must be a clear and explicit response returned. If even one of these conditions is lacking, the fundamental offense is not established.
It is also prescribed for *bhikṣuṇīs* (the same rule and training). For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if a man and woman have previously been intimate but later separated and subsequently reunite;
if it is for the sake of a parent’s illness or if they are imprisoned; if it is for the sake of a faithful upāsaka who is ill or imprisoned;
or if it is for the sake of the Triple Gem, or to visit a sick bhikṣu and others, one may carry a letter and go, as well as [the most urgent matters].
If [the offense] has not yet been prescribed by the rules and so forth, this constitutes non-offense. As recorded in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:

"If a man has many wives, some of whom he favors and others whom he does not, and a bhikṣu says to him, 'You should regard them equally and strive to treat them with impartiality,' and he replies, 'I shall follow the Teacher's instruction.'"
At that time, a bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya if he reconciles a husband and wife who are quarreling.
He incurs a sthūlātyaya if he reconciles them when they are already in discord.

However, there is no offense if, for the sake of the Buddha’s work or the Sangha’s work—specifically to prevent a deficiency in the service of the Buddha—he encourages their reconciliation. This also applies if a woman is returning to her home.
If one exhorts [a woman] to return early to her husband’s house, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. There was a man who kept many horses, but none were born of good stock;
he requested a bhikṣu to seek a mare giving birth to a horse from a certain household for him. When the bhikṣu sought it for him, he incurred a *sthūlātyaya*.
There were two bhikṣus; one had a daughter, and he said to his daughter: "This is yours."
The husband. If one who has a son says to his son, "This is your wife," at the moment these words are spoken, both incur the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) states: "If a husband and wife are angry with each other, and the husband has not yet declared, 'She is no longer my wife,' if they reconcile, [the offense is] theft."

*Lañca*: If she has already declared, "He is not my husband," and [the monk] acts as a go-between, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If he receives her words and understands her intention, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If he receives her intention but does not receive her words, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If he only receives her words but does not understand her intention, there is no offense.
If the matter of matchmaking has already been completed, and a bhikṣu later comes to assist, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Prohibition. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: When a preceptor bhikṣu arrives at a donor’s house, he speaks as follows:
"This girl has grown up; why does she not go forth to marry? This boy is already of age; why does he not take a wife? If it is asked, "Why this girl... [the prohibition applies].
If she does not go to the husband’s house, or if this man does not go to the wife’s house, both incur an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "The offense of matchmaking is established by the determination of three factors: first, the determination of the principals, which consists of conveying the man’s intention to the woman."
One conveys the woman’s intent to the man; thus two matters are established: namely, the matter of marriage between a man and a woman, and the matter of illicit intercourse.
Three times are established: even down to a single moment. Regarding those who act as intermediaries, there are those who are honorable and those who are lowly.

"Honorable" refers to the head of the household, whose word is taken as definitive; the opposite of this constitutes the "lowly. If one receives a message and goes to inquire, or returns with a report—these two [constitute the process].
If one addresses a person of high status with words appropriate for an inferior, one incurs the root offense.

If one uses words for an inferior to reply to a person of high status, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). There are three factors by which a reply is established even if no words are spoken:

first, the designated place; second, the fixed time; and third, the manifested sign. If one sees [the other] staying in such-and-such a place, one knows the matter is settled; this is called "designation" (*kāla*).
As for the place: if one sees me at a certain time, it signifies that the matter will be accomplished; this is called "fixing the time.

If one sees me holding an alms bowl or wearing new clothes, one knows the matter is appropriate; this is called "manifesting signs. When these three things are performed and understood by the other party, it constitutes a formal return of the proposal.
Whether it concerns matchmaking by pointing to the womb, or the birth of a son or daughter, or both being male...
If it concerns a woman, or a *paṇḍaka* (meaning one whose gender changes every half-month), it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one says, "There is a girl in that family;
why do you not seek her out? with the intent to act as a matchmaker, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. Even a single word that corresponds to the act of matchmaking constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a disciple says to his teacher, "I wish to act as a matchmaker for another," [the teacher must intervene].

As for the matter: when the teacher heard these words and silently consented, he incurred a *sthūlātyaya* offense. (The teacher, being ignorant of the Vinaya regulations and failing to properly instruct his disciples, thus incurred this transgression.)

If one is well-versed in the Vinaya, they will immediately reprimand and stop such behavior upon hearing of it; this is what constitutes a true guide. The *Śīlapratyaya-sūtra* states: "To release captive animals and reunite their mates."

Saṃghāvaśeṣa. (In this Vinaya, regarding the act of matchmaking for animals: because one merely informs a bhikṣu beforehand without knowing whether [the act] has occurred or not, it is classified as a *duṣkṛta*. In the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, regarding the case of seeking a stallion for breeding: although the location was clearly indicated, the impulse for sexual misconduct still reached its object; since the matter was not witnessed with one's own eyes, it is [treated differently].)

Therefore, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one releases [the organ] so that it joins again, this constitutes viewing what is contrary to the Dharma with the eyes and giving rise to sympathetic approval in the mind; since there is no absence of desire-taint (*rāga*), one commits the fundamental offense. (The underlying intent of the extended application and the proximate regulation is contained herein.)
These precepts are established identically in the Mahāyāna. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "A bodhisattva should rescue and deliver all sentient beings and bestow the pure Dharma upon them;
yet, if one instead assists others in committing sexual misconduct, this is a lack of compassionate heart."
The Combined Collection of the Vinaya on Restraint and Maintenance, Volume Three:
Phonetic Explanations. *Makata*: in the Sanskrit language, this means "monkey. *Harada*: this means "pool."
As for the name "River," it was merely established by the translator based on its meaning.
This pond is located about five or six *li* outside the city walls of Vaiśālī, beside the garden of Āmrapālī. It was formerly dug by a troop of monkeys for the Buddha.
The Vālukā River—also called the Vālukāmukha River, the Bakku River, or the Bakumaha River—is correctly known by its Sanskrit name as Bakumati;
this translates as the "River of Supreme Wisdom" (Jñānavatī).
*Mṛgadanta* should be transliterated as *Mṛgāra*; this means "Deer-tooth" (*mṛgadanta*).
It is also called "Joyful-Head" (*xǐzǒng*); thus, the name is "Deer-Joy. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* refers to him as the "Deer-staff Śramaṇa"; "Deer-staff" is his name.
As for "Śramaṇa," it refers to one who has the appearance of a śramaṇa: having shaved the head but leaving a small tuft of hair (*cūḍā*), and wearing dyed robes.
He had two garments: one to cover his body and one to place upon his shoulder.
He entered the monastery to seek refuge, and as a bhikṣu, he gathered leftover food to sustain his life. Consequently, the bhikṣus hired him to carry out killings.
*Shè*: The pronunciation is *shì*. It refers to the movement of venomous insects.
*Tà*: The pronunciation is *tà*. It means to tread upon or trample.
*Yì*: The pronunciation is *yì*. It refers to a wooden stake or a wedge. It is also called a *zhí*. In the *Zuozhuan*, Zang Jian died after using a stake (*yì*) to probe his wound.
"Yi-fa" (relying on and eliciting): "yi" means to rely upon. It refers to relying on the spiritual capacity [of the listener] to elicit and raise [the teaching].
"Hang" (pronounced *héng*) refers to a horizontal beam in a roof.
"Qiang" (with the departing tone) refers to setting a snare on a path to trap birds and beasts.

"Gui-yi" (tortoise-divination) refers to the scorching of a tortoise shell; "yi" (divination) refers to the practice of *bupiyi* (divining by means of change). Both are methods for pursuing good fortune and avoiding misfortune.
*Cāṇḍāla* is translated here as "butcher"; they are the most base and despised class in the Western Regions, not permitted to dwell with the four castes, but living only among their own kind.
Whenever they enter a city or town, they carry bamboo staffs in their hands, upon which [they hang]...
The red banner serves to distinguish those who are base and lowly.
*Xiá* (pronounced *xiá*) means to draw near; it refers to familiarity, proficiency, and practice.

"Eloquence" (*biàncái*) refers to the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), also known as the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*catasro jñānapratisaṃvidaḥ*). This is due to their wisdom.

Because they are clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated without obstruction: first, the unimpeded eloquence regarding meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), which refers to knowing the principles and meanings of all phenomena;
second, the unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), which refers to penetrating the designations of all phenomena and their distinctions without obstruction;
third, the unimpeded eloquence regarding language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), which refers to [the mastery of] the names and meanings of all phenomena.

Fourth is the unimpeded eloquence of analytical exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). This means that, in accordance with the inclinations of all sentient beings and their diverse languages and dialects, one expounds the Dharma for them so that each may attain understanding;
this is because one’s discursive explanation is unhindered and perfectly integrated.
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of "covering" or "obscuring. They are also called the five "heaps" (*rāśi*).

The term "heap" carries the meaning of "accumulation," referring to the accumulation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), because they cover the true nature (*dharmatā*). By means of these five factors, sentient beings accumulate and form a body;
furthermore, based on this body, they accumulate conditioned phenomena such as afflictions (*kleśa*), thereby undergoing immeasurable births and deaths. First, form (*rūpa*).
The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). "Form" (*rūpa*) has the meaning of substantial resistance. Because the six faculties, such as the eye and ear, are combined and accumulated, it is called form.

Second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). "Sensation" (*vedanā*) has the meaning of experiencing and receiving. This refers to the six consciousnesses corresponding with the six sense objects.

There are six accumulations of feeling; therefore, it is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). Third is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): "perception" carries the meaning of conceptualization.
This refers to the six consciousnesses corresponding with the six sense objects to form the harmonious accumulation of the six perceptions;

therefore, it is called the aggregate of perception. Fourth is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): "formations" carries the meaning of flux and volitional activity. This refers to the volition of the six consciousnesses...

Perception (*saṃjñā*): The various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that perform wholesome and unwholesome actions, which combine and accumulate, are therefore called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

The five aggregates of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*): "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) has the meaning of discernment. This refers to the six types of consciousness, such as those of the eye and ear, which illuminate and differentiate upon the objects of the various sense-fields; because they combine and accumulate, they are called the aggregate of consciousness.
The six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*) signify the sense of entering or proceeding toward [objects].

This refers to the six faculties—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—which serve as the bases for the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness through mind-consciousness) and are capable of entering the six kinds of objects: form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena;
therefore, they are called the six entrances.

The eighteen *dhātus* (realms) are themselves the divisions of the realms. Because sentient beings are deluded regarding both mind and form (*rūpa*), form is divided into eleven realms—namely, the five sense organs and the six sense objects.
Mind is divided into seven realms—namely, the six consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, and the mental faculty (*manas*).
Since all these belong to the mind, they are distinguished as seven.
"Attaining concentration" refers specifically to the three samādhis and the three gates of liberation.

"Samādhi with applied thought and sustained thought" means that when the initial mind is in dhyāna, it is called *vitarka* (applied thought); when the subtle mind discriminates the flavor of the dhyāna, it is called *vicāra* (sustained thought).
When one enters the first dhyāna with a mind corresponding to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), then all [defilements]...
Both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) are entirely upright; therefore, it is called the *samādhi with vitarka and vicāra*.

As for the *samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra*, this refers to when one is about to enter the second dhyāna with a mind associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
At that time, the mind of conscious awareness has already ceased, yet the conceptualizing thought that relishes the flavor of dhyāna still remains. First.
All concentrations and contemplations are entirely upright; therefore, it is called the samādhi with no vitarka and with vicāra.

The samādhi with neither vitarka nor vicāra refers to entering the second dhyāna and so forth up to the cessation of perception and feeling by means of a mind associated with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
All thoughts that differentiate the flavor of meditative absorption and the consciousness of awareness are [eliminated].
Because these have ceased, it is called the samādhi without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are the three gates of liberation. This means observing that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions;
their intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty, devoid of self and what belongs to a self. If one can thus penetrate this understanding, then...
Because one attains mastery over all phenomena, it is called the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
Since one knows that all phenomena are empty, one observes that characteristics such as male and female, or identity and difference, are in reality unobtainable.

If one can thus penetrate the signlessness of all phenomena, one immediately attains mastery; therefore, it is called the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). If all phenomena are signless...
Thus, one has no aspirations or seeking within the triple world. If there is no aspiration or seeking, one does not create the karma of birth and death;
consequently, there is no suffering of karmic retribution, and one attains sovereignty. Therefore, it is called the Gate of Liberation through Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣamukha*).
It is also called the gate of liberation through wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).

Samādhi (*samāpatti*) is so named because it is free from erroneous and inverted perceptions and apprehends its object; furthermore, it is called samādhi because it does not undergo any [further] sensations (*vedanā*).

Regarding the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*): knowing present phenomena is called the knowledge of phenomena. Present phenomena refers to the specific individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and so forth.
Regarding subsequent knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*): knowing the remaining phenomena is called subsequent knowledge. "Remaining" refers to the past and the future.

It is called inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) because it arises subsequently to the knowledge of past phenomena, followed by the knowledge of present phenomena, and then knows [future phenomena]. Why is this so?
Because one first knows them through direct perception, and only thereafter does one know them through inference.

Regarding "conventional knowledge" (saṃvṛtijñāna): it is also called conventional knowledge because it knows the differences in the practices of sentient beings and knows the various distinctions among the names and designations of phenomena; therefore, it is named conventional knowledge.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): it is called the knowledge of others' minds because it knows the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) of all sentient beings without any obstruction.

Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path constitute the Dharma of the Four Truths (*catvāri satyāni*). The *Dharmadhātu-krama* states: "These four are collectively termed 'truths' (*satya*)."

The term *satya* (諦) has the meaning of being "thoroughly real" (*śraddhā-avabodha*). These four truths (*catvāri satyāni*) were specifically taught for the sake of those who follow the Śrāvaka vehicle, because they seek to generate understanding through hearing.
Thus, it is necessary to rely upon the teachings to manifest the underlying principle. Now, to clarify that the teaching and the principle are not in vain, it is said they are "thoroughly real.
If a result were produced by a cause, then the cause should necessarily precede the result; however, in this case, all [truths] first present the result and subsequently [the cause].
Regarding the causes: because the teaching gates employ skillful means to guide sentient beings, they all present the fruit first and the cause afterwards.
The first two truths are mundane dharmas; in order to lead them to know suffering so as to sever its origin, the fruit is presented first and the cause second.
The latter two truths are supramundane dharmas; in order to lead them toward cessation through the cultivation of the path, the fruit is likewise presented first and the cause second.
Furthermore, regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): "suffering" takes the sense of pain and affliction as its meaning.
All conditioned mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are constantly oppressed and afflicted by the calamities of impermanence; therefore, they are called suffering. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Innumerable sentient beings have three kinds of physical suffering: old age, sickness, and death; three kinds of mental suffering: greed, hatred, and delusion; and three kinds of suffering in future lives."

The hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—summarized thus—consist of the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, and so forth; these are all the afflictions of birth and death within the triple world.
To examine birth and death with discernment, one finds that they are indeed suffering; therefore, it is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The three sufferings are:

the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); the eight sufferings may be understood accordingly. As for the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), "origination" refers to that which summons [suffering].
"Accumulation" (*caya*) is its meaning. If the mind is associated with fetters and karma, it will certainly accumulate the suffering of birth and death in the future;

therefore, it is called "accumulation" (*samudaya*). Upon careful examination, all afflictions, delusions, and karmas truly can accumulate the fruits of suffering—birth and death within the three realms—in the future;
thus, it is named the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*). The Truth of Extinction (*nirodha-satya*) is also called the Truth of Cessation (*nirvāṇa-satya*).

Cessation (*nirodha*) is quiescence. Cessation takes the meaning of extinguishing non-existence as its definition. Once the fetters and karma are exhausted, there is no longer the affliction or entanglement of birth and death;
therefore, it is called cessation. Because all afflictions, fetters, and latent tendencies are extinguished, the karma of the three realms is likewise extinguished.
If the karma and afflictions of the three realms are extinguished, this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Because the cause has been extinguished, the fruit is extinguished; when one relinquishes this retribution-body, the fruits of suffering in future lives will never again continue.

This is called entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana without remainder). To examine the truth of Nirvana: it is indeed quiescent extinction, and therefore it is named the Truth of Cessation. As for the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*):
The Way (mārga) takes "penetration" as its essential meaning. The True Path and the Aids to the Path support one another and are able to reach Nirvana;
therefore, they are called the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya). Examining these two paths, they truly support each other and are able to penetrate to Nirvana without fail.

Therefore, it is called the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). As for the "Right Path": the actual contemplation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) and the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), as well as the practice of wisdom that takes principle as its object, is called the Right Path. As for the "Aids to the Path":
the various remedial methods (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) and meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) within the context of attaining understanding and contemplation are called the Aids to the Path.
Regarding seals, many ancients fashioned them upon signet rings, much like people today attach seals to the handles of fans;

this was for the sake of convenience. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, the Buddha permitted bhikṣus to possess seals as a means of identification and verification, yet he did not permit their attachment to signet rings or precious ornaments; the use of brass [seals] was permitted.
It is made from five kinds of materials: stone, red copper, white copper, ivory, or horn. Furthermore, there are two types of seals:

first, those belonging to the community (*saṃgha*), and second, private ones. If it is a seal for the community, one may carve an image of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, with two deer placed on either side, kneeling and prostrating beneath it.
One should inscribe the name of the original donor who built the monastery. As for a private seal:
One should carve them into the form of a chain of bones, or in the shape of skulls, so that upon seeing them, one may give rise to revulsion and renunciation.
Generally, whenever the Vinaya mentions hand-mudras or finger-mudras, they all conform to this principle.
*Tīrthika* is translated here as "extremely evil" (*ji'e*). It is also called "ultimate" (*bi-jing*), because they ultimately lack the nature for *nirvāṇa*;
these are the *icchantikas* who lack the [Buddha-]nature.
Regarding the four lines on the plantain bearing fruit: the appearance of the plantain producing flowers is like nectar within the petals of a lotus.
It is as sweet as honey. If this flower blooms, the branch itself will perish. When bamboo and reeds flower and bear fruit, the bamboo grove follows in ruin.
A mule is not born of its own accord; it is produced through the mating of a donkey and a horse.
If a mule becomes pregnant, it will inevitably harm its mother.
The Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati) is so called because its inhabitants create the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) themselves and take pleasure therein.
This heaven dwells supported by space. According to the treatises, eight hundred years in the human realm constitute one day and night for this heaven;
thus, twenty-eight thousand eight hundred years in the human realm constitute one year for this heaven. If the lifespan of beings in this heaven is eight thousand [years],...
One *kalpa* corresponds to two hundred and thirty billion, four million years in the human world.
Kālodāyin is also named Udāyin; this translates as "Black Radiance" (*Kṛṣṇaprabha*), and is also called "Coarse Black" (*Karkaśakṛṣṇa*) because his face was dark and his eyes were red.
He was of the Brahmin caste and was born on the same day as the Buddha. Originally...
The king’s minister, because the World-Honored One had left home and attained the Way, was moved by the father-king’s longing to see him; he therefore dispatched Kāla to go and welcome him.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him and called out, “Come, Bhikṣu! Whereupon his beard and hair fell away naturally, and he became a bhikṣu by nature.
However, his mind was full of desire. Later, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin woman who pressured him into misconduct.

This was unlawful, yet the Venerable One did not comply with their actions. He became filled with rage and resentment, mutilated his own body, and falsely accused the Venerable One, reporting it to his father.
His father assembled a crowd of five hundred Brahmins and together they dragged the Venerable One;
however, the Venerable One possessed such great strength that they could not move him even a single step. At that time, the Buddha perceived through his insight that this was the final instruction.
The Admonition Concerning Udāyin: When the Buddha’s physical strength was failing, the assembly beat him nearly to death and dragged him before the king.
Although the king knew for certain that the matter was false, he still rebuked him three times. The Venerable One felt extreme shame and remorse, and subsequently went to where Śāriputra was.
He prostrated himself and related the preceding events in detail. Śāriputra then preached the Dharma to him and gave him instruction.
He aroused a courageous mind, whereby all his fetters and delusions were eliminated, and he realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Having attained this fruit, he thought to repay the Buddha’s kindness and proceeded to teach and transform others. The Buddha declared:
"Among my śrāvaka disciples who teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to attain the noble fruits, Kālodāyin is the foremost. Thus it was with the Venerable One in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He converted eighteen hundred million households and caused them to attain the fruits of sainthood.
Later, a daughter-in-law of a violent and wicked family had an illicit affair with a thief, who cut off the Venerable’s life and discarded his corpse in a refuse heap.

This was the ripening of karma from deeds previously committed by the Venerable, which he must now repay. On the fifteenth day, during the *poṣadha*, the Buddha did not see the Venerable and knew that he had died. The Buddha...
Surrounded by a great multitude, he arrived at the city gate at night and emitted a great radiance that filled the entire city.
The gates opened of their own accord. The king, his consort, ministers, citizens, and women were startled awake and rushed forth;

they followed the Buddha to the site of the refuse heap, where they brought forth the Venerable One’s corpse, bathed it with fragrant water, placed it upon a precious palanquin, and proceeded to an excellent location.
They burned him with fragrant wood and collected his relics. They erected a stupa at the side of a crossroads to make offerings to them, serving as a field of merit for humans and devas.
The reason for citing this at length now is to show that the Venerable One established the Dharma-gate by manifesting the conditions of his transgression.
A Wheel-Turning Sage King, a supreme wheel-turning monarch, accomplishes the seven treasures and is endowed with the four virtues, ruling over the four continents.
As for the seven treasures: first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the white elephant treasure; third, the dark-blue horse treasure;
fourth, the divine jewel treasure; fifth, the jade woman treasure; sixth, the steward of wealth treasure; and seventh, the commander of the army treasure. As for the four virtues: first, longevity...
First, his life shall not be cut short; second, his body will be robust and free from ailment; third, his countenance will be upright and handsome; fourth, his treasuries will be filled with jewels.
By means of the ten wholesome dharmas, he shall exhort and transform sentient beings, and preside over the four great continents.

Regarding the term "non-Buddhist practitioners of incantations and arts" (*tīrthika-mantra-vidyā*): those who study principles contrary to the truth, who follow their own deluded sentiments, and who do not turn back toward internal awakening are called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Their various lineages possess scriptures that have been transmitted from generation to generation; they take the study of their own doctrines as their profession.
Whether they remain householders or leave the home life, they mostly rely on their own magical arts and are people of arrogant pride. They are classified into nine types.
There are sixteen kinds.
[The term] *bì* (thigh) refers to the sound above the skin; it denotes the thighs, the calves, the stomach, and the abdomen.
One should practice mindfulness of the Buddha as the first; these are known as the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). First, mindfulness of the Buddha, the compassionate Teacher. Second...
1. Mindfulness of the Dharma: the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. 2. Mindfulness of the Sangha: the field of merit for devas and humans. 3. Mindfulness of Precepts:
purifying body and mind. 4. Mindfulness of Generosity: universally relieving the poor and destitute. 5. Mindfulness of the Heavens: constantly receiving peace and happiness.
*Mén* (捫): the pronunciation is *mén*; it means to stroke or hold. *Mō* (摸): the pronunciation is *mò*; it means to press or feel with the hand. This refers to stroking and feeling with both hands.
*Bǐ* (髀): the pronunciation is *bǐ*; it refers to the thigh bone.
Cǎo jié (the character for jié is pronounced jiǎ and is identical to gē; gē refers to the stalks of grain). Gē refers to the straw of harvested grain; its husks are removed to be made into mats.
Niè (with the entering tone) means to hold or to press down.
The "special ox" (*te niú*) is an ox three years of age.
*Liáo* is pronounced as *lí*. Guo Pu states: "A black ox is called a *liáo niú*; this black variety originates from beyond the southwestern frontiers."
The character for *mò* (牸) is pronounced *zì*; it refers to a female ox.
*Mó-dèng-gā* (摩鄧伽) is also written as *Mó-dēng-gā* (摩登伽), which translates to "Original Nature" (*prakṛti*).

She was a courtesan skilled in great illusionary arts who once used incantations to delude Ānanda; fortunately, the Tathāgata’s divine incantation went forth to protect him, and her evil spell was finally [neutralized].
He attained extinction and further joined the *Lengyan* (Śūraṅgama) assembly, where he realized the third fruit of the path.
*Bānì* is translated as "tranquility" (*śānti*), and is also translated as "cessation" or "stopping. It is also called "resting.
Because external conditions have thus been stilled and severed, one is then at peace and free to attend to the affairs of the Dharma. The *Fayuan* states: "Seeking the West..."
The existence of *bhaiṣajya* (chanting) is like the existence of *zàn* (eulogies) in the eastern lands. As for *zàn*, it forms chapters based on prose;
as for *bhaiṣajya*, it consists of short verses that flow as hymns. Comparing their significance, though the names differ, the substance is the same.

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "I allow you to chant. Chanting refers to spoken words; it allows for the citation of passages from within the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
To summarize the essential words and sublime phrases, one directly reveals their meaning; hence it is called *bhāṇaka*.

Regarding "familiar with the Tripiṭaka," "familiar" means to have practiced well and studied with refinement. This refers to the profound, mysterious, and subtle meanings of the teachings and principles of the Tripiṭaka.
There is nothing it does not penetrate.
Regarding "ripened fruit" (*vipāka-phala*): this refers to the maturation of the fruit at a different time, namely the eighth consciousness.
Because this consciousness can contain and store the seeds of all phenomena, it brings the various sense faculties and consciousnesses to maturity.

It is the fruit [of maturation]. Just as with the various faculties such as the eye, one now receives the fruits of pleasure and pain as retribution due to causes of good and evil created in the past;
likewise, if one creates causes of good and evil now, one will also experience the fruits of pleasure and pain in the future.
Therefore, it is called the "fruit of ripening" (*vipāka-phala*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: The son of the householder Mṛgāra was named Kāla. He was intelligent, wise, and possessed of keen faculties;
whenever people questioned him, he would always resolve their doubts. While he was suddenly preoccupied with other affairs, there was a man who had a daughter.
When sisters-in-law came to seek [a husband], they would go to ask Kāla whether he was suitable or not.

Whether it was for a person seeking a wife for themselves or seeking one for their son, they likewise went to ask whether he was acceptable or not. Later, when Kāla left the household life to become a monk, he remained just as he had been according to the original dharma.
The "Gate Master" (Menshi) refers to the true, pure, and world-saving Dharma-gate of the Triple Gem.
When lay followers, whether men or women of good faith, take refuge in the Triple Gem, the master to whom they pay homage is called their Gate Master.

Regarding "female" (*pin*) and "male" (*mu*): "female" refers to female livestock. Among those that fly, they are called "hen" (*ci*) and "cock" (*xiong*); among those that run, they are called "female" (*pin*) and "male" (*mu*).
Compiled by the Vinaya-master of Honglu at Baohua Mountain in Jinling, the Śramaṇa Duti. Volume Four of the *Compendium of the Cessation and Maintenance of the Vinaya*.
The sixth precept concerning the excessive size of private dwellings:
If a bhikṣu seeks to build a house for himself, being the owner and acting for his own sake, he must build it according to the prescribed measurements. Regarding these measurements: [text follows]
It shall be twelve spans long and seven spans wide inside. A bhikṣu must be brought along to designate the site;
that bhikṣu shall point out a location that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a bhikṣu seeks to build a hut for himself where there are difficulties or obstructions, without an owner and for his own use, yet does not bring a bhikṣu to designate the site, and if it exceeds [the prescribed dimensions]...
Regarding the measure of the builder: it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The origin story: While the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, he permitted the bhikṣus to build private dwellings.
At that time, a bhikṣu from the country of Aṭavī, having heard that the Buddha had granted permission, immediately began building a large private dwelling for himself with great effort.
They were numerous and constantly engaged in searching and begging, which caused the lay devotees to feel weary and avoid them.

There was another bhikṣu who wished to build a dwelling and began cutting down a tree himself. The tree deity thought of striking the bhikṣu, but fearing it would violate the principles of propriety, he went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha praised and comforted him, then indicated another place for him to dwell. At that time, Mahākāśyapa arrived at the city of Khaṇḍava.

When the householders saw him from afar, they each fled to avoid him. Kāśyapa asked them about the reason, and they explained it all in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha assembled the Saṃgha and established this precept.
Because of matters concerning dwelling places, disputes and resentment regarding dwellings, and base actions and afflictions, he formulated this training rule.
This is the section on the fundamental category of theft from the first chapter.
Explanation of the meaning: the text is divided into two sections. From "If one builds a house for oneself" onwards, it clarifies the primary regulation;

from "If a bhikṣu [builds] in a place that is difficult or obstructed" onwards, it concludes by manifesting the violation. The Vinaya states: "To seek for oneself" means to beg for materials at various locations.
"Seeking. Regarding "one who has no patron": this refers to one who does not have even one, two, or many patrons acting on their own behalf;
rather, they seek it out themselves and construct it themselves. "It should be made according to measure":

herein, the measure is twelve *vitasti* (the span of a hand) in length and seven *vitasti* in width. (*Vitasti* refers to the span of a fully extended hand. Length is measured vertically, which is the depth of the room; width is measured horizontally, which is the breadth of the room.)

Regarding the width: the Buddha’s body is one *zhang* and six *chi* tall. One *zhai-shou* (span) corresponds to sixteen inches by the current small-scale measure; thus, the depth is one *zhang*, nine *chi*, and two *cun*, and the width is one *zhang*, one *chi*, and two *cun*.
If it were too large, it would be cumbersome; if too small, it would be cramped. To avoid these two faults, this measurement was established. Regarding difficult terrain:
where there are tigers, wolves, lions, or other predatory beasts, down to even ants—if one is not troubled by such insects and animals, one should cultivate and level the ground. If there is...
If there are stones, trees, or thorns, one should have them excavated. If there are ditches, pits, ponds, or pools, one should have them filled in.
If one fears inundation by water, one should establish embankments in advance. If the land is claimed by others, [one must address it accordingly].

"We should together eliminate any obstacles so that others have no cause for complaint. This is called a "difficult place" (*durga*). A "hindering place" (*pratibandha-sthāna*) is one where even a grass cart cannot turn around.

Regarding this, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "A non-hindering place is one where on each of the four sides there is space sufficient for twelve ladders, with a gap of one 'fist-forearm' (*muṣṭi-hasta*) between each ladder, allowing those performing the work to come and go all around to plaster, repair, and cover the structure;
one *muṣṭi-hasta* is calculated as two feet. Once that monk building the house has verified that the site is free of difficulties and hindrances, he proceeds to...
Within the Saṃgha, he shall perform three formal requests according to the prescribed ritual. At that time, the assembly of monks should examine whether this bhikṣu is trustworthy or untrustworthy.
If he is trustworthy, they should immediately grant permission for him to act. If he is untrustworthy, the entire Saṃgha should go to that place to observe him.
If the assembly of monks does not go, they should dispatch a trustworthy member of the Saṃgha to go and observe him. If he...

If there is an obstacle and an impediment; or if there is no obstacle but there is an impediment; or if there is an obstacle but no impediment—in all these cases, one should not grant the assignment of the site.

Only if it is a place where there is neither obstacle nor impediment should the assignment be granted through the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation;

this ritual procedure is explained in the section on "performance and maintenance"). Therefore, it is said: "That bhikṣu shall designate a location that is free from obstacles and free from impediments."
Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, when that person is building the hut, it should be known that from the initial placement—
whether of stones, earth, brick-clay lumps, or even until the work is finished— it must be done in accordance with the Dharma.
The Determination of Offenses: Regarding those who violate this rule— If the Saṃgha has not authorized it: one offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for building in excess of the prescribed dimensions;
one offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for building where there is a site of danger; one offense of *duṣkṛta* for building where there is an obstruction;
and one offense of *duṣkṛta* if there is no site of danger but there is an obstruction; and one offense of *duṣkṛta* if there is a site of danger but no obstruction.
Regarding obstructed sites: one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Saṃgha has not formally assigned [the site], it is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. There is no offense for building that does not exceed the prescribed measurements.
Whether there is danger and obstruction, or no danger but obstruction, or danger but no obstruction—all cases are as described above.
If the Saṃgha has already made a formal assignment, there is no offense. Regarding making [a structure] that exceeds the prescribed measure: one saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Whether there is an obstacle and an impediment, or no obstacle but an impediment, or an obstacle but no impediment—all cases are as explained above.
If the Sangha has already made a formal assignment, there is no offense provided that one does not construct it in excess of the prescribed measure.
If there is an obstacle and an impediment, or if there is an obstacle but no impediment, one incurs an offense as described above.
If one constructs [a dwelling] but it is not completed, or if the Saṃgha has not authorized it, or if it exceeds the prescribed dimensions, each case constitutes one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Whether there is an obstacle or hindrance, or no obstacle but a hindrance, or an obstacle but no hindrance, the offense incurred is as stated above.
If one causes another to build a house that is completed, whether the Saṃgha has not authorized it or it exceeds the prescribed measure;

or if the Saṃgha has already authorized it but it exceeds the measure; or if the Saṃgha has not authorized it but it does not exceed the measure—in all such cases, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, as described above.
This applies whether there are obstacles and hindrances, no obstacles but hindrances, or obstacles but no hindrances; the resulting offense is as stated.
