There are cases where there is obstruction but no difficulty; cases where there is obstruction and there is difficulty; and cases where there is difficulty but no obstruction.

In each of these, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense as described above. Furthermore, if the construction is undertaken but not completed, if the Saṃgha has not authorized it, or if it is constructed in excess of the prescribed dimensions, or if it is built in a place that is both difficult and obstructed—in each and every such case, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one constructs a dwelling by marking the ground with a cord, it should be measured according to the prescribed dimensions; if it exceeds those dimensions, one commits an offense.

If one instructs another to work according to the cord and ink-line, and that person following the instruction builds it according to the rules but exceeds the dimensions, that person who followed the instruction commits an offense.

If that person instructing another to work according to the cord and ink-line has them build it exactly according to the rules, yet fails to inform the owner [of the excess], the builder commits an offense.

If one commits [the offense] by instructing another to build according to the plumb line and the carpenter’s square, such that it is built in accordance with the Dharma, the instructor is guilty of an offense even if they did not inquire whether it was being built in accordance with the Dharma.

If the Saṃgha has not authorized [the construction], and one perceives that it has not been authorized, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if there is doubt as to whether it has been authorized, it is likewise [an offense]. If it has not been authorized...
If one perceives what is a formal assignment (*vibhāga*) as not being a formal assignment, or if there is doubt regarding a formal assignment, it is all a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives or doubts that [the construction] exceeds the prescribed measure, it is likewise.

If one perceives an obstacle where there is an obstacle, or doubts whether there is an obstacle; or if one perceives no obstacle where there is an obstacle, or perceives an obstacle where there is no obstacle—and in all such cases of doubt—it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The same applies if one perceives or doubts that it is a restricted place (*vighāta-sthāna*).
This precept requires six conditions to constitute a full offense: first, constructing a private dwelling for oneself without an owner; second, not seeking the authorization of the Saṃgha;

third, having the perception that authorization has not been granted; fourth, exceeding the prescribed limits in violation of the regulations; and fifth, having the perception that one has exceeded those limits.
The six chambers have already been constructed. If there is a deficiency in the conditions, the offense is established as a preliminary effort (*prayoga*).

This also governs the *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); [this is] because they follow the same rules but have distinct training, and due to the arising of difficult circumstances, they are not permitted to dwell in an *araṇya* (wilderness).
For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This constitutes an offense.

Regarding the exemptions from offense: there is no offense if one builds according to the prescribed measure; if one builds less than the prescribed measure; if one builds with the formal authorization (*saṃgha-vinīta*) of the Saṃgha;

if one builds in a place that is neither difficult nor obstructive; if one builds according to the legal layout; or if one builds for the sake of the Saṃgha, for a Buddhist shrine (*stūpa*), a lecture hall, a grass hut, a leaf hut, or a small shelter sufficient for the body;
and in cases where the precept has not yet been promulgated. These constitute non-offenses.

Regarding the construction [of a hut], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When constructing a hut, if one hands over a brick or a lump of clay, or piles up bricks and so forth, it is all a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If the doors and windows are already completed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Upon its final completion, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If the monk who is the owner of the hut does not relinquish the precepts, nor die, nor give [the hut] to the Saṃgha...
If a bhikṣu, within this room, fumigates his bowl, recites or chants, or engages in contemplation (meaning practicing meditative concentration and seated dhyāna),
he incurs an offense of *vyatikrama* for all such uses.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Build a dwelling for me," and having said this, he departs;

if the work is not yet finished when the first bhikṣu returns, but it is completed upon his arrival, this dwelling is not in accordance with the Dharma. (One should still request instructions [from a qualified person], ensuring that the measurements correspond and that there are no obstacles or hindrances.

In such a case, what fault would there be? It is because the former person relied on a scale that violated the regulations; thus, an offense is incurred. If one obtains a dwelling that was already completed [before the instruction was given], there is no offense.

The *Mūla-vinaya* states: "If one constructs a small hut for oneself or causes another to construct it in any of these three types of locations—impure places, places of contention, or places where there is no access—one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each such transgression.
First, regarding impure places: these are locations where there are burrows of snakes, scorpions, insects, or ants. Second, regarding places of contention..."
Near a royal palace, a deva temple, a householder’s residence, a non-Buddhist hermitage, or a bhikṣuṇī convent;
or where there is a fine tree that must be felled; or the three places where one does not proceed: where there is a river or a well, or where one faces a precipice or a pit.

The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one has requested the site for a dwelling but does not construct it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one constructs a dwelling when the materials are not present before one, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If [the dimensions] are reduced by one span (*vitasti*) in length, or increased by one span in width, or if they are reduced..."
One may not construct [a dwelling] that is excessively long; how much less so one that is both long and wide beyond the prescribed measure?
If two or three people build a house together, or if a single bhikṣu or a single śrāmaṇera builds it, there is no offense. Why is this?
Because an individual does not have a share in a house. If the house is divided into sections and an individual receives a share of a house, they incur the saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

This precept is established identically in the Mahāyāna. It refers to what the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* calls "evil seeking" and "excessive seeking," and what the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* calls "having many desires and lacking contentment."
Citing Scriptural Authority: Because a bhikṣu sought to build a house for himself, the Buddha, after rebuking him in various ways, addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, by the side of this Ganges River, there was a brahmacārin with a conch-shell topknot who constantly dwelt on this riverbank."
My countenance was haggard and my body emaciated. At that time, I went to him and met with him, asking for the reason.
He replied to me, saying: "There is a dragon king in this water named Maṇigandha.
He came forth from his palace and approached me, coiling his body around me and covering my head with his own. At that time, I thought to myself:"
"The nature of dragons is violent and impetuous; I fear they might harm my life. It is out of this anxiety that my appearance has become such as it is.
At that time, I said to the brahmin, "Do you wish for this dragon to remain forever in the water and not come out to your location?
He replied to me, "I truly wish for this dragon not to come to my place. I then asked:
"Brahmin, does that nāga wear a necklace? He replied, "Beneath the nāga's neck is a fine necklace.
The Buddha said to the Brahmin, "When this nāga emerges from the water and comes to where you are, you should rise to greet him and say:"
"Nāga King, stop for a moment. Give me the necklace from beneath your neck and come here; furthermore, speak this verse:
'I now require such as this, the fine necklace beneath your neck; with a heart of faith and joy, bestow upon me these exquisite jewels.'"
When that brahmin had accepted my words, at a later time the dragon king emerged from the water.
Seeing him from afar, the brahmin went to meet him and spoke a verse. Then the dragon king replied to the brahmin with a verse, saying:
The wealth and treasures I have acquired are all because of this jewel; yet you, a beggar, shall not come to see me again.
You are handsome, upright, and pure, yet you have sought this jewel to alarm me;
you shall not come to see me again. Why did you give this jewel to you?
Thereupon, the Dragon King immediately returned to his palace and never emerged again. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One who seeks much is not loved; Seeking too much brings forth enmity and hatred. The Brahmin sought the dragon’s pearl."
Thus they shall no longer see one another.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu dwelling in a forest who, after midnight, was disturbed in his meditative concentration by the mournful cries of various birds calling to one another.
I instructed that bhikṣu to say to the birds: "I now urgently require both of your wings."
"Come with me. At that time, the flock of birds left the forest and never returned. You bhikṣus should know this:
even dragons, beasts, and flying birds do not delight in people’s begging; how much less so should humans? To seek much without satiety is improper.
Is it not a case of resentment and hatred?
Regarding the seventh precept on building a large dwelling without assigning it [to others]:
if a bhikṣu wishes to build a large dwelling for himself that has a patron, he must take other bhikṣus with him to designate the site.
Regarding the site: that bhikṣu should designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a bhikṣu builds a large dwelling on a site with difficulties or obstructions, for himself, and it has a patron, yet he does not take other bhikṣus to inspect and designate the site, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Garden in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, King Udayana and the Venerable Channa were close friends and acquaintances. The king said to him, "Build a dwelling as you please.
Now, near the city there was a Nyagrodha deity-tree where many people and horses traveling to and fro would rest beneath it. Channa cut it down.
Having done so, he built a large house. The lay devotees (gṛhapati) criticized and disparaged him. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and thus this precept was established.

Because it gave rise to conflict and dispute, and in order to prevent such censure and transgression, this training rule (śikṣāpada) was promulgated; it constitutes the fundamental category of theft within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
Except for cases exceeding the prescribed measure, there is no offense; all other violations are as stated above.
The establishment of the conditions and the application of the four [factors] may be understood by analogy and need not be elaborated here.
This precept is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna; the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "Practicing the dhūta path, and even during the summer retreat..."
Dwelling in these places of difficulty, one shall not enter them at all.
Eighth, the precept against groundless slander:
if a bhikṣu, being overwhelmed by anger, [accuses] a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense of a groundless pārājika offense...
Slandering the Dharma. Desiring to destroy their pure conduct, if at another time— whether questioned or unasked—
one knows that this matter was spoken without basis, yet says, "I spoke these words out of anger," if a bhikṣu makes such a statement,
it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain. At that time, the Venerable Trapusa-māra-putra, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, thought to himself, "I ought to provide service for the Saṃgha by means of my own strength. He then went to inform the Buddha.

The Buddha instructed the bhikṣus to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) to appoint Trapusa-māra to distribute the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha, as well as to assign [other duties].
Next, they received the invitation for a meal. At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Maitrībala, who was the lowest-ranking member of the assembly.
Having received a poor-quality room and bedding in accordance with his seniority, he became angry and said, "Dravyamāra is partial; he gives the best things to those he likes."
"To those who do not rejoice, one gives evil. How can the Saṃgha appoint such a person? On the following day, monks were appointed to accept invitations.

The bhikṣu Cidì was appointed. When it was his turn to go to the donor's house, the donor, hearing that the bhikṣu Cidì was next in line to receive food, spread out a worn-out sitting mat outside the gate and prepared coarse food. Cidì became doubly enraged.
She then sent her younger sister, the bhikṣuṇī Cīrṇā, to falsely slander the Venerable One during an assembly of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, saying, "The Tāpasa Māra has come to violate me.
Knowing this, the World-Honored One intentionally questioned the Venerable One, and the Venerable One replied.
If these do not even exist within dreams from birth, how much less could they exist during the waking state? The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"There are two kinds of people who will invariably enter hell. What are the two? Those who do not lead a pure life yet claim to lead a pure life, and those who, being truly pure in their conduct, falsely accuse them with groundless charges of impurity. These are the two. Thus did the Tathāgata reprove them in various ways.
Having rebuked the bhikṣu Cīrṇabhūmi, [the Buddha] established a precept for the bhikṣus. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
It was formulated as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) due to the false accusation regarding the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and because of an inability to endure afflictions (*kleśa*).

This is the explanation of the meaning of the category of the first section on the root of lying. The text is divided into three parts. The section beginning with "Overwhelmed by malice" clarifies the cause of the false slander. If, regarding...
"At another time" and below clarifies the arousal of remorse and the disclosure [of the offense]. "If a bhikṣu speaks thus" and below establishes the specific offense committed.
The Vinaya states: "One who is angry" becomes angry due to ten unwholesome factors; among these ten matters, one becomes angry with each one individually (the *Dharmasaṃgraha* states:

namely, resentment, hatred, calumny, deception, arrogance, indignation, wrath, stinginess, delusion, and jealousy—one becomes angry because of these ten matters). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The nine grounds for vexation and improper objects."

One gives rise to anger. Regarding the tenth, resentment (*upanāha*): ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) have instances of displeasure; even Arhats may possess anger (*vyāpāda*). From a mind of indignation (*krodha*), one gives rise to resentment. Indignation toward others is called anger; indignation within oneself is called resentment.

The *Nanshan Chao* states: "A bhikṣu manifests his function through the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-samaya*) and takes a compassionate mind as his essence. To say now that he is 'covered by anger' means that this very essence is obscured; it contravenes the six harmonies and leads to the arising of slander. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:

"When a single thought of anger arises, eighty thousand gates of obstruction open. Regarding the "roots," there are three kinds of roots: first, the root of seeing; second, the root of hearing; and third, the root of doubt.

The root of seeing (*dṛṣṭimūla*) is as follows: one actually sees someone committing an offense against the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one sees them stealing five *kārsāpaṇa* or more than five *kārsāpaṇa*, or one sees them taking a human life;
or if another person has seen it, one hears of it from them—this is called the root of seeing. The root of hearing (*śrutimūla*) is as follows:

one hears that someone has committed an offense against the holy life, one hears that they have stolen five *kārsāpaṇa* or more than five *kārsāpaṇa*, one hears that they have taken a human life, or one hears them praising themselves for having attained the state of a superior person (*uttarapuruṣadharma*).
Regarding the Dharma: if one says, "I heard it from him," this is called the root of hearing (*śrutamūla*). As for the root of doubt (*vicikitsāmūla*), there are two ways in which doubt arises.
Doubt arising from seeing (*darśanaja*) occurs, for example, when one sees a woman entering or leaving a forest naked and without clothing.
The body is defiled by impurities; the hands grasp a blood-stained knife; one is accompanied by evil associates—this is called doubt arising from what is seen.

Regarding doubt arising from what is heard: if one is in a dark place, and hears the sound of a bed, or the sound of a straw mat shifting, or the sound of bodily movement, or the sound of conversing, or the sound of sexual union—if [one hears these]...
If one hears the report: "I have violated the holy life"; or hears it said: "He stole five coins or more than five coins";
or hears it said: "I killed a person"; or hears it said: "I have attained the state of a superior person"—this is called doubt arising from what has been heard.

Apart from these three bases, if one further slanders another by means of other matters, this is called being baseless. [This is] for the purpose of destroying that pure practitioner. (For the purpose of destroying...)

That person’s name of purity cannot be shared with the Saṃgha because they do not participate in the common legal affairs of the community. Regarding the phrase "at another time," etc.: if an interrogator is approached by another bhikṣu who comes to interrogate him according to the Dharma, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If an investigator asks, 'What did you see? Did you see sexual misconduct? Did you steal five coins? Did you kill a human? Or did you claim superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*)? [The accused should ask: 'How did you see it? On account of what did you see it? Where did you see it?'"
This is called "investigation. To not inquire in this manner is called "non-investigation. If one does not inquire, that person is acting out of malice;

though they may later realize their error and speak of it, seeking purity by confessing their own groundless slander, even if they feel regret for their transgression after the fact, the offense was already established at the moment the slander was uttered during that lifetime—how could it be permitted that they might be cleared by such a confession?

The Determination of the Offense: Regarding those who commit an offense herein, if one has not seen, heard, or suspected [an act], yet claims to have seen, heard, or suspected it—regardless of whether the other person is pure or impure—and slanders them by means of a *pārājika* rule, such that the speech is clear and distinct, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If one speaks but does not make it clear, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). (In this section, the offenses are explained reciprocally; fearing that the correct regulations might be obscured, each subsequent item is listed in order so that one may know what has been transgressed.)
If one has not seen, heard, or suspected, yet gives rise to the perception that one has seen, heard, or suspected, and later forgets that perception, yet says "I saw, heard,
or suspected" and slanders another with a *pārājika* offense, it is also as described above.

Not having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense], yet suspecting that another has such [a perception], one later says they have no such suspicion; or, having seen, heard, or suspected, one slanders them with a *pārājika* offense—this is also as described above.
Or, not having seen, heard, or suspected, yet giving rise to doubt, one later forgets that doubt and says they saw, heard, or suspected, thereby slandering them with a *pārājika* offense.
It is also as stated above.

When there is no doubt regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected, yet one says there is doubt; or when one slanders another with a *pārājika* offense based on what was seen, heard, or suspected—this is also as stated above.
If one has not seen, heard, or suspected [an offense], yet harbors no doubt regarding these matters, and later, having forgotten that lack of doubt, says "I saw, heard,
or suspected it" and slanders another with a *pārājika* offense, it is also as described above.
Not having seen [an offense], yet having the perception of having seen it, and later forgetting that perception, one says "I heard" or "I suspect," and defames another with a *pārājika* offense;

this is also as described above. Not having seen [an offense], yet having the perception of not having seen it, while actually having heard or suspected it, one defames another with a *pārājika* offense; this is also as described above.
Not having seen [the offense], yet later forgetting that he did not see it, he says, "I heard there was doubt," and slanders him with a *pārājika* offense; this is also as described above.
Not having seen [the offense] and being without doubt, yet saying, "I heard there was doubt," and slandering him with a *pārājika* offense; this is also as described above.

There is no doubt regarding what was not seen; there is no doubt regarding subsequent forgetfulness. To speak of "doubt regarding what was heard" and to slander [another] with a *pārājika* offense is also as described above;
"doubt regarding what was heard" is likewise.
Excluding the four *pārājika* offenses, regardless of whether the person previously was pure or impure, if one further slanders them with other non-monastic qualities,

saying they have committed a bordering offense (*antāpatti*), that they have violated a nun with a thieving mind while receiving the precepts, or that they have broken [the rules of] the inner or outer paths.
If one commits the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), or if it concerns a non-human, an animal, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite, and the statement is clear and distinct, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If the statement is not clear and distinct, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

This also applies if one uses a finger-sign, a letter, or dispatches a messenger to convey the intent; likewise, if one uses groundless charges regarding the four *pārājika* offenses or the thirteen kinds of [offenses].
If a bhikṣu slanders [a bhikṣuṇī], knowing and being certain [of the facts], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if he is not certain, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If he slanders her with one of the eight *pārājika* dharmas—(1) sexual misconduct, (2) theft, (3) killing, (4) lying, (5) touching with a defiled mind, (6) the eight matters with a defiled mind, (7) concealing another’s grave offense, or (8) acquiescing to an act of formal censure—or if he slanders her for having committed a border-line offense (*antarakappa*), up to the point of having both sexual organs, these constitute slandering according to the non-bhikṣuṇī dharma.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is also as above, with the exception of the bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī. To defame another person with groundless charges constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
"another person" refers here to the three lower groups [of the saṃgha] as well as upāsakas and upāsikās.
This precept is established as an offense through five conditions: first, the presence of a mind of anger; second, the absence of the three roots [of faith, shame, and dread];

third, the matter being one of the four pārājikas, which are not the dharma of a bhikṣu; fourth, slandering a person who has received full ordination; and fifth, speaking with clarity. If even one of these conditions is lacking, the offense is merely a preliminary effort (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa; for śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta.
This constitutes an offense.
Exemptions from offense: If one speaks based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected; if one speaks with a factual basis; if one speaks in jest;

if one speaks rapidly; if one speaks alone; if one speaks in a dream; if one intended to speak of this but spoke of that by mistake; or if it was prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute no offense.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one slanders another by citing each individual offense among the *pārājika* rules, or by citing each individual rule among the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* matters, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.

If one slanders another by citing each individual rule among the thirty [rules] or the ninety [rules], one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense. This also applies to the four matters that may be censured and to the *saṃgha*.

Within the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), for each instance of slander, one commits an offense of transgression against the *vinaya* to be confessed with mental regret (*vyañjana-vinayātikrama-saṃtāpanīya*).
For a bhikṣuṇī, there are eight *pārājika* offenses and nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; if she slanders regarding any one of these, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one slanders regarding any one of the thirty matters or the one hundred and forty-one *pāyattikas*, one commits an offense of transgression against the *vinaya*. [The same applies] by means of the eight...

Regarding the *kṣudrānuśāsanīya-dharmas* (minor rules of training) and the *saṃghāvaśeṣa-dharmas*, if one slanders [the preceptor] regarding each individual offense, there is a violation of the *vinaya* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).
As for the eighteen matters of a *śikṣamāṇā*: if one slanders [the teacher] regarding each of these, she must once again undergo the training in the precepts;

such an offense constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*. The eighteen matters are: 1. Not distinguishing between robes; 2. Sleeping apart from one's robe; 3. Touching fire; 4. Consuming food after having had enough; 5. Destroying living seeds; 6. Discarding impurities upon green grass; 7. Climbing high places without permission; 8. Touching precious objects; 9. Eating leftover food kept overnight; 10. [And so forth...]

(1) Destroying the ground; (2) refusing almsfood; (3) damaging growing sprouts; and the six original rules of training: (4) sexual contact with a defiled mind; (5) stealing less than five coins; (6) taking the life of an animal;

(7) minor lying; (8) eating at improper times; and (9) drinking alcohol. These are called the eighteen matters). Regarding the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, if one slanders them one by one, they should be ordained again;

such an offense constitutes a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya). This applies down to the five precepts of a layperson; if one slanders or violates them one by one, it is likewise an offense.
Regarding the *Vinayottaragrantha* (律攝),

it says: "If an upāsaka (i.e., an upāsaka) slanders a bhikṣu, one should perform the *pātra-nyāsa* (覆鉢) karmavācanā for him (this rite is explained in the section on 'Performing and Maintaining' [作持])."

This precept is established identically in the Mahāyāna. If one speaks of it to an outsider, one commits a grave offense; if one speaks of it to a fellow practitioner of the Dharma, one commits a light offense.
To cite scriptural evidence, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When a person dwells in this world, an axe grows within their mouth. For this reason...
One who cuts off one's own body does so because of having uttered evil words.
Ninth is the precept against taking a partial aspect to slander:
if a bhikṣu, out of anger, takes a partial aspect from a matter that belongs to a different category and slanders a bhikṣu who is not one guilty of a pārājika offense.
If one slanders another with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense, desiring to destroy that person’s pure conduct,
and at a later time— whether questioned or not— it is known that this was taken from a portion of a different matter, and that monk says of himself,
"I spoke these words out of anger," then for having spoken such words, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣu Mātṛceta descended from Vulture Peak and saw a large ram engaging in sexual intercourse with a ewe.
He then compared the ram to the Venerable Ṭhappa and the ewe to the bhikṣuṇī Mātṛceta. He went and said to the bhikṣus: "Previously, because there was no..."
This was a denial based on a root-offense. He had personally seen it with his own eyes. When the bhikṣus questioned him, he claimed that Dharmaruci was not guilty of this and was a pure person;
he had previously seen a ewe engaging in sexual intercourse while descending from Mount Lingyan, and he spoke by drawing an analogy based on that similar incident.
When the bhikṣus heard and understood this, they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. This...

This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). This training rule was established because of the false claim to have practiced the celibate life (*brahmacarya*) and due to an inability to endure afflictions (*kleśa*);
it belongs to the category of the fundamental types of lying from the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
Explanation of the Meaning: The text is divided into three sections as above. "Anger" is as explained above. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"The 'separate categories' refer to the four *pārājika* offenses. If one commits even a single one among them, one is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya."
One loses the status of a bhikṣu; therefore, it is called "a different portion" (*anyabhāga*). Regarding "a fragment": this refers to various matters of deportment. (The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:

"As for 'the remaining portion,' Tvaṣṭṛ and Maitrāyaṇī were humans, while the sheep was a non-human. Because the sheep was treated as a human, it is called 'the remaining portion. 'The remaining portion' is identical to 'a different portion'.").
The other meanings are the same as explained previously. Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, one commits an offense if an impure person resembles an impure person.
They have the same name, the same clan, and the same appearance. Because of these matters, one person slanders another.
Or, an impure person resembles a pure person; they have the same name and clan, and because of these matters, one person slanders another.
If a pure person resembles an impure person and their names and surnames are identical, one may defame that [pure] person on account of the other.
Or, if a pure person resembles another pure person and their names and surnames are identical, one may defame that [pure] person on account of the other.
If he sees that when [the person] was formerly a householder, they committed sexual misconduct, theft of five coins or more, or took a human life, and then says to others:

"I see this bhikṣu committing sexual misconduct, theft, or murder"— this refers to what was done while [the person] was still a householder observing the upāsaka precepts, not after they had gone forth.
[This concerns matters subsequent to receiving full ordination at home.

If one hears that [the person] previously, while living as a householder, committed sexual misconduct, theft, or killing; or if one hears them claim for themselves the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), one should then say:
"I have heard that this bhikṣu has committed sexual misconduct, theft, killing, or false speech."

If a bhikṣu, in this manner, slanders a bhikṣu with matters concerning the four rootless offenses that belong to a different category, if he speaks clearly, it is all a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if he speaks unclearly, it is all a *sthūlātyaya*.

As for other offenses committed, whether light or heavy, as well as those that are non-offenses and so forth, they are all regulated identically to the Mahāyāna, each and every one as previously stated.
The tenth is the precept against not relinquishing the practice of schism in the Saṃgha:
If a bhikṣu desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, and through skillful means adopts the practices that lead to such a schism, persisting in them and refusing to relinquish them.
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not accept the principles that lead to a schism and persistently hold to them without relinquishing them. Venerable sir, you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha.

Being in harmony with the Saṃgha, may you be joyful and free from dispute, studying under the same teacher as one body, like water and milk blending together. Thus, within the Buddha-dharma, there will be increase."

He dwells in even greater peace and happiness. When that bhikṣu thus exhorts him and he persists in his refusal to relinquish [the matter], those bhikṣus should exhort him three times to relinquish it.
If he relinquishes it upon the third exhortation, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Circumstances: The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain. At that time, Devadatta, for the sake of gain and offerings, mastered supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
He converted Prince Ajātaśatru, causing him to give rise to faith and joy, whereby he received great offerings; yet he alone did not equal the Buddha, and thus jealousy arose in his heart.
He immediately lost his supernatural powers and, wishing to gather a following, waited for an assembly of the Buddha’s great multitude.
At that time, he went to where the Buddha was and requested the Buddha’s entrustment, saying: "World-Honored One, my years are now advanced and my life-span exceeds that of ordinary men;
I have long practiced the Way and should dwell in quietude, maintaining myself in silent composure.
World-Honored One, as you are the King of all Dharmas, it would be fitting to entrust the Saṅgha to me, and I shall protect and sustain it. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "I am still..."
"I did not entrust the Saṃgha to Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana; how much less could I entrust it to you, a foolish person with a body like spit and snot?
How could it be entrusted to you? At that time, Devadatta immediately gave rise to an intolerant mind.

He then instructed Ajātaśatru to harm his father and dispatched men to harm the Buddha, but they failed. He went in person to the summit of Vulture Peak and seized a rock, hurling it from afar at the World-Honored One.
Consequently, his ill repute spread abroad and his offerings were cut off.

He then began to solicit alms from house to house together with five people of his own (the phrase "together with five people of his own" refers to four companions: first, Svāgata, who was of high intelligence and great talent, and thus ranked foremost;

second, Khaṇḍadravya, a close friend of Devadatta; third, Kuṣīnara, a disciple of Devadatta; fourth, Kālodāyin, whose seven sisters were all bhikṣuṇīs and who possessed great influence). The Buddha prohibited this, declaring it not permitted.
Regarding eating separately from the assembly, he then thought: "It is unprecedented! Gautama has cut off people's food.

I should rather break up his monastic community; after my own death, I may gain a reputation by saying that although Gautama possesses great supernormal powers and unimpeded wisdom, Devadatta was able to destroy it. He then took four bhikṣus as his companions. With...
The Teacher taught the bhikṣus with five dharmas, saying: "The Tathāgata has always praised those who practice *dhūta*, who have few desires and are content, and who delight in renunciation.
I now have five dharmas which are likewise superior *dhūta* practices for those with few desires, who are content, and who delight in renunciation.
First, to beg for food for as long as life lasts; second, to wear rag-robes for as long as life lasts; third, [to dwell at the foot of a tree for as long as life lasts]..."
1. Sitting on the bare ground for as long as life lasts; 2. Not eating ghee or salt for as long as life lasts;
3. Not eating fish or meat for as long as life lasts. "We shall practice these together so that the newly ordained and ignorant bhikṣus may have faith and joy.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "Devadatta today wishes to sever the four noble..."
The four supports (namely, robes, food, bedding, and medicine). With countless skillful means, the World-Honored One rebuked Devadatta:
"Do not sever the four noble lineages. Do not teach the five points to the bhikṣus.
Do not now employ skillful means to accept the dharma that causes schism in the Saṃgha and persist in holding to it without relinquishing it. You should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha."
He knew that breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha was an extremely evil act, resulting in a grave offense for which one would suffer punishment in hell for an entire kalpa, beyond all remedy.

The World-Honored One, employing various skillful means, caused Devadatta’s intent to break the Saṃgha to momentarily cease, and had the Saṃgha perform the formal ritual of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to reprimand Devadatta. If others were likewise...
If one who employs skillful means intends to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, they too shall be rebuked and admonished by means of this *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
It was for this reason that the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus. This was enacted due to a matter concerning the Saṃgha and the affliction of false wisdom;
it belongs to the category of the fundamental types of falsehood within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
Exegesis: The text is divided into four sections. From "If a bhikṣu wishes to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha" onwards, it clarifies the procedure for addressing one who is causing a schism.
From "That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu" onwards, it clarifies the words of formal admonition and the request to desist according to the Dharma.
From "When that bhikṣu is thus admonished" onwards, it clarifies the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion and three proclamations) of reprimand; [it continues] "if he does not desist."

The following section concludes the offense of defying admonition. The Vinaya states: "Those who are in harmony" refers to those who perform the same *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) and recite the *prātimokṣa* together.
"Sangha" refers to four bhikṣus, or five, or ten, or even an infinite number. "To break" means to cause dissension.
There are eighteen matters that constitute a schism: dharma and non-dharma; discipline and non-discipline; offense and non-offense; light and heavy;

with remainder and without remainder; grave and not grave; customary practice and non-customary practice (the *Śāriputra Vinaya* states that "customary practice" refers to the formal motions consisting of one motion, two motions, or four motions, as well as the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the ordination of the fourteen persons); established rule and non-established rule; taught and untaught; and dwelling in a schism within the Saṃgha.

"Regarding the Dharma: it refers to abiding in these eighteen matters (abiding means holding firmly and not abandoning them. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: 'Having contemplated the schism in the Saṃgha, he gathers his disciples, maintains his own heterodox tenets, and seeks out many evil associates;

for this reason, he stubbornly clings to them and does not abandon them. The subsequent phrases are all explained according to the meaning of the *Vinayaviniścaya*). That bhikṣu should admonish that bhikṣu (admonition means awakening a person through direct speech.

This admonition is a private admonition, not a formal *karmavācanā* within the Saṃgha. Although there is no formal *karmavācanā*, one uses words to restrain him, causing him to eliminate his evil views): "Venerable Sir, do not destroy [the Saṃgha]."

"Those who are in harmony with the Saṃgha," etc. (These three phrases serve as a reprimand; the meaning is that the harmonious assembly must not be split. If it is split, one will certainly fall into hell and suffer for an eon, unable to be cured).

"Venerable sirs, you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha," etc. (These are words of exhortation, intended to show that by not splitting the harmonious Saṃgha, not only will there be no suffering in hell, but furthermore, there will be great benefit).
"Joyful" means that they are well-increased [in merit] and each person’s mind is delighted. "Without contention" means that their views are identical and they accept one another.

Joy (because there is no contention or dispute). Those who study under the same teacher (meaning they train within the teaching of a single Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, without giving rise to divergent views; for although the Tathāgata’s teachings are divided into twelve, their essence is not distinct).
Like water and milk blending together (meaning that when water and milk are mixed, they share a single characteristic and a single flavor, with no difference in color or taste;

this is a metaphor for the four castes of different lineages who, upon leaving the household life and entering the Tathāgata’s Dharma, are all equally called sons of Śākya and equally practice liberation; as their conduct accords with the principle, they are of one characteristic without distinction). Within the Buddha-Dharma, there is increase.

"Abiding in peace and happiness" means that since they share the same training and their conduct does not contradict the principles, they are well able to subdue the afflictions of the three poisons. This causes the accumulation of wholesome dharmas to increase and bring about peace and happiness, so that the Tathāgata’s holy teaching may be propagated and long endure in the world.
When a bhikṣu thus admonishes another and the latter stubbornly persists and does not relinquish [the offense], that bhikṣu should admonish him up to three times.

As for "three admonitions," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The three admonitions consist of three admonitions in private, three admonitions before many people, and three admonitions within the assembly; it does not mean merely three admonitions in total."

The third section states: "There are two things that cause a schism in the Saṃgha: false speech and similar speech. (Regarding 'similar speech': it refers to words that imitate the noble language and resemble the Vinaya regulations, yet are in fact neither Dharma nor Vinaya.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* says: Because of his delusion, Devadatta gave rise to heterodox views and brought about a schism in the Saṃgha. Regarding outward appearance and other matters, he altered the Buddha’s correct rules and established five self-imposed practices.

He slandered the three pure teachings and exhorted the ignorant and small-minded to practice these five dharmas. As for the five practices: first, not eating milk or curd, because calves would suffer from hunger; second, not eating fish or meat, because doing so involves killing living beings; third, not consuming salt, because there is much [salt]..."

1. Because of dust and dirt. 2. Wearing unhemmed robes, because it wastes the labor of weaving. 3. Not dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage), because staying in a dwelling generates merit. Regarding clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that medicine is included within three [of the four requisites].

The fourth [requisite] produces the joy of renunciation and the joy of cultivation, thereby giving rise to the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Thus, there are four noble lineages. Furthermore, there are two matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha: performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and taking up voting tallies (*śalākā*).
If there are one, two, or even three bhikṣus, although they may seek expedient means, they cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha;

nor can bhikṣuṇīs and others cause a schism in the Saṃgha. If this group consists of four or more, and that group consists of four or more, and they cast the voting tickets for a schism and perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā), this constitutes a schism of the harmonious Saṃgha. [They will fall] into hell.
One shall undergo punishment for one kalpa without remedy. Those who are able to reconcile them shall obtain the merit of Brahmā and enjoy happiness for one kalpa.

Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu employs means to break a harmonious Saṃgha, accepts the methods for breaking the Saṃgha, and persists in holding to it without relinquishing it, that bhikṣu should admonish him, saying: "Venerable sir, do not [persist]."
"You are about to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. Do not accept the practice of causing a schism; do not persist in it and refuse to relinquish it.

Venerable sir, you should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and free from dispute, like water and milk mixed together. Within the Buddha-dharma, this will lead to increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness.
Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha must carry out a formal reprimand and you commit a grave offense. If...

"Good at using words. (Regarding "using words": this refers to accepting a remonstrance and abandoning the matter. To say it is "good" means that while the original offense is avoided, one merely commits a minor offense of preparatory action (*prayoga*).
This is what the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* calls the three admonitions in private.)

If they do not accept the words, or if one causes a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, or a king, or a high minister, or various followers of heterodox paths—such as śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas (where "followers of heterodox paths" refers to those who have left the household life as non-Buddhist practitioners;

and "seeking" means seeking to listen)—and if a bhikṣu, in accordance with the Vinaya and the Dharma, wishes to admonish such a person, he should first say to that person: "Venerable sir, I now wish to admonish you; you should receive and listen to my words."
That person should respond by saying, "I have already admonished you. If monks from another region hear of this and their words are trusted, they should seek [to intervene].
If they accept the advice, it is well. (Regarding the mention of monks from another region: these are the close friends of that schismatic; thus they trust one another's words.
This refers to the three admonitions before a large assembly as described in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.)

If he does not comply with the verbal instruction, one should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having performed the announcement, one should further request: "Venerable sir, I have finished the announcement;

there remains the formal act (*karman*). You should now relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform a formal act against you and you incur a grave offense once again. If he complies with the instruction, it is well.
If he does not comply with the instruction, the first *karmavācanā* (formal motion) should be performed.
Having performed the first *karmavācanā*, one should further request: "Venerable sirs, I have finished the formal motion; two *karmavācanās* remain.
You should relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform a *karmavācanā* against you again and you incur a grave offense. If he complies with the instruction, it is well.
If he does not desist from his speech, a second *karmavācanā* should be performed. Having performed the second *karmavācanā*, one should further entreat him:
"Venerable sir, I have completed the first of the two *karmavācanās*; only one *karmavācanā* remains.
You should relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform another *karmavācanā* for you and you incur a grave offense. If you can relinquish it..."
If he does so, it is well.
If he does not relinquish it, the third *karmavācanā* (this refers to the three admonitions within the assembly according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*) is recited for him.
If he still does not relinquish it after the third *karmavācanā*, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If he relinquishes it after the *jñapti-dvitīya-karmavācanā* is completed, there are three *sthūlātyaya*s.
If one relinquishes after the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the first *karmavācanā* have been completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses;
if one relinquishes after the motion has been completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense; if one relinquishes before the initial motion is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one, while all [the formal motions] have not yet been announced, employs means to break the harmonious Saṃgha and accepts the practice of breaking the harmonious Saṃgha, persisting in it without relinquishing it, it is entirely *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

"All have not yet been announced" means before the community of monks has performed even one *jñapti-tri-karman* (one motion followed by three proclamations). If one is admonished three times in private...

If, among a group of many people, one does not relinquish [the offense] after three admonitions, each instance constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Here, I have clarified only the wording of the admonition and the speech of the reprimand; the ritual procedures (*karman*) are all contained within the *Zuochi* (Manual of Liturgical Practice).
If one admonishes in a manner that does not conform to the Vinaya regulations, even if the admonition is performed, it is not valid. The same applies to the three lower categories of offenses.

If, when the Saṃgha is performing the formal act of admonition (*karma*) against one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, a bhikṣu instructs [the schismatic] not to relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If he does not perform the admonition but instructs him not to relinquish it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs him not to relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇī commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If she does not perform the admonition but instructs him... [the bhikṣuṇī commits a *duṣkṛta* offense].
"Do not discard it. This is a *duṣkṛta* offense. With the exception of monks and nuns, if there are others who instruct [someone] not to discard it, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
(By "others" is meant the three lesser groups.)

This precept constitutes a full offense only when five conditions are met: first, there must be the intention to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; second, the assembly of like-minded partisans must be complete;

third, one must not relinquish the course despite repeated admonitions; fourth, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) must be performed according to the Dharma; and fifth, the threefold proclamation (*jñapti*) must be completed.
If any of these conditions are lacking, the offense incurred is mitigated.
Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa (the same rule and the same training); for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This constitutes an offense.
Exemptions from offense: [one is not guilty] if one abandons [the matter] upon the first admonition; or if the admonition is carried out by an illegal separate assembly;
or if the admonition is carried out by an illegal united assembly; or if it is a legal separate assembly; or if it is a legal-similar separate assembly;
or if it is a legal-similar united assembly; or if it is neither Dharma nor Vinaya, nor taught by the Buddha; or if no admonition has been carried out at all; or if [the schism] is broken.
Regarding evil friends: one should destroy such evil associates. If there is one who employs means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, one must obstruct them so that the schism does not occur.

If there are two or three persons who assist in the means to cause a schism through formal ritual (karmavācanā), or if they intend to perform a ritual that is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya—whether for the sake of the Saṃgha, for a stūpa, or for the sake of their preceptors (upādhyāya) or teachers (ācārya), including their co-preceptors...
O Ācārya, if one acts to the detriment of a spiritual friend or causes them to have no place of residence, as well as in cases where the precepts have not yet been established at the outset,
there is in all such instances no offense.
Regarding the practice of gathering [the Sangha]: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if one knows a person intends to cause a schism in the Sangha, the bhikṣus should say to him:
"Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the Sangha. The offense of causing a schism is grave; it leads to rebirth in the evil realms and entry into hell.

We shall provide you with robes and alms bowls, teach you the scriptures, assist you in recitation, and instruct you in the inquiry of the Dharma. If he still does not desist, they should say to those who have influence: [continue as follows].
The upāsaka Balasena said, "Long-lived one, this man wishes to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should go and admonish him with firm words to make him desist.
The upāsaka should say, "Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha. The offense of causing a schism is grave; it leads to rebirth in the evil destinies and entry into hell.
I shall provide the Venerable One with robes and bowls, as well as medicinal broth for his ailments. If you do not find pleasure in practicing the holy life..."
Such a person may return to lay life; I shall give you my wife and provide for all your necessities.
If he still does not desist, one should pull out his tally and expel him. Once he has been expelled, one should proclaim:
"Venerable sirs, a schismatic has arrived; you should take note of this yourselves. If, despite such precautions, he still causes a schism, this is called "schism."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "I do not see any other dharma that destroys the human aspiration for the Path as much as fame and gain.
It was for the sake of gain and offerings that Devadatta caused a schism in the Saṃgha. Devadatta brought about a schism in the Saṃgha by accomplishing eight unrighteous acts:
[1] gain versus lack of gain; [2] praise versus lack of praise; [3] honor versus dishonor; and [4] delighting in evil and following evil associates. There are these four matters.
This is called "schism in the Saṃgha. It refers to preaching the five practices, distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*), or conducting monastic affairs separately within a boundary (*sīmā*).
Furthermore, if a king, a high minister, or any other group of six (the seven groups excluding the bhikṣus) causes the Saṃgha to be discordant, it does not constitute a schism.
Likewise, if from one bhikṣu up to seven bhikṣus are in discord, it is also not a schism. If [it is less than that]...
If one asks the Elder to perform monastic affairs, this constitutes a lack of harmony, yet it does not constitute a schism in the Saṃgha.
If they do not eat together, sit separately during meals, or engage in quarreling and verbal abuse, these also are not termed a schism.
A schism occurs only when eight or more bhikṣus within a single boundary divide into two factions and perform monastic affairs separately; it is in this context that [the act] is performed.
The leader shall fall into the great hell for one kalpa and cannot be saved.
When that bhikṣu desires to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, and the other monks see, hear, or know of it, they should appoint one bhikṣu who is on friendly terms with him to go and admonish him.
If he desists, he should perform one *duṣkṛta* confession. If he does not desist, many bhikṣus should be sent to admonish him. If he desists [at this stage], [the same applies].
He should confess two *duṣkṛta* offenses. If he still does not relinquish [the view], the Saṃgha should go to him and admonish him.

If he relinquishes it, he should confess three *duṣkṛta* offenses. If he still does not relinquish it, he should be admonished by means of a formal motion and threefold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
If one renounces after the announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses and one *sthūlātyaya*.
If one renounces after the first *karmavācanā* (the first formal motion) has been made, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses and two *sthūlātyayas*.
If one renounces after the second *karmavācanā* has been made, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses and three *sthūlātyayas*. If one renounces before the third *karmavācanā* is completed...
Three *duṣkṛta* offenses, three *sthūlātyaya* offenses, and three formal acts (*karmavācana*). Whether the [schism] is relinquished or not, it is all a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of schisms: schism of the formal act (*karmabhedaka*) and schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakrabhedaka*). As for the schism of the formal act..."
To perform a separate *poṣadha* ritual within a single boundary (*sīmā*) constitutes a schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*cakrabheda*). "Wheel" refers to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

It causes people to abandon the eightfold noble path and enter onto a false path. [This applies] if it is done contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha’s teaching. However, if it is done in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, it does not constitute a schism.
The third admonition is concluded. If he does not relinquish [the offense], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. That bhikṣu should immediately enter the midst of the *saṃgha* and announce by himself:
"Venerable elders, I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. It would be well if I were to confess it immediately."
If one does not speak [of the offense] immediately, from that time onward, it is called the number of days of concealment (*paticchāda*). Furthermore, it is said:

if one does not first admonish with gentle words but instead proceeds directly to the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to admonish, the person performing the *karman* incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one expels [a person] before the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been performed, the person performing the *karman* incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, before the three-fold proclamation (*tri-vācikā*) has been made, one separately requests another person within the boundary (*sīmā*) to perform the *karman*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense due to the cause of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
If the Saṃgha is aware of this, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: "Of all other precepts, none were first violated; this precept was first violated by Devadatta because he did not relinquish it despite the three-fold admonition of the Saṃgha."

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: To break the wheel of the Saṃgha constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) that is irreversible and classified as a transgression against the fundamental precepts (*ānantarya*).
To break the Saṃgha through ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) constitutes a grave offense that is not a transgression against the fundamental precepts and is repentable.

Breaking the wheel of the Saṃgha requires at least nine persons: one person claims to be the Buddha. Breaking the Saṃgha through ritual procedure requires at least eight persons, provided no one claims to be the Buddha. This is what is meant by "breaking the Saṃgha."

The wheel [of the Saṃgha]. Whether within or outside the boundary (*sīmā*), it completely destroys [the unity]. To destroy the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha, it must be within the boundary; one performs the *karmavācanā* separately to destroy the wheel of the Saṃgha.
It is necessarily a bhikṣu who destroys the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha; a bhikṣuṇī is also capable of destroying the wheel of the Saṃgha.

To destroy the Saṃgha of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is also to destroy the Saṃgha of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The destruction of the wheel of the Saṃgha occurs only in Jambudvīpa.

(Since all Buddhas appear in Jambudvīpa in the south), the schism of the *karmavācanā* community occurs throughout the three continents (excluding only Uttarakuru, because the monastic community dwells there in small numbers; thus it is said to be "the three continents").
This precept is established as common to the Mahāyāna. If the wheel of the Saṃgha has not yet been split, it is subsumed under the category of teaching with an evil mind or a mind of hatred;
however, if the wheel of the Saṃgha has been split, it constitutes a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense and does not admit of repentance.
Appendix: Examination of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. It states: "Regarding those who have caused a schism in the Saṃgha: if one makes offerings to them, it is called 'giving to a field of merit.
If one receives full ordination from them, it is called 'receiving full ordination. Once one has realized [the error], one should depart;

if one does not depart, they are called an associate of those who have caused a schism. As an associate of those who have caused a schism, one should not speak with them or dwell together with them for as long as life lasts."

They may eat together, but they do not share in matters concerning the Three Jewels; they do not share in the *poṣadha*, the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), or the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*);

they do not share in formal legal acts (*karmavācanā*). They may have seats and couches in common with other renunciant followers of external paths; if such a person wishes to sit, one may sit with them, but one must not offer a seat to them.

(According to the Vinaya, even a person who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha is still called a field of merit and is still considered one who has properly received full ordination. This is because the offense of causing a schism is a *sthūlātyaya*, and it does not constitute the loss of the fundamental precepts as would be the case with the commission of a *pārājika* offense.)

Because its essence remains, it is still called a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). It is like a golden staff that, though broken, is gold at both ends; since the precepts have not been lost, one is still a member of the Saṃgha, which causes those of firm faith to practice giving with equanimity. At the time of initial ordination, this was not yet realized.

If one receives full ordination with a sincere heart, and the intention behind receiving it is genuine, how could one not obtain the precepts? However, if one later realizes [the error], according to principle there can be no communal residence; how could one willingly act as an associate of those who have split the Saṃgha? For this reason, one should depart.
The eleventh precept: Not abandoning an evil faction that causes schism in the Saṃgha.
If there are one, two, three, or even countless monks who act as a faction, and these monks say to another monk, "Venerable sir, do not admonish this monk;
this monk is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya."
“Monks, regarding what this monk has said, we rejoice; regarding what this monk has said, we approve. That other monk says:

“Venerable sirs, do not speak thus. Do not say that this monk is a monk who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya, and that ‘regarding what this monk has said, we rejoice; regarding what this monk has said, we approve.’”
It may be so. However, this bhikṣu is not one who speaks according to the Dharma; he is not one who speaks according to the Vinaya.
Venerable sirs, do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. You should desire harmony within the Saṃgha, venerable sirs.

Be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing without dispute, sharing the same teacher and training, like water mixed with milk. Thus, within the Buddha’s Dharma, there will be increase and peaceful dwelling.
When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him and he persists in his refusal to relinquish [the matter], those bhikṣus should admonish him up to three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. At that time, the faction of Devadatta employed skillful means to assist in the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha.
He spoke to the bhikṣus, saying: "Do not disparage what Devadatta has said. Devadatta is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma;
he is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya. We accept and approve of what Devadatta has said. Thus spoke the bhikṣus.

Kau reported this to the Buddha. After the Buddha had rebuked Devadatta and his faction in various ways, he directed the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure and admonition (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

He further declared that if there are such factions who assist one another in destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha, they too shall be subject to such a formal act of censure and admonition. Thereupon, he established this precept for the bhikṣus. This is the precept.
The matters by which [the schism] is occasioned, as well as the arising of afflictions, are all fundamentally of the same kind as described above.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning, the text is divided into four sections. The section beginning with "If a bhikṣu has a faction" concerns those who assist in breaking the Saṃgha and instead obstruct the presentation of a formal admonition.
The section beginning with "That bhikṣu says, 'Venerable Sir, do not speak thus'" clarifies the admonition directed toward them.

Regarding the faction of those who follow what is not the Dharma: when a bhikṣu has been thus admonished, and after the formal proclamation and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the ritual of a motion followed by three proclamations) have been clearly made with a reprimand, if he does not relinquish [his position], the offense of defying the admonition is established. The Vinaya states: "There are two ways of being compliant" (*anuvartaka*).

"Compliance" means to conform to the wrong and oppose the right, following and remaining [with them]; that is, to assist in breaking up the faction. First is compliance through the Dharma: teaching according to the Dharma and increasing their precepts.
They increase the mind [of concentration] and increase wisdom; they recite and receive [the teachings]. They are compliant in two ways regarding clothing and food:

they provide robes, bedding, food and drink, seats and bedding, and medicine for the sick and infirm. Regarding those who speak according to the Dharma and the Vinaya (the *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Speech that is complete in its phrasing is 'Dharma-speech'; speech that accords with reason without error is 'Vinaya-speech';

furthermore, that which can lead to the true meaning is called 'Dharma-speech,' and that which utters gentle words is called 'Vinaya-speech')"—we who rejoice in them find that all their actions accord with our own hearts.
"Those of us who accept [this] (meaning: we vow to receive and uphold whatever he has taught)," and "Venerable Sir, do not speak thus," etc., (meaning:
exhorting him to follow the orthodox schools and abandon the heterodox factions; the rest is explained as above).
The Offense: Regarding the offense herein, if a monk forms an unlawful faction and says to other monks, "Venerable sirs, do not admonish this monk;
this monk is one who speaks according to the Dharma, one who speaks according to the Vinaya. What this monk says, we accept."
One should admonish this group of bhikṣus, saying: "Venerable sirs, do not speak thus. These bhikṣus are speakers of the Dharma;
these bhikṣus are speakers of the Vinaya. What these bhikṣus have spoken, we accept and approve.
Yet these bhikṣus are not speakers of the Dharma, nor are they speakers of the Vinaya. You must not cause a schism in the Saṃgha. One should say: "You ought to..."
"Help to bring about harmony in the Saṃgha, Venerable One! Be in harmony with the Saṃgha; be joyful and free from dispute, like water and milk blended as one.
Within the Buddha-Dharma, there will be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness. You should abandon this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
It is well if you comply with these words; if you do not comply, the Saṃgha shall perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman)."
Up to the third formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*) of the admonition, whether the offense committed is abandoned or not, and whether it is light or heavy, all are the same as previously stated.
The conditions for the offense are the same as before.
Furthermore, this also governs the *bhikṣuṇī*s’ *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses (governed by the same rules and studied together), as well as those of the *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī*.

This is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing); this constitutes an offense. Regarding the exemptions: herein, those who do not commit an offense are as previously stated (as clarified according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*).

From this point downward, regarding the three precepts, there is no provision for commanding the fourfold assembly, kings, great ministers, or other monks from other regions whose words are trusted, to seek counsel and abandon [the offense]; rather, it is only for the monk to [confess] in a secluded place.

He should be admonished. If he does not desist even when admonished in private, the Saṃgha should immediately perform a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-trikarman*) to reprimand him. The reason this differs from the previous case is that in the former instance, the individual established a false doctrine for himself as the leader to split the Saṃgha; therefore, the compassionate concern of the Sages was all the more urgent, employing various expedients in succession.
Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it says: "If one bhikṣu is subjected to formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) and four other bhikṣus follow him, this is called 'schism' (*saṃghabheda*).

If one who is widely known, well-acquainted, learned, a person of great virtue, and clearly understands the meaning of the Tripiṭaka performs an exclusion for [a transgression] that has not been seen (*adarśana-pravāsanīya*), he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense, because he causes a division within the local community (*upāsama-saṃgha*). As for what is called 'exclusion,' there is both the one who performs the exclusion and the one who is excluded."

In the Dharma, there is a distinction between what is lawful and what is unlawful. If those who perform the act of suspension (nāśana) act in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, then the offense belongs to the one suspended and those who follow the suspended person. If those who perform the suspension act contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya, then the offense belongs to those who performed the suspension and the Saṃgha.

However, even if a bhikṣu who acts according to the Dharma is unjustly subjected to suspension, he will certainly not perform separate monastic affairs within the boundary (*sīmā*) to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. Furthermore, those who are widely learned and well-informed should not be subjected to the suspension for "not seeing" an offense.

This does not mean that one should tolerate their transgressions out of fear or affection, failing to discipline them. For if one were to expel a single person, many others might follow suit, which would inevitably lead to a schism and the division of the Saṃgha. Rather, one must employ skillful means to exhort and guide them so that they recognize their own faults.

Therefore, one must not hastily perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*); if one does so hastily, one will instead incur the fault oneself. This is because, lacking the ability to weigh the situation properly, one fails to use skillful means to secretly protect the monastic community.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If, when others offer admonition, one aligns their mind with the evil faction, even if they do not speak [in support], they commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If they do not agree in speech but their heart delights in causing a schism, they commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense. This applies even if it is the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*) that is being divided."
One should not grant instruction. One should tell her: "Sister, you must first achieve harmony before seeking instruction.
If a bhikṣuṇī community, without consulting the bhikṣus, arbitrarily establishes its own rules and gathers a following, they incur a sthūlātyaya offense.
As for those śrāmaṇeras who have been censured, or other bhikṣus...
If one provides robes, food, and drink to support and nourish someone who is causing schisms among others' disciples, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
However, if one acts with a virtuous intention, desiring to subdue them through temporary means of guidance and attraction, there is no offense.
This precept is likewise established by the Mahāyāna as described above.
Twelfth: The Precept Regarding Refusing to Submit After Being Expelled.
If a bhikṣu resides in a village or a city and defiles families and engages in evil conduct, he defiles families and...
It is seen that you have heard [of these matters]. It is also seen and heard that you have engaged in misconduct. Monks, you should say to that monk:
"Venerable sir, you have defiled families and have engaged in misconduct. It is both seen and heard that you have defiled families, and it is both seen and heard that you have engaged in misconduct.
Venerable sir, since you have defiled families and engaged in misconduct, you should now depart from this village; you need not remain."
This is what that bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, there are bhikṣus who possess affection, hostility, fear, and delusion;
among bhikṣus who have committed such identical offenses, some are expelled while others are not. The bhikṣus reply:
"Venerable sir, do not speak thus—that there are [bhikṣus] who possess affection, hostility, fear, and delusion—[for] there are such..."
Regarding bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, some are expelled while others are not; yet these bhikṣus are without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion.
Venerable sir, this bhikṣu defiles families and engages in evil conduct; that he defiles families has been both seen and heard, and that he engages in evil conduct has also been both seen and heard.
When this bhikṣu is thus admonished and persists in his refusal to relinquish [the misconduct], that bhikṣu...

One should admonish three times for the purpose of making him relinquish this matter. If he relinquishes it after the third admonition, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there were two bhikṣus in the village of Kālīma; one was named Aśva.

"Master, the second is named Pūrṇamāsa. He performs unrighteous acts: he plants flowering trees himself, waters them himself, plucks the flowers himself, makes garlands himself, and carries the garlands himself to give to others; he also teaches others to act in this same way.
Furthermore, if there are women in that village, he sits and rises on the same bed as them, eats and drinks from the same vessel as them, and converses with them in jest."
From those who engage in singing, dancing, and performing as entertainers; or who teach others to do so while singing along themselves;
or who perform comedies, play drums and reed organs, blow conch shells, and accept employment for jesting and laughter—there were at that time many bhikṣus who went to the village of Karṇa for alms.

Their Dharma robes were neatly arranged, their gait was composed and orderly, and they walked straight ahead with downcast eyes, not looking left or right. When the laypeople saw them, they [reacted] in reverse...
Considering this to be improper, they did not provide them with food or drink. When the bhikṣus inquired into the reason for this, they reported the matter in full to the Buddha.

The Buddha commanded Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to go and perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya*) against them. The two venerable ones received the command and went there;
having assembled the Saṃgha, they performed the formal acts of *utkṣepanīya*, *smṛti-vinaya*, and the imposition of punishment (*daṇḍa-karman*) against those two individuals.
Then those two men said, "The Saṃgha possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion. There are other bhikṣus who have committed the same offense;

The Case: Up to three admonitions; if he relinquishes [the offense], it is well. If he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying in the city of Kauśāmbī, in the garden of the householder Sundarika.

Exegesis: The text is divided into four sections. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the nature of being ill-tempered and contravening the teachings.

From "That bhikṣu admonishes this bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the relinquishing of ill-temper through admonition. From "When that bhikṣu is thus admonished... onwards, it clarifies the performance of the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion).

"One should personally accept admonitory speech" (these are words of instruction). "Venerable Sir, admonish the bhikṣus according to the Dharma. The bhikṣus...

Because they admonish one another, the community of the Buddha’s disciples attains the flourishing and intensification of wholesome dharmas. Because they flourish, the True Dharma is able to abide long in the world. Because the True Dharma abides for a long time...
