If one exceeds this limit—specifically, for those who did not receive the *kaṭhina* cloth during the later retreat (*paścima-varṣa*), from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month, during this one-month period, the keeping of the five items such as extra robes is permitted;

whereas for those who received the *kaṭhina* cloth during the earlier retreat (*pūrva-varṣa*), from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, during these five months, the five privileges are permitted. If one exceeds that one month or five months, it is entirely an improper time for keeping extra robes. Whatever robe-cloth is obtained [during these periods] is termed...

[This refers to] out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*). There are ten kinds of robes. As stated above, "if one needs them, one may accept them" means that if one desires to obtain robes, one may accept them provided they are suitable for possession.

"Having accepted them, one should quickly make them into robes" means that once the materials for the robes have been obtained, one should promptly complete whichever of the three robes is missing or damaged, and maintain them according to the Dharma.
If it is sufficient, it is good (meaning that the materials for robes are already sufficient in quantity to produce one robe without deficiency).

If it is insufficient, it is permitted to keep it for one month (meaning that the materials for robes are either lacking or insufficient to make one robe; therefore, it is permitted as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: Ānanda obtained a small piece of cloth and gave it to the bhikṣus, who sprinkled water on it by the riverbank and stretched it out to make it long and wide.

The Buddha went to the riverbank and, knowing the reason, asked about it. They replied, "Because the materials for the robe were insufficient, we sprinkled water and stretched it out to make it long and wide. The Buddha said, "Have you perhaps obtained more?")

[The Buddha asked: "Is there a place where you expect to obtain robes? He replied, "There is. The Buddha asked, "When can they be obtained? He replied, "In one month. The Buddha said, "From now on, I allow those who have a place where they expect to obtain robes for insufficient clothing to wait for one month, so that they may become complete."

Regarding the establishment of the offense: among these, the transgressor is one who, when ten days have passed and the robe-material is sufficient, does not cut it, nor join it with thread, nor sew it into a robe, nor perform a ritual of pure giving (*śuddhaka-dāna*), nor give it away to another;
and on the eleventh day, at the appearance of the dawn, [the offense is incurred].
According to the number of robes [received], there is an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If the robes received together are insufficient, and by the eleventh day the robes received together become sufficient, then on that eleventh day one must cut and sew them into a robe.
Whether using thread to join them, or whether not cutting and sewing them into a robe, or whether not joining them with thread—if [one does not do so]...

If one performs a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*) but does not give it away to another person, then at the appearance of the dawn on the twelfth day, one incurs the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) according to the number of robes possessed.
This applies even up until the twenty-ninth day when the full set of robes is complete; the case is the same.

If the robes are insufficient, whether within thirty days they are sufficient or insufficient, whether they are robes of the same kind or not of the same kind, one must that very day cut, sew, and make them into robes, or even give them away to another.
If one does not cut them, or does not give them away, until the dawn of the thirty-first day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; this [robe] must be relinquished.
The fallen robe should be relinquished to the Saṃgha—whether to many people or to a single person. It must not be relinquished to a separate group;
if it is relinquished [in such a manner], the relinquishment is invalid, and there is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, after the robe has been relinquished within the Saṃgha, it is not returned; or if, at the time of its return, someone instructs that it not be returned;

or if it is not returned and is instead made into a *pariśuddha-dāna* (pure gift); or if it is sent to another person; or if it is taken to make the three robes (*tricīvara*); or if it is made into a *pārikkāra-cīvara* (miscellaneous robe);

or if it is intentionally damaged; or if it is burned; or if it is made into something that is not a robe; or if it is worn repeatedly until it is ruined—in all these cases, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Luo: Regarding this precept, the methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning the robe and so forth are explained in detail within the section on "Practicing and Maintaining.
This precept constitutes a full offense only when four conditions are met: first, harboring greed and arrogance; second, the acquisition of sufficient robe-material.

It is not permitted during the three periods [of the day]. Fourth, it is a violation if one accepts and keeps [the robe] without sewing it, or if one gives it as an impure gift and lets the period expire.
This is also governed by the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for *bhikṣuṇīs* (governed and studied together). For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
These constitute an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: If one has sufficient robe-cloth within ten days; or if one cuts it; or if one joins it with thread; or if one sews it into a robe;
or if one lacks sufficient robe-cloth until the eleventh day when it becomes sufficient—in these cases, one must cut it and so forth.
This applies likewise up to the twenty-ninth day. On the thirtieth day, whether the cloth is sufficient or insufficient, or whether it is the same [as before], [one commits an offense].
The same applies to the requirement that it be cut and so forth on that very day. There is no offense if one takes and wears [the robe] after it has been stolen, lost, burnt, or washed away;
or if another gives it to one to wear; or if one makes it for someone else; or if the monk who was entrusted with the robe passes away, travels far away, or there are circumstances of difficulty;
or if one does not cut it and so forth; or if it was prior to the initial promulgation of the precept. These constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the collection [of robes], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu obtains a robe that is insufficient, he may set it aside in the hope of obtaining more.

On the day he actually receives the robe, if he does not obtain what he had hoped for, yet neither abandons his hope nor ceases his seeking, and he continues to strive diligently, then his expectation is indeed "hope.
Furthermore, if he abandons his non-hope and subsequently obtains this robe, he must make it into a finished garment within ten days. If...
If it is sufficient, it is well; if it is insufficient, one should wait, even up to thirty days, and it is likewise so.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If on the twenty-ninth day one obtains the expected robe—whether it be a fine *pūrva-cīvara* or a coarse *pūrva-cīvara*..."

Regarding the declaration of purity (*śuddhi*) for newly acquired robes, one may further retain them for one month because of the desire for conformity. If one anticipates obtaining coarse robes, one may likewise retain them for another month.
In this manner, proceeding by successive stages according to one's preference, it is done out of a desire for conformity; however, it must not exceed one month.
This precept, within the Mahāyāna, is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; therefore, it does not prohibit their possession or maintenance.
However, if one possesses them for oneself alone and does not bestow them as gifts upon others, one also incurs the fault of being stingy, greedy, and hoarding excessively.
The fourth: The precept on taking robes from a nun.
If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: This precept was established in three stages. The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha.
There was a bhikṣu wearing a worn-out, patched saṃghāṭī. When the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā saw it, she [made a request].
Feeling compassion, he immediately removed the expensive *saṃghāṭī* he was wearing and gave it to him, taking the other’s worn-out *saṃghāṭī* in exchange to wear himself.
On another occasion, he went to pay respects to the World-Honored One. Knowing the situation, the World-Honored One asked him intentionally, "Why is the robe you are wearing so worn out?
He explained the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should not act in this way."

"I permit you to keep and possess five robes that are complete and sturdy. As for other robes, you may dispose of them as you wish—either by giving them away or through the ritual of pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*).
Why? Because even when women wear fine garments, they are still not considered beautiful; how much less so with tattered clothes.
Thereupon, he assembled the community of monks and first established this precept. Subsequently, all the bhikṣus were cautious and fearful, and did not dare to accept [robes] from their relatives.
A bhikṣuṇī took a robe. The Buddha said: "If she is not a relative, one cannot deliberate upon it to know whether it may be taken or not, nor its quality—whether it is fine or coarse, new or old.
However, if she is a relative, one can deliberate upon it to know its presence or absence, whether it may be taken or not, and its quality—whether it is fine or coarse, old or new.
Therefore, I permit [a monk] to take a robe from a relative bhikṣuṇī. This is the rule.
Second is the establishment of the precept regarding robes. Furthermore, within the Jetavana, the two divisions of the Saṃgha received donated robes.

When they were being divided, the bhikṣus mistakenly received the robes of the bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs mistakenly received the robes of the bhikṣus. The bhikṣuṇīs took their robes to the monastery and exchanged them.
The bhikṣus again informed the World-Honored One; therefore, he permitted their exchange. This was the third establishment of a precept. This is...
This is a *pratikṣepaṇasāvadya* (prohibited offense). This training rule was established due to the mind of greedy attachment.

Regarding the explanation of its meaning, the text is divided into two sections. From the phrase "if not from a relative" (*apratisaṃstutāyāḥ*) onwards, it clarifies what constitutes an offense, with the exception of trade.

This clarifies the distinctions made according to the circumstances. The Vinaya states: "Those who are not relatives" refers to those who are not relatives on the father's or mother's side, extending back through seven generations.
"Relatives" refers to those who are relatives on the father's or mother's side, extending back through seven generations. [Regarding] "neighbors": five households constitute a neighborhood.

Five neighboring households constitute a *li*. It is also said that *li* means "to stop," for fifty families dwell together therein. A father has six kin: paternal uncles, brothers, sons, and grandsons. A mother has six kin: paternal aunts, maternal aunts, brothers, and their children and grandchildren.

The seven generations refer to the great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father, son, grandson, and great-grandson. There are ten kinds of clothing as mentioned above. Regarding trade: it refers to exchanging clothing for clothing.

One exchanges clothing for what is not clothing; or one trades what is not clothing for clothing; or one trades with a needle, a needle-case, a knife, thread, small articles, or even a single pill of medicine, and so forth, to obtain clothing.
Regarding the offense: among these, the transgression is as follows—excluding cases of exchange—if a bhikṣu takes the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

The procedures for relinquishing the robe, performing the confession (*pratideśanā*), and returning the robe are explained in the section on "Practicing and Maintaining" (*karmavācanā*). If, after having relinquished the robe, one does not return it, [the offense remains].
The offenses incurred are as stated above.
This precept constitutes a full offense only when five conditions are met: first, there is a mind of greed, attachment, or prideful instruction;
second, the object is a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative; third, one perceives her as a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative; fourth, the items are not for barter.
The five robes and their materials must be of the prescribed measure.

This also constitutes an offense for a bhikṣuṇī (a *duṣkṛta* offense; the rule is the same, though the training is different). For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is defined as an infraction.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: taking robes from a relative nun; trading them for the sake of the Sangha or the Buddha’s shrine;
and cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute no offense.

Regarding the acquisition [of robes], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, and although he has agreed to exchange it, he does not give it himself, nor does he instruct another to give it;

nor does he personally tell the bhikṣuṇī, "I shall give you this robe at such a time," nor does he instruct someone else to say this to her; yet, if he returns the bhikṣuṇī’s original robe [to her], this is [an offense].
One should give it; one should give another robe. Having cut the original robe and returned it, this is not called "exchanging" (meaning that after the nun's robe has been cut, it is then returned).
Having obtained that whole robe, to give a diminished robe in return is not called "giving. One should give a complete and sufficient robe.
Having taken that robe, to give a bowl—whether a small bowl, a *kaṇḍārika*, or food and drink—and so forth.
Giving other items [in exchange] does not constitute a trade; one should give the robe itself.

If a bhikṣu takes the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and does not pay its value, nor instruct someone to pay it, nor speak of it himself, nor instruct another to speak of it, and then departs, leaving the range of sight and hearing, he commits a pāyattika offense. This applies even if, after taking the robe, he does not pay its value, and so forth.
One must not instruct another in speech; whether sitting, lying down, or entering meditative concentration, [to do so] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative gives a robe to a familiar śrāmaṇera, saying: "Śrāmaṇera, I give this robe to you;
take this robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu, and you will obtain merit," and the bhikṣu accepts it—[this is an offense].
Being free from fault, one should speak thus to a familiar śrāmaṇerī, śikṣamāṇā, upāsaka, or upāsikā:
"I give this robe to you; you should take this robe and offer it to the venerable bhikṣu [Name]."
One may acquire merit. For a bhikṣu who takes [an item], there is no offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: To take clothing from a non-relative śikṣamāṇā or śrāmaṇerī constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
If one takes clothing from a relative who has violated the precepts or holds wrong views, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: If one perceives a person who is not a relative as a relative, or suspects that a person who is not a relative is a relative, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, or suspects that a relative is a non-relative, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a nun gives a robe to the Saṃgha, or gives it while preaching the Dharma for them, or when she is receiving full ordination, or gives it because she has seen [the monk] being robbed,
or if the nun, having received much gain and support, takes her clothing and belongings to the place of the bhikṣu, places them on the ground, requests that he accept them, and then departs—
taking them in such circumstances constitutes no offense.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "To accept clothing that is of the proper measure constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; to accept clothing or other items that are not of the proper measure constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding this precept, the Mahāyāna does not distinguish between whether the donor is a relative or a non-relative; rather, it simply considers whether the gift is acceptable or unacceptable."
In the final age, one must carefully guard the Dharma-gate and especially avoid all grounds for suspicion.
Fifth is the precept regarding having a nun who is not a relative wash one's clothes:
if a bhikṣu has a nun who is not a relative wash an old garment, or dye it, or beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Pāyattika. Origin Story:

This precept has two levels of enactment. When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Venerable Kālodāyin and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā sat with their bodies uncovered, looking at one another with lustful intent.
The Venerable One subsequently discharged semen, which soiled his *antaravāsaka*. A nun requested that he wash it for her.
Having obtained this garment, she immediately took some of the semen with her fingernails in a secluded place and placed it both in her mouth and in her urinary tract.

Consequently, she became pregnant. When the other nuns questioned her and learned the reason, they reported the matter to the World-Honored One. The monks, in turn, informed the World-Honored One, who rebuked Kālī.

[The Buddha] said, "Light! This was the first establishment of the precept. Thereupon, the bhikṣus were each cautious and fearful, not daring to have their relatives—nuns—wash, dye, or beat their old clothes.
Out of compassion, the Buddha granted permission, further adding the words "non-relative.
This was the second establishment of the precept. Because it was established to eliminate the affliction of lustful defilement, it constitutes the first section on sexual misconduct.
The fundamental category. Explanation of the meaning:
The Vinaya states that "non-relatives" are as described above. Regarding "old clothing," it refers to any garment that has once been worn on the body (the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"that which has stains or grease on its surface is called old clothing"). There are ten types of clothing, as described above (the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "one may have a female renunciant, even down to a granddaughter, wash them").

One must not have a female relative who has left the household life—such as a daughter-in-law or a wife—wash [the robes] (unless she is a blood relative). Regarding washing, dyeing, and beating: the *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states that "washing" refers even to immersing them once in water;
"dyeing" refers even to placing them once into a dye solution; and "beating" refers even to striking them once with the hand or tapping them once.

**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe, or dye it, or beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) for all three acts.
If she washes, dyes, but does not beat it, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *duṣkṛta*.
If she washes it but does not dye or beat it, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *duṣkṛta*. If she... [does not wash... [text continues]
If one causes [a nun] to wash, dye, or beat [the cloth], there are two *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses and one *duṣkṛta*. If she does not wash, dye, or beat it, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.

(The robe is forfeited once; this constitutes a pure *pāyattika* offense. Depending on whether there are three, two, or one [of the actions], one must perform confession. If one causes a nun who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat a new robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning robes under this precept are explained within the section on "Active Observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). If one has relinquished a robe and fails to return it, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept constitutes a full offense only when four conditions are met: first, the recipient is a nun who is not a relative; second, she possesses lustful attachment.
1. The mind [is set upon it]. 2. It is an old garment. 3. It has already been washed, dyed, and beaten. 4. Having finished washing, dyeing, and beating it.

This also constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* (the rule is the same, though the training is different). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. These constitute an offense.
Regarding those cases where there is no offense: if one washes, dyes, or beats a garment for a relative; if one washes, dyes, or beats it because it is an old garment;
if one washes, dyes, or beats it because one is ill; if one washes, dyes, or beats it for the sake of the Saṃgha or a Buddhist monastery (stūpa); if one washes, dyes, or beats a borrowed garment;
or if it was prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one instructs a non-relative to wash, dye, or beat [the robe], yet a relative washes, dyes, or beats it;
or if one instructs a non-relative to wash, dye, or beat it, yet a relative and a non-relative together wash, dye, or beat it;
or if one instructs both a relative and a non-relative to wash, dye, or beat it, yet the relative washes, dyes, or beats it..."
If one has a relative and a non-relative wash, dye, and beat [the cloth] together, yet it is the non-relative who washes, dyes, and beats it;

or if one has a relative and a non-relative wash, dye, and beat them together, yet both the relative and the non-relative wash, dye, and beat them together—in all such cases, one commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If the robe is not yet fit for washing, dyeing, or beating, yet one has a non-...

If one causes a relative to wash, dye, or beat [the robes], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one causes a relative to wash, dye, or beat them, but they are not a relative to perform the washing, dyeing, or beating, there is no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: If it is a nun who is not a kinsman, and one perceives her as not being a kinsman, yet causes her to wash, dye, or beat [the robes], one commits an offense.

Regarding the offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*): if it concerns a nun who is not a relative, yet one suspects she is so, it is also an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If it concerns a nun who is a relative, yet one perceives her as not being a relative, or if one harbors doubt regarding a nun who is a relative, in both cases one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one causes a nun to wash a robe on behalf of one's upādhyāya or ācārya, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one first washes it oneself and then further orders [the nun] to wash, dye, or beat it, these are all *duṣkṛta* offenses."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Regarding this precept, whether the robes are of measured size or unmeasured size, all constitute an offense.
The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one causes a nun who is not a relative to wash a *niṣīdana*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if she washes a rug, a pillow, or similar items, it is a *duṣkṛta*."

The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one is old or ill and lacks the strength [to wash], or if a bhikṣuṇī, out of reverence and respect, wishes to wash it for one's sake, or if it is a disciple—none of these cases constitute an offense."
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna alike. Internally, it protects the monastic regulations; externally, it silences worldly censure.
Examination of the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If a robe must be washed, one should either wash it oneself or have a disciple do so, but not with such lack of care that the robe is damaged.
Generally, there are five benefits to washing robes: they remove foul odors..."
The cloth is light; lice and nits do not breed upon it; the body is free from itching; it readily accepts dye; and it is fit for long-term use.
Conversely, failing to wash the garment results in five disadvantages. Wearing dyed robes also has five benefits: it accords with the physical appearance and deportment of the noble ones (*ārya*);
it causes one to abandon arrogance; it prevents the accumulation of dust and grime; it prevents the breeding of lice and nits; and it is soft to the touch.
Because soft [robes] are easy to maintain, there are five faults in washing them excessively: they cause rapid deterioration; they become unfit for hard use;
they cause mental fatigue in their enjoyment; they involve useless toil; and they obstruct various wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, there are five faults in wearing fine dyed robes: they increase one's own arrogance and conceit, and they give rise to envy in others.
Therefore, it causes others to perceive one as having a seductive appearance and a lustful nature; it causes great hardship and toil when seeking [a spouse];
it obstructs the cultivation of wholesome qualities; and through excessive attachment, it damages clothing and renders it unfit for use. Excessive beating also has five faults.
In this regard, furthermore, because the bhikṣu Nanda had beaten his robe excessively, the Buddha said: "One who uses robes should not beat them, nor beat them excessively.

If one receives from a donor a robe that has been beaten excessively (meaning it has been carefully pounded until it becomes glossy), and it possesses a fine luster, one should soften it before using it.
Or, one may place it in the open air and rub it to cause the luster to fade; or one may use water."
It is used by sprinkling and soaking. Thus we know that it prohibits excessive beating (excessive beating meaning extreme beating), but does not prohibit beating altogether.
The sixth precept regarding begging for robes from those who are not relatives:
If a bhikṣu begs for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except during the [designated] time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. "At other times" refers to when a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost, burned, or carried away by water;
this is called "at other times.
Regarding the origin of this precept, there were six enactments. The Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī. There was an elder who, at dawn...
In the morning, he went to the garden. Having finished his tour and inspection, he turned his carriage toward the Jetavana Monastery.
There he saw the Śākya son Upananda paying homage and listening to the Dharma. As Upananda preached the Dharma to instruct and transform him, he exhorted him with joy. The elder then asked:
"What do you require? Please tell me. He replied, "I require nothing. The elder pressed him insistently, saying, "If you have anything you need, do not hesitate.
He replied, "Stop, stop! Even if I were to have something I required, you would not be able to give it to me.
The elder requested again, whereupon he said, "You may take what you are wearing. The elder was himself dressed in costly garments.
"A broad and long white cotton cloth of high value. The householder replied, "Come to my home tomorrow; I shall give it to you.
Upananda said, "I told you before that even if you had what was required, you could not give it to me;
now the result is as I said. The householder said, "It is not that I will not give it to you; it is simply that you must come tomorrow. If [you come], I will give this to you."
[The Buddha said: "A robe, or even one of better quality—if I were to immediately take this robe and give it to you, I would not be able to enter the city without a robe.

Nanda pressed his request persistently and would not stop. The elder was displeased, yet he took off his robe and gave it to him. He then mounted his carriage, wearing only a single garment, and entered the city.
The gatekeeper suspected that he had been robbed by bandits. The elder explained the circumstances in detail. The laypeople (gṛhapati) then criticized and disparaged him.

This means that although donors give without weariness, the recipients should know contentment. Because the Buddha knew this, he established the rule that one must not solicit robes from householders;
this was the first formulation of the precept. Thereupon, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to solicit robes from their own relatives who were householders.
The World-Honored One then permitted them to beg for them; this was the second formulation of the precept.
Later, a great number of bhikṣus, having completed their summer retreat in the kingdom of Kosala, took their robes and bowls and set out for the place where the World-Honored One was.
Because it was too hot to travel during the day, they traveled by night and consequently lost the correct path.
They were plundered by bandits and stood outside the gate of the Jetavana with their bodies exposed. The bhikṣus suspected them of being Nirgranthas and informed Upāli, who then questioned them.
Knowing the reason for this, he immediately borrowed a robe and went to see the Buddha. After the Buddha had comforted him with inquiries, he fully explained the circumstances.

The Buddha then established a precept: it is a *duṣkṛta* offense to walk about naked. At such times, one should cover one's body with soft grass or tree leaves and proceed to the vicinity of the monastery.
If a long robe (*saṃghāṭī*) is already available, one should take it and wear it; if not, those who know [the rules]...

If a fellow bhikṣu has an extra robe, he should take it and wear it. If he knows that his companion has no robe, he should ask the Saṃgha what kind of robes are available for distribution; if there are any, they should be given. If there are none, he should ask whether there are any bedding materials.
"If there is [something], it should be given. If it is not given, one should personally open the storehouse and look.
If there are mats, floor coverings, cotton cloths, or blankets, one should tear them apart, take them, and cut them into robes to cover one's body while going out to beg for robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to take items from this place to go to that place. When the Buddha said, "I permit [it]," the bhikṣus...

The Buddha’s robes were taken away, lost, burned, or washed away by the river; fearing and being cautious, he did not dare to wear the robe belonging to the Saṃgha. The Buddha said, "I permit you to wear it.
After he had obtained that robe, he did not return the Saṃgha robe to its original place. The Buddha said, "This should not be done.

Once you have obtained [the new] robe, you should wash, dye, and sew it, and then restore the [original] robe to its proper place. If one does not do so, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma. At that time, there was a bhikṣu...

Regarding the loss of robes through theft, misplacement, fire, or being carried away by water, [the monks] were fearful and cautious, not daring to ask for robes from non-relatives—whether laymen or laywomen.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to ask. Thus, there arose the exception of "other times" and so forth.

Therefore, this precept was first established as a strict prohibition, but subsequently underwent six successive revisions of the rule to provide accommodations; this was due to the arising of afflictions.
This causes distress and makes others unhappy, while increasing one’s own greedy seeking. This training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established due to incidents involving derision and suspicion.
**Explanation of the Meaning:** The text is divided into two sections. From the phrase "if not a relative" (*na saṃstuta*) onwards, it clarifies what constitutes an offense.

From the phrase "except at other times" (*anyatra samayāt*) onwards, it clarifies the exceptions to the rule. The Vinaya states: "Relatives and non-relatives are as described above for householders; begging is as described above."

This refers to obtaining [robes] by begging from them. The previous fourth precept prohibits begging from renunciants; among renunciants, the rule was established specifically regarding *bhikṣuṇīs*. This precept prohibits begging from householders;

among householders, regardless of whether they are male or female, it is not permitted to beg from anyone who is not a relative. There are ten types of robes. Regarding "except at other times" as mentioned above (this means that in cases of hardship, begging is permitted).

Regarding "having one's robes taken away" (*ācchinnacīvara*): the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, "If a king takes them, if bandits take them, if a woman takes them out of lustful desire, or if parents or relatives take them..."

"Desiring to cause him to renounce the path, he took away [the robe]. Regarding the loss of the robe: this refers to losing it oneself, or hiding the robe and later forgetting its location, or hiding it for so long that it becomes rotten and cannot be worn.
Regarding the burning of the robe: this refers to its being consumed by fire. Regarding the drifting away of the robe: this refers to its being carried off by water."
Regarding the determination of the offense: herein, the transgression constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for a bhikṣu.

The procedures for relinquishing the robe, performing the confession (*pratideśanā*), and returning the robe are clarified within the section on "Practicing and Maintaining" (*karmavastu*). If, after having relinquished the robe, one does not return it, the offense is as described above.

This precept requires five conditions to constitute the full offense: first, teaching out of greed for gain or pride; second, begging when no hardship exists; third, the recipient being not a relative;
fourth, the price, color, and dimensions being as requested; and fifth, the robe having already come into one's possession.
Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (the same rule applies to those of common training). For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if one's robes have been stolen, lost, burned, or carried away by water;
if one begs from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative; if one begs from a relative;

if one begs from a fellow renunciant (the term "fellow renunciant" excludes those ordained in other paths); or if one begs on behalf of another, or if another begs for one's sake; or if one obtains them without having asked; and...
In the beginning, before the precepts were established, these [acts] constitute no offense.

As recorded in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "If a bhikṣu begs for clothing from one who is not a relative—whether he goes himself to beg, sends another to beg, or begs by making gestures of cold or heat—what is the gesture of cold? If a bhikṣu..."

During the winter months, when it snows at night (the reason for specifying "night" is that in the time reckoning of the Western Regions, time is not expressed in terms of days, but rather discussed in terms of nights), one should put on worn-out old clothes and go to the house of a donor (*dānapati*), manifesting the appearance of shivering from the cold. At that time, the donor prostrates at one's feet and asks:
"Ācārya, do you have no seasonal robes? Why are you so frozen? One replies: "I had none while your parents were still alive."
"You have always made robes for me at the proper times. Now that your parents have passed away, who will make them for me?
"It is not only your parents who have died; my own parents have also met with impermanence. The donor then said, "Do not harbor resentment."

"I shall make a seasonal garment for you. This is called begging under the pretext of cold. If he obtains a robe through this, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).

What is the pretext of heat? If, during the great heat of the fifth or sixth month, a bhikṣu wears a thick woolen robe and perspires, he goes to the house of a donor and manifests the appearance of heat, speaking as above.
If he obtains a robe through this, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. If he says...
The Request for Dharma. How does one preach the Dharma? For the sake of robes, this bhikṣu recites a verse to a donor, saying:
"One who gives clothing shall be born in the most excellent place; One who delights in the act of giving receives the karmic reward of humans and devas.
Born in heaven, they obtain a beautiful form, Adorned with celestial jewel crowns."
Because of giving robes to a bhikṣu, one naturally obtains robes in every birth;
this is called "begging for the sake of the Dharma. If one obtains [such a robe], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If one begs for a water-strainer, a small patch for clothing, a head-tie, a bandage for a wound, a seam-strip for a robe, or a single strip of cloth within a robe, in all such cases [the same applies].
No offense: if one begs on behalf of one's *upādhyāya*, or on behalf of one's *ācārya*. An offense of *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya):
if one begs on behalf of a *stūpa* or the Saṃgha.
No offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are three kinds of offenses, namely: price, color, and measure. Regarding "price": if a bhikṣu speaks to a householder...
If a layperson gives me a garment of high value, if I obtain that garment, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if I do not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This applies even down to a garment worth two hundred or three hundred coins; the offense is likewise [in these cases]. (This refers to the large coins of the Western Regions, as explained previously in the section on the precept against stealing.)

Regarding color: if a bhikṣu says to a householder, "Give me a blue garment," or a yellow, red, white, or black garment, or even a garment of cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) and so forth—the offense is likewise. Regarding measurement: if a bhikṣu says to a householder...
If one requests from another a robe of four cubits, five cubits, six cubits, or even up to eighteen cubits, and the offense is likewise incurred;
or if one requests a robe of such a color and measurement, yet receives something else instead—these are all *dukkaṭa* (offenses of wrong-doing).
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: At the time of begging, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

Regarding the robes obtained—if their price, color, or measurement correspond to what was requested, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture); if they do not correspond, there is no offense.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: If two people together beg for a single garment, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing).
To solicit from a relative who is impoverished is a *duṣkṛta*. To solicit more after having been given a small amount is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one is not a relative and was previously invited to give a garment—“invited” meaning that one did not go to beg but the other person spontaneously offered it—and subsequently solicits from them when they are impoverished, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To give... [is a *duṣkṛta*].

If one requests more than was initially asked for, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. To request on behalf of another is also a *duṣkṛta* offense. (According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, if one seeks on behalf of another, there is no offense, provided it does not originate from one's own mind but rather follows the instructions of another.

However, according to the *Sarvāstivāda*, both cases constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is because, seeing the poverty of others, one fails to give rise to compassion; instead, desiring that they act for one's sake, one employs such expedient means. This refers to the noble regulations which, based on conditions, investigate causes to determine what is permitted or prohibited.)

This precept is for the sake of sentient beings within the Mahāyāna. Although the training may differ, one must nevertheless deliberate upon whether a donor is capable or incapable of giving, and whether [the gift] is acceptable or unacceptable;
thus, one should skillfully protect the minds of others and cause their pure faith to increase.
Appendix: Examination of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu has a robe within a distance of three *yojanas*, if he loses his *saṃghāṭī* or *uttarāsaṅga*, he should not beg for one.
If he loses his *saṃghāṭī* or *uttarāsaṅga*, but his *antarvāsaka* remains, he should not beg for one.
If he loses all three robes, but his *vraṇapaṭṭa* (wound-covering cloth) remains, he should not [beg for them]."
If one has lost the three robes, the wound-covering robe, or the rain-bathing robe, one should not beg for them.
If one has lost the three robes, the wound-covering robe, or the rain-bathing robe, but the bedding and mats are still present, one should not beg for them.

If one has lost the three robes, down to the bedding and mats, but the surplus cloth (surplus cloth refers to the remaining materials sufficient to make a robe) remains—measuring two cubits in length and one [cubit] in width—one should not beg for them.
The cubit. One should not beg for it. Why? Because this bhikṣu should go wearing these lower robes. He may receive his previous robes within a distance of three yojanas.
If there are various obstacles on the way such that he cannot reach the robes, he may beg for them;
there is no offense.
*Vinaya-zhichi-huiji*, Scroll Five, Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings: Yama Heaven.
"Yama" is translated here as "Good Time" (*shan-shi*). It is also called "Time-Portion" (*shifen*), meaning that at every moment they proclaim [the Dharma].
Because it is joyful, they distinguish day and night by the opening and closing of lotus flowers. This deity dwells suspended in space.
According to the treatise, two hundred human years constitute one day and night for this deity;
thus, seventy-two thousand human years constitute one year for this deity. If the lifespan of this deity is two thousand such years, that corresponds to [human time]...
It has been fourteen hundred and four million years.
"Pingfu" (屏覆) means that which screens and that which covers; "ping" is for the purpose of concealing, and "fu" is a lid or canopy.
"Zhai Upāsikā": "zhai" is its name, or it refers to one who observes the eight precepts of the fast. Upā—
*Posi* (婆私) is sometimes written as *upāsī*, which is the same as *upāsikā*. Master Xuanzang says that *upāsikā* means "female lay follower" (*jìnshì nǚ*) in the language of Tang;
this refers to one who draws near to and serves the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
If a woman living at home has received the three refuges and the five precepts, she is then able to personally serve the community of Buddhist nuns. [Old]...
The terms *upāsaka* and *upāsikā* are both corruptions. Some say that one who observes the eight precepts is called a *upāsikā*, meaning she dwells near (*upāsika*) the Arhats.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states: "One who observes the eight precepts for one day and one night is called a *kalyāṇī-upāsikā* (virtuous female lay follower), because this person, with a virtuous mind, dwells apart from the breaking of precepts."
Viśākhāmātṛ (or Vaiśākha) is translated as "Distinct Branch" (*biezhi*); it refers to the lunar mansion *Ārdrā*.
She was named after the constellation under which she was born. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Viśākhā’s husband was named Mṛgāra.
Mṛgāra revered Viśākhā just as he revered his mother. Consequently, people of the time called her 'Viśākhā-Mṛgāra'."
Regarding the mother and son: the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states that he was the younger brother of King Prasenajit and the son of Dharmaghoṣa.
In the past, Dharmaghoṣa fled from his country due to a crime and reached the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, where he settled and took a wife.
Thus this daughter was born. This daughter possessed eloquence and wisdom; later, she married the minister Viśākha of Śrāvastī as his seventh son’s wife.
King Prasenajit, having heard of her wisdom and eloquence, immediately appointed her as his sister-in-law.
Afterwards, thirty-two eggs were born; from each egg emerged a child, whose countenances were dignified and handsome, and who were peerless in their valor and strength.
The prowess of a single man could match a thousand men. At that time, Viśākhā’s faith was awakened and her understanding opened; she invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and the entire family attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Later, when the Buddha again preached the Dharma for them, they immediately attained [Arhatship].
Among the upāsikās, Anāgāmī was foremost in wisdom and eloquence.
Kuīyīnhuāi tilted her head from within the doorway and looked askance.
The term for "light-omen" (*mingxiang*) in Sanskrit is *aruṇa*. The *Śīla-vibhaṅga* (Shanjian lü) states: "*Arūna* in the Han language means 'light-omen'.
The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā-bhāṣya* (Tonghui zhigui) states: "In this region, dawn is defined as two *kē* before the sun rises;
this constitutes the light-omen. Furthermore, it is also limited by the point at which the lines on the palm become visible.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this is called "the time when the earth is clearly perceived," meaning that the colors of the earth are seen with clarity.
Furthermore, to the north of this Jambudvīpa, there is a great king of trees named Jambūnada-gold. When the sun shines upon that tree, it appears black;
when it shines upon its leaves, they appear green; and when it passes the tree and shines upon the realm of Jambudvīpa, [it appears yellow].
Thus, there is the color white; among the three colors, white is the primary one.
"To bring calamity upon oneself" means that sorrow and distress are all created by oneself and are not related to external matters.
It is what is meant by the saying: "One who commits their own misdeeds cannot survive."

The "Six Groups of Monks" (Ṣaḍvargika), also known as the "Sixfold Assembly," refers to those who gather in groups to perform various acts contrary to dignified decorum, entering and departing in large parties. They are: first, Nanda; second, Upananda; and third, Kālodāyin.
Caturdanta, Aśvinī, and Pūrṇa—these six men were without anything they did not understand;

they were thoroughly versed in the inner teachings of the Tripiṭaka and were highly proficient in the arts and crafts of the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*). Nanda and Upananda were both excessively greedy, though some say they were also excessively wrathful;
they were skilled in mathematics, the movements of the yin and yang, and in expounding the Dharma and engaging in debate.

Kālodāyin was characterized by excessive desire and was profoundly skilled in the way of archery; he attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) after studying the Abhidharma and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Channa was characterized by excessive anger—and it is also said he had excessive delusion—and was likewise skilled in the way of archery;
he understood the Abhidharma and later attained the exhaustion of outflows, becoming an Arhat. Aśvaka and Punarvasu were characterized by excessive delusion, and they too...
He was said to be prone to anger. He was skilled in music and various forms of humor; he was capable in all matters and adept at preaching the Dharma and engaging in debate.
He also understood the Abhidharma. These six men were all from noble families; they influenced one another and formed a close bond as friends.
They propagated the Buddha’s teachings, serving as the pillars of the Dharma-gate within and acting as the upholders of the Buddhist religion without.

They are great protectors, meaning they manifest through great skillful means (*mahopāya*). Each has his own disciples; nine people together constitute sixty, and for this reason they are called the "Group of Six" (*ṣaḍvargika*) bhikṣus.
*Śuṣka-śoṣa* refers to the disease of thirst; it is also called the disease of parched withering, because one's skin and flesh become emaciated.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* calls it the "disease of total depletion. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that there is a worm named "Fat-Biter" (*meda-bhakṣaka*) which dwells within the fat channels inside the body.
If one commits excesses or sleeps too much, this worm becomes enraged and does not [consume the fat].
It causes the digestion of food and drink to fail, or gives rise to diseases such as scabies or consumption (śoṣa).
Regarding the method of planting trees in the Western Regions, one tree is planted at intervals of seven *dhanus* between eight trees.
For eight trees, there are only seven intervals. Seven times seven amounts to forty-nine *dhanus*.

Taking four *hasta* of an average person as one *dhanu*, with eighteen *cun* making one *hasta*, and seventy-two *cun* making one *dhanu*, forty-nine *dhanu* (seven times seven) total thirty-five *zhang*, two *chi*, and eight *cun*. Whether it be without boundary markers or if it is circular...
The circumference is forty-nine *zhang* and one foot two inches; this constitutes the boundary.

According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, twenty-four finger-widths (*aṅgula*) of an average person constitute one cubit (*hasta*). This corresponds to the *hu* (official tablet) foot-measure: fifteen inches constitute one cubit.
The measurement of seven *dhanus* (bows) may be calculated accordingly. A cubit is measured from the elbow joint to the tip of the fingers.
The *Mūla-vinaya* of the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā states:
In the city of Takṣaśilā, there was an elder who, not long after marrying his wife, gave birth to a daughter. Her body possessed three virtues, like a blue utpala lotus.
First, his body was golden in color, like a flower garland. Second, his eyes were deep blue, like flower petals.
Third, his fragrance was rich and pervasive, like the scent of flowers. Because of these [characteristics], he was given the name Utpala (Blue Lotus).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: Her appearance was upright and handsome, and her complexion was the color of the *utpala* lotus.
In a time long ago, during many kalpas past, this person was a Brahmin girl. When her parents and family members went to sea to gather treasures, she remained behind;
unable to support herself, she lived together with various courtesans and sold her beauty to provide for her own needs.
This woman’s physical appearance was not beautiful, and no one ever came to visit her. She constantly reproached herself, wondering why she alone was so unfortunate.

At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha whom everyone revered and honored. Someone said to her, "If you can make offerings to the Pratyekabuddha, you will have whatever you desire in every lifetime, according to your wishes. Consequently, she prepared exquisite food and drink, using *utpala* [flowers].
She covered [the Buddha] above with *ro-hua* flowers and offered them to the Pratyekabuddha, immediately making this vow:
"May I, in every lifetime, always obtain the female form, being peerlessly beautiful and respected by all people; furthermore, may I attain the merits obtained by this śramaṇa."
"May I attain this. For that reason, in this present life, I was born as a woman with the most excellent countenance.

By virtue of my original vow, I have now attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and am praised by the Buddha; among the bhikṣuṇīs, I possess the greatest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and am the foremost."
Regarding the bhikṣuṇī who maintains the five robes: according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, they are:
first, the saṃghāṭī (i.e., the *saṃghāṭī*); second, the uttarāsaṅga (i.e., the *uttarāsaṅga*);
third, the antarvāsa (i.e., the *antarvāsa*); fourth, the kaṣāya (i.e., the *kaṣāya*, the lower garment); and fifth, [the saṃkakṣikā].
The *saṃkakṣikā* is the shoulder-covering garment; it is called the "arm-pit-concealing undergarment.
The *Huìzhèngjì* was authored by the Vinaya Master Yǔnkān of the Tang dynasty, and its text is frequently cited in the *Zīménjìngxùn*.
However, the complete work has not been seen; it is presumed to have already been lost.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā is also called Toulananda or Tulonanda.
According to the analysis, *sthūla* means "great" (*mahat*) and is also termed "coarse" (*audārika*); "coarse" carries the sense of "great. *Nanda* translates here as "joy" (*pramuditā*).
This bhikṣuṇī was proficient in and mastered the Tripiṭaka; she was skilled in preaching the Dharma and was the most eminent among the group of six bhikṣuṇīs.
She was the one known as Citrā. The *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-sūtra* states that she was the sister of Ānanda.
"Jiāhuìjié" (爪扴扴) has the phonetic value of "jiǎ" (甲). It refers to using the fingernails to scrape and gather impurities.
"Shēn" (娠) means being pregnant.
"Jīhuán Jīngshè" (祇桓精舍): "Jīhuán" (祇桓) is a corruption of "Jītá" (祇陀); this is translated as "Victorious Monastery" (勝精舍).

Regarding this, the *Śākyaputrīya-vamśa* (Shìjiā pǔ) states: "Because it is where those who have stilled their minds reside, it is called a *vihāra* (jingshè). Furthermore, it is said that it is not a place inhabited by the coarse or violent;

therefore, it is called a *vihāra*. The *Yìwén lèi* states: "It is not because the building itself is exquisite, but rather because it is the dwelling of practitioners who are refined and disciplined;
therefore, it is called a *vihāra*. According to the *Gǎntōng jì*, this refers to the foundation of the Jetavana Monastery.
The site consists of eighty *qǐng* of land and one hundred and twenty courtyards. Measured approximately from east to west, it is nearly ten *lǐ*;
from north to south, it is over seven hundred *bù*. It was constructed jointly by the two men, Jeta and Sudatta. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Sudatta took gold and spread it as he gathered it across the ground; within a single day, there were only five hundred *bù* of gold that had not yet been covered. Jeta...
Jeta then said to Sudatta, "As for the remaining area that has not yet been covered, there is no further need for gold. Please grant it to me;
I shall personally erect a gatehouse for the Buddha so that the Tathāgata may always pass through it when entering and leaving. The elder Jeta then built the gatehouse himself.
Within seven days, the elder Sudatta completed a great residence sufficient to accommodate three hundred people.
There are sixty-three meditation halls in quiet locations; the winter quarters and summer halls are each distinct from one another.
All necessary implements are fully provided. The *Faxian zhuan* states: "Going twelve hundred paces west of the southern gate of Śrāvastī city is the site where the elder Sudatta built a vihāra."
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* of the Kośala kingdom states: "The kingdom of Kośala is the birthplace of the Buddha.
As the Buddha said in a verse to King Bimbisāra: "There is a wondrous and excellent land situated at the edge of the Snowy Mountains;
Abundant, prosperous, and rich in various treasures, it is named Kośala. I was born therein, among the sons of the Śākyas of the Solar Lineage. [Heart]
Disgusted by old age, sickness, and death, he left the household life to seek the Buddha-way. Various sūtras state that the Buddha was born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu;
why, then, does this treatise say he was born in the kingdom of Kośala? However, Kośala is the name of a capital city.
Because it is adjacent to [Kapilavastu] and both belong to the same territory of Central India, [the two are treated as one].
*Nirgrantha*—translated here as "the detached" (*li xi*)—is the general name for non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*).
It is also called *Nigantha* or *Nigandha*; it should properly be transcribed as *Nikanlanta*, yet it is translated as "unfettered" (*bu xi*).
Those non-Buddhists (tīrthika) pluck out their hair and go naked, possessing no stored goods; they beg for food with their hands and eat whatever they obtain immediately.
*Yojana*—also called *yuzhen na*—is a name for a distance measurement in India. It is large.
The *Śāstra* states: "There are three distinctions regarding the *yojana*: the large is eighty *li*, the medium is sixty *li*, and the small is forty *li*.

The *Commentary on the Mūla-karman* says: "As for what is called a *yojana*, since there is no direct equivalent, its meaning corresponds to one postal station (*yi*) in the Eastern Land [China], which is approximately thirty-odd *li*.
The old term 'youxun' (yojan) is a corruption. If one follows the Western [tradition]..."
Regarding the local customs of the region: four *krośas* constitute one *yojana*. Calculating one *krośa*, it amounts to eight *li*;
thus, four [of them] amount to thirty-two *li*. We have now established this as the distance for a single postal station (*yì*), so that there may be no excessive delay from afar.

The *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) states: "This term has no direct equivalent [in Chinese]. It refers to a temporary lodging where a Wheel-Turning King halts during his tour of inspection, similar to the guesthouses and postal stations (*ganyou*) of this land.
The character for 'ye' (冶) is pronounced 'yǎ'; it means to adorn or decorate."
