Part Seven: The Precept on Contentedly Accepting Robes.
If a bhikṣu has lost his robes, had them stolen, burned them, or had them carried away by water,
and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative invites him and offers him many robes, that bhikṣu should receive the robes with contentment. If he accepts more than that,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Narrative: When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there were many bhikṣus who encountered bandits and lost their robes.
They came to the Jetavana Monastery, where a lay follower (upāsaka) heard of this and, knowing that they possessed many fine robes, followed after the bhikṣus.
[The monks] intended to take [the robes]. The bhikṣus replied, "Stop, stop! We have already made our offerings; we ourselves possess the three robes and do not need them.
The group of six bhikṣus said, "Venerable sirs, if your three robes are sufficient, why do you not take some and give them to us?
Or will you give them to others? When the bhikṣus then took [the robes] and gave them [to them], those who had few desires...

The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha regarding this precept: "This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Because of soliciting robes, afflictions arise, causing others distress and increasing one's own greed and seeking.
Due to such matters of reproach, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established."
Explanation of the Meaning: The text is divided into three sections. From "If one loses a robe, etc. downward, it clarifies the circumstances of difficulty.

From "If it is not a householder who is not a relative" downward, it clarifies the permitted exceptions. From "If [the time] exceeds this" downward, it establishes the offense incurred. The Vinaya states:
"Regarding those who are not relatives and the ten kinds of robes, as mentioned above: if one loses a single robe, one should not accept [another]; if one loses two robes..."
There remains one robe, or perhaps two, three, or four layers; these should be torn apart to make individual robes.
If all three robes are lost, that bhikṣu should accept only what is sufficient. There are two kinds of sufficiency:

first, the sufficiency of a householder, which is to accept whatever clothing a layperson provides (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: the upper garment of a layperson is eleven cubits long and three cubits wide; the lower garment is...).

Seven cubits in length and two cubits in width; one must not beg for more than this amount. This refers to the clothing materials used by laypeople, who provide them according to their own means, whether long or short.

A bhikṣu should not seek more than this. (The ancient measure used was the Zhou *chi*; one *chi* equals eighteen inches, and eight such inches constitute one cubit. Second, the three robes of the renunciant’s contentment (*tṛpti*). (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu’s upper robe is new, it should be made double-layered as a *saṃghāṭī*, measuring three cubits vertically and five cubits horizontally; this is the *saṃghāṭī*. If it is a *nivāsana*, also known as a *kūlacīvara*, it measures two cubits vertically and five cubits horizontally; this is the lower garment (*antaravāsaka*). The dimensions of the other two robes are as follows...")
What has been explained above concerns the amount of cloth for making robes by those who have left the household life; one must not seek more than this.

If a layperson (*gṛhapati*) offers robes at their own discretion—meaning a donor who possesses many robes invites the bhikṣus to take as much as they wish—this is not the same as the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation at the end of the summer retreat). If the cloth is fine, thin, or not durable, it should be taken and made into a robe.
If it is double, triple, or quadruple thickness, one should provide borders and attach patches on the shoulders to protect against dirt and grease.
In that place, one should install hooks and fastenings. If there is any remainder, one should ask the householder:
"What shall this remaining robe-material be cut and made into? If the donor says, "I did not give this to you because you lost your robe;

I gave it to you, Venerable Sir, of my own accord"—meaning, "It was not given as an inducement for recovering a lost robe, but is the surplus of wealth from my own spontaneous offering—why must you tell me? It is simply for the Venerable Sir to use as you please."
Regarding the offense: herein, if a bhikṣu accepts robes beyond the limit of sufficiency, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture).

The procedures for the forfeiture, confession, and the returning of the robe are explained in the section on "Practicing What Is Held. If, after having forfeited it, one does not return it, and so forth, [the respective offenses apply].
The offense is as described above.
This precept incurs the full offense only when three conditions are met: first, there is an invitation to accept offerings at will; second, one perceives the object and gives rise to greed;
and third, one accepts it without knowing contentment.
Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (the same rule applies to those of common training). For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if one takes only what is sufficient; if one takes less than what is sufficient; if a householder gives many robes;
if the material is fine, thin, or not durable; if one makes a robe of two, three, or four layers with borders, or adds patches to areas stained by grime and oil, or installs hooks and toggles;
or if there is a remainder and one asks the householder, "What shall I do with this? and so forth.
If [the rule] had not yet been established, and so forth, this constitutes no offense.
As the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu requests from another a layperson’s upper or lower garment..."

It is obtained according to the prescribed measure. If one begs for more, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); if one obtains it, there is an offense of forfeiture and expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If one begs for a monk’s upper and lower robes, the matter is likewise the same.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "If one begs for upper and lower robes from a layperson, even if they are insufficient, one should not beg further.

If one begs further, one incurs an offense (specifically, the *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of begging; the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense upon obtaining the robe). If there is a surplus, it need not be returned to the donor.
If one begs for upper and lower robes from a bhikṣu, if they are insufficient, one must beg further; if there is a surplus, it must be returned."

If one does not return it, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Some say that for a bhikṣu, "upper garments" refers to the three robes (*tricīvara*), while "lower garments" refers to the skirt (*antaravāsaka*).
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣuṇī loses five robes, she may receive two; if she loses four robes..."

One may accept a single robe. If one has lost the three robes, one must not accept [another]. However, if a friend or a donor makes a spontaneous invitation, or if it is one's own property, one may accept it as one pleases.
This precept of the Mahāyāna is for the sake of sentient beings; whatever is offered, one should accept it according to the invitation.
However, one must avoid censure and inspire faith; these cannot be dispensed with.

Citation: The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "If the three robes are stained with grease or filth upon the shoulder, one should substitute a patch at the spot where they rest on the shoulder.

It should be one and a half cubits (*hasta*) in length and one span (*vitasti*) in width (one span being the Buddha’s one *vitasti*, which is two chi and seven cun in length and one chi and six cun in width).
Sew it onto the four edges; when it becomes soiled, tear it off and wash it. This is from the *Tri-sahasra-vidhi*.
[One] patches the four corners.
Nowadays, those who make the three robes (tricīvara) all take a small square piece and patch it upon the shoulder, outside the area where grease and dirt collect;
this is called "Mount Sumeru. Furthermore, two small pieces are added to both sides, which are called...
Regarding the sun and moon, those [images] pasted on the four corners are called the Four Heavenly Kings; such errors as these—where do they appear in the Vinaya scriptures?
The eighth precept concerning the greed for begging:
if a bhikṣu, and a householder or a householder’s wife, prepares the price for a robe for a bhikṣu and buys such a robe to give to a certain [person]...
"O Bhikṣu, if a bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering (*pravāraṇā*), goes to a layperson's house and speaks thus:
'Excellent, layperson! Buy such and such a robe for me and give it to me, so that it may be fine,' and if he should obtain a robe [in this manner]..."
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. Origin Story:
This precept has two enactments. When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a certain bhikṣu who entered the city to beg for food.
He heard a householder and his wife discussing how they were preparing the price to buy a robe to give to Upananda. Upon returning...

He informed him. Upāli asked about his family and learned of it. The next day he went there and said, "If you wish to give me a robe, it should be made wide, large, new, fine, and sturdy, so that I may accept and wear it. The householder criticized and complained about this.
When the bhikṣus heard of it, they informed the Buddha. This was the first establishment of a precept. Thereafter, the householder acted according to his own will.
He invited a bhikṣu and asked him, "Venerable sir, what kind of robe do you require? At that time, the bhikṣu was hesitant in his mind and did not dare to answer.
Furthermore, there was a lay devotee who wished to make an expensive robe for the bhikṣu; this bhikṣu, however, had few desires and was content.
"One need not seek robes of great value; if one desires something inferior, there may still be hesitation and one may not dare to ask for it as one wishes.

The Buddha said: "If a householder allows a bhikṣu to seek whatever he desires, [the bhikṣu] should respond: 'From this day forward, we permit the bhikṣus to have few desires and know contentment, and thus to seek what is inferior.
Therefore, the previous phrase regarding not accepting invitations at will is added. This is the second formal enactment (niyama)."

This is the precept (*śīla*). It was established because [a monk] forcibly demanded fine robes, thereby causing mutual provocation and distress. This constitutes a category within the fundamental types of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) from the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].

Regarding the explanation of its meaning, the text is divided into three parts. The section beginning with "The householder" clarifies the private arrangement for procuring robes; the section beginning with "That bhikṣu... [clarifies the offense].
It is best for one to go personally to clarify the matter. If one obtains the robe-cloth and subsequently completes the transaction, an offense is incurred. The Vinaya states:

"A layman and a laywoman" (referring to a husband and wife of firm faith who, with a single mind, deliberate together to plant the seeds of merit). Regarding "the price of the robe": this refers to gold, silver, the seven treasures, and so forth (regarding the procurement of the robe-price:
"procurement" means to prepare and provide it in advance for storage). There are ten types of robes as mentioned above. There are two kinds of seekers.

1. Seeking a donor for the price: [The donor] provides a garment of great value, even increasing it by one *māṣaka* (one *māṣaka* in the Western Regions is equivalent to sixteen small coins in this region; "one part" here refers to one small coin). 2. Seeking the garment:
Speaking to a layperson, saying, "Make a garment of such width and length," even increasing it by one thread, saying, "Excellent, layperson! (This is praise and exhortation).

These are his words, intended to cause the donor to provide even more exquisite and refined items. "Such and such garments" refers to garments that are vast, new, fine, firm, and dense (firm meaning solid;

dense meaning compact and substantial). "For the sake of excellence" indicates that his current seeking is insatiable; this is precisely the mental state that serves as the cause for the karmic action.
Regarding the offense: among these, the violation occurs if a bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering (*pravāraṇā*), goes to seek a costly and wide robe.
If he obtains one, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; if he does not obtain one, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning robes under this precept are clarified within the section on "Active Observance. If one relinquishes them and fails to return them as required, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept fulfills three conditions before the full offense is established: first, the presence of a covetous intention; second, going in person to seek them out.
The third [condition] is that what was sought has already been obtained.

Furthermore, this rule applies equally to bhikṣuṇīs, for whom it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (the same rule and training as for the bhikṣus). For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This constitutes a transgression.
Regarding the exemptions for non-offenses: if one first accepts an invitation to a *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) and then goes to seek [food];
or if one seeks with moderation and in reduced amounts; or if one seeks from relatives, from renunciants, or seeks on behalf of another;
or if another seeks for one's sake; or if one obtains it without having sought it; as well as in cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the selection [of robes], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "As for 'being choosy,' there are three kinds of choosiness.
First, the choosiness of contentment: if one is given a fine robe, one says, 'I need a coarse one';
this is called the choosiness of contentment. Second, the choosiness of discontent: if one is given a coarse robe, one says, 'If you give me a coarse robe...'"
"It is not right to touch me; I am a person of high status. You should give me fine clothing. This is called the fault of being dissatisfied with what one has and desiring more.

If one commits this, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Third is the excellence of being content with coarse things: If one is given fine clothing, one says, "I do not need such fine clothing.
I am a forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*); like a deer, I dwell in the wilderness in an open space. If one is given coarse [clothing]... [one accepts it].

It is sufficient to ward off cold, heat, wind, and rain; this is called "coarse contentment. If one obtains such, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, if the required standard for contentment is not met, it is permitted to request [finer material];

however, if the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* provides fine thread while one requests coarse, one also commits an offense. Yet, the permission rests with the donor: if the donor first invited [the monk] at his own discretion and requested [material], but the robe has not yet been made, the offense lies with the donor. This is because when the robe is already finished, he requests coarse material again;

fearing that the donor might feel pressured or constrained, even if he gives it, the donor’s heart is not pleased. Regarding the permissions and prohibitions in the two Vinayas: one is intended to quell greed, regulating internally to eliminate evil; the other is intended to quell... [text ends].
[This was said] to censure [such behavior], to protect outsiders, and to increase their faith; it is not without profound significance.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To solicit fine items from one's relatives constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: If one sends a messenger, a letter, or a seal, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one asks for goods from a relative who has abundant wealth and many possessions, there is no fault; however, if [the relative] is poor, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one has previously invited a donor who has abundant wealth and property, and encourages them to prepare a fine meal, there is no fault; however, if [the donor] is destitute, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: If one has already initiated the preparatory effort before full ordination (*upasampadā*), but only acquires the object after having been fully ordained—if one seeks it with an excessive price, color, or measure, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*);
once it enters one's possession, it is an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If one begs from gods and the like...
If one begs for silk threads, embroidery, small pieces of cloth, or the like, there is no offense.
This precept is likewise established in the Mahāyāna; it concerns seeking improperly and seeking excessively, thereby failing to show compassion toward sentient beings.
The ninth precept concerning greedily seeking together:
If a bhikṣu, two laymen or a laywoman provide the price for a robe for that bhikṣu, and [the bhikṣu] takes such a price for a robe...

If one purchases such robes and gives them to a certain bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu—without having previously received an invitation from a householder—goes to the houses of two householders and says: "Excellent!
Prepare such and such robe-funds and make a single robe for me for the sake of its excellence," and if he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Exegesis: The origin story (*nidāna*) of this precept is also due to the aforementioned individuals.
Regarding the gravity of the offenses therein, the relinquishment and confession, the restoration of the robes, and the circumstances of non-offense, all are identical to those previously described.
The only difference is that [the Buddha] exhorted the two householders to collaborate on making a single robe so that it might be exquisite and fine.
The tenth precept concerning the solicitation of robes more than six times:
If a bhikṣu, a king, a great minister, a brahmin, a householder, or a householder’s wife sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣu,
saying, "Take this price for a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu," that messenger...
He goes to where the bhikṣu is and says to him, "Venerable sir, for your sake, I have sent this price for robes;
please accept it. That bhikṣu should say to that messenger: "I should not accept this price for robes.
If I need a robe, I shall accept one that is appropriate for the time and pure. The messenger says to the bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, is there anyone who attends to your affairs?"

The bhikṣu who requires robes should say, "There is. [He should say: "Whether it be a monastery attendant or an upāsaka, this person is a steward for the bhikṣus and constantly attends to their affairs.
Then, having delivered the price for the robe to that steward, the messenger returns to the bhikṣu and speaks thus: "Venerable sir, regarding the specific steward whom you designated—"
"I have already provided the price for the robe. Venerable sir, knowing the proper time, go there and you shall obtain the robe.
A bhikṣu who needs a robe should go to the person in charge of affairs and, after reminding them twice or three times, should say: "I need a robe.
If, after reminding them twice or three times, he obtains the robe, that is well. If he does not obtain the robe, [he may do so] up to four or five times...
If he stands silently before her for a second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth time, and obtains the robe, it is well.
If he does not obtain the robe, and he continues to seek it beyond that point and obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go to the place where the price for the robe was received, either going himself or sending a messenger, and say:
"Previously you sent a messenger with the price for a robe to give to a certain bhikṣu; that bhikṣu has not obtained the robe at all.
You should take it back so that it is not lost. This is the proper course of action.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī.
In that city, there was a high minister who was a close friend of Upananda. He sent a messenger with the price for a robe to give to him.
Upananda immediately took the messenger into the city and gave the price for the robe to a long-time acquaintance, an elder, to hold for him. At another time, the minister asked the messenger:
"I previously sent the price for robes to have them made for Vāṇada; did he wear them for me? He replied, "He did not.
The minister then ordered the robe-price to be reclaimed. Upon hearing this, Vāṇada immediately went in haste to the house of that elder to demand the robes.
At that time, the elders of the city had assembled, and there was a prior regulation that those who failed to attend would [be punished].
"A fine of five hundred [kārsāpaṇas] has been imposed. I am now going there for a moment. Venerable Sir, please wait a short while;
do not let me have to pay the fine. Bhadananda said, "That cannot be. First give me the price for the robe so that I may have it made.

The householder had the robe made, and when the assembly had concluded its session, he paid the five hundred [kārsāpaṇas]. At that time, that householder and all the other lay devotees were completely... [exhausted/overwhelmed].
They all reviled him with suspicion. The Buddha, knowing this, established a precept for the Saṃgha. This is a prohibitive offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya).
Because of taking impure wealth and failing to protect the feelings of others, resulting in distress and confusion, he formulated this training rule (śikṣāpada).

**Exegesis:** The text is divided into six sections. The passage from "Whether it be a king or a high minister" up to "now for you to receive the price of robes" clarifies that a donor has dispatched a messenger to deliver a gift of robes.
The passage from "That bhikṣu should speak thus to the messenger" up to "always acting as an attendant for the bhikṣus" clarifies the observance of the precepts by the bhikṣu.
He shall not accept money or precious objects. That messenger shall go to the person in charge of affairs, and so on, until he reaches the place where he may obtain robes and such items.

When it is clear that he must report back, the monk who requires robes should go to the person in charge of affairs and remain standing silently before him for four, five, or six times; if he obtains robes, it is well. Thus it is explained.

Relying on the regulations, one requests clothing to protect the pure faith of others. If one does not obtain clothing after exceeding this limit of seeking it and so forth, it clarifies that one has violated the regulations;

by requesting beyond the limit, one commits an offense against the fundamental precept. If one does not obtain clothing, from the point of the source of the price for the clothing until "this is the proper time" and so forth, it clarifies that one does not lose the trust of the donor, having informed the master [of the gift] and taken it. The Vinaya states: "The king, the great minister, and so forth, as above."

As for the *brāhmaṇa*: there are those born as *brāhmaṇas* (*jāti-brāhmaṇa*). "Born" refers to being descendants of Brahmā; they are the noble lineage of the five regions of India, which does not exist in other countries.

Therefore, the five regions of India are all called "Heavenly Regions" (Tianfang). A householder (*gṛhapati*)—excluding kings, ministers, and noble laypersons—sends a messenger to deliver the price for robes to a bhikṣu (meaning he dispatches men, women, or eunuchs as messengers;
"price for robes" refers to holding gold, silver, the seven precious gems, ivory, and so forth, to serve as the value of the robes).

He gives such a price for robes to a certain bhikṣu (this refers to a donor indicating it to his messenger; it is the act of giving when one who personally delights in respect and offerings bestows it). I...

"One should not accept the price for this robe" (The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: According to the rules for bhikṣus, one must not accept or possess gold, silver, precious gems, and so forth, nor grain, millet, rice, beans, villages, gardens, slaves, oxen, sheep, or vehicles.

These gold, silver, precious gems, and so forth, the Saṃgha should accept. If there are fields or orchards, these too should be held in common by the assembly. They should be entrusted to the monastery's attendants (*kappiyakāraka*) or other laypeople to calculate the shares, collect the taxes, and provide for the Saṃgha).

"If I require a robe, I shall accept it when it is appropriate and pure" (Appropriate time refers to the time when a bhikṣu has need of a robe, or when the Buddha has permitted that bhikṣus may accept [the offering]).

At that time, "pure" means not violating the prohibitions of the World-Honored One and being free from all obstacles and difficulties. If it is a time when one is fit to receive [the robe-material], I shall accept it to complete the robe and maintain it as my possession.
Whether it be a *gāmaṇi* (village headman) or an *upāsaka*, these are the attendants for the bhikṣus who constantly perform services for the bhikṣus.

(That is to say, the *gāmaṇi* refers to the temple servants (*śrāmaṇera*); because they were granted by King Prasenajit, they should not be subject to the king's conscription. They constantly perform various communal duties for the Saṃgha and serve the bhikṣus. The *upāsaka*...)

"Upāsaka" here means "lay follower. This refers to one who has taken refuge in the Triple Gem, observes the five precepts, and is capable of drawing near to and serving the Saṃgha, desiring to become a bhikṣu or acting as an attendant.

When it says "that messenger goes to the attendant," it means that the messenger goes to the person indicated by the bhikṣu, delivers the price for the robe, and entrusts him with the instruction to purchase a pure robe at the appropriate time.
"Go to that bhikṣu to receive it. (This means: "Venerable sir, know that the time has come for you to obtain the robe;

go to the place of that person in charge of affairs, and you shall receive a robe that is pure and in accordance with the Dharma. "The bhikṣu who needs a robe should go to the place of the person in charge of affairs" (this means:
when this bhikṣu requires a robe, he should go slowly to the place where the person to whom the price for the robe was entrusted resides). "If [he goes] two or three times..."
On the contrary, one should remind [the steward] by saying, "I require robes" (this refers to speaking back and forth two or three times to cause the steward to remember;

"to remember" means to fix upon a specific month and day for when the robes will be made). That steward—whether at home, in the market (where buying and selling occur), or at the place of work (meaning a place where various tasks are performed)—should be told: "I now require robes; please make robes for me. This is [the procedure].

One should remind [the steward] two or three times. If one obtains the robe after being reminded two or three times, it is well (this means that by acting in accordance with one's own request, one causes others to joyfully provide it, without needing to seek further).
If one does not obtain the robe after being reminded four, five, or six times while standing silently before him, then that steward—whether he is a householder or... [text fragmentary].
If he is at his place of work, the monk should go before him and stand silently.
If the person in charge asks, "Why are you standing here? the bhikṣu should reply, "You yourself should know.

If the person in charge says, "I do not know," and there is another who does know, he should say to that person, "That person knows" (as for those referred to as "others who know," they are generally...).

If I were to entrust my belongings to another, or if I were to borrow clothing from a fellow traveler for use, I would certainly inform one person so that there is witness when I later seek them back, thereby avoiding disputes; this is the compassionate instruction of the Buddha.
If a bhikṣu makes one verbal demand, he may wait two periods of silence before seeking the garment; if he makes two verbal demands, he may wait four periods of silence;

if he makes three verbal demands, he may wait six periods of silence (after three periods of formal recollection, he is permitted to wait for six periods of silence to seek the garment). If he makes one verbal demand, it is calculated as equivalent to two periods of silence.

[The monk] remains silent. Even if he requests [the robe] three times, this is equivalent to six instances of silence; he must not remain silent and request the robe again. As for the term "violation," it refers to breaking the World-Honored One’s formal regulation regarding the six instances of silence.
Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu requests [the robe] more than three times by speaking, or stands silently for more than six times and thereby obtains the robe, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.

The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning this robe are explained within the section on "Active Observance. If one has relinquished the robe but fails to return it, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, harboring a mind of greed; second, failing to protect the minds of others.
Third, the offense of seeking [the robe] in violation of the regulations;
fourth, when the robe has already entered one's possession, both the regulations and the forfeiture for a bhikṣuṇī apply (the same regulation, same training).

This is the division of shared property. If one says, "Just take the robe; I myself shall explain the matter to the owner of the robe," and at that time receives the robe and takes it away, there is no offense.

"You should return to the place from which you received this robe-cloth. It would be well if you were to report it thus.

This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well, for the purpose of avoiding reproach and increasing the pure faith of others.
The eleventh rule concerning the request for cotton to make bedding:
If a bhikṣu makes a new bed or mat using wild silkworm cotton, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying in the country of Āṭavī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were making new bedding out of wild silk cotton (*tūla*).
They were seeking either unprocessed silk cotton, or processed silk cotton, or dyed silk cotton, or undyed silk cotton.
Regarding "whether new or old": they went to a silkworm-raising household and said, "We need silk. The host replied, "Wait a moment; you must come when the cocoons are ready.
The group of six bhikṣus stayed nearby waiting, watching as the cocoons were being dried. At that time, the silkworm pupae made a noise. The layperson criticized and disparaged them.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who established the precept. This is a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural offense).

This is an offense. Because it involves taking the lives of various sentient beings, it increases craving and greed, causes one to neglect one's own wholesome qualities, and damages the right faith of others;
therefore, this training rule was established. It constitutes the fundamental category of killing within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "Regarding 'various materials' (*miśra*):

these include *karpāsa* (cotton), *kośaka* (a type of plant fiber), *kṣaumam* (flax), or *śāṇa* (hemp) and *kauśeya* (silk). According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are two kinds of *kauśeya*: first, raw fine silk; second, spun silk.

To make a new bedding (*śayanāsana*)—the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that 'new' is of two types: first, newly manufactured; second, newly acquired. Here, 'newly manufactured bedding' refers to woolen rugs (*kaṭhina*). This has two [types]..."

There are two types [of cotton garments]: first, those stuffed with padding; second, those woven from yarn. Neither is permitted for use. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Regarding garments made of cotton, there are two kinds: first, spreading out carded cotton and stuffing it, according to the method used for making felt;

second, spinning cotton into thread and weaving it to form a garment. Making these two types of garments is called 'making bedding' (*śayanāsana*). 'Bedding' is not merely a sleeping mat; it is a general term for clothing."

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu uses mixed wild silk cotton for himself to make a new bedding, and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If he makes it but it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If he instructs another person to make it and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he instructs another person to make it but it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If he has it made for another person, [the offense is determined accordingly].
It is not accomplished; [if one does so], it is all *duṣkṛta*.
This must be relinquished. As for relinquishing it therein: if one chops it finely with an axe and mixes it with mud, or applies it to a wall, or applies it to a plastered floor.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the presence of craving and attachment; second, a mind devoid of compassion;
and third, the completion of the bedding and furniture.

This also governs the *bhikṣuṇī*s, for whom it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing). [The rule is] the same in its application, though the training is different. It also applies to *śikṣamāṇā*s, *śrāmaṇera*s, and...
Māni-tukila (mānattukkaṭika); this constitutes an offense. Regarding the exemptions for non-offenses:
if one obtains [the material] already finished; or if one chops it with an axe and mixes it with mud to plaster walls or mounds;
or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—these are non-offenses.

Regarding the acquisition [of robes], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one makes the three robes—whether using the warp or the weft, whether the center or the edge, whether the internal seams, the borders, or the patchwork—if they are completed, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The use [of such a robe] constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
It must be relinquished within the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha should not return it, nor may it be used for any other purpose. It may only be spread upon the ground. And...
It is used to construct screens, curtains, and canopies.

Regarding self-destructive relinquishment: when one cuts bedding with an axe, the mind of craving and attachment is severed along with the descent of the axe. It causes—
It shall never be restored; therefore, it is called "abandonment through self-destruction" (*svayaṃ-bhaṅga-tyāga*).

One thereby repays past debts and no longer wanders within the three realms. Why is this? Because by consuming the products of their bodies, one becomes bound by those very conditions.

Twelfth: The Rule Concerning Black Woolen Bedding.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding cover using entirely new pure black wool from rams, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall on the side of the Monkey River in the city of Vaiśālī.
Many Licchavis practiced sexual misconduct; they made blankets from pure black wool and wore them while walking about at night so that people would not see them.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus imitated this practice. The Licchavis said to them: "We [did this] for..."
"This was done intentionally out of lustful desire; for what purpose have you done this? Having heard this, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
For the sake of the Saṃgha, the Buddha established this precept: because of attachment to beautiful forms and further seeking after fine textures, they neglect their duties and increase their greed;
therefore, to prevent such lack of benefit, he enacted this training rule (śikṣāpada).
**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "Pure black" refers to wool that is either naturally black or dyed black. Regarding "the wool of the *rūḍhaka* sheep" (*rūḍhaka* is pronounced with a level tone;

*rūḍhaka* is the name for a foreign sheep whose wool is exceptionally soft and fine, like the downy fleece of a lamb here in this land [the character *ér* is pronounced *ní*]). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In this country, black sheep’s wool is precious."

The rule regarding not permitting clothing made from black sheep’s wool also has two types: first, to select, process, and weave black sheep’s wool to make fine felt; second, to spin it into thread and weave it into cloth to make clothing. Both of these types of clothing are termed *pariṣkāra* (requisites).
This sheep’s wool may be used to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), which are to be formally accepted and maintained.

**The Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if a bhikṣu himself uses pure black wool from a ram to make a new bedding mat, and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture).
If he makes it but it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If he instructs another to make it and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he instructs another to make it but it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This also applies if he makes it for another.
Whether [the bedding] is returned or not, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
The method for relinquishing and confessing this precept, as well as the rules for returning bedding and so forth, is explained in the section on "Maintaining by Action.

Once one has completed the relinquishment of the bedding before the Saṃgha, if one does not return it, or instructs another not to return it, or makes a *pariṣkāra-dāna* (pure gift) of it, or gives it away to someone else, or repeatedly [uses it], [it constitutes an offense].
Regarding the spreading of a rug: it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for every step [of the process].
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the presence of a mind of greed or pride; second, that the wool is entirely black;
and third, that the rug has been completed.
If a bhikṣu commits it, it is a duṣkṛta (the same rule, but different training); for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if one obtains what is already finished; if it has been cut or torn;
if it is thin and folded to make two layers; if it is made into a mat; if it is made into a pillow; if it is made into a small square sitting cloth; if it is made into a lying-blanket;
