This precept is studied identically in the Mahāyāna; its meaning is the same as that regarding bedding made from wild silkworm silk.
Thirteenth: The Offense of Deficiency in the Making of a New Bedding.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he should use two parts of pure black wool, three parts white, and four parts variegated.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated, [he commits an offense].
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made new bedding out of pure white sheep’s wool.
The lay devotees all criticized and disparaged them, saying, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, resemble..."

If the king or a high minister (according to the customs of the Western Regions, only the king, high ministers, and elders wear fine, expensive, white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) to manifest their nobility;

others dare not wear it), the bhikṣus, having heard of this, inform the Buddha, who then establishes the precept as before. This training rule was formulated because of attachment to beautiful colors and other such qualities.
Explanation of the Meaning: The text is divided into two sections. From "When making a new bedding" (*navakam sayyāsanam*) onwards, it clarifies the formal regulation.
From "If a bhikṣu does not [use... onwards, it concludes the section on transgressions. The *Vinaya* states: "White" refers to either naturally white hair or hair dyed white.

"Variegated color" (*pāṇḍuvarṇa*) refers to the hair on the head, the ears, or the legs; or any other variegated-colored hair. (The character *máng* is pronounced *máng*; it means mixed-colored hair). The *Vinayavibhaṅga* says:
The hair on the head, feet, and belly—because the head, feet, and belly are the places of movement, the hair there is coarse and harsh).

If one makes a bedding of forty *pala*, twenty *pala* must be pure black, ten *pala* white, and ten *pala* variegated (*śabala*). (The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one *pala* is four *liang*. The *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra* states that one *pala* is one *liang*.

These differ because they refer to different weights; thus, the translations vary. Following the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* here, forty *pala* weigh ten *jin*. Therefore, five *jin* should be black, two and a half *jin* white, and two and a half *jin* variegated).
If one makes a sitting mat of thirty *bāla* and a bedding of twenty *bāla*, the weight shall be calculated accordingly:
two parts black wool and one part each of white and variegated wool. (This is because black wool is difficult to obtain, white is next most difficult, and variegated is easy to find;

furthermore, black and white are fine, soft, and expensive materials that increase one’s self-indulgence, whereas variegated wool is coarse in texture and not of high value, thus it does not increase one’s desires.)

**The Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one makes a new bedding for oneself without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated, and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one causes another to make it and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one makes it for another person, [the same applies].
Whether the relinquishment is accomplished or not, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The procedure for relinquishing and confessing this precept, as well as the method for returning bedding and other items, is clarified in the section on "Practicing and Maintaining" (*karmavācanā*). If one has completed the relinquishment but fails to return the items, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the presence of an affectionate intent; second, the division of two parties in violation of the teaching;
and third, the completion of the act.
Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta (the same rule, different training); for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.

Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if it is made according to the prescribed measurements; if the formal announcement (*jñapti*) was insufficient and a variegated cloth was used to complete it;
if one makes a purely variegated garment; if one obtains one that has already been completed; if it is cut into strips; if it is dyed to change its color (*kāsāya*);
if it is used for pillows, mats, or bedding; and in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—these constitute no offense.

Regarding the gathering [of wool]: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if one uses mostly black wool while forming the perception that it is [a permissible amount], or forms the perception that it is less than the limit and then adds more—whether making it oneself or having another make it—one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. To use it constitutes a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.
If one uses mostly white wool while forming the perception that it is [a permissible amount], or forms the perception that it is less than the limit and then adds more... [the same applies].
The offense is likewise. If one uses even a small amount of inferior hair (that is, brindled hair) while forming the [same] perception, the offense is likewise.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one uses black [wool], even if it exceeds [the limit] by one [strand], there are two *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses;
if one uses white [wool], even if it exceeds by one, there are two *dukkaṭa* offenses; if one uses brindled [wool], even if it falls short by one, there are two *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses."

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Alternatively, if black [pigment] is easily obtained while other colors are difficult to seek, the weight may be increased or decreased, and it shall be valid;
there is no offense. (This refers to what is produced from the local soil; the allowance is granted in consideration of the specific circumstances)."
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well, because it restrains worldly censure externally and protects the monastic regulations internally.

Fourteenth: Regarding the ordination of one who is less than the required age—if a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat, he must keep it for six years; if it is less than six years, he may not make another without first disposing of the old one.
Regarding "new": except by means of a formal monastic act (*saṃgha-karman*), it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

The Origin Story (*nidāna*): This precept has two stages of enactment. When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus took offense at their bedding—whether it was too heavy or too light, too thin or too thick—and because they would not discard it, they made new ones. As it was with them...
He was constantly seeking out bedding and requisites, accumulating them in great numbers. A bhikṣu who was content informed the Buddha, and this was the first formulation of the precept.
Later, at another time, a certain bhikṣu contracted the disease of consumption; for a minor reason, he wished to travel among the people.

He thought to himself, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that bedding must be kept for six years. If one does not discard it before the six years are up and instead makes a new one, one commits an offense against the precepts.
I possess a rag-robe bedspread that is so heavy it is unbearable to carry; how should I proceed?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) on his behalf to allow him to make a new bedspread.
Thus, as in the case of the formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃghakarma), this is the second formulation of the precept. It was established to prevent those who do not take pleasure in its use;
for those who cherish new and fine things, this training rule (śikṣāpada) was ordained.
**Exegesis:** The text is divided into three sections. 1. "Making a new bedding and keeping it for six years" clarifies the original regulation (*prathama-vidhi*). 2.
"If one makes a new one before six years have passed without relinquishing the old" clarifies that an offense is incurred.

3. "Except by formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-karman*)" clarifies the subsequent dispensation (*anujñā*). Regarding "before six years": the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states this means "less than six rainy seasons"; the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states, "Even if one is unwilling, one should keep it for the full six [years]."

[The offense of] committing [a transgression]. Regarding the violation herein: if a bhikṣu, having not yet completed six years, does not relinquish [the old bedding] and instead makes new bedding, if it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture);
if it is made but not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If he causes another person [to make it], [the same applies].

Regarding the maker: if one makes [an item] and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if it is made but not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one makes [an item] for another person, whether it is completed or not, it is in all cases a *dukkaṭa*.
The methods for relinquishing this precept, returning bedding and furniture, and performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) are explained within the section on "Practicing and Maintaining.
If one has relinquished the bedding and fails to return it, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the intention to possess out of greed; second, holding [the animal] for less than a year;
third, not having received formal authorization through *karmavācanā*; and fourth, the completion of the act.
Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta (the rule is the same, though the training is different);
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if the Sangha has granted permission; if six years have been completed; if one discards [the old] before the six years are up;
if one makes a new one because the old one is missing or destroyed due to other circumstances; if another person makes one and gives it to him; if he obtains one that is already finished;
or if it was prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute cases of no offense.

Regarding the acquisition [of a new rug]: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if an old rug is present before one, and one discards it to make another, one commits an offense (the "rug" refers to bedding).

If an old rug is present before one, and one makes another without discarding it, one also commits an offense. If an old rug is not present before one, yet one discards [an existing one] to make another, one also commits an offense.

If an old rug is not present before one, and one makes a new one without discarding [an existing one], all such cases constitute a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. To use [such a rug] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the offense of a bhikṣuṇī:

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that if a bhikṣu makes a new bedding within this year, and further makes another item during that same year, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) for the second instance and commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. This applies to the first maker.

There is no offense. Although it is not within the same year, if one makes another mat in the second year, and likewise in the third, fourth, or even fifth year, making a new one each time, the offense is the same as before.
If, during this [first] year, while the new bedding has not yet been finished, one makes another; and when both are completed, one says, "I shall keep the former and discard the latter."
Subsequently, one may either retain the later [item] and discard the earlier one, or incur the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for the later one while there was no offense for the earlier one.
If the initial undertaking was not yet completed, and in the second year—or even the third, fourth, or fifth year—both are finally completed at the same time:
The same applies to the offense incurred by relinquishing or retaining [the robe] before or after [the prescribed time].
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "Except in cases of formal monastic authorization (*saṃgha-karman*): if one is ill and has not yet recovered, one may act according to one's own will.
If the illness has already been cured but recurs, there is no need for further authorization; the previous authorization may be used."

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When a monk who is aged or infirm has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding his woolen blanket, he should personally record the date and duration of its loss due to his inability to maintain it.
Once his illness has been cured, he must resume maintaining this same old blanket. Thus, the blanket must have been used for a full six years from that time.
If a monk’s illness is cured yet he does not resume maintaining it for the full six years, he commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well, for it involves cherishing the offerings of the faithful and subduing greed and attachment.

Examination: The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that when the Buddha was residing at the hermitage in the Kalandaka Forest (the kingdom of Kalandaka), a severe and biting wind arose and the bhikṣus suffered from the cold.
At that time, the administrators (vaiyāvṛtyakara) possessed bedding and mats that had all been kept for six years.
Because the precepts have been established, they dare not construct anything new; because they endure the cold, all building activities have been suspended.

Having understood this, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying: "In all matters of administrative construction, if a bhikṣu possesses bedding and furnishings and, though less than six years have passed since their acquisition, cannot avoid the cold, that bhikṣu should request [permission] from the Saṃgha. Six.
Within the year, he shall further prepare a bedding mat. It is permitted for the Saṃgha to grant him formal authorization through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
If the Saṃgha recognizes that the person is trustworthy, they shall immediately grant him this rule. Alternatively, they may have him bring his old bedding mat to the midst of the Saṃgha;
if it is too long, it should be cut short, and if it is too short, it should be lengthened by adding wool.
If it is too wide or too narrow, adjust it according to the requirements of the situation. If there are torn places, they should be mended with hair-felt.
If it is so completely shattered that it cannot be repaired, the Sangha should perform a formal *jñapti-karman* (announcement) to authorize its disposal.
Fifteenth: The Precept on Not Patching.
If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take a piece from an old one, measuring one span in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one to spoil its color.
If he makes a new sitting mat and does not take a piece from an old one, measuring one span in length and breadth, to patch it...
The new [robe] is superior because it is dyed with a discolored hue. This constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The origin story (*nidāna*):
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the World-Honored One sent someone to request a meal.

It is the constant practice of the Buddhas that after the bhikṣus have accepted an invitation, they should go throughout the various rooms and see that the old sitting mats are strewn about everywhere in disorder, with no one to collect them.

Thereupon, they instruct the bhikṣus to make new sitting mats and to take a piece from the old ones measuring one span in length and breadth to patch onto the new ones for the sake of discoloration. However, the group of six bhikṣus did not...
Based on the Buddha’s teachings, after the Blessed One had rebuked him in various ways, he established a precept for the Saṃgha;
this training rule was formulated in order to prevent such a spirit of contempt.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: There are circumstances where the World-Honored One does not attend the place of an invitation, but instead sends someone to request food.
These are: first, to remain in secluded meditation; second, to preach the Dharma to the devas; third, to observe those who are ill;
fourth, to inspect the bedding and furniture; and fifth, to establish the precepts for the bhikṣus.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: For the sake of five benefits, the World-Honored One inspects the monks' quarters once every five days.
First, to see whether the śrāvaka disciples are attached to conditioned affairs; second, to see whether they are attached to worldly discourse;
third, to see whether they are attached to sleep, which hinders the practice of the Path; and fourth, to observe the sick bhikṣus.
Fifth, for a young bhikṣu who has recently gone forth, seeing the Tathāgata’s dignified and orderly deportment, he gives rise to a heart of joy.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning, the text is divided into two sections. The first section clarifies that if one is making a new sitting mat, one should take [a portion] from an old one. The latter section explains its [purpose].
The Correct Regulation: If one makes a new sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) without taking a portion from an old one to form the binding edge, an offense is committed. The Vinaya states:
When making a new sitting mat, if the old sitting mat is not yet worn out and has no holes, one must take a piece from it, wash, dye, and treat it, then stretch and pull it to flatten it for cutting.
One should take a piece measuring one span (*vitasti*) in length and breadth and patch it onto the new mat; if it is to be patched along the edge, it should be done accordingly.

If the center is of a discolored hue (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "To make it discolored means that when using it, one desires it to be durable. As for the 'seating mat' (*niṣīdana*), it refers to what is spread out for sitting or lying down;

it is also called the 'clothing for sitting anywhere' (*yathāsukha-vastra*). It is permitted to keep it because it protects the body, protects the robes, and protects the bedding. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *niṣīdana*, also known as *niṣīdantaka*).

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one does not take up an old [sitting mat] to patch over it with a new one for the purpose of discoloring it, but instead makes a new sitting mat, then if it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture). If it is made but not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one causes another to make it, and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if it is made but not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The same applies if one makes it for another.
Whether it is accomplished or not, both constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning items such as sitting mats (*niṣīdana*) are explained in the section on "Practicing What One Holds.
If one has relinquished them and does not return them, one incurs the aforementioned offenses.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, acting out of indulgence in craving; second, violating the regulation by not patching [the robe];
and third, completing the making of a new one.
This also applies to the *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom it is a *duṣkṛta* (the regulation is the same, though the training is different). It also applies to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and... [śrāmaṇerīs].
Māni-tuk-kila (a minor offense of wrongdoing).
This constitutes a transgression. Exceptions where there is no offense: if one takes a worn-out [material] to patch over a new one for the purpose of discoloring it;
if one has no [old material] of one's own and makes a new one; if someone else makes it for one; if one obtains one that is already finished; or if it is entirely old.
If one acts [in this manner], or if it concerns the very first instance before the precepts were established, these are considered non-offenses.
According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, if an old [robe] completely covers a new one, or if it is entirely torn to pieces.

If it is unable to be patched to serve as a new one, there is no offense. At that time, the bhikṣus did not take their sitting mats (niṣīdana) when traveling to stay elsewhere, fearing they would commit the offense of being separated from their robes.
The Buddha said: "I have ordained that bhikṣus must not stay overnight apart from their three robes;
this does not refer to the sitting mat. Nevertheless, bhikṣus should not intentionally fail to carry it with them, nor should they forget to do so through negligence."
There is no offense [in this case]. A bhikṣu should not go outside without his sitting mat (niṣīdana). One who violates this commits a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should not accept a single-layered niṣīdana (if made of a single layer, it will not last long in use, as it diminishes the merit of the gift). One should not..."

Regarding staying overnight apart from one's *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), the *Lekha-śāstra* states: "If one stays overnight apart [from it], there is no need to relinquish it; one should merely perform the confession of a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "The *niṣīdana* should be made of two layers and folded into three parts; it should be cut to the proper dimensions."
[The term] "leaf" (*pattra*) is the same as the leaf of the three robes (*tricīvara*).
This precept is studied by followers of the Mahāyāna as well.
To cite scriptural evidence, the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "That which is 'old' refers even to that which has been used for a single sitting; this is what is meant by 'old. (4)

Take one side of the border, whether square or round, and paste it onto a new cloth. If you cannot paste it, you may also tear it into fine strips and mix them onto a new cloth; this is likewise permissible.
The *Śīla-pratyaya-sūtra* states: "Because it is taken, it serves as a border; its four sides are used to disfigure its color.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "Regarding the bedding that has been taken: from the longest [piece], take one span (*vitasti*) from the middle of its width.
Tear it lengthwise according to the width, and divide it into narrow strips to serve as borders; then apply these borders all around."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When taking a new sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), one should patch it with an old one at the four corners.
Examining this in detail across various sections of the Vinaya, it is prescribed that when making a *niṣīdana*, one should use an old mat to serve as a border around its four edges.

The patches are applied to the four corners because they serve to alter the color and eliminate finery, to ensure durability for long-term use, to protect the body and bedding, and to prevent greed and excessive attachment to the faithful’s offerings. Nowadays, makers of such items take various colors;
however, when new cloth is used to patch the four sides and corners, it only serves to further increase the mind’s craving for beauty and leads to the wasteful expenditure of the faithful’s gifts.
This is a gift of material things; how much less could one falsely claim that the four corners constitute the Four Heavenly Kings?
The *Nanhai Jiguī Neifǎ Chuán* (Record of the Inner Dharma Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states: "The practice of spreading out mats for prostration is not observed in the Five Indic Regions.
However, what is required by the Vinaya regulations is intended solely for the time of sleeping and lying down, in order to protect the felt mats and seats of others when using another's property."

The new and the old must both be replaced [with a cloth]. Regarding such personal items, if they are old, they are not required; do not allow them to become defiled, thereby impairing the faithful offerings.

This is not for the purpose of prostration. Monks in the various lands of the South Sea carry a piece of cloth three to five feet long, folded like a napkin, which they use as a replacement for prostrations. When kneeling, the stūpa remains upon their shoulders. Thus it is in the Western Regions.

When bhikṣus came and saw this, they all smiled with amusement. (The text) states that according to the *Jiguī zhuan* (Account of Returning Home), these were likely monks from the borders of the Five Indias who had previously entered China;
their erroneous customs and lingering practices had long been habituated into a prevailing custom. If one enters a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), one cannot avoid following the crowd.
One must know that spreading out one's sitting mat (*kaṭhina*) and performing prostrations is not a formal regulation of the Vinaya. If one performs [it]...
Regarding the visualization of honoring the dharma-robe: I hope this may absolve the transgression of violating the teachings.

To begin with, the purpose of prostration is to humble oneself in order to manifest the utmost reverence; logically, there should be no spreading out of mats to support one’s body while performing it.
Yet, there are still those devoid of shame who select fine silk and brocade, matching colors to display their beauty, and have their attendants spread them out and lift up their robes for them.
To treat the Great Sage with such disrespect is to delude oneself through arrogance toward one’s superiors; how could one hope to escape the retribution for such a sin?
Sixteenth, regarding the precept on carrying wool from afar:
if a bhikṣu traveling on a road obtains wool and there is no one to carry it for him, he may carry it himself for a distance of up to three yojanas.
[The offense of] *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for traveling more than three *yojanas* while carrying [an item] oneself when no one else is available to carry it.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, Upananda was traveling on a road.
He obtained a great deal of wool and carried it on the head of a staff as he walked along.

When the lay followers saw this, they all spoke with reproach and disdain, saying, "How can these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya clan engage in the buying and selling of wool? When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.
This training rule was established because of the resulting censure and reproach.
Regarding the explanation of its meaning, the text is divided into two sections. The section beginning with "While traveling on a road, one obtains wool" clarifies the actual regulation.
If there is no one to carry it, one may carry it oneself for a distance of up to three *yojanas*; beyond that, the offense is established. The Vinaya states:
"Whether traveling on a road or staying at a residence, if one requires wool, one may take it (whether obtained through a gift from another or found as discarded refuse).
If there is no one to carry it—meaning no *kappiya-kāraka* or other layperson—one may carry it oneself for up to three *yojanas* (approximately a journey of one hundred *li*). If...
If someone is carrying [an item], one should say to that person: "I have this object; you should assist me in carrying it.

However, that bhikṣu must not assist in carrying it along the way (meaning that since there is already a pure person acting as a carrier, the bhikṣu himself must not again assist in carrying it midway, lest he disparage the dignity of the Saṃgha).
Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu carries [an item] himself for more than three yojanas, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he causes another person to carry it, or assists in carrying it along the way, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes a bhikṣuṇī to carry [wool] beyond three yojanas, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one causes a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī to carry it beyond three yojanas, it is a duṣkṛta offense—except for wool.
If one carries any grass, leaves, hemp, or the like beyond three yojanas, it is a duṣkṛta offense. Furthermore, if one carries other [items]...
If one places an object on the head of a staff while walking, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The procedure for relinquishing and confessing this precept, as well as the rules regarding the return of wool and other items, is explained in the section on "Observance through Action" (*karmavastu*). If, after having relinquished the item, one does not return it and so forth, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept constitutes a full offense only when three conditions are met: first, it must be wool; second, one must carry it oneself beyond the prescribed limit;
and third, there must be a mind of attachment.
This also applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom it is a *duṣkṛta* (the rule is the same, though the training is different). It also applies to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and [śrāmaṇerīs].
Māni-tukila; this constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if one carries it for three *yojanas* or less than three *yojanas*;
if someone else carries it partway so that one does not assist in carrying the remainder; or if one causes a bhikṣuṇī or members of the three lower assemblies to carry it.

It is not an offense in three cases: if one carries woolen gear (such as a fine woolen mat or woolen cords), or carries hair from the head, neck, or feet, or makes a cap, or makes a covering for leather sandals, or in cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept. These constitute non-offenses.

Regarding the collection [of wool]: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if a bhikṣu carries wool while traveling on a road and forgets something at a distance of one *yojana*, he may return to retrieve it;
once retrieved, he may return to his original location for a total distance of three *yojanas*. He must not exceed this limit; if he does, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he forgets an object at a distance of one and a half *yojanas* and is able to return for it, and having returned... [text ends].
If one goes again after having already departed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If one walks straight on for three *yojanas*, crossing over with one foot constitutes a *vyatikrama* offense;
crossing over with both feet constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. If two people each carry a load, [the same applies] up to three *yojanas*.
Having exchanged them, each person again obtains three *yojanas*; for three people it is nine *yojanas*, and for four people it is twelve *yojanas*.
If there are many people in this manner, the limit is set according to the number of individuals; they simply must not carry a heavy burden once more.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: One may have a *kappiyakāraka* (pure person) carry [the items]. If no such person is available, one is permitted to carry them oneself;
however, one must not carry them on the head or bear them on the back. To do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
Regarding the seventeenth precept concerning a nun dyeing wool:
if a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Pāṭidesanīya: Origin Story.

There are two enactments regarding this precept. When the Buddha was staying at Anupiya, the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus made new bedding and had the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī wash it.
Having dyed and carded wool, their hands were stained with dye. They went to pay homage to the World-Honored One. Upon seeing them, the World-Honored One questioned them and learned the reason.
He rebuked the group of six bhikṣus; this was the first instance for which he established a precept for the Saṃgha.
Later, the various bhikṣus each had doubts and did not dare to have their relatives—bhikṣuṇīs—wash, dye, or card wool. The Buddha further permitted this; thus it came to be.
This is the second formulation of the precept. Because one's own craving obstructs another's correct cultivation, this training rule was established;
it constitutes the fundamental category of sexual misconduct from the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].

**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "If one who is not a relative washes [the robe] as described above, down to the point of immersing it once in water to dye it, or even immersing it once in dye and tearing it apart;
down to using the hand to tear a single piece apart" (*bò*, pronounced *bó*; meaning to wave, to separate, or to split).
(That is to say, the analysis and discernment of the principle).
Regarding the determination of the offense: herein, if one causes a nun who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for each act.
If she washes and dyes it but does not card it, there are two *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *duṣkṛta*.
If one washes [the robe] but does not dye or tear it, there are two *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not wash it but dyes and tears it, there are two *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *duṣkṛta*. If one neither washes nor dyes it but tears it, there are three *duṣkṛtas*.
If one causes a non-relative *śrāmaṇerī* or *śikṣamāṇā* to wash, dye, or tear it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This precept concerning the forfeiture and restitution of wool and so forth is explained within the section on the observance of formal acts (*karmavācanā*). If one has forfeited the item but fails to return it, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept fulfills three conditions before the full offense is established: first, it must be sheep’s wool; second, it must belong to a nun who is not a relative.
When the three [procedures] have been completed as prescribed, it simultaneously constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for the *bhikṣuṇī* (the same rule applies, though the training is different).
For the *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative washes, dyes, or card-cleans [the wool];
or if one washes, dyes, or card-cleans it for the sake of a sick person; or if one washes, dyes, or card-cleans it for the sake of the Saṃgha, the Buddha, or a stūpa;
as well as cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute no offense.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: If one perceives a nun as not being a relative, or entertains doubt regarding her status, and causes her to perform the three tasks—specifically, the handling of wool—one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
An appended examination: The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that the reason for establishing the precepts for the bhikṣus was to promote the "superior Dharma" (*adhika-dharma*).

If the community of bhikṣuṇīs were to engage in tasks such as washing and dyeing, they would neglect their primary spiritual duties; consequently, they would lack majestic virtue and destroy the superior Dharma.
The superior dharma. Furthermore, for the purpose of ceasing unwholesome dharmas, there is a sequential causal condition; moreover, for the two assemblies, each has its own pure dharma.
The eighteenth is the precept against accepting gold and silver.
If a bhikṣu takes money in his own hand, or gold and silver, or instructs another to take them, or accepts them when they are placed on the ground,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a high minister in the city who was a close friend and acquaintance of Upananda. On another occasion, he obtained a large amount of pork and ordered his wife to set aside a portion for him.
It happened to be a festival day in the city, where various musical performances were held and people remained awake throughout the entire night.
At that time, the minister’s son was also among them. He did not sleep throughout the entire night. Being hungry and exhausted, he asked his mother, "Is there any leftover meat?
His mother said, "The meat is all gone; only the portion belonging to Baddhālinda remains.
The son immediately took five coins and said to his mother, "Take these coins and buy more meat to give to him; give this meat to me. In the early morning, Baddhālinda put it on.
Taking his robe and bowl, he went to the house of a high minister and sat down upon a seat. At that time, the minister’s wife told him the reason for her visit.
Upāli (Bhadanta) said, "If it is for my sake, you may give me money; there is no need for meat. She immediately placed the money on the ground and gave it to him.
Then Upāli took the money, left it at a market stall, and departed. The king, the ministers, and the laypeople all [discussed this] together.
They spoke words of reproach, saying: "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not renounce gold, silver, money, or treasures.

At that time, there was a minister named Mukuṭa, who possessed great power and was skilled at providing explanations. He caused the multitude to cease their reproaches and to become joyful, faithful, and understanding.
He then went to pay homage to the Buddha and reported these circumstances to him. The Buddha told the minister: "It is as you have said."
Within the True Dharma, there is much benefit and no transgression. Why is this? The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, have renounced precious treasures and do not cling to ornaments.
If they were to handle gold, silver, coins, or jewels, they would then be subject to the five desires.
To be subject to the five desires is not the dharma of the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya. If one sees a śramaṇa, son of the Śākya, because of me...
If one acts as a teacher yet grasps gold, silver, coins, or treasures, it is certain that he is not a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya.
You should know that the sun and moon have four afflictions: they are not bright, not pure, unable to illuminate anything, and devoid of majestic power.
What are these four? The asuras, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist are the great afflictions of the sun and moon. So too are the śramaṇas and brahmins...
The gate also has four defects: it is not bright, it is not pure, it cannot illuminate anything, and it lacks majestic power.

What are these four? Not renouncing the drinking of alcohol; not renouncing sexual desire; not renouncing the handling of gold and silver; and not renouncing wrong livelihood for one's own sustenance.
When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who had few desires and were content felt resentment and reproached [the gate].
After Vāḷananda had finished, he addressed the Buddha to establish this precept. This is an offense of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

It was established for the sake of stopping slander, for the sake of extinguishing strife and contention, and for the sake of perfecting the noble lineage. Thus was this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) ordained; it belongs to the fundamental category of theft within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].

**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "As for 'money' (*kākaṇī*): on its surface there are inscribed figures and symbols (the exterior being round to symbolize heaven and the interior being square to symbolize earth, with the name of the king placed in the center to symbolize how heaven and earth give birth to humanity).

As for 'gold and silver': the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* says: 'Precious things include gold, silver, *muktika* pearls, coral, *śukti* (mother-of-pearl), and *aśmagarbha* (agate). Regarding these various treasures:

those that have been fashioned or not yet fashioned, those that possess marks or do not possess marks—those that have been fashioned into various vessels are 'fashioned'; those that are merely the raw treasure and have not been made into vessels are 'unfashioned. Those that possess marks are either treasures fashioned into vessels, or those bearing the mark of letters, or those bearing the mark of a seal.'"

Regarding "not taking by hand": this refers to not making it into a vessel or treasure, not making it into a written character, and not making it into a seal. Regarding "teaching another to take it": this means teaching another person to take it for one's own sake. Regarding "receiving it when placed on the ground":

this refers to receiving it when another places it on the ground, rather than receiving it from the hand of another. Although this is neither taking it by one's own hand nor teaching another to take it, because one receives it when another places it on the ground, it is nonetheless prohibited; in all these cases, it is due to the mind of greedy accumulation, and therefore they are all equally forbidden.

Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu takes gold, silver, or coins with his own hand, or instructs another to take them, or receives them by placing them on the ground, in all such cases it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture).
This must be relinquished. Regarding this relinquishment: if there is a faithful and devoted park-keeper or a lay follower (upāsaka), one should say to them, "This is not for me;

you should know this. (This is the method of relinquishing precious objects before a layperson. Having thus relinquished it before that layperson, one must confess the offense before a single pure bhikṣu;
this is clarified in the section on "handling and keeping"). If that person takes it back and gives it to the bhikṣu, [the bhikṣu may accept it].
For the sake of those people, I, the Buddha, shall accept the instructions to have a pure attendant (kappiyakāraka) take charge of them.

If one obtains pure robes, alms bowls, sitting mats (niṣīdana), or needle cases, one should hold them as property belonging to others and receive them for the purpose of keeping them; [one should maintain the thought that these are the belongings of others, without the slightest intention of possessing them as one's own, even if one acquires such items.]

It is called "purification" (*pariśuddhi*). One must still present it to a fellow practitioner of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*). What should be exchanged? What should be accepted so as to purify it? Furthermore, "purifying" means to utterly exhaust thoughts of craving and not harbor any notion of gold or silver.
If that lay follower (*upāsaka*) takes [the object] and gives it to a bhikṣu for a pure robe, bowl, sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), or needle case, the bhikṣu should accept and keep it.

(This is the method for returning precious objects to a layperson; because that "purifier" knows the Dharma, once he has taken the object, he sees what robes or requisites the bhikṣu lacks and immediately fashions and sends them, so that the bhikṣu may obtain them.)
There is no need for barter; this is appropriate for the time. One may accept and keep it as pure. If, after he has taken it, he does not return it, one should have another bhikṣu say to him:
"The Buddha has a teaching for the sake of purification; you should return that bhikṣu’s property. (This is the method for when a layperson does not return precious goods.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha has a teaching," it refers to the rule established by the Buddha that allows bhikṣus to employ skillful means to purify precious objects; it does not mean that he is actually giving it to you. If the other bhikṣu does not speak [to the owner], [the fault falls upon him].
In such a case, you should go there yourself and say: "The Buddha has given this to you for the sake of purification;

you should now give it to the Saṃgha, to the stūpa, to your preceptor (upādhyāya), to those who share your preceptor, to your teacher (ācārya), to those who share your teacher, and to your fellow students, relatives, and friends.
Or, return it to its original owner. Why? Because we do not wish to cause them to lose it."
Because it is a gift of faith. If one does not speak to that person, even though they know what it is and see it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense (knowing it and seeing it refers to the *śuddhi-dharma*).
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the presence of a mind of greed or pride; second, the object being gold, silver, money, or precious gems;
and third, receiving and possessing it without pure speech (*viśuddha-vāk*).
Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (the same rule applies to those of equal training). For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one speaks knowing it to be so;
or if there is a trustworthy attendant of the monastery who wishes to prevent the loss of that faithful offering (the full text of which is as above in the section on relinquishment);
or in cases such as when the precept has not yet been established—these constitute no offense.
The third section states: A bhikṣu found some money among the graves and brought it back himself. The Buddha said, "It should not be accepted.
That bhikṣu required copper; the Buddha said, "Smash it so that its characteristics as currency are destroyed, and only then may you take it with you."
Regarding the practice of acquisition, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: A sick monk may employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure attendant) to keep [items], but he must not be greedily attached to them.

If it is an object subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), once it has been relinquished among the Saṃgha, it may not be returned; the monks of that community should likewise not divide it up.
If there is a surplus, it should be placed among the inexhaustible goods (the inexhaustible goods being those belonging to the *cāturdiśa-saṃgha*).

Any interest or profit generated from them may be used for the construction of dwellings or for robes (namely, bedding and curtains within the monastic quarters), but they must not be consumed as food. Whenever a bhikṣu obtains money, [it should be treated in this manner].

When the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has concluded, one should not take the value of the robes for oneself; rather, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle allowable items) take charge of it.

If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should point to the ground near one's feet and say, "Know that [the value] is placed here on the ground," and then use grass, leaves, bricks, tiles, or the like for oneself.
Throw it from afar onto [the ground] above. Wait for a *karmadāna* (attendant) to come and inform them, according to what is used in that particular country.
Whether it be copper coins, iron coins, coins made of foreign resin, leather coins, or bamboo tally-sticks—if they are all things that should not be grasped, one must not take them up.

Alternatively, there may be items used in certain countries whose characteristics are not auspicious, or those whose characteristics are auspicious but are not used in that country; to grasp any of these constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
A nun’s offense is not permitted in the country; her characteristics are not fulfilled. If she takes [it] by holding copper or iron, there is no offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The Saṃgha should appoint, by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, one bhikṣu to be the person who discards gold, silver, and money.
That bhikṣu should discard these items in a pit, in fire, in flowing water, or in the wilderness."
In the midst [of the assembly], one should not mark the place. If it is held at another location, it may not be taken up again.
That bhikṣu should not ask the Saṃgha, "What should be done with this object? Nor should the Saṃgha instruct him, saying, "Do this" or "Do that.

If he neither discards it nor asks, but instead has a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) trade it for food and clothing for the Saṃgha and gives it to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha may accept it. If it is to be divided, [the same applies].
Only those who have committed an offense are not permitted to receive a share; those who have not committed an offense may do so.
Even if a layperson offers food to a bhikṣu, if the bhikṣu does not know it is pure, a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") must accept it for the purpose of purchasing pure items.

There were some bhikṣus who wished to travel to a distant place and requested provisions from a householder. The householder then sent a messenger with gold, silver, coins, and goods to accompany them. Upon arriving at their destination...
The amount was very large. The messenger returned and informed the master. The master said, "I have already given it as a gift; you should not take it back.

You may take it to the monks' quarters and offer it to the Saṃgha. The Buddha said, "I permit pure men (śūdra) to receive it on behalf of the Saṃgha, so that it may be exchanged for items required by the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus themselves should not handle such affairs."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one takes precious objects with one's own hand, if they are few, they should be discarded.

If they are many, even if one obtains the consent [of others], one should say to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle such items): 'Because these are impure, I should not take them; you should take them. Once the *kappiya-kāraka* has taken them..."
He said to the bhikṣu, "Give this object to the bhikṣu. The bhikṣu said, "This is an impure object; if it were pure, I would accept it.
If he cannot find a trustworthy person to purify it, he should make it into bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions.
He should enter among the monks and say: "Venerable sirs, I personally took up precious objects and committed a pāyattika offense. I now confess it."
[The offender] discloses [the offense] and does not dare to conceal it, confessing the transgression. The Saṃgha should ask: "Have you relinquished this treasure?
If he replies, "I have relinquished it," the Saṃgha should ask: "Do you see your fault? If he replies, "I see my fault," the Saṃgha should say to him: "Henceforth, do not commit it again.
If he says he has not relinquished it, the Saṃgha should issue a formal command to make him relinquish it. If they do not issue such a command, the entire Saṃgha incurs an offense.
*Duṣkṛta* offense: If, having been exhorted [to desist], one does not relinquish it, that bhikṣu commits a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: If for the purpose of constructing buildings or similar works, one should seek grass, wood, vehicles, and manual laborers;
one should not seek gold, silver, money, and the like. If one takes currency used by various regions, one commits the offense of relinquishment (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If one takes currency not used in one's own country, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one takes red copper, brass, bronze, iron, lead, or tin, there is no offense. If others offer the price for robes and one wishes to have them, one may accept them;
having accepted them, one should immediately form the intention that they belong to those [donors] and keep them, entrusting them to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a steward).
One should not hold it oneself. If there is no *kappiyakāraka* (a person who makes things permissible) to hold the object, one should address a single *bhikṣu*, saying:
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind. I, [name], have obtained this impure object.
I shall take this impure object and exchange it for pure wealth. Having said this three times, one may use it as desired; do not harbor any doubt.
Furthermore, if there are thieves in a monastery, one should securely hide and take up all the stūpas, monks' belongings, gold, silver, money, and treasures before departing.
If there is no one with deep faith, a pure resident or a lay devotee should employ a *śrāmaṇera*;

if there is no *śrāmaṇera* either, the bhikṣu should dig a pit with his own hands to hide and take them up. As for what I have taught regarding difficult circumstances, these matters are indeed difficult.
After [the robe] has been sent away, one must not proceed with it.

The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If it is another's property or property belonging to both oneself and others, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense without forfeiture [of the object]. 'Property belonging to both' refers to that which is shared with others.
If, during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the donor provides the price for robes to the community of bhikṣus, this constitutes an entrustment. This is the gift.

One should accept them while maintaining mindfulness as the primary focus. The bhikṣus should seek out a person of respectful faith—whether a temple attendant (karmadāna) or an upāsaka—to serve as a pure donor (śuddha-dāyaka).
(This is the method for requesting a pure donor of gold, jewels, grain, or rice; it is explained in the section on "Performing Retention").

If a bhikṣu obtains objects such as gold or jewels, provided he perceives them at that time as the property of a donor and takes hold of them, there is no offense, as they are intended to be set aside.
If one obtains impure items from afar, one may hold them with the mental intention that they belong to a donor;
as long as the donor remains alive, there is no offense whatsoever. If no donor can be found, one should take the gold, silver, or other such items and say before a single bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me. I, the bhikṣu [name], have obtained these impure items."
Wealth. One should take this impure wealth and exchange it for pure wealth. This should be recited three times, and one should then carry it oneself or have another person carry it.

(According to the *Caturvargika Bhikṣu-karmavācanā* compiled by Master Huaisu, this method was also adopted therein. In these degenerate times of the Eastern Land [China], it is truly an easy-to-practice expedient;
therefore, among the methods for carrying items, this one is to be followed. If a bhikṣu obtains gold, silver, or the like while on a journey...
Because it is the provisions for the path, one should carry it oneself, or have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle such items) or a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) carry it.
It should be understood that regarding gold, silver, and so forth, the prohibition applies only to personal possession (*svīkāra*) by the *śrāmaṇera*; it does not forbid his handling them.
This precept is permitted for the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings; however, it must be held and managed by a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person").
If no such pure person is available, one may personally take hold of it provided that one’s mind is free from attachment and one maintains the intention to bestow it upon the two fields of merit.
If, out of a greedy mind, one keeps it for oneself without practicing altruistic benefit, this constitutes a violation through defilement, characterized by excessive desire and a lack of contentment.
Citation: The *Zhimen jingxun yinchao* (Explanatory Notes on the Admonitions for the Monastic Community) states:
"First, fields, houses, and gardens; second, planting and cultivating seeds; third, storing grain and silk; fourth, keeping servants and attendants; fifth, raising and tethering birds and beasts;
sixth, money, treasures, and precious objects; seventh, felt mats, bedding, cauldrons, and tripods; eighth, ivory, gold-ornamented couches, and various heavy articles—these are the eight."

The names of the Sūtras, Śāstras, and Vinaya are extensively listed among the common enumerations; however, it is revealed that [possessing these] is improper. Furthermore, the Vinaya and Sūtras state:
"If there are those who possess [these], they are not my disciples. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also says: "They will certainly not have faith in my Dharma and Vinaya.
For these eight reasons, all of them increase greed and destroy the Path, defile the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and result in impure fruits; therefore, they are called "improper" (*akalpa*).

It is pure. It continues until it says: "In the Vinaya, matters are addressed according to specific circumstances; because those of lesser capacity have narrow minds, many allowances were made for the possession [of wealth].

The Nirvāṇa Sūtra states: 'If there are no disciples to provide for one's needs, or if the times are famine-stricken and food and drink are difficult to obtain, I permit my disciples to accept and possess gold, silver, vehicles, fields, and houses, in order to protect and uphold the True Dharma.'"

Grain and rice are among the necessities easily obtained through trade; although it is permitted to accept and store them, such items must be received through a formal act of pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*) from a donor of sincere faith.
The *Huìzhèngjì* states: "The above clarifies that for the Mahāyāna, both the capacity [of the practitioner] and the teaching are urgent;

the following clarifies that for the Hīnayāna, both the capacity and the teaching are relaxed. Regarding the Vinaya, which concerns matters of fact, a violation of a factual matter is minor; this demonstrates that the primary intent of the Sūtras lies in the principle."

From the perspective of principle, [the Mahāyāna] is weightier. Those of small capacity have narrow minds; because they are incapable [of the higher vows], [the Prātimokṣa] is opened for them. Conversely, because those of the Mahāyāna are capable, it is weightier.
Yet worldly people conversely claim that the Lesser Vehicle requires the precepts while the Great Teaching is universal—how much error this is!
Appendix: Examination of the *Sudarsana-vinaya*. It states that there are four ways of utilizing offerings. First is "theft-like utilization":
if a bhikṣu who lacks the basis of precepts receives food and drink according to the order of the Saṃgha, this is called theft-like utilization. Second is "utilization as debt":
if a bhikṣu receives from others food, drink, clothing, dwellings, beds, mats, or bedding... [if he is] intelligent... [text continues].
One who has left the household life with clear wisdom and faith should, at the time of receiving food, bring mindfulness to mind with every morsel;
this should likewise be done even when using bedding and seating. If one is of dull faculties, one should bring it to mind once before eating;
when using robes, one should first bring it to mind in the morning. This is provided that they are not using them merely to ward off cold, heat, or shame.
Using [robes]. If one accepts food, drink, or medicinal decoctions without being afflicted by hunger, thirst, or illness, this is called using with debt.

The dead flesh should have long since rotted and stunk; there must surely be some extraordinary sign. He took it back home and placed it in a suitable location.
After half a month had passed, it had become two pieces. Another half-month passed, and each of the two pieces had five embryos.

The four afflictions of the sun and moon refer to the four types: asuras, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist.

Alternatively, they are considered five afflictions by dividing smoke and clouds into two separate afflictions. As the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The orbs of the sun and moon are obscured by five veils;
thus they are not bright, do not illuminate, are not expansive, and are not pure. First, there are clouds, such as those found during the height of summer. There are also sparse clouds.
First, [smoke] arises and in an instant increases until it completely covers the void, obscuring the disks of the sun and moon so that neither appears.
Second, smoke is like that from burning grass and wood in a forest or wild field; suddenly, the smoke completely covers the void, obscuring the disks of the sun and moon so that neither appears.
Third, dust is like when a great wind swirls and strikes during a severe drought, and the clamorous dust suddenly [covers the sky].

It arises and completely covers empty space, obscuring the disks of the sun and moon so that neither appears. The fourth type of mist is like that of autumn and winter, when mountain and river mists arise;

furthermore, it is heard that in foreign lands, when rain has first cleared, the sun shines upon the valleys and plains, causing vapors from the earth to surge upward and disperse as a fine spray, completely covering empty space and obscuring the disks of the sun and moon so that neither appears.
When the five classes of asuras fought with the devas, the devas used the sun and moon as their banners.
By virtue of the majesty of the sun and moon, the devas were always victorious at that time. Consequently, the asuras were constantly filled with resentment and sought to destroy the sun and moon.

However, due to the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, they could not destroy them despite exhausting all their wisdom and arts; they finally resorted to shielding them with their hands.

Part Nineteen: The Precept Against Buying and Selling Precious Objects.
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha. At that time, Upananda went to the marketplace and exchanged money for more money, taking it away with him.
When the laypeople saw this, they all reviled and disparaged him. There were some bhikṣus of few desires...

The Venerable Kāśyapa heard that the Buddha had formulated this precept due to the afflictions of greed and pride; thus, he established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which belongs to the category of the fundamental offenses of theft in the first section.
Regarding the explanation of its meaning: the *Vinaya* states that "various kinds of buying and selling" refers to [dealing with] gold, whether refined or unrefined, silver, whether refined or...

[It includes] wrought silver (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "wrought" refers to vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth; "unwrought" refers to ingots of gold or silver, as well as fragments of gold or silver), and coins. There are eight kinds of coins.
Gold coins, silver coins, iron coins, copper coins, white-bronze coins, lead-tin coins, wooden coins, and resin coins.

Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects—exchanging finished gold for finished gold, or even exchanging them for coins—it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture).
This should be relinquished. Regarding the relinquishment herein, it is no different from the preceding rule on handling precious objects (the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules).

There are only twenty-seven types of methods for returning [the object]. Among these, the eleventh—making bedding out of mixed wild silk floss—and the eighteenth—handling precious objects oneself—both lack a method for returning [the object], as clarified within the section on "Making and Possessing."
This precept constitutes a full offense only when three conditions are met: first, the presence of a mind of greed or pride; second, the accumulation of precious objects for exchange;
and third, the completion of the exchange.
This rule applies equally to *bhikṣuṇīs* (with the penalty being a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), as well as to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*.
This is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) and constitutes a transgression.

At a house where rice was being served, he immediately asked for the price. [The host] replied, "Householder, do not speak such words; this is not something we ought to do.

When the outsider obtained the cloth, he returned to the park where he resided and showed it to the other outsiders. Among them was one of wisdom who said, "You have been deceived by him."

At the time of sale, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). If he fears that the price of grain will be high at a certain time and thinks, "I shall now purchase this grain so that, by relying upon it, I may recite the sūtras, practice meditation, and cultivate the Path," and when the time comes the grain becomes very expensive, if he eats more than what was provided by his upādhyāya...
Ācārya, if one performs meritorious deeds and others profit from selling the surplus, there is no offense.
If a *karmadāna* (monk in charge of affairs) hires laborers, rents carriages, horses, men, or boats, and uses impure speech in doing so, it is all a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).
If a monk serves as the monthly steward for the Saṃgha and goes to the market to purchase ghee and oil, or to buy rice and beans...
When seeking all manner of goods, if one uses impure speech, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (viniya-āpatti).

If one buys for oneself, and so forth—in all such cases—if one does not use pure speech, it is an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). If a bhikṣu, while engaged in buying and selling, utters words of reproach or disdain, saying of the goods previously possessed by another:
"This is good, this is bad; it is coarse or fine; the measure of the bushel or scale is large or small," or speaks of the quality of the incense—[these constitute offenses].

Regarding odors and so forth: there is no offense. Suppose a donor, for the sake of a bhikṣu, gives money to a shopkeeper and says, "If a certain bhikṣu comes every day seeking something, give it to that bhikṣu according to his wishes.
When the bhikṣu later comes to request it, whether he uses pure or impure speech, there is no transgression.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one wishes to engage in trade, one should instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) by saying, 'For my sake, exchange this item for that item.
Furthermore, one should mentally resolve: 'May they obtain my profit, and may I not obtain their profit.
If one engages in trade personally, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) if one trades with the five classes of monastics or with laypeople."
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one buys for profit but does not sell for profit, there is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of buying, but no offense at the time of selling.
If one buys without seeking profit but sells for profit, there is no offense at the time of buying, but there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) at the time of selling.
If one travels to another region to buy goods, having originally had no intention of seeking profit, yet obtains a profit when selling them upon arrival there," [there is no offense].
There is no offense.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If, at the time of buying or selling, one does not speak according to reality, or uses false and adulterated measures or weights to deceive others, one incurs the offense of lying (*mṛṣāvāda*).
At the moment one obtains the goods, one commits the offense of theft (*steya*). Whenever one possesses property..."
When buying or selling, one must first fix the mind and have no intention of seeking profit; whatever profit is obtained in the course of the transaction is entirely without fault.
Even when making the three robes, one should not engage in trade with the aim of making a profit.
When there are communal goods present that one wishes to sell, the Elder (Upādhyāya) should first establish the base price; he must not, on this account, proceed to call for bids. He should...

One may give it only to one who offers the highest price at the very end. If one does not truly wish to purchase it but falsely increases the price offered by another, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If, when the robe has been proclaimed as obtained, one puts it on before the payment for its value has been returned, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
The *Nidāna* states: A bhikṣu should not determine the price for a layperson, nor should he negotiate the high or low value of the price.
If there is no layperson to pay on his behalf, he may personally pay the price two or three times; beyond this, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: To purchase food with such impure items, for every mouthful, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

To purchase clothing and wear it, for each instance, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). If one exchanges goods with another and the other person later regrets the transaction, the goods should be returned;
however, if more than seven days have passed, they should not be returned. If one seeks a more expensive garment by offering a lower price, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If...
It must be an object. If the three attempts to solicit [the price] are unsuccessful, one should seek out a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") and have them purchase it.
This precept is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna.
To cite scriptural evidence, the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states: "This offense of buying and selling is, among all *pāyattika* offenses..."
Among these, the most serious is trade. It would be better to be a butcher than a merchant. Why?

A butcher kills only animals, whereas a merchant deceives and harms everyone—without regard for whether they are monastics or laypeople, noble or foolish, or whether they observe the precepts or violate them.
There is no one they do not deceive, and they constantly harbor malicious intentions. Even if they deal in grain, their hearts always hope to...
When the world suffers from famine, frost, hail, and calamities; when one dwells amidst the accumulation of salt and stored goods;

and when one’s mind constantly harbors the hope for rebellion and disorder in the distant regions, blocking the royal roads—such are the evils of the merchant who traffics in these goods. This is the nature of the merchandise he sells.
If food is prepared for the community of monks, the monks should not eat it. If a dwelling for the Saṃgha of the four quarters is built, they should not reside within it.

If a stūpa or an image is made, they should not bow toward them. Furthermore, it is said that although the Buddha himself would pay homage with his mind, ordinary bhikṣus who maintain the precepts should not make use of these objects.
If such a bhikṣu dies, these objects belong to the community of monks.
Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for the distribution [of property]: A question is asked: "If one did not enjoy this property while alive, why perform the *karmavācanā* upon death?

The answer is: "The transgression of the offense of trade and sale is extremely grave. If the Saṃgha were to consume this property while [the owner] was still living, although they would indeed be violating the precepts, because they are among the fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) of the Sangha, they would nevertheless be permitted to enjoy it. Because [they] receive [it].
Because it was used and subsequently produced [revenue] without interruption, its acceptance and use within the Sangha’s field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) were not permitted;

in this life there would be no merit, and in the future one would incur grave offenses. For these reasons, I did not dare to act further. Since the bhikṣu has died, there is no longer any cause for buying or selling;
therefore, I authorize its acquisition through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).
The twenty-first precept concerning the keeping of an extra bowl:
If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl without having made it a formal gift, he may possess it for up to ten days; if he exceeds this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Origin Story: There were two stages to the establishment of this precept. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept their fine alms bowls and set aside those that were not fine; in this way, they constantly sought out fine bowls until they eventually accumulated a great many.
A householder visited their quarters, saw this, and spoke with derision and reproach, saying it was like a potter’s shop selling bowls. All [the monks]...
Having heard this, the bhikṣu who was content informed the Buddha; this was the first establishment of a precept.

At that time, Ānanda obtained a precious bowl from the kingdom of Soma (the bowls of this country were blue and beautiful like the Jambu tree). He wished to give it to Mahākāśyapa, but Kāśyapa was away.
Fearing he would commit the offense of keeping an extra bowl, he went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha asked Kāśyapa: "In how many days will he return?"
He returned and reported, saying, "I shall return in ten days. From this, it was permitted to keep [the robe] for up to ten days;
this is the second established precept. Because of the attachment to accumulation, afflictions increase and the cultivation of right practice is hindered;
therefore, to prevent and sever this, this training rule was enacted.
Explanation of Terms: The Vinaya states that there are six kinds of alms bowls:

iron bowls, bowls from the country of Soma, bowls from the country of Ugara, bowls from the country of Ujjayini, black bowls, and red bowls. In brief, there are two main types: iron bowls and clay bowls.
The large [alms bowl] holds three *dō* (斗), and the small holds one *dō*. This is the measure of the *pātra* (Sanskrit: *pātra*; also called *pātrā*; translated here as "bowl").

In meaning, it is translated as "appropriate vessel" (*ōgi*), signifying that its substance, color, and measure must all conform to the Dharma. Regarding the substance, it is either clay or iron. Regarding the color, it is blackened or reddish by firing, or the color of a peacock's throat, or the color of a pigeon.
Regarding the measure, it follows the distinctions of large and small as divided in the Vinaya.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Among the various differing explanations of the masters of the treatises, one single meaning is taken as correct.
There are three types of alms bowls (*pātra*): the superior receives three *pātra*s of rice, one *pātra* of soup, and half a *pātra* of other edible foods;
the inferior receives one *pātra* of rice, half a *pātra* of soup, and half [a *pātra*] of other edible foods."
Soup. The space between the upper and lower [levels] is called the "middle bowl. The Sanskrit term *pātra* (or *pattha*) is translated here as "sheng" (升).
Three *pātras* of rice equal two *sheng* of the Qin measure; a Qin *sheng* is equivalent to only seven *he* (合) of the present-day measure.
One *pātra* of soup, along with other edible food amounting to half a *pātra* of soup, constitutes one and a half *pātras*. When receiving food, one should leave...
Regarding the empty space within the bowl: it must not be filled too full; it is best to ensure that the fingers do not touch the food.

As for the offense: if a bhikṣu receives a bowl on the first day, and receives another bowl on the second, third, fourth, or even up to the tenth day, and keeps them until the dawn of the eleventh day, [he commits an offense] during those ten days.
If one obtains a bowl, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense upon its total acquisition. This applies whether the bowls were obtained intermittently within ten days or all at once on a single day.

It remains an offense unless the bowl is formally given away as a pure gift (*viśuddhi-dāna*), or unless it is sent to another person, or unless it is lost, or unless it is intentionally destroyed, or unless it is rendered non-bowl (that is, discarded and no longer maintained as a possession).
The application [of this rule] is as clarified in the *Dīrghacīvara* (Long-Robe) precept: in all such cases, one commits an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

The procedures for forfeiting, confessing, and returning the bowl for this precept are explained in the section on "Practicing Retention" (*karmavācanā*). If, after having forfeited it, one does not return it, and so forth...
The offense is as described above.
This precept incurs the full offense only when three conditions are met: first, it is an extra bowl; second, there is the intention to possess it out of greed;
and third, ten days have elapsed.
The regulation for Bhikṣuṇīs regarding the Nissaggiya Pācittiya (identical regulation, same training): for Śikṣamāṇās, Śrāmaṇeras, and Śrāmaṇerīs, it is a Duṣkṛta.
This constitutes an offense.

Exceptions where there is no offense: within ten days, if one performs a formal act of purification (*pariṣkāra-dāna*); if one gives it away to another; if one has the perception that it has been stolen;
if one has the perception that it is lost, broken, or carried away by water; if one takes up and uses a lost bowl or a burnt bowl (meaning it was destroyed by fire during the process of fumigation);
if one uses it for the sake of another; if the monk to whom the bowl was entrusted dies; if one travels far away; if one leaves the monastic life; or if one is attacked by thieves or wild beasts.
It is not an offense in cases such as being swept away by water and other such calamities, or when not giving [the bowl] to another because it was before the precept had been established.
The third section states: "The *kañcaka* (small bowl), the *kṣudra-pātra* (minor bowl), and the *anupātra* (subsequent bowl) are permitted to be kept even if they are impure."
The fourth section states: A bhikṣu should not possess a wooden bowl; this is the bowl of non-Buddhists.

If he possesses one, he is to be dealt with according to the Dharma (an offense of *vinayātikrama*). He should not possess a stone bowl; this is the Dharma-bowl of the Tathāgata. If he possesses one, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
He should not possess a bowl made of gold, silver, various jewels, or incense; these are the practices of laypeople (*avadātavasana*). If he possesses one...
One incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. [However,] it is permitted to accept an iron bowl, provided it has been properly processed by smelting.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It is not permitted to place a partition inside the bowl. However, if a partition is made with a cake or rice, there is no offense."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The almsbowl is the insignia of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. A bhikṣu must not place impure substances within it.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should carry the almsbowl in accordance with the Dharma; one must not use it to discard sweepings, to hold leftover food, or to hold [food] beyond the proper measure."
One should drink during the midday meal. One must store incense and medicine [in a vessel] and lift it up with care, guarding it as one would one's own eyes.

After the midday meal, one must not use the alms bowl for drinking. It is permitted to use vessels made of copper, iron, or clay for drinking; it is also permitted to have a separate vessel for consuming gruel.
If one obtains two bowls, one should ask the Upādhyāya or Ācārya, "Which of these two bowls is superior? If the two teachers do not know, [one should ask someone else].
