One should distinguish [the bowls] and use each for five days. One who possesses superior [qualities] may keep it; one who is inferior should give it to another.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If one has purchased another's bowl but has not yet returned the price, one may not keep it.
Even if the owner of the bowl says, 'Just use it, and I will return the price later,' one still may not keep it until the price has been returned."

Thereafter, one should accept and keep it (this refers to the fact that those engaged in trade fear that prices may fluctuate; whenever a bhikṣu transacts with a layperson, he must first settle the matter clearly and decisively to avoid censure or dispute).

If, after purchasing a bowl and having completed the payment, the owner of the bowl has finished fumigating it and informs the bhikṣu, yet the bhikṣu does not go to retrieve it and ten days pass, he commits an offense of relinquishment (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). If the owner of the bowl has finished fumigating it and another person learns of this and conveys it [to the bhikṣu]...
The Bhikṣu-vinaya states: "Even if a bhikṣu has kept [an extra bowl] for more than ten days, he does not commit an offense.
The Mātṛkā says: "If a bhikṣu possesses a single bowl and does not accept it [as his formal possession], he commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika)."

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: If [the bowls] are of deficient measure or excessive measure, or if they were intended for others, or for the purpose of ordination (*upasampadā*), or for providing for one's needs—provided they are not distinguished [as being kept for oneself]—there is no offense. "Not distinguishing" means that they are kept for ten days or less.

Furthermore, there is no offense in storing soup or vegetables, or in keeping two small bowls for drinking water, as well as a salt dish and a spoon; all of these are without fault. Moreover, regarding...
Within the large bowl, small bowls may be kept according to their capacity; if it accords with one's needs, keeping many does not constitute an offense.

One should further keep one large bowl to prevent the occurrence of deficiencies. This differs from the non-Buddhists who use vessels made by sewing leaves or who eat while holding their hands in a hollowed position;
such practices are difficult to maintain and difficult to provide for, and do not possess the marks of a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). The World-Honored One permitted only one, not many.
It is not few. It is in accord with the Middle Way for sustaining the body and cultivating one's practice.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one keeps a white iron bowl or an unbaked clay bowl, all such bowls that do not meet the prescribed measure constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.

(*Vinayasamgraha* states: "If they are necessary and one keeps many, there is no offense; however, as these are essential implements, even if many are kept, they are permitted because there is a limit to them. In this context, if one keeps white iron...")

Regarding the "equal bowl" (patra) and the formation of an offense: since it is an object no longer fit for use, yet one continues to accumulate and store it, stinginess and greed reach their extreme; therefore, it is thus punished. However, the actual transgression lies in the mind, not in the object itself.
This precept is not studied in the same way by those of the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings.
Examination of the attached text: The *Caturvargika* states: "One should not paint images of grapes or lotuses in the bowl, nor draw the svastika symbol or one's own name upon it.
One should not wrap the four sides or the rim of the bowl, nor cover it entirely."
Regarding the patching of the alms bowl: one should patch two parts and leave one part unpatched. If there are holes from which stars can be seen, they should all be patched.
If food enters a hole, it should be picked out as soon as possible; if the remainder cannot be removed, there is no offense.

It is permitted to make a bag to hold it, with a strap to sling over the shoulder, and to carry it under the arm with the opening facing outward. (Because a bhikṣu was carrying his bowl under his arm with the opening facing his side on the road...)

While traveling, he encountered rain. His foot slipped and he fell to the ground; his alms-bowl (pātra) pressed against his ribs, which subsequently caused him illness. For this reason, it was prescribed that the opening [of the bowl] should face outward. Nowadays, it is said that when entering a village to beg for food, the opening faces outward, but once the food has been received, the opening turns toward the ribs.

This is a mistaken tradition, as there is no authoritative source to rely upon. If a bowl breaks, it is permitted to repair it. If one who makes bowls leaves the household life, it is permitted for them to make bowls for the bhikṣus;
it is permitted to keep tools for making them, and it is permitted to fumigate the bowls. One should construct a fumigation furnace, such as a cauldron or a jar, of various kinds.
Sow the mud with apricot seeds and hemp seeds, and enclose the mud with ash. Level the ground to create an incense-bowl site;
place a support and set the bowl upon it. Cover the bowl with a lid and heap ash around its four sides, pressing it down with the hand to make it firm.
Alternatively, heap fresh cow dung around the four sides and burn it; one should perform the fumigation in this manner.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: When the Buddha first appeared in the world, the community of monks had no bowls.

The Buddha commanded Śakra Devendra to have a celestial master craftsman fashion one hundred thousand bowls, which were placed in the marketplaces of the world. In the Sanskrit language, they are called *kaṃsī*.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* translates it as a "shallow iron bowl. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A bowl is half the size of a *kaccara*, and a *kaccara* is small. The *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"A *kaccara* fits into a small bowl; a small bowl fits into a medium bowl; a medium bowl fits into a large bowl.
According to this, the *kaccara* is the smallest among the four types of bowls. Generally, those of the Vinaya school say that one bowl is equivalent to three *kaccaras*.

Upon examining various sections [of the lexicons], this explanation has never been found. As for the character *lù* (鐼), according to the *Haipian*, its pronunciation is *fén* (墳) with the meaning "iron";
it is also pronounced as *shì* (飾) and *bēn* (奔) in the level tone, meaning "a wooden vessel. Even in the *Zihui*, its phonetic glosses place it among the category of iron.
The twenty-second rule: Regarding the precept on seeking a fine bowl for one who possesses a bowl.
If a bhikṣu possesses a bowl that has fewer than five patches and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its excellence, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
That bhikṣu must go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it; [the Saṃgha] shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among their own and give it to him.
One should hold it; one should even hold it until it is broken. This is the proper time. The origin story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the bowl of Upananda had been broken.
He entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to a householder to request a bowl. The householder immediately purchased a bowl and gave it to him. He then went to various other households...
The householder families also sought [alms] in this same manner. By breaking one bowl, they obtained many bowls.
At another time, various lay devotees gathered in one place and each said to themselves, "We have acquired immeasurable merit because we gave bowls to Baddhālita."
Because of this, all the lay devotees (gṛhapati) collectively censured them, saying they lacked shame and remorse; they would break one bowl and keep many bowls in possession.
Although the donors never grew weary of giving, the recipients knew no contentment. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who then established this training rule (śikṣāpada).
Because of their craving for fine things, their afflictions (kleśa) increased and they incurred the world’s censure; thus, he ordained this precept.
**Exegesis:** The text is divided into three sections. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards clarifies the offense incurred for intentional transgression. From "That bhikṣu...
onwards clarifies the procedure for relinquishing [the bowl] within the Saṃgha. From "Even unto... onwards clarifies the method for maintaining and mending the bowl. The Vinaya states:

"Five mends" refers to each mend being two finger-widths apart (a "mend" means to join or patch; it refers to sewing together and reinforcing). "Not leaking with fewer than five mends" refers to the bowl currently being maintained in use.

Although this alms-bowl is broken, its repairs do not yet total five; it holds soup and rice without leaking and remains fit for use and practice. Nevertheless, out of a desire for something new and for the sake of excelling others, he further begs a second bowl from another person.
**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken with fewer than five patches and is not leaking, yet he seeks a new bowl, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If it has five full patches and is not leaking, yet he seeks a new bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This [new bowl] must be relinquished.
As for the relinquishment herein: that bhikṣu should relinquish it before the Saṃgha within this residence.
(Selecting a place other than his current residence). Once he has relinquished it and finished the confession, the Sangha should perform a *karmavācanā* to grant him a bowl.

If this bhikṣu’s bowl is of high value or fine quality, it should be set aside; the lowest and most inferior one should be taken and granted to him by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

After the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* has been performed, that bhikṣu should make a formal announcement regarding the bowl and inquire of the Saṃgha in due order, saying, "It shall be held and given to the Elder.
If the Elder wishes to take this bowl and give it away, he should take his own bowl and give it to the next seat.

If it is given to that bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should accept it; he should not withhold it for the sake of protecting the Saṃgha (meaning he should take what ought to be taken, without necessarily setting it aside to protect the Saṃgha).
Furthermore, he should not, on account of this cause, maintain a most inferior bowl. If he does so maintain one...

*Dukkaṭa* (this refers to the fact that the Saṃgha should not, on account of such conduct involving a transgression regarding the bowl, intentionally take up the very lowest bowl and bring it to the assembly with the intent to exchange it for that fine bowl.

If one accepts it while harboring a prior mind of greed for excellence, how can they be considered a pure member of the assembly? Therefore, this is punished as an offense. This clarifies the specific section within the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*; the text is abbreviated and the meaning is implicit).
If the second *sthavira* takes this bowl, he should take the bowl of the second *sthavira* and give it to the third *sthavira*. If it is given to him...
"Kauṭilya, that bhikṣu should accept it. He should not refuse it out of a desire to protect the Saṃgha, nor should he, for this reason, accept and keep the very lowest bowl.

If he accepts it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense. In this manner, passing it along in succession even to the lowest-ranking monk, if one takes this bhikṣu’s bowl and returns it to him, or if one takes the bowl of the very lowest-ranking monk and gives it to him [he should accept it]."

These are the procedures for the forfeiture and confession of this bowl, as well as the rites of returning the bowl, using the bowl, and entrusting the bowl—namely, the *jñapti* (motion) and the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation).

These are clarified within the context of "practicing observance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) [in accordance with the *Mūla-vinaya*. According to that, a person of fivefold virtue is appointed to handle the bowl; there is also a formal motion to the assembly, which is likewise included within "practicing observance"].
That bhikṣu must guard this bowl and must not place it where tiles or stones might fall upon it, nor place it beneath a leaning staff, nor...
One must not place [the bowl] beneath a hanging object; one must not place it on the road; one must not place it upon a stone;
one must not place it beneath a fruit tree; one must not place it on uneven ground.

A bhikṣu must not hold two bowls with one hand, except when using the fingers to separate them at the center. One must not hold two bowls with one hand while opening a door, except when exercising careful attention.
One must not place [the bowl] inside the threshold or beneath the door leaf. One must not hold the bowl and place it beneath a rope bed or a wooden bed, except for a momentary placement.
One must not place it between a rope bed and a wooden bed. One must not place it on the corner of a rope bed or a wooden bed, except for a momentary placement.
One must not stand while rinsing the bowl, even to the point of breaking it. A bhikṣu must not...
Therefore, one should not intentionally break a bowl, nor should one intentionally cause it to be lost. If it is intentionally broken, one must not treat it as anything other than a bowl.
If, after having discarded it, one does not return it, one incurs an offense as described above.

This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the presence of a mind intent on greedy accumulation; second, that one possesses a bowl that has been mended and is free of leaks;
and third, that one has already obtained a fine bowl through begging.
The regulation for Bhikṣuṇīs regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (shared rule and shared training): for Śikṣamāṇās, Śrāmaṇeras, and Śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This constitutes an offense.

There are five cases where one does not commit an offense when accepting [a bowl]: if it is mended with fewer than five patches; if one seeks a new bowl because the existing one has fewer than five patches;
if one asks for it from a relative; if one asks for it from a renunciant; if one seeks it on behalf of another; if another seeks it for one's sake; if one obtains it without having asked for it;
if one receives a bowl when it is being given to the Sangha and it falls to one's turn; or if one purchases and keeps it using one's own funds.
Furthermore, there is no offense in cases such as when the precepts have not yet been established.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken but can still be mended with a single patch, even if it has not yet been patched, he may still use it.
If he seeks another bowl, at the time of seeking, he commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); once he obtains it, he commits an offense."
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: If one perceives what is not good as good, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one perceives what is good as not good, there is no offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu who maintains a patched bowl intentionally breaks it, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
However, if his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), teacher (*ācārya*), or spiritual friends, out of compassion for him because washing the bowl hinders his practice, hide it away;
and if, not seeing it, he asks for another, there is no offense. He should accept and maintain one bowl that he receives. If he receives two bowls, [he should keep] one...
The alms bowls enter the Sangha’s pure kitchen (*śuddha-kūṭī*). This continues until ten bowls are obtained;

nine bowls enter the Sangha’s pure kitchen (the "pure kitchen" refers to a consecrated area established by *jñapti-karman*, not the modern-day kitchen). If one obtains the value of a bowl, it is likewise.
The *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states: "If one begs for and obtains many bowls, one should relinquish them with a single intention."
Regarding those who delight in sensual pleasures, others should agree with them.
This precept is studied by followers of the Mahāyāna as well.
Appendix for examination: The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states that there are five kinds of molten or moist substances that should not be used to mend a bowl: namely, black...
Sugar, beeswax, lead, tin, and realgar (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: these five substances fall away when applied to a heated object).
There are five methods for repairing an iron alms-bowl: first, to plug the hole with a small nail; second, to attach a small iron plate and hammer it in until firm;
third, to cut the four edges like fish-teeth so that they interlock internally and externally; fourth, to cover the hole with an iron plate and fasten it all around with nails.
Fifth, the use of powdered materials. There are two kinds: first, filings of iron; second, powder from a grinding stone.

The former is used to repair iron bowls, and the latter to repair earthenware bowls. When using the powder for patching, mix it with oil and thoroughly grind it within an iron bowl using an iron hammer.
Only then should it be used to fill the hole, immediately burning it over a low flame to make it hard. If it is coarse or rough...
Furthermore, apply oil and fumigate it according to the prescribed method. If the earthenware bowl has cracks or pores, fill them with a mixture of sand and silt and dry it over a fire.
If it is cracked or broken, carve it into the shape of a drum-waist and fill it with iron plugs;
then coat it with clay and use it after fumigating it with fire. In general discussion regarding bowls, there are four kinds of perfection. First:
1. Perfection of substance: this refers to it being made of iron. 2. Perfection of characteristics: this refers to its being solid, without holes or seams, and not susceptible to stains or grease.

3. Perfection of measure: this refers to it being a large bowl. 4. Perfection of the place of acquisition: this refers to obtaining it through distribution among the community or obtaining it from a donor.
The twenty-third precept concerning robes woven by a non-relative weaver:
If a bhikṣu personally solicits thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into the three robes,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī. At that time, Bhadanta wanted to sew a *saṃghāṭī*.
He entered the city and went to the houses of various lay devotees (*gṛhapati*), seeking thread everywhere.

Having begged for a great deal of thread, he took it to a weaver and had him weave it into the three robes (*tricīvara*). He himself prepared the shuttle and personally supervised the weaving. The lay devotees saw this.
They were thus criticized and disparaged. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who established this precept because such criticism arises from causing distress to things.
This constitutes the fundamental category of theft within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].

**Explanation of the Meaning:** The Vinaya states: "To beg for oneself" means to personally go begging from place to place. "Threads" refers to ten kinds, namely the ten types of cloth threads mentioned above.
[There are four cases regarding the weaver and the provider of the thread: 1. The weaver is not a relative (*ñāti*), and the one who provides the thread is not a relative.

2. The weaver is not a relative, but the one who provides the thread is a relative. 3. The weaver is a relative, [but the provider is not]. 4. [The weaver is] a relative, and the one who provides the thread...
This refers to one who is not a relative. However, it is prohibited by the rule against those who are not relatives;
the offense is established therein. Regarding the transgression in this matter: if the weaver is not a relative and the one providing the thread is also not a relative.
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: If one personally supervises the weaving, weaves it oneself, or winds the thread onto the shuttle, in each case there is the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

The method for relinquishing, confessing, and returning the cloth for this precept is explained in the section on "The Practice of Observance" (*dhāraṇā*). If, after having relinquished it, one does not return it, and so forth, [the corresponding offenses apply].
The offense is as described above.

This precept incurs the full offense only when three conditions are met: first, seeking out and following instructions out of greed or pride; second, begging for thread from one who is not a relative;
and third, having that non-relative weave a robe without providing payment.
The regulation for Bhikṣuṇīs regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense is the same as that for the Bhikṣus (same regulation, same training).
For Śikṣamāṇās, Śrāmaṇeras, and Śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if the weaver is a relative; if the one who provides the thread is a relative;
or if one weaves for oneself a bowl bag, a leather sandal bag, a needle case, a woolen mat, or a meditation belt; or if one makes a waistband, a cap, or socks;
as well as cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute no offense.

Regarding the act of gathering [wool]: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if one personally begs for thread, it is a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (an offense of transgression through mental regret); if one obtains it, it is a *vyatikrama-āpatti*;
and if it is woven into cloth, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one weaves it oneself, or causes the fivefold assembly (*pañcavarga*) to weave it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "If the donor himself possesses faith and has them weave it, or if one provides payment to the weaver, there is no offense.
However, if one makes false claims of one's own superior virtues with a deceitful mind in order to obtain goods, it is an *āpatti-duṣkṛta*."
One may incur a *pārājika* offense (a *pārājika* refers to a defeat) all at once.

Even for one who possesses genuine virtue, if they cause a weaver distress—even though they are personally related to him—by acting at an improper time or by manifesting strange gestures, they incur an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) or a *pācittiya* (offense requiring confession). All such instances result in an *dukkaṭa*.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one possesses few robes, one should properly beg for robes; one should not beg for thread to make robes.
If one requires thread for sewing a robe or making a belt, there is no offense."
The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one requests [cloth] on behalf of the Saṃgha, there is no offense.
This precept is not shared in the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings.
The twenty-fourth: The Precept Against Encouraging the Weaving of Fine Robes.

If a monk, when a householder or a householder’s wife has employed a weaver to weave a robe for that monk, goes to the weaver’s place before having been invited to do so and says: "Weave this robe for me;
weave it very well, making it broad, large, and firm. I shall give you a small amount as payment. If that monk gives him the payment...
Even for the value of a single meal, if one obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

The Origin Story: This precept has two enactments. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there was a householder in the city who provided high-quality thread and had a weaver weave a robe for Upananda. The weaver...
He went to the monastery and spoke to Upananda. Upananda immediately dispatched a weaver to produce a cloth that was both vast and of fine quality. The weaver said that the thread was insufficient.

Upananda went to the house of a lay devotee and begged for more thread. The laywoman brought out her thread box, and he took whatever fine thread he desired at his own pleasure and gave it to the weaver.
The weaver said that the payment was too small; Upananda then further promised to provide him with the necessary price.
The householder returned from elsewhere and asked his wife, "Has the robe you were weaving previously been finished?
His wife replied that it was finished and brought the robe for him to see. The householder said, "This is not the robe I previously had woven. The wife then explained the circumstances in detail.
The householder immediately became critical and disparaging. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha. This was the first formulation of the precept.
Thus, after the precepts had been established, lay devotees made spontaneous invitations to offer robes to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare accept. Furthermore, there were lay devotees who wished to give expensive robes to the bhikṣus;

however, because the bhikṣus were of few desires and contented, they wished for something less valuable and were hesitant, not daring to accept. The Buddha said: "If it is a prior invitation made during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony..."
And when asked for something inferior, he answered as he pleased; therefore, the phrase "not previously invited to a *pravāraṇā*" was added.

This is the second formulation of the precept (*śikṣāpada*). Because it had invited public censure and suspicion, this training rule was established. It belongs to the category of the fundamental offenses of theft within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. The first, beginning with "The layman and the laywoman sent a weaver," clarifies the matter of covetous seeking.
The second, beginning with "This bhikṣu provided the price," establishes the offense committed. The Vinaya states: "The layman and the laywoman are as described above.
There are ten kinds of robes, as mentioned above. [The phrase] "Give me a very fine weave" means to make it exquisite; it also carries the sense of making the robe vast, solid, and dense. Broad...

"Those that are sufficient" means they are measured by the vertical length of the foot. "Large" means they are measured by the horizontal span of the foot. "Firm" refers to being solid; "fine" refers to being dense and subtle. "Even down to the value of a single meal" means, at the very least, the wage for the labor of providing one meal.
Regarding the offense: among these, the transgression occurs if a bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation for the *pravāraṇā*, goes to seek robes.
If he obtains them, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if he does not obtain them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning robes under this precept are explained within the section on "Practicing and Maintaining" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*). If one relinquishes them and fails to return them as required, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept constitutes a full offense only when five conditions are met: first, seeking something superior out of greed or pride; second, not having previously accepted an invitation.
Third, going three times to entrust [the task] to the weaver; fourth, agreeing to increase the price; fifth, taking possession once the robe is finished.

This also includes the regulation for *bhikṣuṇīs*, which constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (the same rule applies to those of common training). For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
These constitute the transgressions.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one has previously accepted an invitation for a *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) and then goes to seek [food];

if one seeks with moderation and in reduced measure; if one requests from relatives; if it is for the sake of another or another is acting on one's behalf; if one obtains it without having requested it;
or if it concerns the initial period before the precept was established—these constitute cases of no offense.
Regarding the acquisition [of robes], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one says to a weaver, "Weave this well for me; weave it firmly and tightly;
beat it [to make it smooth]," one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinayātikrama* offense. When the weaver applies his hand and beats the cloth during weaving, for each stroke, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he obtains it in this manner, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If one merely goes to encourage [the weaver] and obtains a robe without paying a price, it is a *vyatikrama*.
Regarding Vinaya offenses, the *Mūla-vinaya* states: If, for the sake of obtaining robes, one rises from one's seat, adjusts one's robes,
takes two sets of five types of food and so forth, goes to the weaver’s place, and hands them over while urging him to weave well, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense in each case.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: Regarding this robe, regardless of whether its dimensions are appropriate or inappropriate, one incurs an offense in all cases.
If, for the sake of a weaver, one instructs them to weave well and—without providing food, utensils, or the price for food—obtains a fine robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing).
If one sends a messenger, a letter, or a seal, and promises to provide food, utensils, or the price for food, yet obtains a fine robe [without having given them], [it is likewise an offense].
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: If one has yarn of one's own and causes a weaver to weave it, there is no offense.
This precept is likewise established in the Mahāyāna; it concerns seeking what is improper and seeking excessively.
The twenty-fifth [offense] is the precept against taking back a robe out of anger after having given it.
If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or instructs another to seize it, saying, "Give me back my robe;
I will not give it to you," and if that other bhikṣu returns the robe and he takes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Nanda’s disciple was skilled at exhorting and converting others.
Upananda said to him, “Travel through the countryside with me; I shall give you a robe.
After Upananda had given him the robe, the other monks asked him, “For what purpose did you travel with Upananda? He replied, “I am a fool.”
The people did not know how to recite the precepts, nor did they know how to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony or the formal legal acts (*karmavācanā*).
Later, when that bhikṣu did not follow along, Upāli (Baddhananda) demanded back his former robe. When the bhikṣu refused to return it, Upāli became enraged and forcibly seized it.
The bhikṣu cried out loudly, "Do not do this! Do not do this! Hearing the sound, all the bhikṣus from the neighboring cells came together in a great assembly.

Questioning him as to the reason, he informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. Because of this matter regarding the taking of robes—and out of intolerance for negligence and the affliction of censure—he formulated this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
This constitutes the fundamental category of theft within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
**Exegesis:** The text is divided into three sections. First, "giving robes to a bhikṣu" clarifies that he delights in giving voluntarily.
Second, from "if he becomes angry" onwards, it clarifies taking them back through anger. Third, from "if the bhikṣu returns the robe" onwards, it establishes the offense committed.

The Vinaya states: "There are ten kinds of robes as mentioned above" (*Vinayaviniścaya* says: "The phrase 'giving a robe' is a general heading. When giving a robe, if one says, 'You may serve as my servant,' and if [the recipient] does not...").

"Acting as my messenger to seize his robes; later, he becomes angry. "Later" refers to a different time. "Angry" (*krodha*) means manifesting signs of distress through bodily action (*kāyakarman*); "resentful" (*pratigha*) means harboring internal indignation and anger within the mind.
"Seizes" refers to the fact that, based on his original intention to have certain expectations, when those desires are not fulfilled, he consequently takes the robes back by force.

Regarding the offense: among these, the transgression occurs if a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or instructs another to seize and conceal it;
this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If he seizes it but does not conceal it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If [an object] is attached to a tree, a wall, a fence, or even to a clothing rack, a bed, or bedding, and one takes it away from its place, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if one takes it without removing it from its place, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning robes regarding this precept are explained under the section on "active observance. If one relinquishes them and fails to return them as required, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept constitutes a full offense only when four conditions are met: first, it was originally given to another; second, the recipient is pure.
Monks, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense through three causes: (1) taking back [the object] out of anger; (2) concealing it by moving it from its place; and (3) storing it away.

This is also regulated for *bhikṣuṇīs*, who likewise commit a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This constitutes an infraction.
Exemptions from offense: If one does not speak with anger, saying, "I regret it; I will not give you the robe; bring it back to me";
or if that person, knowing the other's heart has changed its mind, immediately returns the robe; or if another person says, "This bhikṣu wishes to regret his decision and return the robe to him";
or if one borrows another's robe and wears it, and while wearing it improperly, it is seized [from one]. If...
If there is fear that the robe will be lost; or if there is fear that it will be damaged; or if that person has broken the precepts, broken their views, or broken their deportment;
or if they have been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*); or if they have been expelled (*pabbājaniya-kamma*), or are subject to expulsion;

or if it is for the sake of a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacariya*)—in all such cases, taking [the robe] away without hiding or storing it, as well as when the rule had not yet been established, constitutes no offense.

Regarding the method of distribution, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There may be cases where what is given collectively is taken individually, or what is given individually is taken collectively;
there may be cases where what is given collectively is taken collectively, or what is given individually is taken individually. If it is taken collectively, one incurs one *pāyattika*;
if it is taken individually, one incurs numerous *pāyattikas*. When giving robes, if one says: 'I shall give them to those who stay by my side.'"
If one who does not abide [in the precepts] takes [the robe], or says, "I will give it to you if it suits your fancy," and then takes it back if it does not suit his fancy;
or if he gives it for the sake of receiving the scriptures, and then takes it back because he does not receive the scriptures—in all these cases there is no offense.

Or, if one sells a robe but has not yet received the payment, and while the payment is not yet complete, he takes the robe back—there is no offense. Or, if a disciple is incorrigible, [one may take back the robe] in order to discipline him.
If one seizes [the robe] out of subjugation, and after having subdued the person returns it, there is no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one instructs a bhikṣu to seize another's robe while the robe has not yet left the body, both incur a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If it has left the body, both incur a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). The owner incurs the fault of relinquishment. (The "owner" refers to the former [owner]).
Regarding "one who gives clothing": the forfeiture refers to the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one seizes the robes of a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī..."
*Duṣkṛta*. If one seizes the robes of a *śrāmaṇera* who has received the precepts and is undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*;
or those who are blind, deaf, mute; or those who have not been seen [to be worthy of] banishment; or those who have not abandoned evil and heterodox views and have been banished—all are *duṣkṛta*.

If one seizes the robes of one with a deranged mind, a distracted mind, or a diseased mind; or one who has committed the four grave offenses (*pārājika*) or the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*); or one who belongs to the five classes of people [unfit for ordination]—all are *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣuṇī takes the robe of another bhikṣuṇī, or the robe of a śrāmaṇerī who has received the full precepts, or even the robe of one who has committed the five heinous crimes or belongs to the five types of persons [who cannot receive ordination], it is entirely a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). If she takes the robe of a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

If she first gives her own robe to another with the fundamental intention [of giving]—meaning she truly intends to give it so that the robe already belongs to the other and the other becomes its owner—and later, for the sake of causing annoyance, temporarily...

If one takes back [a robe] that was given away, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The robe must be relinquished to another; the confession is for a *pāyattika* offense. "Relinquishing the robe to another" means that it is still returned to that person.

If one originally gave the robe as a permanent gift and later took it back permanently, one must calculate its value; if it reaches five *māṣakas*, a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) is committed (since a value of five *māṣakas* constitutes a serious transgression).
If one temporarily lent the robe to another and later took it back out of anger with the intent to cause them distress, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one seizes [the robes] for the purpose of subduing [the offender] so that they may abandon unwholesome dharmas, there is no offense in the temporary confiscation. (According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, seizing the robes of those with broken precepts or wrong views constitutes no offense:

first, one gives the robes to them for the sake of upholding the precepts; later, because they commit offenses such as breaking the precepts, one seizes them back. This is a means of subduing the mind, and therefore it is not an offense. However, according to the *Sarvāstivāda* regulations, seizing the robes of a śrāmaṇera who has received the full precepts, or even those of a person who has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*), constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.)

Since he was originally one who had been granted [the robe] because he was under formal accusation for study, yet first gave it out of compassion and later took it back out of anger, his joy and wrath were inconsistent and he acted according to his own whims and views; this is why he incurred the offense.
This precept is shared with those of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the twenty-sixth precept on medicinal substances kept for seven days:
if a bhikṣu has an illness, he may consume residual medicines—namely ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—for up to seven days. If...
If one consumes [the medicine] after seven days have passed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the monks were afflicted by wind-related ailments during the autumn months;

their bodies became withered and dry, and they developed malignant sores. The Buddha permitted the consumption of the five kinds of medicine at any time, whether it was the proper time or not, when one was ill. Thus spoke Piṅgiya.
Kātyāyana was staying in Rājagṛha. He was widely renowned and had a large following of disciples.

He obtained great quantities of the five kinds of medicinal substances—ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—which his disciples accumulated, stored, and distributed throughout various places.
The quarters became foul and filthy. When the elders saw such hoarded messes scattered about, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying they were like the storehouses of King Bimbisāra.
A monk who possessed contentment heard this and informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. This is an offense of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
It was formulated as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) due to the affliction of greed regarding the matter of medicine for the sick.

**Exegesis:** The text is divided into two sections. The first, beginning with "In cases of illness," clarifies the permission to take medicine. The second, beginning with "If [the time] passes," establishes the nature of the offense.
The Vinaya states: "The sick person is instructed by a physician to take such-and-such kinds of medicine.

Regarding "medicine": ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar (*śarkarā*). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of illness: first, those primarily consisting of hunger and thirst; second, those adventitious illnesses numbering four hundred and four. The conditions for all illnesses do not exceed three types, namely..."

Wind, heat, and phlegm—these three types of illness can be eliminated by three medicines: oil removes wind; clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and rock honey remove bile-fever (*pitta*); honey and aged granulated sugar can remove phlegm.

For those with combined illnesses, one should employ all these medicines together to treat them. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Regarding the four hundred and four illnesses: there are one hundred and one wind illnesses, one hundred and one fire illnesses, one hundred and one water illnesses, and one hundred and one combined illnesses."

Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu acquires and stores medicinal substances on the first day, and continues to acquire and store them on the second, third, fourth, and even up to the seventh day, such that when the dawn of the eighth day appears, he still possesses those medicinal substances acquired during the seven days.
All are subject to the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). (The phrase "one day" is as explained in the precept concerning the keeping of extra robes.
If, within seven days, one obtains medicine either on alternate days or on only a single day, and the dawn of the eighth day breaks, all are subject to forfeiture.

If medicine obtained within a seven-day period has not been formally offered away (*apariṇata*), nor has it been given to another, and if it is neither lost, nor discarded, nor spoiled, one may use it as non-medicine—meaning that if it is ghee or oil, one may use it to light a lamp, or to anoint the feet, or to anoint the doors and windows; or if it is honey or rock sugar, one may give it to the pure attendants (*śucika*) of the monastery.
However, if one takes it without the intention of treating it as a close friend’s gift and does not relinquish it, then at the appearance of the dawn on the eighth day, it is entirely forfeited.
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense regarding medicinal substances and does not relinquish them, but instead exchanges them for other medicines, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and one *duṣkṛta*.

The methods for receiving various medicines under this precept, as well as the methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning the medicines, are explained in the section on "Practical Observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). If...
If one discards [the medicine] and does not return it, etc., the offense incurred is as described above.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, it must be seven-day medicine; second, there must be a mind of greedy possession.

After three times seven days have passed, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* (the same rule applies to her fellow students); for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is defined as an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: If it is medicine that has exceeded seven days; if ghee or oil is used to lubricate the hinges of a door;
if honey or rock sugar is given to a park keeper; if, upon reaching the seventh day, it is discarded and given to a bhikṣu to eat;
if, before the seven days have elapsed, it is returned to that bhikṣu, who should then use it to anoint his feet, light a lamp, or for other such purposes. This applies to the first case as well.
If the precepts have not yet been promulgated, etc., this constitutes no offense.

The *Vinayasamgraha* states: If seven days have elapsed and one perceives them as having elapsed—or suspects they have—and [the garment] is discarded, it is an offense of expiation (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If fewer than seven days have elapsed but one perceives them as having elapsed—or suspects they have—one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If [one wears it] for the sake of a fine appearance, or if it is worn...

Regarding flavors: if one seeks robustness or nourishment while maintaining a deceitful mind toward the precepts, or partakes in various medicinal substances, these all constitute offenses of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
When receiving seven-day medicine, at the time of actual consumption, one should inform a fellow practitioner of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*) by saying:
"I have already finished taking the medicine for one day; six days remain, and I shall take it. This applies accordingly up to the seventh day.

[The Buddha] knew. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one has a serious illness, it does not constitute an offense to consume food. When these four types of nourishment are being digested, one should form this thought:

'I am consuming this for the sake of treating my illness, not for the sake of delicious flavors. (The four types of nourishment are ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar. Rock sugar is [forbidden] outside of the proper time."
One must not eat at improper times (vikāla) without permission. There are five types of persons who are permitted to eat at improper times:

those traveling on a long journey, the sick, those unable to obtain food, those who eat very little, and those at a place where water is being distributed, provided it is mixed with water before drinking.

(In recent times, there have been some who preach and perform liturgical repentance ceremonies, claiming that rice, sugar, dried tangerine peel, and orange cakes may be used as medicinal food and thus may be eaten at improper times without restraint. These individuals all follow their own arbitrary whims and allow junior students to imitate them; yet, upon a thorough investigation of the Vinaya texts of the five schools, no such practice has been found.)
[Permit me to] explain and listen.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
The twenty-seventh: the precept against seeking and using rain-clothing at an improper time.
If a bhikṣu has one month remaining of the summer retreat, he should seek a rain-bathing robe; he should use it for bathing during the final half-month.
If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bathing robe more than one month before the end of the retreat, or uses it for bathing more than half a month before that time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī. Viśākhā, Mother of Mṛgāra, invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal the following day.
At the time of the meal, it rained heavily. The Buddha said, "This rain is the last rain; it shall be the same for the four continents.
He then ordered all the bhikṣus to go outside and bathe in the rain. A maidservant came and announced that the time for the meal had arrived.

Seeing from afar that the bhikṣus were all bathing naked, she suspected they were non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthika). She returned and informed her mistress, who again commanded her to go and invite them.
When the Buddha arrived at her house and had finished accepting the offerings, the Mother Viśākhā requested eight boons from the Buddha.
"May you grant food to the visiting bhikṣus; for these visiting bhikṣus have come from afar and do not know where they should go.
May you grant food to the traveling bhikṣus; for some, on account of food, have been unable to keep up with their companions. May you grant food to the sick bhikṣus."
If he does not obtain food suitable for his illness, he will pass away; if he obtains food suitable for his illness, he will recover.

I pray that you grant medicine to the sick bhikṣu, so that if he does not obtain medicine suitable for his illness, he will not pass away, and if he obtains medicine suitable for his illness, he may recover.
I pray that you grant food to the attendant, so that because he seeks it for himself, he does not neglect nursing the patient. I pray...
She provided the bhikṣus with gruel. In the early morning, she sent a maidservant to the saṃghārāma to invite the Saṃgha, announcing that the time had come.

She saw that all the bhikṣus were bathing naked in the rain. She made eight vows to provide for them as long as she lived, saying, "I pray that you will grant me the provision of rain-bathing robes for the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs. The Buddha granted them all. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard of this.

The Buddha permitted the keeping of a rain-bathing robe (*vassikasāṭikā*). Thereupon, [monks] constantly sought rain-bathing robes at all times—spring, summer, and winter—and did not relinquish their rain robes even when they were no longer needed, using them for other purposes. Even when they possessed a rain robe, they would still bathe naked.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who, due to the afflictions of greed and pride, established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. The first, beginning with "one month remaining of spring," clarifies the regulation regarding the procurement and use [of the rain-bathing robe].
The second, beginning with "if a bhikṣu exceeds one month," establishes the offense incurred. As for what the Vinaya calls the "rain-bathing robe" (*varṣāśāṭī*), there are ten types as listed above.
On the sixteenth day of the third month, that bhikṣu should seek a rain-bathing robe.

On the first day of the fourth month, he should use it. (This is calculated by taking the fourth month as one period; from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month constitutes the spring period.

When it is said here, "one month remains at the end of spring, he should seek a rain-bathing robe," it means that three months of the spring period have already passed and only one month remains—specifically, from the sixteenth day of the third month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month. Within this single month, he should seek it, and by the first day of the fourth month, he should use it. As for its dimensions, the length...)

Short. This is explained in the eighty-ninth precept among the *pācittiya* offenses. However, since this robe is intended to prevent the difficulty of procuring one when it is urgently needed—such as when the rainy season is approaching and the days of the retreat are near—it is permitted to seek it out one month prior to the end of summer.

One should not seek [robes] at this time, nor is it permitted to seek them during the summer retreat. Since the primary purpose of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is the practice of the Path, one should not engage in seeking or acquisition, for fear that it would cause the abandonment of one's principal practice.

The Determination of the Offense: Regarding those who commit an offense herein, if a bhikṣu seeks robes before the sixteenth day of the third month and uses them before the first day of the fourth month, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning this robe are explained in the section on "Practicing the Observance" (*dhāraṇa*). If one relinquishes it and fails to return it, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept constitutes a full offense only when three conditions are met: first, a lack of reverence for the teaching; second, [the period] exceeds one month; and third, [the robe is not returned].
If one obtains a robe and uses it more than half a month before [the prescribed time], it constitutes an offense.
This also governs the *bhikṣuṇī*s; for them, it is a *duṣkṛta* (a minor offense), though the rule is the same while the training is different.
For *śikṣamāṇā*s, *śrāmaṇera*s, and *śrāmaṇerī*s, it is also a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one requests [the rain-cloth] on the sixteenth day of the third month and uses it on the first day of the fourth month;

or if, having relinquished the rain-cloth, one subsequently puts it to another use; or if one wears a bathing robe for the purpose of bathing; or if one has no rain-cloth and makes one into a bathing robe;
or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—these constitute no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu intends to observe the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*), he should seek a rain-bathing robe during the final month of spring.
If a bhikṣu intends to observe the later retreat (*paścimavarṣā*), he should think: "Since they are seeking robes, why should I not seek one as well?
If he succeeds in obtaining one [at that time], he commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If a bhikṣu...

If a bhikṣu who has entered the later retreat (*paścimā varṣā*) takes a rain-bath robe (*varṣāśāṭī*) and continues to keep it until the end of the eighth month, he commits an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If a bhikṣu who has entered the earlier retreat (*pūrvā varṣā*) thinks: "Since that person still keeps his robe until the end of the eighth month, why should I not do the same?

and then keeps it [beyond the proper time], he also incurs an offense of expiation with forfeiture. If bhikṣus each seek robes according to their respective summer retreats and keep those robes [within the prescribed limits], there is no offense.

[This refers to] one who is without offense (*anāpatti*). Although the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is divided into the earlier and later periods, each period lasts for a full ninety days; thus, the two periods cannot be treated as equivalent examples of one another.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This robe must not be accepted. It must be kept as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*) and must not be given away as a formal gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*).
One must not wear this rain-robe to enter rivers or ponds to bathe. Nor may one wear it to bathe during light rain."
One must not bathe naked; one should wear a *śāṭaka* (an inner short skirt). Nor should one wear other old garments or rain-clothing while performing various tasks.

When it is time to bathe during heavy rain, or if the rain suddenly stops and there is still moisture from dirt on the body, one may put on [the rain-clothing] and enter other water to bathe; there is no offense. If a bhikṣu, at the time of eating, wishes to...
One may smear oil on the body. Whether it is during illness or in a place frequented by many people, one may fasten both ends [of the garment] to serve as a barrier against the rain.
This rain-bathing robe may be used for four and a half months (referring to the final fortnight of spring and the four months of the summer retreat).
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it must be relinquished. A single bhikṣu shall announce within the Saṃgha: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today the Saṃgha relinquishes the rain-bathing robe."
"Bath-cloth. Thus it is said three times. If one discards it on the sixteenth day, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*. Once discarded, it may be used as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*).
It may also be formally purified (*pariśuddha*) in the presence of a monk who is a *jñāti* (relative or acquaintance).
Furthermore, one may enter other bodies of water to bathe and perform various types of work; there is no offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "A bhikṣuṇī may possess a bathing robe, but she may not possess a rain-bathing robe;
a bhikṣu, however, may possess a rain-bathing robe. There are generally two purposes for this: first, during the rainy season, it serves to screen the four sides while bathing within;

and during the heat of the summer, it likewise serves as a screen while bathing within. Second, because there is much rain during the summer months, it is used to constantly wrap the three robes when carrying them."

If one observes the practice and there is an intercalary third month, one should not seek [the robes] during the preceding three months. A bhikṣu incurs no offense if he does not keep a rain-bathing robe.
This precept is studied in common with the Mahāyāna.
The twenty-eighth precept concerning the keeping of urgent offerings after the time limit:

If a bhikṣu has not yet completed the ten days before the end of the three-month summer retreat, and the bhikṣus receive an urgent offering of robes, the bhikṣu, knowing it to be an urgent offering of robes, shall accept it.
Having accepted it, he may keep it until the time for robes. If he keeps it beyond that time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Śaikṣa Dharma: Pāyattika*. Origin Story:
While the Buddha was staying at Verañjā, after the summer retreat had concluded, a brahmin invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal;
having finished eating, he offered robes. The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to accept these summer robes. When the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) heard this, they immediately [acted].
At that time, he constantly begged for robes; even before his *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) had concluded, he both begged for robes and accepted them.

Furthermore, after Upananda had completed his *varṣā* at one location, he heard that robes had been obtained in great abundance at another location. He then went everywhere to receive a share of those robes and, taking them with him, entered the Jetavana.
When the monks of few desires learned of this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet establish a formal precept (*śikṣāpada*).
At that time, King Prasenajit dispatched his two ministers, Liśadatta and Punnaka, to suppress a rebellion.
Having received their orders, the two ministers thought to themselves: "We do not know whether we shall return from this expedition;
we ought to prepare food and offer robes in advance for the Sangha. However, because the rainy season retreat had not yet concluded, the bhikṣus did not dare accept the robes and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to accept *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robes).

Based on this, the precept was established. The explanation of the meaning is divided into two sections: from "If ten days have not yet elapsed" below, it clarifies the permission to receive and store [the robe];

from "If [ten days] have passed" below, it establishes the offense incurred. The Vinaya states: "Regarding *ātyayika-cīvara*, if one accepts it, one obtains [the benefit]; if one does not accept it, one loses [the benefit]. (This refers to the donor.)

If there is an urgent matter and one goes out on official business: if the robe is currently present at that time, it may be given; if it is not present, it is lost. Regarding the types of robes, there are ten kinds as mentioned above. Regarding the time for robes:
after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, there is a one-month period before the *kaṭhina* robe is accepted; once the *kaṭhina* robe has been accepted, there is a five-month period.

"Ten days remaining" after the *pravāraṇā* refers to when ten days remain [of the month], specifically from the fifth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth day; hence the expression "ten days remaining. If a bhikṣu encounters an emergency...
Regarding the gift of robes: one should know that this is a "gift of urgent robes" and accept it. Having accepted it, one may keep it for ten days.
Until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*, if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, one may keep it for one month; if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread, one may keep it for five months.

If there are nine days remaining until the *pravāraṇā*, or eight days, or seven days, and so on down to when there is only one day remaining until the *pravāraṇā* (which is the seventh month, tenth day).

Four days have passed; it is now only fifteen days since the morning [of the robe-offering], hence it is said that "one day remains"). When one obtains an *ātyayika-cīvara* (a robe given as an urgent offering), knowing it to be an *ātyayika-cīvara*, one should accept it.
Having accepted it, one should keep it for one month if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread at the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*, or for five months if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread.

**The Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if a bhikṣu receives an urgent offering of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) and keeps it beyond the preceding limit or the subsequent limit, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If one receives [the robe] before the fifth day of the seventh month—provided one has not accepted the *kaṭhina* robe—it is called "keeping beyond the preceding limit" (*pūrvātikrānta*), and one commits an offense. One may keep it until the fifteenth day of the eighth month; if one keeps it beyond the fifteenth day of the eighth month, one commits an offense.

If one has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, one may keep it until the fifteenth day of the twelfth month; if one keeps it beyond that, one commits an offense. These two cases are called "keeping beyond the subsequent limit" (*paścātikrānta*).

The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning this robe are clarified within the section on "Active Observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). If one has relinquished the robe but fails to return it, one incurs an offense as described above.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, it must be an urgently offered robe; second, the mind must harbor greed and arrogance.

Regarding the three types of receiving and keeping [excess robes] beyond the prescribed time limits, this is governed concurrently with the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for *bhikṣuṇīs* (the same rule applies to those of common training).
For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is defined as an infraction.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one obtains an urgent gift-cloth (*ātyayika-cīvara*), it is not an offense provided one does not exceed the [prescribed] time before or after.

Furthermore, if one's robes have been seized by bandits, lost, burned, or carried away by water, it is not an offense to exceed the time limit, provided one maintains the perception that they were indeed seized, lost, burned, or carried away.
If the road is perilous and impassable, or if there are many dangers from bandits, thieves, and fierce beasts; or if the river is in high flood;
or if there is the danger of being imprisoned by a king or the threat to one's life; or if there is the difficulty of practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*);

or if the bhikṣu to whom the entrustment was made has died, gone away, been harmed by thieves or beasts, or been swept away by water—then if [the messenger] passes beyond [the limit] under such circumstances, there is no offense, as well as in the case of the first instance.
If the precepts have not yet been established, this constitutes no offense.
According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, there are five types of "urgent offering robes" (*ātyayika-cīvara*):
those offered for one's own illness, those offered for the illness of another, those offered at the time of death, and those offered for the deceased.
Or if one gives when about to depart; or if it is during the summer retreat; or if at some time the donor wishes to give with their own hands, then taking [the robe] is also not an offense.

If a bhikṣu has been appointed to store the robe, or if the donor says, "When I return from my journey, I shall give it with my own hands," then even if the time limit has passed, keeping it is also not an offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: Regarding "urgent robes" (*akālaka-cīvara*), these may be offered by a king, a queen, a prince, or high-ranking officials and generals to the Saṃgha.
This is because the virtuous intentions of such noble persons are difficult to encounter.

Furthermore, when a woman is about to marry and leave her own home for her husband’s family, she loses her autonomy; therefore, she offers property to the Saṃgha so that she may regain her independence. If...
Giving to the sick ensures benefit for both the living and the deceased; such instances are all termed "urgent robe-gifts" (*ātyayika-cīvara*).

Apart from urgent robe-gifts, all robes belonging to the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) must await the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. If one distributes them during the middle of the retreat, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

This precept may be observed by those of the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings; however, it must be done through a formal, pure act of giving (*śuddha-dāna*). According to the previous discussion, this concerns the twenty-ninth rule:
the offense of being separated from one's robe for more than six nights during the final month of the rainy season retreat.
If a bhikṣu, having completed the three months of the summer retreat and the month of Kārttika having elapsed,
dwells in an araṇya in a place where there is suspicion or fear, and while dwelling in such a place, wishes to leave any one of his three robes behind in a village residence,
he may, for a valid reason, stay apart from his robes for up to six nights. If he exceeds this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Pāyattika. The Origin Story:

The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. After the bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat and one month of the *kārttika* period had passed, they were residing in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*). At that time, there were many bandits who plundered and seized their robes and bowls. All...

They came and stayed together at the Jetavana Monastery. The Buddha, knowing the reason for this, permitted them to remain and stay in that place, with each person leaving their robes inside the monastery.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had granted this permission, they immediately left their robes inside the monastery, entrusted them to a bhikṣu who was a friend, and went out.
The one who had received the entrustment took the robes out and dried them in the midday sun.

The bhikṣus questioned him regarding the reason for this and reported it to the Buddha, who established the precept. Due to the afflictions of delusion and pride, he formulated this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).

Regarding the explanation of its meaning, the text is divided into three sections. The section beginning with "When the three months of the summer retreat have ended" clarifies the completion of the full summer residence and the subsequent relocation. If there is...
The phrase "doubt and fear" below clarifies that it is difficult to grant permission [to leave]. If one exceeds [the limit] below, the offense is established.

"The three months of summer have ended" (meaning from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month). "The subsequent month of Kārttika" (Kārttika is translated here as the Pleiades;

because the Pleiades constellation governs this month, it refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month; this is the one month following the fourth month of summer). "Full" (refers to those who completed the later retreat on the sixteenth day of the fifth month).

On the first day, one begins the formal sitting (sitting in retreat). Although one follows those who have entered the preceding *anvārohaṇa* (rainy season retreat) and has already performed the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the merit of that single summer has not yet been completed. One must necessarily remain for this full month so as to complete the ninety days and thus not violate the rules regarding the breaking of the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
The Vinaya states: "A forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) is located five hundred *dhanus* from a village. In the country of Cāmara, one *dhanus* is four cubits (*hasta*) long;
using the medium cubit as the standard (one person’s cubit being one chi and eight cun in the Zhou measure), five hundred *dhanus* is equivalent to five *li*. There [is such a place].
Regarding "fear due to suspicion": there is the fear of thieves within the village.
When a bhikṣu dwells in such a place and wishes to leave one of his three robes (*tricīvara*) inside the village, the three robes refer to the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *antarvāsaka*.
"Inside the village" refers to a settlement or hamlet. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One of the robes" means either the *saṃghāṭī* or the *uttarāsaṅga*...)

The Saṃgha: one may entrust a single robe according to what is measured, but one must not entrust an *antarvāsa* (lower garment), because it is worn against the body; nor may two be entrusted, because one cannot wear only one when entering the Saṃgha for prostrations or begging for food.

There are circumstances under which one may stay apart from one's robes (these "circumstances" refer to matters concerning a stūpa, matters concerning one’s *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, or other matters; in brief, these include matters related to the Three Jewels, illness, and nursing the sick).

"Staying apart from one's robes" means being separated from the robe that has been entrusted. This applies even up to six nights (*ṣaḍ-rātra*) (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: starting from the sixteenth day of the seventh month, in successive order...).

At night, it was permitted for a bhikṣu observing the *āraṇyaka* retreat to stay apart from his robe. The reason it was permitted was that during these six nights, it is the time when bandits set out; therefore, it was permitted. When those six nights have ended—

On the seventh night, before the appearance of the dawn light, if one relinquishes the three robes, or holds them in hand, or reaches a place where a stone could be thrown (this "place where a stone can be thrown" does not refer to the *āraṇyaka* boundary; rather, it refers to the outer limit of the village dwelling where the robes are deposited).
Regarding the offense: among these, if a bhikṣu has completed six nights and, before the appearance of the dawn light on the seventh night,
does not relinquish his three robes, does not hold them in his hands, and does not remain within the range of a stone’s throw,

and thus spends the night separated from his robes when the dawn light of the seventh night appears, he commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (expiation involving forfeiture) in its entirety.

The methods for relinquishing, confessing, and returning this robe are explained within the section on "Practicing and Maintaining" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*). If one has relinquished it but fails to return it, one incurs an offense as described above.

This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: (1) the period lasts from one day up to six nights; (2) out of negligence, one does not go [to return it] despite being instructed.
Regarding the place where the robe is kept: third, discarding it without forming the mental resolve; fourth, when the dawn has already appeared.
These also apply to the *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom it is a *duṣkṛta* (the rule is the same, though the training is different).
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.

Exceptions where there is no offense: if one has the perception that it was stolen; the perception that it was lost; the perception that it was burned; or the perception that it was swept away; or if the boat crossing is impassable;
or if the road is dangerous and difficult; or if there are many bandits; or if there are fierce beasts; or if the river water has risen in a flood; or if one is held by force.
If one is imprisoned, or faces a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya), and thus does not relinquish the robe, does not hold the robe,
and does not go within the range of a stone’s throw, these cases— being among those for which the precept had not yet been established— are considered non-offenses.
