To say what one has not seen, heard, touched, or known, while knowing it to be a falsehood, is a *pāyattika*.
One forms the thought, "I shall speak falsely," and at the time of speaking falsely, one knows it is a falsehood; having spoken the falsehood—[this constitutes the offense].
Knowing it to be a false speech, one commits a *pāyattika* for lying.
One forms the initial thought, "I shall speak falsely"; while speaking falsely, one knows it is a false speech;
and having finished speaking falsely, one does not recall having spoken falsely—thus one commits a *pāyattika* for lying.
One does not originally form this thought: "I shall speak falsely. At the time of speaking falsely, one knows it is false speech;
after having spoken falsely, one knows it was false speech. Therefore, false speech is a *pāyattika* offense.
One does not originally intend to speak falsehood. While speaking, one knows it is a falsehood; after having spoken the falsehood, one does not recall that it was a falsehood.
Therefore, this is a *pāyattika* offense for speaking falsehood.
What one has seen is different; what one has endured is different; what one desires is different; what one has touched is different; what one has conceived is different;
what one’s mind [perceives] is different—all such matters are false speech. To speak each of these clearly is a *pāyattika*; to speak them without clarity is a *dukkaṭa*.
If, when the precepts are being recited, one is reminded even after being asked three times...
There is an offense, yet it is not termed a *duṣkṛta*.
This method for the confession of the ninety *pāyattika* offenses is explained in detail within the section on "Performance and Maintenance" (*karaṇīya-dhāraṇa*).
From this point onward, there will be no further prolixity.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the intention to speak falsely; second, the statement being untrue;
third, the speech being clearly articulated; and fourth, the listener understanding the meaning.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise a pāyattika (the same rule applies to those of the same training).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.

Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: speaking according to the facts based on one's intention; having perceptions derived from what has been seen, heard, touched, or known, and speaking in reliance upon those perceptions;
and cases such as when the precept has not yet been established—these constitute no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu says anything that contradicts his own mind, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If he speaks without contradicting his own mind, there is no offense."

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "There are cases where false speech constitutes a *pārājika* offense, because one falsely claims to possess superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) that one does not actually possess.
There are cases where false speech constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, because one baselessly slanders another monk with such qualities.
There are cases where false speech constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, such as when one speaks of possessing superhuman qualities [without meeting the criteria for the other offenses]."
If one slanders another with groundless charges, it is not full [of offense] (not full meaning that the statement is incomplete).

Alternatively, there may be false speech that falls under a *pāyattika* offense, such as slandering another with groundless charges of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, or other violations within this precept.

Alternatively, there may be false speech that falls under a *duṣkṛta* offense, such as the false speech of the three groups of disciples. Alternatively, there may be false speech that is without fault, such as that which was previously committed.

For example, suppose a layperson originally broke the precepts because they lacked a teacher or a community of monks; having returned to become a bhikṣu, since they lacked a teacher or a community of monks and had never received the precepts, they subsequently broke them.

There is no longer a precept-essence (śīla-tattva) to be protected; therefore, in both cases, there is no offense of violating the precepts. Nevertheless, by committing evil karma, one cannot escape the retribution of suffering. Whether one speaks falsely by dispatching a messenger or speaks falsely by means of a written letter, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one speaks falsely without prior intent, or speaks falsely through error, confusion, or a slip of the tongue, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
This applies whether one is discussing the meaning of the Dharma, transmitting someone else’s words, or speaking anything at all.

Do not judge all things as either right or wrong; do not arbitrarily grasp at anything as being correct. Always ensure that you rely upon and investigate the fundamental source, for if there is such a basis, there will be no fault.
This precept is established equally in the Mahāyāna; however, it may be waived for the sake of saving and aiding sentient beings—this is called "skillful means speech" or "beneficial speech.
If it does not serve to save or benefit others, one still commits an offense.

Appendix: Examination of the *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha*. It states: "A disciple of the Buddha says: 'One should always speak the truth and should not make oaths, for doing so serves only to clear one's own name while manifesting that others do not believe one.
Even if one is falsely slandered, one should still not take an oath (the term 'xue' means to wash or cleanse)."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: One must not recite incantations for oneself, nor may one recite them for others. One must not make a vow with an object for oneself, nor may one make such a vow for others.

This is because reciting incantations and fleeing into hiding are of the same nature. One must not flee into hiding oneself, nor cause another to flee into hiding. Reciting incantations and fleeing into hiding are of one kind.

The third section states: At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus encountered some minor matter, they immediately uttered curses (to curse means to submit a written petition to deities, as is done today).
They said: "If I do such a thing, may I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma.
If you do such a thing, you too shall fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma."
The Buddha said: "It should not be done in that way. Listen: if one speaks these words, 'If I do such a thing, I take refuge in the Buddha;
if you do such a thing, you also take refuge in the Buddha,' when a householder sneezes or comes to prostrate at one's feet."
One should offer a blessing, saying, "May you live long. If a junior monk sneezes, one should offer a blessing, saying, "May you be free from illness.
If a senior monk sneezes, one should say, "Namo."
The second [offense] regarding disparaging the precepts:
If a bhikṣu utters disparaging words concerning the categories of the precepts, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus settled a dispute.

The incident: He reviled the bhikṣus in various ways. The bhikṣus were ashamed and, losing their composure, were unable to speak. When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
For the sake of the Saṃgha, he established this precept. This is a natural offense (prakṛti-sāvadya) arising from the affliction of intolerance regarding matters concerning renunciants;
thus, this training rule was enacted. It belongs to the category of the fundamental types of false speech in the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].

Commentary on the Meaning: The Vinaya states that those who disparage others by way of their lineage include those born into low-caste families, those of low occupations, and those of low arts and crafts.
The lowly castes are the Caṇḍālas, the scavengers, the bamboo-workers, and the cartwrights.
Those of low caste are the Kauṇḍinya (this is a minor clan of the Jñātṛka in India) and the Kauśināga (this is a low-born lineage in India).

The Bhāradvāja (this is one of the eighteen clans of the Brahmins; they originally resided among the Jñātṛka). Furthermore, if one is not originally of low caste but practices low arts, one is thereby of low caste.
As for those of low occupation: they trade in pigs and sheep, slaughter oxen, and hunt with hawks and falcons.
Fishermen; thieves; those who capture thieves; city guards; judges; those of lowly crafts—namely, smiths, carpenters, potters, leatherworkers, barbers, basket-makers;
or it is said they are transgressors (meaning those who have committed offenses of the seven categories);
those with many dependents; the bald and blind; the bald and sightless; the lame, the crippled, the deaf, and the mute; and others.
If one is subjected to various afflictions, such as being reviled face-to-face with words like, "You were born into a *caṇḍāla* family," and so forth, up to being subjected to various afflictions;
or if one is reviled through metaphorical insults, such as, "You resemble one born into a *caṇḍāla* family," and so forth, up to being subjected to various afflictions;
or if one reviles by way of self-comparison, saying, "I was not born into a *caṇḍāla* family," and so forth...

When people who are afflicted by various misfortunes revile one with wholesome dharmas, saying: "You are an araṇyaka, a beggar for alms, one who wears robes made of rags from dust heaps," and so on, up to "you are a practitioner of dhyāna";
or if they revile you through analogy, saying: "You resemble an araṇyaka," and so on, up to "you resemble a practitioner of dhyāna";
or if they revile you by comparison, saying: "I am not an araṇyaka," and so on, up to "I am not a practitioner of dhyāna" (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* says).

Regarding slanderous speech (*paiśunya-vāda*): it refers to uttering words that manifest and expose matters intended to disparage others. For this reason, harmony of mind brings joy, and harmony of speech prevents contention; all such discordant states are not speech in accordance with the Vinaya.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if a bhikṣu speaks disparaging words concerning another’s lineage, whether by direct abuse, by metaphorical abuse, or by comparing himself to them, if he speaks clearly and intelligibly, it is a *pāyattika* offense in every case.
If he speaks but does not do so clearly and intelligibly, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense in every case.
If a bhikṣu speaks of wholesome dharmas while reviling others by comparing them to others, or by comparing himself to them,
whether he speaks clearly or not, it is entirely a duṣkṛta offense.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, there must be a mind of disparagement; second, the object of disparagement must be a bhikṣu or another’s parents;
third, one must disparage them with words of lowliness; and fourth, both the speaker and the listener must understand what is said clearly.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise a pāyattika (the rule is the same and the training is shared).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: speaking for the sake of mutual benefit; speaking for the sake of the Dharma; speaking for the sake of the Vinaya;
speaking for the sake of instruction; speaking out of intimacy or affection; speaking in jest; speaking inadvertently during the course of conversation;
speaking alone; speaking in a dream; or intending to say one thing but mistakenly saying another—and furthermore...
If [the offense] has not yet been established as a precept and so forth, it constitutes no transgression.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are seven types of disparagement: disparaging based on lineage, occupation, physical appearance, illness, offenses, verbal abuse, and afflictions (*kleśa*).

(Now, because we are in the final age, people engage in much strife; for this reason, I have extensively cited the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* to clarify the characteristics of transgressions in detail. Do not grow weary of its prolixity. Regarding what is generally referred to herein as...)

The *sthūlātyaya* offenses are all independent minor grades (*mṛdu-pakṣa*) and are categorized identically with the offense of reviling the Saṅgha; they do not arise from the first two categories [of the Prātimokṣa]. Regarding caste, there are superior, middling, and inferior types.
If one says of an inferior person, "You are a *caṇḍāla*, a wool-worker, a weaver, a potter, or a leather-worker," and thereby causes that person to feel shame, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one says, "Your parents were such as these," one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one says, "Your preceptor and ācārya are like this," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says, "Your companions and friends are like this," it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

If one says, "You are of intermediate caste" (meaning you are neither born of a noble lineage nor the offspring of a low-born family), with the intent to cause them shame, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If you speak thus regarding your parents, you commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If you speak thus regarding your two teachers, you commit a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If you speak thus regarding your companions and friends, you commit a *vinayātikrama* offense of mental regret (*cittavipratisāra*).
As for the highest [offense], if one says to another, "You are of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa caste," with the intent of making that person feel ashamed, it is likewise [an offense].
An offense of transgression against the Vinaya: you have [associated with] such persons as your parents and two teachers; all are offenses of transgression against the Vinaya.
You have [associated with] such persons as your companions and spiritual friends; this is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya, to be confessed with a mind of regret.

Occupations are of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior. The inferior are those such as you—namely, a butcher, a seller of pigs, a fisherman, a hunter, a bird-catcher, a snare-setter, a city-guard, or an executioner.
To speak such words with the intent to cause another to feel shame constitutes a *pāyattika*.
"Your parents were like this" is a *pāyattika*. "Your two teachers were like this" is a *pāyattika*.
Thullaccaya: "Your friend and companion is like this"—this is a *vibhaṅga* offense.

"The one who sells incense, the shopkeeper, the farmer, the vegetable grower, or the messenger is like this"—if you speak such words with the intent to cause them shame, it is a *thullaccaya*. "Your parents are like this"—*thullaccaya*.

If you speak thus regarding your two teachers, it is an offense of transgression against the *vinaya*. If you speak thus regarding your companions and friends, it is an offense of transgression requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*).

Furthermore, if you are a goldsmith, a silversmith, a jeweler, a copper-smith, or a shopkeeper, and you speak such words with the intent to cause them shame, it is an offense of transgression against the *vinaya*. If you speak thus regarding your parents or your two teachers, [it is likewise].

An offense against the Vinaya: "Your friend and companion is like this. If one says this, causing the other to feel shame through a transgression of the mind involving remorse (*viniścaya-citta-kaukṛtya*), there are three grades:
inferior, middling, and superior. The inferior grade consists of saying things such as, "You are blind, hunchbacked, have clubbed feet, or saw-toothed [teeth]," thereby making the other feel ashamed;
this is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). "Your parents are like this" is also a *pāyattika*.
"Nyati! Your two teachers were like this. *Thullaccaya*. "Your companions and friends were like this. *Dubbhāsita*.
"The middling ones—your great black, great white, great yellow, and great red [complexioned ones]—were like this.
If one speaks these words to cause another to feel shame, it is a *thullaccaya*. "Your parents were like this. *Thullaccaya*.
If you say of your two teachers, "They are like this," it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*viniya-āpatti*).
If you say of your companions and spiritual friends, "They are like this," it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya with mental regret (*viniya-citta-vipratisāra-āpatti*).

If you say of those who possess the thirty-two marks and the halo of golden light, "They are like this," with the intent to cause them shame, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. If you say of your parents and your two teachers, "They are like this," [it is likewise].
All incur an offense of *vinaya*-transgression. It is the same for a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Regarding those with offenses of *vinaya*-transgression who feel remorse, there are no such things as inferior, middling, or superior illnesses; all are classified as inferior.

You [who suffer from] diseases such as scabies, sores, leprosy, abscesses, hemorrhoids, jaundice, malaria, consumption, emaciation, and insanity—regarding these various kinds of ailments, act [as follows].
To speak these words with the intent to cause another to feel shame constitutes a *pāyattika*. "Your parents were like this" is a *pāyattika*.
"Your two teachers were like this" is a *sthūlātyaya*. "Your friends and associates were like this" is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

"There is no such thing as minor, middling, or major offenses; all offenses are collectively termed 'downward' (inferior). You have committed a *pārājika* offense, even down to a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.

If one speaks these words with the intent to cause the other to feel shame, it is a *pāyattika*. (In this context, the mention of committing a *pārājika* offense refers to disparaging [the person] out of a light-hearted mind;

The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu reviles a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu, it is a *pāyattika*. [If she] reviles the other three, [it is likewise]."
[The offense is] *duṣkṛta*.

This precept is likewise established in the Mahāyāna. If one merely reviles or groundlessly slanders another good person, it is subsumed under the "slandering and reviling" precept with a light penalty.
If one combines this with self-praise, it is subsumed under the precept of "self-praising and slandering others" with a heavy penalty. If [the offense] increases...
Regarding those who commit offenses through superior afflictions, they lose the bodhisattva precepts.
As for the third precept against divisive speech:
if a bhikṣu engages in divisive speech, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus would whisper behind one person's back and repeat it to another; they would whisper behind another's back and repeat it to this person. Thus they continued without ceasing, until they reached the midst of the Saṃgha.
Where there had been no cause for dispute, strife arose; where there was already strife, it was not extinguished. The bhikṣus...

Having understood this, he addressed the Buddha to establish the precept: "This is a natural offense (prakṛti-sāvadya). Because of the afflictions associated with keeping a retinue, this training rule was promulgated;
it belongs to the category of the fundamental types of lying in the first section."

Exegesis: The Vinaya states that "slanderous speech" refers to a bhikṣu inciting discord among bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and followers of external paths and heterodox teachings, including śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and so on, even down to followers of external paths and heterodox teachings, śramaṇas, and... [the passage continues].
The Brahmins further incite various non-Buddhists, Brahmins, bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs to engage in strife.
Those who incite them say: "You are a *caṇḍāla*, or even of the *vāṇija* caste; you are a seller of pigs and sheep, or even a barber.
You have violated the seven classes of precepts (*saptāpatti-skandha*). You have caused others to become bald, blind, and sightless."

Regarding the various types of patients: if there is a monk who causes a schism, it is entirely due to that monk’s instigation and discord (according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, this precept is also called "slanderous speech," meaning to alienate those bound by kindness and righteousness, incite strife and contention, cause dissension among the community, and obstruct the practice of the path).
Regarding the establishment of the offense: among these, if one speaks with divisive intent and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if the meaning is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the presence of a motivating mind; second, the act of conveying a message back and forth;
third, the recipient being a bhikṣu; and fourth, the clear communication and understanding of what was said.
If a *bhikṣu* commits this simultaneously, it is a *pāyattika*; for a *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, or *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This constitutes an offense.

Regarding those cases where there is no offense due to following permission: breaking away from evil spiritual friends and evil companions; when two or three people perform illegal and non-disciplinary *karmavācanā* acts;

speaking repeatedly to the Saṃgha, the Stūpa, one’s preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), spiritual friends, or relatives about matters that are meaningless and unbeneficial; and cases such as when the precepts had not yet been established—these constitute no offense.
Regarding the offense:

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one forms the thought, 'I wish to cause him to be separated from that person and to come over to my side,' whether he is actually separated or not, it is a *pāyattika*."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Among these, there are eight types of offenses: first, seed; second, performance; third, action; fourth, transgression;
fifth, illness; sixth, signs; seventh, affliction; eighth, abuse. Of these eight matters, the three matters of seed, performance, and action..."
If one communicates [these matters] to a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa, or a merchant’s son, it is a duṣkṛta.

If one communicates them by means of the eight matters to the fourfold assembly (the fourfold assembly refers to the bhikṣuṇīs and the three groups of novices), it is a duṣkṛta. If one communicates them to laypeople or to those who are not ordained teachers, or if one sends a messenger or a letter, in all such cases it is a duṣkṛta.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu has no prior enmity or grievance, but happens to hear [the dispute], or having heard it, desires to bring about its cessation through skillful means so as to prevent further strife, there is no offense."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If a layperson within a monastery intends to commit an evil act or harass a bhikṣu, one should address them with harsh and urgent words to cause them to submit. If they do not submit, one must not go directly to the king;
first, one should speak to that evil person’s acquaintances, and then to the king’s consort, the princes, the ministers, and so forth. If this person...
Abandon it immediately and cease; do not allow the matter to proceed.

This precept is established identically in the Mahāyāna. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "To instigate strife between two parties and to slander or deceive a worthy person constitutes a minor defilement offense."
The fourth precept concerning sleeping in the same room as a woman:
If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika. Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Ānanda [departed] from Śrāvastī...
While traveling toward the kingdom of Kosala, he arrived at a village where there was no dwelling for monks.
He heard that a courtesan lived there permanently with her family, so he went there and took up lodging at the gate.
At that time, several elders who were on business also came to seek lodging; they sat down very close to him. The courtesan felt compassion for them and invited the Venerable One inside.
Inside the dwelling, the Venerable One sat cross-legged with his mindfulness fixed before him. At the beginning of the night, the courtesan came seeking to commit sexual misconduct;
the husband remained silent and did not respond, nor did he look at her. When the latter part of the night arrived, the courtesan again removed her clothes and approached to seize him.
The Venerable One leaped into the air. The courtesan felt shame, put on her clothes, joined her palms, and repented.
When the Venerable [Mahākāśyapa] arrived at his own dwelling, he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for her.

The courtesan attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*), received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and became a laywoman (*upāsikā*). On the following day, the Venerable accepted her offerings, preached the Dharma, and departed.
Upon reaching the monastery, he recounted these circumstances to the assembly of monks. Among them was one of few desires...

The bhikṣus felt resentment and complained, reporting the matter to the Buddha, who then established the precept. Because women give rise to the affliction of sexual desire, this training rule was enacted;
it constitutes the fundamental category of the first section concerning sexual misconduct.
Exegesis: The Vinaya states: "Woman" refers to a human female who possesses consciousness and whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not severed.
"Dwelling" (*śālā*) refers to a structure with walls on all four sides and a roof covering above; or it may have a front porch without walls; or it may be covered, though not completely enclosed.
Or if it is covered but has openings.
Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu is already there when a woman arrives later; or if the woman arrives first and the bhikṣu arrives later;
or if both arrive at the same time; and if he lies down on his side with his flank touching the ground, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
*Pāyattika* (the sound *pāyatti* means "to turn sideways in an improper manner"). It is a *pāyattika* offense to turn over [in bed] accordingly.
If one sleeps in the same room as a female deity, nāga, yakṣa, or ghost-spirit, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one sleeps in the same room with a female animal—whether capable of transformation or incapable of transformation—it is a *duṣkṛta*. During the day...
If a woman stands while a bhikṣu lies down, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, she must be a human female; second, they must be in the same room without a partition between them;
and third, he must be lying on his side on the ground.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; the same rule applies to bhikṣuṇīs. For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: If a bhikṣu does not know that there is a woman in the room when he stays there;
or if the bhikṣu arrives first and the woman arrives later, and the bhikṣu is unaware of her presence;
or if the dwelling has a roof but lacks enclosures on all four sides, or has partial or minimal enclosures; or if it is fully enclosed but lacks a roof, or has only a small or partial roof.
Whether under cover or in the open, while walking or sitting within this room, if one falls to the ground due to dizziness,
if one is seized by force, if one is bound by others, or if there is danger to life or danger to one's pure conduct— as well as in cases where the precept has not yet been established—
these constitute non-offenses.

Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: if there is a partition within a single room such that there are separate doors, there is no offense. If the rooms are different but there is no partition, it is a *pāyattika*.
If they share a room and share a partition, it is a *pāyattika*. If the rooms are separate and the doors are different, there is no offense.
If a woman is inside a room with a bhikṣu, and half of her body is within the room, it is a *vyatikrama* offense. [If] the woman is inside the room...
If a bhikṣu has half of his body inside a building, he commits a *vyatikrama* offense.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: If a woman is on an upper story and the bhikṣu is below, or vice versa;
or if the ladder has been removed and the door is securely locked; or if the ladder has not been removed, one should install a bolt and key; or even if they are in the same room, by...
If objects obstruct the way so that passage is cut off, there is no offense. If it were not so, at the appearance of the light of dawn, all would incur a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if the female small animal is incapable of sexual intercourse. If she is under the protection of parents, a husband, or others, and one sleeps with her, there is no offense.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If they share the same roof but have separate partitions; or if it is a large assembly for preaching the Dharma; or if it involves one's mother, sisters, or close relatives who are ill;
or if there is a trustworthy man present; or if one does not lie down alone with another—none of these constitute an offense."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "To sit through the entire night without lying down does not constitute an offense.
This precept is studied identically in the Mahāyāna.
The fifth [precept] concerns the rule against staying for more than three nights with those who have not received the full ordination.
If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received full ordination, exceeding two nights and reaching a third night, it is a pāyattika.

Regarding the origin of this precept: there were two stages of its establishment. When the Buddha was at Kalandaka-nivāpa, the group of six bhikṣus stayed overnight with several elders in a lecture hall.
At that time, one among the group of six fell asleep with a distracted mind.
He was unaware of anything as he rolled over and exposed his body. A bhikṣu covered him with a robe, but he rolled over again and exposed his body;
this happened three times. The householder mocked and ridiculed him, and the bhikṣu, being contented, felt ashamed and reported the matter to the Buddha.
This was the first establishment of a precept. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:

"I do not permit you to sleep together with those who have not yet received the full ordination. When it was time to send Rāhula out, Rāhula had no place to stay, so he went to the latrine to spend the night.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, went to the latrine, led him in, and stayed with him in his own room for one night.
At dawn the next morning, he assembled the Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You all lack a heart of compassion. Thus...
He drove out the young boy, saying, "Is this son of the Buddha not protecting my wishes? Therefore, he permitted them to stay for two nights;
this was the second formulation of the precept. This training rule was established due to the affliction of non-serenity regarding the matter of staying overnight while asleep.
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. The first clarifies the formal regulation regarding staying overnight with those who have not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

The second, beginning with "exceeding two nights," establishes the offense incurred. The Vinaya states: "Those who have not received the full ordination" refers to everyone except bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
this includes the three lower groups of renunciants as well as laypeople (*avadātavasana*) and so forth. "Staying in the same room" is as follows:

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If staying for two nights were not permitted, there would inevitably be various causes for affliction as well as circumstances leading to the loss of life. Out of a heart of compassion, one is allowed to stay for two nights; however, in order to protect the Buddha-dharma, staying for three nights is not permitted."
Regarding the determination of the offense: whether there is an offense or no offense within this is entirely as stated above.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, that the other person is one who has not received full ordination;

second, that one is not ill oneself and there are no other exceptional circumstances; third, that one stays together in the same room for up to three nights; and fourth, that one does not depart before the dawn has appeared.
If a *bhikṣuṇī* does so as well, it is a *pāyattika* offense (the same rule applies to those of the same training).
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This constitutes an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one sleeps in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination, on the third night one must stay in a separate room.
If it is outdoors, or when there is wind, rain, snow, or cold outdoors, one must return to the room to sit."
When it reaches the ground—that is, when the light of dawn appears—if one is too old or ill to sit, one should use a curtain to screen oneself.
Whether it reaches the neck or the armpits, the bottom of the curtain must reach the ground; it should be made of a dense material so that not even a kitten can pass through.
If traveling on a road where there is no canopy or curtain, and if there is a person who has not yet received full ordination whom one trusts, one should speak to them as follows:
"While you sleep, I shall remain awake. When a bhikṣu wishes to sleep, he should call out to wake the other, saying, "I shall sleep; you remain awake.
If you sleep, you will have no merit. This refers to one who, having not yet repented for the offense of the precept regarding sleeping in the same room, subsequently sleeps again in the same room.
The offense increases further. After having confessed the transgression, one should stay in a separate room; however, one may again stay together [with others].

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one stays together for more than two nights and then stays together with another person on the third night, it is a *pāyattika* offense, because of the continuity with the previous person. If, after staying together for two nights, one moves elsewhere...
In other cases, after staying apart for one night, there is no fault in returning to stay together again. If one remains seated throughout the night, there is no offense.
The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: When one is ordered to stay outside for the third night, one should not be sent out of the monastery grounds or away from the eaves;
one need only leave the immediate precinct of one’s own room. However, if there is fear that evil bhikṣus might provide conditions for the breaking of precepts, [one should depart].
Upon reaching the third night, one should have the śrāmaṇera go to the room of a virtuous friend.

If such a person is not available, he should be expelled together with those who commit evil deeds, or the bhikṣu should take the śrāmaṇera himself and lie down elsewhere. This applies if one has already entered the rains retreat.
If one is unable to go, one should generate the thought of providing protection. During the three months [of the rainy season retreat], there is no offense for staying overnight with a śrāmaṇera.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If, after the retreat, an evil bhikṣu comes into the monastery, the preceptor should..."
One may share a room with a śrāmaṇera and stay there until the end of the summer retreat; do not harbor any doubts regarding this.
Once the summer retreat has concluded, those capable of doing so may expel him; however, those who cannot expel him should take the śrāmaṇera and go to another monastery.
If they are on a journey, even if they have stayed for more than two nights, they should sleep throughout the night; do not give rise to doubts.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a sick bhikṣu has a śrāmaṇera attend to him, there is no offense even if he lies down.
However, among them, a bhikṣu who is not ill should not lie down."
The *Mūlamūlakā* states: It is not permissible to sit together with laypeople, novices (*śrāmaṇera*), those undergoing training (*śikṣamāṇā*), or those under separate residence (*parivāsika*).
However, there is no offense if there is a compelling reason.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.

An appended examination: The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states that if there are difficult circumstances and no other bedding available, one should fold the seven-robes (*saptaka*) into four layers and lie upon them;
the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) should be folded and placed beneath the head, or used to cover the body. The five-robes (*pañcaka*) [are also permitted].

To satisfy one's internal needs. Whenever lying down to rest, one should lie on the right side with the feet placed one upon the other, the body remaining motionless, forming the mental image of light, dwelling securely in right mindfulness, free from afflictions of the mind, and keeping the robes undisturbed.

One should know the proper measure regarding sleep and maintain the thought that one shall rise early. During both the first and last watches of the night, one should constantly cultivate wholesome qualities. This is the sleep of a śramaṇa.

Regarding the method of resting: if one is free from the suffering of illness, one should not lie down during the day. If, while sleeping or resting, one is disturbed by others, one should move to another location.
Sixth, one should not recite the precepts together with those who have not received the precepts.
If a bhikṣu recites the scriptures together with one who has not received the precepts, it is a pāyattika.

The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Khānumata. Six groups of bhikṣus were in the lecture hall with several elders, reciting the Buddha’s sūtras with loud voices, just like brahmins reciting their texts; their noise disturbed those practicing meditation.

There was a bhikṣu who was contented with little, who addressed the Buddha regarding the matter of instruction and requested that a precept be established. Consequently, this training rule (śikṣāpada) was formulated;
it belongs to the category of the fundamental types of false speech in the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
Explanation of the Meaning: The Vinaya states that "those who have not received the precepts" refers to everyone except bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding "reciting the meaning of phrases, not the meaning of phrases, nor the meaning of words": this means reciting together with others.
"Neither before nor after: 'Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas.

Regarding "non-sentential meaning" (asamvyañjanārtha): it is like one person who has not yet finished saying "Commit no evil," while a second person anticipates the preceding words and says "Commit no evil.
Regarding "sentential meaning" (savyañjanārtha): the two persons recite together, neither before nor after.

"Commit no evil" is not the literal meaning of the word *zhu*. For example, when one person has not yet uttered the word *zhu*, and a second person repeats the preceding word *zhu*—as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"Even though a bhikṣuṇī has received full ordination, she may not teach [the Dharma]. If she is to bestow a sūtra upon a disciple, she should instruct her, saying: 'Wait until my recitation is finished, and then you should recite.

If she does not follow these instructions, she shall not be permitted to teach again. As for "Dharma," it refers to that which is spoken by the Buddha, that which is spoken by the śrāvakas, and that which is spoken by ṛṣis and devas.

The Buddha approved this, and all [these teachings] were named *Dharma* (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The reason for establishing the precepts for the bhikṣus is to distinguish them from non-Buddhists; to differentiate them from his disciples;
to analyze the language so that they may understand it clearly; and because the true meaning is not valued for its sound").
Regarding the offense: among these, the transgression consists of reciting together with one who has not received the precepts.
Whether by oral instruction or by written transmission, if it is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*; if it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one speaks clearly or unclearly to devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and animals who possess the power of transformation, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If the teacher does not instruct by saying, "I have finished speaking; you may speak now," [and the student speaks], it is an offense for the teacher.
Dukkaṭa. This precept constitutes the full offense only when three conditions are met: first, the other person has not yet received full ordination; second, one has not previously instructed them;
and third, one recites together with them in a loud voice.
If a bhikṣu commits this act together with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika (for both; the same rule applies to those of the same training).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions for non-offenses: "I have finished speaking; you may speak now. Or, one person has finished reciting while another writes it down.
Or, two people are engaged in the same task and recite together, or speak very rapidly, or even make mistakes in their recitation.
Furthermore, cases where the precept had not yet been established at the outset—these constitute non-offenses.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one causes a person who has not yet received full ordination to recite a sūtra together with oneself, it is a *pāyattika*.

'Reciting together' means reciting at the same time; that is, while the sound of one's own recitation has not yet ceased, the other has already finished reciting, or while the other's recitation is not yet complete, one resumes reciting.
For every such phrase, it is a *pāyattika*."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one teaches a person who has not yet received full ordination using incomplete verses—whether it be a verse (one *gāthā* consisting of four lines), each such verse constitutes a *pāyattika*;
or whether it be a passage from a sutra (a single unit of meaning within a dharma-explanation or a parable), each such instance constitutes a *pāyattika*;
or if one speaks by individual phrases (referring to speaking only a single line within a four-line verse), each such phrase constitutes a *pāyattika*. This is termed 'incomplete flavor.'"
The phrase "insufficient" (*paryāpta*) is also like this (the phrase "obscure" (*mūḍha*); that is, even a single line is not yet complete).

The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: If one speaks while eating, if one speaks due to a hurried temperament, or if one recites together as the standard text, or when giving instruction, one should first inform the other person, saying:
"Do not speak at the same time as I. Even if they do so simultaneously, there is no offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.

To cite scriptural evidence, the *Śīlapratyaya-sūtra* states: "If a bhikṣu explains even a single phrase of the dharma of the precepts to one who has not received the precepts, it is a pāyattika (an offense requiring expiation).
[This was established because the Buddha knew that the group of six bhikṣus was speaking words of the Vinaya to śrāmaṇeras, and thus he enacted the rule]."

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If there are laypeople who seek out faults, or who have a mind to steal the Dharma, or who lack faith and respect, or who are non-Buddhists, and one causes them to listen to teachings consistent with the Vinaya—if they hear them..."
In all such cases, one incurs an offense of transgression.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: "If one recites together with a Dharma-master a text he has composed, there is no offense.

(Based on the intent of these three Vinayas, the emphasis lies solely on the *vinaya*. Indeed, the names of the five categories of offenses are the laws for fully ordained monks; they must never be allowed to be heard by śrāmaṇeras and others.)
Appendix: Examination. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: There are five types of persons to whom one should not preach the *Vinaya-piṭaka*:
namely, those who are by nature ignorant; those who deliberately pose heterodox questions; those who ask questions without seeking to resolve their doubts;
those who ask out of a desire to mock or tease; and those who ask with the intent to find fault. The opposite of these five types of persons [are those to whom it may be taught].
It is said that this does not constitute an offense. One who receives the Dharma must maintain the three dignified postures as an act of respect; therefore, one should not lie down.

Regarding the method for a disciple to receive instruction—whether old or young—upon arriving before the teacher, one should join the palms, bow with a stooped body, and only then request to ask questions.
One should inquire whether the four elements are at ease, cultivate reverence and esteem, maintain a straightforward mind free from flattery, and resolve all doubts with single-minded devotion.
"Understand this well and do not let it be forgotten. If you have no doubts, receive the teaching as usual, prostrate at the teacher's feet, and withdraw.
If the teacher goes out, follow behind him. If the teacher sits, you should squat or sit on a low seat.
The teacher, in turn, should respect the student and not treat them with contempt, but should teach the Dharma with an open mind."

One should be without stinginess, skillfully guiding and skillfully answering. Possessing patience and compassion, one should harbor no resentment or malice, ensuring that those who receive the teachings feel no weariness or distress.
One should always attend to them as a servant and instruct them frequently; even those of dull nature should be given special instruction.
If one uses a chanting or melodic tone when transmitting the Dharma, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
However, there is no offense if one chants or recites the sūtras with a melodic intonation in a secluded place while preaching the Dharma or offering praise.

One should not chant or recite non-Buddhist texts or treatises; yet, if for the sake of subduing followers of other paths, one knows oneself to have the capability, one may do so three times each day.
When the two parts [of the day] are favorable, one should study the Buddha-dharma; during the one part that is unfavorable, one should practice external texts.
One should not calculate months and years to establish three divisions. The night is also divided into three periods: at the beginning and the end, one practices meditation and recites the sūtras;
in the middle, one settles the mind and sleeps. If one acts as a brāhmaṇa and recites books, reading them according to their sections and phonetic rhythms, one attains [merit].
This is an offense against the Dharma. However, if it is local dialect, national laws, or seasonal verses for the purpose of acting as a chant leader (*cangdao*), there is no offense.
One should also study the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*; if a nun comes to request instruction, one should teach her according to the Dharma.
If there are any doubts, they shall be well explained. When reciting or preaching, if one forgets the location or place, one may speak of any one of the six great cities.
If one forgets the names of the king, the great lords of the earth, or the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*), one should freely invoke the names of King Śrīgupta and the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Śuklā Upāsikā: Furthermore, in a monastery where bhikṣus reside, on the eighth and fourteenth days of every month, at the time of the morning meal, the *ghanṭī* should be struck to assemble the great assembly. Incense and flowers should be offered, and the Dharma should be heard.
If non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) should come, one should employ skillful means to have them depart. One should invite the elders and maintain a mind of sincere reverence. Skillfully...
Regarding dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*): one should proclaim the noble teachings and must not seek profit as a means of livelihood; to do so constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
Furthermore, if an elder (*sthavira*) preaches what is not the Dharma, he should be restrained. Moreover, a teacher of the Dharma should not take on many disciples.
They were taken as attendants. As for those who personally declined to go, there was no offense (for a refusal is essential).
Once they had arrived at that place, the Dharma-preacher sat upon the lion throne, with a high desk placed before it to support the scriptures. Incense and flowers were solemnly arranged;
if one were to preach to others without being invited, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The seventh rule concerns speaking of another’s grave offense:
If a bhikṣu knows that another has committed a grave offense, and he speaks of it to someone who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha.
Pāyattika. Origin Story:

This precept was established in three stages. When the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, there were monks practicing *parivāsa* and *mānatva* who sat in the lower seats. The group of six [monks] spoke to the others...

The laypeople said, "These individuals have committed such offenses; therefore, the Sangha has punished them by relegating them to a lower status. Their conduct in walking and sitting is flawed. When the bhikṣus heard this, they felt shame.
Those who delighted in training in the precepts criticized and disparaged them. The group of six bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
This was the first formulation of the precept. Once the precept had been formulated, some bhikṣus did not know what was grave and what was not grave;
some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were apprehensive and cautious. The Buddha said, "If one does not know, there is no offense.
This was the second formulation of the precept. At that time, Śāriputra was [honored] by the assembly...
[The Buddha] said: "Appoint [someone]. Within the assembly of kings and among the people, one shall speak of the transgressions of Devadatta.

Regarding what Devadatta has done, do not say it is the Dharma, the Sangha, or the Buddha; you should know that this was done by Devadatta. Having heard the establishment of these precepts, Śāriputra gave rise to a sense of awe and caution.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the Saṃgha: "There is no offense for those appointed by the community."

Therefore, there is the statement regarding the *saṃghakarma* for removal. This is the third formulated precept (*śikṣāpada*). Because of the matter of one who had not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*) being unable to endure afflictions (*kleśa*), this training rule was established;
it belongs to the category of the fundamental types of false speech in the first section.
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. From "Knowing that another... onwards, it clarifies what has been committed as an offense. From "Except for the Saṃgha...
onwards, it demonstrates the permitted exceptions. The Vinaya states: "Regarding those who have not received the precepts, it is as previously explained.

As for 'grave offenses,' these refer to *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. To speak toward one who has not received the full ordination (meaning to recount and expose the transgressions previously committed by another person) constitutes an offense."

"Except by formal monastic procedure (*saṃgha-karman*). "Monastic community" (*saṃgha*) refers to those who share the same formal procedure and the same recitation of the precepts (excluding cases where the community has assembled in harmony and is authorized to assign a penalty for an offense;
this is clarified in the section on "maintaining through performance").
Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, if one speaks clearly and fully, it is a *pāyattika*; if one does not speak clearly and fully, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
With the exception of a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), if one speaks of any other offense to a person who has not received full ordination, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one speaks of a grave offense that one has committed oneself to a person who has not received full ordination, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Dukkata: except for monks and nuns, if one speaks of a grave offense (dauḥśīlya) committed by another person to someone who has not received the full ordination (upasampadā), it is a duṣkṛta.

(The "other persons" refers to the three minor assemblies and the two assemblies of laypeople who have received the precepts. Pāyattika: [If one speaks of] a grave offense while perceiving it as a grave offense;

or if there is doubt regarding a grave offense; or if it is not a grave offense but one perceives it as a grave offense. [In these cases, it is a pāyattika. If it is not a grave offense... [it is a duṣkṛta].
Harsh speech and suspicion are both *duṣkṛta* offenses.

This precept requires seven conditions to constitute the full offense: first, there must be the intentional mind of speaking; second, it must be a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) with the perception that it is a grave offense;
third, the other person must not have previously known [of the matter] and must perceive it as unknown; fourth, it must not be for the sake of serving the Saṃgha.

[The Buddha] said: "It is an offense. There are five [conditions]: first, it is one who has received the full precepts; second, speaking to one who has not yet received the precepts; third, the speaker and the listener both understand what was said.
This also applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom it is a *pāyattika* (the same rule applies to those of common training). It also applies to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*."
For a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if she does not know; or if the Saṃgha has appointed her, and she perceives what is coarse and evil as not being coarse and evil.
If a layperson has already heard of this grave offense, or if it occurred before the precept was first established, there is no offense.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "Even though a bhikṣuṇī has received full ordination, she must not speak [of such matters] to him."

(Because the Bhikṣus are honored and superior, there is fear that the Bhikṣuṇīs might treat them with contempt; out of compassionate protection for the Saṃgha, the Buddha prohibited speaking of [the offense] to them.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: If one speaks of another's grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to an ignorant layperson while perceiving or suspecting them to be ignorant, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one speaks of it to a knowledgeable layperson while perceiving or suspecting them to be ignorant, [one incurs a *pāyattika* offense].

[In such cases], one incurs *dukkaṭa* (an offense of wrong-doing). There is no offense if, regarding a household of which one was unaware, one forms the perception that they were already known [to others];

or if the matter has been discussed in detail by the assembly; or if at some time the people have all heard and known it—just as when a mural painting is viewed by everyone together, one says, "I did not know it alone, but spoke [of it]," there is no fault.
"The people have all heard and known it" refers to the assembled Saṃgha, and does not refer to worldly persons who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one instructs someone to speak toward person A, but speaks toward person B; or if one instructs them to speak of this offense, but speaks of that offense—in all such cases, it constitutes a *pāyattika*."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If a monk is appointed by formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to confess his offense, and another monk speaks on his behalf, it is a *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing).
This is because he was not appointed by the Saṃgha; yet, having accepted the appointment, he requests another to speak for him. Since this transgresses the *vinaya*, he cannot avoid being at fault.
If he instructs [the offender] to speak to this person, but instead speaks to another person or in another location, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If the Saṃgha... [performs the ritual... [text continues].
To speak [of the *karmavācanā*] at will, at any time, or in any place constitutes an offense. Regarding the *karmavācanā*, there is no offense [if the speaker intends for a third party].

In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is taught that if one speaks toward person B while facing person A, because their mind harbors malice and lacks the thought of benefit, a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) is established. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is stated that if one causes [the announcement] to be directed toward this person while facing that person, it is all due to mishearing the *karmavācanā* and erring in its direction; therefore, a light offense (*duṣkṛta*) is established.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The reason for establishing the precepts with the bhikṣus is to provide great protection for the Buddha-dharma.
If one were to speak of the faults and evils of a bhikṣu to a layperson (avadātavasana), that person would consequently lack respectful faith toward the Buddha-dharma."
It would be better to destroy a stūpa or damage an image than to speak of a bhikṣu’s transgressions or faults to one who has not received full ordination.

If one speaks of such grave offenses, it constitutes a violation of the Dharma-body. If one speaks of offenses belonging to the second category (the *pāyattika* rules), one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding the speaking of the matter of the offense:
this refers to the specific acts committed, such as sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth. These constitute an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense.
This precept is established by the Mahāyāna as well. The *Fanwang jing yishu* (Commentary on the Brahma Net Sūtra) states: "There are two types of those who speak ill [of others]:

first, the 'submerging mind,' which seeks to cause another to lose their reputation, profit, and so forth; second, the 'punitive mind,' which seeks to cause another to be bound in fetters and the like.
These two mentalities are both karmic offenses (*karmādhipati*), and one will certainly violate a grave precept (*pārājika*). However, if one speaks with a mind of encouragement or..."

If one is commissioned to preach, none of the offenses are committed. Furthermore, if one has committed the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses, and the person before whom one preaches has already lost their precepts, then by preaching after they have lost their precepts, one incurs only minor stains.
The eighth precept concerning speaking of the superhuman states (*uttari-manussa-dhamma*) to outsiders:
If a bhikṣu speaks of the superhuman states to a person who has not received the precepts, saying, "I have seen this;
I know this to be true," it is a *pāyattika*.
The Origin: This precept originated with the bhikṣus of the Vālukārāma, as explained in detail in the first section [of the Vinaya].
The difference here lies in the distinction between what is factual and what is not; therefore, the gravity of the offense is divided into heavy and light.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "To now obtain that which was previously unobtained, and to proclaim one's attainment of the qualities of a superior person (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*) to one who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*)—because such a person, being unordained, appears to seek fame and profit and seems to possess greed—it is for this reason that this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established."

This is the first section on the categories of the roots of falsehood (originally established as a precept for instructing śrāmaṇeras; according to the *Śikṣāsamuccaya-nidāna-sūtra*). **Exegesis:** The Vinaya states:

"Human phenomena" refers to the human realm (*pudgala-dhātu*), the human aggregates (*skandha*), and the human sense-bases (*āyatana*). "Superior human phenomena" refers to the various dharmas that lead to liberation.
To claim for oneself: "I possess mindfulness, right reflection, ethical discipline, aspiration, and non-negligence"—[to speak thus when one does not possess these] constitutes [an offense].
There is progress of the mind; there is concentration and right concentration; there is the Path and spiritual practice; there is wisdom and vision; there is attainment and fruition.
(The various uses of "there is" and so forth are explained in detail within the first chapter. Here, it says "superhuman states" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) but does not say "super-celestial states.

This is because the Buddha appeared among humans and established the precepts among humans, as the *Prātimokṣa* discipline exists among humans. Furthermore, humans are superior to devas; humans can cultivate wholesome dharmas and frequently realize the Noble Path, whereas the devas are attached to pleasure and cannot apply themselves diligently to cultivation. Therefore...)

It simply says: "Exceeding humans" already includes exceeding devas within its scope. "Truth" refers to the reality of one's own person. To commit the offense of *pārājika* is to realize this dharma for oneself.
Regarding the transgression herein: if such a thing truly exists, and one speaks of it toward a person who has not yet received the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If one speaks clearly, it is a *pāyattika*; if one speaks unclearly, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one uses hand gestures, writing, or makes signs to send someone, and the meaning is conveyed clearly, it is a *pāyattika*; if it is not conveyed clearly, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one speaks clearly to devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or animals capable of transformation, [it is a *pāyattika*]. If it is not clear, [it is a *dukkaṭa*].

If one speaks clearly [of such things], it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one speaks to a person who has received the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and who does not consent [to hear it], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, there must actually be superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*); second, there must be a desire for fame.
With a mind of profit, (1) one speaks to three persons who have not yet received the precepts; (2) the person before one understands the meaning.

This constitutes a dual offense: for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika* (the same rule applies to fellow students); for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as an offense.
Exemptions from offense: if one acts out of overweening pride; if one declares it to be the result of karmic retribution rather than something attained through cultivation;
if one truly attains [the state] and informs a like-minded bhikṣu; or if speaking in jest, speaking to oneself, or speaking in a dream.
Furthermore, there is no offense in cases such as when the precepts have not yet been established.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā*, if one truly attains the four fruits of the path, or even attains the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and speaks of it to others, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one speaks thus for the sake of fame or profit, claiming "I am pure," it is likewise an offense.
If one upholds the precepts and truly recites the Tripiṭaka, yet speaks to others according to the sūtras as recited, according to the meanings as understood,
or according to what can be answered in debate, it is entirely *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "To manifest the appearance of an arhat constitutes a *vyatikrama* requiring mental repentance (*citta-kaukṛtya*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one who has received the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) speaks [of such matters] without being asked, for every word there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense are: if one speaks at the time of entering *nirvāṇa*, or if one speaks after a person who has received the full precepts has first asked."
The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: To manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) before laypeople constitutes an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).

There is no offense, however, when one manifests rare and extraordinary events for the purpose of clarifying the holy teaching, or when one desires to subdue the minds of those sentient beings being converted; although such acts are spoken of, they do not constitute an offense.
The *Mātṛkā* states: To speak to one who is insane, mentally distracted, or seriously ill constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept is studied identically in the Mahāyāna.
Ninth: The precept against speaking with a woman for more than [the permitted duration].
If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except when a man capable of understanding is present, it is a pāyattika.

Regarding the origin of this rule: there were three stages of its enactment. While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Kālodāyin went to the house of an elder while on his almsround;
standing before his sister-in-law, he whispered the Dharma into the ear of his nephew’s wife. The sister-in-law...
Seeing this, they became suspicious and said, "If one is preaching the Dharma, one should speak aloud so that we may hear it. Why do you speak only into our ears?
A bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard of this and rebuked Kāla. He went to inform the World-Honored One, and thus this first precept was established.
At that time, there were women who invited bhikṣus to preach the Dharma; however, because of the Buddha's prohibition of the rule, [they were unable to do so].
Fearing they might engage in improper discourse, he therefore established the rule for preaching the Dharma: "One must not exceed five or six words. This was the second formulation of the precept.
The bhikṣus again felt apprehensive; thinking that there was no man present who understood [the teaching], they ceased and did not preach the Dharma to women.
Therefore, the phrase "provided there is a man who understands" was added, resulting in the third formulation of the precept.
This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). It was established as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) due to the affliction of derision arising from the matter of preaching the Dharma;
it belongs to the category of the fundamental types of sexual misconduct in the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "Five-word [utterance]" refers to "form is non-self," and so on, up to "consciousness is non-self.

"Six-word [utterance]" refers to "the eye is impermanent," and so on, up to "the mind is impermanent" (*Vinayavibhaṅga* states: "Speech corresponding to five or six [categories] is called 'five-six word speech.

'Exceeding' means that what should be five exceeds five and reaches six; what should be six exceeds six and reaches seven"). "A man who understands" refers to one who discerns matters that are coarse or not coarse (*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If [the person] is blind...").

One who is deaf or asleep is also called an ignorant man. As for an intelligent man: if he is less than seven years old, or more than seven years old but does not understand the meaning and flavor of good and bad speech, he is not called intelligent.
If he is seven years old or more than seven years old and understands the meaning and flavor of good and bad [speech], he is called intelligent.

**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except in the presence of a man capable of understanding, and the preaching is clearly articulated, it is a *pāyattika*. If the preaching is not clearly articulated, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

This applies even if the recipient is a female deva, nāga, or yakṣa, or a female animal, provided she is capable of transformation. To preach for more than five or six sentences in such cases constitutes an offense.
Whether understood or not understood, all constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This precept fulfills four conditions before the full offense is established: first, it must be directed toward a layperson who is not a deceptive person or a woman;
second, there must be no other layperson present who understands the language; third, the teaching exceeds five or six words; and fourth, the words are spoken [with the intent to instruct].
It is clearly understood.
This also governs the *bhikṣuṇīs* for a *pāyattika* offense (the same rule applies to those of common training).
For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Exemptions from offense: If one speaks five or six words; if one speaks more than five or six words in the presence of a man who understands;
if one bestows the five precepts upon a laywoman (*upāsikā*) in the absence of a man who understands, and explains the dharma of the five precepts;
if one bestows the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) and explains the dharma of the eightfold fast; or if one explains the dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path or the ten [precepts].
Regarding wholesome dharmas: if a woman asks about their meaning, there is no man who knows them who should not answer. If she does not understand, he may explain them extensively.
This includes cases such as when the precepts have not yet been established; in these instances, it is not an offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: Having finished speaking five or six words to a woman, one says, "The Dharma of the rules is correctly limited to this much," and rises from the seat to depart.
If there is a further cause or condition, one returns to sit again and speaks for her; in such a case, there is no offense.
If, after having finished speaking five or six words, another woman arrives, and one speaks for that subsequent woman, it is likewise [permissible].

Furthermore, it is not an offense to speak for an unlimited number of women. Nor is it an offense if a woman comes to listen while one is reciting a sutra oneself, or if she asks about the essential meaning of the doctrine, provided that one explains it so as to enable her understanding, even if it exceeds five or six words. In all such cases, there is no offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: A "woman" refers to one capable of receiving sexual desire.
If she is a barren woman (*śilā-strī*) or a young girl not yet capable of engaging in sexual desire, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one speaks of worldly, mundane matters, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one speaks of the blessings and rewards of giving (*dāna*) or offers prayers of aspiration (*pariṇāmanā*), there is no offense. One may preach the Dharma for a nun; this applies to all cases.
Because the nuns provide instruction, there is no offense.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Whether the man lacks lustful intent while the woman has a defiled mind, or vice versa, in all such cases one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Even if she is intelligent, one must not speak [to her]. Although she is called a 'woman,' her wisdom may equal that of a man; nevertheless..."
Because one does not speak improper words to this woman, there is likewise no offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well. Because it protects against public censure, one must ensure that no censure arises; only then may one adapt to the circumstances.
Whether the teaching is extensive or concise, there is no offense.
The Tenth Precept on Digging the Earth:
If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the origin of this precept: there are two enactments of this rule. When the Buddha was at the city of Khānumata, the group of six bhikṣus [acted] with the Buddha...
While repairing the lecture hall, [the monks] dug the earth all around it themselves. When the elders saw this, they all reviled them, saying, "They are severing the life-roots of others.
This was the first establishment of a precept. The group of six [monks] further instructed others to dig the earth, saying, "Dig here;
place it there. The elders again reviled them. This was the second establishment of a precept. This is an offense of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), as such base actions cause hindrance.

To abolish improper cultivation, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established. **Explanation of the Meaning:** The Vinaya states: "Earth" refers to ground that has already been excavated or ground that has not yet been excavated.

If it is ground that has already been excavated and has been soaked by rain for four months, it returns to its original state. (The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of earth: earth that is 'living' (*jātā*) and earth that is 'not living' (*ajātā*). In lands with heavy rainfall, the earth becomes 'living' during the eight months; this is called 'shocking' [the earth]. )

The period after the crab's claws appear and before the commencement of *lidong* (the first winter month) is the time when rain is scarce; in such lands, the earth becomes "arable ground" (*jìngdì*) in the fourth month of summer. Any ground other than this is called "non-arable ground. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Arable ground refers to that which has never been dug; if it has been dug previously, it is not [arable ground]."

If the ground is moistened by rain or dampened by other water for three months, it is called "native soil" (*jāti-bhūmi*). If there is no moisture from rain or water for six months, it is likewise called "native soil. Other than this, it is not native soil. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"If the ground consists of four parts, with one part being stone, or if it is earth that has been burnt, these are all not native soil."

**The Offense of Confession (Pāyattika):** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one uses a hoe, or a pickaxe, or strikes with a mallet, or pierces with a sickle or knife, or even scratches the ground with fingernails, or drives a stake into the earth, or sets fire upon the ground—in all such cases, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not instruct another by saying, "Look at this" or "Know this," it is a *dukkaṭa*. (According to the rules for bhikṣus, one must not act directly.)

To say, "Dig this" or "Place that," is pure speech (*viśuddha-vāk*). This causes the *kappiya-kāraka* (the person who makes things permissible) to know for themselves what should be dug and what should be placed. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: For each thing required, one says to the *kappiya-kāraka*, "You know this.

If they do not understand, one speaks again, saying, "You look at this. If they still do not understand, one speaks again, saying, "I need this. If they still do not understand, one speaks again, saying, "Give this to me."
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, it must be native soil; second, there must be no mind of reverence for the teaching;
and third, one must either dig it oneself or instruct another to do so.
This also applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*, who incur a *pāyattika* (the same rule applies to those in training). It also applies to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*.
For a nun, this constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense include: if she says, "Know this" or "Look at this"; or if she is dragging timber or dragging bamboo.

If a fence has fallen to the ground, one should prop it upright. If bricks or stones have been overturned, one should collect cow dung (as this is frequently used for constructing altars and performing fire rituals in the Western Regions).
One may take earth from a collapsed riverbank, or take earth from a rat's burrow, or remove earth from a walking path (*caṅkrama*), or remove earth from within a house.

If one walks back and forth, performs walking meditation, sweeps the ground, or strikes the ground with a staff; or if one does not intentionally dig, or if it concerns the initial period before the precept was established—these are cases of non-offense.

Regarding the practice of digging: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if one causes a bank at the edge of a river to collapse by treading upon it with the foot, for every step taken, it is a *pāyattika*.

If the earth collapses while walking along the edge of a bank, there is no offense. If a *karmadāna* bhikṣu has much property belonging to a stūpa or property belonging to the Saṃgha that he wishes to bury in the ground, or if it is located in an exposed area where the soil is loose, he must not dig it himself; rather, he should have [another] do so.

The *karmadāna* (lay attendant) shall know this. If it is a burial site in a covered place, one may dig up the remains oneself. If one strikes a wooden peg (*śaṅku*) into the ground, there is a *vinayātikrama* offense;

if one injures [the earth] even as much as the leg of a mosquito, there is a *pāyattika* offense. The same applies to pulling out a peg. If the dead soil has been soaked by rain, a bhikṣu must not take it;
he should have the *karmadāna* take it, but only as far as the limit reached by the rain's saturation. Thus it is said.
If one takes it oneself later, there is no offense. To dig the earth is a *pāyattika* offense; if it is half sand, it is a *vyavahāra-vinaya* offense; if it is pure sand, there is no offense.
If a clod of earth is so heavy that one person cannot lift it and it breaks [when dropped], it is a *pāyattika* offense; if it breaks with less than one person’s weight, there is no offense.
This should be understood to apply analogously to stones, ginger-stones, and ash.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one digs into ground that does not produce vegetation, for every single act of digging, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one digs into ground that produces vegetation, for every single act of digging, it is a *pāyattika*. If one digs in a muddy place, up to the depth of a knee, for every single act of digging, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one draws lines on the ground with the hand, even to the depth of a mustard seed, [for every single act, it is a *duṣkṛta*]."

To dig where there are paintings is a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, if one digs in places where gold, silver, and other ores are naturally found; in places where orpiment, red ochre, or white clay occurs;
in places where rock is naturally present; in places of black stone; in sandy places; or in places where salt is naturally found, there is no offense.
