The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu is engaged in construction and wishes to establish the foundation, having obtained an auspicious star and awaited a favorable moment, and there being no *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant), he may himself drive a stake into the ground to mark the boundary; if it is four finger-breadths deep, there is no offense."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the other three assemblies dig the earth for no purpose, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If they take dry soil, there is no offense.
(Based on this, one should understand that for the three assemblies when there is a valid purpose, digging is not prohibited; the same principle applies to cutting grasses and trees.)
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
The eleventh: the precept against destroying a village of spirits.
If a bhikṣu destroys a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Origin: The Buddha was staying at Kalandaka-nivāpa. There was a certain bhikṣu who, while repairing a dwelling, cut down trees with his own hands.
The Buddha, knowing this, rebuked him and established a precept for the Saṃgha. This is an offense of prohibition (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya).

It was formulated due to the matter of seeds and the "village of spirits" (bhūta-grāma), arising from the affliction of lack of compassion and the resulting censure. Thus was this training rule (śikṣāpada) enacted.

**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "A *preta* (ghost) is a non-human being. (*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: "A *preta* means 'fearful. This refers to their being empty and cowardly, possessing much fear.

Furthermore, it means 'awe-inspiring,' for they can cause others to stand in awe of their majesty. A *deva* (spirit) means 'capable. Those of great power can move mountains and fill the seas; those of lesser power can manifest, hide, and undergo transformations. "A village" refers to all grasses and trees. Because they are cut down or destroyed, it is called "ruining" a village.

There are five kinds of villages (*according to the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the five types have not yet been translated from the Sanskrit; here they are rendered based on the *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya*).
The Vinaya states: (1) Root-propagation refers to plants such as the fragrant rhizome (*xiangfuzi*), sweet flag (*changpu*), and ginger; these all grow from roots.
(2) Stem-propagation (which is synonymous with branch-propagation) refers to trees such as the pomegranate, willow, *bodhi*, *pippala*, and grapevine;
these all grow from stems. (3) Node-propagation refers to plants such as sugarcane, bamboo, and reeds; these all grow from nodes. (4) Sprout-propagation refers to the orchid (*lan*).

Fragrant fruits such as the orange and the citron (for these various seeds can only be produced through splitting and cracking). Fifth are the seed-plants, namely rice, wheat, beans, mustard, and so forth (as these all produce seeds from seeds;

however, because ghosts and spirits take refuge and dwell within these five types—just as humans rely upon villages—they are called "villages of ghosts and spirits"). The *Śīla-hetupratyaya-sūtra* states: "There are spirits who rely on tree roots; there are spirits who rely on tree branches; some rely on the bark; some rely on the inner bark;
some rely on the clefts in the bark; some rely on the buds; some rely on the leaves; some rely on the flowers; and some rely on the fruits. This applies to all medicinal herbs."

All trees possess spirits. The reason these spirits dwell therein is that they subsist on their fragrance. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "Those ghosts who dwell beneath trees did so because they saw people planting them to provide shade for others, yet they maliciously cut them down to take the wood for their own use;
consequently, they fell into the midst of trees, constantly suffering from cold and heat."

**Establishing the Offense:** Regarding the transgression herein: if, with respect to the five types of living seeds, one perceives them as living and proceeds to cut, parch, or boil them oneself, or instructs another to cut, parch, or boil them, it is a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
If one acts while harboring doubt as to whether they are living or not, or instructs another to do so, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one perceives what is living as non-living, or perceives what is non-living as living, [there is no offense].
If there is no doubt that it is living plant matter, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If it is living plant matter and one perceives it as such, and one cuts, fries, or cooks it oneself, or instructs another to cut, fry, or cook it, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If it is living plant matter but one suspects it so, and one cuts it oneself, or even instructs another to cook it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If it is living... [text ends]
If one perceives what is not a living plant as a living plant; or if one perceives what is not a living plant as a living plant while it has become a living plant;
or if one perceives what is not a living plant with doubt—all these are *duṣkṛta* offenses.
This applies if one drives a stake into a living tree, or sets fire to a living plant, or cuts off more than half of it.
To cut living plants or trees constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; to cut plants or trees that are half-dry and half-living constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one does not say, "Look at this," while knowing it is so, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, knowing it is living plant life; second, perceiving the living plant life as such;
third, intending to destroy it oneself or instructing another to destroy it through impure speech; and fourth, the actual severance of the plant.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise a pāyattika (the rule is the same for those of the same training).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: it is said that one does not commit an offense if one observes and recognizes [the situation].

This includes: cutting withered or dry grass and wood; dragging timber or bamboo across living plants and trees; erecting fences or barriers; clearing away ditches, bricks, or stones; taking cow dung;
or, when a path is covered by living grass, using a staff to push aside the obstruction to clear the way; or supporting it with tiles or stone pillars. And so forth.
It is not an offense if one cuts or damages grasses and trees while clearing the ground for a walking path (*caṅkrama*), or while sweeping the ground where one walks to and fro,
or if one accidentally pulls up or cuts living grasses and trees, or in cases prior to the initial formulation of the precept.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (or relevant Vinaya text), in its third section, states: "One should not eat impure fruit; one should consume it after performing five kinds of purification methods:
first, purification by fire (even a single touch with fire); second, purification by knife (damaging it with a blade); third, purification by a sore (natural blemishes on the fruit itself)..."
Fourth, purity through pecking by birds (where the bird has previously pecked and wounded it). Fifth, purity through being unfit for sowing (unfit to serve as seed or not yet matured).
Among these, one may eat the first and last two types of pure food in their entirety. Regarding the remaining three types of pure food, one should remove the seeds before eating them.
Furthermore, there are five other methods of purification: if the skin is partially peeled; if the skin is completely stripped away; if it is rotten; if it is split open; or if...
Regarding dried and withered [food] (self-offered and dried): one should not eat impure fruits or vegetables; one should not perform the ritual purification (*parikarma*) oneself;

one should not take them up with one's own hands. One should have another person perform the purification and place them on the ground. Having had another person perform the purification, one should not eat them without having formally accepted (*pratigraha*) them.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: If grapes, fruits, or melons are gathered into a single heap, one may apply fire to three or four spots [with the sound "zhù" (pronounced like "zhǔ" in "sting")];
this constitutes purification (*pariśuddha*). If using a knife or fingernails, each individual item must be purified separately.
If one purifies them oneself with a knife or similar tool, there is no offense at the time of eating; however, at the time of performing the purification, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one eats plants propagated from roots, they must also undergo five kinds of purification, namely: peeling, cutting, breaking, washing, and fire.
If one eats stalks or leaves, three kinds of purification are required, namely: cutting with a knife, fire, and washing.

When performing purification, it should be done as a collective purification (*saṃketa-śuddhi*) within a single heap or a single vessel; if one item is purified, this is termed collective purification, and the remaining three groups [of practitioners] do not need to act."

Therefore, to intentionally kill grass or trees constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, if they are burned by fire, or broken, or cut, and one knows that they will certainly not grow again, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu allows grass to grow in the courtyard of his residence, he should instruct a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) to take care of it (meaning he should let the attendant know so that the attendant may personally remove it).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: In certain lands, when grain is gathered into heaps, one fears that non-human beings (*amanuṣya*) might steal it; therefore, one burns the top with ash and fire to mark it.

This constitutes purification (*viśuddhi*). If the *karmadāna* (steward) has granary grain that has not yet been purified, and fearing that young bhikṣus do not know the Dharma, he has a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) perform the fire-purification until the granary grain is exhausted, the bhikṣus may always speak [of it as pure].
If one says, "I shall pound it," there is no offense. If one picks up dry cow dung mixed with living grass, it is a *pāyattika*.
The *Mātṛkā* states: to cover living grass with ash, soil, or sand is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one says to another person, "Take these fruits; I wish to eat them," it is a *duṣkṛta*. To swallow raw fruit that has not been purified is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one swallows [the food] whole (meaning it remains in the mouth), it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one bites through it, it is a *pāyattika*. To pick off a fungus from a tree is a *duṣkṛta*.
To strike a ripe fruit so that it falls is a *duṣkṛta*. To strike an unripe fruit so that it falls is a *pāyattika*.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If, after the purification by fire, sprouts have grown, it is pure at the place where the sprouts have grown, but not at places other than where the sprouts have grown;
one may eat [the fruit]. If flowers or fruit are required, one may grasp a branch of the tree and have a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) take them down; there is no offense."
One must not allow the tool to break. If the tree is so high that a lay attendant (*kappiyakāraka*) cannot reach it, a monk may embrace it while the attendant takes hold of it;

there is no offense. If a falling tree crushes a monk but he does not die, even if he has an axe or other tools in his hand, he should rather maintain his resolve to die than cut the wood or dig into the earth to save his own life. Why? Because of digging into the earth.
Cutting down trees incurs a *pāyattika* offense. A person of wisdom would rather die maintaining the precepts than live by violating them—such as when a tree falls upon a person.
A bhikṣu may cut down trees or dig the earth to save a life; this does not constitute an offense.

(One must know that while one should abide by the regulations for oneself and not violate them out of compassion, the permission to act is granted to save a life; this is entirely identical to the intent of the Mahāyāna teachings. If someone sets fire to a monastery, [the bhikṣu] may [act] to protect his dwelling place.
If one clears away grass or digs up soil in order to extinguish fire, there is no offense.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If, while walking upon living grass or mossy ground, one gives rise to the thought of causing damage to the grass, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) according to the extent of the damage.
However, if one merely intends to walk [without such a harmful intent], there is no offense."
There is no offense [if it is unintentional]. If one pulls up a mushroom from the ground, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There are three precepts that bring great benefit to the Buddha-dharma:

first, one must not carry burdens; second, one must not kill plants or grasses; third, one must not dig the earth. If these three precepts were not established, kings would cause the *bhikṣus* to engage in cultivation."

Regarding the labor of cultivation: there are these three precepts. When the king has stilled his mind, the three assemblies [of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and śrāmaṇeras] serve as pure attendants (*śuddha-puruṣa*).

Therefore, there is no offense. (In the *Mūla-vinaya* and various other schools’ *Śaikṣa-dharmas*, śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs all incur an *duṣkṛta* offense; this is because those rules were established to ensure they follow the monastic decorum of the Vinaya. That it says here there is "no offense" correctly clarifies that this is a special exception for those who are not of the same class as the Great Saṃgha.)
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
To cite the scriptural authority, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:

In the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, there was a nāga king named Elāpattra who manifested in the form of a young brahmin (*maṇava*). Carrying a chest full of gold, he traveled everywhere, reciting a verse and asking:
In what place is the king supreme? What is it that becomes stained by defilement?
Who is the fool who is stained despite being undefiled? Where does the fool grieve? Where does the wise person rejoice?
What kind of union and separation Is said to be true happiness?
If there were anyone who could explain it, he would immediately offer a golden casket as an act of veneration; however, no one was able to provide an explanation.
He gradually traveled to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and again proclaimed the same thing. Someone reported to him, saying, "There is a man of supreme wisdom."
"Residing in an araṇya, there is one named Nārada; you should understand this meaning. Before long, Nārada arrived.
The Dragon King questioned him with a verse, and having heard it, Nārada committed it to memory and replied, "Twelve years hence, I shall explain it to you.
The Dragon said, "That is too long and too distant," and gradually requested a reduction until it was seven days. At that time, Nārada immediately went and informed the five [disciples].
"O Bhikṣu," [the King said]. The Bhikṣu replied, "You should ask the Buddha. He then went to the Deer Park, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and sat down.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he realized the fruit of Stream-entry (srotāpatti). He then requested ordination.

The Buddha said, "First explain the meaning of the verses to the young Brahmin (māṇava), and only then may you go forth. He should have answered thus: "The sixth king is the supreme locus of defilement."
"Thus, one gives rise to attachment where there is no defilement, and speaks of defilement where none exists. This is the fool; the fool grieves over this, while the wise person rejoices in it.
To be able to separate from that which is a source of craving—this is called true peace and happiness. If he did not understand, [the Buddha] spoke further in verse:
"If a person hears sublime words and understands them as superior cultivation of concentration, yet hears them and does not comprehend their meaning..."
"Because people are heedless, if he should again doubt you, you may cut a leaf with your fingernails in his presence.
If he asks whether the World-Honored One has emerged from seclusion, reply that he has already emerged. If he asks where he is, reply that he is at the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground (Mṛgadāva).
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Mālatā went to the dragon’s abode and answered him in full as above. That dragon then transformed himself into gold.
The Cakravartin King went to where the World-Honored One was. The Buddha said, "You foolish man!
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you received the Buddha’s prohibitory precepts but were unable to maintain them, resulting in this inferior body of a long-lived nāga.
Why now do you again give rise to a deceitful mind? You should now restore your original form. The nāga said, "World-Honored One, I am a nāga."
His body was beset by many enemies and evils, and he feared that sentient beings might harm one another.
The Buddha commanded Vajrapāṇi to protect him. The Dragon King went to a separate location and resumed his original form;
his body had seven heads, and the distance from head to tail was two hundred *yi* (meaning two hundred *yojana*). Upon each head, there grew a great *eḷa* tree.
The tree was shaken by the wind, causing pus and blood to flow out and soil his body;
it was foul-smelling, loathsome, and constantly swarming with flies, maggots, and various insects that bit and fed upon him day and night.

At that time, the Dragon King appeared in his true form before the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand aside, and said: "I pray only that the World-Honored One will grant me a prediction."
"On what day shall you cast off this dragon body? The Buddha said, "In the future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, a Buddha will appear in the world named Maitreya;
he will bestow upon you the prediction of enlightenment, and you shall be freed from your dragon body. The Dragon King wept with grief.
From all their eyes, tears flowed forth simultaneously, forming fourteen rivers that surged and roared with rapid currents.

The Buddha commanded them to cease, lest they cause harm to the kingdom. The dragon prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and suddenly vanished. The great assembly then asked about the causes of his past deeds.
The Buddha said: "In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this dragon left the household life to practice within the Buddha-dharma.

He was well-versed in the Tripitaka and fully trained in the gates of meditative concentration. While practicing walking meditation beneath an Īrā tree, he exerted himself with such vigor that the leaves struck his head."
Even though he endured it, later, his mind became weary and he arose from meditative concentration. Summoning his mindfulness, he began to walk in meditation (*caṅkrama*).
The leaves struck his head again with extreme pain, and he gave rise to a mind of anger. With both hands, he snapped off the tree leaves and threw them to the ground, saying these words:
"The Buddha Kāśyapa, what fault did he see in an insentient object that he established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*)?"
Causing him to undergo such suffering. Due to that fierce poison of a hateful mind and his violation of the precepts, he died and fell among these dragons.

An examination of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: Whenever a *bhikṣu* in charge of administrative affairs intends to cut down a tree for the purpose of construction, seven or eight days prior, he shall set out various sacrificial offerings beneath that tree and recite the *Tri-saraṇa-gamana Sūtra* (the Three Refuges Sūtra). [Note: The text refers to the "Threefold Recitation" (*tri-kṛtva-uddeśa*), which refers to the three sections of the *Prātimokṣa*.]
[Recite the verses]. The senior bhikṣus should offer prayers of blessing, expound upon the ten paths of wholesome action, and praise virtuous deeds.
Furthermore, they should say: "If there are devas who have long resided in this tree, you should seek another dwelling.
This tree now belongs to the Triple Gem for the purpose of construction. After seven or eight days have passed, we shall have a lay attendant cut it down. If...
When felling a tree, if unusual signs appear, one should praise the merit of generosity and renunciation and explain the faults of stinginess and greed.
If unusual signs still appear, one should not fell it; if no such signs are present, it may be felled (but this must be done by a lay attendant and not by oneself).
*Vinaya-zhichi-huiji*, Scroll Eight: Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings.
The Bhikṣu Xiànglì (Elephant Power), also named Xiàngshǒu (Elephant Head), and also known as Fǎshǒu (Dharma Hand). In the country of Śākya, there was one named Xiàngshǒu.
Village. He was known by that name. He was a son of the Śākyas. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* records the Buddha’s prophecy:
"This person has committed three kinds of unrighteous acts, namely, stinginess and greed, delusion, and anger; he shall fall into hell. A verse says:
"If one gives rise to an unwholesome mind and accomplishes greed, anger, and delusion, this body commits evil of its own accord, and [the retribution] returns..."
Furthermore, it harms oneself; just as the plantain tree destroys its own body when it bears fruit, so too does this [affliction] harm itself.

That which is free from greed, hatred, and delusion is called wisdom. One who does not harm their own person is called a superior man. Therefore, one should eradicate the great afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
*Tiè* (pronounced *dì*) refers to a sneeze caused by nasal congestion. Whenever monks or laypeople in the Western Regions sneeze during acts of veneration, they all offer the wish:
"May you have long life and be free from illness. This is like children in this land who, whenever they sneeze, all say: "May you live for a hundred years."

"Defamation" (*kṣepa*) refers to verbal abuse; "abuse" (*kṣipati*) means to speak in a way that brings humiliation upon another. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Defamatory speech" refers to performing acts intended to disparage others. Regarding "leather" (*carman*):
raw hide is called "leather" (*carmā*), while processed hide is called "leather" (*veḍha*). To work with it is the craft of a lowly artisan.
*Bìbǒ* (躄跛): The first character is pronounced *bì*. To have both feet incapacitated is called *bì*;
to have one foot partially incapacitated is called *bǒ*. *Kuàngjiǎo* (踉蹡): The second character is pronounced *kuāng*. It describes the manner of walking with hurried and sudden steps.
*Āraṇya* is also called *āraṇyaka*. It is translated as "a place of seclusion," "a quiet and peaceful place," or "a place of empty stillness.
*Kaivarta* (butcher) is also called *caṇḍāla*, and again *caṇḍāla*. According to Master Ying, this is translated as...
It is called "Adorned with Banners" (Yun yan zhi). One source says it means "Master of Killing. These are those from the western regions who engage in slaughter;
they adorn themselves for their evil deeds and carry bells and bamboo poles as their insignia, hence the name. If this were not the case, [it would be otherwise].
The king will surely punish him; indeed, he may even be feared. The *Faxian zhuan* states that he is called a "wicked person" (*pāpaka*) and lives separately from others.
If he enters a city or marketplace, he ties bamboo [to himself] to distinguish himself from others, so that people may recognize and avoid him, not colliding with him.
Regarding the six great cities: the Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, attained enlightenment in Magadha, preached the Dharma in Vārāṇasī, and entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara;
these, along with Rājagṛha and Vaiśālī, constitute the six cities that were the foremost among the sixteen great kingdoms of the Western Regions.

Regarding the Dharma of the Five Precepts: when the Buddha first conferred the Three Refuges upon his lay disciples, such as Trapusa and Bhallika, he immediately bestowed the Five Precepts upon them, establishing them as upāsakas and upāsikās. If these lay disciples should break these five precepts...
They are therefore not pure men or women. Thus the Sūtra says: "The five precepts are the great prohibitions of the world.
If one violates the five precepts, in heaven one violates the five stars; on earth one violates the five sacred peaks;

in the quarters one violates the five emperors; in the body one violates the five viscera. In this way, there are immeasurable violations against the world. If we consider [them from the perspective of] the transcendental..."
Those in the world who violate the five precepts destroy the fivefold Dharma-body and all Buddha-dharmas. Why is this?

Because the five precepts are the root of the śīla (ethical discipline) of all Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. If one violates the five precepts, one may not again receive the precepts of either the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.
If one can firmly uphold them, these constitute the five great gifts; these five are collectively termed [the five precepts].

As for "precept" (*śīla*), its meaning is prevention and restraint. It can prevent the transgressions of non-volitional unwholesome discipline (*akuśala-avijñapti*) and can cease the evils arising from the three types of action (*trikarma*).
Therefore, it is collectively termed "prevention and restraint."
Regarding the eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), various sūtras and śāstras refer to them by several names:

sometimes as the "eightfold fasting precepts" (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*), sometimes as the "eightfold precepts" (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), sometimes as the "eightfold fasting" (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), and also as the "eight dharmas for nurturing merit.
Although these names differ, the precepts themselves are identical. That is to say, the first eight dharmas are called the "gate-precepts" (*kuan-jie*). "Gate" (*kuan*) means to close or shut off.
There are eight evils. By not giving rise to these transgressions—and finally, by not eating at improper times—one is said to observe the *upavāsa* (fast).
"Upavāsa" takes the meaning of "aligning with the middle. This is because it prohibits the eight evils and causes one to cultivate the Middle Way.
The ten wholesome dharmas are able to counteract the ten unwholesome dharmas— namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech,
covetousness, ill will, and wrong view— and are thus called the ten wholesome dharmas, or alternatively, the ten wholesome paths.
Tiantai says: There are two kinds of the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*): first, cessation (*saṃvara*); second, practice (*caryā*).
Cessation means merely ceasing prior unwholesome acts so as not to afflict others; practice means cultivating superior virtues to bring benefit and happiness to all.

These two are collectively termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*). "Wholesome" takes "conformity with principle" as its meaning. To still distortions and return to the truth is called conforming to principle. Cessation, then, stills the heavy [unwholesome states].
Because inverted unwholesome conduct gradually returns to the goodness of the supreme path, both the abstention from and the performance [of wholesome acts] are termed "good.
Alternatively, they are called "good" because, when applied to the path, they are capable of leading one to the fruit of ultimate bliss.
The character for *chú* (鋤) is pronounced *cú*; it is identical to *zhū* (鉏). It means to remove weeds and assist the growth of seedlings; it also means to execute or to hew.
The character for *jué* (钁), with the radical *kuāng* and the final tone *rù*, refers to a large hoe.
The character 釿 (jìn) means a chisel. The character 鎌 (lián) means a sickle.
A hooked blade is also called a wedge. The character 搯 (tiāo) is pronounced with the *kǔ* and *qiè* finals;
it refers to pinching or pricking with the fingernails.
*Zhe* (pronounced as in "zhè") means red earth.
*Shàn* (pronounced as in "shàn") means white earth.
*Yòu* (pronounced as in "yòu") refers to the fruit; the small variety is the tangerine (*jú*), while the large variety is the pomelo (*yòu*).
*Beilèi* (蓓蕾): the first syllable is pronounced *bèi*, the second *lěi*; it refers to a flower beginning to bloom.
*Zè* (笮): the pronunciation is *zé*; it means to press down. *Cǎn* (剗):
the pronunciation is *chǎn*; it means to shave off or level.
*Jūn* (pronounced *jùn*) is the small variety of *zhēn* (mushrooms).
It has not yet been translated [into Chinese] in the country of Takṣaśilā.
The Nāga King Elāpattra is also called Elāpatra. *Elā* is the name of a tree, which translates as "foul odor.
*Pattra* translates as "extreme" (*parama*). Because this Nāga King damaged the leaves of this tree in the past, [he is so named].
This has caused this most foul-smelling tree to grow upon his head.
"Māṇava" is translated here as "Ju-tong" (Young Scholar).
"Qiè" (篋) is pronounced like "qiè" and refers to a chest or casket.
The kingdom of Vārāṇasī—formerly called Bōluónài—is named after a river. Not far from this river, he established a royal city;
it is also translated as "the city surrounded by a river."
Narada has not yet been translated;
"shi" (駛) means "to cause" (使), or alternatively pronounced with the departing tone, meaning "the swift pace of a horse.
The five bhikṣus refer to the five men, namely Kauṇḍinya and the others.
The Compendium of the Vinaya on Restraint and Maintenance, Volume Nine, compiled by the Vinaya-expounding Śramaṇa Duti of Baohua Mountain in Jinling. Part Twelve:
The Precept Against Annoying Others with Discordant Speech.
If a bhikṣu falsely speaks with evasive words to annoy another, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the origin of this precept: there are two enactments for this rule. The Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
Chanda committed an offense. When the bhikṣus asked him, "Do you yourself recognize that you have committed an offense?
he replied with irrelevant matters, saying: "To whom were you speaking? What matter were you discussing? What principle were you debating? Were you speaking to me, or to someone else?
Who is the one who has committed the offense? From what does the offense arise? I do not see any offense; why then do you say I have one?"

This was an offense. The bhikṣus criticized and complained about it, and they informed the Buddha. The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of *anyavāda* (speaking otherwise) against him.

Thereupon, the initial precept was established: "If a bhikṣu speaks otherwise [than what he intends], it is a pāyattika. Subsequently, he became a source of provocation: when the Saṃgha summoned him, he would not come;
when they did not summon him, he would come. When he should rise, he would not rise; when he should not rise, he would rise. When he should speak...
He did not speak; he spoke when he should not have spoken. The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti* (formal announcement) for him once again. This was the second rule established.

(The two types of formal procedures—the *jñapti-karman* for idle chatter and for causing annoyance—are clarified in the section on "Practicing What is Held"). This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), established as a training rule due to the afflictions of resentment arising from violating trivial matters.
It belongs to the same category as the fundamental basis of the first [grave] offense, lying.
**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "Regarding 'other words' (*anyavāda*): 'To whom were you speaking? ... up to 'I did not see it.

One commits this offense [of *anyavāda*, which is synonymous with *vibhāṣā*]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There are eight matters that constitute 'speaking other words' to disturb others: 1. When a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is being performed, if a bhikṣu assembles with the community to perform an act of subjugation (*tarjanīya-karman*), or even an act of separate residence (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

2. When discussing according to the Dharma, to say that things are neither eternal nor annihilated; this is called 'discussing according to the Dharma. 3. When discussing the Abhidharma, the ninefold Sūtras are what is meant by 'Abhidharma. 4. When discussing the Vinaya..."

1. At the proper time. Whether the *prātimokṣa* is recited in full or in brief, this is called *vinaya*. 2. Not deviating from the subject of discussion. One must not abandon the topic under discussion to discuss other matters; this is called "not deviating from the subject. 3. Not deviating from the person.

One must not abandon the person who originally posed the question to ask another person; this is called "not deviating from the person. 4. Suspending the discussion. When it is time to preach the Dharma, one says, "Let us pause for now and discuss this later"; this is called "suspending the discussion. 5. Disturbing others with irrelevant speech. [This refers to] speaking in a way that annoys or troubles others.
As for the Venerable Channa’s use of improper speech to annoy others, this is called the eighth matter).

Regarding the determination of the offense: herein, if one uses improper speech before the Saṃgha has made the formal announcement (*jñapti*) regarding such speech—saying things such as "To whom are you speaking?
and so forth—it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense. If, however, after the announcement has been made, one acts in this manner...
Regarding "other speech": all such instances constitute a *pāyattika*.
If the Saṃgha has not yet performed the formal announcement (*jñapti*) regarding causing disturbance—such as calling someone who does not come and so forth—all such instances constitute a *duṣkṛta*.
If, after the announcement has been completed, one causes such disturbance to the Saṃgha, all such instances constitute a *pāyattika*. If...
If an elder summons one to come and one does not come, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept constitutes its full offense only when four conditions are met: first, one has committed a transgression oneself; second, one conceals it and defies admonition.
Third, making a formal announcement (*jñapti*) three times; fourth, verbally or through silence causing provocation.

These are governed by the same rules as for *bhikṣuṇīs* (a *pāyattika* offense), and the same applies to fellow students. For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This constitutes an infraction.
Exemptions from offense: If one does not understand because of hearing [the words] repeatedly; or if there is confusion in the speech of others; or if one asks, "To whom were you speaking?
and so forth, up to "I do not see this offense" (this is no offense for speaking otherwise); or if one intends to perform an illegal or non-vinaya *karmavācanā*;
or if it concerns the Saṃgha, a stūpa or monastery, or the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and those associated with the preceptor, or the instructor (*ācārya*) and those associated with the instructor.
Lí. If one performs an unbeneficial *karmavācanā* against former or current acquaintances and others; if one does not grant reconciliation when summoned but fails to come;
if one eats in a single sitting and does not perform the *atirikta-bhakṣaṇa-vidhi*; if one is summoned to rise but does not rise;

or if, during a house collapse, a fire, or threats from wild beasts and bandits, one instructs them not to rise but they nevertheless rise; or if one asks about these matters with an evil mind—[in such cases, it is an offense].
This is the explanation regarding persons and dharmas. It is not an offense [if one speaks] without giving rise to provocation or vexation.

Furthermore, there is no offense in cases such as speaking in a low voice, speaking rapidly, speaking in a dream, speaking to oneself, intending to say this but mistakenly saying that, or when the precept has not yet been established. These constitute non-offenses.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one answers differently when questioned within the Saṃgha, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one answers differently when questioned among a multitude, before one's *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, or before various elders, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense."
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: If one violates with a defiled mind a reasonable teaching given by the Saṃgha or those worthy of respect, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one utters words of violation or provocation regarding a teaching that is not reasonable, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one violates or provokes someone who does not understand the language, this is also a *dukkaṭa* offense. If one has been appointed to oversee communal affairs...
If one acts with a defiled and evil mind—performing what should not be done and failing to do what should be done—one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If there is no defiled mind, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu sees a hunter pursuing deer or other game entering the monastery, and the hunter asks, "Have you seen any deer pass by here?", he should not say that he has seen them.

If it is a cold season, he should reply, "You may enter the heated room and warm yourself by the fire. If it is a hot season, he should reply, "You may enter the cool room and drink water. If the hunter...
He said, "I am not weary. To answer your question about the fleeing deer, you should first examine your own fingernails.
He replied, "I see my fingernails. If he asks again, one should observe the great void. He replied, "I see the great void. If he says:
"I do not ask about fingernails or the great void; rather, I ask whether there are sentient beings who can be killed here—would this be an offense?
One should then look in all four directions and reflect thus: "In ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are fundamentally devoid of sentient beings.
One should reply: "I see no sentient beings. In these cases, there is no offense. However, if asked otherwise... [the remainder of the text follows].
If one answers according to the facts, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "If one treats the three teachers or the precepts with contempt, it is a *pāyattika* for each instance; if one treats other bhikṣus with contempt, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a teacher orders one to sweep the floor and one does not sweep, or if one sweeps contrary to the instructions, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*."

Duskṛta (the precept on lack of respect; found in all other schools but absent in this school alone. Its general meaning is the same as this [precept], so it has been collected here and included therein so that no transgression may be overlooked).
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
The thirteenth: the precept against reviling.
If a bhikṣu reviles [another], it is a pāyattika offense.

The Origin Story: There are two origins for this precept. When the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, the monk Ṭhapassamāla was appointed as the steward to manage the bedding and seating of the Saṅgha and to assign meals.
At that time, the bhikkhu Mettiya, in a place where he could see but not hear, said to his companion: "Ṭhapassamāla has favoritism."
Out of anger, fear, and delusion, other bhikṣus said to him, "Do not speak in this way. He replied, "I did not speak to his face; I was merely censuring him in private.
The Buddha, knowing the circumstances, established the precept for the first time, saying: "If a bhikṣu censures another in a disparaging manner, it is a pāyattika offense."
Furthermore, at a place where they could hear but not see, they said to one another: "There are those who harbor attachment, hatred, fear, and delusion. The bhikṣus said to them:
"The Buddha has not prescribed a precept stating that disparaging others constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. They replied: "We do not disparage him; we are merely reviling him.
For this reason, the second formulation of the precept was established. This is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), arising from the act of slander and the underlying state of anger.
Out of resentment and affliction, this training rule was established; it belongs to the category of the fundamental types of false speech in the first section.

Regarding the explanation of its meaning: the Vinaya states that if one reviles another face-to-face at a distance where they can see but not hear, saying things such as "you have attachment," and so forth.
If one reviles another from behind, or at a distance where the ear hears but the face is not seen, and speaks of [faults such as] attachment and so forth, the offense is established.
Regarding the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu, out of dislike, reviles another bhikṣu and his words are clearly understood, [he commits an offense].

*Pāyattika* for those who are not clear about it; *Dukkaṭa* for one who, having been instructed by a senior monk (*upādhyāya* or *sthavira*), harbors resentment and reviles him, or for one who accepts such instruction and then harbors resentment and reviles him (*Dukkaṭa*). (In the case of the instructor, by analogy, it is likewise difficult to escape this offense.)
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the presence of a mind of anger; second, the person appointed by the Saṃgha;
third, the utterance of words of disparagement or abuse; and fourth, that the speech is clearly articulated.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise a pāyattika (the same rule applies to those of the same training).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions for non-offenses: if a person actually possesses such a matter and, fearing future regret, speaks to them so that they may confess according to the Dharma;
or if it was spoken in jest, or spoken in a dream; or if one intended to speak of this but mistakenly spoke of that;
or if it occurred before the precept had been established—these are considered non-offenses.
Regarding the rules for taking food, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one feels disdain but does not reprimand, one incurs a *vinayātikrama* (offense against the discipline).
If one reprimands but does not feel disdain, one incurs a *vinayātikrama*. If one both feels disdain and reprimands, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
If one feels disdain but does not reprimand, it refers to taking food from one's own vessel and comparing it with the vessels of those sitting nearby.
At the midday meal, he spoke these words: "Is it equal? This was a case of disliking [the distribution] but not censuring it.
As for censuring but not disliking, one merely says there is attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion, without comparing it to the portion one has received oneself.
(The case of both disliking and censuring may be understood by analogy with this.)
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: To disparage a person appointed by the Saṃgha constitutes a *pāyattika*;
to disparage other persons constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mātṛkā* states: To revile an animal constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept is likewise established by the Mahāyāna.
The fourteenth: the precept on failing to put away the bedding of the Sangha.
If a bhikṣu takes a rope bed, a wooden bed, bedding, or a sitting mat belonging to the Sangha and spreads it out in an open space, or instructs another to do so...
[If a monk] spreads [a seat] and departs without picking it up himself, nor instructing another to pick it up, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, there was an elder in the city who provided a meal for the Saṃgha.
Seventeen groups of bhikṣus took the Saṃgha’s sitting mats and spread them out in the open air, where they walked back and forth while waiting for the food.
When the time arrived, they did not gather [the bedding] up and proceeded directly to the meal.

Consequently, the monks' sitting mats were covered with wind-blown dust and soil, damaged by insects and birds, and became filthy and impure. The bhikṣus criticized and disparaged this, and they informed the Buddha, who established the precept.
This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of prohibition). Because it arose from negligence regarding bedding, he formulated this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).

Explanation of the Meaning: The text is divided into two sections. The first clarifies that monastic property belongs to the Saṃgha and is for the use of the Saṃgha by citing the passage "if one takes a monastic corded bed.
The second, beginning with "if one spreads [it] as instructed," establishes the offense incurred. The Vinaya states: "Property of the community is for the sake of the Saṃgha.

Regarding "belonging to the Saṃgha": it has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha. Regarding "for the sake of the Saṃgha": it is being prepared for the Saṃgha but has not yet been relinquished to the Saṃgha. Regarding "belonging to the Saṃgha": it has already entered the Saṃgha.

It has already been relinquished to the Sangha. As for the rope bed (*śayanāsanam*), there are five types: those with curved legs, straight legs, bent legs, those with notched legs, and those without legs.
The wooden bed is likewise of five types. Regarding bedding (*śayanāsanam*): it may be used for sitting or for lying down. A cushion (*bimbohana*) is a sitting cushion;
it is placed in the open air (meaning it is uncovered, as the roof is not inside a building). Whether one spreads it oneself or instructs another to spread it—(spreading refers to...)
[Arrange it properly]. If there are resident bhikṣus, a *māmādika* (steward), or a supervisor there, one should say to them:
"I now entrust this to you; you must guard and look after it. [This refers to instructing someone to lift [the robe]; "lifting" means to collect and store it well].
If there is no one at all, one should lift it and place it in a secluded spot before departing. If there is no secluded spot, and one knows for certain that this place...
There shall be no damage. Once it has been made secure, one should cover the coarse part over the fine part and depart (this refers to "lifting oneself up").
If one can return immediately, one should go. If there is heavy rain but one can return quickly without damaging the sitting mat, one should go.
If there is moderate rain and one can return while walking [there], one should go. If there is light rain and one walks only a short distance (a "short distance" means slowly... [one should go].

[This refers to] walking slowly. When one has obtained [a robe] and returns, one should depart [from the dwelling]. (The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "The reason the Tathāgata instructs the bhikṣus to protect their bedding and mats is that he perceives five kinds of faults:

first, not to let them be blown by the wind; second, not to let them be scorched by the sun; third, not to let them be rained upon; fourth, not to let them be covered with dust and soil; and fifth, not to let insects or birds discharge impurities upon the bedding and mats.")
Regarding the offense: among these, the transgression occurs if one proceeds without having made the necessary preparations. Upon first exiting the gate, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

(The original cause concerned bedding and mats laid out in the open air; the present regulation concerning the gate refers to the main gate constructed by Prince Jeta at the Jetavana monastery in Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Since that area was spacious, there was indeed open ground within it.)
It should be understood according to the *Kāla-vinaya* (the Discussion on Time). However, the standard is defined by merely crossing the threshold of the monastery gate.

If one foot is outside and one foot is inside, and one intends to leave but does not, or subsequently regrets it, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If two persons sit together on a single bed...
The junior monk (*navaka*) should collect [the bedding] and depart. "Junior" implies that the senior monk (*sthavira*) ought to collect it;

yet if the senior monk does not collect it at all, the junior monk commits a *pāyattika* offense. Furthermore, because this is contrary to proper decorum (*anācāra*), he incurs a *dukkaṭa* (this refers to the loss of the respectful etiquette due to which one more offense of improper conduct is added).
If the senior monk tells the junior monk that he should collect it, but the junior monk does not collect it, the senior monk commits [an offense].

*Pāyattika*. (This means that the senior monk (*sthavira*) should instruct the junior monk (*navaka*). Since he does not himself perform the act of lifting [the bedding], nor does he instruct another to lift it, even though he is a senior monk, he incurs the fundamental offense.
If two persons neither go before nor after, and both fail to lift [the bedding], both incur a *pāyattika*.

If there are other empty rope-beds, wooden beds, squatting stools, small tables, bathing benches, or the outer and inner covers of bedding; or if it is a mat spread on the ground; or if one takes up ropes, cords, or wool—[in these cases, no offense is incurred].
If one leaves bedding or mats exposed in an open space and departs without putting them away, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If one spreads out monastic bedding in an open space and enters a room to sit in *dhyāna* (meditative reflection) without putting it away, it is a *duṣkṛta*. (*Dhyāna* refers here to the practice of seated meditation.)
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the private use of monastic property; second, spreading it out in an open space;
third, departing without putting it away; and fourth, having both feet pass through the doorway.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; the same rule applies to bhikṣuṇīs (the training is identical for those of the same school).
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: as previously assigned; or if it is only a light rain and one can return after traveling a short distance;

or if one has gathered up other items such as empty beds and departed; or if one is bound by forceful power; or if one does not act due to the two difficulties of life or the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya);
or if one departs in proper sequence; or if two people are sitting together, the junior person should gather [the bedding]; or if [it has already] been gathered.
Entering a room for reflection, as well as cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precepts—these constitute non-offenses.
Furthermore, the *Samantapāsādikā* (Shanjian lü) states: "To fail to report another's private property [when it is lost] is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one does not put away their own bedding, nor causes another to put it away, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When the bhikṣus have finished eating, if there are laypeople who sit upon the monks' bedding or couches, they should wait until the laypeople have finished eating.
If there is someone who is ill and cannot wait long, they should leave; as soon as they see [the situation], [they should act accordingly]."

One should pick up [lost items]. If the door-bolt or the door-key is lost and there is no place to put it away, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises and one does not pick it up, there is no offense.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: If there are no bhikṣus, one should inform a śrāmaṇera; if there is none, one should entrust it to a nearby donor.
If there is no donor, one should survey the four directions, secretly hide the door key, and only then depart as one pleases.

If one remembers [the duty] but fails to secure it, one incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*). If one forgets, one incurs only a minor offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If one encounters [a situation] on the road...
When a bhikṣu arrives, one must point out the location of the door-key. There are five kinds of persons who are unfit to be entrusted with it:
namely, those who are shameless, those who harbor enmity, those who are aged and infirm, those who are afflicted by illness, and those who have not yet received full ordination.

If a bhikṣu has agreed to take charge of another's belongings while on the road, but fails to take them up within the monastery from the first watch of the night until the appearance of the dawn light; [he incurs an offense].
If one picks it up without damaging it, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If one picks it up after damaging it, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
Examination: The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "Regarding all clothing belonging to the Saṃgha, it is not permissible to use it without interposing another object as a lining.
Furthermore, the object used for the lining must not be thin or tattered. If one uses [the Saṃgha's clothing]..."
Regarding bedding and seating materials: if they become damaged, one should not remain silent and neglect them.
If there are tears or holes, they must be sewn and patched. If they are torn or broken, they should be joined back together.
If they are beyond repair, they should be used as lamp wicks, or made into brooms, or chopped and mixed with mud to coat walls, or used to fill crevices. Thus [should one act].

The merit of giving increases. Disciples and followers should, on the eighth, fifteenth, twenty-third, and the final day of each month, inspect the bedding and requisites of their preceptor, dusting them and exposing them to the sun. If they do not do so, they all incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If there are no disciples, one must attend to these matters oneself. Furthermore, when listening to the Dharma, one should not [give rise to... with others.
A bhikṣuṇī, a layperson, or a śrāmaṇera should not sit in close proximity on the same woolen mat or seat; likewise, one who is under training (śikṣamāṇā) should not share a seat with others.
However, there is no offense if there are difficult circumstances. A bhikṣu with no years of seniority (anupasaṃpanna-varṣa) should not sit on the same seat as one with three years of seniority;
one with one year of seniority should not sit on the same seat as one with four years of seniority; nor should one with two years... [of seniority sit with one with more].
One who has attained seniority by having completed three summer retreats may sit on the same seat as others.

If the space in a layperson’s house is cramped, even if one sits on the same seat as one's *upādhyāya* (the preceptor, translated here as "Teacher"), there is no offense. It is permitted for three people to sit on a single bed;
however, two people should not lie down together on one bed. This applies provided they possess a sense of shame. If they lack such shame, it is not permitted.
Regarding the offense: if one is on a journey and sleeps with a large cloak (*mahāpatta*) between oneself and another, separated by the cloth, there is no offense.

If there is a donor who spreads clothing on the ground to invite the assembly of Dharma practitioners, wishing for them to tread upon it, or if a lion throne adorned with jewels has been covered with the clothing of a layperson, the bhikṣu should give rise to a sense of compassion and depart.
The perception of impermanence: stepping upon or sitting on [a rug] does not constitute an offense, provided it is for the purpose of inspiring faith and respect in non-Buddhists.
If a donor lends a monastic rug or mat, it should be given to them; when the matter is concluded, one should have it returned. If it becomes soiled, it should be washed.

If the monastery is burned by fire, one should first take out one's own robes and bowl, and then take out the permanent assets of the Sangha, having those who are physically unable to do so gather them in one place.

The "guardian" (referring to one who is powerless, yet whose intent lies in being able to guard, though unable to maintain practice). If that fire were to be extinguished, one should not rashly enter the great waters and drift away;
this case should also be judged accordingly.
This precept is shared by those training in the Mahāyāna.
The fifteenth is the precept regarding not putting away bedding in a communal dwelling:

if a bhikṣu, in a communal dwelling, spreads out bedding belonging to the Saṃgha—whether spreading it himself or instructing another to spread it—and then departs; or if he sits [and does not put it away]; [he commits an offense].
If one lies down and, upon departing, neither raises [the bedding] oneself nor instructs another to raise it, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, there was a visiting bhikṣu who said to a resident bhikṣu:
"I have spread out my bedding and stayed overnight in a peripheral monk's cell. Later, at another time, he did not inform [the resident].
The resident bhikṣus then departed. The monastic bedding became moldy and ruined; it was eaten by insects and its color faded.

Because the former residents had not been seen for a long time, when visiting bhikṣus arrived at the room and inspected it, they saw this and expressed their reproach and disapproval. They reported this to the Buddha, who established the precept. This is an offense of prohibition (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya).
It was formulated as a training rule (śikṣāpada) due to the matter of bedding and the underlying affliction of disrespect.
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. From "In the monastery quarters" onwards, it clarifies the use of communal property by the Saṃgha;

while the substance [of the property] pertains to all four directions, the objects themselves are restricted to the specific residence. From "When departing" onwards, it establishes the offense incurred. The Vinaya states:

"Communal property, such as bedding and furniture, shall be entrusted, guarded, and maintained as described above. If there is no one to whom it can be entrusted and one does not fear its loss, one should move the bed away from the wall."
He raises the legs of the bed, places pillows, bedding, and requisites inside, and covers them with other bedding before departing.

If he fears they might be damaged, he should collect the bedding, rugs, and pillows, place them on a clothing rack, and stand the bed upright before leaving. (The previous precept concerned the open air;

this differs in that it concerns a monastic dwelling. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states: "A 'dwelling' may belong to the community of monks or to an individual; it is at least small enough to accommodate a visiting bhikṣu performing the four deportments of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.")
[Regarding] sitting and lying down).
Regarding the offense: if one departs without employing such a means [of returning], and goes outside the boundary, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is outside the boundary and one foot is inside the boundary, and one returns with regret and does not go further, there is no offense.
All *duṣkṛta* offenses: if one has agreed to go but does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If, having returned immediately, one remains outside the boundary for two nights, and on the third night before the dawn has appeared, one does not personally go to the dwelling or send a messenger to inform the *māmakī* (the owner) or the administrator, saying, "Please take care of these items," it is a *pāyattika*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the utilization of monastic property; second, departing without either taking it up oneself or informing the owner;
and third, both feet having crossed the boundary.
If a monk commits this offense, it is a *pāyattika*; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is likewise a *pāyattika* (the same rule applies to those of the same training).
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if one departs after performing the aforementioned sequence of actions; or if the dwelling is ruined, collapsing, or burned by fire;
or if there are circumstances of difficulty; or if the third night has passed and the dawn light has appeared, yet one does not go personally nor dispatch a messenger with a message;
as well as cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.

Regarding the rules for gathering [the bedding]: the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states that if one spreads monastic bedding (*śayanāsana*) in an inner room and there is no enclosure, one must remain at least one stone’s throw away;
otherwise, it is an *duṣkṛta* offense (this is based on the distance reached by a stone thrown by an average person). At two stone’s throws away, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: when intending to leave, one should sprinkle the floor inside the dwelling to make it clean and sun the pillows and mattresses.

One should inform the owner regarding dry bedding. Regarding bedding and mattresses, one should inform the person in charge. If staying overnight at a layperson's house, one should point it out and inform them when departing.
If it is a straw mat, one should ask when leaving: "Where shall these straws be placed?
and arrange them according to the host's instructions. If the host says, "Just go; I will take care of it myself," one should fold up one corner slightly before departing.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Even when a bhikṣu is in a layperson's house, when using grass for bedding, he must also leave behind the grass upon which he has slept.
He should inform the donor, saying: 'If you wish to keep it, then keep it. If he fails to do so, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
This precept is likewise established in the Mahāyāna.
The sixteenth precept on forcibly taking up residence:
If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu is already staying at a dwelling, yet comes later and forcibly spreads out bedding in the middle of it to stay overnight.

He should think: "If they find it cramped, they will naturally avoid me and depart. To act with such a motive and for no other reason constitutes an improper demeanor (*anācāra*), which is a *pāyattika* offense.
The Origin Story: This precept has two origins. The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus were traveling on a road in the kingdom of Kośala.
They arrived at a village where no other bhikṣus resided. The group of seventeen addressed the group of six, saying: "You are our seniors; you ought to..."
[The group of seventeen] first sought lodgings, saying, "We shall seek them later. The group of six replied, "You go ahead yourselves; we will not seek lodgings.
Thereupon, the group of seventeen went and sought lodgings, spreading out their bedding and settling there for the night.
When the group of six learned of this, they went to them and said, "Arise! You must stay according to the order of seniority. [Thus spoke] the group of seventeen.
He did not consent. They then forcibly spread bedding within the seating area. The group of seventeen monks spoke out in a loud voice, saying, "Venerable sirs, do not do this!
Among the assembly, there were monks of few desires who felt reproach and went to inform the World-Honored One. This was the first establishment of a precept.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether a place was a previously inhabited dwelling or not. Later, they realized it was a previously inhabited dwelling;
some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were apprehensive and cautious. The Buddha said, "If one does not know, there is no offense.
Therefore, for the sake of the Saṃgha, this was the second formulation of the precept. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) arising from matters concerning bedding and furniture.
Out of a sense of indignation, this training rule was established.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning, the text is divided into two sections: from "knowing that a previous bhikṣu... onwards concerns taking up residence out of pride and strength;

from "creating such causes and conditions... onwards establishes the commission of the offense. "Knowing" (means either knowing by oneself or being informed by another, indicating it is not a case of ignorance). "A previous bhikṣu" refers to one who has already been residing there.

"Abiding therein" means that the bhikṣu was already there, dwelling in peace and quiet. "One who arrives later" refers to a bhikṣu who arrives subsequently and, relying on his influence, acts with even greater intentional insolence;
he spreads his own bedding atop the bedding of another and sits or lies down upon it. The Vinaya states: "In between" means either at the head-end or at the foot-end.

Regarding bedding on both sides [of the body]: whether it be a bed of grass, a bed of leaves, or even a bed spread upon the ground, one should reflect as follows—[the term "reflect" indicates that this is not verbal speech, but rather an unwholesome thought arising within the mind; namely, being oppressed by the suffering of crowding, one thinks: "He shall naturally avoid me and depart from afar; why must I employ words to send him away?
By means of such causes and conditions, and no others (meaning: one employs the aforementioned forceful means to cause the other to avoid oneself voluntarily, and not for any other purpose or cause).

Furthermore, that which is not in accordance with dignified deportment (meaning that those who arrived first have never offered a polite request for departure, while those who arrived later insist on staying overnight, thereby disrupting the four modes of conduct; this is unsuitable for the Sangha).
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding those who violate this rule, for every time they turn over onto their side so that it touches the bed, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, there must already be someone present in the place; second, the mind must harbor a sense of disturbance or agitation.
The section on the three types of strong bedding is concluded.

This also governs the *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense (the same rule applies to those of common training). For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. These constitute the transgressions.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if one did not know beforehand; if [the other] has already spoken and remained [there]; if it is spacious and does not cause obstruction;
if there is an acquaintance who instructs one to spread [the bedding] therein; if one falls to the ground; or if, due to illness, one turns over and falls upon it.

If one is imprisoned, if there is a threat to life, if there is a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or if it concerns a precept not yet established at the outset, these constitute non-offenses.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the dwelling place is small, a single bhikṣu shall spread [the bedding] across one entire dwelling space."
Having spread the bedding and the *niṣīdana* over it, he either prostrates and pays his respects to the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, or departs to receive the scriptures.
Later, when another monk arrives, he removes the previously placed *niṣīdana* and spreads his own *niṣīdana*.
Having sat down, he recites the *bhāṣya* in a low voice. When the resident monk who arrived first sees this, he thinks: "Who could possibly interrupt him?"
The Dharma: one should immediately take one's own *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and depart. Subsequently, for a *bhikṣu*, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to sitting in meditation while ill. If one comes later and lies down on another’s bed, if that person is a senior (*sthavira*), one should say to them:
"Venerable sir, do you not know that the World-Honored One has established the precepts? If the *bhikṣu* who is lying down is a junior, one should reprimand him.
"You are not well-behaved; you do not understand the characteristics of the precepts. You do not know that the World-Honored One has established these rules.

How could you later lie down to sleep upon another's bed? If a bhikṣu is walking in meditation in a certain place and sees a bhikṣu who arrived earlier, he should move away to another spot (*'other place' means that there was already another bhikṣu walking in meditation at this location, and the bhikṣu who arrives later also walks in meditation there). If a bhikṣu sleeps at night..."
At that time, although one may cause trembling or speak in one's sleep, if one does not form an intention to cause disturbance, there is no offense. To disturb a *bhikṣu* is a *pāyattika*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one is able to spread [the bedding], it is a *pāyattika*; if one is unable to spread it, it is a *dukkaṭa*."
If, for the purpose of annoying others, one closes or opens a door; closes or opens a window (the term "xiang" refers to windows);
lights or extinguishes a fire; lights or extinguishes a lamp; chants the *brahman* hymns, recites scriptures, preaches the Dharma, or engages in debate;
or performs any such act that is disagreeable to another—each such instance constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Appendix: Examination of the Rules The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "In the rooms for defecation and urination, one does not follow seniority.
Whoever arrives first shall enter first. Once the act of voiding is finished, one must not remain there for long. Regarding the place for washing the feet, one must follow the order of seniority.
As for the utensils of the Saṃgha, down to the dyeing vessels, whoever uses them first must wait until their task is completed before others may use them."

One should act according to seniority; those who have already taken [an item] first must not be dispossessed. Furthermore, one should not place a small amount of dye in a vessel with the intention of causing it to stagnate, thereby obstructing its use by others.
When reciting scriptures, if someone has already taken their seat before you, you should not require them to rise and make way based on seniority.
Once the monastic razor has been used, it should be returned to its original place.
One must not remain [there]. Furthermore, one should prepare for future needs such as these. Those who do not act accordingly shall all incur an evil offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
(The seventeenth: The precept against dragging another out of a room.)
If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, does not wish for him to remain in the saṃgha’s dwelling and either drags him out himself or instructs another to drag him out, it is a pāyattika.
The Circumstances: The Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery. The group of six and the group of seventeen were dwelling in the same quarters as before.
After the group of seventeen had entered the monastery, swept and sprinkled the rooms, spread out bedding, and settled in for the night, the group of six learned of this.

He immediately went to the room and ordered him to rise, taking the seat according to the sequence of seniority in the precepts. The group of seventeen replied, "Venerable sir, you are indeed our senior;
however, we have already spoken [to you], and we cannot rise now. The group of six forcibly pulled him up; being angry and displeased, they drove him out of the room.
The Buddha established this precept for them: it is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) because, due to matters concerning bedding and seating, one causes vexation to others.
The formulation of this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
Explanation of the meaning: “Being angry with others” means harboring displeasure, causing others unease, and acting out of misconduct. Regarding “expelling”: the *Mūla-vinaya* states:
Some say "drive them out," or "pull them out by hand" (whether doing it oneself or employing others).
Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, if one pulls them out oneself, or instructs another to pull them out;
or if one pulls many people out through many doors, there are multiple *pāyattika* offenses. If one pulls many people out through a single door, there are multiple *pāyattika* offenses.
If one leads a person out through many doors, there are multiple *pāyattikas*. If one leads a person out through one door, there is one *pāyattika*.
If one carries another's belongings out, or carries objects and throws them outside the door, or shuts another inside the door, it is likewise for all such acts.
Dukkata. This precept incurs the full offense only when three conditions are met: first, there is a mind of anger toward another; second, the other is a faultless bhikkhu;
and third, one drags them outside the door.
If one governs [the offense] concurrently, it is a *vinaya-pāyattika* (for monks; the same rule applies to those of the same training).
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Exemptions from offense: If one departs in succession without a mind of malice; or if, after staying together for two or three nights, one sends away a person who has not received the precepts;
or if that person has broken the precepts, broken their views, or broken their deportment;

or if they have been expelled (meaning the Sangha has already performed the act of expulsion against them); or if they are subject to expulsion (meaning the offense committed by the bhikṣu is one for which expulsion is required, but the Sangha has not yet performed the formal ritual of expulsion); or if there is...
There is no offense in cases involving danger to life, difficulties regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*), the expulsion of such persons, or when the precepts have not yet been established.
As the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one brings a person whom [the other] does not like to live in the same room with him, [desiring to]..."
If one causes [a person] to leave on one's own, whether they leave or not, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To pull out a *bhikṣuṇī* or any of the other three assemblies is a *duṣkṛta*.
However, if one pulls out a shameless person, or if one intends to subdue a disciple, there is no offense.
If one leads [the person] out, there is no offense.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If there is a bhikṣu who is quarrelsome and frequently violates the precepts, views, and proper conduct..."

If such a person acts out of anger, or if they lack a virtuous mind, they incur an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). [Regarding "acting out of anger": this refers to manifesting skillful means to subdue them, rather than actual anger;
thus, there is no offense. Regarding "lacking a virtuous mind": this means being devoid of compassion and acting without the intent to subdue; for this reason, one incurs an offense.
If one drags a pure *bhikṣu* out of a place that is not a monastic dwelling, one incurs an *duṣkṛta* offense. If it concerns a person who has broken the precepts, the assembly should...
They shall be driven out together; if they lean against the gate or embrace a pillar, they must all be hewn down, and the matter of their expulsion shall be brought to an end.
Afterwards, the monks should repair the places where they were hewn and cut. If the disciples and others hope for such a punishment of evil, [they should act accordingly].
When leading [the person] out of the room, there is no offense. However, one should not cause them to leave their dwelling place.

If they have not broken the precepts or committed a transgression, but are merely difficult to converse with, one should employ the "method of dragging the halter" to subdue them. (The "method of dragging the halter" means to temporarily set them aside, neither conversing with them nor engaging in communal activities;

it is like a wild horse that is difficult to tame, which should be restrained by its halter and then abandoned. If dragons or snakes should suddenly appear in the dwelling place, one should snap one's fingers.
He instructs him, saying: "O worthy one, you should go far away; do not disturb the bhikṣu.
If he does not leave even after being told this, one should take a soft object and entangle him with it to lead him away. Do not bind him with hair-ropes or the like, lest he be injured.
Release him carefully in a thicket of grass. Once he has entered his hole, only then should you depart. This is the method for discarding fleas and lice.
One should place it upon an old cloth or fabric, adjusting its position according to the cold or heat of the season.
If such materials are unavailable, one should place it in a crevice of a wall or a hole in a pillar, allowing it to sustain itself naturally.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If camels, oxen, or horses are within a stūpa or monastery, and one drives them out for fear of defiling or damaging the stūpa or monastery, there is no offense.
This precept is likewise established in the Mahāyāna.
The Eighteenth Precept on Sitting or Lying on a Bed with Removable Legs in a Multi-Story Building:
If a bhikṣu, in a room or upon a multi-story building, sits or lies down on a rope bed or a wooden bed with removable legs,
it is a pāyattika offense.
**The Origin Story:** The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

A group of bhikṣus were living on an upper story of a multi-storied building. They sat upon beds with removable legs; as they sat, they were not composed, and because the floor of the building was thin, the legs of the beds came loose and fell onto the bhikṣus who were sleeping below.

They were injured, and blood flowed from their bodies. Bhikṣus who possessed a sense of shame and remorse criticized and reproached them for this. Consequently, the Buddha established a precept concerning lying down.
This training rule was established because of the presence of [faulty] objects and a lack of care regarding dignified deportment.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning: the *Vinaya* states that "a room" refers to either a communal monastic cell (*saṃghārāma*) or a private cell.

A "multi-storied building" (*kūṭāgāra*) refers to one where the head [of a bed] does not reach the ceiling. A "bed with removable legs" refers to a bed whose legs are inserted into sockets; because they are not secured with wedges, the legs become detached. (From the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*).

It is said: Regarding the rules for sitting and reclining, one must always be composed and careful; if one is not attentive and careful, injury will inevitably result, and furthermore, one’s dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) will be impaired.

The offense is established as follows: among these, if one sits or lies down such that the side of the body touches the bed, or turns over, it is a *pāyattika* offense—provided this is not a bed with detachable legs, or a single-seated chair, or a wooden plank, or a bathing bench.
All such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
