This precept incurs the full offense only when four conditions are met: first, the floorboards of the upper story are thin; second, there are people below the upper story;
third, the bed is broken or its legs have come loose; and fourth, one sits or lies down without careful composure.
If a *bhikṣu* commits this simultaneously, it is a *pāyattika*; the same rule applies to his fellow students.
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
The exceptions where there is no offense are as follows: sitting on a bed with rounded legs, straight legs, curved legs, or no legs;
if there is a wooden floor covering on an upper story of a multi-storied building; if one sits on the bed turned upside down; if one sits after having removed the legs of the bed;
and in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established. These constitute no offense.
Regarding the practice of gathering: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if there is no one sitting beneath a pavilion, there is no offense.
This precept is largely identical to the [preceding] rule for fellow students.
Number nineteen: the precept against pouring water containing insects onto mud or grass.
If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings, and he himself pours it onto mud or grass, or instructs another to pour it, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the origin of this precept: there were two enactments. When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, Chanda was constructing a large building.

They used water containing insects to mix with the clay and instructed others to blend it. When the laypeople saw this, they criticized them for lacking a heart of compassion and for harming the lives of many sentient beings;
thus, this was the first establishment of a precept. At that time, the bhikṣus had doubts, not knowing whether there were insects or not;
some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained fearful and cautious. The Buddha said, "If you did not know [that there were insects], you do not commit an offense."

This was the second precept established. This is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). It was formulated as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) due to the affliction of a lack of compassion regarding the use of water;
it belongs to the same category as the fundamental offense of killing in the first section.

**Explanation of the Terms:** *“Knower”* (the one who knows): This refers to either knowing through self-examination or knowing through the words of others. *“Water”* (udaka): This refers to water from ponds, rivers, wells, and so forth, including even thin gruel and similar liquids.

*“Insects”* (saprāṇa): The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: “Water with insects” refers to those caught by a strainer or those visible to the naked eye. *“To pour”* (siñcati): This means to sprinkle; it is also a synonym for the general use of water.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* explains that there are two types of water usage: internal and external. Internal usage includes things such as food and drink; external usage includes things such as sprinkling, washing clothes, and bathing. Since this rule pertains to external usage, its internal usage is prohibited as later forbidden. Both of these uses clearly manifest the compassionate protection of sentient beings.
[This refers to] subtle [beings].

Regarding the offense: among these, the transgression occurs if one knows that water contains insects and yet uses it to sprinkle on mud or grass, or if one throws grass or soil into that which contains insects;
this constitutes a *pāyattika*. Excluding water, if there is curd-milk (*dadhi*) or fermented rice-gruel (*mantha*) containing insects...
If one pours clear curd-liquor or barley-gruel used for soaking onto mud or grass, or instructs another to pour it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places earth or grass into such fermented liquids as those containing insects, or instructs another to do so, [it is likewise a *pāyattika*].
A *pāyattika* offense:

if there are insects in the water and one perceives them as such, it is a *pāyattika*. If there are insects in the water but one suspects it, it is a *pāyattika*. If there are no insects in the water but one perceives them as such, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If there are no insects in the water but one suspects it, it is a *dukkaṭa*. All such cases are *dukkaṭa*.
This precept fulfills three conditions before the full offense is established: first, knowing that the water contains insects; second, perceiving it as containing insects;
and third, personally instructing others to pour it out for use.
This also applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*, who commit a *pāyattika* offense (the same rule applies to those training together). It also applies to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*.
For a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This constitutes an offense.

Exceptions where there is no offense: if she does not know there are insects; if she perceives them as being without insects; if the insects are large and she touches the water with her hand to make them go away;
if she strains the water and sprinkles it on the ground, or instructs another person to sprinkle it; and in the case of the initial period before the precept was established.
...and so forth. These constitute non-offenses.
According to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*: "To pour [water] oneself" constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for each breath (the term "breath" here signifies a pause).
If one instructs another to pour [water], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for every word spoken.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "In ponds, rivers, and other water-filled places, there are many insects and fish; if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, diverts the water..."
Whenever the lives of insects or fish are severed, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; if they do not die, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

If one dams this water source so that it is cut off, then for the lower half [of the stream], according as the lives of insects are severed or they do not die at that time, the offense incurred is the same as before.
This precept is established identically in the Mahāyāna.
An appended examination: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu is constructing a dwelling and requires water—from a river, a pond, or a well—he must strain it until a vessel is full;
he may then use it only after checking that there are no insects. If there are still insects present, he must [strain it] again."
Filter it and examine it closely. If there are still insects after three layers of filtration, one should dig a separate well and examine it as before.
If there are still insects, one should abandon the task at hand and go elsewhere. The birth of insects is impermanent;
they may have been absent previously and now exist, or they may exist now and later cease to be. Therefore, monks, day by day—
Examine it closely; if there are no insects, then use it.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "There are three ways of killing living beings: killing sentient beings out of greed for their hair, horns, skin, or flesh;
killing sentient beings out of hatred, resentment, or malice; and killing without any desire for gain and without any anger."
To harm and kill sentient beings is called killing out of delusion. To use water containing living creatures for this precept is what is meant by killing sentient beings out of delusion.
This is the twentieth precept concerning the concealment of a room’s defects beyond three layers.
If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, including its doors, windows, and other decorative fittings, he must direct that the roofing and thatching be limited to two or three layers.
If they exceed this, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying in the city of Kauśāmbī at the Sundarika Park. Chanda constructed a large dwelling;
after he had finished one layer of thatching, there was still straw remaining, so he added a second layer, and yet there was still straw remaining, so he added a third layer.
He thought to himself, "I cannot constantly beg for straw from my donors," and so he continued adding layers until the roof collapsed and the dwelling fell into ruin. All those who lived there...
The laypeople saw this and all reviled and disparaged it. At that time, a bhikṣu who was contented heard of this and informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense by prohibition). It was formulated as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) due to the afflictions of greed and arrogance regarding the matter of dwellings.
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. From "constructing a large dwelling" (*mahallaka*) onwards, it clarifies the process of construction.

From "if it exceeds" onwards, it establishes the offense incurred. The Vinaya states: "A 'large dwelling' (*mahāśālā*) refers to one that uses many materials" (the *Vinayavibhaṅga* states: "There are two kinds of large residences: first, those large in physical dimensions;

second, those large in the quantity of donated materials. This refers to being large in dimension, built for a donor"). Furthermore, "other decorations" refers to carving, engraving, and painting. Regarding "coverings," there are two types.

Covered lengthwise; covered crosswise. (According to my observation of all the dwellings constructed in the Western Regions, they consist of wooden-framed houses with flat roofs, with walls plastered with lime and covered with various materials—such as thatched reeds, straw, or wooden planks.)

Doors, windows, walls, paintings, carvings, and various other exquisite designs—their ornate decorations are manifold. What is now referred to in the Vinaya as "and other such ornaments" is a general term.

When that bhikṣu has directed the two sections of the covering (where "sections" refers to the measured divisions) and the third section is not yet finished, he must depart to a place where he is neither seen nor heard.

Regarding the establishment of the offense: among these, the transgression occurs as follows. If two sections have been covered and the third section is not yet finished, and one does not go to a place where one is neither seen nor heard, then upon the completion of the third section, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one leaves a place where one is heard and goes to a place where one is seen, or leaves a place where one is seen and goes to a place where one is heard, in all such cases it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, seeking to build a dwelling; second, desiring to construct it with solidity;
and third, exceeding the prescribed dimensions after the inspection is complete.
This also applies to bhikṣuṇīs as a *pāyattika* (identical regulation for those of the same training). It likewise applies to śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.
For a nun, this is a *duṣkṛta* offense; thus it constitutes a transgression.
Exceptions where there is no offense include: if the path by water or land is cut off, or if there is danger from bandits, danger from wild beasts, or if the waters have risen in flood.
If one is under the influence of powerful forces; or if one is bound; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
or if one has been instructed [to leave] up to the third joint but has not yet finished; or if one does not go to a place where [the instruction] is neither seen nor heard;
or if it concerns a case prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these are non-offenses.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "In constructing a dwelling, there are three methods—superior, middling, and inferior—each with its own specific limits.
If one were to use the superior or middling method of roofing for an inferior dwelling, it would be because of the excessive weight."
Because it is completed all at once (*sakṛt*). If one uses grass for the covering, for every blade of grass there is a *pāyattika*.

Regarding the method of roofing for a middle-sized or larger dwelling, because it is likewise a heavy construction, if one uses grass for the covering, for every blade of grass there is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the method of roofing according to the superior, middling, or inferior [sizes], because it is completed all at once, once the dwelling is finished, there is one *pāyattika*.
If the wall is not completed all at once, there is no offense.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "When building a wall, if it is made of wet mud, from the initial preparation of the ground and laying of the foundation until the walls are first raised, they should be built in two or three layers, applying the molds for the bricks.
To exceed this limit constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. If [the wall] is made of fired [bricks]..."
Bricks, as well as stone or wood—should the donor wish for a rapid completion, even if the weight exceeds the prescribed limit, there is no offense.

(According to this school, as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, up to the third stage, if one abandons the work before it is finished, there is no offense; other schools hold that the offense is incurred only upon reaching the fourth stage. Here, we follow the regulations of this school;
other schools should merely be understood accordingly.)
This precept is shared with the Mahāyāna.
Twenty-first: Regarding the precept against going oneself to instruct nuns—if a bhikṣu goes to instruct bhikṣuṇīs without being appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī requested of the Buddha that he allow the bhikṣus to provide instruction and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs. The Buddha commanded Ānanda to assign the elder monks in turn to go [to the nuns’ quarters].
At that time, it was Paṇḍaka’s turn; however, the Venerable One could recite only a single verse. When he arrived to receive the bhikṣuṇīs...
Having been invited with formal rites and having recited a single verse, he immediately entered the fourth dhyāna. The group of six nuns addressed one another with mocking words:
"We previously said that the bhikṣu Panthaka is a fool who only knows how to recite a single verse.
When he comes to teach us and has finished speaking, what else will he have to say? Now he is silent; it is exactly as we said. There were some [who]... Arhats.
The arhat bhikṣuṇīs, having heard what the Venerable One had said, were all greatly delighted.

In this manner, he recited the verses three times and entered the fourth dhyāna three times. When the Venerable One emerged from concentration, he observed the minds of the bhikṣuṇīs; some were filled with joy.
There were some who did not rejoice; they immediately ascended into the void, manifested various supernatural transformations, preached the Dharma, and departed.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went there themselves to instruct and admonish them, yet they did not speak the True Dharma, but instead spoke all manner of worldly discourses, even including laughter, dancing, and limping.
The group of six bhikṣuṇīs were exceedingly delighted, while the arhatī bhikṣuṇī, with a heart of reverence—

Therefore, [the Buddha] remained silent and spoke no word. Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Buddha. The Buddha ordained that within the Saṃgha, a formal procedure consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) must be used to appoint a teacher for the nuns.
Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus immediately went outside the boundary and appointed one another to go [as teachers].
Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Buddha again. The Buddha ordained that one must be accomplished in ten qualities before being permitted to teach the nuns. First, the precepts...

1. Being fully endowed with the Vinaya; 2. Having heard much and being able to recite the characteristics of the two divisions of the precepts; 3. Being capable of making definitive judgments without doubt;

4. Being skilled at preaching the Dharma; 5. Having left the household life from a noble family; 6. Having a handsome and upright appearance; 7. Causing the assembly of nuns to rejoice upon seeing her.
8. To preach the Dharma to the community of nuns in a manner that is capable of inspiring them with joy. 9.
To don the dharma robes without having gone forth under the Buddha and thereby commit a grave offense (pārājika). 10. To have reached twenty years of age or more (i.e., twenty *varṣa* of seniority).

For such cases as these, one may bestow the instructions and precepts upon nuns; thus the rule was established. This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), arising from greed regarding matters concerning nuns.
Fearing that [the practice of teaching nuns] would incur worldly reproach and provoke afflictions dependent on external conditions, this training rule was established.

This constitutes the fundamental category of sexual misconduct within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa]. (According to the *Mūla-vinaya*: One who possesses seven qualities should be appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct nuns: 1. observance of the precepts; 2. extensive learning; 3. standing in the rank of seniority; 4. proficiency in the language of the capital city;
5. never having defiled a nun with one’s body; 6. being well-versed in distinguishing the eight *pārājika* rules; 7. being well-able to explain the eight *gurudharma* rules.)
**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "The Sangha" refers to those who share a single recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and a single *karmavācanā*.

"Appointed" refers to one appointed from within the Sangha by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (this procedure is explained in the section on formal acts). Regarding the "instructor": there are eight rules that must not be transgressed.

When a bhikṣuṇī of eighty years' standing (*śata-varṣā*) sees a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, she must rise to meet him, welcome him, inquire after his well-being, and prostrate before him, requesting him to be seated.
(1) One must not revile a bhikṣu. One must not slander them by saying they have broken their precepts, broken their views, or broken their deportment.

(2) One must not bring up a bhikṣu’s offenses, nor cause them to be reminded of them, nor force them to confess them. One must not obstruct another bhikṣuṇī from seeking the removal of her offense, nor obstruct her from the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*.
One must not speak of a bhikṣu’s faults; however, a bhikṣu may speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s faults.
(3) Regarding the faults of a bhikṣuṇī: she must first train in the śikṣamāṇā precepts; (4) having done so, she must request the full ordination from the Saṃgha.
(5) If she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must undergo the mānatva penance for half a month within both divisions of the Saṃgha.
(6) Every half-month, one should seek out an instructor from within the Saṃgha. (7) One should not observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in a place where there is no bhikṣu.
(8) Upon concluding the summer retreat, one should go before the assembly of monks and request the three matters for the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*):
what has been seen, heard, or suspected. These eight matters should be respected, honored, and praised throughout one’s entire life.

One should transgress [this rule]. (Regarding these Eight Rules of Respect: when a nun first seeks ordination, the Buddha has already declared that she must first request the Saṃgha for instruction every half-month. Now, Mahāprajāpatī requests this again because he wishes to initiate the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for appointing a messenger.
However, that which is to be taught is precisely these Eight Rules that must not be violated).

**The Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one goes to preach the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed when the Saṃgha has not appointed them, or on a day other than the designated teaching day, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If the Saṃgha has appointed them, they should arrive at the appointed time; the nun should also meet them at the appointed time.
If they do not arrive at the appointed time, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The nun should go out to meet them for half a *yojana*.

If one goes to welcome [a guest] and provide for their needs, yet fails to do so, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one goes to preach the Dharma to someone who has not been appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, a deliberate violation of the rule out of a greedy mind; second, the act of instructing a bhikṣuṇī;
and third, both feet having entered the doorway.
Furthermore, for a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta (the same rule applies, though studied separately); for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions from offense: as stated above, if one was appointed by the Saṃgha to go [on an errand] and arrives at the appointed time;

or if there are various difficult circumstances that cause delay and obstruction such that arrival at the appointed time is impossible; or if it concerns the very first instance before the precept had been established—these constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the timing for instructing nuns, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One must not instruct them from sunset until the first light of dawn has appeared.
One must not do so in a secluded or private place, nor in an exposed place; rather, one should do so in a place that is neither too secluded nor too exposed, such as a lecture hall or beneath a tree.
Furthermore, one must not instruct them on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the month, nor on the first, second, or third day.
On that day, one should go to provide instruction from the fourth to the thirteenth day. One must not instruct a community of nuns who are not in harmony.
Upon arrival, one should ask whether the community of nuns is in harmony. If they are in harmony, one should send a messenger to summon them.
If she does not come, one should grant her the *chanda* (consent) for instruction; however, one must not provide partial instruction, nor may one provide instruction with long-winded speech.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one who has not been appointed instructs a bhikṣuṇī, for every word [spoken], it is a *pāyattika* offense. This is the procedure for instruction.

For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one enters the dwelling place of nuns without being appointed by the Saṃgha for the purpose of instruction, for every step taken, it is a *pāyattika*. If one foot has entered the door, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This excludes cases where a bhikṣuṇī is ill.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If one does not first recite the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) but instead recites other teachings first, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If, however, one has already recited the Eight Rules of Respect and subsequently recites other teachings, there is no offense."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu should recite the bhikṣuṇī precepts so as not to let them be forgotten.

Why is this? Because women are prone to forgetfulness and their wisdom is easily distracted. After my parinirvāṇa, they should inquire about the rules of training from the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*).

These precepts are studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well. If one observes the capacity [of the recipient] and knows there will be great benefit, there is no offense. However, this applies only to the final age."
The Dharma is especially worthy of careful deliberation.
Appendix: *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) asks: "What is the difference between *anuśāsana* (instruction) and *avavāda* (teaching)?
It answers: “That which prevents what is unbeneficial is called instruction; that which provides what is beneficial is called teaching. Furthermore, it teaches one to abide [in the Dharma].”
Because it causes one to abide in right mindfulness, it is called "instruction" (avavāda). Because it teaches one to abide in clear comprehension (saṃprajanya), it is called "guidance" (anuśāsana).
Furthermore, because it causes one to cultivate mundane wholesome dharmas, it is called "instruction"; because it causes one to cultivate supramundane wholesome dharmas, it is called "guidance.
It is by such distinctions that they differ.
The twenty-second precept concerning instructing nuns until sunset:
If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a pāyattika offense.

The Origin: The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. At that time, Nanda—[the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that this is not the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda]—was appointed by the community of monks to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Having finished his instruction, he remained silent.
Mahāprajāpatī requested him again, and so on up to three times. Nanda possessed a beautiful voice, and those who heard him took delight in listening. Eventually, [he reached...]
At sunset, the nun left the Jetavana Monastery and entered the city of Śrāvastī. Since the city gates were already closed, she stayed overnight within the moat surrounding the city wall.
At dawn, she was the first to enter the city. When the elders saw her, they slandered her, saying, "She has spent the night with a bhikṣu."

The Buddha, knowing that [the offense] was committed for the sake of the Saṃgha, established this precept (śikṣāpada) because of the matter of public censure. This constitutes the fundamental category of sexual misconduct within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
Regarding the explanation of its meaning: the Vinaya states, "That bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, should [proceed] even unto..."

One should return before sunset. (This precept was not established for a bhikṣu going to a nunnery; rather, it was established for a bhikṣuṇī returning from a monastery at dusk. This is based on the preceding account of its origin.)
(As may be known from the subsequent opening).
Regarding the offense: herein, if one teaches until sunset, it is a *pāyattika*.
Excluding the case of teaching, if one receives the scriptures, recites the scriptures, asks questions, or engages in other matters until sunset, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Dukkata: except for bhikkhunīs, if one recites the sūtras for other women, or receives the sūtras from them, or questions them, or engages in other such matters until sunset, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
If it is evening and one perceives it as evening, it is a *pāyattika*. If it is evening and one suspects it is so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is evening but one does not perceive it as such, or if it is not evening but one suspects it is so, in all these cases it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, one must personally instruct bhikṣuṇīs within a monastic monastery;
second, the bhikṣuṇī monastery must be separated from the city by a wall; and third, it must be evening, and one must perceive it as evening.

If a *bhikṣuṇī* is also subject to this regulation, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense (the same regulation, different training). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding those cases where there is no offense: if she listens while preaching the Dharma at a ferry crossing; if she listens while traveling with merchants at night during a Dharma discourse;
if she listens while preaching the Dharma within a nunnery; if she listens because she was invited as a teacher on the day of the *poṣadha* when she encountered a Dharma discourse;
and in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—these constitute non-offenses.

Regarding the determination of the proper time, the *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Even if it is within the prescribed time, if the assembly of nuns stands rather than sitting, or if they are occupied with distracting activities that do not cease, or if one preaches the Dharma while the body is constrained by some impediment, this is also called 'improper time.
Furthermore, if the original intention of the donor was to request the Dharma master to preach through the night, or if the nunnery is nearby..."
If one faces a city gate; or if the city gates are not closed at night; or if the nuns' monastery is within the city;

or if the community of nuns is at the residence of a layperson—in all these cases, there is no offense. As for the person appointed to instruct the nuns, once they have been appointed, they shall instruct them for as long as they live;
it is not necessary to appoint another.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
The twenty-third [offense] regarding instructing nuns:
if a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus, "The bhikṣus teach [the Dharma] for the sake of food and drink," [he commits an offense].
Regarding the *bhikṣuṇī*: it is a *pāyattika*.
The origin story (*nidāna*): The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when the *bhikṣuṇīs* heard that the instructor (*śāstṛ*) was coming, they went out half a *yojana* to welcome him, provided him with lodging, and prepared food, drink, and bathing facilities. [The group of] six [monks] did not...
Having been appointed by the Saṃgha, he gave rise to a mind of jealousy and said, "These bhikṣus have no genuine sincerity; they instruct the bhikṣuṇīs solely for the sake of food and drink.
A bhikṣu of few desires, having heard this and knowing the truth, censured the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks and reported it to the Buddha, who then established the precept.
Out of a mind of jealousy, this training rule was established.
Regarding the offense: if a monk, for the sake of food or drink, instructs a bhikṣuṇī;
or for the sake of food or drink, teaches her to recite, receive, or inquire about the sūtras; and if he speaks so that she understands clearly, it is a pāyattika.
If it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, there must be a mind of envy; second, one must instruct a bhikṣuṇī;
third, the false speech must be for the sake of food and drink; and fourth, the speech must be clearly articulated.

If a *bhikṣuṇī* does so, it is a *duṣkṛta* (the rule is the same, though the training is distinct for her). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if the matter is indeed as stated; if one instructs a nun for the sake of providing food and drink;
if one teaches her to recite or receive the scriptures, or answers her questions, for the sake of food and drink; if speaking in jest, speaking in private, or speaking in a dream;
if intending to say one thing but saying another; and in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—these constitute no offense.
Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: it states that if one says [the teaching] is for the sake of medicine, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: if one says it is for the sake of making offerings that one instructs bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one says that the bhikṣu practices the twelve *dhūta* austerities...

If one practices walking meditation, sitting meditation, reciting sutras, or performs various meritorious deeds solely for the sake of making offerings or seeking benefit, each instance constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
This precept is studied identically in the Mahāyāna.
The twenty-fourth: The precept concerning giving robes to a nun who is not a relative.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for trade, it is a pāyattika offense.

The Origin Story: This precept was established in three stages. While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms and was fully endowed with dignified deportment. At that time, a certain bhikṣuṇī saw him and conceived a virtuous mind toward him;
she repeatedly invited the bhikṣu, but he did not accept her invitations. On another occasion, when the community of monks at Jetavana was distributing robes...
This bhikṣu, taking his share of robes, went out the door. Seeing that bhikṣuṇī approaching, he wished to fulfill his previous intention of offering them to her;

she did not accept them at first, but he immediately gave the robes to that bhikṣuṇī, who accepted them without hesitation. This bhikṣu repeatedly spoke of this to others with feelings of reproach and dissatisfaction.
A bhikṣu of few desires and possessing a sense of shame heard of this and informed the World-Honored One. This...
This was the first formulation of the precept. Later, the bhikṣus did not dare to give robes to their relatives who were bhikṣuṇīs.

The Buddha said, "I allow you to give them. This was the second formulation of the precept. At that time, the two assemblies of the Saṃgha divided the robes together; monks and nuns took them by mistake.

They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to exchange them. This was the third formulation of the precept. Because this led to censure and suspicion, he established this training rule (śikṣāpada); thus it was the first [of its kind].

Section on the Root Categories of Sexual Misconduct (Note: Regarding the common error in the distribution of robes between monks and nuns, it is said by donors: "This is the robe of a bhikṣu; this is the robe of a bhikṣuṇī. However, originally there were not two distinct styles of robes.

If there were two styles, then exchange or wearing them would not be permitted. Now, a corrupt tradition claims that the outer seams of a monk’s robe face outward, while the outer seams of a nun’s robe face inward. This statement is found in no Vinaya regulations of any school).
Exegesis: The Vinaya states that "relatives" are as defined above. "Robes" are of ten kinds, as described above.
"Bartering" means exchanging with one another; for instance, trading robe for robe, or even trading non-robes for robes, needles for knives, or thread, down to a single piece of medicinal herb.
**Establishing the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: giving a robe to a nun who is not a relative constitutes a *pāyattika*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the recipient must necessarily be a nun who is not a relative and is without fault;
second, the object must not be for barter or other such purposes; third, the robe-material must be of the prescribed measure.
If a *bhikṣu* commits it as well, it is a *duṣkṛta* (the same rule, different training). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: trading with one's own relatives; giving to a stūpa, to the Buddha, or to the Saṃgha;
and cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one gives clothing of the proper measure, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one gives clothing or other items that are not of the proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: If one gives clothing to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative but has broken the precepts or holds wrong views, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one gives clothing to any of the other two groups of female renunciants (śrāmaṇerī or upāsikā) who are not relatives, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.

However, there is no offense if one gives clothing for the purpose of managing household affairs, for the purpose of skillfully preaching the sūtras and Dharma, or for the purpose of encouraging extensive recitation of the sūtras and precepts.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one sees someone who has encountered misfortune and lacks clothing, one may give it to them; or if one receives [the gift] as an act of giving (*dāna*), there is no offense.
This precept is studied identically in the Mahāyāna. However, in this age of the Final Dharma (*paścimaka-dharma*), one must exercise extreme caution.
The twenty-fifth: The precept concerning making robes for a nun who is not a relative.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika. Regarding the origin of this rule:
This precept has two enactments. When the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, there was at that time...
A bhikṣuṇī wished to have a saṃghāṭī robe made. She took it to the monastery; Kālodāyin, being skilled in the methods of tailoring robes, immediately cut and sewed it for her.
He fashioned it into the likeness of a man and woman engaged in sexual intercourse. When the bhikṣuṇī arrived, he folded the robe and handed it to her, saying:
"You must not rashly open this robe to look at it, nor must you show it to others. If it is time for the formal announcement..."
"Arrival" (meaning that when a donor invites the Saṃgha and announces that the time for the meal has come, they go to the offering). Wearing this robe, he walked behind the bhikṣuṇīs.
When the laypeople saw this, they clapped their hands and laughed loudly. Mahāprajāpatī asked and learned the reason;
she then informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus in turn informed the World-Honored One. This was the first establishment of a precept. At that time, the bhikṣus...
Out of fear and caution, they did not dare to make robes for their relatives who were bhikṣuṇīs. The Buddha permitted this; it was the second formal rule (śikṣāpada) established.
Because this led to public censure and suspicion, this training rule was promulgated.
Explanation of Terms: The Vinaya states that "relatives" are as defined above, and there are ten types of robes as listed above (*Vinayasamgraha* states:
"making a robe" refers to cutting, sewing, washing, and dyeing).

**Establishing the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one makes a robe for a nun who is not a relative, it is a *pāyattika* offense for every amount of cloth cut with the knife;
it is a *pāyattika* offense for every stitch and every needle.

Furthermore, it is a *pāyattika* offense for smoothing it out, pulling and stretching it, pressing it with the hand, rubbing it, or grasping the corners to pull it into shape, or for applying patches.
Regarding the conditions: whether one asks for thread or joins the thread, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, that the nun is not a relative; second, that there is an intention to joke or mock.
Third, making robes by one's own hand.

This also prohibits bhikṣuṇīs, for whom it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense (the same rule applies, though studied separately). For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is defined as a transgression.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if one acts for a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative; or for the sake of a stūpa;
or if one borrows [an item] and washes, dyes, or repairs it before returning it to the owner; or in cases such as when the precept has not yet been established—these constitute no offense.
Regarding the taking [of robes], the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When taking the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If a nun sends a messenger to bring robe-material to have a robe made, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if she causes another person to have it made, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If she has it made into a robe that is not of the proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
If one washes [the robe] with *lavaṇa* (salt), for each individual act, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept is studied in common by the Mahāyāna.
The twenty-sixth: the precept against sitting in private with a nun.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
The origin story: The Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī.
Kālodāyin was handsome in appearance, and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was likewise so. Both of them harbored lustful intentions. At that time, Kālo...
At dawn, Udāyin went to the place where Thullanandā was staying and sat together with her outside the gate.
When the lay devotees saw this, they all spoke in disapproval. A monk who possessed contentment and a sense of shame, having heard of this, informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.

Because this gave rise to public censure and suspicion, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established. It belongs to the category of the fundamental offenses of the first section concerning sexual misconduct.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning, the Vinaya states: "In one place" means there is one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī.
"A secluded place" refers to a place hidden from sight or a place hidden from hearing. "Hidden from sight" means it is obscured by dust, mist, or darkness.
"Out of sight" means being in a screened or concealed place, up to a place where one cannot hear the sound of normal conversation.
Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu sits alone in a screened place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*.
If she is blind but not deaf, or he is deaf but not blind, it is a *duṣkṛta*. [The same applies if] they stand.
If one remains [seated], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, being in a secluded place; second, with only a single nun present; and third, sitting together on the same seat.
If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits it, it is a *duṣkṛta* (the same rule, but different training). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if a bhikṣu has a companion; or if there is a wise person (a "wise person" refers to a layman who understands good and evil and can speak of them);
or if while walking he suddenly falls to the ground; or if he falls while suffering from illness; or if he is seized by force and imprisoned;
or if there is danger to life, or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or if it concerns cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To sit in a secluded place with two other nuns is also a *pāyattika* offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"If one returns to sit after having walked in meditation (*caṅkrama*), it is a *pāyattika*. For every time one rises and returns to sit," [it is likewise].
One incurs that many *pāyattika* offenses.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "The term 'sitting' here refers to the specific condition for committing the offense; even other modes of conduct constitute an offense against this precept, as do the Mahāyāna fellow students."
The twenty-seventh precept: Traveling with a nun.
If a bhikṣu agrees to travel along the same path with a bhikṣuṇī, from one village to another, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The appropriate times are: when traveling with merchants, or when there is suspicion, fear, or terror; these are called the appropriate times.
At that time, regarding the origin of this precept: there were three enactments. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The group of six bhikṣus and the group of six bhikṣuṇīs were traveling through the human realm of Kośala. When the lay devotees saw them, they all...
[They were] criticized and disparaged. This was the first establishment of a precept. At that time, various bhikṣus did not first make an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī;
they encountered her unexpectedly on the road and, out of apprehension and caution, did not dare to travel together. The Buddha said, "If there was no prior appointment, there is no offense.

The twenty-eighth precept concerning traveling in a boat with a bhikṣuṇī:

The Origin Story: This precept has two origins. When the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, there was a woman from Vaiśālī who had married a man from Śrāvastī.

The husband pursued him until he caught up. He slandered and beat the Venerable One so severely that he nearly died.

The Thirty-first Precept: Regarding the Acceptance of More Than One Meal’s Alms.
If there is a place where a monk is offered a single meal, a monk who is not ill should eat only that one meal. If he accepts more than this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

[The] Origin Story: This precept has two enactments. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there was at that time a village without a monastery in the kingdom of Kośala.
A householder built a residence for the bhikṣus and constantly provided for them.
They provided them with food and drink. Those who resided there were permitted to eat only one meal daily.

However, the group of six bhikṣus stayed at that place for one night and obtained excellent food and drink, so they remained. On the second night, they again obtained excellent food and drink, and thought to themselves:
"The very reason we travel on pilgrimage is precisely for the sake of food; now we have already obtained it. They...
At this dwelling place, he ate repeatedly. The householder criticized and disapproved of this; thus was the first precept established.

Later, while Śāriputra was traveling, he arrived there and fell ill. Fearing that he might violate this precept, he set out on his way despite his illness, whereupon his condition grew increasingly severe.

Therefore, the phrase "free from illness" was further added. This is the second formulation of the precept. Because eating at improper times led to the censure and suspicion of the laity, this training rule (śikṣāpada) was established.

Explanation of the Terms: The Vinaya states: "A dwelling place" refers to staying there for one night. "Food" refers to even *kāla-bhojana* (meals at the proper time)—the phrase "even" here being an abbreviation that omits the five types of *khādya* (solid food).

"One who is ill" refers to one who has departed from that village; "one whose illness has increased" refers to [as the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states]: "a sick person, down to one wounded by a bamboo leaf."
**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a monk who is not ill stays overnight at a single lodging and receives food beyond that, for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika*.
Excluding food, if he further receives other items such as undergarments, lamp oil, or oil for anointing the feet, it is all *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, being free from illness or hardship; second, having a mind of greed;
and third, swallowing more than permitted.
This also applies to *bhikṣuṇīs*, who incur a *pāyattika* (the same rule applies to those training together). It also applies to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*.
For a nun, this is a *dukkaṭa* offense; this constitutes a transgression.
It is not a transgression in the following cases: receiving food for one night; receiving food while ill; if laypeople invite her to stay and eat;
or if a donor invites her to a meal in a fixed sequence, such as eating at the home of one person today and another tomorrow.
There is no offense in cases such as when people are eating, when the paths by water or land are obstructed, due to various difficult circumstances, or when the precept has not yet been established.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one stays overnight and does not eat, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing) to stay at another location.
Eating therein constitutes a *pāyattika*.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
The thirty-second: the precept concerning eating in succession (*saṃkramaṇa-bhojana*).
If a bhikṣu eats by taking successive portions of food, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense. The "appropriate times" are: when one is ill, when robes are being distributed.

These are called the appropriate times. (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "The appropriate times are: when one is ill, when working, when traveling on a journey, and when robes are being distributed; these are the times.")
The Origin Story: This precept was established in three stages. While the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, he was traveling through the countryside with the bhikṣus.

There was a śramaṇa brahmin who, with five hundred wagons filled with food and drink, followed the World-Honored One through winter and summer, waiting for an opportunity to provide an offering. However, [he could find no such opening].
He did so and went at once to tell Ānanda, saying, "Please inform the Buddha on my behalf that I wish to spread food and drink upon the ground so that the Buddha and the Saṅgha may tread over it;
this shall serve as an offering to the Buddha. The Buddha then permitted the making of cakes and gruel.

When the time came for the monks to receive these offerings, the lay devotees of the country of Anāpinḍada heard that the Buddha had allowed the Saṅgha to eat gruel and cakes, and they were all greatly delighted, thinking, "We have gained a wonderful opportunity to prepare them."

[This was] for the sake of merit. There was a minor official of little faith who, seeing that the Buddha and the Saṃgha had received great offerings, conceived the thought of them as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
He prepared rich and delicious food and invited the Saṃgha; however, because the monks had already accepted another invitation and were eating thick gruel, they could not eat much.
The official resented this. The Buddha said: "One must not, having already accepted an invitation, eat thick gruel."
Regarding porridge: it should be marked with a blade of grass; it is improper for it to be otherwise. At that time, the Buddha returned to the city of Rājagṛha.
There was a young musician who had little faith, and his situation was likewise. For this reason, he did not permit "successive eating" (also known as "repeated eating").
This was the first establishment of a precept. At the places where sick bhikṣus were invited to eat, there was no food or medicine suited to their illnesses.
If there were wholesome food or medicine suitable for their ailments, they feared and hesitated to eat it, dreading that they might violate the precepts.
The Buddha permitted sick bhikṣus to eat by "successive invitations" (saṃkramaṇa); this was the second establishment of a precept. Furthermore, there was a householder who also invited [them].
The Buddha and the Saṃgha were offered food and robes. A bhikṣu, being cautious and apprehensive, informed the Buddha.

Because [the practice of] "successive meals" (*paryāyeṇa bhojana*) was permitted at the time of offering robes, there was a third establishment of the precept. (Although this precept allows for such an exception, one must still not eat past noon; there is evidence for this in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*). This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
It was formulated as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) due to the afflictions of excessive indulgence in eating, the neglect of tranquility, and the incitement of public reproach.

**Exegesis:** The text is divided into two sections. The first clarifies the original enactment regarding "successive eating" (*paryāya-bhojana*); the second, beginning with "except at other times," clarifies the subsequent allowances.
The Vinaya states: "Successive eating" refers to invitations (*nimantraṇa*). There are two types of invitations: invitations by turn for the Saṃgha and individual invitations.
"Eating" refers to rice, parched grain flour, cakes, and so forth. "The sick" refers to those who are unable to eat while remaining in a single sitting. "Delicious food" refers to...
This is sufficient. Regarding the donor of robes: after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, if there is no *kaṭhina* robe, the period is one month;

if there is a *kaṭhina* robe, the period is five months. Furthermore, regarding other times for food and robes (*Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "That is to say, there is a donor who gives a bathing robe, or other garments such as shawls, or even items such as cowries, to serve as the price for robes").
**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if on this day one receives many invitations for meals, one should personally accept one invitation and give the remainder to others.
One should give them away by saying: "Venerable sir, I must go there; I now give this to you.
If a bhikṣu does not relinquish the previous invitation and accepts a subsequent invitation for a meal, he commits a *pāyattika* offense for every mouthful swallowed.
If one does not relinquish a subsequent invitation and eats at a prior invitation, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense for every swallow.

This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the absence of any permissible exception; second, not relinquishing the prior [invitation] while accepting the subsequent one.

If the three types of food have already entered the throat, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* (the same rule applies, though with different training requirements). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, and a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if one is invited to receive what is not food; or if the food is insufficient; or if there is no one to invite one to eat;
or if one has already eaten and subsequently obtains more food; or if there is both a preceding meal and a subsequent meal at the same location;
as well as cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.

Regarding the practice of eating: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the Buddha said, "From this day forward, out of compassion and for the benefit of sick bhikṣus, I permit three kinds of 'sufficient food' (pūrva-bhakta) to be eaten—namely, those possessing excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.
If one cannot be satiated at a single invitation, one may accept a second invitation, but one must not accept a third. If one cannot be satiated at the second location..."
One should accept a third invitation, but one should not accept a fourth invitation. At the place of the third invitation, one cannot be satiated;

having accepted it, one should eat gradually until midday (by "midday" is meant that it is understood that one must not pass noon). It is permitted to eat frequently on festival days. (The following passage contains nine sentences in total:

the first three clarify invitations for food when one has robes; the middle three clarify invitations for food when one has no robes; the final three clarify invitations for food when one’s robes are uncertain.)
One should cause the bhikṣus to know the time for the exception. Within these causal conditions, there are further prohibitions; one must first exercise careful deliberation before proceeding.

If a bhikṣu receives an invitation for food and clothing, and he accepts that invitation for food and clothing when they are available, he does not commit an offense. Eating [there] also does not constitute an offense.

Furthermore, regarding invitations involving both clothing and food: if one accepts an invitation for which there is no clothing or food, one does not commit an offense. As for "food": it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

This means that at the time of the initial invitation, it was stated that there would be both clothing and food; however, when the bhikṣu arrives to accept the invitation, there is only food and no clothing. Therefore, at the time of accepting the invitation, there is no offense; yet, if he accepts the food, he commits an offense immediately.

Furthermore, there is the invitation involving both clothing and food. If that [invitation] involves clothing and food, or if it involves food but no clothing, it is not an offense for one to come and accept the invitation.

Regarding "eating": it is a *pāyattika* offense (this refers to a case where a monk knows the invitation includes clothing, yet forms the thought that clothing is not certain; having arrived at the invitation, if he eats when clothing is present or absent, he commits the offense immediately.
Accepting the invitation and coming is not an offense. This concludes the first three phrases).
Furthermore, regarding invitations where neither clothing nor food are provided: if one accepts such an invitation despite the lack of clothing and food, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If one eats, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). This refers to an invitation given at a time when no clothing is provided; it does not accord with the principle of permissible exceptions. One should properly decline the host in order to protect the faith of the donor; this is what is meant by being a "holder of the Vinaya" and a pure bhikṣu. If, upon hearing an invitation, one immediately goes and both accepts the food and eats it, both [the host and the guest] commit an offense.

Furthermore, regarding an invitation where there is no clothing or food [for the host], yet the host possesses clothing and food, if a bhikṣu comes to accept the invitation, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

However, if he eats, he does not commit an offense. (This means that at the time of the invitation, the host says there is no clothing; the bhikṣu perceives that there is clothing and comes to the invitation. Once arrived, there is indeed clothing. Therefore, while accepting the invitation violates the rule and constitutes an offense, eating when clothing is present does not constitute an offense.)

Furthermore, regarding an invitation that originally included neither clothing nor food: if the invitation was for one who has both clothing and food, yet he comes and accepts the invitation when there is no clothing and no food, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If he eats, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). This refers to an original invitation where there was no clothing; the bhikṣu forms the thought that clothing will be provided, but upon arriving, he eats while having no clothing.
Therefore, both parties commit an offense. (The three points herein are concluded.)

Furthermore, there is the case of an invitation regarding robes and food versus no robes and food. If that [inviter] invites while having both robes and food, and the monk comes to accept the invitation thinking there may or may not be robes, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he eats, it is a *pāyattika*. (This means that at the time of the donor's invitation, they say "there may or may not be robes," and thus it is not an occasion where an exception is granted.
That bhikṣu also forms the thought that robes are uncertain, yet having arrived, he accepts food without robes; both constitute an offense.)

Furthermore, there is the case of an invitation where robes are provided and an invitation where robes are not provided. If one accepts an invitation where robes are provided, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). As for eating, there is no offense.

(This means that although at the time of the invitation it was said that robes were not certain, the bhikṣu forms the perception that robes are provided; yet upon arriving, robes and food are indeed present. Therefore, accepting the invitation is permitted, but eating constitutes an offense.
If one accepts the invitation where robes are provided and then eats, there is no offense.)
Furthermore, there is the case of an invitation for those with or without robes. If one who has no robe comes to accept such an invitation, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If they eat, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). (This refers to when one clearly knows that the invitation is indefinite, yet forms the thought that there will be no robe, and having arrived, if they accept food while without a robe, they commit both offenses.
The final three phrases are concluded.)
There is no offense if one receives many invitations for food and clothing; if each invitation arrives with both food and clothing, there is no offense in all cases.
The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one has first accepted an invitation for food without clothing, and subsequently accepts an invitation for food with clothing, there is no offense."
Regarding the offense:

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states that if, in a single house, within a monastery, or in an araṇya, one eats repeatedly for the sake of seeking plumpness and vigor, or out of a fondness for fine food, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). This applies if it is done with a contemptuous mind or through hypocrisy.
To not eat [the meal] also constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "Whether it be a meal assigned by the Saṃgha, a meal in a separate room, or if a layperson comes to receive the eight precepts..."
If one partakes of an offering or regular food, there is no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "When performing [a ritual] or while traveling on a journey, eating in succession (turning from one meal to another) constitutes no offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "All vegetables, all parched flour, and all fruits are not 'food for every occasion' (*sarvatra-bhojana*), nor are they 'separate meals' (*pṛthag-bhojana*)."
Regarding communal meals: if one has not yet finished eating, and there is an abundance of *śāli* rice, there is no offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna.
Citing evidence from the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*: "Ānanda had previously accepted an invitation, but at that time he forgot and did not remember it; furthermore, it was the same [as before]."
The Buddha accepted the invitation of King Prasenajit. As he placed the food in his mouth, he recalled that he had received two invitations and had not yet granted the other one.
Out of reverence for the Buddha, he did not dare to spit out the food; yet, out of adherence to the precepts, he did not dare to swallow it.
Knowing Ānanda’s remorseful state of mind, the Buddha told him to mentally transfer the portion to the other person and then eat. [This was reported to] Upāli.

He asked the Buddha, "Can others also do so? The Buddha said, "With the exception of five kinds of people: first, those practicing meditation (whose minds are focused exclusively on the Path so that no discursive thoughts arise);

second, those dwelling alone in a forest hermitage (āranya) where there is no one to converse with; third, those traveling on a long journey (who may momentarily forget mindfulness while on the road);
fourth, those who are chronically ill; and fifth, those staying with relatives during times of famine. Apart from these, it is not permitted for anyone else."
The thirty-third precept on eating in a separate group:
If a bhikṣu eats in a separate group, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense. "Other times" refers to the time of illness and the time of making robes.

The time for giving robes; the time when traveling on a road; the time when riding in a boat; the time when a great assembly has gathered; the time when śramaṇas are being given food—these are the proper times.
Regarding the origin story: this precept was established in eight stages. The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha. At that time...
At that time, Devadatta instructed others to harm the Buddha and further incited King Ajātaśatru to kill his father. His evil reputation spread abroad and his offerings were cut off;
consequently, he and five of his own followers went from house to house to beg for food. For this reason, the rule was established that one must not eat separately from the community.
This was the first formulation of the precept. There were sick bhikṣus who, out of fear and caution, did not dare to eat apart from the community.

The Buddha, knowing this, permitted it; this was the second formulation of the precept. At that time, after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony had concluded, the bhikṣus were making robes during the month of Kārttika.
The upāsakas, mindful of the fatigue and hardship of the assembly, came to invite them for a meal. [The bhikṣus] replied, "Please invite only three people; as for us..."
"One should not eat apart from the community. The Buddha said, "It is permitted when making robes. This was the third establishment of the precept.
At that time, there was a householder who wished to offer food and robes and came to invite them. He replied, "Please invite only three people for the meal; we may not eat apart from the community.
The Buddha said, "When receiving robes as an offering, one may eat apart from the community. This was the fourth establishment of the precept. There was...
"O monks, while traveling along a dangerous road with a group of lay devotees (gṛhapati), the time for alms-seeking arrived.
He said to the lay devotees, 'I wish to go into the village to beg for food; please wait for me briefly, and we shall return together.
The lay devotees replied, 'This road is suspicious and terrifying; we shall provide you with food and drink, so do not come back later. The monk said, 'But...'"
[The Buddha said: "With three people, we may not eat separately from the group. They then entered the village to beg for food, but their companions moved forward and left them behind.
Their clothing was plundered by bandits. The Buddha said: "If traveling on a dangerous road, I permit eating separately from the group.
This was the fifth precept established. [Later,] while traveling with various lay devotees by boat, they went downstream, just as before...
This was opened because they had been robbed by bandits; this is the sixth precept established. At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were traveling and arrived at a small village.
The lay devotees thought to themselves, "The community of monks is large while the village is small;
we should provide food for the Saṃgha so that they do not suffer from exhaustion. They immediately went to the monastery and requested that the monks accept a meal the following day.
The bhikṣus replied, "We request only three people; we may not eat in a separate group. The Buddha said, "When the great assembly has gathered, it is permitted to eat in a separate group.
This was the seventh precept established. At that time, the nephew of King Bimbisāra wished to go forth among the śramaṇas of the non-Buddhist paths.
After providing a meal, he went to inform the king. The king asked him, "In whom do you wish to go forth?"
He replied, "I have gone forth among the Nirgranthas. The King asked again, "Have you ever provided food for us, the śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas?
Thereupon, he prepared a meal and invited the Saṃgha; however, they did not accept it, answering as before.
The Buddha said, "It is permitted for śramaṇas to receive food from a separate group when a meal is being offered. This was the eighth precept established.
This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of prohibition). This training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established because of Devadatta.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning, the text is divided into two sections: the first clarifies the original enactment regarding eating in a group apart from others;

the second clarifies the subsequent allowances regarding "other times" and so forth. The Vinaya states: "Eating in a group apart from others means: if there are four persons or more than four persons" (*Pañcavargīya-vinaya* says: "if within the boundary...").

To invite four or more individuals separately is called "eating in a separate group" (*pṛthaggaṇabhojana*). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Eating in a separate group means eating individually. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "A 'separate group' refers to those who do not eat in the same place.

If four bhikṣus are within the same boundary, even if only one person does not eat together with them, it is all termed 'eating in a separate group. Regarding "food," this refers to rice, parched grain flour, dried cakes, and so forth (the five types of staple food prescribed here; there is no offense regarding other foods).

Regarding "when making robes," this refers to the period after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, during which there is either a month without the *kaṭhina* robe or a month with the *kaṭhina* robe.

The fifth month. ... up to making a single "horse-tooth" stitch upon the robe (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: when making robes, if food is difficult to obtain, one is permitted to eat separately from the community).

If food is easily obtained, it is not permitted [to accept it]. Regarding the time for the distribution of robes (*cīvara*), it refers to the aforementioned periods of one month or five months, as well as other times when food and robes are offered (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"The time for the distribution of robes refers to the measurements of a wiping cloth, a lower garment, a waistband, a shoulder-cloth, and so forth"). Regarding those traveling on a journey, it refers to anyone coming or going within a distance of half a *yojana*.
Regarding those traveling by boat, it refers to those traveling up or down by boat within a distance of half a *yojana*. Large...
Regarding "a gathering of the assembly": if there are four people eating, having one person in excess causes trouble;
if five, ten, or even a hundred people, having one person in excess causes trouble. (This means that when there are many people, food is insufficient. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"As for a gathering of the great assembly, whether for a Dharma matter or for other reasons, when the Saṃgha assembles, the minimum number is four resident bhikṣus and four visiting bhikṣus; this is called a 'great assembly. Even if a great assembly has gathered, if food is not difficult to obtain, [the following] is not permitted. [The rules concerning] alms-giving to śramaṇas.
"Those who eat" refers to those other renunciants outside this community of Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, as well as those who have gone forth from among the non-Buddhist sects.
If a bhikṣu has no reason for taking a meal apart from the community (where "reason" refers to the special occasions, etc.), that bhikṣu should immediately rise and say:
"I have no reason for this meal apart from the community; I wish to request permission to leave."
[They] go out. If there are two or three people, they may eat as they please. If there are four or more than four, they should divide themselves into two groups and enter to eat in turns.
If a bhikṣu has a reason for eating separately from the group and wishes to enter to seek [food], he should do so.
One should announce: "I have a reason for taking separate food and wish to enter. One should enter according to the order of the senior monks (*sthavira*).
Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu takes separate food, it is a *pāyattika* for every swallow;
if there is a reason but one does not announce it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, there is no separate group; second, one receives [the food] from a full assembly;
third, the food reaches the throat.
This also applies to the *bhikṣuṇī*s (a *pāyattika* offense, governed by the same rule for those of common training). It also applies to *śikṣamāṇā*s, *śrāmaṇera*s, and *śrāmaṇerī*s.
For a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This constitutes an offense. Regarding the exemptions:
there is no offense if it is at any other time; or if three or four people eat together with one another;
or if one departs for a valid reason; or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established. These constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the rules for eating separately from the community (*pṛthag-bhaktika*), the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of separate meals: first, invitations; second, begging.
For example, if a lay devotee approaches four bhikṣus and formally invites them to eat, saying, 'May the Venerable Ones accept this,' this is called an invitation.
If they accept at the same time and eat in one place, all four commit an offense (that is, a *pāyattika* offense). This applies if they accept the invitation simultaneously."

Each departs and each receives; each eats and incurs no offense. However, if one is invited separately and departs separately, yet arrives at the householder’s home together and receives food at the same time, one incurs an offense.
This is called "incurring an offense by receiving an invitation. Regarding "incurring an offense by begging":
it is as when four bhikṣus who beg for food see a householder and say to him, "Give food to us four," and then either depart together or [depart separately].
Each departs; if one accepts food all at once, one incurs an offense. This is called "incurring an offense by begging.
If four people have been invited and among them is one who understands the Dharma, and they wish to eat together but fear committing an offense, they should employ a skillful means.
At the time of eating, they overturn their bowls and do not accept the food. The householder asks, "Why do you not accept? They reply, "Simply give food to three people; I wish to..."

Recite the prayer of merit. After the three people have finished eating, one may then receive food; this does not constitute an offense. If invited for rice but given gruel upon arriving at the house, there is no offense.
The *Śāriputra-vinaya* states that there are two benefits for prohibiting eating separately from the group (*pṛthag-bhakta*): first, to protect the donor accordingly.
Out of compassion. Second, because of the power of the bhikṣu who has broken all evil desires:
if three bhikṣus eat separately in one place and a fourth person takes a portion of their food, there is no offense.

If traveling on a road or by boat, if one arrives yesterday and receives food today, or if one travels tomorrow and eats today, it is all a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). [The cause is that while traveling together, they could not keep pace with their companions.]
Regarding the difficulty [of the rule], it is permitted [to eat] on one day and then on another; however, if it is not for a permitted reason, receiving food [on those days] constitutes an offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If three people eat and one does not eat, or if three are fully ordained (*upasampanna*) and one is not yet fully ordained, there is no offense.
If food is sent to them, even down to giving a single spoonful of salt to them in a communal setting, [it is likewise permitted].

In all such cases of eating, there is no offense. Alternatively, if a donor says, "I shall give food to everyone who comes in," or if a donor builds a separate room and says, "I shall give food to everyone who stays in my room," there is likewise no fault.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If four bhikṣus are within the same boundary, and among those four there is one who possesses a permissible condition (*kṣānti-pratyaya*), whether it be a meal for the Saṃgha or a meal for private use, there is no offense in either case."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "When the Saṃgha is about to eat, four kinds of signals should be given:
first, striking the *gandī*; second, blowing the conch; third, beating the drum; and fourth, making a proclamation, so that those within the boundary may hear and know.

These four kinds of signals must be performed according to the established rule; one must not allow them to be confused or disordered, lest the monastic law fail. If the Saṃgha eats without performing these signals..."
Regarding "eating": to eat that which is impure is called stealing the food of the Saṃgha;
it is not termed the offense of eating separately from the assembly (for stealing the food of the Saṃgha, one commits the offense of theft by calculating the monetary value).

If one eats while making a sign [to exclude others], even if there are bhikṣus within the boundary or none at all, whether many or few—if one knows whether there are bhikṣus or not, or whether they will come or not—but provided that [the conditions for exclusion] are not met...
There is no fault in prohibiting [certain individuals]. If there were such a prohibition, even if the *gandī* were struck, the meal would not be pure;

this is called "stealing from the Saṃgha" (where "prohibition" refers to barring incoming visiting bhikṣus). If within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) there are two or three locations, each with its own beginning and end, yet the Saṃgha performs only one *poṣadha*, then at the time of the meal, if the *gandī* is struck for each location individually, there is no prohibition whatsoever.

Pure and without fault: if a donor invites four or more persons to eat within the boundary of the *poṣadha* (confession) area, they should invite one person from the sequence of the Saṃgha to the place where the *poṣadha* is held.
If one portion of food is sent [to them], and not otherwise, there is an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*).
It is the same for two or three locations (this refers to cases where many places have jointly established a legal meal and share the same boundary). If [the groups] each arrive...
At the place of the *poṣadha*, one person from among the Saṃgha should be requested [to oversee]. If one portion of food is sent [as a representative], then it is pure regardless of the location.
If one does not request one person from among the Saṃgha and does not send one portion of food, one falls into an offense (*āpatti*).
If, within the boundary of a village, there is no monastic boundary (*saṃgha-sīma*), yet two donors invite four or more [monks] to eat at two separate locations, [the following applies]:

Strike the *gandī* bell. From the two locations, mutually invite one person each. If a portion is sent [to another location], and there are monks from that other location present, they should enter according to the Dharma; even if it is only one person who does not do so, it constitutes an offense.

When the Sangha is eating, the *karmadāna* (the "one with authority"—meaning one who exercises mastery over the matter) may, using communal property (*saṃghika-vastu*), separately prepare rich and delicious food for four people.
Regarding eating: although four people may be present, there is no offense of eating separately from the group (*pṛthag-bhaktika*) in those two instances; however, the food is not pure.

All cases of eating separately from the group involve food provided by a donor (*dānapati*). If it is *saṃghika* (monastic) food, there is entirely no offense of eating separately from the group, yet it is eating that is not in accordance with the Dharma.
As for *saṃghika* food, if it is not pure, one frequently incurs the offense of stealing from the Saṃgha.

If a donor’s household invites four or more monks for a meal, even if the *gandī* has been struck, if the donor prohibits it and one knows that a single monk cannot eat there, all [who eat] incur an offense of transgression (*pācittiya*). (The "prohibitor" refers to the donor;
although he prohibits it, future monks should not eat separately from the group. If one knows that a single monk cannot eat there, one incurs an offense.)
The *Śīla-hetu-pratyaya-sūtra* states: The mother Viśākhā separately invited the Buddha and five hundred arhats for a meal.
