The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda: "Is there any bhikṣu who has made an announcement within the Saṃgha to distribute [the food]?
He replied, "No. The Buddha said, "I pity this Viśākhā for failing to obtain even a single merit. Why is this so?"
If one eats alone or eats with a single bhikṣu, one gains great merit and attains great fruit.
If, within the assembly of bhikṣus, one does not announce a private gathering, one commits a pāyattika offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
An appended examination [of the sources] states that the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* mentions five causes for requesting food early and eating it in one’s own room:
first, being a newly arrived guest; second, being about to depart on a journey; third, being afflicted by the suffering of illness; fourth, being a caregiver for the sick; and fifth...
Regarding those who hold administrative duties:
the *Mātṛkā* states that if one is an inspector, it is no fault to first take a portion for oneself from the meal offering and eat it.

(Regarding this "separating from the assembly," there are two meanings. First, to act separately for the sake of the assembly, as clarified in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts. Second, to be separate from the assembly, as explained in the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*. Thus, when begging for food, one may not go with four companions; when accepting an invitation, one must be sent according to the prescribed order of the Saṅgha.

For the regular meals within the monastery, the *gaṇḍī* gong must be struck. Invitations to private quarters are not permitted unless there is a specific reason. The sacred regulations are clear; how could they be neglected or transgressed? Alas!

At present, in monastic residences, private kitchens are commonly established where fine delicacies are served at will, leading junior students to imitate such practices and turn their backs on the rules. I pray that those of wisdom will reflect: this illusory body is not solid, and exquisite food cannot be preserved forever. As a constant model for teachers, the responsibility lies in upholding strict regulations. How can these be allowed to fall into ruin?)
The thirty-fourth precept concerning receiving more than three bowls when invited:
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson who invites him with cakes, parched flour, and rice, and if the bhikṣu desires them, [he may accept].
One should accept two or three bowls. Upon returning to the monastery, one should divide them to give food to the other bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts more than two or three bowls and, upon returning to the monastery, does not divide them to give food to the other bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Origin Story: There are two enactments regarding this precept. The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī.
There was a woman from a great village who had married into the kingdom of Ujjayinī; she returned to her parents' home and offered food to the bhikṣus. Later, at another time...
Her husband sent a messenger to summon her back. She immediately prepared food and adorned herself, and they set out together.
There were some bhikṣus who had come to the father’s house at the time of their alms-round. When the daughter saw them, she gave all the food she had prepared to them;
only after she had finished preparing more did she return. Before she could arrive, her husband had already taken another wife. Furthermore, outside the city of Vārāṇasī, a multitude...
A large caravan of merchants was staying overnight together with their companions. A certain monk who lived on alms received food from a merchant who was devoted to the faith and departed.
As he traveled along, he passed the word on to the other monks until all had finished begging for food. At that time, the leader of the merchants was just entering the city to purchase more grain.
The other companions, having set out earlier, were left behind and could not catch up on the road; they were subsequently [attacked] by bandits.
The monks heard of this and informed the Buddha. This was the first formulation of the precept. Thereupon, the sick monks were apprehensive and did not dare to accept food beyond the limit.
The Buddha said, "I permit those who are ill to accept food beyond the limit. This was the second formulation of the precept.
This is an offense of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). It was established as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) because of the affliction of greed arising from excessive food.
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. From "When arriving at the house of a layperson" (*śveta-vastra-gṛha*) onwards, it clarifies the method for receiving food.

From "If one is not ill" onwards, it establishes the offense incurred. The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu is invited to the house of a layperson and is offered cakes or parched grain flour (*piṣṭaka* or *cūrṇa*), he should inquire of the host.
If the host says, 'This is food for a woman returning from her husband’s home,' or 'It is the food of a merchant on the road'... [The text continues with the specific conditions for the offense.]
Regarding provisions for the journey: one should eat and then go out and return to the monastery to inform the bhikṣus:
"In such-and-such a house there is food for a woman returning home, and there are provisions for merchants on the road. If you wish to eat, you should eat and then go out."

If one wishes to take food back, it shall not exceed two or three bowls—this being the limit for what I do not bring back now (the measure of a bowl has upper, middle, and lower grades, as described above).
If one takes back a single bowl of food, it must be shared equally upon returning (meaning that those dwelling within the same boundary share the benefit and divide it evenly).
One should say to the other bhikṣus: "If there are those who have gone to that house, they may eat there immediately. If [one] brings [it back],...
Regarding those returning from their almsrounds: they should take two bowls back. I have already returned with one bowl;

had I returned with two, we would have shared the food between us. He further addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "If there are any who go to that house to beg for alms, they may eat right there at that house.
Those who wish to bring food back should take only one bowl back; I have now already returned with two bowls."
"If you have brought back all three bowls, divide them and eat together. Address the other bhikṣus, saying:
'If you wish to go to that house to beg for alms, you may eat there immediately; if you wish to bring it back, be careful not to bring it back.
I have already brought back three bowls.'"
**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu who is not ill receives more than two or three bowls of food from a household and then departs through its gate, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is inside the gate and one foot is outside the gate, and he makes a movement to leave but then stops, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*.
If he does not inquire [about the meal] upon returning, it is also a *dukkaṭa*.
If a wife eats the provisions for a merchant’s journey, she commits a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If she takes them to a monastery and eats them alone without distributing them to the other bhikṣus, or if she does not inform the other bhikṣus [of her intention to eat them], [she likewise commits an offense].

All such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, that the food belongs to a woman returning home or to the provisions for merchants on a journey;
second, that one is not ill oneself; third, that one receives more than three bowls; and fourth, that one carries it out through the gate.
If a monk simultaneously disciplines both a bhikṣuṇī and a śikṣamāṇā, it is a pāyattika for both (the rule is the same for those of common training).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one does not contravene the aforementioned regulations; if the person brings it themselves to the monastery and one may accept it;
or if they bring it to the nunnery and one may accept it; as well as cases such as when the precept has not yet been established—these constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the collection [of alms], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one collects using the large bowl, one should take only one bowl; one should not take two.
If one collects using the medium bowl, at most one may take two bowls; one should not take three.
If one collects using the small bowl, at most one may take three; one should not take four. To collect beyond these limits constitutes an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "In brief, if a bhikṣu takes another's food when it exceeds the quantity of four and a half *śērs* of cooked rice, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
However, if the donor permits him to take as much as he wishes, there is no fault."
There is no offense.
The *Vinayaviniscaya* states: "If one takes more than three bowls from non-humans or from those belonging to other religious sects, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) in all such cases.
If one eats more than three [mouthfuls] at the same sitting, except for cakes and parched grain flour, it applies only to other items, or when the donor..."
If one takes it with joy and according to one's own will, there is no offense in either case. There are three ways in which one falsely squanders the offerings of the faithful:
first, when a donor gives with faith to one who upholds the precepts, but the recipient, having accepted it, gives it to one who violates the precepts;

second, when a donor gives with faith to one who possesses right view, but the recipient, having accepted it, gives it to one who holds wrong views; third, when one accepts more than is necessary and does not eat it oneself, and so forth.

To receive a single handful of food for a long time—excluding the case of a donor who has previously granted permission to eat at will—these three matters are all termed "wasting the faithful's offerings" and shall bring about evil retribution. (A "handful" refers to what is held by both hands; it is also a measure of grasping.)
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
The thirty-fifth: the precept against eating without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food).
If a bhikṣu has finished his meal and subsequently accepts an invitation, yet eats without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta*, it is a *pāyattika*.
[The Section on] the Origin of the Story. The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. He praised the practice of eating a single meal a day.

Thereupon, the bhikṣus partook of whatever they had—roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, boiled rice, parched grain, or dried cakes—and whether they drank gruel or took medicine, they all followed this rule.

Consequently, their bodies became emaciated and their complexions grew haggard. The Buddha then permitted them to eat until full in a single sitting—whether it be rice, parched grain flour, cakes, or other foods.
(The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: "Regarding eating in a single sitting: even if a venerable elder arrives, one should not rise. Once the food has been received, one should not leave the seat.

This applies even down to the serving of salt or the receiving of leaves for eating; in all such cases, one must not rise. For sick bhikṣus who are unable to eat in a single sitting, he permitted them to eat repeatedly.

Regarding eating: there is no rule for a sick person to stop eating (the *pātrāvadāna*). At that time, if various sick monks received excellent food and could not finish it all, yet their attendants had already stopped eating (*pātrāvadāna*), they did not dare to eat it themselves and thus threw it away. Flocks of birds then clamored and squabbled over it.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] permitted attendants who had already stopped eating to consume the leftovers. At that time, the monks received food early in the morning.

Having set it down, he entered the village for alms. After eating, he returned and picked up the food he had set down to give to the bhikṣus. Since those bhikṣus had already finished their meal, they did not dare to eat it.
The Buddha permitted them to take the food they had received and eat it after performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual of leftover food).
There was an elder with many acquaintances who entered the village for alms and obtained a great quantity of food, which he gathered together in one place and ate. He took...
He returned with the assembly of bhikṣus; having already finished their meal, they also did not dare to eat.

The Buddha permitted them to take food from that place back and eat it by performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite (the rite of leftover food). One should speak these words for the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite as follows: "Venerable Sir..."
"I have eaten my fill; I already know this and have observed this. This constitutes the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhaktavidhi* (the ritual for leftover food).
He [the donor] should take a small portion of food and say to that bhikṣu: "I have ceased; you may take and eat it. This is called the *śeṣa-bhaktavidhi*.
At that time, there was a gluttonous bhikṣu in Śrāvastī who did not know what constituted having eaten his fill or not having eaten his fill, nor did he know the ritual for leftovers.

Eating. If one obtains food that has not been left over, one may eat it. The bhikṣus, feeling resentment and reproach, informed the Buddha, who then established this precept. This is a prohibitive offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya);
it was formulated because of gluttony and lack of contentment, and thus this training rule (śikṣāpada) was enacted.

Exegesis: The Vinaya states that "food" refers to the five types of formal food (*pañca-bhojanāni*). Among these five foods, if one eats any one of them until fully satiated, there are five ways of constituting a completed meal (*pūrṇa-bhakta*).

The first is knowing the rice (referring to the five formal foods; others are not termed "completed meals"). The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If porridge has just begun to thicken when standing upright..."

If the spoon does not overturn the flour, or if one draws a line with a finger when mixing it with water and a trace remains visible, these all constitute a completed meal (if otherwise, they do not). Second, knowing it has been brought [to one] (meaning that someone hands it over and one receives and accepts it from them).

Third, knowing the prohibition (meaning that once one has finished eating, one expresses with mind and speech that no more is needed). Fourth, knowing the deportment (meaning that one may receive food while in any of the four modes of deportment).
Fifth, knowing the relinquishing of deportment (meaning that one who is sitting may walk, stand, or lie down; and likewise, one who is lying down may sit, walk, or stand).

**The Definition of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, having finished his meal and abandoned the formal posture, eats without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food), there is a *pāyattika* for every swallow.
This applies even if he eats *khajjaka* (hard foods such as branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, oil, sesame, or black rock-honey) after grinding them into a fine powder;
if he has finished his meal and does not perform the *khalupaścādbhakti*, he incurs [the offense].
And he eats it; for every swallow, there is a *pāyattika*.

If, having already finished eating, he performs the *khalupaṭiggahaṇa* (the ritual of "leftover food") for another; or if he knows that another has already finished eating and performs the *khalupaṭiggahaṇa* for them;
or if he takes food with his own hand and performs the *khalupaṭiggahaṇa*; or if he holds food and places it [in the bowl].
Regarding the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of leftover food): if one has a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) hold the food while performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* ritual;
or if one covers good food with inferior food while performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* ritual;

or if one receives the *khalupaścādbhakti* ritual from another and carries it all away—such cases do not constitute a valid *khalupaścādbhakti* ritual. In all such instances, it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If one has finished eating and perceives that one has finished eating, it is a *pāyattika*. If one has finished eating but suspects that one has finished eating, or if one has not finished eating but perceives that one has finished eating, or if one has not finished eating but suspects that one has finished eating—in all these cases, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires five conditions to constitute the full offense: first, having received food until satiated; second, the perception that one has had enough;
third, having abandoned the formal posture; fourth, not performing any further ritual procedure; and fifth, eating again so that the food enters the throat.
Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta (the same rule applies, though studied separately; according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a bhikṣuṇī commits the same offense).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: perceiving food as non-food; not having received [the food] while performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) ritual;
performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual for what is not food; taking [food] oneself while performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual; performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual without placing it on the ground;
giving it to another from the point where one's hand reaches, or receiving it from another who has performed the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual; or in cases of illness or for one who is ill.

Regarding leftover food (*ucchista-bhojana*): if one has not performed the ritual for "remaining food" (*kṛta-śeṣa-kalpa*), or if it was before the precept was first established, these constitute non-offenses.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "For the sake of two benefits, the ritual for receiving leftover food (i.e., the ritual for remaining food) is permitted."

First, due to the circumstances of a bhikṣu tending to the sick; second, because a bhikṣu has insufficient food due to certain circumstances. The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "There are five kinds of *pūṣanī*, which may be eaten as solid food (the term 'eaten' here carries the sense of taking and chewing). First, rice. Second, [gruel]. Third, [curry]. Fourth, [vegetables]. Fifth, [fruit]. These are what may be chewed and swallowed. Furthermore, there are five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods), which may be chewed and swallowed: first, roots; second, stalks; third, leaves; fourth, flowers; fifth, fruits. These are what may be chewed and swallowed. There are also five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), which may be consumed by licking: first, milk; second, curd; third, fresh butter; fourth, clarified butter; fifth, oil. These are what may be licked and consumed. There are also five kinds of *lehya* (lickable foods), which may be licked and consumed: first, honey; second, molasses; third, raw sugar; fourth, rock sugar; fifth, granulated sugar. These are what may be licked and consumed. There are also five kinds of *peya* (drinks), which may be drunk: first, water; second, juice; third, tea; fourth, medicinal decoctions; fifth, fermented grain drinks. These are what may be drunk. There are also five kinds of *coṣya* (suckable foods), which may be sucked and consumed: first, sugarcane; second, bamboo shoots; third, lotus roots; fourth, dates; fifth, jujubes. These are what may be sucked and consumed. There are also five kinds of *bhakṣya* (eatable foods), which may be eaten: first, parched grain; second, parched rice; third, parched barley; fourth, parched wheat; fifth, parched millet. These are what may be eaten. There are also five kinds of *abhyavahārya* (things to be swallowed), which may be swallowed: first, meat; second, fish; third, dried meat; fourth, dried fish; fifth, dried meat and fish. These are what may be swallowed. There are also five kinds of *paribhoga* (enjoyments), which may be enjoyed: first, bedding; second, seats; third, clothing; fourth, medicine; fifth, miscellaneous items. These are what may be enjoyed. There are also five kinds of *upabhoga* (uses), which may be used: first, vehicles; second, ornaments; third, musical instruments; fourth, lamps; fifth, incense. These are what may be used. There are also five kinds of *pariṣkāra* (requisites), which may be possessed: first, robes; second, bowls; third, needles and thread; fourth, waistbands; fifth, water-strainers. These are what may be possessed. There are also five kinds of *upakaraṇa* (accessories), which may be kept: first, staffs; second, sandals; third, umbrellas; fourth, fans; fifth, whisks. These are what may be kept. There are also five kinds of *paricaryā* (services), which may be performed: first, washing feet; second, massaging the body; third, fanning; fourth, shaving; fifth, bathing. These are what may be performed. There are also five kinds of *vaiyāvṛtya* (attendant services), which may be rendered: first, sweeping the ground; second, spreading grass mats; third, arranging bedding; fourth, preparing water for washing; fifth, lighting lamps. These are what may be rendered. There are also five kinds of *karmānta* (tasks), which may be undertaken: first, building a monastery; second, constructing a stupa; third, making robes; fourth, making bowls; fifth, making furniture. These are what may be undertaken. There are also five kinds of *śikṣāpada* (precepts), which must be observed: first, the precept against killing; second, the precept against stealing; third, the precept against sexual misconduct; fourth, the precept against false speech; fifth, the precept against intoxicants. These are what must be observed. There are also five kinds of *dhuta-guṇa* (ascetic virtues), which may be practiced: first, wearing rag-robes; second, wearing robes made of discarded materials; third, wearing robes made of felt; fourth, eating only one meal a day; fifth, eating from a single vessel. These are what may be practiced. There are also five kinds of *saṃlekha-dharma* (methods of austerity), which may be applied: first, reducing food intake; second, reducing sleep; third, reducing conversation; fourth, reducing social contact; fifth, reducing possessions. These are what may be applied. There are also five kinds of *pratisaṃlayanadharma* (methods of seclusion), which may be maintained: first, staying in a forest; second, staying at the foot of a tree; third, staying in an open space; fourth, staying in a charnel ground; fifth, staying in a dwelling with few people. These are what may be maintained. There are also five kinds of *viharadharma* (modes of dwelling), which may be adopted: first, dwelling in a mountain cave; second, dwelling in a valley; third, dwelling on a riverbank; fourth, dwelling on a sandbar; fifth, dwelling in a thatched hut. These are what may be adopted. There are also five kinds of *caryādharma* (modes of conduct), which may be followed: first, walking meditation; second, sitting meditation; third, standing meditation; fourth, lying down meditation; fifth, mindful movement. These are what may be followed. There are also five kinds of *samādhi* (concentration), which may be cultivated: first, the concentration of emptiness; second, the concentration of signlessness; third, the concentration of wishlessness; fourth, the concentration of the four foundations of mindfulness; fifth, the concentration of the four right efforts. These are what may be cultivated. There are also five kinds of *prajñā* (wisdom), which may be developed: first, wisdom arising from hearing; second, wisdom arising from reflection; third, wisdom arising from cultivation; fourth, conventional wisdom; fifth, ultimate wisdom. These are what may be developed. There are also five kinds of *vimukti* (liberation), which may be realized: first, liberation through the destruction of the outflows; second, liberation through the exhaustion of the outflows; third, liberation through the cessation of the outflows; fourth, liberation through the non-arising of the outflows; fifth, liberation through the non-attachment to the outflows. These are what may be realized. There are also five kinds of *nirvāṇa* (nirvana), which may be attained: first, nirvana with remainder; second, nirvana without remainder; third, nirvana with both remainder and no remainder; fourth, nirvana with neither remainder nor no remainder; fifth, nirvana beyond all conceptualization. These are what may be attained. Third, due to the circumstances of a bhikṣu who is ill; fourth, due to the circumstances of a bhikṣu who is traveling; fifth, due to the circumstances of a bhikṣu who is performing a ritual service. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, eats solid food after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, eats soft food after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, eats hard food after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, eats lickable food after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, eats drinkable food after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, eats suckable food after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, eats eatable food after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, eats swallowable food after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, enjoys enjoyments after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, uses uses after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, possesses requisites after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, keeps accessories after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu, due to these five kinds of circumstances, performs services after noon, he commits no offense. If a bhikṣu

1. Barley and bean rice; 2. Three types of parched flour (*piṣṭaka*); 3. Meat; 4. Cakes; and 5. Five kinds of *khādaniya* (food to be chewed)—this term "chewed" (*khād*) carries the sense of masticating.

These refer to roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits. If one first eats the five types of chewed food, along with milk, curd, vegetables, and so forth, and subsequently eats the five types of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), there is no offense.
However, if one first eats the five types of soft foods and then eats the five types of chewed food, [it constitutes an offense].
Eating [meat], as well as milk, curd, vegetables, and so forth, is termed an offense. One should know that there are five expressions for when one has not yet finished eating:
namely, when food is being offered, if one does not require it immediately, one should respond by saying: "Wait a moment," "Go ahead," "Hold on," "Wait a while," or "Wait until I have eaten."
Furthermore, if one says, "Wait until I have finished," it is called "not yet sufficient. If the word "and" (or "also") is absent, it constitutes a prohibition against being satisfied.

If one has not actually finished but intends to act as if finished, even if one speaks of being finished, it does not constitute being finished; one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), because the speech does not accord with the Dharma.
If one obtains leftover food and consumes it after performing the ritual procedure (*kappiya-kāraṇa*), one dwells in personal comfort and [the donor] gives [merit].
The host shall obtain merit. When one wishes to perform the ritual, one should wash the hands and receive food.

Holding it, one approaches a *bhikṣu* who has not yet finished eating, or one who, though already finished, has not yet left his original seat (meaning he has not relinquished his dignified posture). Facing him, one performs the ritual.
If that person has not yet signaled that they have had enough, one should take two or three morsels and, having eaten them, announce to him: "This is your portion; enjoy it as you please."

One may eat. This refers to a case where the person has not yet signaled that they have had enough; in such a case, one may eat without offense. However, if one has already signaled that they have had enough, it is not permissible to eat.
One should press down with the hand and inform them as previously described. There are five cases in which the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of declaring "enough") is invalid:
first, when one is inside the boundary (*sīmā*) while addressing someone outside the boundary; second, when the two parties are out of reach of one another; third, when standing at the side.
Fourth, [the donor] is behind [the recipient]. Fifth, the person ahead leaves their seat. Reversing these [conditions] constitutes an offense.
If one person performs the ritual while others partake of the food, there is no violation for anyone.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It is permitted for one person to perform the 'leftover food' (*kṛtapiṇḍa*) rite, and all others may then eat it.
If a bhikṣu brings food and wishes to perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite, he should do so over the bowl; specifically, the food within the bowl is what is designated as "leftover food.
The food remaining in the alms-bowl (*pātra*) is not so designated. If the liquid from the food in the bowl flows into [the vessel], [it is likewise considered leftover].
Within a bowl, both [types of food] may be designated as "leftover food" (vighasa).

If one seeks to designate two bowls together as leftover food, yet the person before one stops eating from only one bowl, then that single bowl alone is designated as leftover food. This applies whether it be cakes or vegetables.
If two bowls are covered together horizontally, both may be designated as "leftover food" (*vighasa*). The same applies to various other types of vessels.

If a bhikṣu has already finished his meal, and a great donor arrives bringing various kinds of food and drink, he should ask whether there is a *vaiyāvṛtyakara*—such as the monthly director (*māsika-vinaya*) or an administrator—who has not yet finished eating; only then may those [remaining items] be made into leftover food. If...
If he has already finished his meal, he should perform it for an elder who has not yet finished.
If the elder is modest and cannot do so in the midst of the assembly, they should move the elder to a secluded place and perform it there together.
If the elder has already finished his meal and a visiting bhikṣu arrives, he should ask him; if that visitor has not yet finished his meal, he should then perform it for him. If...
Once the guests have finished eating, the Sangha should employ skillful means so as not to violate the donor’s wholesome intention.

If there is a senior *śrāmaṇera* among the assembly (a "senior" being one whose age has reached twenty), he should be taken to the boundary of the precepts (*sīmā*) and ordained with full precepts (*upasampadā*).

After teaching him the ritual for leftover food (*vighasa-dharmatā*), he may then eat. (The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* is identical to this; its ritual procedures are detailed in accordance with the Vinaya within the section on "Practices and Retentions").
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
To cite scriptural evidence, the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "If a bhikṣu receives offerings from others in an improper manner, he falls because of those offerings.
There are two kinds of such falling: first, consuming the offerings of others while failing to cultivate the Path according to the Dharma, allowing the mind to run wild and become unrestrained."

[The first case is] negligent; there is no good record to be made. Second, giving to those who transfer their gifts: such giving is not in accordance with the Dharma, and because of these two circumstances, one shall fall into the three miserable realms.

Regarding those to whom one should give: if one's parents are poor and suffering, one should first cause them to receive the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Wholesome Actions, and only then bestow gifts upon them.
If they are not poor, even if they have received the Refuges and Precepts, it is not appropriate to give to them [in that manner].

Furthermore, there are other objects of giving: those who repair stūpas, those who serve the Saṃgha, and those who maintain monastic dwellings. One should calculate their labor and provide them with the corresponding wages;

if one gives more than that as an act of generosity, one will fall into the realm of those afflicted by disease. If one gives food to the sick as an act of generosity, one should do so with a mind of loving-kindness, providing what is appropriate;
if one gives food by mistake as an act of generosity, one will fall into the prison of infants.
If one encounters a woman who is pregnant, one should bestow [alms] upon her with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), without expecting any recompense for what is given or received.
If someone comes to a monastic dwelling to beg, if they already possess provisions, there is no need to give; however, if they have no food, giving to them is without fault.
If a bhikṣu does not practice meditation, does not recite the scriptures, and does not attend to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha, yet receives from others...
Giving is giving. If one gives while knowing that the recipient lacks these three types of action, both the giver and the receiver fall into transgression.
It would be better to swallow iron balls and die than to eat the faithful offerings of others without observing the precepts.
Furthermore, if one has already eaten to satiety and eats more by force, it will not increase one's physical appearance or strength, but will only increase one's afflictions.
Therefore, one should not eat without moderation.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, how could one give rise to the three kinds of evil karma—of body, speech, and mind—on account of food?
If, out of greed for food, one gives rise to the three types of evil karma, the wealth obtained [thereby]..."
"Regarding material things, everyone says together that when one later undergoes the fruits of suffering, there is no one to share them.
Furthermore, observing all sentient beings who undergo physical and mental suffering for the sake of food and drink, how could I give rise to greedy attachment toward this food?
Moreover, it is because of food and drink that the body grows; yet I have now left the household life to receive the precepts."
The practitioner of the path, desiring to cast off the body, now craves this food; how then can he ever succeed in abandoning this body?
Having contemplated thus, although he partakes of food, it is as if he were eating the flesh of his own child in the wilderness—his mind feels revulsion and finds no pleasure in it at all.
He deeply contemplates the fault of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in this way, and next contemplates contact-food (*sparśāhāra*), as if being flayed.
The ox is being devoured by immeasurable worms. Next, one contemplates the food of thought (*manahāhāra*) as being like a great mass of fire.

The food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is like three hundred spears. If a bhikṣu goes begging for alms, he should beforehand form this thought: "May I obtain what is good; may I certainly obtain much; may I obtain it quickly. This is not called [proper] eating. One should cultivate the perception of revulsion toward such food. [Note:

The character 啑 appears to be a scribal error for 噉 (to devour/eat). The term 矛*贊 likely represents a specific type of weapon or a transcription error for 鏃 (arrowhead/spearhead); it is rendered here as "spears" based on the context.]
Wholesome dharmas will decline day and night, while unwholesome dharmas will surely increase. If you wish to beg for food, you should first make this aspiration:
"May all who beg be fully satisfied; may those who give this food obtain immeasurable merit."
"If I obtain food, I shall use it to heal this poisoned body, cultivate wholesome dharmas, and benefit sentient beings.
When one makes such a vow, the wholesome dharmas cultivated increase day and night, while unwholesome dharmas gradually diminish and are extinguished.
The thirty-sixth: Causing another to commit the offense regarding the rule on leftover food (*atireka-bhojana*).

If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has already finished his meal, yet, having been invited, he does not perform the *atireka-bhojana* rite and persistently invites him to eat, saying, "Venerable one, take this food," and does so for no other reason than the desire to cause the other to commit the offense, it is a *pāyattika*.

[The Exhortation]. The Origin Story: This precept has two enactments. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there was a gluttonous bhikṣu who was rebuked by a bhikṣu acting in accordance with the Dharma, who said: "It is unprecedented! You are now a glutton."
Regarding those who are gluttonous: they do not know contentment with what has been eaten, nor do they leave over what has not been sufficiently eaten; they eat without leaving any remainder.

Having heard these words, they harbor resentment in their hearts. Later, at another time, seeing that bhikṣu who had finished eating without performing the *khalupaścādbhaktika* (the rite of leaving food), they earnestly invite him to eat, wishing to cause him to violate the precepts. He then accepts and eats it, and the greedy bhikṣu acts in the same manner.
The Buddha rebuked him for his transgression. A monk of few desires then addressed the Buddha; this was the first formulation of a precept.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether they had already eaten or not yet eaten, nor did they know whether they were sufficiently fed or not sufficiently fed.

Later, when they realized they had already eaten and were sufficiently fed, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained apprehensive and cautious. The Buddha said, "It is because you did not know."

There is no offense; therefore, "knowingly" is added. This is the second formulation of the precept. Because one would provoke another to commit an offense by cross-examining them regarding their fault, this training rule was established due to the affliction of malice.

Exegesis: The Vinaya states that there are five kinds of food, as mentioned above. "To offer food with earnest persistence" means to repeatedly and frequently invite [the recipient] and urge them insistently to chew and eat.

"Desiring to cause another to commit an offense" means desiring to cause that bhikṣu to incur an offense on this account and to give rise to remorse and distress; this is not the occasion for hearing or listening to [the teaching].

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if that bhikṣu accepts the food and eats it, for every swallow, both [the giver and the eater] incur a *pāyattika* offense.
If he gives it to him to eat, but he does not eat it and discards it; or if he accepts it but does not eat it and sets it aside;
or if, having accepted it, he transfers it to another person—the one who gave it [in these cases] incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If he does not do so...
Regarding the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of leftover food): if one gives it to another as leftover food so that they may eat it, the giver commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one gives food to a sick person with the intent to cause another to commit an offense, or if one gives the remains of a sick person's food to another with the intent to cause them to commit an offense, [the same applies].
If, after having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food), one gives it to another with the intent that they commit an offense, the giver incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

If the recipient has already finished eating and perceives that they have finished eating, it is a *pāyattika*; if there is doubt as to whether they have finished eating, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If the recipient has not yet finished eating but perceives that they have finished eating, or if there is doubt as to whether they have finished eating, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the other person has already finished eating and abandoned their formal posture;
second, one perceives them as having finished eating and intends to cause them to commit an offense; third, one offers food with earnest entreaty that has not yet undergone the ritual preparation;
and fourth, the other person accepts it and consumes it without performing the *kṛtya-śeṣa* (remaining-food) rite, such that it enters their throat.
If a bhikṣu commits this simultaneously, it is a *duṣkṛta* (an offense of wrong-doing); [if he does so] separately, it is a *śaikṣa-dharma*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if one did not previously know it was *pūrva-bhakta* (already-eaten) or *apūrva-bhakta* (not yet eaten);
if one gave it [to another] and had them discard it, set it aside, or give it to someone else, and that person then took and ate it;

if one gave food that had not yet undergone the *atirikta-āhāra* (leftover-food) ritual and had them perform it before eating; or if one gave the leftovers of a sick person and did not cause another to eat it.

It is not an offense in the following cases: when one performs the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of "making food leftover") oneself and does not cause another to commit an offense; and when it concerns the very first instance before the precept had been established.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu who has finished eating and has not yet performed the *avaśeṣa-karma* (the act of declaring the meal finished)," [he may take more].
Regarding food: if one accepts an invitation to eat the fifteen kinds of food at will, whatever food is eaten constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
All barley, millet, rice, hemp, and panicled millet—so long as they have not been made into parched grain, cooked rice, or cakes—are termed "similar foods" (*pratibhakṣa*).

Once they have been transformed into parched grain, cooked rice, or cakes, they are all termed "proper foods" (*bhakta*). (The five improper foods together with these five similar ones constitute the fifteen kinds.)
This precept is shared by those training in the Mahāyāna.
The thirty-seventh: the precept against eating at improper times.
If a bhikṣu eats food after the proper time, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Nidāna: The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, the people of the city were celebrating a festival with various musical performances.
Nanda and Upananda went to watch; the crowd gave them food, and having finished eating, they continued watching until dusk before returning.
Furthermore, at sunset, Kālodāyin entered the city to beg for alms, and the sky was overcast and dark.
He arrived at the house of a woman who was pregnant. As the woman came out carrying food, she encountered a thunderstorm.

Seeing his face for a brief moment, she thought it was a ghost; terrified, she fell to the ground (because of the Venerable’s dark and radiant countenance). He replied, "I am not a ghost; I am the wife of Kālodayin.
She immediately spoke in anger, saying, "O Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, you would rather burst your own belly than come here at night!"
While they were going on almsround, the bhikṣus felt resentment and reproached Nanda, Upananda, and Kāla, reporting the matter in full to the Buddha.

For the sake of the Saṃgha, he established this precept; it is an offense of prohibition (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya), instituted because their excessive greed invited public censure. Thus was this training rule (śikṣāpada) enacted.
Exegesis: The Vinaya states that "the proper time" (*kāla*) refers to the period from when the first light of dawn appears until midday.
According to this rule, the same applies to food throughout the four continents. "Improper time" (*vikāla*) refers to the period from midday until the first light of dawn has not yet appeared.

Regarding "food," there are two types: *khādaniya* (solid food) and *bhojaniya* (soft food), as described above. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the shadow at midday has passed by even the width of a hair or the blink of an eye, it is immediately improper time.")
**The Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one eats food at an improper time, for every swallow there is a *pāyattika*.
If non-time medicine is taken after the improper time has passed, it is a *pāyattika*. If seven-day medicine is taken after the seven days have passed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If life-long medicine is consumed without a valid reason, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If it is neither [proper] time nor...

If one perceives it as the improper time, it is a *pāyattika*. If it is not the improper time but one suspects it is, or if it is not the improper time but one perceives it as such, or if it is the proper time but one perceives it as the improper time or suspects it is, in all these cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, eating at an improper time; second, the perception that it is an improper time; and third, [the act of eating].
If the food enters the throat, it constitutes an offense: for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika (the same rule applies to her fellow students);
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This is defined as an offense.

Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: eating black rock honey; or, in the case of illness, taking emetic or purgative medicines and being permitted to boil barley so that the husks remain unbroken, straining the juice, and drinking it; or if the substance is spat out from the throat and then swallowed again;
or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—these constitute non-offenses.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna.
To cite scriptural evidence, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The World-Honored One is by nature free from eating at improper times;
therefore, from the time the Tathāgata was born into the royal palace until his parinirvāṇa, he never once consumed food at an improper time. This is said to be the nature of all Buddhas."
One should always abide in the Middle Way and not cling to the two extremes; therefore, one abstains from eating at improper times to manifest the Middle Way.

Thus, the regulation of eating only at midday is established. That one may eat before midday symbolizes the preliminary practices (*pūrvayoga*), which have the meaning of attaining realization, and also causes the body and mind to obtain immediate benefit.
By not eating after midday, one experiences less drowsiness and sleep, and is free from the ailment of undigested food, so that the body becomes light.
It is peaceful and the mind easily attains concentration; because there is such a principle, one is thus enjoined to eat at midday.
The *Vinaya-samādhi Sūtra* states: "The devas eat early in the morning; the Buddhas of the three periods of time eat at midday;
animals eat when the sun sets; and ghosts and spirits eat at dusk. Therefore, the Buddha established the precept to sever the causes of the six realms of existence, so that they may be made equal."

Regarding the food of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, the *Chushi jing* (Sutra on Dwelling in the World) states that the Buddha said there are five blessings in not eating after midday: first, little sexual desire; second, little sleep;
third, attaining single-mindedness; fourth, no downward-moving wind (flatulence); and fifth, the body attains peace and happiness, and illnesses do not arise.
The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"There are certain donors who construct monasteries and provide abundant provisions for the sake of the monks of future generations. Yet, some who resemble renunciants approach the stewards at improper times to request food.
What kind of offense do the one who gives and the one who eats incur? And what kind of [consequence] does the original donor incur?"
“Merit. The Buddha said, “One who eats at an improper time is a person who has broken the precepts; such a person is a thief.
One who gives at an improper time is likewise a person who has broken the precepts and is also a thief. They have stolen the property of the donor and act contrary to the donor’s intent.
Because the object has been lost, the donor gains no merit; there is only the merit of the initial resolve to establish [the offering]. Śāriputra said, “[May we] receive [it] at the proper time.”

"Eating at the proper time. If one has not finished eating during the proper time and eats again at an improper time, or if one accepts food during the proper time and then eats it at an improper time, would one still obtain merit?
The Buddha said: "One who is pure regarding eating at the proper time is a field of merit;
such a person is a renunciant, is the Saṃgha, is a true friend to devas and humans, and is a guide for devas and humans. As for one who is impure..."
They are hungry ghosts who violate the precepts and commit theft; they are the dwelling place of sin.

Those who demand food at improper times, whether it be the proper time or not, and who give it away at inappropriate moments, are called "those who oversee the food. They are known as the evil Māras who retreat from the Path, and they are termed the three evil realms.
Because they are like broken vessels and lepers who destroy the fruits of goodness, the Brahmins do not eat at improper times, nor do the non-Buddhist practitioners of Brahmacharya.
"Even a commoner does not eat with such depravity; how much less should my disciples, who know the Dharma and practice the Dharma, act in this way? Anyone who acts thus is not my disciple.

Such a person who violates the Dharma—whether by stealing salt or vinegar, even in a single lump or a single pinch—and who steals or accepts what is stolen, shall die and fall into the Hell of the Scorched Intestines (*Jiao-chang*).
There they shall swallow glowing iron balls. Upon emerging from that hell, they shall be reborn as a pig."
Among dogs, they eat various impurities; then they are reborn as evil birds, whose cries people find strange;
later they are reborn as hungry ghosts within monasteries, dwelling inside latrines and devouring excrement and filth for hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
Even when they are subsequently reborn among humans, they are poor, lowly, and base; whatever they say, people do not trust or believe. This is worse than stealing the property of a single person.
The offense is still relatively light. This is because it deprives many people of their field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and cuts off the path to transcendence (*lokottaramārga*).
Examination: The *Vinayamātṛkā* (序) states: When a bhikṣu was ill and took a purgative, he became faint and distressed after midday.

The Buddha ordered that he be given boiled rice-pollen juice to drink. After it was given, his distress still did not cease. The Buddha then ordered that he be given bamboo shoot juice. It was given...
The illness did not subside at all. The Buddha ordered that rice gruel be placed in a bag and squeezed to extract the liquid for him to drink; yet the disease still did not improve.
The Buddha then directed that he be taken to a secluded place and given the rice gruel.
The *Mūla-nidāna* states: There was a sick bhikṣu whom a physician instructed to take flour mixed with water as a non-time meal (*vikālabhojana*).
The Buddha said: "There are toothless oxen that eat barley; later, they excrete the grains. One may use these whole grains as flour and consume them at a non-time.
If he is still not cured after consuming this, one may use raw barley flour, stirring it with a large amount of water."
Filter the substance, and only then should it be consumed. If it is not cured even after consuming it, the Buddha said:
"The physician shall prescribe that one consume a drink made from roasted flour (maṇḍa), whether thick or in the form of a ball; it should be consumed as desired.
Regarding all such matters, whatever I have permitted for the sake of the sick outside of the proper time, none of these should be done once the illness has been cured."

The *Mūla-ekottara-karman* states: There are five kinds of fruits. Whether at the proper time or the improper time, whether one is ill or not, one may eat one *harītakī* at will. This is called *devadāru*. Second is *vibhītaka*;
third is *āmalaka*, which is the *yugan-zǐ* (Chinese gooseberry) of the southern hills, shaped like a *bīnlang* (betel nut); eating it removes wind. Fourth is *mṛdvīkā*...
“Ssu” (粟) refers to black pepper (*marica*). “Wu pi-p’o-li” (五畢茇利) refers to *k’ou-chiang* (蒟醬).

The *Caturvargika-vinaya-karmavācanā* states: “In the event of illness caused by thirst, it is permitted to accept non-time [liquids] such as fruit juices or honey syrups, provided they are clear like the color of water;
these may be accepted after purifying them with drops of water. This applies to those suffering from wind-heat illnesses.
Regarding the causes and conditions: it is permitted to accept five kinds of seven-day medicines.

There are also causes and conditions regarding illness for which it is allowed to accept medicines to be taken for as long as one lives—namely, all salty, bitter, sour, and pungent substances unfit for regular food, such as ginger, pepper, and the like, up to powders, pills, decoctions, and ointments made from white-arts (Atractylodes). However, non-time [afternoon] drinks must not be kept until the following morning.
If seven-day medicine is not consumed by the eighth day, it may not be kept.

The *Nanhai Jiguinei fa zhuan* (Record of the Inner Law Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states: When food remains on the tongue after eating, if grease persists and one has not yet rinsed with pure water, any saliva or drool that has already been produced must be discarded externally.
If the designated time for consumption has passed, one further commits the offense of taking food at an improper time (*vikāla-bhojana*).

(Text). Thus it has been transmitted down through the generations. Regarding the previous [rules] on eating in succession (*paryāya-bhojana*) and eating separately from the community (*gaṇa-bhojana*), these were permitted as exceptions within the precepts;

they were spoken of as being allowed under the rule against eating at improper times (*vikāla-bhojana*). However, although those former rules were permitted, they still occurred when one had passed the midday limit and was at liberty to eat.
Furthermore, there is lamentation that we have long been infected by perverse customs, which are difficult to eradicate quickly. Some say, "It is the Master’s command."

I ordered it opened, but upon thorough investigation, there was no authoritative scripture to rely upon. Some say that one must practice "participating in study" (canxue). Yet, even during the Buddha’s lifetime, there were no kitchens;

how much more so now in monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) and forest hermitages (*araṇya*)? At dawn there is a light meal, and in the evening tea and water—these provisions are more than double those of the Sage’s era.
How can their refined cultivation compare to that of the former sages? It is not merely that the śrāvakas of the Western Regions fixed the day by the sun's shadow.
Thus it should be practiced. Indeed, among the ancient virtuous ones of this land, there were many who observed the pure fast (*śucivratā*).
Their exemplary conduct and noble regulations are all recorded in the biographies (*avadāna*). I pray that you will follow in their footsteps to inspire future students.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the late meal is called "medicine-stone" (*bhaiṣajya-śilā*), this is not the eternal path of the Dharma King followed equally by both ordinary beings and sages; nothing surpasses the single practice of the ancients.

Regarding the provisional application of time, do not rely on constant usage; I have now appended a discussion of this here to clarify that it lacks a scriptural basis and has no authoritative support.
The thirty-eighth precept: On the Consumption of Leftover Food.

If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika (the *Mūlasaṃghabhedaka-vinaya* states: "Eating food that has been touched by others or food from the previous day is a *sthūlātyaya* offense").
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. At that time, the Venerable Kāla was also residing there, constantly sitting in meditation and contemplation.
When the time arrived, he entered the city to beg for alms; the food was easily obtained, and he had this thought:
"Why do I weary myself by entering the city for alms every day? It would be better to eat what I first obtain;
as for the food obtained later, I shall carry it back. He acted exactly according to this thought.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not see Kāla at either the morning or the midday meal, and they suspected that he had died, or had gone on a long journey, or had left the monastic life, or had been harmed by a wild beast.

Later, having seen [the offense] and inquired into its cause, he informed the Buddha, who established the precept. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of prohibition), instituted because of its being contrary to the Dharma;
thus this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was formulated.
Explanation of the meaning: The Vinaya states that "stale food" refers to anything received on one day and kept until the next day; all such things for a śramaṇa...
Among the sons of the Śākya who have received the full ordination, none are pure. There are two kinds of food: formal food (*bhojana*) and non-formal food (*abhojana*), as described above.
Regarding the determination of the offense: herein, if one eats food that has been kept overnight, for every swallow there is a *pāyattika* offense.
One who eats at an improper time commits a *pāyattika* offense. One who eats for more than seven days after the seventh day commits a *pāyattika* offense.

To consume medicinal substances permitted for life as long as there is no cause of illness constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. If one perceives what was prepared overnight as having been prepared overnight, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one suspects it was prepared overnight, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If it was not prepared overnight but one perceives it as such, or if one suspects it was not prepared overnight, both are *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the leftover food has been kept overnight; second, there is the perception that it is leftover food kept overnight;
third, one consumes it again until it enters the throat.
This also applies to bhikṣuṇīs as a *pāyattika* (with the same rule for those of common training). It also applies to śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.
For a nun, this is a *duṣkṛta* offense; this constitutes a transgression.

As for the exemptions where there is no offense: if she has received food overnight and gives what remains to her parents, to those working on a stūpa, or to those building a dwelling after having calculated the price;
or if there are holes or cracks in her bowl through which food enters, and she washes it according to the Dharma, leaving the remainder.
[This applies to cases] such as when one has gone out, or at the very beginning before the precept was established; these are considered non-offenses.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "If a *mahābhikṣu* stays overnight with food that he has not received with his own hand, it is called 'storing within' (*antar-śayana*);
if he eats it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If he receives it with his own hand and then stores it overnight, it is called 'storing leftovers' (*vighasa-śayana*)."

To eat [forbidden food] is a *pāyattika*. If one first takes fruit oneself and later receives it from a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle such items) before eating it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There are two kinds of contact with food that are without offense: first, when a pure monk touches it by mistake;
second, when a monk who has broken the precepts and lacks shame or remorse touches it. Regarding celestial food (*dibba-anna*), it may be accepted after midday for a period of seven days.
The *Mūla-nidāna* states: "Any remaining cakes or fruits should be given to a śrāmaṇera; they may be eaten by him when returned the following morning.
If one gives them with the intention that they be kept for oneself, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of giving and a *pāyattika* offense at the time of eating.
If there is no intention whatsoever [to keep them], there is no offense."
The *Muktaka* states: If a sick person is poor and has only such leftover, defiled food as ghee or oil, they may consume it without offense.
When a bhikṣu is traveling, he may have a śrāmaṇera carry his provisions; he may also have the śrāmaṇera lift up or set down [his belongings] for him.
Furthermore, when bhikṣus are traveling on the road and ought to carry provisions, if there are no laypeople and no śrāmaṇeras, they should exhort a donor to give them.
If there is no donor either, they should take them with them themselves. Later, seeing a layperson, they should exchange them for food;
if there is no place to exchange them, they should divide [the provisions] into two portions and say to the layperson: "Take one portion. Once that person has entered...
With his hand, he should say to that person: "Take my food; I shall take your portion. They may exchange and eat this way, though it is difficult to find such an opportunity.
On the first day, one must fast. On the following day, if someone offers food, one may accept and eat it;
if no one offers anything, one may take for oneself a single *muṣṭi* (a handful) and eat it. By the third day, there will again be nothing.

Regarding the one who bestows [the food]: one may eat two "tiger-fist" handfuls. When this reaches the fourth day and there is again no one to bestow it, one may take it according to one's own needs and eat until satisfied;
there is no offense. Later, when provisions for the journey are exhausted, if one sees ripe fruit fallen on the ground, one should take it and perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*).
Having received it, one should eat it. If a pure attendant (kappiyakāraka) is difficult to find, one should eat it after having been handed it over.

If there is no one to hand it over, one may take it oneself and eat it with the thought that one is on Uttarakuru. Regarding fruit ripened on a tree that has not yet fallen to the ground, one should climb the tree oneself, shake it, and cause it to fall;
then, taking it oneself, one may eat it. These aforementioned allowances are all for the sake of difficult circumstances. If...
Except in times of difficulty, [these actions] are all strictly prohibited.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If many bhikṣus travel together, each individual bhikṣu, including even a single young śrāmaṇera, shall carry his own provisions.
When it is time to eat, they shall divide them among themselves. Once the śrāmaṇera has received his portion, he says to the bhikṣus: 'Now...'"
One may take the portion belonging to a śrāmaṇera and exchange it with a venerable elder (bhadanta). Having obtained it, one may further exchange it with the second seat-holder.

By proceeding in this manner through successive exchanges until reaching many portions of food, there is no offense. If the śrāmaṇera does not understand the Dharma, the bhikṣu may carry the food himself.
If one gives [the food] to a śrāmaṇera, and it is subsequently exchanged so that one obtains food, there is no offense.
This precept is studied in common with the Mahāyāna.
The thirty-ninth: the precept against taking food for oneself.
If a bhikṣu eats food that has not been formally offered, or places medicine in his mouth—with the exception of water and tooth-sticks—it is a pāyattika.

Regarding the origin of this precept: there were two stages of its establishment. When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who constantly went on alms-round and wore robes made of discarded rags (pāṃsukūla).
At that time, the lay devotees (gṛhapati) of the city [prepared offerings] for their deceased father...
If a mother, brother, sister, husband, wife, son, or daughter prepares food and performs a sacrificial offering at a crossroads,
at a gateway, by a riverbank, or even under a tree or in a shrine, and a bhikṣu takes that food for himself and eats it, householders will criticize and disparage him.
When those of few desires hear of this, they inform the Buddha, and thus the first precept is established.
At that time, the bhikṣus became doubtful and did not dare to take tooth-sticks or pure water for themselves.
The Buddha said, "Excepting water and tooth-sticks, there is no offense. Thus, the second precept was established. This is a prohibitive offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya);
because it was contrary to the Dharma, this training rule (śikṣāpada) was enacted.
Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. The first clarifies the original enactment; the second, beginning with "except for water and so forth," clarifies the subsequent allowances.
The Vinaya states: "There are five ways of receiving: receiving hand-to-hand; or receiving from one who holds an object in their hand;
or receiving from one who holds an object in theirs; or receiving from one who holds an object in their hand; or receiving by passing an object from a distance."
Both the giver and the receiver are aware of this; there is no obstruction or resistance in between, and it falls into the hand. Furthermore, there are five ways of receiving:

receiving with the body what is given by the body, receiving clothing what is given as clothing, receiving with a bent elbow what is given with a bent elbow, and receiving with a vessel what is given in a vessel.

Or, there may be circumstances where it is placed on the ground and given. (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: The Buddha thought to himself, "Whenever bhikṣus do not receive food [directly], such faults arise. Therefore, I now command all... )

"O Bhikṣus, having accepted food that is fit to be eaten, one should cause others to witness it; thus, as taught by the Buddha, one should accept and eat it. 'Medicines' refer to ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar."

Regarding the *yāñcī* (tooth-stick): [The fourth section states: The Buddha said, "One should chew the tooth-stick. There are five faults in not chewing it: first, foul breath; second, inability to distinguish flavors; third, the aggravation of the heat-element (*ūṣman*); fourth, lack of appetite; [and fifth, the accumulation of impurities]."

The five eyes will not be clear. There are five benefits to chewing a tooth-stick; the opposite of these may be inferred. Regarding the length of the tooth-stick: the longest permitted is one *vitasti* (a span), and the shortest permitted is four finger-breadths in length.
One should not chew it in a crowded place, such as a heated room, a dining hall, or a walking path; rather, one should do so in a secluded spot.
**Establishing the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one takes food into one's own mouth without having received it, there is a *pāyattika* for every swallow.

If one consumes non-timely medicine (*akālabhaiṣajya*) after the designated time, or consumes seven-day medicine (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*) after the seven days have passed, in all such cases there is a *pāyattika*.
If one consumes life-long medicine (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*) without receiving it when there is no valid reason, there is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one does not receive [the robe] and perceives it as not received, it is a *pāyattika*. If one does not receive [it] but suspects [it], or if one receives [it] while perceiving it as not received, or if one receives [it] while having doubt, these are all *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the food has not been formally received; second, one perceives it as not having been received;
and third, one takes it for oneself and swallows it.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise a pāyattika (the rule is the same for both).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.

Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if food falls into a bhikṣu’s alms bowl while he is begging for food due to being blown by the wind or carried off by a bird, he may remove it—even down to a single fingernail—and eat what remains;
furthermore, there is no offense for those who were practicing before the precept was first established. These constitute cases of no offense.
Regarding the practice of tasting food: the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one is permitted to taste food to ascertain its saltiness or blandness, provided that one does not swallow it.
One is permitted to accept food from devas, nāgas, ghosts, or monkeys; likewise, one may accept food based on the donor’s verbal instruction. However, one must not accept food that is thrown.

(In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, accepting food thrown from a distance is permitted when there is a specific cause or necessity. In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, such "thrown food" is not permitted because it involves disrespect. While the underlying circumstances are the same, they differ in terms of what is allowed and what is prohibited.)
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "In general, one receives food for two reasons: first, to sever the causes and conditions for theft; second, to establish a witness.
Receiving food from a non-human being constitutes receiving food, but it does not constitute establishing a witness.
Therefore, receiving food from non-humans or animals is permitted when there is no human available to grant the food, as such circumstances are remote and isolated. If...
Among humans, non-humans, animals, and ignorant children, [the offering] is not permitted in any case.
The *Mūla-mātṛkā* states: When one is in the midst of receiving food, if it has not yet been obtained and consequently falls to the ground, one should receive the food again.
If there is no donor, one may take it oneself; having removed the impure portions, the majority may be eaten.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
To cite scriptural evidence, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "In the past, there was a bhikṣu who traveled with a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
They came to the foot of a tree where there were fruits upon it. The non-Buddhist said to the bhikṣu, 'Climb the tree and gather the fruit. The bhikṣu...
He replied, "According to the dharma of us bhikṣus, one should not climb trees. He said again, "Then shake the tree to take the fruit.
He replied, "In our dharma, one must not shake a tree to make the fruit fall. The outsider climbed the tree, took the fruit, and threw it down to him.
When he spoke of taking and eating the food, [the monk] replied, "In my Dharma, one must not eat without having first received it.

The non-Buddhist developed a heart of faith and reverence, realizing that the Buddha’s Dharma was pure. He immediately followed the bhikṣu and went forth within the Buddha’s Dharma, receiving full ordination; shortly thereafter, he attained the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Appendix: Examination of the Record The *Neifa zhuan* (Record of the Inner Dharma) states: The Sanskrit term is *dantakāṣṭha*. *Danta* is translated as "tooth" (*da*). *Kāṣṭha* is simply "wood.
How could one fail to recognize that this refers to a tooth-stick? To name it "willow branch" (*yangzhi*) is incorrect.
Willow trees are extremely rare in the Western Regions; translators have thus erroneously transmitted this designation as "the Buddha’s tooth-wood," though the tree is in fact not a willow.
I personally witnessed this at Nālandā Monastery. However, among the religious and laity of the Five Indias, chewing tooth-sticks is a constant practice;
even three-year-old children are all taught to do so from an early age. As for mountain retreats, one should primarily use branches of oak or vines of kudzu.
For level plains, one may use paper mulberry, peach, locust, or willow as one pleases; alternatively, large trees may be split and used. Or...
It may be cut into small strips; thus it will benefit both the noble teachings and the worldly stream.
Forty: The Precept Against Seeking Fine Food When Not Ill.
If a bhikṣu obtains fine food and drink—milk, curd, fish, or meat—and if a bhikṣu [seeks] such fine food when not ill...
If one seeks food for oneself when ill, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: This precept was established in two stages. The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī.
There was a merchant chief who was an almsgiver (*dānapati*) to Baddhālī. He went to that man’s house to seek various foods. The merchant chief asked: "Now..."
"What is the trouble? he thought, reflecting on this food. He replied, "I have no suffering or distress; I simply wish to obtain some mixed food.
The merchant leader criticized and disparaged him. A bhikṣu who went for alms heard of this and informed the Buddha. This was the first establishment of a precept.
At that time, all the sick bhikṣus were fearful and cautious, not daring to beg for themselves, nor daring to beg for the sake of a sick bhikṣu. They obtained [nothing].

[The monks] then did not dare to eat. The Buddha granted permission for all [of these]. This was the second formulation of the precept (*śikṣāpada*). It was established because of the arising of public censure.

**Explanation of the Meaning:** The Vinaya states: "Delicacies" (*praṇīta-bhojana*) refers to milk, curds, fish, and meat (milk and curds being drinks; fish and meat being foods). As for "the sick," it refers to...
If one is unable to finish eating during a single sitting, it constitutes an offense.
Regarding the transgression herein: if, being without illness, one personally begs for such fine food for one's own sake and eats it, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every swallow.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the food must be fine and mixed; second, one must seek it for oneself while not being ill;
and third, it must be taken into the mouth and swallowed.
If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits this, it is a *duṣkṛta* (the same rule applies, though studied separately; according to the *Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, this constitutes an offense of reproach).
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if one begs for oneself while ill; if one begs on behalf of someone who is ill; if one has obtained food through begging and eats it;

if one acts on behalf of another or another acts on one's behalf; if one obtains food without having begged; or if it concerns the initial period before the precept was established—these constitute cases of no offense.
Regarding the rules for gathering [alms]: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if one solicits [food], it is a *pāyattika*; if one does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Mūla-vinaya* states: if one begs when not ill and eats when not ill, there is *dukkaṭa* at the time of begging, and one falls into the offense (*āpatti*) upon eating;
if one begs when not ill but eats when ill, there is *dukkaṭa* at the time of begging, but there is no offense at the time of eating.
If one begs when ill but eats when not ill, there is no offense at the time of begging, but at the time of eating, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense).
If one begs when ill and eats when ill, there is no offense. If, while begging for food, another person brings out rice and one desires something else, [one may take it].
"Do not accept their food; remain silent. When he asks, "Venerable sir, what do you require?
this statement expresses that one may act according to one's own wishes. If something is required, it may be sought accordingly; there is no offense.
Furthermore, when a donor sees a bhikṣu, he says: "If you have anything you require, please ask for it as you wish.
If the bhikṣu seeks whatever object he may find, there is no offense.
In this Mahāyāna precept, there are also illnesses for which one must not eat fish or meat. If one eats them, the offense incurred is a minor defilement (*mṛdumala*).
*Vinaya-zhichi-huiji*, Scroll Ten, Glossary of Pronunciations and Meanings.
Regarding the "Village Without a Dwelling": At that time, there was a village in the kingdom of Kośala that had neither a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) nor a lodging for travelers.

A householder, for the sake of merit, constructed a dwelling and provided all manner of food and drink to the visiting monks, yet he could only offer a single meal and was unable to provide more. Thus, he established this through the practice of merit.
Therefore, other vinayas all refer to it as the "House of Merit" (Puṇya-śālā).
The *Śramaṇa-brāhmaṇa* has not yet been translated. Other vinayas mostly refer to him as the "Agidatta-brāhmaṇa."
The term *vinaya* is the Sanskrit for *karmadāna*, which is translated here as "one who manages affairs" (*zhīshì*) and also as "one who gladdens the assembly" (*yuèzhòng*).

The two characters *wéi-nà* combine both the Chinese and the Sanskrit: *wéi* (綱維, "to maintain the framework") is the Chinese word, while *nà* is the Sanskrit term, with the three characters *karmadā* having been omitted.
*Miè* (pronounced *miàn*) means "to turn one's back. To "turn one's back on the compass and square" (*miè guījǔ ér gǎicuò*) refers to deviating from the standard rules.

*Chuǎi shí* (揣食) and *chuǎi chuī* (揣吹)—the former being pronounced with the rising tone—refer to "lump food" (*piṇḍāhāra*), which is also called "segmental food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). It is so named because it possesses distinct physical segments or portions.
The nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) refers to the mental factor of contact associated with the first six consciousnesses.

It generates joy and pleasure toward its objects, such as when watching a theatrical performance one remains satiated even without eating all day. Furthermore, various tactile sensations of coolness and warmth can nourish the body.
The nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) refers to the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*) associated with the sixth consciousness.
It generates aspiration toward desirable objects; through the nourishment of this mental intention, the sense faculties increase.
