If one intentionally commits a fundamental offense and does not comply with the admonition, it is a *pāyattika* (an offense requiring expiation). [This refers to] the commission of the root offense itself; failing to comply with the exhortation results in a downfall.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, performing an improper act oneself; second, possessing a mind that defies the admonition.
If, after being admonished three times,
one does not accept [the correction], both the bhikṣuṇī commits a pāyattika (the same rule applies to her fellow students), while the śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera,
and śrāmaṇerī commit a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if an ignorant person comes to offer admonition, one may reply, "You should ask your teacher or preceptor;
once you have studied the sūtras and learned the method of admonition, you may then offer it. If you do so, it shall be accepted.
Or, if speaking in jest, or speaking while alone, or while dreaming, or if intending to say this but mistakenly saying that, and so forth.
If [the rule] was not yet established at the beginning, this constitutes no offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
Examination: The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "That which is spoken by one who is venerable should not be obstructed; whatever instruction is given [should be followed]."
One should not oppose them; rather, one should remain silent, dwelling in respectful conduct, free from envy and anger, having eliminated sinful thoughts, and always providing honor and support.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "One should not accept the admonitions of five types of persons: first, those who lack a sense of shame and remorse; second, those who are not broad-minded..."

[The student] studies. Third, they constantly seek out the faults of others; fourth, they delight in quarreling and strife; fifth, they wish to discard their robes and return to lay life. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"Regarding those who were previously admonished, there are six types of persons: first, those whose minds harbor love and hatred."
1. Those of dull faculties and lacking wisdom; 2. Those who have seen or heard little; 3. Those who act for the sake of gain and fame; 4.

Those who act for the sake of the happiness of the present life, desiring only to take care of themselves; 5. Those who have newly gone forth and still harbor attachment to their wives and children—these six kinds of people will suffer harm if admonished.
If one issues formal instructions or admonitions, their words will be of no benefit; rather, one should respond to them by saying: "Only you yourself..."
One should observe one's own bodily actions as wholesome or unwholesome, without observing whether others act or do not act.
If the opposite of these six points occurs, then one should mutually admonish one another.
The fifty-fifth precept on intimidating others:
If a bhikṣu intimidates another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
The origin story: The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. The Venerable Bhikṣu Nāgapāla constantly...

He attended to the Buddha’s left and right, providing whatever was required. It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that when they are walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), if those making offerings stand at the head of the path, once the first watch of the night has passed, they invite the Buddha to enter his room; the World-Honored One remained silent.
The same occurred during the middle watch and the latter watch of the night. That man thought to himself, "I shall now surely terrify him.
The Buddha had him enter the room, whereupon he immediately turned around, donned a *kambala* (woolen garment), and made the terrifying sounds of a non-human being, saying, "Śramaṇa, I am a ghost!
The World-Honored One replied, "You should know that this foolish person’s mind is likewise evil. At dawn, the World-Honored One was pure and serene.
The Saṃgha was assembled. Having rebuked him, [the Buddha] established this precept for the bhikṣus.

This training rule (śikṣāpada) was promulgated due to the incident of derision and the underlying affliction of lack of tranquility. (According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "This good bhikṣu was instead seized and bound; he feared the Buddha and doubted [him]. This is the Sanskrit term.)
Exegesis: The Vinaya states: "To terrify" means to frighten a person by means of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects (*dharmas*).
Regarding "forms": these may take the shape of an elephant, a horse, a ghost, a bird, a beast, or other such forms. Regarding "sounds":

these may include the sound of conch shells, the sound of drums, or the sounds of elephants, horses, and so forth. Regarding "odors": these include the scent of roots, bark, flowers, leaves, fruits, and so on, as well as various [other fragrances].
Odors. As for flavors: sour, sweet, bitter, astringent, salty, pungent, and so forth. As for tangibles:
whether it be cold, hot, light, heavy, fine, coarse, smooth, rough, soft, hard, and so forth. As for mental objects (*dharma*):

speaking to another person and saying, "I dreamt that you would die," or "you will lose your robes and bowl," or "you will abandon the path," or likewise regarding one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*), or one's parents.
If one who is gravely ill should die [as a result], it constitutes an offense.

Regarding the transgression herein: if one uses form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena to terrify another person, and does so with clear articulation, it is a *pāyattika*; if the articulation is not clear, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires five conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the person must be a bhikṣu; second, one must harbor the thought that the person is a bhikṣu;
third, one must intend to cause them fear; fourth, one must harbor the suspicion that one is causing them fear; and fifth, both the speaker and the listener must understand what is said clearly.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; the same rule applies to bhikṣuṇīs (the training is identical for those of the same school).
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: sitting in a dark place without a lamp; being in a place for defecation or urination;
showing colors and such to others without the intent to cause fear; if these things actually exist; if one sees such signs; if one sees them in a dream;
if one is about to die; if one has renounced the path; if one has lost one's robes or bowl; or even [if it concerns] one’s parents.
When one is gravely ill and facing death, one should say to that person:

"I have seen such various signs of transformation in you—whether spoken in jest, or spoken hurriedly, or spoken to oneself, or spoken in a dream; what I intended to say was this, but I have mistakenly said that."
Furthermore, there is no offense in cases such as when the precepts have not yet been established.

The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "If, by means of things such as loathsome sights or sounds, one causes fear or distress by telling another person, 'Piśācas and the like are coming to kill you,' it constitutes an offense regardless of whether that bhikṣu actually experiences fear or not."

If one understands the meaning of these words, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If, by means of such things as pleasant forms or sounds, one says, "The king wishes to come and kill you," one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
This applies even to a person under training (who is also called a *śrāmaṇera* who has obtained the precepts).

If one causes alarm or distress to a person who is currently engaged in repentance, or to any other person, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). However, there is no offense if one speaks of the hells, animals, or hungry ghosts with the intention of transforming and guiding them, provided that they thereby become free from the fear of rebirth. If one suspects that a person is a bhikṣu, or perceives a bhikṣu as not being a bhikṣu, or suspects that a bhikṣu is not a bhikṣu—in all these cases, there is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one perceives a threat as a threat, or suspects a threat as a threat—in all these cases, there is a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one does not perceive a threat as a threat, does not suspect a threat as a threat, and perceives what is not a threat as a threat—[there is no offense].
If one harbors thoughts of fear, lack of fear, or doubt [regarding this rule], it constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense.

The fifty-sixth: the precept against bathing more than once a day.
If a bhikṣu bathes every half-month, a bhikṣu who is not ill should accept this; he must not exceed it, except at other times.

This is an offense of expiation (pāyattika). "Other times" refers to: the heat of summer, the time of illness, the time of labor, the time of wind and rain, and the time of traveling on a road. These are the [permitted] times.
The Origin Story: This precept has six regulations. The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
In the kingdom of Magadha, there was a pond where King Bimbisāra had permitted the bhikṣus to bathe in it at all times. Later at night, the group of six bhikṣus entered the water to bathe.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, accompanied by a woman he favored, also arrived there and heard the sound of the bhikṣus bathing. Then...
He remained silent and waited for him. The group of six monks used various fine medicinal powders to wash one another until the first light of dawn appeared;
yet the king was still unable to bathe. All the ministers criticized and disparaged this, so he established the rule that one may bathe once every half-month.

This was the first formulation of the precept. During the height of the summer heat, the bodies of the bhikṣus broke out in blisters and rashes, yet they were fearful and cautious [not to violate the rule].
[The monks] dared to bathe. They informed the Buddha. The Buddha permitted bathing frequently during times of heat; this was the second rule established.
Furthermore, a sick bhikṣu’s body became foul-smelling and filthy from the impurities of excrement, urine, and vomit. Fearing transgression and acting with caution, he did not dare to bathe.
He informed the Buddha. The Buddha permitted bathing frequently during times of illness; this was the third rule established. Furthermore, the various bhikṣus... [were making...]

At that time, their bodies were covered in sweat and grime. Out of apprehension and caution, they did not dare to bathe. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted them to bathe frequently during work. This was the fourth precept established.
Furthermore, when various bhikṣus were traveling through wind and rain, their bodies became sweaty and covered in dust.
Out of apprehension and caution, they did not dare to bathe. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted them to bathe frequently during times of wind and rain. This was the fifth [precept].

This was the formulation of the precept. Furthermore, while traveling on the road, various bhikṣus suffered from bodily heat; they broke out in blisters and rashes, and were covered in sweat, grime, and dust.

Out of fear and caution, they did not dare to bathe. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted them to bathe frequently while traveling on the road. This was the sixth formulation of the precept.
This training rule was established because of excessive affliction caused by the practice of bathing.
Regarding the explanation of its meaning, the text is divided into two sections: from "bathing once every half-month" downward, it clarifies the original enactment;
the section on "other times" and so forth clarifies the subsequent allowances. The Vinaya states: "The hot season" refers to the forty-five days of spring and the first month of summer.

(This refers to the period from the first day of the third month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month; this one and a half months is the final forty-five days of spring. From the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, this one month is the first month of summer.
These two and a half months are collectively called the "hot season. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "In India, it becomes hot early; this is called the Indian hot season.

Thus, depending on the location, whether the heat arrives early or late, one should count these two and a half months as the period for bathing therein without offense). Regarding the "sick," even having a foul body odor qualifies. Regarding "work," even sweeping qualifies.

"A traveler" refers to one who comes or goes for a distance of at least half a yojana. (At times such as these, if one does not bathe, the body and mind will be ill at ease; the Buddha, out of compassion, observed their capacities and the timing, and thus granted permission.)

Regarding the offense: among these, the transgression is as follows. Except during the [permitted] times, if one bathes more than once—whether dousing the entire body or half the body—it is a *pāyattika*.
If one makes preparations for bathing with the intent to bathe but does not go through with it, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, one’s own lack of a valid exemption; second, the presence of a mind of contempt for the instruction;

The fifty-seventh precept on lighting fires in the open air:
If a bhikṣu, being without illness, lights a fire in the open air for himself to warm his body, or instructs another to light one,

The Origin Story: This precept was established in three stages. When the Buddha was staying at Khānumata, the group of six bhikṣus were unable to speak freely in the presence of the senior monks.
They left their cells and went out onto the open ground, where they gathered various firewood and grasses to kindle a fire for warming themselves.
At that time, there was a venomous snake within an empty tree; driven by the heat of the fire's energy, it emerged from a hollow in the tree.
[The fire] went out. The bhikṣus were all startled; they took the burning wood and scattered it in all directions.

The flying embers set the Buddha’s lecture hall on fire. This was the first establishment of a precept. There was a sick bhikṣu who, out of fear and caution, did not dare to light a fire nor instruct another to do so.

He informed the Buddha, and for this reason [the Buddha] granted permission. This was the second establishment of a precept. Furthermore, there was one who wished to boil [medicine] for a sick bhikṣu...

Whether it be porridge, soup, or rice; whether it be fumigating the bowl, dyeing robes, lighting lamps, or burning incense—if one fears and hesitates and does not dare to perform these acts, the Buddha permits them all.
This is the third established precept. It was formulated because of the affliction of frivolous play, establishing this rule of training.

Section Fifty-eight: The Precept on Taking Another’s Property.
If a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case— whether he hides them himself or instructs another to hide them—
even if it is done in jest, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. A householder invited the Saṃgha for a meal the following day;
having prepared the offerings during the night, he went to the monastery at dawn the next morning and announced that the time had come.

At that time, the group of seventeen monks took up their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases, and sat down on one side to practice walking meditation, pacing back and forth while waiting for the mealtime to arrive. [Then] the group of six...
He waited for the moment when the other turned his back and took [the object] to hide it. When the time came for him to search, he could not find it;
meanwhile, the group of six monks had been playing with it beforehand. Other bhikṣus, having observed this, censured them and reported the matter to the Buddha.

Because of this act of frivolity and the underlying affliction of a lack of tranquility, the Buddha established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*). This constitutes the first category of the fundamental offense of theft.

**Explanation of Terms:** *“Concealing” (藏):* A euphemistic term for hiding. *“Robes” (衣):* The three robes (*tricīvara*) and other garments. *“Alms bowl” (鉢):* The two types of vessels—iron or ceramic—that are of the prescribed measure.

*“Sitting mat” (坐具):* That which is spread out for sitting or reclining. *“Needle case” (鍼筒):* A container for storing needles. These are the six essential articles that a *bhikṣu* must carry with him at all times.
*“Down to joking” (下至戲笑):* Whether one intentionally causes another to feel vexed by hiding [the items], or hides them as a means of mockery and ridicule.
Regarding the establishment of the offense: among these, the transgressor is one who either hides it themselves or instructs another to hide it, even if done in jest;
this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the intention to mock while hiding it; second, the object must be a *bhikṣu*.
There are six items. If that person searches for them but does not find them, it constitutes an offense:
a *pāyattika* for a *bhikṣuṇī* (the same rule applies to those of common training), and a *duṣkṛta* for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*. This is defined as an offense.
Exemptions from offense: If one takes up an object after having correctly ascertained its identity and substance;
if one takes up an object because it has been blown away or soaked by wind and rain while left in the open air;

if one takes up an object because the owner is haughty by nature and has left the six requisites in disarray, with the intent of admonishing them; or if one takes a robe on loan and the other person does not [return it].

If one gathers [the items] for fear of losing them and then picks them up; or if, on account of these robes, bowls, or other belongings, there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya);
or if it concerns matters for which the precepts have not yet been established—these are non-offenses.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: To conceal the belongings of the other four assemblies, or even the property of animals, constitutes a *duṣkṛta*;
to conceal the property of two assemblies constitutes a *pāyattika*; and to conceal the property of the remaining three assemblies all constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If one searches for it and finds it, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one searches for it and does not find it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one hides an empty needle case and does not find it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: To conceal items that it is permissible for a śramaṇa to possess constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika);

to conceal items that are not permissible to possess constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Furthermore, if one arbitrarily conceals or takes possession of items subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya), impure robes, robes of reduced measure, items belonging to those under training (śikṣamāṇa), or the property of non-Buddhist brahmins and others, in all such cases one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu entrusts his robes to another bhikṣu, and that [recipient] stores only his own robes and does not store the other's, and they are stolen by a thief, there is no offense."
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
The fifty-ninth: the precept against taking for oneself a garment given as a pure gift.
If a bhikṣu gives a garment to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and later...
If one takes back and wears a robe without informing the owner, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The group of six monks, having truly given their robes to a close and dear monk, later took them back and wore them without informing the owner. When the other monks heard of this, those who possessed few desires and a sense of shame [were concerned].

"Vexation" (kui) refers to resentment and reproach. [The monks] informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. Due to the matter of clothing and the affliction of negligence, he formulated this training rule (śikṣāpada).
This constitutes the fundamental category of theft within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
Explanation of the Meaning: The text is divided into two sections. From "giving to a bhikṣu" onwards, it clarifies that the gift of robes has an owner.

From "not informing [the recipient]" onwards, it establishes the offense committed. The Vinaya states: There are ten kinds of robes as mentioned above. Regarding "one who gives a robe," there are two types of *viśuddha-dāna* (pure gifts).
The first is the *tattvika-viśuddha-dāna* (true pure gift), which is defined as: "This is my extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) which has not yet been purified; now..."
For the sake of purification, one gives to an elder; this constitutes a "true purification" (*bhūta-visuddhi*). Second is the "successive purification gift" (*paramparā-visuddhi-dāna*);
[the method for successive purification gifts is explained in the section on "making and holding" (*karaṇa-dhāraṇa*), whereas here the regulation concerns true purification gifts].
**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one takes and wears a truly pure robe without informing the owner, it is a *pāyattika*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, it must be a truly pure [robe]; second, one must take it without informing the owner.
Third, to take [an object] for oneself and use it arbitrarily constitutes an offense.
This rule applies equally to *bhikṣuṇīs*, who commit a *pāyattika*; likewise for *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, who commit a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as a transgression.

Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if it is a true act of pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*); if one speaks to the owner regarding their attachment [to an object] and then performs a successive act of pure giving;
if one takes possession according to one's own will whether spoken to or not; and in cases such as when the precept has not yet been established—these constitute non-offenses.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.

among the one hundred [offenses], they should be marked with a dot after being purified.

If one entrusts an undyed robe to the house of a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the garment must be entirely white or of a primary superior color; second...

One shall not keep [robes] that have been dyed with the three types of colors in a way that ruins them, nor shall one keep them after marking them for purification. These three acts constitute the category of the three robes;
they must be worn and used in their current state.
This also applies to *bhikṣuṇīs* (a *pāyattika* offense, governed by the same rule and training). It also applies to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*.
For a nun, it is a *duṣkṛta*; this constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one does not contravene the aforementioned regulations; if the color of the robe has faded and it is dyed again;
or if it concerns the very first instance before the precept was established—these constitute cases of no offense.

Regarding the methods for dyeing: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if one obtains a garment of blue-black (*nīla*), it should be purified by means of black clay (*mṛttikā*) and madder (*mañjiṣṭhā*)—“black” refers to the color of clay, while “madder” (pronounced qiàn) is a plant used for dyeing crimson.
If one obtains a garment of black clay, it should be purified by means of blue-black and madder. If one obtains a garment of madder, it should be purified by means of blue-black and black clay.
If one obtains garments of yellow, red, or white, they should be purified by means of the three: blue-black, black clay, and madder.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should make marks using three types of colors. If one wears [the robe] without making these marks, it is a *pāyattika* offense for every instance of wearing it;
if one does not wear it, it is a *pāyattika* offense for every night it remains overnight."

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Down to the cloth for wiping the bowl, the towel for wiping the feet, the bowl bag, and the waistband—all of these must be dyed with a 'ruined color' (*khaṇḍa-varṇa*) and kept after having performed the purification by marking (*tri-bindu-śuddhi*).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"With the exception of the three robes (*tricīvara*), all other garments need only be worn after performing the purification by marking with three dots; there is no [other requirement]."
Regarding discoloration: if it is not pure blue, light blue, or azure, one may use such spots as a means of purification to make the lining of a robe.
As for the *saṃkakṣikā* (this is translated as "inner garment," resembling a short skirt), its exterior appearance must not be visible; it may be worn [only when hidden].

If it is made as a garment intended to be visible, one must never wear it in red, yellow, or white. The same applies to colors that are not pure or are overly large, with the exception of *puṭa* (leather boots).

All other robes, bedding, and such items must be used after performing the three-dot purification (*tripuṇḍra-śodhana*); to use them without having performed the three-dot purification constitutes a transgression.
If one performs the three-dot purification on a robe that already possesses the proper color using the five primary colors, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
Excluding the five primary colors, there are pure yellow, blue, saffron, and indigo; furthermore, one must not wear any shade of green.
Even if yellow, red, or white are purified by three dots, wearing them is still an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When performing the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*), the maximum size is four finger-widths; the minimum is like a pea.
Whether one, three, five, seven, or nine [patches], they must not be shaped like a flower.

If many small, miscellaneous new items are combined to patch a single area, the purification is performed once for that area. If each is patched individually, the purification must be performed for each one.

If one makes a new robe, one should perform the ritual of purification (*kappabindu*) at one corner; if it is mended with one or even half a strip of cloth, the purification must likewise be performed.
This precept is equally prescribed in the Mahāyāna.
The sixty-first precept: The Prohibition Against Taking Life.
If a bhikṣu intentionally kills the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
Origin Story: This precept has two enactments. The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. Kāḷudāyin...
Upatiṣya was displeased. Seeing the crows, he made a bamboo bow and shot at them. At that time, several lay devotees (gṛhapati) entered the garden to pay homage to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Having seen this, they criticized and disparaged him, saying, "The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they lack a heart of compassion.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the World-Honored One. This was the first establishment of the precept. The Buddha established the precept.
[The Buddha] had finished [speaking]. At that time, as the bhikṣus sat, rose, walked, and came and went, they killed many small insects.
Among them, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were apprehensive and cautious. The Buddha said, "If one does not know [of the living being], there is no offense.
He further added the words "intentionally killing it," and thus established the second precept for the Saṅgha. This is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), arising from the matter of life.
Out of compassion for sentient beings afflicted by defilements, this training rule was established; it constitutes the fundamental category of killing within the first section of the precepts.
Regarding the interpretation of the meaning: the Vinaya states that "animals" refers to those incapable of transformation, and "killing" means to sever their life-force.

Whether one kills by one's own hand or instructs another to kill, including the use of poisons or lethal implements (the term "killing" implies an intentional desire to harm living beings, not an unintentional error).
The determination of the offense is explained at length as in the first chapter on the *pārājika* offense of killing.
Regarding the offenses herein: if one intentionally kills with a murderous intent, it constitutes a *pāyattika*. [The text continues: ...at that time...
If one kills [an animal] and it does not die, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the intention to kill; second, the object being an animal; third, the perception that it is an animal;
and fourth, the certainty that its life will be ended.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; the same rule applies to bhikṣuṇīs. For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one does not kill intentionally; or if one hurls tiles, stones, knives, or staves toward another place and the life is accidentally taken;
or if a bhikṣu, while engaged in building a dwelling, loses a tile or stone from his hand and accidentally kills;
or if it is a brick, a wooden staff, or a rafter of the roof—such cases where death occurs because the hand could not restrain the falling object; or if one is supporting [someone]...
When rising from illness, when lying down, or when entering or leaving a room; when all have died without any harmful intent;
and in cases such as the initial period before the precepts were established—these constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the inclusion [of animals], the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "As for animals, those other than nāgas are included.

(Although nāgas are indeed animals, they are capable of transformation and possess supernatural powers; they protect the lands and preserve the True Dharma, and their functions are similar to those of the devas. Therefore, killing a nāga constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense.
This same principle applies to those who cannot transform, as stated in our own Vinaya; thus, they are excluded).

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, causes harm to an animal even as small as a single finger, and that creature dies as a result, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Or, if it does not die at that time but later dies because of this, he also incurs a *pārājika* offense. If it does not die later either, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If one causes a person who is insane to commit an act of killing, although that person commits no offense, the instructor incurs the fundamental offense.
Regarding animals: if one perceives an animal as an animal, it is an offense of falling (pāyattika); if one suspects it is an animal; or if one perceives an animal as a non-animal;
or if one perceives a non-animal as an animal; or if one suspects it is a non-animal—in all these cases, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
The *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states: "If one intends to cut a vine but mistakenly cuts a snake, there is no offense.
If one intends to cut a snake but mistakenly cuts a vine, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). If one intends to kill this insect but mistakenly kills that insect;
or if one intends to cut an insect but cuts the ground; or if one intends to crush an insect but crushes the earth—in all these cases, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*."
This precept is established in common by the Mahāyāna. Because a bodhisattva protects sentient beings, one must not kill any living being whatsoever;
to kill is to commit a grave offense.
Appendix: Examination The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: If birds or sparrows nest and roost upon the corridors of a dwelling and cause a clamor, one should have someone inspect the nests.
If there are no chicks or eggs, they should be immediately removed and discarded. If there are chicks or eggs, one should wait until they depart before removing them.
If there is a bee hive, it should be removed if there are no young bees. If there are young bees, one should wrap it with thread; thus, it will not continue to grow.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Those who delight in killing are not welcomed by any living beings.

Conversely, because all sentient beings find joy in relying upon those who do not kill, such people experience peace and happiness in their minds when their lives are about to end, remaining free from doubt and regret.
Whether they are reborn in the heavens or among humans, they will always attain a long life. This is [the teaching].
It serves as a causal condition for attaining the Way, even leading to the attainment of a Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan.
Those who kill living beings undergo various forms of physical and mental suffering in both this life and future lives; those who do not kill are free from these manifold sufferings.
Thus, to kill another is in fact to kill oneself. Would a person of wisdom ever willingly kill themselves?
The sixty-second precept: The prohibition against drinking water containing insects.
If a bhikṣu knowingly drinks water that contains insects, it is a pāyattika offense. Regarding the origin of this rule:
there are two enactments for this precept. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the group of six [monks]...
A bhikṣu took water containing various insects and drank it. When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged him.

A bhikṣu of few desires, having heard of this, informed the Buddha. This was the first formulation of the precept. At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether there were insects in the water or not;
later, when they did find out, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained apprehensive. The Buddha [said]:

It was stated that there was no offense because [the monk] did not know [there were insects]. Consequently, with the added knowledge that the water contained insects, the Sangha further established the second precept.
This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); it was enacted as a training rule because the taking of sentient beings' lives occurs when utilizing water.
It belongs to the fundamental category of killing within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
**Explanation of the Terms:** "Knows" means either knowing by oneself or being informed by another that "there are insects in the water.
There are two kinds of insects: first, those seen as soon as one looks; second, those seen only after straining with a filter (*parisrāvaṇa*).

"Water" refers to all water from rivers, ponds, springs, wells, ditches, and canals. There are two ways of using water: first, internal consumption, which refers to what pertains to the internal body.
Enjoyment consists of bathing, drinking, eating, chewing tooth-sticks, or washing the hands and feet; this constitutes internal enjoyment.
Second is external enjoyment, as explained previously in the nineteenth precept (this is interpreted according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*).

Regarding the offense: among these, one who knows that water contains mixed insects and drinks or uses it, or drinks or uses fermented grain water (*yāsa*), vinegar, or the like containing mixed insects, commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If there is water with living beings and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*. If there is water with living beings but one suspects it so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is water without living beings but one perceives it as having them, or if there is water without living beings but one suspects it so, both are *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, water containing insects; second, the perception that there are insects; third, failing to inspect or filter the water;
and fourth, drinking or using it so that it passes down the throat.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise a pāyattika (the rule is the same and the training is shared).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if one did not previously know whether there were insects or not; if coarse insects touched the water and caused it to flow away;
if one strained the water before drinking; or in cases such as the very first instance before the precept was established—these constitute no offense.
This precept is established equally in the Mahāyāna.

To cite scriptural evidence, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "In the kingdom of Pāralī, there were two bhikṣus who traveled together as companions to Śrāvastī to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
On the way, they became exhausted with thirst and found no water. Upon reaching a well, one bhikṣu..."
The Buddha drew water and drank it immediately. Another bhikṣu examined the water and saw insects in it; he did not drink. The bhikṣu who had drunk the water asked him, "Why did you not drink?
He replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not drink water containing insects.
The other urged him again, saying, "Venerable sir, just drink. Do not let yourself die of thirst so that you may fail to see the Buddha. He replied, "I would rather perish..."
He did not violate the Buddha’s precepts, yet he died of thirst. As the monk who had been drinking water gradually approached the Buddha, the Buddha asked him, "Where have you come from?
He further asked, "Do you have any companions? The monk then answered the matter in full detail. The Buddha said, "Foolish man!
You did not see me, yet you thought you had seen me. That deceased monk had already seen me previously. (The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:)

That practitioner of the precepts died while abstaining from alcohol and was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Having attained a complete celestial body, he went first to the Buddha’s dwelling, paid homage to the Buddha, and heard the Dharma. He attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and received the three refuges;

therefore it is said, "He has already seen me first. (The account is the same in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*). If a bhikṣu is negligent and indolent, failing to restrain his sense faculties, then although he dwells in the same place as me, he is far from me. Although he sees me, I do not see him. If there is a bhikṣu who...
On the other shore of the ocean, those who are able to be heedful, diligent without indolence, and who restrain their sense faculties—though they may be far from me, I always see them;

they are always near to me. (This is explained in terms of the *dhātu* [realms]. If explained in terms of the *adhvan* [time periods], then a person who is heedless, even if born in an age of sages, is no different from the age of the final dharma.)

Those who are heedful, though born in the final age, will not differ from the True Dharma. The Buddha-body is truly eternal; fundamentally, there was neither his appearance in the world nor his parinirvāṇa. I pray that those of deep faith and wisdom do not give rise to the notion that this is merely the Semblance Dharma or that the Dharma has been extinguished, thereby abandoning themselves.

You must vow to be diligent and untiring, properly restraining the sense faculties and strictly purifying the *vinaya*. Do not treat minor transgressions lightly. Always act as if you were face-to-face with the Compassionate Countenance and personally receiving the clear instructions. If you practice without ceasing, you shall see that the single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa remains solemnly undispersed.
Appendix: An Examination The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Regarding 'insects,' this does not refer to fish, turtles, and the like;
rather, it refers to tiny creatures such as *jūka* (water striders) and *śalabhaka* (mayflies), even down to those with extremely minute forms that can be seen by the eye.

One should not examine them with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), nor should one have someone with poor eyesight examine them. At the very least, one may have someone who can see the fine lines on the palm of the hand examine the water."
One must not be too hurried nor stay for too long; it should be like the time it takes an elephant to turn around once.

If there are extremely minute insects in the water, one must not use that water for washing hands or face, or for the great and small calls of nature (the character *jié* is pronounced *yú*; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to a person without a right arm;
here the meaning is taken to refer to these insects, which are legless and crawl backward).
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: There are five kinds of eyes with which one should not examine water for insects: first, eyes afflicted by sores; second, eyes with cataracts or opacities;
third, eyes that are deranged or insane; fourth, eyes impaired by old age or illness; and fifth, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). For how long should one examine the water? It is said:

for the duration it takes for a cart drawn by six oxen to turn around. If one examines the water once while following the current and finds no insects, [the purity lasts] for the distance of one *krośa*.
One may drink from a *rośa* (one *rośa is said to be five *li*, or alternatively two *li*) at will, provided that no other river flows into it in the interim.
If there is a downstream river or a river flowing upstream, one may use the water within a distance of one *vyāma* (one *vyāma* equals eight feet) after having inspected it once.
There are five kinds of pure water: first, pure water for the *saṃgha*; second, pure water for an individual; third...

1. Purification by straining; 2. purification by four spring-sources; 3. purification by well-water; 4. purification by a person who is known to be observant of the precepts and who protects living beings; and 5. purification by water that has been observed.

If one knows that the person [providing the water] is one who maintains the precepts and protects life, then even if one does not personally inspect it, there is no offense in drinking or using the water when it is obtained.
It should be understood that for all such observations of water, from sunrise until the appearance of the dawn light, one may always use it accordingly.
There are five types of filters for straining liquids: first, the square sieve; second, the dharma-jar; third, the kuṇḍikā;
fourth, the pouring sieve; and fifth, the corner of the robe.

The fourth *fen* states: "One should not travel without a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*). Even for half a *yojana*, if one does not have one, one should use a corner of the *saṃghāṭī* as a wooden strainer.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "It is also permitted to keep a water-strainer tube (*parisrāvaṇa-daṇḍaka*), made of copper, iron, bamboo, wood, pottery, or stone."
Cover the mouth with fine cloth; the use of discarded rags (pāṃśukūla) is not permitted.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "Bind the head with silk, and tie a thin cord around the neck to hold the mouth shut, then sink it into the water."
Lift the head until half is above [the water] (if the mouth is fully submerged, it will be difficult to insert). Once it is full, draw it out; furthermore, one must inspect for insects.
Any jar or pitcher with a wide opening, regardless of its size, may have its mouth covered with silk to fetch water at any time; this is most convenient. (Note:
*chao* is pronounced with the fourth tone and means "broad"; *xiang* is the same as *gang*.)

The *Jizhu men jingxun* (Admonitions for the Gate of the Black Robes) states that the fundamental principle of the *lunang* (strainer) is as follows: For those who have left the household life, the cultivation of compassion (*maitrī*) is the root.

Compassion is defined as bestowing happiness, and it takes the abstention from killing as its priority. Although the species of beings may be minute, their desire to preserve their lives is no different [from our own].

This strainer is thus an instrument for practicing compassion and a condition for aiding sentient beings; through it, great conduct arises, and the ultimate Way is thereby accomplished. (This is why King Bimbisāra...)

The generals Li Shiduo and Pūrṇa received the five precepts for laypeople; whenever they were on campaign by royal command, they always carried water-strainers suspended from their bows. How much more so, then, for a monk who practices compassion and protection—how could he ever allow himself to lack one?
The sixty-third precept: The Precept Against Intentionally Annoying Others.
If a bhikṣu intentionally annoys another bhikṣu, causing him even for a moment to be unhappy, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: This precept has two stages of enactment. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, at that time ten... [text continues]
The group of seven bhikṣus went to question them. They asked, "Venerable sirs of the group of six, how does one enter the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth dhyānas?

How does one enter emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? How does one attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, and the fruit of an arhat? The group of six replied, "It is just as you yourselves do."
As for what was said: they had already committed an offense of *pārājika* and were no longer monks.

The group of seventeen [monks] then went to where the senior (*sthavira*) monk was and asked him, "If there are monks who ask such questions as, 'How does one enter the first dhyāna up to attaining the fruit of arhatship?'—what offense do they commit? The senior monk replied, "There is no offense. Immediately...
Having observed this, the six groups and the seventeen groups became suspicious and troubled; they went and informed the World-Honored One.
This was the first formulation of the precept. After the precept had been thus formulated, at one time the bhikṣus gathered in one place and discussed the Dharma and the Vinaya together.
A certain bhikṣu withdrew, his mind filled with doubt, and said: "Those bhikṣus have caused me to doubt. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense for one who did not act intentionally. This was the second formulation of the precept.

It was established as a training rule (śikṣāpada) due to the incident of playful mockery and the affliction of restlessness (auddhatya). (According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, the bhikṣu Udāyin saw...)

After the group of seventeen had received full ordination (*upasampadā*), they conceived a malicious intent and said to them: "Although you have undergone the ritual procedures, you have not actually obtained the precepts. What is the use of exhausting yourselves by further seeking academic training? (Therefore, this rule was established).

**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "Those who harbor doubts and distress" refers to [those who doubt] regarding birth, age, the reception of precepts, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), or transgressions;
these constitute the "Dharma. Regarding those who harbor doubts concerning their birth, one asks:
"How long has it been since you were born? The person replies: "It has been this much time since I was born. [The questioner] says: "It has not been that long for you."
“Born. You were born like other people; you were not born at such a time. This is called doubting regarding the time of birth when questioned.
Regarding doubting regarding the age when questioned: one asks, “How many years old are you? and the person replies, “I am so many years old.
[The questioner] says, “You are not that many years old, like other ordained persons; you have not yet reached that age. This is called questioning regarding the age.

Regarding "arising of doubt at the time of receiving the precepts": one asks the person who has received the precepts, "When you received the precepts, your age was less than twenty, and furthermore, the assembly within the boundary was separate [from the formal act]. This is called 'arising of doubt at the time of receiving the precepts. Regarding "arising of doubt at the time of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure)":

one asks, "At the time you received the precepts, the *jñapti* (motion) was not accomplished, and the *karmavācanā* was not accomplished; it was contrary to the Dharma. This is called "arising of doubt at the time of the *karmavācanā*."
A separate assembly. This refers to raising a doubt regarding a *karmavācanā*. Regarding the arising of doubt concerning an offense:
one says to another, "You have committed a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *duṣkṛta*, or a *durbhāṣita*.
This is called the arising of doubt concerning an offense. Regarding the arising of doubt concerning the Dharma: you...
Regarding the dharmas thus questioned: one commits a *pārājika* offense. Such a person is not a bhikṣu;

this is called "giving rise to doubt regarding the Dharma," which causes one to be unhappy for even a brief moment (thirty such moments constitute one day and night; that is to say, it causes another’s mind to be uneasy for a short duration).

**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu intentionally causes doubt in another bhikṣu—whether regarding his birth, his age, or even the time of his ordination—and speaks so as to be clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he speaks but is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the person addressed is a bhikṣu; second, there is an intentional mind of malice or suspicion;
and third, the words spoken and heard are clearly understood.
If one simultaneously disciplines [a nun], it is a *pāyattika* offense for the bhikṣuṇī (the rule is the same and the training is shared).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if the matter was indeed so; if it was not done intentionally to cause annoyance;
if spoken in jest; if spoken rapidly; if speaking to oneself; if spoken in a dream; if intending to say one thing but mistakenly saying another;
or if it occurred before the precept had been established—these constitute cases of no offense.
Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: If someone comes wishing to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), if they have reached twenty years of age, one should grant them full ordination.
If they have not reached it, one should say: "Stay here and wait until you have reached [the required age].
If they nevertheless proceed to receive full ordination elsewhere, one must not express doubt or regret; to do so constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense. If...

The same applies to those with impaired faculties and those who are ill (these two preceding phrases refer to the collective inclusion of those such as the hundred-fold excluded persons). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Causing the other four assemblies to fall into doubt or regret constitutes a *duṣkṛta*; causing the two assemblies [of monks and nuns] to fall into doubt or regret constitutes a *pāyattika*;
causing the other three assemblies to fall into doubt or regret constitutes a *duṣkṛta*."
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: If one speaks with the further intent of causing doubt or regret through other matters, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

That is to say, speaking to a bhikṣu and saying, "You sleep too much, you eat too much, you talk too much," etc., [claiming], "Such a person is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya," thereby causing him to doubt and regret, is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This precept is shared with the Mahāyāna.
The sixty-fourth: the precept against concealing another’s grave offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense and conceals it, he commits a pāyattika.
The Origin Story: This precept has two origins. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Upananda frequently committed offenses and spoke of them to a bhikṣu who was his close friend, instructing him not to tell anyone.
Later, the two men quarreled, whereupon that bhikṣu immediately told other bhikṣus about the offense he had committed. When the other bhikṣus heard this...

He informed the Buddha. This was the first formulation of a precept. At that time, there were bhikṣus who, having heard the Buddha formulate the precepts, did not know whether they had committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) or not.
Later, they realized it was a grave offense; some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained doubtful.
The Buddha said, "If you did not know, there is no offense. He then formulated the precept once more. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). By...
This training rule was established because of the affliction of concealing past associates and their offenses.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning: the Vinaya states that "grave offenses" (*sthūlātyaya*) refer to the four *pārājika* and thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules.

"Concealing" means to hide one's transgressions and fail to disclose them. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Concealing an offense causes the Buddha-dharma to be impure and fosters unwholesome qualities."

Regarding the offense: herein, if one speaks after knowing it is the time for the light meal (*prāsaṅgika-bhojana*), it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one speaks after knowing it is after the light meal until the first watch of the night, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one speaks after knowing it is from the first watch until the middle watch of the night, it is a *duṣkṛta*. In all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

When midnight has passed and one intends to confess during the latter part of the night but has not yet done so, at the moment the light of dawn appears, it is a *pāyattika* offense—except for concealing a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) or other offenses, which are *duṣkṛta*.

To conceal a grave offense oneself is *duṣkṛta* (this refers to the minor offenses that arise from the successive concealment throughout the night). Except for a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī concealing a grave offense of another person, it is *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding others (referring to the three lower groups of the ordained and the two groups of lay practitioners who have received the precepts):

if it is a grave offense and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*; if there is doubt regarding a grave offense, it is a *pāyattika*. If it is not a grave offense but one perceives it as such, or if there is doubt regarding what is not a grave offense, in all such cases it is a *dukkaṭa*.

This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the person must be one who has received full ordination; second, the offense committed must be a grave offense (sthūlātyaya);
third, with the perception that it is a grave offense, one conceals it from others; and fourth, the concealment continues until after the appearance of the dawn.

The regulation for Bhikṣuṇīs is a *pāyattika* (the same regulation applies to those of the same training). For Śikṣamāṇās, Śrāmaṇeras, and Śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense. (Question:

According to the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya, if a Bhikṣuṇī conceals another Bhikṣuṇī’s abandonment of a *pārājika* offense, she commits a *pārājika*. Why is this [present case] fixed as a *pāyattika*? From which of the two meanings does it follow? Answer: There is a slight difference.

If a Bhikṣuṇī conceals another Bhikṣuṇī’s commission of sexual misconduct, for that one matter she incurs a heavy offense; for other precepts, she follows the lighter penalty. Therefore, it is formulated here as a *pāyattika*).
Exemptions from offense: If one did not previously know [the gravity of the act] and perceived it as not being a grave offense;
or if one speaks to another person, or there is no one toward whom to speak; or if, having resolved to speak, the dawn has already broken before one has spoken;
or if one does not speak due to a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya); or in cases such as when the precept was not yet established at the outset.
This constitutes no offense.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun), there are three types of concealing another's grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*): first, concealing another's four *pārājika* or *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses results in a *pāyattika* offense;
second, concealing [the commission of] shedding the Buddha’s blood or causing a schism in the Saṃgha requires a face-to-face confession (*pratyekamukha*).
Regarding the *sthūlātyaya*: for the three offenses below the third category, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one sees another commit an offense, one may speak of it to a single person and then stop. If one hears of it or suspects it, there is no need to speak of it."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not go and speak of this to just anyone; one should speak it to a virtuous bhikṣu.

If that offending bhikṣu is violent, or if, relying on the power of a king or a high minister, he creates the conditions for taking life and harms those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should reflect thus:
'The karmic retribution for his offenses will surely come to him of its own accord; he himself shall know it. It is, for example, like..."
If a fire breaks out, one should merely save oneself; how could one concern oneself with other matters? This would be without fault.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Fearing that it might become an obstacle to [the Dharma], or that because of this the Saṃgha might be divided."
If one conceals [the offense], there is no transgression.
This precept is established identically in the Mahāyāna; it is the same as the precept regarding not instructing others to repent of their offenses.
Appendix for examination: The third section states, "If one possesses five internal qualities, one should exhort another at the proper time and not at an improper time."
At that time, he was truthful and not false; beneficial and not harmful; gentle and not coarse;
and compassionate and not angry.
The fourth section states: The Buddha told Upāli: "If one's physical deportment is impure, one's speech is impure, and one's livelihood is impure;

if one has heard little and does not know the Sūtras, has heard little and does not recite the Vinaya, and if one’s eloquence is not clear or illustrative—such as a white sheep—one should not censure others.
If one is fully endowed with all these qualities, one should [censure] at the proper time."
One should raise the charge against another’s offense according to the Dharma. Furthermore, this bhikṣu may have both affection and respect for me, in which case he should raise the charge;
or he may have affection but no respect, in which case he should raise it; or he may have no respect but possess affection, in which case he should raise it;

or even if he lacks respect, if he is able to cause one to abandon evil and turn toward the good, he should raise it; or if there is a bhikṣu whom that person holds in high esteem and respects, [he should raise it through him].

One who has faith and devotion should be subject to *ukkhepanīya-kamma* (an act of suspension) so that they may abandon evil and practice virtue. If there is no one at all [who possesses these qualities], the Saṃgha should entirely set them aside and expel them, saying:
