This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, being seated among the assembly while disregarding the precepts and refusing to listen;
second, knowing for oneself that one has committed an offense yet concealing it and failing to reveal it; third, falsely claiming that one only recently became aware of it.
If a monk [performs] both [acts], it is a *pāyattika* offense for the bhikṣuṇī (the rule is the same and the training is identical).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding those cases where there is no offense: if one has never heard the recitation of the precepts before and hears it for the first time now;

or if one has never heard the detailed exposition before and hears it for the first time now; or if speaking in jest; or speaking to oneself; or speaking in a dream; or if intending to say this but mistakenly saying that;
or in cases such as when the rule had not yet been established—these constitute no offense.

Regarding the observance of the *poṣadha*: the *Vinayaviniścaya* states that if, at the time of the *poṣadha*, one utters words of ignorance—whether due to afflictions, forgetfulness, sleep, or a distracted mind—and fails to hear each individual precept, one incurs a downfall offense (*pāyattika*).
If one hears a training rule unique to the bhikṣuṇīs and speaks in such a manner [of ignorance], one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one shares the same training rules, one incurs the fundamental offense. If one is aged and infirm and lacks the capacity for discernment, there is no offense in speaking according to the facts.
At the time of the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony), one should have a person who is proficient and well-versed in reciting the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* recite it for the assembly.
Prior to the striking of the *ghanṭā* (bell), all *bhikṣus* should reflect upon their own offenses and confess them according to the Dharma. However—
Later, one should attend the assembly.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), one should recite the two divisions of the *vinaya*. If one is unable to do so, one should recite one division.
If one is still unable, one should recite the precepts of the first category and the verses at the time of the *poṣadha*."
One should explain the five categories in detail. If one is unable to do so, one should recite the first category and the verses;

as for the remainder, since the Sangha hears it regularly, those who do not recite it commit a *vinaya-āpatti*. Within the Sangha, one who is skilled should speak, while others should listen with single-minded attention;
they must not practice dhyāna or engage in other activities. This applies to the four matters, and so on up to the seven.
Regarding the methods for settling disputes: if one acts contrary to what is not permitted during the proceedings, one incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
If one acts contrary to everything that is not permitted, it is a *pāyattika*. This offense cannot be confessed before an individual;

it must be confessed before someone within the assembly who maintains the precepts, possesses majestic virtue, and is respected by others as difficult to offend. That person should reprimand them, saying: "Venerable sir, you have lost your excellence."

[If] during the fortnightly recitation of the Prātimokṣa, you do not show respect, do not attend with a single-minded focus, and do not listen to the Dharma with attentive ears, having been rebuked, you must confess a *pāyattika* offense. (The intention behind this rule is to reprimand one individual in order to admonish the entire assembly;

it is to discipline that one person who is ignorant and does not study the precepts, thereby causing the multitude to revere and trust the Vinaya and take pleasure in studying the precepts. Therefore, the confession must necessarily be made before the assembly, in the presence of those whose virtue and majestic dignity inspire reverence and are difficult to approach.)
This precept is shared with the Mahāyāna.
Seventy-fourth: Violating the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action) precept.
If a bhikṣu has already participated in a communal *karmavācanā*, and subsequently speaks thus: "The bhikṣus act according to their personal favoritism toward the assembly..."
Regarding "giving property belonging to the Saṃgha":
it is a *pāyattika*. The origin story (*nidāna*) is as follows: The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.

The Venerable Trapuṣabhadra was appointed by the assembly to oversee the affairs of the Saṃgha. Because he was occupied with the affairs of the Saṃgha and the affairs of the stūpa, someone [initially]...

When a monastery was being established, when the first quarters were built, and when the first well was dug, donors held assemblies and gave offerings, yet [the Buddha] did not have the leisure to attend them.
His robes became worn and torn. At another time, there were expensive robes offered to the Saṃgha; the monks deliberated together and, by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, granted them to him.
The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks was also present in the assembly. Later, they spoke words of regret and slandered the Saṃgha.

The Buddha established this precept because of the incident involving quarreling and discord, due to the affliction of intolerance; thus he formulated this training rule. (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"There are nine duties for the administrator (*karmadāna*). First, the duty of managing and assigning beds and seats. Second, the duty of managing and appointing invitations for assemblies. Third, the duty of managing and distributing rooms and quarters. Fourth, the duty of managing and distributing clothing and utensils. Fifth, the duty of managing and distributing incense and flowers. Sixth, the duty of managing and distributing fruits and vegetables. Seventh, the duty of managing and supervising warm water.

Eighth, the duty of managing and distributing various cakes and foods. Ninth, the duty of knowing how to grant [privileges] at will to those capable of performing the tasks. 'Administrator' means the presiding officer.)

Explanation of the Meaning: The text is divided into two sections. The first section concludes the account of what is performed by a harmonious assembly (*saṃgha*) through a collective formal act (*karmavācanā*).
The second section, beginning with the words "If he speaks thus," explains how one who has acted contrary to their own feelings subsequently regrets it and slanders the Saṃgha. The Vinaya states:
"Those who are intimate" refers to those who sit, rise, and converse with one another as closely as a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or a teacher (*ācārya*). These are the ones intended here.

Regarding "property of the Saṃgha": it refers to items made for the sake of the Saṃgha and already given to the Saṃgha, or items already promised to the Saṃgha—ranging from robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases down to drinking vessels and water containers.

"Giving" means to divert property belonging to the Saṃgha and bestow it upon a single individual. This is the method of giving a robe through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement), as explained in the section on "Holding What Has Been Made."
Regarding the offense: among these, the transgression occurs when one has first participated in a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) within the community and later regrets it.
If the statement is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*; if not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires five conditions to constitute a full offense: first, one must personally harbor a covetous mind; second, the other person must be willing to give;

third, there must be a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) performed with the assembly; fourth, after the gift has been made, one subsequently obstructs it; and fifth, the words [of obstruction] must be clearly articulated.

If a monk simultaneously censures both a bhikṣuṇī and a śikṣamāṇā, it is a pāyattika offense for the former; it is a duṣkṛta offense for the latter. This applies equally to śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, for whom it is likewise a duṣkṛta offense.

This constitutes an offense [for the monk]. (Śrāmaṇeras and others may not participate in the formal *kaṭhina* procedures of the Saṃgha; if they privately criticize the great monks, they too are at fault.)
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if the matter is indeed so; or if one speaks in jest; or even if one intended to say this but mistakenly said that;
as well as in cases prior to the initial formulation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the distribution [of goods], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If items that are to be distributed among the Saṃgha arrive, one should take them in turn.
If one does not wish to take them, it is permitted to pass by and not take them. If someone asks, 'Why do you not take them?
one should reply, 'This is not what I require; I wish to take other items. If one requires them later, one may take them without fault."
If one distributes items, saying, "Take as you please; whoever needs them may take them for themselves," there is no offense.

There are three types of prohibitions: 1. Prohibiting at the time of giving: one incurs a *vyatikrama* (offense of transgression) against the Vinaya. 2. Prohibiting before the gift has been given: one incurs a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (offense of mental regret).
3. Prohibiting after the gift has already been given: one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If among the monastic community there are those who perform manual labor, and if they are virtuous elders who are impoverished, the harmonious Saṃgha may give to them as much as it possesses.
To say that they should not be given anything constitutes a transgression in every case."
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
Seventy-fifth: The Precept Against Departing Without Granting Consent.
If a bhikṣu, while the Saṃgha’s deliberation on a matter has not yet concluded, departs without granting his consent, it is a pāyattika.
The Origin Story: This precept has two origins. When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī, the community of monks gathered in one place and discussed the Dharma and the Vinaya.
At that time, the group of six monks said to one another, "Look, these monks have gathered in one place;
it appears they wish to perform a formal ritual (*kamma*) against us. They immediately rose from their seats and departed.
The assembly said, "There is business for the Saṃgha; you should all stay and not depart. Yet they nevertheless departed.
Among them were those who delighted in training in the precepts, who felt resentment and reproach, and reported the matter to the Buddha. This was the first establishment of a rule.

At that time, various bhikṣus were occupied with affairs of the Saṃgha, affairs of the stūpa, or caring for the sick, and they had doubts. The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I authorize the giving of one's consent (*chanda*). Therefore...

There is a statement concerning the arousal [of desire] without having consented. This is the second training rule (śikṣāpada) established because of the lack of tranquility regarding the discussion of legal matters (dharmakarma) and the presence of afflictions (kleśa).

Explanation of the Meaning: The Vinaya states that "Saṃgha" refers to those who share a single recitation of the *Poṣadha* and a single *Karma*. "Settling" (*vinicchaya*) means deliberation. As for "matters," there are eighteen matters that cause schism in the Saṃgha:

[disputes concerning] what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya; what is an offense and what is not an offense; whether it is light or heavy; whether it is a residual offense (*sāvaśeṣa*) or a non-residual offense (*anavaśeṣa*);
whether it is a grave offense (*duṣkṛta*) or not a grave offense; whether it is a customary practice or not a customary practice; and whether it is a formal rule (*prajñapti*) or not a formal rule.

Regarding the prescribed and the non-prescribed teachings: [the rules for] granting consent (*chanda*) are explained in detail within the section on "performing and maintaining" (this constitutes one opening of three).
As for the offense: if one goes outside the door, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is inside the door and one foot is outside the door, or if one makes an effort to go while not actually going, or if one intends to go—[these constitute offenses].
If one does not depart [from the assembly], it is all *duṣkṛta*.
This precept fulfills three conditions before the full offense is established: first, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed and the assembly has gathered;
second, one departs abruptly without having granted consent (*chanda*); and third, both feet have crossed the threshold of the door.
If one simultaneously presides over [the trial], it is a *pāyattika* offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* (the same rule applies to those of the same training).

For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This constitutes an offense. (Regarding the three lower groups, there is no formal procedure for adjudication; the principle of granting consent is the same as for the *saṃgha*. As for their offenses, they are governed by the same rules as established in the later *Pañcavargika-vinaya*).

Exceptions where there is no offense: when there are matters concerning the Three Jewels or the care of the sick; when one has granted consent (*chanda*) but is unable to do so because the mouth is clenched;

when the *karmavācanā* is contrary to the Dharma or the Vinaya; or when one departs without granting consent for the purpose of causing harm or disadvantage to a stūpa, the Saṃgha, one's two teachers, or friends—such as these cases, as well as instances prior to the initial promulgation of the precepts.
This constitutes no offense.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed under a roof, for every instance one goes out, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a formal act is performed in the open air, going beyond the distance of one fathom from the face of the Saṃgha constitutes a *pāyattika* offense."
If one who possesses supernormal powers leaves the ground by a distance of four finger-breadths, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one leaves while the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal legal procedure (*karmavācanā*) without having been dismissed, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one leaves after coming to a private room where a legal procedure is being conducted, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
However, whether during a formal legal procedure of the Saṃgha or a private legal procedure, a *śrāmaṇera* is permitted to rise and leave from within.
It is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The same applies to *śikṣamāṇās* and *śrāmaṇerīs*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one must attend to defecation or urination for a brief moment, provided it does not interrupt the affairs of the Saṃgha, there is no offense.
This includes when preaching the Dharma or the Vinaya, listening to many bhikṣus recite the sūtras, receiving the sūtras from others, or listening to others recite the sūtras."

One must inform [the preceptor] before departing. To depart without informing him constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense. If one who is reciting a sūtra stops the recitation and departs while speaking of other matters, there is no offense.

(If one who is listening to another receive the recitation of a sūtra also incurs an offense for departing without informing [the preceptor], it is for two reasons: first, due to a light-mindedness that lacks faith and the thought of respecting the teaching;
second, because their deportment is negligent, thereby lacking the conditions for sympathetic joy.)
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
The seventy-sixth: The precept on regretting after having given consent.
If a bhikṣu, having already given consent, subsequently regrets it, it is a pāyattika.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Among the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*), there were those who had committed offenses.

Fearing that the Saṃgha would formally reprove them, these six men followed one another at all times without parting, so as to prevent the Saṃgha from performing a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) against them.
On another occasion, while the group of six was making robes, the Saṃgha, perceiving an opportunity, sent for them. They replied, saying:
"We were unable to go because we were making robes. The Saṃgha said, "If you cannot come, you may have one or two bhikṣus bring your consent (chanda).
They then had one bhikṣu bring the consent. The Saṃgha immediately performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for this bhikṣu.
When this bhikṣu returned and informed the group of six (ṣaḍvargika), the group of six regretted their actions and said, "The one who performed that ritual was not [authorized]."
They performed a formal act (kamma), but the kamma was not validly accomplished. "I gave my consent (chanda) for that matter, not for this one," he said.

The monks censured the group of six (ṣaḍvargika), and they subsequently went to inform the Blessed One. Because of this, the Buddha established the precept out of concern for the affliction of remorse.
Thus, this training rule (śikṣāpada) was formulated.

**Exegesis:** "Having given one's consent" (*chandadāna*) means that when the Saṃgha has a formal matter (*dharmakarma*), one has previously mentally expressed their desire and granted permission. "Regretting it later" (*paścāt-tāpa*) means that after having given consent, one subsequently feels remorse in the mind.

This precept is largely identical to the preceding one; there is a slight difference therein: the former refers to knowing the matter beforehand and collectively consenting to the *karmavācanā*, yet later regretting and slandering the Saṃgha; this [present case], however, concerns not knowing [the matter] and later obstructing the consent already given.
(2) Regarding the *karmavācanā* for the intent to destroy both types of precepts, which causes the prior matter to fail:
As for the offense incurred herein, if one has already given consent (*chanda*) and later regrets it, saying [the words] clearly and intelligibly, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly and intelligibly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, it must concern a monastic matter conducted according to the Dharma; second, the formal ritual of granting consent (*chanda-karman*) has been performed;
third, remorse arises in the mind; and fourth, the expression of regret is clear and complete.
If a *bhikṣuṇī* commits this simultaneously, it is a *pāyattika*; for a *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, or *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This constitutes an offense (the application of the rule to *śrāmaṇeras* and others is as in the preceding *Pañcavargika*).
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if the matter is actually as described and it was not a formal ritual (*kamma*), or if the ritual was invalid;
if one says, "This is not a ritual," or "The ritual was invalid"; if speaking in jest, speaking to oneself, speaking in a dream, or if intending to say this but mistakenly saying that;
and for those cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute no offense.

Regarding the taking [of consent], the *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If one has already given consent to another, but later gives rise to regret, and because these afflictions have arisen, the mind lacks shame and remorse, then when addressing a suitable object while perceiving them as a bhikṣu and speaking to them, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"Except for matters concerning the formal acts (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha; regarding all matters adjudicated by the Saṃgha, once they have been performed through collective consensus (*sāmagrī*), [the decision stands]."
To later express regret and censure [a formal act] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If the Saṃgha has performed any formal act (*karmavācanā*) in accordance with the Dharma, and one subsequently censures it, saying "it is not valid," this is a *pāyattika* offense. This excludes the formal acts of the Saṃgha;

it refers to all matters that are not formal acts (i.e., matters not accomplished by the procedures of a single motion, a second motion, or a motion followed by three proclamations). If the community of monks is in harmony and collectively decides upon a matter, to later censure it again constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one follows the Dharma and the Vinaya, it is a *pāyattika*. If, although one sees the royal decree, the monastic rule (*saṃgha-karman*) does not accord with the Vinaya, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If the Saṃgha performs any formal act (*karman*) that is contrary to the Dharma, and at that time one lacks the power to change it and thus remains silent without rebuking it, yet later says it is improper, there is no offense.
Offense. This precept is studied by those in the Mahāyāna as well.
The seventy-seventh: the precept against eavesdropping on a dispute to hear what follows.
If a bhikṣu, after monks have engaged in mutual quarreling and dispute, listens to these words and reports them to the other side, it is a *pāyattika*.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the bhikṣus were quarreling.

The group of six bhikṣus listened to these words and reported them to the other side, causing disputes to arise where none had existed before, and preventing those already existing from being settled.
It can be extinguished. The bhikṣus, having investigated and understood the cause, informed the Buddha, who established the precept. This is a natural offense (prakṛti-sāvadya);
it was formulated as this training rule due to the affliction of intolerance arising from the act of causing disturbance.

Exegesis: The Vinaya states that there are four kinds of disputes: disputes regarding speech (*vāda-vivāda*), disputes regarding accusations (*anuvāda-vivāda*), disputes regarding offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*), and disputes regarding matters (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*).

To listen to these words and report them to another means: to eavesdrop on others in a secluded place, seeking out their faults and subsequently relaying them to one another, thereby inciting anger and agitation.
Thus, a minor matter begins and develops into a major dispute; once a major dispute has arisen, it cannot be pacified.

**The Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one listens to the quarreling speech of others, whether from path to path, from path to non-path, from non-path to path, from high to low, or from low to high—going there and hearing it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;
not hearing it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one employs the means to go but does not go, [it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense].
If one agrees to go together but does not go, it is an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta* (transgression) in all cases.
If two persons are conversing together in a dark place, or in a secluded place, or while walking ahead, one should snap one's fingers or clear one's throat to alert them.
If one does not do so, it is an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta* for all [who fail to do so].
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, knowing that other bhikṣus are quarreling; second, going to a secluded place to listen;
and third, clearly understanding what is said.
If she governs both [the monks and nuns], it is a *pāyattika* offense for the bhikṣuṇī (the same rule applies to her fellow students).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one intends to perform an act that is contrary to the Dharma or contrary to the Vinaya;
or if one goes to listen in order to become aware of matters that would cause harm or lack benefit to a stūpa, the Saṃgha, or one's two teachers or friends;
as well as cases such as when the precepts have not yet been established—these constitute non-offenses.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Regarding the offense of going to listen to a dispute, it is because such an act can destroy the Buddha-dharma and cause the Saṃgha to split into two factions;
therefore, the rule was established that the listener commits an offense.

As for the offense of listening from a high or low place, this is because the matter of the dispute is grave, and thus differs from cases such as the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the *saṃghakarma*, and so forth. Within this context, the dispute—
If a person or others who do not engage in dispute come to listen, whether one speaks to them or not, one commits an offense in all cases.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To listen in silence to the speech of the other four assemblies constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one goes to listen for the sake of reconciliation, there is no offense.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "With every step taken toward going, it is a *duṣkṛta*; upon reaching the place where one hears [the talk], it is a *pāyattika*.
If one goes to listen in order to reform oneself, there is no offense."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If two bhikṣus are conversing privately inside a hall and another bhikṣu wishes to enter, he should snap his fingers or move his foot to make a sound.
If the people inside remain silent, he should turn back and leave. If they continue speaking without ceasing, it is no offense to enter.
Furthermore, if one bhikṣu is already sitting inside the hall while two other bhikṣus are conversing privately... [from here].
When a visitor arrives, the bhikṣu who is already seated should make a sound. If the visitor remains silent, the bhikṣu inside the hall should go out.

The same applies to those walking in front or behind. If a bhikṣu quarrels with another bhikṣu, harbors resentment, and utters such insults as, "I shall surely kill this wicked man," and the other bhikṣu hears this, he may say to him: "Please take care of yourself."
Vigilance. I have heard an evil report that certain visiting bhikṣus have made this statement:
"We shall steal from such-and-such a storehouse, such-and-such temple property, such-and-such food from the *śaikṣa*-kitchen, or the robes and bowls of such-and-such a person.

Upon hearing this, the administrative official (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) should remain silent and return to the midst of the Saṃgha to announce: "Venerable sirs, regarding such-and-such a storehouse, such-and-such temple property, such-and-such..."
The robes and bowls of such-and-such a person from the Sangha’s pure kitchen must be guarded. When I hear an evil sound, I shall cause you to know it beforehand.
If a bhikṣu has many disciples, he should inspect them at dusk to see whether they are acting according to the Dharma in their various rooms.

If he hears them speaking worldly talk, he must not immediately enter and reprimand them; rather, he should wait until they come to him of their own accord, and only then reprimand them, saying: "You..."
Having left the household life with a mind of equal faith and consuming the offerings of the faithful, one ought to practice seated meditation and recite the sūtras.

Why do you discuss worldly and unrighteous matters? This is not in accordance with the wholesome dharmas of one who has left the household life. If you hear the sūtras being expounded, you should listen to their meaning.
When engaging in questions and answers, one must not immediately enter into praise. One should wait until they have come of their own accord, and only then offer words of commendation.
You are able to discuss the sūtras together and explain their meanings, preaching upon the matters of the Buddha-dharma, just as the World-Honored One said when bhikṣus assemble.
One should practice two things: first, noble silence; second, discourse on the meaning of the Dharma.
This precept is established identically in the Mahāyāna.
The seventy-eighth: the precept against angrily striking a bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika. The origin story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Among the group of six bhikṣus, there was one bhikṣu.

Out of anger, [the Buddha] struck the seventeen bhikṣus. Those who were struck raised their voices and cried out loudly. When the other bhikṣus heard this, they became aware of it and censured him with disapproval.
They informed the Buddha, who then established this precept. This was formulated due to the incident involving companions and the affliction of intolerance;
it constitutes the fundamental category of the first section on killing.

**Exegesis:** "Not rejoicing" means that the mind is entangled by anger and resentment, such that a state of displeasure arises. The Vinaya states: "To strike" refers to using the hand, a stone, or a staff. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"To strike" refers to the body, its parts, or the preparatory acts of the body. "The body" refers to the entire body. "Parts of the body" refers to the hands, feet, elbows, knees, teeth, or nails—these are called the parts of the body.
"Preparatory acts of the body" refers to striking with a staff, wood, tiles, stones, or the like, or throwing them from a distance; these are called the preparatory acts of the body.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one strikes a bhikṣu with the hand, a stone, or a staff, it is a *pāyattika* in all cases.
Excluding the staff, hand, and stone, if one strikes him with anything else—such as a door-bolt, a curved hook, the handle of a whisk, or the handle of an incense burner—it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, there must be a mind of malice; second, one must personally carry out the beating;
and third, the person before one must be a bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; the same rule applies to bhikṣuṇīs (the training is identical for those of the same school).
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if one has an illness requiring someone to strike them; or if one is choking on food and requires striking on the spine;
or if one does not hear when spoken to and is touched so as to enable hearing; or during sleep, if one lies down upon another (where "lying" means placing oneself upon);
or if there is mutual contact while walking back and forth in meditation; or if the tip of a staff accidentally touches [another] while sweeping the ground; and so forth.
If [the offense] occurred before the precepts were first established and so forth, this constitutes no violation.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*: "Striking a śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts (i.e., a śrāmaṇera undergoing *śikṣamāṇa*)—whether he be blind, one-eyed, deaf, or mute—or striking a bhikṣu undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*, all constitute a *pāyattika* offense.
(Blindness refers to losing both eyes; being one-eyed is called "blind" [in this context]; being deaf refers to the loss of hearing.)

If one already has such a disease prior [to ordination], they are included among those with the sixteen minor prohibitions and may not receive the bhikṣu precepts. If, however, one has already received full ordination (upasaṃpadā) and subsequently develops this disease, they remain a bhikṣu. Such individuals as these should indeed be treated with compassion.

The *Mātṛkā* states: Striking three kinds of persons constitutes a *duṣkṛta*: namely, one who dwells as a thief (i.e., one who enters the Path with a thieving mind), one who was originally not in harmony (one who lacks a teacher or is hostile), and one who has originally violated the precepts (one who has committed the four *pārājika* offenses and lost the nature of a bhikṣu).
If one throws objects such as sand or beans at the assembly of bhikṣus, for every [bhikṣu] struck, one incurs that many *pāyattika* offenses; if they do not strike anyone, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

*Dūṣaṇa* (offense of wrong-doing). The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one strikes a person who possesses the appearance of a bhikṣu—whether they observe the precepts or have broken them—while perceiving them as a bhikṣu, or while harboring doubt regarding their status, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
This also applies if one perceives or suspects someone who is not a bhikṣu to be a bhikṣu."
If one strikes a pillar, a wall, or other objects with a distracted mind, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
However, there is no offense if one acts for the benefit of others without a mind of ill-will.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To strike any of the other three assemblies, or even an animal, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Sudarśana-vinaya* states: "If one strikes a woman with lustful intent, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: To strike a bhikṣuṇī constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; to strike any of the three other assemblies constitutes a *vinayātikrama*.

Even down to a layperson, it is a *vinayātikrama* requiring mental repentance (*cittavipratisāra*). If wicked elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, pigs, dogs, or the like approach, one must not strike them.
One may, however, take up a staff, wood, tile, or stone and strike the ground to create a terrifying appearance. If a domestic animal approaches...

Entering a stupa or monastery, one must not jostle or strike images, nor damage flowers, fruits, or trees; furthermore, one may use a staff, wood, tiles, or stones to strike the ground in order to frighten [wild animals] away.
This precept is equally established in the Mahāyāna. If one strikes back in retaliation for being struck, the offense constitutes a light defilement (*mṛdukalmāṣa*). If there is no provocation...
If one gives rise to anger, as well as the fetters of intense resentment and malice, and refuses to accept an apology when another seeks repentance, this constitutes a grave offense.
Since a bodhisattva ought to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings, how could he instead respond with anger and physical assault?
The seventy-ninth precept on striking a bhikṣu with anger:
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu with his hand, it is a pāyattika (the word "搏" is pronounced "bó").
The Origin: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The group of six monks struck the group of seventeen monks with their hands.
Those who were struck raised a loud cry. When the bhikṣus heard this, they inquired into the matter and reported it to the Buddha, who then established the precept.
This training rule was enacted because of the incident involving companions and due to the affliction of intolerance; it constitutes the first section on the root of killing.

This is the same category. Explanation of the meaning: "Brandishing" (po) means to gesture (yi). To gesture is to manifest a form or image; it refers to raising one's hand toward another to display the appearance of striking, thereby causing the other person to be terrified.

In the preceding precept, the mind’s original intention was actually to strike, and since the blow did not land on the body, the full offense was not incurred. In this precept, there was no such thought from the outset; one simply brandished the palm. By merely brandishing it, the full offense is incurred. This is why the two precepts differ, and thus they are formulated separately.
**Establishing the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if, out of anger and displeasure, one strikes a bhikṣu with the hand, it is a *pāyattika*.
Excluding the hand, if one strikes with a door-bolt, a whisk handle, a censer handle, or the like, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the presence of an angry mind toward another; second, the person before one is a bhikṣu...
If he strikes her body with his hands or feet three times, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for the *bhikṣu*;
the same rule applies to the *bhikṣuṇī*. For the *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is defined as an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if another person intends to strike you and you raise your hand to ward them off; if a fierce beast or a thief approaches;

if someone comes brandishing a weapon and you raise your hand to ward them off; furthermore, all instances where the act was not intentional, as well as cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept—these constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the act of exposing oneself: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that if one turns the palms of the hands or feet toward another, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one raises any other part of the body toward another, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one makes a threatening gesture with the hand that reaches [the victim], it is a *pāyattika*;

if it does not reach, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one forms the intention to strike and makes a threatening gesture with the hand, at the very moment the hand is first raised, one incurs the full offense (*mūla-āpatti*).
If one raises the hand toward many bhikṣus, the offense is incurred according to the number of persons; if [one acts] toward a bhikṣu..."
When cowherds harbor resentment toward one another, one should go to them and seek their forgiveness (*kṣamāpanā*).
One must not go to seek an apology while the anger in one's heart has not yet subsided.
Nor should they act like a lion, maintaining a stubborn and rigid mind and refusing to grant mutual forbearance. If they are unwilling to endure it, one should dispatch a wise person to mediate.
One should immediately reconcile them and swiftly cause the dispute to cease. A junior monk should go to the side of the angry bhikṣu;
upon reaching his personal space (*śeṣa-bhāga*), he should prostrate to him and say, "May you be free from illness.

When seeing bhikṣus engaged in quarreling, one should mediate and resolve it without taking sides. One should not go to look at a place where laypeople are fighting, for fear of being drawn in as a witness.
Therefore, as stated above, those who do not act in accordance with this will all incur *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Regarding the gravity of this precept in the Mahāyāna, it is as explained above.
This is the eightieth: the precept against groundlessly accusing another of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense out of anger.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger, slanders another with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The group of six bhikṣus, out of anger, slandered the group of seventeen bhikṣus with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who then established this precept. This is a rule of essential nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

Regarding the offense: because [the Buddha] could not endure the afflictions arising from those who practice the holy life together with him, he established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*). This belongs to the category of the fundamental types of lying in the first section.

**Explanation of the Meaning:** The Vinaya states that there are three "bases" (*mūla*): namely, what has been seen, heard, or suspected. This is as explained in the section on the thirteen matters (*trayodaśa-vastu*).

(The difference between them is this: there, one slanders another with the four *pārājika* offenses on groundless charges; here, one slanders by means of each individual item among the thirteen matters.)
Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, if one speaks and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the other person must be a bhikṣu; second, one must personally harbor a mind of anger.
Third, to slander [a monk] with groundless charges of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; fourth, to speak such words clearly.

These rules apply concurrently to *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom they constitute a *pāyattika* (the same rule applies to those of common training). For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if the basis of seeing, hearing, or suspecting is such that one speaks the truth with the intent to cause repentance and without slandering;
or if speaking in jest, speaking to oneself, speaking in a dream, intending to say this but mistakenly saying that;
or in cases such as when the precept has not yet been established—these constitute no offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: To slander a bhikṣu is a *pāyattika*; to slander a bhikṣuṇī is a *sthūlātyaya* (this *sthūlātyaya* is lighter than a *pāyattika*);
to slander any of the other three assemblies is a *vinayātikrama*; to slander a layperson is a *vinayātikrama* with mental regret (*cittavipratisāra*).
This precept is established equally in the Mahāyāna. To speak [of one's faults] to a fellow practitioner constitutes a light offense; to speak of them to an outsider constitutes a grave offense.
The eighty-first: the precept against entering the palace gates without authorization.
If a bhikṣu enters the residence of a Kṣatriya king of the water-sprinkling lineage while the king has not yet gone out and the treasures have not yet been stored away,
and he crosses the threshold of the palace gate, it is a pāyattika.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī. At that time, Queen Mallikā paid homage to the Buddha and heard the Dharma.

Having attained the realization of the fruit [of stream-entry], she exhorted King Prasenajit until he gained faith and joy, permitting the bhikṣus to enter and leave the palace gates without obstruction. When Kālodāyin went on his almsround, he entered the royal palace in succession.
At that time, the king and his consort were lying together during the day. When the consort saw him approaching from afar, she immediately rose and adjusted her robe;
as she did so, the robe she was wearing brushed against the seat, causing him to sit down. The consort, having lost her garment and being left exposed, crouched down in shame.
The Venerable One returned to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣus: "The foremost treasure of King Prasenajit is now..."
Everyone saw this. The bhikṣus interrogated the Venerable One, and having learned of his conduct, they censured him and informed the Buddha, who then established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).

This was because [the monk] had gone to the royal palace, which led to criticism regarding the affliction of lust. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Udāyin had a reason to go to the lady Mallikā’s quarters; he entered the palace too early."
**Exegesis:** The section beginning with "If a bhikṣu" clarifies the scope of the conduct [in question]. The section beginning with "If he passes beyond" establishes the offense incurred.
The Vinaya states: Regarding a Kṣatriya of the water-sprinkling royal lineage, when he succeeds to the throne, he takes water from the four great oceans and the horn of a white bull;
he collects all manner of seeds, fills [the horn] with them, and places it upon a golden palanquin.
Above, the various minor kings carry the king on a palanquin, where he sits together with the first queen.
The great Brahmin pours water upon the crown of the king’s head. If he is of the Kṣatriya caste, water is poured upon his head;

thus is the king established, and for this reason he is called a "Kṣatriya King Consecrated by Water. [Regarding] the "Consecrated Lineage" (Kṣatriya—this means "Lord of the Field": at the beginning of the kalpa, there was a person of virtue whom the multitude established [as ruler]).
He divided the fields and lands for the sake of the multitude; because he was noble and possessed sovereign power, they inherited him as their clan name.

If he were of the Brahmin caste, the Vaiśya caste, or the Śūdra caste, he would be consecrated with water and thus established as king, also known as a Kṣatriya king of the "water-sprinkled head" lineage.
As for "not yet emerged": the king has not yet emerged, the court ladies have not yet returned to their original places, and the treasures have not yet been concealed.
Gold, silver, pearls, tridacna shells, agate, crystal, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, and all manner of precious jewels and necklaces had not yet been put away.

(The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The various wives took turns serving as night-watchmen for the king. At that time, Queen Mallikā wore a garment of pearl netting beneath her, and over it a garment of polished mother-of-pearl.")

The inner body is externally revealed, as when one has spent the night with a king and immediately puts on these robes. "Not yet having hidden the treasure" means not yet having hidden these ornaments. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* says:

When the king has already gone outside but the queen has not yet risen, at the time of their union, the precious robes she wears are light and translucent, revealing the inner body from the outside to arouse desire; because she has not yet hidden these robes, it is called "not yet having hidden the treasure. Furthermore, women are the "treasure" of men; if the queen has not yet covered her body with other garments, this is also called "not yet having hidden the treasure.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "Treasure" refers to things held in high esteem, as well as the beauty of women—all such things are termed "treasure."
Regarding the offense: among these, if the king has not yet departed and the treasure has not yet been concealed, and one crosses the threshold, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is outside and one foot is inside, and one forms the intention to leave, or if one has made an appointment to go but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Except for the case of a Kṣatriya king, if one enters the homes of other minor local kings, powerful nobles, or wealthy elders,
and crosses their thresholds, it is entirely a duṣkṛta offense.

This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, it must be within the palace of a great king; second, the king has not yet departed and the treasures have not yet been stored away;
third, it must be at the gate of the inner quarters; and fourth, both feet must have entered inside.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; the same rule applies to bhikṣuṇīs (the same training for those of equal training).
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if the king has already departed; if the court ladies have returned to their original quarters;
if all precious treasures have been removed and stored away; if one has something to report or petition; if one has been summoned; if one is taken away by force;
if there is a threat to life; if there is a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or if it concerns cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precepts—these constitute non-offenses.
Regarding the threshold, the *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: There are three kinds of thresholds: first, the threshold of a city gate;
second, the threshold of a royal palace gate; and third, the threshold of the inner harem gate. Entering the first two gates incurs an *āpatti-duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing);

entering the inner harem gate incurs a *pārājika* offense (a grave offense involving expulsion). (*Kun*, the threshold, refers to the short crossbar placed between the two doorposts on either side of a doorway; its meaning is identical to that of *yǔ*.)
This precept is established by the Mahāyāna as well; it is especially something to be observed with caution in the final age. Even if one is summoned or invited, one should not enter hastily.
However, there is no offense if one possesses great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and majestic virtue (*tejas*).
Appendix: Examination of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that there are ten kinds of faults for entering a royal palace.
First, if the king and his consort are staying in one place, when a bhikṣu enters, the consort may smile, which causes the king to immediately become suspicious.
Is it not that the bhikṣu has committed a base and evil deed in a private, secluded place? If this were not so, for what reason would he be seen laughing?
Or perhaps he had the intention to commit an evil act. Second, when the bhikṣu entered the palace, the queen became pregnant;
the king then gave rise to this thought: "Is it not that the bhikṣu engaged in unwholesome conduct with her, causing her to become pregnant? Third...
First, when the bhikṣu enters the palace, the king loses precious treasures and various kinds of jewels;

Seventh, when a bhikṣu enters the palace, a high-ranking and influential minister who has been dismissed from his position thinks to himself:
"Is it not because the bhikṣu has slandered me to the king that I have fallen into this undesirable situation?
Eighth, when a low-ranking minister is granted a great reward by the king, people say in discussion: "Is it not because of the bhikṣu..."
The bhikṣu acted as his intermediary. Ninth, when the king frequently went forth with his army to campaign against other kingdoms, everyone discussed it, saying:
"Is it not because the bhikṣu has been deliberating with the king that he repeatedly causes us to be exhausted by military expeditions?
Tenth, when the bhikṣu entered the palace while the king was away on a campaign, he told the warriors: "Whatever is obtained [in battle], all of it..."

[The property] belonged to them personally. Later, once [the rebellion] was suppressed, the King reclaimed it. The people discussed this, saying, "This is a bhikṣu who instructed the King to seize our property.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "For this reason, you should not enter the inner palace at will, lest the fourfold army lose its peace and security. This is not something a bhikṣu ought to do."
The eighty-second precept concerning the handling of precious objects:
If a bhikṣu takes hold of a jewel or a jeweled ornament, or causes another to take hold of it, except within a monastery or a lodging place, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu takes hold of one within a monastery or a lodging place, [there is no offense].
"O Jewel! If it is adorned with jewels, whether you take it up yourself or instruct another to take it up, you should form this thought: 'If there is an owner who recognizes it, they shall take it.
You should act on such grounds and no others."

The Origin Story: This precept was established in three stages. While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī, there were disciples of non-Buddhist sects who, while traveling along the road, stopped to rest by the roadside and departed after leaving behind a bag containing a thousand pieces of gold.
Later, a large number of bhikṣus arrived and also stopped to rest by the same roadside; they saw this bag of gold and said to one another:
"Take this for now; if there is anyone who recognizes it as his own, he shall return for it. He traveled several *li* when he remembered and hurried back.
He immediately took the bag out and gave it to him, but the man instead claimed it was insufficient. He went to inform King Prasenajit, who investigated and confirmed its falsity.

The king then confiscated the man's household wealth along with the gold, transferring them to the state treasury. Those who delight in studying the precepts and possess a sense of shame and remorse heard of this and came to know of it.
The monks were censured, saying: "How can one take gold and silver with one's own hands, causing a layperson to be punished by the authorities and having their family property confiscated?
Because of this, they informed the Buddha; this was the first establishment of a precept.

At that time, Visākhā Mātṛ entered the Jetavana monastery, removed her necklaces and ornaments, and placed them beneath a tree before going to pay homage to the World-Honored One. The Buddha preached for her.

The Dharma. With his mind fixed on the Dharma, he forgot to take [the items] and returned home. When a bhikṣu saw this, he feared he had committed a transgression of the precepts and did not take them, reporting the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha permitted that if one sees abandoned property within a saṃghārāma, it should be taken up for the sake of preventing its loss.
Furthermore, the phrase "within a saṃghārāma" was added; this was the second formulation of the precept. Moreover, the assembly...
While traveling along a road, a number of bhikṣus arrived at an uninhabited village and took up lodging in an empty workshop belonging to a craftsman.
At that time, the craftsman had placed both finished and unfinished gold and silver items in the workshop before departing.
For the sake of guarding them, the bhikṣus remained awake throughout the entire night. The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
When staying overnight in another's house, if there are items within the dwelling, one should collect and secure them so that they are not lost;
furthermore, the addition of the phrase "at the place where one stays" constitutes the third formal precept.
This is a prohibitive offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya), established as a training rule to restrain the affliction of greed regarding precious objects.

Exegesis: The text is divided into two sections. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards clarifies the original formulation of the rule (*prātimokṣa*). The section beginning with "Except for monasteries (*saṃghārāma*)...

clarifies the subsequent permissions (*anujñā*). The Vinaya states: "Precious things" refers to gold, silver, pearls, amber, *śukti*, agate, *musāragalva*, lapis lazuli, shells, jade, and wrought or unwrought gold.
"Ornaments" refers to copper, iron, lead, tin, and white bronze. By means of these...

"Jewel" (*ratna*) refers to adornments. (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Items of the jewel category refers to various weapons such as bows and swords, as well as musical instruments such as drums and flutes.

"Saṃghārāma" (translated here as "Garden of the Community") is as explained above; it is also translated as "Community Courtyard. "Courtyard" (*āra*) is a term following the conventions of this land, being a name for a residence, a garden, or a pavilion. As for the current designation of monastic dwellings as "temples" (*si*), "temple" is also a public administrative term in this land referring to the residences of feudal lords.

When Western monks first arrived, they temporarily stayed at the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu Si*). Later, they built the Baima Monastery (*Baima Jingśe*) and requested to reside there. Although their place of residence was later moved, they retained the title "Temple" (*Si*) to commemorate their original site.

From this time forward, these were all called *si* (temples). Regarding "those who stay as guests" (*ji su chu*), this refers to lodging in the houses of laypeople (*bai yi*). As for the phrase "one should form this thought," etc., this correctly clarifies the meaning of the provisional allowance (*sui kai*).

That is to say, whether in a monastic temple or when staying as a guest, although one is permitted to personally handle or have others handle gold, silver, and the seven treasures, one must first maintain this mindfulness: "I shall not harbor even the slightest heart of greedy attachment; if a master comes and recognizes them, I will give them back to him, and only then shall I take them.

The phrase "for such causes and conditions and no others" means that apart from the cause and condition of forming such a thought and returning [the items] to their owners, there are no other [permissible reasons].
There is no other expedient means by which one may seize it).
Regarding the offense: herein, if one seizes it oneself or instructs another to seize it, it is a *pāyattika*.
Whether in a monastery or within a layperson’s house, if one seizes it oneself or instructs another to seize it—whether it be a jewel or an object adorned with jewels—it is an offense.
Seize it. Examine the characteristics of the bag and the vessel: the characteristic of being enveloped by consciousness, the characteristic of being bound by consciousness.

One should untie the bag and examine it to know how many parts are joined together, how many are not yet joined, how many are square, how many are round, and how many are old or new. If there should be anyone seeking [to buy] it, [one may sell it].
One should ask them, "What does your object resemble? If it corresponds, one should return it;

[Regarding] all *duṣkṛta* offenses:
this precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, it must be genuine material consisting of the seven treasures or ornaments made of those treasures.
Second, there is no opening for an exemption. Third, taking it up oneself or instructing another to take it up constitutes an offense.
This rule applies equally to *bhikṣuṇīs* (a *pāyattika*, with the same regulation and training). For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. These are the offenses.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if it concerns the collection of ornaments for the worship of stūpas or temples for the sake of preservation;
or if it pertains to the period prior to the initial promulgation of the precepts—these constitute cases of no offense.

Regarding the rules for gathering [precious objects], the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one takes hold of various precious objects with one's own hand, or causes another to take hold of them, if they have already been polished and treated, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if they have not yet been polished and treated, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This applies even to taking hold of imitation lapis lazuli."
It is also an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) if one grasps ornaments for adorning the body; in all such cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* (falling offense).
Even if one grasps a garland made from barley stalks, it is an *dukkaṭa*. If one grasps various musical instruments, such as the lute (*vīṇā*) or conch shells, [it is likewise an offense].
If there are strings and frets, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. Even for a single-stringed lute made of bamboo, holding it constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
If various conch shells are fit to be blown, grasping them incurs a *pāyattika*; if they are unfit to be blown, one also incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding all musical instruments, whether fit or unfit [for use], the gravity of the offense incurred is the same. If...
When grasping a bow: if it has a string and a notch, one incurs the offense of a *pārājika* (or *sthūlātyaya*, depending on the context); if it lacks these, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
If a sword has a blade or an arrow has a point, one incurs the full offense; otherwise, it is an *dukkaṭa*.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: To handle counterfeit pearls is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding gold, silver, precious floors, couches, and seats in the human realm, a bhikṣu should neither walk upon nor sit upon them.
Regarding gold, silver, precious floors, couches, and seats in the heavenly realms, a bhikṣu may sit upon and use them.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "One should not eat from a precious vessel.

Whether going to the heavens or to the dragon palaces, if there are no other miscellaneous vessels available, one may even take and use a precious golden vessel; this is permitted because there are no other miscellaneous vessels.

However, if one is in the human realm, where vessels are mostly made of clay or tile, it is strictly prohibited. Even if one has attained the state of a true noble one (ārya) who is free from outflows (anāsrava), one must still observe the Buddha’s regulations, for [the distinction between] ordinary beings and noble ones..."
Because they follow the same path).
The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one uses a moonstone or a sunstone to produce water or fire, there is no offense even through physical contact.
This precept, in the Mahāyāna, is for the sake of sentient beings; it does not depend on the location, but is determined solely by the capacity and circumstances of the individual.
Citation: The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: While the Buddha was at Vulture Peak, he entered the city to beg for alms and encountered a heavy rain.
The water swept away the cliffs and caused them to collapse, revealing a hidden treasure. He addressed Ānanda, saying, "You should observe that this is a great, harmful poison.
Ānanda replied, "Truly, it is a fearsome poison. A man gathering roots and fruits heard of this and went to see it; having seen it...
Regarding the hidden treasure, he thought to himself: "May this poisonous venom always sting me; I shall not shrink from the pain even for my parents, wife, children, and kinsmen.
He then took it all back home and used it as he pleased. When King Ajātaśatru saw his great wealth and prosperity, [he became envious].
A messenger was sent to inquire: "In what place did you obtain the king’s hidden treasure? He replied, "I did not obtain it. They seized him and brought him before the king.
When the king questioned him himself, he likewise said, "I did not obtain it. The king then acted according to the law, having his kinsmen bound and delivering him to the executioners.
That man wept with grief as he followed the executioners, crying out in a loud voice: "Ānanda, this is..."
"Poisonous harm! This is indeed poisonous harm! Having been brought before the executioner, he spoke these words. According to the law, the matter must be reported back to the King.

The King then summoned him back and questioned him. The man related the details of his past karmic conditions in full. At that time, the King had recently begun to have faith in the Buddha-Dharma; unconsciously, tears flowed from his eyes, and he declared:
"Because you encountered the World-Honored One and obtained these precious treasures, although your crime deserved death, I now release you along with your retinue.
You should take these goods and offer them to the Buddha and the Sangha. Having been granted this pardon, he prepared superior offerings and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he immediately attained the first fruit of enlightenment (*srotāpanna*). For this reason, it was not permitted for bhikṣus to handle precious objects.

Appendix: Examination. The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "If one sees another's property outside the monastery, one should cover it over with leaves, grass, or the like to ensure it is concealed.
One should not regard this as an act of negligence or abandonment. If the owner comes to claim it, one should take it back to one's residence."
If one privately takes up an item and for seven or eight days no one comes to claim it, it should be deposited in the monastic storehouse.
If after five or six months still no one comes to claim it, it should be used for the benefit of the Saṃgha by purchasing durable utensils.

If the original owner later comes to claim it, one should exhort them to donate the item to the Saṃgha. If they are unwilling to donate it, one should repay them the original value. If they demand interest, [it should be paid].
One should tell them: "In accordance with the precepts established by the Buddha, we return this object to you; it is improper for you to further demand interest upon it.
