"Venerable sir, if you do not establish the precepts, you are not even able to see this object, let alone obtain it.
If, even after this, you still do not understand, you should take him to a lay follower (upāsaka) and say:
'I originally possessed only this much, which I have now returned in its entirety; yet now I am being falsely accused. At that time, the lay follower should rebuke him, saying:"
"Son, you have already received more than enough of these goods. Yet now you go so far as to slander the bhikṣus. You may leave;
I shall act as your adversary to adjudicate this matter. If it is a precious object and no one comes to claim it, let it remain as above for three years.
Then, according to the place where it was obtained, it shall be used within that boundary. If it should nonetheless cause schism in the Saṃgha..."
Regarding the repair of a cell, stupa, or courtyard: if one uncovers a treasure while digging the earth, the *karmadāna* (lay attendant) is not to be trusted.
One should inform the King; if the King requires it, he should give it [to the monastery], or if it is offered as a gift, it should be used.

Even if it has already been used, should the King learn of this and demand it back, one should request that the property of the stupa or the property of the Sangha be returned. If there is a trustworthy *karmadāna*, one may take [the treasure] and set it aside for three years.
This concludes [the section on] using [proceeds] for the construction of stūpas or for the affairs of the Saṃgha as described above.
If there is an iron seal upon a treasure cache bearing a name, one should likewise answer truthfully. The same applies to property obtained from the construction of new monastic dwellings.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: If a lost treasure is found within a monastery, for the sake of its protection, when one is about to depart, it should be entrusted to someone who knows the Dharma and fears transgression, with the instruction:
"If the owner comes to claim it, you must return it. If no owner appears after a long time, it may be used by the Sangha.
Should the owner later come to claim it, one should lead them to show the monastic quarters and say: "This was the property of a donor. If...
One must not grant permission to enter. If one wishes for [the donor] to obtain the original [merit], one should speak to a faithful lay devotee and extensively exhort them.
The eighty-third precept: Entering a village at an improper time.
If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
The Origin Story: This training rule was established in two stages. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Upananda entered a village at an improper time and played dice with several householders. The householders, being defeated and driven by stinginess and envy, said:
"A bhikṣu enters a village in the early morning for the sake of alms; he enters a village at an improper time [for other purposes]."
"For what reason? When the bhikṣus heard this, they censured and reproached Baddhananda and reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.

This was the first establishment of a precept. Furthermore, because there were among the bhikṣus those who had business for the Saṃgha, business for the stūpa or monastery, or business such as attending to the sick, the Buddha permitted them to enter a village after having entrusted their affairs; therefore, the rule against entering without entrusting [one's affairs] was added.

[The Buddha] spoke. This was the second rule established for the sake of discipline. Because entering a village had invited the censure and slander of the laity, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was enacted.
**Explanation of the Meaning:** The *Vinaya* states: "Proper time" (*kāla*) refers to the period from when the first light of dawn appears until midday.

"Improper time" (*akāla*) refers to the period from after midday until the first light of dawn has not yet appeared (the *Vinayavibhaṅga* states that there are two divisions of improper time: first, past noon; second, before the first light of dawn). "Village" (*grāma*) has four [types].
The types of villages are as described above. Regarding "not informing a bhikṣu" (which means not notifying other bhikṣus):
if there are matters concerning the Saṃgha, the stūpa, or attending to the sick, one should entrust one's affairs to another bhikṣu before departing.

If one is staying alone in a single room, one should entrust one's affairs to a neighboring room. The entrustment should be performed in this manner: go to a bhikṣu, assume the proper demeanor, and say: "Venerable One..."
He reflects thus: "I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, shall enter a village at an improper time and go to such-and-such a house in such-and-such a town or village.
The person before him replies, "So be it."

**The Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one enters a village at an improper time without having made an announcement, the moment the first foot crosses the threshold of the village gate, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is inside the gate and one foot is outside the gate, or if one makes the effort to go but does not go, or if one intends not to go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept constitutes a full offense only when four conditions are met: first, the mind is heedless; second, the time has already passed midday;
third, there is no valid reason for not having announced one's arrival; and fourth, one has already entered the village.
If a monk administers [the punishment] to a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika (for both, the rule is the same for those who study together).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions where there is no offense: if the path passes through a village; if one has something to announce; if one is summoned; if one has accepted an invitation;
if one is seized by force; if one is bound and led away; if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya);
or if the precept has not yet been established—these constitute cases of no offense.

Regarding the procedure for formal announcement (*jñapti*): the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that "other bhikṣus" refers to those seen with the eyes (all such announcements must be made face-to-face with the person concerned to be valid;
hence the phrase "seen with the eyes"). If, after the announcement has been made, one enters a village and then returns to the place of residence, it is considered as having already been announced.
Furthermore, if one enters a village without [first] informing [another monk], it is a *pāyattika*.

If one enters a village without having informed [another] and passes through any number of large or small alleys, for each such alley traversed, there is a *dukkaṭa*. For each house of a layperson entered, there is a *pāyattika*.
However, if any of the eight calamities (*aṣṭā-vighnāni*) arises, there is no offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If a monastery is located outside a village, to leave the monastery without informing others and reach the city gate constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If two bhikṣus are dwelling in an *araṇya* (forest hermitage) and wish to travel, they must inform one another in succession."
If one person has already announced their departure and another person subsequently wishes to depart, they should inform the other bhikṣus.
If there are no other bhikṣus, they should form this thought: "When I see a bhikṣu on the road, at a gate, or near a village, I shall inform him.
Having made this announcement, they may then enter.

The *Mātṛkā* states: "If there are no bhikṣus, one should inform a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā" (this means that if one encounters these three groups of nuns, one may inform them; it does not mean specifically going to a nunnery to inform them).
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If there are no bhikṣus, one may entrust [the food] to another layperson (referring to a temple attendant who is a 'pure person') without offense.
This precept is studied identically in the Mahāyāna."
The eighty-fourth precept on making high beds:
If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Tathāgata, excluding the space for the mortise holes at the base.
If they exceed this height, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Kālodāyin, having foreknown that the World-Honored One would surely come by this path, immediately prepared a high and fine seat upon the road and invited the Buddha to view it.
The Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and said to them: "This foolish man harbors evil within; he has prepared a high and vast seat."
Regarding the bed: [the Buddha] rebuked Kāḷudāyin for acting solely for his own sake and established a precept for the community.
Due to the matter of bedding and the affliction of arrogance and indulgence, he formulated this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states that there are five kinds of beds: beds with curved legs, beds with straight legs, beds with bent legs, beds with removable legs, and legless beds.

Regarding "the eight finger-breadths of the Tathāgata" (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The eight finger-breadths of the Tathāgata mean that one finger-breadth of the Tathāgata is two *cun*").

"Except for the part that enters the step-hole above" (meaning: excluding the leg of the bed which enters the wooden step; it is eight finger-widths high from below). "Having finished cutting" (meaning:

having measured [the leg] to exceed eight finger-widths, one must cut it off before using it). "If it exceeds" (meaning: if it is higher than eight finger-widths, it does not conform to the prescribed regulation).
Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, if one commits it oneself or instructs another to do so and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one commits it oneself or instructs another to do so and it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, arrogance and self-indulgence; second, excessive attachment to the object;
and third, the completion of the bed.
This also applies to *bhikṣuṇīs* (a *pāyattika* offense), as well as *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs* (the same rule applies).
For a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if the feet are eight finger-breadths high; if they are less than eight finger-breadths;
if another has already offered them and one cuts them to use; if the feet have been removed; or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established. This is the [explanation].
There is no offense.

The third section states: "Except for a jeweled couch, one should sit on any other [seat] in the house of a layperson" (the custom in the countries of the Western Regions is that there are no chairs or benches;
one simply sits cross-legged upon small couches. As for the term "jeweled," this refers to those used by kings, high ministers, and elders).
Regarding the proper procedure for cutting [the hair], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should cut it and then repent. If one has not yet cut it, the Saṃgha should order him to do so;
if they do not order him, he shall not comply. In all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: If one receives the gift of a high bed, one should form this thought: "This bed is not in accordance with the Dharma;
I shall cut it down. If one accepts it without forming such a thought, it is a *pāyattika*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one sits upon it oneself for the entire day, it is one *pāyattika*.
If one rises and then sits again, each instance constitutes a *pāyattika*. If one sits upon another’s bed, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If a visiting bhikṣu arrives and, in the course of receiving assignments, obtains an oversized bed, he should say to the administrator: "Lend me a saw."
Question: What should be done? Answer: It is said that this bed exceeds the prescribed measurements. One wishes to cut it down to the proper size.

If [the donor] says, "Do not cut it," and the donor sees this and becomes displeased, then if [the monastery] will not remain there for long, one should dig into the ground and bury the legs so they reach the proper height. If [the monastery] will remain there for a long time, [one should leave them as they are].
One should bury [the legs] level with the ground; wooden tubes may be used to encase the legs so that they do not rot.
If one is sitting on a high-legged chair at a donor’s house, one must not sit with the legs dangling; one should request a footstool, or seek out bricks or wood to support the feet.

If one sits on a high chair within a *puṇya-śālā* (a hall for merit), there is no offense—this is because such a place is established to protect the feelings of others, and thus it is permitted accordingly.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The reason this does not constitute a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense is that it has been cut short.
Having been cut to the proper measurement, one must confess before the Saṃgha."
This precept is shared with the Mahāyāna.
Precept 85: Regarding the Use of Cotton Down for Mattresses.
If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed, a wooden bed, or a large or small mattress stuffed with cotton down, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six monks made beds and large or small cushions stuffed with cotton wool.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized them, saying, "They have no heart of compassion; they are like kings and ministers who take the lives of living beings.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. This also arose from matters concerning bedding and furniture, as well as pride.
Because [monks] were indulging in afflictions, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established.
Explanation of the meaning: The *Vinaya* states that "cotton wool" (*tūla*) refers to the flowers of the white poplar tree, the willow tree, or the *pūtīka* plant (cotton wool is also called *dūla*;

*dūra* is the name of a tree; the wool grows from the tree, hence the name is established, similar to what is called "willow down"). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (*Sapoduo lun*) states: "Cotton wool is a type of grass."

"Wood-Flower Cotton" (*tūla*) is a general term for [cotton down] (as the *Vinaya* explains it by citing the white poplar flower and other such sources). Regarding "storing": the *Vinayaviniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that this refers to spreading the cotton upon a bed and then using a single-layered cloth (*kaṭhina*) to cover it as appropriate.
A "large cushion" is for the purpose of sitting and reclining; a "small cushion" is for the purpose of sitting alone. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* states:

"Tūla cotton is forbidden because it is an item possessed by persons of high status, because it is loathed by people, and because it readily breeds insects. Furthermore, if one lies upon something soft and warm, one will later suffer from cold; moreover, it becomes coarse and hard, making it unbearable. For these reasons, it is prohibited and not permitted."
Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, if one acts oneself or instructs another to act and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) for both.

If one acts oneself or instructs another to act but it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for both. If one acts on behalf of another and it is completed or not completed, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the presence of a mind of pride, greed, arrogance, or haughtiness; second, the material being *tūla* cotton;
third, the act of storing it oneself or having another do so; and fourth, the completion of the storage.
If a bhikṣu commits this offense, it is a pāyattika; the same rule applies to a bhikṣuṇī (they share the same training).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a dukkaṭa. This constitutes an offense.
Exemptions from offense: if it is *kaurava* grass, *muñja* grass, or *śāṇa* grass;
or if one uses wool, cotton, or tattered rags; or if it is used as a shoulder-support; or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established.
This constitutes no offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If one sits, for every sitting there is a *pāyattika*; if one lies down, for every lying down there is a *pāyattika*.
If another offers [the seat] and one accepts it, there is a *pāyattika*. One must first abandon [the seat] and then perform the confession (*deśanā*). If...
Not so; the offense is likewise grave.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One must tear it out and destroy it, and only then repent of the transgression. If it has not yet been destroyed, the Saṃgha should issue an order for it to be destroyed."
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one scatters or stores cotton wool (*tūla*) and the like upon a private bed or seat belonging to the Saṃgha, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
The stuffing must be removed, and the offense must be confessed. When confessing the offense before another, that person should be asked:
'Has the stuffing been removed? If one does not ask this, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one stores a pillow to support the head or the feet, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*. If one is ill, there is no offense.
This precept is studied identically in the Mahāyāna."

The character *zhí* (挃) is pronounced *zhì*. It means to strike or push. Specifically, it refers to touching or poking with one's fingers.
*Yù* (pronounced *hé*) refers to the threshold; it denotes the horizontal beam at the bottom of a door that serves as the boundary for the inner gate.
*Gé* (pronounced *há*) refers to a small gate within the interior.
*Lian* (pronounced with the third tone) refers to a carriage pulled by people walking; it is called a *lian* because it is drawn by men as they travel.
It is a type of carriage.
*Chu* (pronounced *chu*) means to degrade or dismiss.
*Tíng*: the sound of *tíng*. It refers to the stalk of a herb.
*Zàn*: the sound of *zàn*. It refers to a bowstring.
*Shù*: the sound of *shù*. It means sharpness; it is now used for the arrowhead.
There are briefly four types of *pāṭala* trees. The leaves of the white *pāṭala* are round, like the skin of a pear;
its white wood resembles that of the willow, hence it is named the "white willow. The leaves of the green *pāṭala* are long, while those of the red *pāṭala* turn crimson when the frost descends.
The grain and texture are also red. The nature of yellow-ash wood (*huángyángmù*) is hard and compact, making it difficult to grow.
"Willow flowers" refers to the drooping branches of the slender willow. The *Bencao* states that the upright wood reaches a height of about ten feet.
Withering in autumn and flourishing in spring, there are those that initially produce yellow stamens; as the flower gradually dries, the downy fluff emerges, which is called willow-cotton (*liùxiù*).
People collect it to use as bedding or cushions. Beneath the fluff are black seeds that fly along with the cotton.
Wherever they encounter moisture, they immediately take root; if they fly into a pond or pool, they grow in dark, shaded places as floating plants.
Water-moss (ping). People often place it in a vessel filled with water and submerge cotton絮 therein; after several days, it covers the surface and forms a thick layer.
It can also be woven into felt to serve as a substitute for wool. It is extremely soft and exceptionally cool, making it suitable for infants to sleep upon, owing to its cooling nature.
"Pútái-huā" (蒲臺華) is also called "púlí-huā" (蒲梨華). "Pú" (蒲) should be written as "pú" (蒱), and "tái" (臺) should be written as "tái" (薹);
it refers to the *vatsaka* grass.
"Chán" (禪) has the pronunciation "dān"; it refers to a garment that has no lining.
The *kaurava* grass has not yet been translated [into Chinese].
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* refers to it as *mañjaka* grass, while the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* calls it *mañju* grass;
these are all one and the same.
*Sāpā* grass, also called *pāpā* grass, is extremely soft; it is translated as "greasy" (*ni*). It supports the shoulders;
"supporting" (*zhi*) is synonymous with a "cushion" (*jian*).
