Chapter Eighty-six: Making Bone, Ivory, or Horn Needle Cases.
If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, having hollowed it out and polished it smooth, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a craftsman who was devoted to the faith;
he made needle-cases from bone, ivory, and horn for the bhikṣus. Because of this, he neglected his household business until his wealth and property were completely exhausted.

They no longer possessed clothing or food. The people of the world criticized them, saying that by seeking blessings they had instead obtained calamity. A monk possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, having heard of this, informed the Buddha.
Due to the matter of the needle cases and the resulting affliction of public censure, he established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).

Explanation of Terms: *The Maker*: (Whether making it oneself or having another make it). *Bone, Ivory, or Horn*: (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Bone" refers to the bones of elephants, horses, oxen, camels, dragons, and so forth.

"Ivory" refers to the tusks of elephants, fish, pigs, and so forth. "Horn" refers to the horns of oxen, rhinoceroses, deer, sheep, and so forth). *Needle Case*: (This is one of the six personal requisites of a bhikṣu. There are two types of construction: first, the cylindrical form; [second, the flat form]).

The two combined forms: if one uses the three aforementioned types [of materials] to create these two forms, it is not permitted in all cases. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "There are two kinds of needle-cases that should be kept: first, reed; second, iron. Furthermore, there are those made from one's own resources that should be kept, namely:

copper, iron, stone, and red copper. Regarding "hollowing out and scraping": "hollowing out" (*kū*) refers to cutting open the interior to make it empty; "scraping" (*ka*) refers to planing and shaving the exterior to polish its surface.
Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, if one commits it oneself or instructs another and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) in all cases.
Whether one does it oneself or instructs another to do it, if it is attempted but not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) in all cases.
This precept fulfills three conditions before the full offense is established: first, there must be a mind of greedy attachment; second, the object must be bone, ivory, or horn;
third, it must be completed and put to use.
This also governs the *bhikṣuṇī*s (who commit a *duṣkṛta* offense under the same rule but with different training), as well as *śikṣamāṇā*s, *śrāmaṇera*s, and *śrāmaṇerī*s.
For a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exemptions: there is no offense if one uses iron, copper, lead, tin, pewter, bamboo, wood, reeds, or grass;
or if it is the very first instance before the precept was established. These cases constitute no offense.
Regarding the timing for confession, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should confess after having broken [the saṃgha]; if one has not yet broken the saṃgha, one should be commanded to do so.
The *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One should smash [the offense] and then declare it while confessing. The person being confronted should ask as follows:
Have you broken the needle case? If one does not ask this, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Because it is a minor object, it is not included among the thirty matters; furthermore, it ought to be broken.
If one returns it to the owner and the owner does not accept it, or if one gives it to another, it will cause distress; if one gives it to the Saṃgha, it is contrary to the Dharma."
This is indeed a matter of censure and abandonment.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
Appendix: Examination of the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "One who keeps a needle case should store it securely. If there is a bhikṣu who lacks a sense of shame and remorse..."
One should not lend [these items] to novices or those who have not yet received full ordination. However, they may be lent to those capable of caring for them well.
One should store needles and knives; fearing that iron will develop rust, they should be wrapped in waxed cloth (referring to cloth used for wiping with heated wax).
The eighty-seventh precept concerning the making of a sitting mat beyond the prescribed measure:
If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), he must make it according to the proper measure. Herein, the measure is two spans of the Buddha’s own hand in length.
The width is one and a half *vitasti* (a span). If it is increased beyond that, whether in width or length, by even half a *vitasti*, once the cutting is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.

The Origin Story (*nidāna*): This precept has two stages of enactment. When the Buddha was at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he was inspecting the monks’ quarters and saw that the bedding and mats of the community of monks were spread out in the open air and defiled by impurities. The bhikṣus received [the instruction].
Having returned to the monastery, the World-Honored One, on account of these circumstances, assembled the Sangha and addressed the assembly with a reprimand, saying:

"You should know that this defilement belongs to one who possesses desire, one who possesses hatred, and one who possesses delusion; it does not belong to one who is free from desire, hatred, and delusion.
It is impossible for a bhikṣu whose mindfulness is undistracted to fall asleep; how much more so for an Arhat?"
In the Han [era], from this time forward, it was permitted for the bhikṣus to make *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) for the purpose of protecting the body, the robes, and the bedding.
When the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks made them excessively large, those possessing a sense of shame observed this and informed the Buddha.
This was the first establishment of the precept (*śikṣāpada*). At that time, Kālodāyin’s body was large while his *niṣīdana* was small; he was unable to sit before the Buddha.
Along the side of the path from which he had come, [the monk] pulled at his *niṣīdana* with his hand, wishing to make it wider.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked about it intentionally and permitted that one may increase its width and length by half a *vitasti* each. This was the second rule established;
it was formulated as a training precept (*śikṣāpada*) on account of the matter of bedding.
Explanation of the Meaning: The text is divided into three sections. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the original enactment of the rule.

From "Furthermore, increasing... onwards, it clarifies the subsequent allowances. From "If one exceeds [the limit]... onwards, it establishes the offense incurred. *Nīśīdana* (also called *nīśīdantaka*; in the language of Tang, "reclining mat").

Some call it the "clothing for sitting" (*sui-zuo-yi*); others call it the "foot-lining clothing" (*chun-zu-yi*). This refers to spreading it upon one's seat or bedding when sitting or lying down; whether sitting or lying, it prevents filth from defiling the bedding.

The intent behind its regulation was originally to protect the body, the robes, and the bedding. The *Shisao* states: "Regarding 'for the body,' it is because one fears that if one sits directly on the ground, there may be injury. Next, 'for the robes,' it is because one fears that without a substitute, the three robes will easily be damaged.

Regarding 'for the bedding,' it is because one fears that bodily impurities will soil the monastic beds and mats. As for the measurement (*liang*), this refers to the prescribed quantity to determine the standard for width and length: two *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha’s hand in length and one in width.
A *vitasti* is half a span (one *vitasti* of the Buddha is one Chinese *chi* and six *cun*; that is, the length is three feet two inches, and the width is two feet four inches).
If it is further increased by half a *vitasti* in both width and length (half a *vitasti* is eight *cun*; this means that beyond the standard measurements, eight *cun* are added to each dimension;

thus, the length becomes four feet and the width becomes three feet two inches, which is sufficient for sitting or reclining). Regarding "having cut [it] off" (this refers to making it without following the prescribed measurements; one must have it cut down, and according to the offense, one should seek repentance).

Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, one commits an offense if the length exceeds the prescribed measure while the width does not; or if the width exceeds the measure while the length does not;
or if both the width and the length exceed the measures. This applies whether one performs the work oneself or instructs another to complete it.
If the act is completed, it is a *pāyattika*; if it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the mental desire for it to be wide and long; second, the intentional disregard of the noble prohibitions.

The three acts having been completed, it is also an *dukkaṭa* offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* (the same rule applies, though studied separately); it is also an *dukkaṭa* offense for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, and a *śrāmaṇerī*.
This constitutes a transgression.
Regarding those cases where there is no offense despite the transgression: it is not an offense if one makes [the robe] according to the prescribed measure or less than the measure;

or if one obtains from another a finished garment and cuts it down to the proper measure; or if one folds it double; or in cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept. These constitute non-offenses.

Regarding the proper procedure for cutting [excess material], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should cut it off and then repent. If it has not yet been cut, the Saṃgha should command that it be cut.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If it exceeds the prescribed measure, one commits a *pāyattika* offense once it has been cut. One must repent; it is not sufficient merely to repent without having cut it."
An offense of *vyatikrama* (this refers to the case where one confesses the offense without having cut [the cloth]; it is neither commanded nor permitted).
This precept is studied by those in the Mahāyāna as well.
Examination based on the *Mūla-vinaya-karman*: At that time, there was a bhikṣu who made a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) using variegated materials.
However, when they kept long threads and used them for weaving, the brahmins and laypeople mocked them.
The Buddha said: "In making sitting mats, one should make them double-layered and dye them to change their color."
The third section states: "One must necessarily cut [the cloth] and sew it into strips (*patta*).
A border should be applied to all four sides. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "A *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) should be made in two layers and folded into three parts.

The bottommost part should be cut into strips, identical to the strips of the three robes (*tricīvara*). (This is why Nanshan [Daoxuan] mistakenly cut his bedding; the celestial being’s instruction was based on this very format.)

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A new [niṣīdana] shall be double-layered; an old one shall be four-layered. One should not accept a single-layered niṣīdana, nor should one discard a previously accepted one."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It is permitted to make [a robe] of two layers, but it must not be too thin. This is because one desires to wear something small yet durable.

Furthermore, one must consider the thickness (*pūta*), the measurement of the folds (*cita*), the measurement of the shrinkage, and the measurement when wet. One wishes for it to expand once it has dried. If using *kambala* (wool), it should be made of a single layer;
if using *kārpāsa* (cotton), it should be made of two layers. This is the 'robe according to the sitting' (*niṣīdana-anurūpa-cīvara*). It is not [permitted otherwise].

One may use them as the three robes (*tricīvara*). One must not give them away as a formal gift (*śuddha-dāna*), nor take them to carry firewood, grass, or miscellaneous items; they may only be spread out for sitting.
If traveling on a road, one may fold them long and place them upon a robe-bag on the shoulder. Upon reaching the place of rest, one may take them up and sit upon them.
If it is placed back in its original location, one should cover it with the center [of the robe]. When wishing to sit, one should unfold it slowly;

first press down with the hands and only then sit. Master Yijing’s commentary states: "The intention behind this regulation is that the *niṣīdana* was originally intended as a cushion for bedding to prevent damage;
it was not meant for other uses. However, its large size is equal to one's own body, reaching to the top of the head..."
There remains one *vitasti*; in this case, it corresponds exactly to the bedding. If its measurement were smaller, it would not suffice as a replacement for the bedding.
Furthermore, according to various schools (*nikāya*), it is commonly stated that one adds one *vitasti* to both the length and the middle [width].
Only the text of our own Vinaya states that one further adds half a *vitasti* to both the width and the length. I have therefore appended this here to ensure clarity.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "To the long [measurement], add one more span (*hasta*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Add one cubit (*vitasti*) to the edge of the thread.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The permission to add to the edge of the thread refers to adding from the side of the weaving, but only at one end."
"Add one span (*vitasti*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: 'Extend it by one span on each side. This means that having cut [the cloth] into three parts, one continues the length at the head;
as for the remaining one part, one applies it to the four corners, or else one does not apply it at all."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: Regarding "increasing the spans," this refers to doubling or tripling the measurement by stitching it together at the ends.
The eighty-eighth rule concerning the offense of making a wound-covering cloth (*vastrakṣatapraticchādana*) in excess of the prescribed measure says:
If a bhikṣu makes a wound-covering cloth, he must make it according to the proper measure. Herein, the measure is four of the Buddha’s own spans in length.
It shall be two spans wide. If it exceeds this measurement once it has been cut, it is a *pāyattika*. The Origin Story:
When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the bhikṣus suffered from various kinds of sores.
Pus and blood defiled their bodies, their robes, and their bedding. The Buddha permitted them to keep a "sore-covering robe" (*vastra-ābādha*) for this purpose. This is the robe to be made.

[The monks] had coarse, hairy garments that chafed their sores; when they lifted their robes, they suffered pain. They informed the Buddha, who further permitted them to cover their sores with expensive, fine, soft cloth.
Afterwards, they wore their lower garments (*nivasana*) and skirts. When visiting the homes of laypeople and being invited to sit, they should say, "I have an ailment.
If [the host] says, "Just sit," they should lift the edge [of the garment] and sit while covering the sore with this cloth.
At that time, when the group of six heard this, they began to make many large and wide wound-covering robes.
When the other bhikṣus saw this and recognized it, they informed the Buddha, who then established this training rule because they had made them in excess of the prescribed measure.
**Explanation of the Meaning** The text is divided into two sections. From the words "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the regulation regarding the dimensions of the robe.

The phrase "having finished cutting," etc., establishes the offense committed. The Vinaya states: "A wound-covering robe" refers to various types of sores and ailments; one wears it to cover the body.

It should be four *tala*-hands in length (meaning a length of six feet and four inches) and two *tala*-hands in width (meaning a width of three feet and two inches). [It must be] cut [to these measurements].
The conclusion and so forth are as above.
Regarding the determination of the offense: among these, an offender is one who—if the length is within the prescribed measure but the width is not;

or if the length is not within the prescribed measure but the width is; or if both the width and the length are not within the prescribed measure—either makes it themselves or instructs another to make it.
If it is completed, all are pāyattika offenses; if it is not completed, all are dukkaṭa offenses; if it is made for another person, whether completed or not, all are dukkaṭa offenses.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the presence of a mind of greed or pride; second, the completion of the act to an excessive degree;
and third, the conclusion of the act by oneself or another.

It also governs *bhikṣuṇīs*, for whom it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) [as the rule is the same but the training is distinct]. It likewise applies to *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*.
For a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if one makes [the garment] according to the prescribed measurement or less; or if one obtains [material] from another and cuts it to the proper measurement.
If it is made in two layers, or if it was made before the precept was first established, these constitute non-offenses.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this wound-covering robe is a personal garment; one must not treat it as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*) or offer it as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), nor may it be used for other purposes.
Once the wound has healed, it may then be treated as one of the three robes or offered as a pure gift.

Usage. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Even after the wound has healed, if one keeps [the garment] for more than ten days, it is a *pāyattika* offense" (this is likely a scribal error in the translation;
it should be the same as the offense of forfeiture for keeping extra robes). One should cut it off and repent. If it has not been cut, the Sangha should order it to be cut.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one has exceeded the prescribed measure and cuts it down, and then performs repentance, there is no offense; however, if one repents without having cut it down, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense (the failure to cut down applies both to the agent and the object)."
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
An appended examination: According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, one is instructed to add the formal ritual for receiving and maintaining [the robe].

Once it has been received and maintained, there will be no fault regarding an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*). As stated in the *Yīfǎbìchúsuǒjùyí* (The Rituals Possessed by a Single Lawful Bhikṣu): "Venerable One, with a single mind..."
"Mindful of me, Bhikṣu [Name], this wound-covering cloth has been made according to the prescribed measure; I now accept it. (Recite three times.
He should reply, "So be it. The response should be, "Excellent. (Based on this, the scribal error in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* can be identified.)
The eighty-ninth precept concerning making a rain-bathing robe of excessive size:
If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe, he should make it according to the prescribed measure. Herein, the measure is six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length.
It shall be two and a half spans in width; if it exceeds this, it must be cut down, and [the offender commits] a *pāyattika*.

The Origin Story: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the group of six bhikṣus heard that Viśākhā, Mother of Mṛgāra, had made a request for the Buddha to permit the bhikṣus to make rain-bathing robes. They then proceeded to make them excessively large.

The rain-bathing robe (*vassikasāṭikā*). Those who delight in training in the precepts expressed their disapproval and reproached [the practice], and they informed the Buddha, who then established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) because the rain-bathing robes were of excessive size.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning: the Vinaya states that a "rain-bathing robe" refers to what a bhikṣu wears while bathing in the rain.
Because it covers the body: its length is six *tala*-hands (meaning a measurement of nine chi and six cun);
its width is two and a half *tala*-hands (a measurement of four chi). Once cut, it is as described above.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if it is excessive in length but within the prescribed measure in width; or if it is within the prescribed measure in length but excessive in width;
or if it is excessive in both length and width—if one makes it oneself or instructs another to make it, and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) in all such cases.
If it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) in all such cases. This applies equally if one does it for the sake of another.
Whether it is completed or not, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
This precept fulfills three conditions before the full offense is established: first, it must be a rain-bathing robe; second, it must be intentionally made in excess of the prescribed measure.
The three acts are completed.

Furthermore, for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta (the bhikṣuṇīs have no rain-bathing robe; according to the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya, they are only permitted to keep a bathing robe, and if it exceeds the prescribed measure, it constitutes a pāyattika).
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This constitutes an offense.

Regarding the exemptions for non-offenses: it is not an offense if one makes [the garment] according to the prescribed measure or less; or if one obtains it from another and cuts it to the proper measure; or if one folds it into two layers;
or if [the rule] has not yet been established at the time of the initial ordination. These constitute non-offenses.

Regarding the proper procedure for cutting [the robe]: the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one should first cut it and then repent; if it has not yet been cut, the Saṃgha should order it to be cut.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that to repent without having cut it constitutes a *vyatikrama-vinayātikrama* offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
Regarding the ninth and tenth precepts concerning the measurement of robes equal to those of the Buddha:
if a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to that of the Tathāgata, or makes one exceeding that measurement, it is a pāyattika offense. Within this:
Regarding the dimensions of the Tathāgata’s robe: it is ten spans (*vitasti*) in length and six spans in width; this is called the dimension of the Tathāgata’s robe. The Origin Story:
While the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Śrāvastī, the Venerable Nanda (who was the Buddha’s younger brother) was four fingers shorter than the Buddha.
When the bhikṣus saw him approaching from afar, they all thought he was the Buddha and rose to welcome him. Upon reaching...

Then he realized it. Both felt shame and remorse. The Buddha permitted Nanda to wear black robes to distinguish himself from others (meaning dyed with black clay to produce a "ruined color" [*kasāya*]).

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The Buddha’s robe color was like gold; when he sewed the patches, he added wool, and the color of the cloth was likewise [golden]. Therefore, Nanda ought to cover it with sand. "Covering with sand" is translated here as "ruined color.
At that time, the group of six monks made robes equal in size to those of the Tathāgata, or they made them excessively large and heavy. The other bhikṣus were displeased.

Reproach. He informed the Buddha, who established this precept (*Vinaya-mūla* states: Upānanda fashioned a large *cīvara*; once the seams were finished, he wore it with only one side open and the rest gathered over his shoulder as he went to various residences, which led to censure and fault;

thus, this training rule was enacted. This was because his body was small and the robe was large, making them incompatible; hence, he wore half of it while gathering the other half over his shoulder).

**Exegesis:** The text is divided into two sections. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards clarifies what constitutes an offense; from "In this regard... onwards correctly explains the measurement of the robe.
The Vinaya states: "There are ten kinds of robes as mentioned above. Regarding "Tathāgata" (the Tathāgata), he is the foremost of the Buddha’s ten titles.

This means that while ordinary beings come but do not go as they should, and śrāvakas go as they should but do not come, only the World-Honored One comes and is able to go as he should, and goes as he should and is able to come; thus he differs from ordinary beings and śrāvakas. [This concludes] the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe.

"Et cetera" means [the robe] is ten *vitasti* (spans) long—equivalent to sixteen feet (*zhang*) by current standards—and six *vitasti* wide, which is nine feet and six inches. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The measurement of the Buddha’s robe is such that the Buddha’s body is sixteen feet tall."
For ordinary people, it is half of that. Regarding the measurements of the robes: they should be halved accordingly.

As for the offense: if a bhikṣu [makes] a robe equal in length to the Tathāgata’s robe measurement but not the standard width, or not the standard length but the standard width, or neither the standard width nor the standard length—[in all such cases, it is an offense]. If both the width and the length exceed the standard...
It is not permissible. If one makes it oneself or instructs another to make it, and it is completed, it is an *pāyattika* offense in all cases.
If it is made by oneself or another but not completed, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense in all cases. If it is made for another, whether completed or not completed, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense in all cases.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the intention to disregard the instruction; second, the desire for it to be broad and long;
and third, its completion beyond the prescribed measure.
It is also applied to bhikṣuṇīs as a *duṣkṛta* (with the same rule but distinct training). It applies likewise to śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.
For a nun, this constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense. This is the rule regarding transgression.
As for the exemptions where there is no offense: if one obtains finished robes from another and they must be cut to the proper dimensions;
or if they are not cut but are folded double; or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—these are instances of no offense.
Regarding the proper procedure for cutting [the hair], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should cut it and then repent; if it has not been cut, the Saṃgha should command that it be cut.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one repents without having cut it, it is an offense of violating the *vinaya* (*vyatikrama-vinayātikrama*)."
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
An appended examination: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one should [make the robe] according to the size of one's own body. There are three types of *saṃghāṭī*:

the superior is five cubits (*hasta*) in length and three cubits in width (a cubit is measured from the elbow joint to the tip of the extended middle finger; for an average person, one cubit is one chi and eight cun). The medium...
The superior [robe] is five cubits long—excluding one fist (meaning four cubits with fingers extended and one cubit when the hands are clenched)—and three cubits wide—excluding one fist.
The inferior [robe] is four and a half cubits long and three cubits wide—excluding one fist.
The *uttarāsaṅga* is likewise; the two middle types of *antarvāsaka* are also thus. The inferior [robe] is... [length].
It is four and a half cubits [in length] and two cubits minus one *vitasti* [in width].
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "In total, there are three grades of the *saṃghāṭī* robe. The superior grade uses the practitioner's own cubit measurements:

three vertically and five horizontally. The inferior grade reduces each dimension by half a cubit. Those between these two are called the middling grade. The seven-strip and five-strip robes likewise have three grades."

The dimensions for these [robes] are all the same as this. Furthermore, there are two kinds of five-striped robes (*pañcakaṇṭhaka-cīvara*): one with two vertical and five horizontal strips, and one with two vertical and four horizontal strips.

These are the smallest permissible dimensions for a robe that is properly maintained (*dhāraṇīya-cīvara*), provided they merely cover the three wheels (the navel and the two knees). [Note: This refers to cases where the upper part covers the navel and the lower part masks both knees.

For those with long forearms, this measurement is appropriate; however, for those with short arms, it may not reach the knees. In such cases, the length of the forearm should be taken as the standard. If one’s body is tall while the forearms are short, [one should follow the forearm length].
This is measured according to the body, not according to the cubit (*hasta*). If it were otherwise, it would likewise be measured according to the body.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The length of the cubit is not fixed; the Buddha commanded that it follow the measurement of one's own body parts."
The present Vinaya states: "Clothing should be tailored to fit the body" (the five, nine, and ten *pātimokkha* rules concluded).
There are four *pātideśanīya* rules.
However, these all arise from greed; they increase greedy delusions and destroy the faith and respect of others. Therefore, the Buddha—
Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya*: this term has no direct equivalent in Chinese. According to the *Shishi yaolan*, based on its meaning, it is translated as "confessing toward another.
However, since all offenses ought to be confessed and repented before others, why is this category alone specifically termed "confessing toward another"?
The *Vinayamūlasaṃgraha* states: "That is to say, when there are bhikṣus currently residing at the monastery, one must confess each instance individually and separately to them.
It differs from other offenses, and thus receives its own distinct name. Furthermore, once the offense has been committed, it must be confessed immediately;
one may not allow it to remain unaddressed. This also distinguishes it from other offenses."
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika*, the *Daśabhāṇavāra*, and our own school, this offense should be confessed before a single person;
by declaring it once and repenting, the offense is eliminated.

The Sūtra says: "One who commits a *pāyattika* (pāratideśanīya) offense falls into hell for a lifespan of one thousand years as reckoned by the Trāyastriṃśa devas—where one day and night equals one hundred years of the human world—which, by human calculation, is thirty-six million years.
This hell is the Kālasūtra Hell; it is so called because the limbs and body are first measured out with glowing iron cords and subsequently cut and sawn apart."
Therefore, regarding the first precept concerning receiving food from a nun who is not a relative:
if a bhikṣu enters a village and, being without illness, takes food with his own hand from a nun who is not a relative.
Regarding the offense of eating [at the wrong time]: that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, I have committed a blameworthy act which ought not to have been done;
I now confess it to you, venerable sir. This rule is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession).
The Origin Story: This precept has two origins. The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī.
At that time, grain was expensive and the people were suffering from famine; it was difficult to obtain food through alms-seeking.
On the first day, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā obtained some food by begging and gave it to a bhikṣu. She did the same on the second and third days. Then, she entered the city with her alms-bowl.
While begging for alms, she encountered an elder on his way to pay homage to the king in a carriage.

His attendants drove people aside, and as the nun sought to avoid the path, she fell into deep mud and lay there with her face buried in the ground. Moved by compassion, the elder ordered his men to help her out;
upon learning the circumstances, he reproached the bhikṣu for his lack of courtesy and deference. He then invited the nun to his home, where he provided her with clothing to wash and food to eat.
[The Buddha] spoke: "From this day forward, you may always eat at my house; do not go elsewhere again.
If you obtain anything from outside, you may give it to others as you please. When the bhikṣus heard this and learned of it, they informed the Buddha.

The World-Honored One, having assembled the ten points of meaning, first established the precept for the Saṃgha. At that time, the bhikṣus all had doubts and did not dare to accept [food from] their relatives.
Regarding food from nuns: there were also certain sick bhikṣus who did not dare to accept food from nuns who were not their relatives. The Buddha permitted them all to do so;
hence the statement that one may take food with one's own hands from a nun who is neither a relative nor ill.

This was the second training rule established. It was formulated due to the affliction of public censure arising from matters concerning bhikṣuṇīs; it belongs to the first category [of offenses], namely killing.
The Root Category: Explanation of the Meaning. The text is divided into two sections. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards clarifies the matter of the offense;

from "That bhikṣu... onwards clarifies the method of repentance. Regarding "entering a village": (the term "village" is used to distinguish it from open spaces outside the village. There are four kinds of villages, as explained above. It is not...

"A relative bhikṣuṇī" (a relative is as defined above; since a bhikṣuṇī is not a relative, one should not seek food from her). "Receiving food with one's own hand when not ill" (if not ill, there is no allowance; the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"ill" does not mean a minor ailment, but refers to scabies, jaundice, festering sores, ulcers, carbuncles, or boils—conditions loathed and despised by others.

"Taking food with one's own hand" excludes cases where food is placed on the ground or given by someone else; it means taking it directly with one's own hand, or holding a vessel and receiving two or five kinds of solid food from another and swallowing it). "This bhikṣu" refers to [the subject].

(The person who has committed an offense) refers to [the transgressor]. "Other bhikṣus" refers to those who have properly received full ordination and maintain the precepts. "Matters subject to censure" refers to actions that are not wholesome and were prohibited by the Buddha;

since one has violated what was prescribed, it is logically appropriate to censure them. "That which should not be done" refers to what is not appropriate for a bhikṣu who possesses contentment, shame, and dread of blame to do.
"Now repenting before the Venerable One" means not daring to conceal [the fault], but speaking of it oneself to clear away the offense committed. This dharma is called the "Dharma of Repentance."

(This sentence concludes by returning to the names of the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, so that one may know how to maintain them. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "The essence of this precept is not a transgression; one should confess it once before a single person.")

**Establishing the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one is not ill and receives [food] with one's own hand, and thus eats it, there is a *pāyattika* (pāṭidesanīya) for every swallow.
This precept requires five conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the nun is not a relative; second, one perceives her as not being a relative.
Doubtful. (1) Being oneself free from illness; (2) taking it oneself within the village; (3) swallowing it with food. These constitute the offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* (the same rule, different training). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, and a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is the offense.
The exceptions where there is no offense: receiving food from a relative nun; if one is ill; if it is placed on the ground for one to take;

if someone else hands it over; if it is within a monastery; if it is outside the village (the allowance regarding being outside the village arises because the conditions for an offense are triggered within the city);
if it is given inside a bhikṣuṇī’s dwelling; and cases such as when the precept had not yet been established. These are the exceptions.
No offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If a bhikṣu is outside the village and a bhikṣuṇī is inside the village;
or if a bhikṣu is inside the village and a bhikṣuṇī is outside the village; or if a bhikṣu is in the air and a bhikṣuṇī is on the ground; or if a bhikṣuṇī..."
If a monk who has entered the state of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) takes [food] while on the ground, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one takes fifteen kinds of food at once, it is one *pāyattika*;
if one takes them one by one, there are fifteen *pāyattikas*. (The fifteen kinds of food refer to the five types of formal meals and the five non-formal meals.)"

[The five types of] proper food, as well as wheat, millet, rice, hemp, and *qiao* (foxtail millet), before they have been made into parched flour, boiled rice, cakes, or other preparations, are all termed the "five similar foods.

The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: If one is not actually a related nun (*ñāti-bhikṣuṇī*) but perceives her as such, or if there is doubt [regarding her status], one incurs the full offense (*pāyattika*).

If she is a related nun but one perceives her as unrelated, or if there is doubt [regarding her relationship], one incurs a *duṣkṛta*. If she is unrelated but one perceives her as unrelated, there is no offense.
Regarding this precept, the Mahāyāna does not distinguish between relatives and non-relatives; rather, one should simply observe whether the recipient is worthy or unworthy.
Nevertheless, in this age of the Final Dharma, it is best to maintain a distance from nuns.
The second precept concerning the prohibition of stopping a nun from giving food:
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson to eat, and there is a bhikṣuṇī therein who points out [food], saying, "Give such-and-such a person soup;
give such-and-such a person rice," the bhikṣu should speak to that bhikṣuṇī as follows: "Sister, please stop for a moment."
The bhikṣus must wait until the meal is finished. If there is not even one bhikṣu present, they should speak thus to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister, please stop; we must wait until the bhikṣus have finished their meal. If this is done, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression, saying:

"Venerable sirs, I have committed a censurable act which ought not to have been done. I now confess my transgression before the venerable ones. This rule is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession).
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There were many bhikṣus there together with the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika).
They were sitting and eating inside the house of a layperson. At that time, the nuns of the group of six asked the group of six for soup and rice, saying, "Give this soup;
give this rice. They skipped those in the middle and did not give them, instead giving [the food] out of order to others.

Among the monks who heard this, those with few desires censured the group of six. They informed the Buddha, who established this precept because of the affliction of disparagement arising from matters concerning food and drink.
This constitutes the category of the fundamental types of false speech within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
**Exegesis:** The text is divided into three sections. From "If a bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the etiquette for receiving food. From "If there is not even one bhikṣu...
onwards, it clarifies the matter of those being converted. From "That bhikṣu... onwards, it clarifies the method of repentance. "The director" (meaning one who assigns the task).

"The giver" (meaning one who does not distribute food equally, but instead bypasses the order to give to specific individuals). "Soup and rice" (indicating that this is not coarse food). "Great" (mahā-).

"Sister, please stop" (*bhagini tiṣṭha*)—here, "sister" (*bhaginī*) refers to an elder sister; according to the Vinaya regulations, when a *bhikṣu* addresses the assembly of *bhikṣuṇīs*, he generally uses the term "Venerable Sister" (*āryā bhagini*).

The two characters "please stop" (*tiṣṭha*) are words used for rebuking and halting; they mean to cause her to pause briefly and wait until the assembly has finished eating. "If there is not even one *bhikṣu*" etc.—this means that within the assembly present before them, there is not even a single person who rebukes and stops that *bhikṣuṇī*.

That *bhikṣu* who eats [in such a manner] incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*). "To repent before the Venerable Ones"—this means that the *bhikṣu* who ate [improperly] should face the assembly of *bhikṣus* present before him and confess his transgression.

This offense differs from the other three precepts in that it is eliminated simply by confessing and repenting before a single person; therefore, it says, "I repent my transgression before the Venerable Ones."

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding those who commit an offense herein: if one eats while not having a single bhikṣu present to admonish and stop them, there is a *pāyattika* (pāratideśanīya) for every swallow.
This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, it must be at the house of a layperson; second, [the food] must be indicated by a bhikṣuṇī.
1. Indicating [the food]. 2. Not preventing [the donor] from stopping [giving]. 3. Receiving the food and swallowing it. These constitute the offense.
(The rule applies equally to the *bhikṣuṇī*, though the training is distinct). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is defined as a transgression.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if she says, "Stop for now"; if the bhikṣuṇī herself acts as the donor;
if the donor provides the food and instructs the bhikṣuṇī to distribute it; or if she does not distribute it by favoring one person over another.
Furthermore, there is no offense in cases such as when the precepts have not yet been established.
As recorded in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "One should say, 'Sister, please stop for a moment; we must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.'"
If he stops, it is well. If he does not stop, one should speak to him two or three times. If the recipient does not respond after being spoken to, there is an offense of *vinaya-āpatti*.
This is the rule for the confession of an offense regarding eating.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If two groups of monks are seated together within one group, and if one person among them says, 'This is a bhikṣuṇī,' then the second group of monks is also said to have spoken [the same].
If they enter separately, sit separately, eat separately, and exit separately—when entering the gate of a donor, the bhikṣus should question the bhikṣu who is exiting."
How is it that a bhikṣuṇī instructs a donor within this [monastery] to give food to a bhikṣu? If she says, "I should ask such-and-such," one should inquire whether they have been restrained.
If she replies, "They have already been restrained," then those who enter are also said to be restrained.
When various bhikṣus go out through the city gate, at that time, one should ask those entering; as for those exiting, if they have not yet been restrained when they exit, [the same applies].
Those who enter should be restrained; if those who exit are restrained, those who enter are likewise said to be restrained.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a śikṣamāṇā or śrāmaṇerī instructs others to serve more food but does not say 'step back a little,' it is a duṣkṛta offense."
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.

Examination: According to this section [of the Vinaya] and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if there is not even one bhikṣu among the assembly who rebukes and stops all the bhikṣus from eating, they all incur an offense; yet the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* requires confession toward only a single person.

One must understand this according to the underlying principle: if the one eating is a junior monk, he should follow the rules of his own division; if the one eating is a senior monk, it should be as prescribed in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
Third, the precept on receiving food from a family under training.

If a *kula-kamma* (formal act regarding a family) has previously been performed for a family, and a bhikṣu, without having been invited by such a family and while not being ill, receives food with his own hands and eats it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying: "I have committed a censurable offense, which ought not to have been done;
I now confess to the Venerable One. This rule is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession).

The Origin Story: This precept has two origins. When the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, there was a household where both husband and wife had attained faith and joy as disciples of the Buddha.
Now, it is the constant practice of those disciples who have seen the Truth that they never begrudge even their own flesh and blood to the bhikṣus, but always provide them with offerings.
Consequently, they became impoverished, and their provisions of food and clothing were completely exhausted. Their neighbors all remarked, "This family was formerly very wealthy;

it is only since they began making offerings to the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya that they have fallen into such poverty. A bhikṣu of few desires and possessing a sense of shame heard of this and informed the Buddha.

The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and one proclamation) for the sake of the householder’s family. (Regarding this ritual method, at the time of its performance...)

Because it was clear that this occurred during the [forbidden] time, a rule was established: "If a bhikṣu knows that a family is a 'protected household' (*śaikṣa-kula*) and, after the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed against them, accepts food or drink in that house, he must confess his transgression before another bhikṣu. This was the first formulation of the precept.
Thereupon, among the bhikṣus, those who had previously accepted invitations from such protected households all harbored doubts; they did not dare to go there again. When they were ill...
The Buddha had doubts and did not dare accept the invitation from a family; the Buddha permitted both [the monk’s hesitation and the family’s request].

Therefore, it was added that one who has not previously accepted an invitation and is not ill must receive food with his own hands. This is the second training rule (śikṣāpada). It was established due to the affliction of public censure regarding the matter of begging for food.
It belongs to the category of the fundamental nature of theft within the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].

**Explanation of the Meaning** The text is divided into two sections. The first, beginning with "If one first performs the *karmavācanā* for a family of learners (*śaikṣakula*)," clarifies the matters that constitute an offense.

The second, beginning with "That bhikṣu," clarifies the method for repentance. Regarding the "family of learners" (*śaikṣakula*): the *Vinayasamgraha* states that this refers to those who have attained the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Because the afflictions and outflows (*āsrava*) of these first three fruits are not yet exhausted, they must still train in their abandonment; thus, they are called a "family of learners. This refers to families of the four castes where such practitioners, while remaining in the household life, have attained the realization of the fruits. If [it were] an Arhat...

Arhats are called those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It is necessary for them to remain far removed from sensual desire and to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) before they can realize the four fruits; this cannot be attained while dwelling in a household. Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual):

it refers to a case where both husband and wife have realized the noble fruits and possess no stinginess toward the Triple Gem. However, because their household affairs have become impoverished, the Saṃgha performs a ritual of protection and exclusion, such that they do not go to their home to receive food and drink. This is distinct from the punishment for offenses; it is the rule of excluding [monks] from entering the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*).
Such a "family under training" (*śaikṣakula*) refers to a family for whom the Saṃgha has already performed the *karmavācanā*. One who is not ill must first accept an invitation [to eat there].
(This means that although the formal ritual (karmavācanā) has been performed for him, he has not yet made a request, nor does he have an illness;

thus, there is no ground for exemption). Regarding the offense: one who, having previously neither received a request nor being ill, receives food or drink with his own hands within such a community of training (śaikṣa), commits a *pratideśanīya* offense for every swallow.

This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, it must be a family of practitioners undergoing the formal ritual (karmavācanā); second, one must not have been invited and must be free from illness;
and third, the food must be received and swallowed.

If a *bhikṣu* commits this simultaneously, it is a *duṣkṛta* (the rule is the same but the training is distinct). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if one has previously accepted an invitation; if one is ill; if the gift is placed on the ground and taken up; if it is received from another person;
if it is given by a family under training (*śaikṣa-kula*) and their wealth subsequently increases such that they request the Sangha to revoke the formal act of training (*śaikṣa-karma*);
and in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset. These constitute non-offenses.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.

An appended examination states: The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says, "If the wife is an ārya and the husband is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or if the husband is an ārya and the wife is an ordinary person, one should not perform the *śaikṣakula-karman* for them. If both husband and wife are āryas and free from stinginess..."

If his greed causes his wealth and goods to be exhausted, the Saṃgha should perform the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of placing one under training) for him. If the Saṃgha possesses gardens or fields, they should be granted to him so that he may know them;
he should be made to fulfill his regular obligations, and the remainder he may use for his own support. If there are no gardens or fields, he shall subsist on whatever he obtains through begging.

One should take food to their home and give them what remains. If one cannot do so, one should bring them to the monastery, provide them with a dwelling, bedding, and seating, and give them food in due order.
One should also provide them with non-time [meal] drinks and, if there are robes available for distribution, one should give them a share as well.
The nuns who belong to that family of practitioners should also be cared for in this same manner.
The fourth precept concerning receiving food in a place of fear:

If a bhikṣu resides in an araṇya—a remote and isolated place where there is apprehension and fear—and if that bhikṣu, while staying in such an araṇya, has not first informed a donor (dānapati), he must not receive food outside the monastery grounds within the saṃghārāma. If he does so... [the rule applies].
If one receives food with one's own hand and eats it within a monastery when not ill, one should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have committed a censurable act that ought not to have been done; I now confess this to you, Venerable sir. This is called the method of confession.

The Origin Story: This precept has two origins. When the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the women of the city of Śrāvastī brought food and drink to the saṃghārāma to make offerings.
Thieves heard of this and waylaid them on the road to harass them. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "From now on, you should tell the [women]..."
"Women, do not go out onto the roads; there is the danger of bandits. If they have already left the city, one should say to them, "Do not go to the monastery;
there is the danger of bandits on the road. This was the first formulation of the precept.
At that time, various donors, knowing beforehand of the danger and apprehension, nevertheless brought food. The bhikṣus, being apprehensive, did not dare to accept it.
Furthermore, there were sick bhikṣus who also hesitated and did not dare to accept [food]. There were also donors who placed food on the ground to give, or instructed others to give it;

the bhikṣus again hesitated and did not dare to accept. The Buddha permitted all of these, adding to the previous rule the instruction that one may accept food with one's own hands even from a donor who has not been informed beforehand, provided one is not ill. This was the second formal precept established. Because...

This training rule was established due to the affliction of censure regarding matters of food and drink; it belongs to the category of the fundamental types of sexual misconduct in the first section [of the Prātimokṣa].
The explanation of its meaning is divided into two parts: from "If a bhikṣu... onwards clarifies the matter of the offense;
from "...should confess before another bhikṣu... onwards clarifies the method of repentance. The Vinaya states: "A forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) is located five hundred [bow-lengths] from a village."

"An archer's range" (meaning one *krośa*, which is five *li*; the *Vinayaviniścaya* states that this was spoken in reference to the specific origin story, though it applies equally to places further away). "Those who are suspicious and terrified."

There is apprehension of fear from thieves and robbers. Regarding the *dānapati* (the term *dāna* is Sanskrit; here it is translated as "giving" (*śe*). The term *pati* is Chinese, meaning "to transcend";

it refers to one who can break through stinginess and envy by practicing giving, thereby crossing the sea of poverty and subsequently attaining great wealth, which leads to the accumulation of merit and provisions). Regarding the sick person: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, "Those with minor ailments, cold ailments, or wind ailments are unable to go outside.
The previous three precepts constitute an offense when committed within a village or a house; this precept, however, gives rise to a transgression because it occurs within the monastery.
The Definition of the Offense: Regarding those who commit this offense— should a forest-dwelling bhikṣu reside in such a remote location and,
having not previously informed a donor, receive food outside the monastery, or within the monastery,
accept it with his own hands when he is not ill, then for every swallow of that food, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
This precept requires five conditions to constitute a full offense: first, being within a monastery; second, being on a remote path where fear or suspicion arises;
third, not having first informed the donor; fourth, having no cause for illness; and fifth, personally receiving the food and swallowing it.

If a *bhikṣu* commits [this offense], it is a *duṣkṛta*; (the rule is the same, though the training is distinct). For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This constitutes an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one has first informed the donor; if one is ill; if the food is placed on the ground for one to take; if one instructs another to give it;
if it is given while one is receiving instructions or listening to the Dharma; if the bhikṣu has private food of his own which he causes to be handed over;
and in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—these constitute no offense.
This precept is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.

Examination: According to both the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya and the Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya, a formal procedure consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) is required to appoint a bhikṣu to observe and guard travelers on dangerous roads.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If a bhikṣu has received the formal authorization (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha, and he knows that a thief has entered therein, he should station a pure person within it. If he sees anyone within who resembles a thief," [he should act accordingly].
One should take this food and say to those carrying it: "Do not come into this place; there are people here who resemble thieves.
If those carrying the food should insist on coming, there is no offense. The person appointed for the *karmavācanā* must necessarily be brave, strong, and capable of repelling the thieves.
If he is unable to repel them, the entire Saṃgha should go to the place where the thieves are. If they still cannot...
One should be able to respond appropriately to the donors (*dānapati*) of the village community so as to cause many people to maintain restraint.
Because this precept clarifies the matter of the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), I have recorded the rules of conduct for the forest hermitage. The third section states:
At dawn, wash your hands. Take up your robes and shake them out; put on the *saṃghāṭī*, placing it either upon your head or over your shoulder.
Wash your bowl and place it in its carrying net. Take your leather sandals and staff. Holding the key, exit the room. Close the door and push it to see if it is secure.
If it is not secure, you should further stabilize it with the bolt (the *argala*, which is used to lock the door). If it is secure, you should fasten the cord.
Looking around inside, if no one sees him, he should hide the door-hook. If someone sees him, he should place it in a concealed spot.
Or, carrying it away, while walking along the road, he should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas.
If he sees someone, he should first greet them, saying, "Welcome. If he wishes to enter a village, he should set his bowl on the ground, put on his outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), and [use] leather...

Having set aside his sandals and struck down his staff, he should leave them by the edge of the village. When entering the village, he should observe the characteristics of the lanes, whether they are open spaces, marketplaces, gateways, or places for discarded refuse.
Upon entering the house of a layperson, he should observe the first gateway characteristic through to the seventh gateway characteristic.
If he wishes to adjust his robes, he should face a wall, holding his staff in his right hand and his bowl in his left hand. He must not [do so while walking].
One should dwell on the path; one should not dwell in a secluded place. One should not go out to meet food. If summoned, one should go.
If one receives boiled rice, dry rice, or the like, they should not be placed together in one spot. If it is in a single bowl, one should separate them with an object.
If one has tree leaves, bark, a *kañcika*, a large bowl, or a small bowl containing flour, these should be wrapped in a hand-towel.
One should not beg from a prominent household, nor should one insistently demand anything.

If one knows that something will be obtained, one should wait until the begging is finished, then leave the village, step off the path, set the bowl on the ground, fold the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), place it upon the head or shoulder, and proceed while constantly reflecting.
One should practice only wholesome dharmas. Upon seeing someone, one should first inquire after their well-being, saying, "Welcome.

One should then sweep and clean the place where food is usually eaten, and prepare the water vessels, vessels for leftover food, seats, foot-washing stones, water for washing feet, and towels for wiping feet.
If other forest-dwelling bhikṣus arrive, one should rise to meet them from afar, take their bowls, provide them with seats, and offer them water vessels and other necessities. Then...
Once he has finished washing his hands with soap powder, he should set aside a portion of the remaining food for later.
If a *sena* (this term means "thief") arrives, he should give it to him; next, he should offer water, and then offer food to that forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣu.
While giving him food, he should attend to his needs by providing salt, vinegar, vegetables, water, a fan, and so forth. If the time for the meal is about to pass, he should...

They eat together. When they have finished eating, one should take their bowls and provide them with water for washing their hands. If there is any leftover food, it should be given to humans or non-humans.
One should wash the vessels containing the remnants, as well as the beds, seats, and other items, and return them to their original places.
One should sprinkle and sweep the dining area. If a *śramaṇa* comes, one should say to them: "This is water; this is for washing the feet; this is food; it is for you."
Because they are equal [in this regard], he should set aside a separate, clean place for eating whenever he wishes to eat.

An araṇya bhikṣu should be well-acquainted with the divisions of the night, well-acquainted with the cardinal directions and their characteristics, and well-acquainted with the stars; he should not spread out fine bedding, but should instead remain vigilant in mind during the first and last watches of the night for contemplation.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "A person who is not foolish is fit to dwell in an araṇya (forest hermitage).

Even if they are not widely learned, provided they clearly understand the characteristics of the precepts, they may also dwell there. (An araṇya is also called a vihāra; it is a place where those who are coarse and violent do not reside, but rather where refined practitioners live.
Nowadays, people have no knowledge at all [of this] yet claim to 'dwell in seclusion'—this is truly lamentable. [The six rules concerning reproachable matters are concluded.]

The seven groups of the *śaikṣa-dharmas* (rules of training) comprise one hundred items in total. The *Shichao* states: "The Vinaya says *śikṣākarani*; this is translated as 'rules of training' (*zhòng xué fǎ*), meaning matters that ought to be learned."

The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "As for the 'rules of training' (*śaikṣadharma*), this refers to all the numerous misdeeds (*duṣkṛta*) and improper utterances (*durbhāṣita*) found within the extensive commentary;
since these are all subsumed within the rules of training, they are collectively termed the 'rules of training.'"
In the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, it is asked: "Other sections do not state 'one should train,' yet this precept alone does so.

What is the reason? The answer is: "The other precepts are easy to maintain, yet their offenses are grave; if one violates them, the offense is established, and one must either repent before the assembly or repent face-to-face with another.

This precept is difficult to maintain, yet its offense is light and easily escaped. If one commits a violation, provided one feels remorse and resolves to train, the offense is immediately extinguished."

Because these precepts are difficult to maintain and easy to violate, one should constantly guard one's thoughts and train in them so as not to incur the offense; thus it is said simply that "one should train.
A sutra states: "If one violates the *śaikṣa* (minor) precepts, one will fall into hell for a duration equal to five hundred years of the life span of the gods of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven."
(Fifty human years constitute one day and night in that heaven). By human reckoning, this is nine million years. This *niraya* is the Saṃjīva Hell.
It is so called because the various sinners each have iron claws grow upon their hands; they tear at one another until the flesh falls away.
Whether it is by the wardens shouting or by the blowing of a cold wind, although the two conditions for reviving differ, they are equal in that they all revive. Thus it is called Saṃjīva.

Appendix: A Comparative Examination of the Precepts for Training (*śikṣāpada*) *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: Sixty-seven rules; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*:
Forty-three rules; *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: One hundred and eight rules; *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: One hundred and thirteen rules;
*Pratimokṣa-sūtra* (Kāśyapīya school): Seventy-six rules.
One should wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) neatly; this is how one should train.
(First) The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭīs* either too high or too low; some made them like an elephant’s trunk, some like a *tāla* leaf, and some with fine pleats.

When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying, "They look like kings or ministers, or like performers who wear such garments for festivals, jests, and comedic recitations.
A monk of few desires heard of this and informed the Buddha. The Buddha assembled the ten points of purpose and established a precept for the Saṃgha.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "The numerous rules of training and so forth were all established as precepts due to matters of formal conduct, public censure, and afflictions;
this [section] provides a general enumeration [of them], while the specific names are not individually listed below."
**Explanation of the Meaning:** "One should wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* is also called *nièhuán-sēng*; this is translated as 'skirt') in a neat and orderly manner.

Regarding "one should wear it in a neat and orderly manner," the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "This refers to being free from the fault of wearing robes in a disordered fashion. The *Vinaya* says: "Disordered" means, for instance, tying the belt below the navel.
Some are drawn high to the waist; some have one corner hanging down like an elephant’s trunk; some have two corners hanging down like the leaves of a *tāla* tree;

or there are fine pleats wrapped around the waist (the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: this refers to folding the edge of the skirt into fine pleats which are gathered together at the waist, shaped like a *tāla* leaf).
This refers to that which is gathered above and dispersed below (as detailed in the *Nèifǎzhuàn*).
Regarding the offense: if one commits this intentionally, one should confess a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅);
because it is committed intentionally, it is a *duṣkṛta* for improper conduct (*anācāra*). If one commits it unintentionally, it is a *duṣkṛta*. (The *Śariputrābhidharma-vinaya* states:)

*Duṭ* means evil; *kila* means to act. One should confess a *duṭ-kila* (pācittiya); this is a fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*), not a transgression of decorum (*airesika-duṭ-kila*). This latter is an offense arising from [the former]. That is to say, by acting intentionally, one commits the fundamental offense; at that time, because it violates the monastic decorum, one further commits one *airesika-duṭ-kila* on top of the fundamental offense.

It should be understood that if the offense is committed, both the fundamental offense and the offense arising from it are established. However, when confessed, the fundamental offense is extinguished, and the offense arising from it is extinguished accordingly, because although their names differ, their substance is the same and there is no need for two separate confessions.

Here, we discuss only the method of confession for those who do not conceal the offense. If, after committing the offense, one conceals it for one day or many days before finally declaring and repenting it, the principle involves eight stages: questioning whether the offense exists or not.

The methods for repentance (*chān-fǎ*) are not universal; they should be prepared according to the sequence [of the offenses]. There are explicit texts governing these regulations, so take care not to confuse them. If one commits an offense through negligence rather than intentionally, this is classified as an accidental transgression (*duṣkṛta*).

It does not necessarily require seeking repentance before another person; it suffices to reproach one’s own mind and resolve never to do it again, and the offense will then be extinguished. Now, in the first section, the gravity of various offenses is explained in detail. For the subsequent sections on the determination of offenses, follow this same principle without variation. Regarding this precept, the formal procedures for repentance, as well as the method of mental reproach for non-intentional offenses, are all clearly elucidated within the section on "Practicing the Observances."
It applies concurrently to bhikṣuṇīs and the three lower groups [of female practitioners]; it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding exemptions where there is no offense: if at times a sore develops at the navel and she wears it low; or if there is a sore on her ankle and she wears it high;
or if she is within a monastery, or outside a village, or while working, or while traveling on a road, or in the case of the most [urgent circumstances].
If [the act] was committed before the precepts were first established and so forth, this constitutes no offense.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If a bhikṣu does not rely on the Buddha’s teaching and, disregarding shame, intends to commit an improper act, he incurs a *pratikṣepaṇīya-duṣkṛta* (offense of mental censure) for grasping and spreading out the robe; if he puts it on his body, he incurs an offense that must be confessed (*pratideśanīya*)."

Regarding *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing): if one puts on robes with a compliant mind but does not do so according to the prescribed rules—whether due to forgetfulness or ignorance—and thus wears them improperly, one incurs only the offense of *cittāpatti* (reproach of mind). Wrongdoing is thus defined;
it should be understood that this applies analogously to the other training rules (*śikṣāpada*).

(The Eighteenth Precept) **Exegesis:** The setting and origin of this rule are as described above. Onlookers criticized [the monks], saying they were like Brahmins.
The Buddha therefore established this precept. The Vinaya states: "To have the body poorly covered" means to expose various parts of the body.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies as previously stated.
There is no offense in cases such as when one has such an illness, or is bound, or the wind blows the robe away from the body, or at the very beginning before the precept was established.
Appendix: Examination of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The *antarvāsa* (inner robe) should be made of a fine material;
if it is coarse, it should be made in two or three layers. If the *antarvāsa* is coarse, the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) should be made of a fine material."
If the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) is coarse, the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) should be made of fine material; if the *saṃghāṭī* is coarse, the *uttarāsaṅga* should be made of fine material.
(Text) Regarding the three robes, it is permitted to distinguish between coarse and fine materials by making them in two or three layers.
The original purpose of this regulation was to ward off cold and shield against heat; ten types [of robes] are detailed in the Vinaya.
Regarding clothing and materials: there is currently a tradition handed down which states that the Buddha ordained that the three robes (*tricīvara*) be made entirely of coarse hemp cloth.
This was simply because when the World-Honored One first left the household life, he cast off his precious garments, and a tree deity offered him a single hemp robe.
This hemp robe, moreover, had been left behind by a *pratyekabuddha* a hundred years prior; it was extremely fine and was not coarse at all. Due to this...

This has not been investigated; the error has persisted for a long time. If one were to say that cotton cloth is forbidden while only hemp cloth is permitted, this would be an unauthorized imposition and is certainly not the text of the Vinaya.
One must understand that the customs of this region differ, and there are customary garments distinct from those [prescribed].
Even if they do not have two or three layers, it is permissible; however, one who has received full ordination and is called a monk must absolutely not be without them.
One should train oneself: "When entering the homes of laypeople, one shall sit while properly covering the body with the three robes that are being maintained. (The nineteenth precept.
Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting of the rule, the origin of the censure, and so forth; therein, what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as the remaining four [points].
The rest is all the same as before; this is the special seating rule.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when sitting, one must not sit upon one’s robe.

One should lift the robe with one hand and press down on the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) with the other, and only then sit calmly and composedly. This applies when eating within the monastery (*vihāra*). And so forth.
Furthermore, O Ācārya: when sitting before an elder bhikṣu, one should sit with the body properly covered.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: When in the house of a layperson, one should not sit with feet crossed;
nor should one sit with the inner ankles overlapping, nor with the outer ankles overlapping, nor with the feet tucked up, nor with the feet stretched out too long, nor with the body exposed.
One must not walk into the house of a layperson while looking left and right; this is how one should train (the twentieth). Commentary on the Meaning:
The setting and origin of the rule are as described above. Onlookers criticized and disparaged [the monks], saying they resembled thieves.
The Buddha established the precept for them. The Vinaya states: "Looking left and right" means glancing about in every direction.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies as previously stated.
There is no offense in cases such as: when one has such an illness; when one is observing the time and seasons; when there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
when one seeks a means of escape by looking for a way to flee in various directions; or when the precept has not yet been promulgated.
Regarding the practice of walking, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When walking, one must not walk with the head bowed like a horse;
rather, one should walk with a level gaze to guard against wild elephants, oxen, or horses. One should walk as if carrying a palanquin, without looking east or west.
If one wishes to look, one should turn the entire body toward the place being observed.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Not looking up" means raising one's eyes to look ahead at a distance of one *vyāma*.
One *vyāma* in measure is four cubits (*hasta*) in length.
One must not enter the house of a layperson or sit therein while looking left and right; this is how one should train. (Twenty-first)

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting, the incitement of censure and so forth, and whether there is an offense or no offense therein—all these, as well as the other four assemblies, are entirely the same as previously described. The only point of difference is the act of sitting.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: When in the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), one should not sit down abruptly if not invited to do so;
nor should one sit down without having carefully observed the surroundings.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When sitting, one must not extend the neck like a horse or lower the head; one should gaze straight ahead.
One must take care not to startle a donor who might approach with a hot vessel and cause their hand to be singed.
If eating within a vihāra, one should sit gazing straight ahead in the presence of the upādhyāya, ācārya, or senior monks (sthavira).
One should train oneself to enter the houses of laypeople in silence. (The twenty-second precept.

The Origin Story: While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, several householders saw the group of six monks entering the houses of laypeople while shouting and clamoring loudly.
They criticized them, saying they resembled Brahmins. Consequently, the Buddha established this precept.
The Vinaya states: "One who is not silent" refers to one who speaks loudly or shouts. Whether it be giving instructions or offering food with a loud voice, the offense is established.
Regarding the offenses committed therein, they are all the same as those for the other four assemblies. As for those who do not commit the offense: [the text continues].
There were times when such illnesses occurred: if one was deaf and could not hear sounds, it was necessary to call out in a loud voice;

or to give instructions in a loud voice; or to offer food in a loud voice; or to run while shouting in cases of danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya); as well as at the very beginning, before the precepts had been established.
Regarding the practice of summoning: the *Vinayaviniścaya* states that if one must call someone and they do not hear it, one should request a layperson to call out loudly for them.
One should train oneself to enter the house of a layperson in silence and sit down. (Twenty-third).

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting, the provocation of censure and so forth, as well as what constitutes an offense and what does not, for all four assemblies, these are entirely the same as previously stated;
the only difference lies in the seating arrangement.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One must not raise one's voice or shout loudly while sitting inside a layperson’s home.
