If one wishes to call out, one should snap one’s fingers. If the person in front does not notice, one should speak loudly to someone nearby.
Furthermore, when eating in a vihāra, or when sitting before the *upādhyāya*, the *ācārya*, or an elder (*sthavira*), one must not raise one's voice or shout loudly.
When one wishes to speak, one should inform the person sitting beside them; in this manner, passing it on successively to the second and third, one should ensure they are made aware.
One must not enter the homes of laypeople while laughing or joking; this is how one should train. (Twenty-fourth)
Exegesis: The setting for the origin of this rule is as described above. Onlookers criticized and disparaged [the monks], saying they were like monkeys.
The Buddha established the precept accordingly. The Vinaya states: "To laugh in jest" means to smile with the teeth exposed.

Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, as well as those involving the other four assemblies, are all identical to what was stated previously. There is no offense in the following cases:
if one has a lip ailment and does not cover the teeth; if one smiles out of joy while recollecting the Dharma; or if it concerns the initial period before the precept was established.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If there is something laughable, one must not bare one's gums and show one's teeth while laughing loudly; rather, one should endure it.
One should give rise to the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and death. If [the laughter] still does not cease, one should cover the mouth with the corner of one’s robe.
The *Mūlamātṛkā* states: "When yawning, one must not cover the mouth; this is a *duṣkṛta*.
One must not sit in the house of a layperson while laughing or joking; this is how one should train. (Twenty-fifth)."

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting of the occasion, the arousal of censure and so forth, what constitutes an offense therein and what does not, and all other matters concerning the four assemblies, are entirely the same as previously stated; the only distinction lies in the separate seating.
One should train oneself in being prepared to receive food. (The twenty-sixth precept. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. A householder invited the Saṃgha to partake in a meal offering.
With his own hands, [the householder] served various kinds of food and drink. The group of six [monks] did not receive the food with proper attention; they cast away the soup and rice.
When the layperson saw this, he said to one another, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame.

They do not receive food with proper attention, but out of greed they take more than they need, like those times when grain is expensive. The Buddha established a precept for them. The Vinaya says: "Improperly."
Regarding "eating while holding the bowl with the hand": this refers to eating while setting aside the soup and rice.
The offense is established as follows: the transgressions herein committed by all four assemblies are entirely the same as previously described. Those who do not commit an offense are as follows:
Or, because the bowl was small, he would discard rice while eating, or it would fall back onto the table; this also applies to cases prior to the initial establishment of the precepts.
As recorded in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "One who receives food with a single-minded focus" means that with the left hand, one holds the bowl with a single-minded focus, and with the right...
One should hold the edge with the hand and receive food in a level bowl; this is how one should train. (Twenty-seventh) The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove. The group of six monks went to a formal invitation and received food until their bowls overflowed.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged them, saying, "They are like hungry people greedily seeking more. The Buddha established the precept, stating:

"To eat unevenly" means to overfill the bowl. Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not within this rule, as well as the remaining matters concerning the fourfold assembly, all are the same as previously explained.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One must not accept rice in a bowl so full that it overflows with the addition of soup and vegetables;
one should leave a space around the rim of the bowl sufficient for the fingers to curl."
One should learn to receive soup in a level bowl (the twenty-eighth training rule).

Explanation of the meaning: Regarding the location where the rule was established, the origin of the censure, and so forth; as for what constitutes an offense and what does not therein, along with the other four assemblies, all are identical to the previous [rules].
Regarding the practice of receiving food, the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: When receiving food, one should observe the bowl so as not to let it overflow.
One should not request an excessive amount of soup or vegetables, for when placing the bowl back down later, there is a fear that it might spill over.
One should train in [the proper manner of eating] such foods as soup and rice. (The twenty-ninth precept.
The Origin Story: While the Buddha was residing at Jeta’s Grove in Śrāvastī, a householder prepared an offering and invited the Saṃgha.
Having personally served the rice with his own hands, he entered the inner quarters to fetch soup and returned; by the time he returned, the group of six had already finished their rice.

After the householder gave them the soup, he again entered the inner quarters to fetch more rice and returned; by the time he returned, they had already finished their soup. The householder criticized and disparaged them, saying they were like people who were starving.
The Buddha established a precept for this matter. The Vinaya states: "Regarding 'unequal distribution,' it refers to when the rice has been exhausted before the soup."
When the rice has been completely consumed, and the soup arrives before the rice has arrived, the soup is already exhausted. Regarding the offense incurred:

the transgressions therein, as well as those involving the other four assemblies, are all identical to what was stated previously. As for those who do not commit an offense: [The text continues: ...the rice has been completely consumed, and the soup arrives before the rice has arrived, the soup is already exhausted. Regarding the offense incurred: the transgressions therein, as well as those involving the other four assemblies, are all identical to what was stated previously. As for those who do not commit an offense: [the text continues].
Sometimes one needs only rice and not soup; sometimes one needs only soup and not rice; or when the time for eating has passed;
or when there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or when eating quickly; as well as in cases prior to the initial formulation of the precept.
Regarding the method of taking [food], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not take the soup first and then the rice.

One should first take the rice and press it down, and then take half the soup. If, according to the laws of the land, soup is served first and rice afterwards, one should receive it using a *kaṇḍolaka* (a small bowl or container).
If such an item is unavailable, one may receive the soup with the alms-bowl (*pātra*). However, when receiving the rice, one should use...
Cover it with your hand and lower the bowl slowly; do not allow the contents to overflow.

If a sick bhikṣu wishes to take a large amount of soup, there is no offense in taking much. (The *kubha* is a small bowl; that is to say, one takes the ladle and receives [the food] in the small bowl.)
One should eat in proper sequence; this is how one should train. (The thirtieth precept. Exegesis:
The setting and origin are as described above. Regarding the censure for going to a meal invitation: it was said that [the monks] were like birds or domestic animals.
The Buddha established the precept. The Vinaya states: "Eating out of order" means taking food from various places within the bowl and eating it.
Regarding the establishment of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein are all identical to those previously mentioned for the other four assemblies.
As for non-offenses: if one is afflicted by hot rice and picks out the cool parts to eat; or if the time for the meal is about to pass;
or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); eating quickly in such circumstances; or in cases where the precept has not yet been promulgated—these are non-offenses.
Regarding the practice of eating: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one must not eat by scooping out the entire contents [of the bowl].
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one must not pick out choice foods from within the bowl.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that one should not eat with arrogance.
One must not eat by scooping from the center of the bowl. This is how one should train. (Thirty-first) Exegesis:

Regarding the setting, the origin of the censure, and so forth; as for what constitutes an offense and what does not within this context, these, along with the other four assemblies, are all the same as previously stated.
The Vinaya says: "To 'scoop' means to place [food] at the four sides and scoop from the center down to the bottom of the bowl."
This is the manifestation of emptiness.
If a bhikṣu is not ill, he must not seek out soup or rice for himself; this is how he should train. (The thirty-second precept. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove. At that time, a householder invited the Saṃgha. He himself...
They served various kinds of food and drink with their own hands. The group of six monks sought food for themselves as if they were starving.
Householders criticized and disparaged them, so the Buddha established a precept on their account.
Regarding the establishment of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein by the other four assemblies are all identical to what was stated previously.
There is no offense in the following cases: if a sick person requests it themselves; if one requests it for another; if another requests it for oneself; if it is obtained without having requested it;
or if it occurred prior to the initial promulgation of the precept.
One must not cover the soup with rice while hoping to receive more; this is how one should train. (The thirty-third precept. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. A householder invited the Saṃgha to provide a meal offering.
The householder personally served the soup and rice. After giving the soup to one of the group of six bhikṣus, he recognized him;
he then went back inside to fetch more soup. The bhikṣu immediately covered the soup with rice. The householder asked, "Where is the soup? The bhikṣu remained silent.
The householder criticized and disparaged him, saying he was like a starving person. The Buddha, on account of this, established a precept.
Regarding the establishment of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein are all identical to those of the other four assemblies.

As for non-offenses: if one is invited to a meal; or if it is for the sake of fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin); or if it is for the sake of the sick, and having been invited to a meal, one gives it back to them;
or if at times one specifically requires soup, or at times specifically requires rice; as well as cases when the precept had not yet been established.
Regarding the practice of receiving food, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu receives food and fears it will soil his robes, he must not cover them entirely;
he should leave one side exposed. If he finishes the food, he may answer 'I have received it' when asked by another.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu is ill and requires a large amount of broth, he may take as much as needed without fault.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "One must not cover the soup with rice or the rice with soup, for this is done with the intention of seeking more and thereby increases the mind of greed.
One should cultivate a sense of detachment toward food and drink; this is what one who has left the household life ought to do.
One should eat whatever is obtained and maintain the mindfulness of having few desires."
One shall not look into the bowl of the person sitting beside them; this is how one should train. (The thirty-fourth precept. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove. A householder prepared an offering and invited the Saṃgha.
He personally served the food and drink with his own hands. Among the group of six, there was one man who received a small portion of food;

seeing that his neighbor’s portion was large, he immediately said to the lay devotee, "You have favoritism, householder. The householder replied, "I am distributing it equally; why do you say I have favoritism?
The Buddha established a precept for this matter. The Vinaya states: "One should look into the bowl of one's neighbor."

Who is more and who is less? Regarding the determination of the offense, those among them who have committed an infraction, as well as the remaining four assemblies, are all identical to what was stated previously. As for those who do not commit an offense: [as before].
If a fellow monk is ill; if one’s vision is dim so that one cannot discern whether food may be accepted or not, whether it is pure or impure, or whether it has been formally received or not;
and regarding cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precepts.

Regarding the practice of inspecting food, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If the person supervising the food inspects it to see where [food] may be taken and where it may not be taken, there is no offense.
If a fellow practitioner or a disciple under one's care is ill, one may inspect the contents of their bowl.
This is food appropriate for the illness; if one does not examine it, there is no offense. If one examines whether the food is suitable for the seniors or juniors, there is no offense.
One should eat while keeping the bowl in mind; this is how one should train. (Thirty-fifth)
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

A householder invited the Saṃgha, and the bhikṣus went to his home and sat down upon their seats. After the group of six bhikṣus had received the soup and rice, they looked around to the left and right.
Unaware of this, his neighbor took the soup and hid it. When he looked for it himself, the soup was not there.
He asked, "I received the soup just now; where is it now? His neighbor monk said, "Where did you come from?
He replied, "I placed the soup here before me and looked all around, yet now it is gone. The Buddha established a precept on account of this. (From the Vinaya)
It says: "The thought of not securing the bowl" refers to looking around to the left and right.
Regarding the offense incurred, it applies equally to all four assemblies as previously stated. As for those who do not commit an offense: [the conditions are as follows].

Or if the eyes of a fellow monk sitting nearby were dim, and he looked on his behalf to determine whether [the food] was pure or impure, or already received or not yet received; or if he himself was checking the time;

or if there was danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and he looked around to escape it; or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established—[in these instances, there is no offense].

Regarding the practice of eating, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One should maintain a composed mind while observing the alms bowl. While eating, one must not leave the bowl set before oneself while conversing with a neighbor.
If there is a necessary reason to speak to those on the left or right, one should touch the upper rim of the bowl with the left hand.
When the food reaches the third person, one should first hold up the bowl in anticipation of the food arriving.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Eat with focused attention; fill the body to nourish the Way. One must not observe others and give rise to feelings of disdain or contempt.
According to the *Lüshe lun* (Kṣudrakavastu), when eating each morsel of food, one should contemplate from where this food comes.
It comes from its place; it emerges from the granary; the granary emerges from the earth. The earth gives rise to life through the combination of seeds;

now, in turn, it nourishes this body of excrement. When lifting a morsel, one should form the perception of it as excrement. With right mindfulness present before one, one should not eat with a distracted mind.
One should form the perception of the food as repulsive, and form perceptions of it as originating from the earth, as a disease, and so forth.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Reflect upon this food; the labor expended is immense.

If one calculates the sweat shed by those who produce even a single bowl of rice and sums it all together, the food is small while the sweat is vast. This food is the result of such hardship; yet as soon as it enters the mouth, it becomes impure.
Within a single night, it transforms into excrement and urine. What was once a delicious flavor becomes something so loathsome that one does not wish to look upon it."

The practitioner reflects to himself: "If I were to become greedily attached to such wretched food, I would fall into the three miserable realms. Contemplating food in this way, one should cultivate revulsion for the five desires.
One must not take large mouthfuls of rice when eating; this is how one should train (the thirty-sixth rule).
Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and origin are as above. Regarding the censure for going to a meal: it was said that [the monks] resembled domestic animals.
The Buddha established the precept for them. The Vinaya states: "A large mouthful" means one that cannot be accommodated within the mouth.
Regarding the determination of the offense: those transgressions committed therein, as well as those involving the other four assemblies, are all identical to what was stated previously.

There is no offense in cases such as when the time for the meal is about to expire, or when there is danger to life, danger to one's celibate life (*brahmacarya*), or when eating quickly, or during the initial period before the precept had been established.
Regarding the method of eating, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One must not take large morsels, nor should one take small ones;
rather, one should eat in portions of two or three grains, like a courtesan. One should eat in a manner that fits the mouth.
An elder should eat slowly and must not finish quickly, lest he remain watching and cause the juniors to eat in a frantic rush and fail to be satisfied.
One must not open one’s mouth wide in anticipation of food; this is how one should train. (Thirty-seventh) Commentary:
Regarding the setting, the origin of the censure, and so forth, as well as what constitutes an offense and what does not, these are all identical to the previous cases for the other four assemblies.
The Vinaya states: "To open the mouth wide" means to open the mouth wide beforehand before the food has even arrived.
This is for the purpose of waiting.
Regarding the gathering [of food], the *Saṃghāṭī-vinaya* states: "When a bhikṣu eats, he should follow the manner of eating of the elephant king of the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*).

Once food has entered the mouth, he uses his nose to mark the boundary between the front and back portions. After the preceding morsel has been swallowed, he continues to place the subsequent ball [of food] inside."
If one has an ulcer in the mouth, it is permissible to open it wide;
there is no offense. One must not speak while holding food in the mouth. This is how one should train.

(Thirty-eighth). Explanation of the Meaning: The setting of the occasion, the arising of criticism and suspicion, and so forth, are as described above. The Buddha established the precept for this case. The Vinaya states:
Regarding "speaking with food in the mouth": when food remains in the mouth, one's speech is indistinct and causes others not to understand.

(This is based on the *nidāna* [introductory narrative], which simply mentions "speaking with food in the mouth. One must know that there are two sets of five [rules] concerning eating; for all such eating and chewing, one must never speak with food in the mouth. Speaking with food in the mouth is the practice of laypeople (*avadātavasana*) and of shameless Brahmins who accept alms;
it is not the proper etiquette for a bhikṣu attending a meal offering.)
Regarding the establishment of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein by the four assemblies are all identical to those previously mentioned. As for non-offenses:

these include cases where one is choking and seeks water, or when there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya), or making a sound while eating, as well as during the initial period before the precepts were established.

Regarding the proper timing for responding to a call, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When the Upādhyāya, Ācārya, or Sthavira calls, if one can respond without changing the tone of one's voice while the mouthful has not yet been swallowed, that is permissible.
If one cannot do so, one should respond after swallowing. If another person objects to this, one should reply:
"Because there was food in my mouth, I did not respond immediately."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: When receiving additional food, one should ask whether more is needed;
one must not disparage or scold the food, nor should one clump rice into balls and toss them into the mouth from a distance. This is how one should train. (Thirty-ninth)
Commentary on the Meaning: The setting for the origin of this rule is as described above. Regarding the censure for going to a meal offering, it is said that one is like a magician.
The Buddha established the precept for this; the Vinaya states: "One who throws from afar first opens their mouth, then takes a lump of rice and throws it from a distance so that it enters."
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, as well as those involving the other four assemblies, are all identical to what was stated previously.
There is no offense in cases where one is bound and food is thrown into one's mouth, or for those who were acting prior to the formulation of the precepts.

Regarding the practice of gathering [fruit]: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if one eats sour jujubes, grapes, or various other such things—even roasted beans—by picking them up and tossing them into the mouth, there is no offense.
One should not let food fall; this is how one should train. (Fortieth) The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove. A householder invited the Saṃgha.
He personally served the food and drink with his own hands. The group of six monks took lumps of rice in their hands and chewed them.

A lay follower named Bāṣpa (or "Half-eater") criticized and disparaged this. The Buddha, on their account, established a precept. The Vinaya states: "To scatter" means that half [of the food] enters the mouth while half remains in the hand.

(This rule was established based on the dining etiquette of the Western Regions; in the present land of the East, one should use a spoon when eating from a bowl. If food is scattered, the penalty shall be the same as prescribed here.)

Regarding the establishment of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein by the four assemblies are all identical to those previously mentioned. As for those who do not commit an offense:
this includes eating thin cakes, scorched rice, melons, sugarcane, vegetables, fruits, and cases where the precepts had not yet been established at the time of gathering.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a ball of roasted flour is too large, one should divide it with the hand so that it may fit into the mouth; the same applies to cakes."
It is also thus.
One should train not to eat making cheeks (puffing out the cheeks). [The forty-first precept. Explanation of the Meaning:
The setting and the origin of the rule are as above. Regarding the censure for going to a meal invitation: it was said that he resembled a macaque. The Buddha, for...
**Formulation of the Precept:** The Vinaya states: "Eating with puffed cheeks" means causing both cheeks to bulge out like those of a macaque.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the transgressions therein, all other members of the fourfold assembly are subject to the same rules as previously stated. **Non-offenses:** There is no offense in the following cases: [list of non-offenses].
There may be such illnesses; or the time for the meal may be passing; or there may be danger to life or danger to the holy life; or one eats quickly;
or it concerns the initial period before the precepts were established, and so forth.
Regarding the practice of "turning food in the mouth," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not turn food around in the mouth. "Food" refers to a mouthful of rice;
one must not take a ball of rice from one cheek and move it to the other. One should chew on one side and swallow while chewing that very side.
One must not make noise while chewing food; this is how one should train. (The forty-second precept. Explanation of the Meaning:

The setting and the origin of the rule are as above. Because [monastics] made noise while partaking of offerings, they incurred the reproach of the laity. Therefore, the Buddha established this precept.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein by the four assemblies are all identical to those previously mentioned.
As for non-offenses: these include chewing dry cakes or parched rice; chewing sugarcane, melons, or fruits;

or cases where the precept had not yet been established at the time of the assembly. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not eat making smacking or slurping sounds, nor may one swallow food whole."
If one makes gurgling sounds, there is no offense if it is due to a disease of the throat.
The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states: "When drinking gruel, one must not make sounds while eating roots, stalks, and the like; do not allow loud noises to be made."
One must not gulp down food with a large mouthful; this is how one should train.
(Forty-third) Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and the origin of the censure are as described above. The Buddha established the precept accordingly. The Vinaya states:
"To gulp" means to open the mouth wide and call out from a distance while gulping.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies. There is no offense in the following cases:
if there is pain in the mouth; if one is eating soup; if one is drinking any kind of beverage; or if it concerns the very first instance before the precept was established.
Regarding the consumption [of food], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one eats thin gruel or soup, one must not drink by slurping so as to make a sound;
one should swallow slowly.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One should not eat by flicking the tongue, nor by smacking the lips, nor by making gurgling sounds, nor by blowing air [upon the food]."

When eating (if one truly has an oral ailment, one should follow the provisions of one's own school; if there is no oral ailment, one should adhere to the *Mahāsāṃghika-mūla-vinaya*), one must not lick food with the tongue; this is how one should train. (Forty-fourth)
Explanation of the Meaning: The circumstances and the arising of the censure are as described above. The Buddha established the precept accordingly. The Vinaya states:
"To lick with the tongue" means to lick morsels of food with the tongue (*piṇḍa*). (A *piṇḍa* is a morsel; it refers to that which is tested or probed.)
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, as well as those involving the other four assemblies, are all identical to what was stated previously.

There is no offense in cases where one is bound, or when the hands are covered in mud, or stained with grease and filth, and one uses the tongue to lick them clean; or in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established.
Regarding the practice of eating: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one must not lick the hands while eating.
If ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar has adhered to the hands, one should take a portion by scraping it onto the rim of the bowl and then eat it.
One must not lick the fingers while eating; however, if honey or salt is on the tips of the fingers, it is permissible to lick them without fault.
One must not flap one’s hands while eating; this is how one should train. (45) Explanation of the Meaning:
The setting and origin are as above. "Reproach" refers to being treated like a king or a high minister.
The Buddha established this precept for that reason. "Flapping" means to move or shake the hands.
Regarding the establishment of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, for all four assemblies, they are entirely the same as previously stated.
As for those who do not commit an offense: there may be such illnesses; or there may be grass or insects in the food; or at times the hands are impure and one wishes to shake them off;
or before having received the food, the hands become soiled by contact and one shakes them off; and in the case of the very first instance.
Regarding the regulations on the precepts and so forth, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When shaking one's hand, one must not shake it toward a neighboring seat.
If food adheres to the hand, one should shake it in front of oneself. If dusting off the bowl, [one should do so in the same manner]."
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One should not sprinkle water from one's alms bowl upon others, thereby soiling their robes;
nor should one harbor envy upon seeing the fine garments of others. All such actions as these are improper."
One must not eat with food scattered in the hand; one should train [in this] (the forty-sixth rule).
Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and origin are as above. "Reproach" refers to appearing like a chicken or a bird.

The Buddha established this precept because [people] were eating with food scattered in the hand—meaning they did not form it into morsels. In this region, when receiving food, both spoon and bowl are used; there is no ritual of forming morsels with the hand. Regarding the offense therein: [it occurs if food falls].
The offenses for all four assemblies are identical to those mentioned previously.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when receiving food, one must not allow even a single grain to fall to the ground.

However, if it falls while a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) is pouring it out, there is no offense. When placing food into the mouth, do not let it fall to the ground; if it should happen to fall by mistake, [there is no offense].
There is no offense [if one acts as follows]: when eating melons, fruits, or sugarcane, one must not discard the rinds, pits, or pulp haphazardly on the ground;
they should be gathered at the edge of one's feet.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If food falls onto grass or leaves that have been received [as a seat], it should be eaten. If there is soil upon it, blow it away."
One should remove [the soil] and then eat. If there is much earth adhering [to the food], one may wash it off with water to make it edible.
One must not hold a drinking vessel with soiled hands; this is how one should train (the forty-seventh).
Exegesis: The setting for the origin of this rule is as described above. Regarding "contemptuous speech," it refers to those who resemble kings or ministers.
The Buddha established the precept for this reason. The Vinaya states: "Defiled hands" refers to hands that have rice mixed with oil clinging to them.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein are all identical to those previously mentioned for the other four assemblies.
There is no offense in cases such as receiving [the gift] upon grass, receiving it upon leaves, receiving it with washed hands, or when the precept had not yet been established.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: One should not eat with fingers bent; one should not eat by sniffing at the food; one should not disparage or revile the food;
and one must not discard water used for washing the bowl inside the residence of a layperson. This is how one should train. (48)
The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jetavana Monastery, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six monks, having finished their meal at a householder’s home, washed their bowls and discarded the rinsing water, leaving even leftover food scattered upon the ground.

When the householder saw this, he criticized and disparaged them, saying they had received too much food and drink, and that they were wasting it in such a messy manner, like starving beggars or like kings.
O Great Minister, the Buddha established this precept. The Vinaya states: "Washing-bowl water" refers to water mixed with rice.
Regarding the offenses incurred therein, they apply equally to all four assemblies, just as previously stated. As for those who do not commit an offense: [the text here indicates the exceptions].

If one receives water in a basin for washing and carries it outside to discard it, as well as cases prior to the initial formulation of the precepts and so forth—consulting the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü), it asks: "Is there no offense in discarding it with the owner's permission?"
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: At the time of eating, one should take food according to the capacity of one's stomach and must not receive more than necessary.

If a *kappiya-kāraka* (lay attendant) suddenly gives too much, before eating it, one should reduce the portion and give it to a neighboring seat-mate. If the neighbor does not take it, one should give it to a *śrāmaṇera* or a *ārāmika* (monastery worker).
When washing the bowl, one must not pour even a single grain of rice onto the ground; if there is any [leftover], [it should be disposed of properly].
It should be collected on a wooden board or upon leaves.

Examination of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: There were some laypeople who had newly built a house and desired for bhikṣus to sprinkle the ground with water used for washing their bowls as an act of auspiciousness.
The Buddha permitted them to sprinkle the ground with water from their bowls that contained no food.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: When someone comes to beg for bowl-water, one should wash the bowl clean, place pure water within it, and recite a *gāthā* three times before bestowing it upon that person.
Whether they wash with it or drink it, it can eliminate ten thousand ailments. One must not place leftover food into the water of the bowl.
The *gāthā* says: "By means of the pleasures of the five worldly desires, or even those of the various devas..."
This pleasure, compared to the bliss of the exhaustion of craving, does not equal even a thousandth part. Because accumulation gives rise to suffering, and from suffering, accumulation arises again;
the Noble Eightfold Path can transcend these, reaching the sublime state of Nirvana. Whoever practices giving will certainly obtain its benefit;
if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely attain peace and joy later. (Although the Buddha personally spoke this verse, it must be [practiced with] true and genuine purity...)

One who purely upholds the precepts shall chant [the mantra] three times while holding their alms bowl; only then will they cure myriad ailments. If one lacks the virtue of the precepts, even if they chant a thousand times, it will be difficult to evoke a response.
One must not discharge feces, urine, mucus, or saliva upon living grass or vegetables, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train.

(The forty-ninth precept. The Origin Story: This precept was established in two stages. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the group of six monks discharged feces, urine, mucus, and saliva upon living grass and vegetables.
When the lay devotees saw this, they reviled them, saying, "They are just like animals."

This was the first time the Buddha established a precept for the Saṃgha. After the precept had been thus established, there was a sick bhikṣu who was unable to avoid living grass or vegetables because he was utterly exhausted;
therefore, [the rule] was again relaxed, stating that there is no offense except in the case of illness. This was the second establishment of the precept.
Regarding the offenses incurred therein, they apply equally to all four assemblies, just as previously specified. According to the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya, it is the same.

If a bhikṣuṇī commits a pāyattika offense— [wherein the formulation for the monks' precepts was established first, while those for the four assemblies were subsequently included; thus the formulation for the bhikṣuṇīs’ minor rules was established later,
each being strictly formulated for its own respective group, hence they are considered more serious]— there is no offense if she voids excrement or urine in a place devoid of grass or vegetables,
and it flows onto or falls upon living grass or vegetables, either by being blown there by the wind or carried there by birds, or if it is her very first [act].
Regarding the period before the precepts were established,
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If, during the summer months, the grass grows so luxuriantly that there is no empty space,
one should stay in places frequented by camels, oxen, horses, and the like, or upon bare tiles and stones, or upon dry grass and leaves."
Regarding the sequence: if there is no [dry ground], one should use a wooden branch to receive it, causing the excrement to fall first onto the wood and only afterwards onto the ground.
If one's hands or feet become soiled by feces, urine, mucus, or saliva, they may be wiped on living grass.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If one is in a place thick with thorny bushes, there is no offense.

If walking through a great forest where branches and leaves are densely interlaced, one should avoid areas frequented by people. If traveling through cultivated fields where there is no open space, one should carry dry leaves."
One should relieve oneself on cloth. If such cloth cannot be obtained, there is no offense.
One must not discharge feces, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva into water, except when ill; this is how one should train (the fiftieth).
Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and the origin of the censure are as described above. Regarding the offenses therein, they apply equally to all four assemblies, just as previously stated.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one has an illness; if while defecating or urinating on the bank, the excrement or urine falls into the water;
if it is blown by the wind or carried away by a bird into the water; or if the precept had not yet been established at the time.
Regarding bathing, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If it rains and water suddenly overflows, one should stand upon a clod of earth, a tile, a stone, bamboo, or wood.
First let the water fall onto the wood, and only afterwards let it fall upon oneself.
If the hands or feet become soiled by excrement or urine, they may be washed in the water. When entering the water to bathe, one must not spit into it. If...
Regarding those at a distant shore: one should spit into one's hand and then discard it.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If the water is not used by people, or if it is seawater, there is no offense.
Even if the water is fit for use, if it is so remote that no one uses it, there is no offense."
The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: Whenever one expels mucus or spits, one should not make a loud noise, nor should one do so frequently.
If one is habitually prone to much mucus and spittle, one should go to a secluded place to do so.
One must not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill; this is how one should train. (Fifty-first). Explanation of the Meaning:
The setting and the origin of the censure are as described above. The Buddha established the precept for this matter. Regarding the offenses therein:
And the other four assemblies are all the same as before. There is no offense if one has an illness, is bound in fetters, or at times has mud or grease on the feet;

or if it is the very first instance before the precept was established. (However, regarding this one precept, when the minor practices were being transmitted throughout the five regions of India, everyone sat in a squatting posture (*utkuṭukāsana*).

This was also consistent in the various countries of the maritime islands. Only in the land of China is the situation different; matters are not uniform there. Those who stand are many, while those who squat are few.)

In a land where squatting is not practiced, one who squats is ridiculed as being "not a man"; in a place where standing is not the norm, one who stands is regarded as a curiosity. Regarding these two paths, there ought to be a rational resolution. For while the Vinaya follows Western (Indian) regulations and the Councils of recitation still listed both permitted and prohibited practices—thus leaving no room for transgression when it came to impurity—the Dharma flowed eastward to China;
those who uphold it should adapt to local customs to avoid public censure. By adhering to the teachings and practicing virtuous conduct, one may hope to remain free from doubt.
Citation from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: The Buddha said, "Even if something is prescribed by me, if it is not considered pure in other regions, it should not be used.
Even if something is not prescribed by me, if it must be practiced in other regions, it must be practiced."
The *Mūla-karman* states: At the time when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I have previously expounded the Vinaya teachings for you extensively, yet I have not yet spoken of them in brief. You should now listen to this summary teaching.
For instance, regarding certain matters that I have neither permitted nor prohibited in the past, if concerning such a matter..."
That which accords with impurity and opposes purity is impure; it should not be practiced.
If a matter accords with purity and opposes impurity, this is pure; it should be practiced accordingly. Question:

For what purpose did the World-Honored One deliver this brief instruction when he was about to enter parinirvāṇa? Answer: After the Great Teacher has passed away, until [the time of] the Noble Ones...
Before the Teaching has vanished, do not allow non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to raise such criticisms:
"Since the World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), yet there are matters in the world that he neither permits nor prohibits, how are his disciples to act?
To prevent this difficulty and to observe for the benefit of future generations, he established these rules. Furthermore, he desired that his disciples...

There is no doubt regarding this matter; one shall attain peaceful dwelling. Therefore, it must be explained: (In general, all those who preside over the Vinaya, I pray that you do not, upon merely hearing this teaching, hastily adopt other fixed prohibitions and falsely claim they accord with the holy teachings.
This would result in prescribing what was not prescribed and relaxing what was prescribed, thereby bringing disorder to the Vinaya. Who could possibly take the blame for such a sin?)

Appendix: Examination of the Rules The Buddha said that one should not suppress the urge to urinate or defecate for long. When departing [the dwelling], one should hold *śocana-tṛṇa* (grass for cleansing).
If others have already gone ahead, one should walk in front of them. Upon reaching the latrine, one should place one’s clothes on a peg, a rack, a tree, or a stone.
Having reached the exterior of the latrine, one should snap one’s fingers or cough so that humans and non-humans may be aware of one’s presence. With the hand...
One should hold the robe firmly so that it does not touch either side of the latrine. One should place the feet firmly and first look for snakes or insects, which should be driven out.
One should not lift the robe before squatting; rather, one should squat with both feet together.

Once squatting, one should gradually lift the robe, taking care not to lean forward or backward toward the sides, thereby preventing feces, urine, mucus, or saliva from defiling the latrine opening. One must not do so.
One should not make a loud noise. The toilet grass should be at least one span (*vitasti*) long and no shorter than four finger-breadths (*catur-aṅgula*).
Grass that has been used and grass that has not yet been used should be placed in separate locations. Having finished, one should slowly rise and gradually lower one’s garments.

Upon reaching the place for cleansing, one should snap one’s fingers to alert both humans and non-humans. One should first look out for venomous snakes, then gradually lift one’s garment and squat; one must not approach the water directly.
Wash the vessel. When washing, do not allow it to make a sound. Having finished washing, one should wipe the water from the body with the hand, or with a leaf, or with a piece of rag.
One should wash the hands with salt-earth, or ash, or mud, or cow dung, or clay bricks, or bathing powder (*śāṭī*).
Having washed, one should gradually lower one's garments and rise to look at the latrine; if there is any impurity, one should sweep it away.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "One should wash [the hands] using the tips of two fingers—namely, the ring finger and the little finger.
One must not preach the Dharma to a person who has reversed their robe or is otherwise disrespectful, except in cases of illness. This is how one should train. (Fifty-second [Precept])

The Origin: This precept has two origins of enactment. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the group of six monks preached the Dharma to people who were disrespectfully wearing their robes slung over one shoulder.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, those who possessed a sense of shame, modesty, and a desire to train in the precepts took offense at the group of six and reported it to the Buddha. This was the first formulation of the precept. At that time, the bhikṣus were uncertain.
Fearing that he might incur an offense by preaching the Dharma to one who was not ill but was instead clutching his robes, the Buddha declared that there is no transgression for one who is ill.

Therefore, the phrase "except in the case of illness" was added; this constitutes the second regulation (hereafter, when preaching the Dharma while exempt from the rule of illness, all subsequent articles shall be governed by this precedent).
Regarding the determination of the offense: those who commit such transgressions among the four assemblies shall all be treated identically as previously stated.
As for those who do not commit an offense: if one preaches the Dharma for a king or a high minister; or if it concerns the period before the precepts were first established;

or if, although they are kings and ministers honored by the world, one considers that they ought to hold the Buddha-Dharma in profound reverence—thinking that even if they were to hear it, what benefit would there be if they harbor arrogance; or if one forgets one's own body for the sake of the Dharma, as was the case with all people of antiquity; and furthermore, considering that [the Dharma] was personally entrusted at the assembly on Vulture Peak—therefore, one must specifically show them respect. This applies to the preacher.

You must自重 (cherish and uphold yourself) by means of the Dharma. If neither party shows mutual respect, both will suffer loss. As for the authority to guide, encourage, and transform others, it must necessarily be exercised by weighing the individual according to their capacity; one must not abruptly deliver teachings suited only for those of inferior faculties.
All precepts should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the practice: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The Buddhas do not teach the Dharma to those whose minds are not focused.
One must not preach the Dharma to sentient beings who have wrapped their necks with robes, except in cases of illness. This is a precept that should be studied. (Fifty-third).
**Exegesis:** The setting for the origin of this rule is as described above. The Buddha established this precept (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"According to the local customs of the Western Regions, the garments worn are not cut or tailored; they are originally woven from a single piece of woolen cloth (*kambala*). These are expensive, fresh white, light, soft, and multicolored. For men, it is wrapped around the waist and passed under the armpits, with a scarf draped across the chest leaving the right shoulder bare. For women, the robe hangs down and covers both shoulders completely. Therefore, the rule now prescribes 'wrapping around the neck.

If one here [in China] wraps the neck with a kerchief, a turban, or other such items, the application of the rule should be understood accordingly. If outward decorum is not observed, inward mindfulness will not be reverent; thus, one should not preach the Dharma to such a person").
Regarding whether an offense has been committed therein or not, as well as for the other four assemblies, all are exactly the same as before.
One must not preach the Dharma to those who cover their heads, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train. (Fifty-fourth)

Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and the origin of the incident are as described above. The Buddha established the precept: "As for one who covers their head—this refers to covering the head with clothing or other items. In India, exposing the crown of the head and walking barefoot signifies the highest respect;

in the Eastern lands (China), wearing the cap and shoes in full array manifests the utmost reverence. However, rites follow national customs, and thus these serve as expressions of devout respect. In this region, apart from the removal of the cap or turban, if one uses any other object to cover the head, one must not preach the Dharma to them.
Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not within this rule, as well as the remaining four assemblies, all are the same as previously stated.

Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: if a bhikṣu, for the sake of the stūpa or the Saṃgha, goes before a king or a landowner, and that person says, "Bhikṣu, preach the Dharma to me," if there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) present, he should form the intention to speak for that person's sake;
if the king listens, there is no offense. Furthermore, if a bhikṣu is traveling through a dangerous and fearful path, [he should] protect...
The people of Vaiśālī said, "Venerable One, please teach us the Dharma. Although he taught them while they had their heads covered, there was no offense.
One must not teach the Dharma to those with their heads wrapped, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train. (Fifty-fifth)

Exegesis: The setting for the origin of this rule is as described above. The Buddha established the precept [the term *guo* meaning "to wrap" is distinct from the meanings of "to bind" and "to cover"].
Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not within this context, as well as the other four assemblies, all are identical to the previous cases.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu, for the sake of the Stūpa or the Saṃgha, approaches a king or a local lord, or even when traveling through dangerous and fearful paths, the permission to speak is granted as stated above.
One must not preach the Dharma to someone with hands on hips, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train (the fifty-sixth rule).

Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and origin are as above. The Buddha established this precept for those with hands on hips—whether with one hand or both hands—one should not preach the Dharma to them.
Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as the other four assemblies, all are the same as previously stated.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One must not preach the Dharma to a person who is hugging their knees, except in the case of illness;
one must not preach the Dharma to a person who is sitting with legs crossed at the ankles, except in the case of illness.
One must not preach the Dharma to those wearing leather sandals, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train. (Fifty-seventh) Exegesis:
The setting and the occasion for the arising [of this rule] are as above. The Buddha established this precept.

In the Sanskrit language, it is called *kavada* or *upānah*, which translates here as "boots"; these are footwear made of leather. (Although in the Eastern Land [China] there is no custom of listening to the Dharma while barefoot, if one is wearing...)

Impure footwear must be discarded and replaced. Other matters regarding what is permitted or prohibited should be understood by referring to the abbreviated teachings. As for whether an offense has been committed therein or not, this applies equally to the other four assemblies.
All [details] are the same as before.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If many people are wearing leather sandals and they cannot be made to remove them, then provided that those who were not wearing them do not speak [of the offense], there is no fault."

One must not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train. (Fifty-eighth) Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and the circumstances for the origin of this rule are as described above.
The Buddha established this precept [as follows]: [Clogs] made of grass are called *fēi*; those made of leather are called *lǚ*; those made of hemp are called *jiǎo*;

and those made of wood are called *jī*. There are also silk clogs (*bòjī*), which are made of silk. In the Western Regions, kings, ministers, and elders all wear sandals adorned with gold, silver, and jewels. According to the underlying principle, it is forbidden to preach the Dharma to anyone wearing such footwear. However, there may be occasions where one acts according to the needs of the situation through skillful means.

[Included] as above, it should be understood. Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not within this context, as well as for the other four assemblies, all are identical to what was previously gathered in the assembly.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu, for the sake of a stūpa or for the sake of the Saṃgha, goes before a king or a landowner, and that person says, 'Bhikṣu, preach the Dharma to me,' he should not say, 'Please remove your shoes,' for fear of giving rise to suspicion."

Therefore, if there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle pure things) nearby, one should pay attention and speak the Dharma for the sake of that *kappiya-kāraka*. Although the king may permit it, there is no offense;
however, one must not preach the Dharma to those on horseback, except when they are ill. This is how one should train. (Fifty-ninth)
The Origin: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that King Prasenajit established a regulation for himself, saying, "If the Buddha is at Jetavana, I shall go there every day in person.
Consequently, he traveled by carriage to Jetavana to see the Buddha, where the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) preached the Dharma to him.
When the various bhikṣus heard this, those who practiced the dhūta austerities and delighted in training in the precepts reproached the group of six.
He informed the Buddha, who then established the precept. Therefore, it is ordained that one should not preach the Dharma to those who are ahead of oneself while one is behind;
to those walking on the road while one is stationary; to those sitting while one is standing; to those on high seats while one is on low seats; or to those lying down while one is sitting.

Furthermore, one should not preach the Dharma to those carrying staffs, swords, spears, blades, or canopies. The origin of these cases is the same as before (here, "vehicles" refers to mounts such as elephants, horses, oxen, and carriages). Among them—
Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as the other four assemblies, all are identical to what was stated previously.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "If a bhikṣu, for the sake of the stūpa or the Saṃgha, approaches a king or a local lord, and that person says, 'Bhikṣu, preach the Dharma to me,' he should not tell him to dismount from his vehicle, for fear that suspicion might arise."
If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) nearby, one should make a mental resolve and speak for the sake of that *kappiya-kāraka*.

Even if the king listens, there is no offense. Furthermore, when traveling on a dangerous road where there is fear, if a guard says, "Venerable sir, preach the Dharma to me," there is no offense in preaching even while he is mounted on a vehicle.
One must not stay overnight in a stūpa of the Buddha, except for the purpose of guarding it; this is how one should train. (The sixtieth precept. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The group of six monks stayed overnight in a stūpa of the Buddha.
When the bhikṣus heard this, those of few desires censured the group of six. They reported the matter to the Buddha, who then established a precept.
At that time, the bhikṣus were doubtful and did not dare to stay overnight for the sake of guarding [the site]. The Buddha also granted permission; this was the second formulation of the rule.
Explanation of Terms: The Sanskrit term is *stūpa*. It is also called a *pútú* (浮圖). In the new translation, it is called a *sùdǔbō* (窣堵波). It is also referred to as a *zhì* (制).
*Ti* (底) is another name for *caitya*. This is translated as "square mound" (*fangfen*) or "round tomb" (*yuanzhong*).

The correct translation is "congregation of characteristics" (*juxiang*), meaning that the manifold virtues of the Tathāgata are gathered here, and it is thus gazed upon by both humans and devas; it refers specifically to the place where the Buddha’s *śarīra* are enshrined.
Furthermore, wherever the Buddha preached the Dharma or walked in meditation, a *stūpa* was erected. Although there may be no [relics]...
It is also called a *stūpa*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "That which contains *śarīra* is called a *caitya*;

that which lacks *śarīra* is called a *cetiya*. (The term *śarīra* has two meanings: first, the whole body; second, fragmented remains. There are three types of fragmented remains: first, bone *śarīra*, which is white in color;

second, flesh *śarīra*, which is red in color; third, hair *śarīra*, which is black in color. Bodhisattvas and Arhats all possess these three types. Only the *śarīra* of a Buddha is not fixed to a single color; through supernatural transformations, it emits radiance that endures for immeasurable kalpas.)

It is eternally present and perfect, benefiting all sentient beings. It is that which has been cultivated through the熏修 (xūnxiū—perfuming cultivation) of morality, concentration, and wisdom, and is the collective gathering of wondrous merits. Rare and difficult to encounter, it serves as the most supreme field of merit during the age of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma. The *Shilaozhi* (Record of Śākyamuni and Laozi) in the *Weishu* states: "After the Buddha had passed away, his body was cremated with fragrant wood.

His sacred relics were divided into fragments, large and small like grains of rice. Striking them did not break them; burning them did not scorch them. They possessed radiant light and divine efficacy, and are thus called *śarīra* (relics). Kings and ministers collected and enshrined them, exhausting themselves in offerings of incense and flowers to pay their respects.

Shrines were built over the tombs, which are called *stūpas*, much like ancestral temples. Therefore, they are at times referred to as 'stūpa-temples' (*tamiào*). This term refers specifically to the Buddha’s stūpas, distinguishing them from those of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas. Even if they are not [the Buddha's]..."
Regarding stupas: one should likewise pay respect to all stupas (buddhas) of the noble ones and sages, and must not engage in such acts as staying overnight within them.

However, this does not apply to those who act for the purpose of protection (meaning that with a respectful mind, one sweeps away dust and debris at dawn and dusk, burns incense and lamps day and night, and guards against unfaithful laypeople who might commit transgressions through arrogance; therefore, staying overnight to provide protection is permitted—this refers to those such as the current masters of incense and lamp halls).
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies.

There is no offense in cases such as when one suffers from such an illness, or is seized by a person of superior force, or when there is a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Regarding the overnight stay and the period before the initial formulation of the precepts, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (The Vinaya in Four Parts) provides the following scriptural evidence: When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, no one dared to shave the World-Honored One’s hair out of reverence for him.
There was only a young boy named Upāli, who was ignorant and had not yet attained anything [of spiritual distinction].

Bhaya had his hair shaved by the Buddha. While his parents stood before the World-Honored One, they joined their palms and said, "It is good that this young child has shaved the World-Honored One’s hair;
does it look well? The Buddha said, "He shaves very skillfully; it makes the body comfortable. However, [the boy] bent his body too far.
The father then said to his son, "Do not bend your body too far, lest it cause the World-Honored One discomfort. Furthermore—
He asked the Buddha, "Is it well? The Buddha said, "It is good. [The son] held his body too straight. His father said to him, "Do not hold your body so straight;
do not cause the World-Honored One discomfort. He asked the Buddha again, "Is it well? The Buddha said, "It is good. [The son] then drew in his breath too coarsely.
His father said to him, "Do not draw in your breath so coarsely; do not cause the Buddha discomfort. He asked the Buddha once more, "Is it well? The Buddha said, "It is good."
"No," the Buddha said, "it is well, but his exhalation is too coarse. The father said to his son, "Do not exhale so coarsely as to cause the Buddha discomfort.
Then the young boy Upāli, having brought both inhalation and exhalation to an end, entered the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda: "This boy has already entered the fourth dhyāna; go and take hold of his hand."
[The Buddha] said, "Take a knife. Ānanda immediately received the instruction and took a knife; using his old hair-receptacle, he gathered the World-Honored One’s hair.
The Buddha said, "You should not use an old vessel. You should use a new vessel, wrapped in new silk cloth and new garments.
At that time, there was a prince, General Gopāli, who had gone to campaign in the west. He requested the Buddha’s hair to take with him for the purpose of making offerings.

The Buddha granted permission. [The monks] did not know how to store it. The Buddha said, "I permit you to place it within a golden stūpa, a silver stūpa, or a stūpa made of the seven precious substances, and to wrap it in silken cloths. They did not know how to carry it.

The Buddha said, "I permit you to carry it on elephants, horses, carriages, litters, or palanquins, or to bear it upon the head or upon the shoulders. At that time, the prince took the World-Honored One’s hair and departed.

He went forth to wage a campaign and returned to his kingdom victorious. For the World-Honored One, he erected a hair-stupa (*keśa-caitya*). This was a stupa from the time the World-Honored One was still in the world.
At that time, various bhikṣus also requested the hair of the World-Honored One and wished to carry it with them, but they did not know how to enshrine it.

The Buddha said, "I allow you to enshrine it in a golden stupa or the like. They did not know how to carry it while traveling; eventually, they carried it upon their shoulders while traveling. At that time...
The upāsakas thought to themselves: "If the Buddha would permit us to erect stūpas for the World-Honored One while he is still alive, we shall build them.
The Buddha granted permission for their construction, yet they did not know how to build them.
The Buddha said: "They should be made square, or with eight corners, or circular. They did not know what materials to use. The Buddha said: "They should be made of brick, stone, or wood."
[The construction] was carried out. All [procedures] were as prescribed above, even down to the ground-covering, which was also as above.
He wished to construct a railing around the four sides of the banner and to provide ornaments and offerings. The Buddha permitted each of these; he allowed the lion figure to be made on the banner.
At that time, the bhikṣus stayed overnight inside the World-Honored One’s stūpa, even to the point of placing the Buddha’s stūpa in the lower room while they themselves stayed in the upper room.

...and so forth. Regarding these twenty-six matters that arose as conditions, the Buddha declared in each case, "It should not be done," and he established the regulations one by one, as listed below.
The *Mūlakacāra* states:
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada requested of the World-Honored One, saying, "I have fashioned [a reliquary] with the hair and nails of the Tathāgata..."
"A stūpa. If the Buddha permits it, I shall construct one. The Buddha told the householder, "You may do as you wish. [The householder] did not know how to construct it.

The Buddha said, "From the descent from Tuṣita Heaven to Jambudvīpa, through the conversion and guidance of sentient beings, up until the site of his parinirvāṇa—[you should construct] the sacred sites of his previous lives (*jātaka*) according to your wishes. (In all other recensions, these matters concerning the stūpas and so forth are missing; only...)

There is a regulation within our school. The reason for recording these details now is to prevent doubts regarding the existence of stūpas during the Buddha’s own lifetime, and to take this as authoritative evidence. Appendix:
The *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* states that there are eight kinds of stūpas, all of which possess *lupan* (exposed tiers).

A Buddha’s stūpa has eight tiers; a Bodhisattva’s, seven; a Pratyekabuddha’s, six; one who has attained the fourth fruit [of Arhatship], five; one who has attained the third fruit, four; and one who has attained the second fruit, three.
The fruit [stūpas] have three tiers; the stūpas of those who have attained the first fruit have two tiers; and the wheel-turning king’s has one tier.
For ordinary monks, there are only plantain leaves and fire-jewels. Although the wheel-turning king’s stūpa has but one tier, a bhikṣu must not pay it homage because it is not a stūpa of an Ārya.
Ordinary monks, however, should pay homage according to their respective order of seniority.
The *Latter Part of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "A Buddha-stūpa is thirteen stories high and topped with a wheel-mark (*cakra*), adorned with various jewels.
A Pratyekabuddha’s stūpa has eleven stories, and an Arhat’s four stories; these too are embellished with jewels.

Although the stūpas of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) are likewise made of jewels, they lack tiered levels, for such kings have not yet escaped the suffering of the various realms of existence within the three worlds. (Regarding the wheel-mark, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The Buddha... [text continues]).

He constructed a stupa for Kāśyapa Buddha, topped with a tiered canopy and a long pole bearing the *cakra* (wheel) emblem. In the sutras, this is frequently referred to as the *xianglun* (wheel-emblem), so named because people look up at it to observe its form; the *lupan* (exposed canopy) is itself the wheel-emblem, differing only in nomenclature.
One must not conceal wealth or property within a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of ensuring its security; this is how one should train.
(The sixty-first rule. Commentary on the Meaning: The setting and the origin of the occasion are as described above.

When the Buddha established this precept, the bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to store wealth in the stūpas even for the sake of securing them. The Buddha then granted permission once more; this is the second [instance].

This is a regulation. (Regarding "property": this refers to clothing, utensils, and equipment. It is not permissible to greedily accumulate these within one's own storehouse, thereby valuing one's personal belongings while neglecting the Buddha’s stūpas.

However, if it concerns items for making offerings to stūpas and images, or property belonging to the Saṃgha, one may temporarily store them away as a provisional measure to ensure they are protected securely and do not go astray.)
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies.
There is no offense in cases such as: for the sake of a secure storage; being held by force; when there is danger to life; when there is danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
or when the precept has not yet been promulgated.
One must not wear leather sandals when entering a Buddhist stūpa; this is how one should train. (Sixty-second precept. Explanation of the Meaning:
The setting and the circumstances for the origin of this rule are as described above. The Buddha established this precept [noting that "wei" refers to tanned leather and "ge" refers to raw leather;
any footwear made of hide is collectively termed "leather sandals"].
Regarding the establishment of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein are all treated identically to those of the other four assemblies.
As for non-offenses: these include cases where one has such an illness, or is seized by force and summoned into the stūpa, as well as instances prior to the initial promulgation of the precepts.
Appendix: According to the *Third Division* (Tṛtīya-khaṇḍa), when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, there was a son of a householder in Campā named Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa.
His parents had only this one son and cherished him deeply. Having been accustomed to comfort since birth, he had never walked upon the ground;
consequently, hair grew on the soles of his feet. At that time, the King of Magadha desired to see him.
The King issued an edict to the lord of Campā, commanding that all the elders bring their sons.
The lord of the city, having received the edict, accompanied the elders and brought the sons there. They requested the King to spread his robes upon the ground.

Then Upāli proceeded to the King’s presence, prostrated himself with his head at the King's feet, and the King, seeing him, was filled with joy and bestowed gold and jewels upon him, saying, "I have already granted this to you."
"Regarding benefits in the present life: the World-Honored One is on Vulture Peak Mountain. You should go there to pay him homage, visit him, and inquire after his well-being;

he shall grant you benefits for future lives. Following these instructions, the elders paid homage to the Buddha, heard the Dharma, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and became upāsakas.
At that time, Śaṇavāsa sought the Buddha’s permission to leave the household life. Because of this—

His parents would not consent, and the Buddha did not grant permission. He returned home and, employing skillful means, entreated his two parents until they finally allowed him to leave the household life to pursue the Path.
In the place where he practiced diligent walking meditation, blood flowed and stained the ground like a slaughterhouse.
Later, he attained the exhaustion of outflows and realized the fruit of Arhatship. The Buddha said to Śoṇa:
"You have been accustomed to pleasure since birth and are unaccustomed to enduring suffering. I permit you to wear a single-layered leather sandal within the monastery.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "I have renounced five elephant kings to leave the household life and pursue the Way.

Should people speak ill of me, saying that I covet a single-layered leather sandal, and if the World-Honored One permits the bhikṣus to possess such sandals, I too shall possess one. At that time, the Buddha remained silent.
He approved of this. Thereupon, for these reasons, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and preached the Dharma accordingly.
By means of countless skillful means, he praised the dhūta practices, those who have few desires and know contentment, and those who delight in renunciation. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"I permit you, for the sake of protecting the body, protecting the robes, and protecting the bedding, to wear single-layered leather sandals within the monastery. At that time...
The bhikṣus wore single-layered leather sandals, which soon became worn through. I permitted them to patch them with tree bark or leather;

they should sew them with thread, and I permitted them to keep awls. If they were in border regions where tiles and stones were abundant, I permitted them to wear double-layered leather sandals and to use leather as bedding.
If they obtained untreated leather, I permitted them to soften it, but I did not permit [handling] it with one hand.
One should carry leather sandals and an alms bowl. One must not possess any large hides, such as those of lions, tigers, leopards, otters, wild cats, wild foxes, or black-skinned animals.
One must not sit upon or lie upon rugs made of leather, brocade, or variegated fabrics.

When defecating, urinating, or washing one's feet, it is permitted to wear leather sandals. However, when in the presence of one’s *upādhyāya* (preceptor) or *ācārya* (teacher), one should bared one shoulder.
One should remove one’s leather sandals from the right shoulder when taking or giving anything, except when in the house of a layperson or while traveling on a road.
If it is dark at night and one fears venomous insects, wearing them is permitted. One should not make bags for bowls, needles, thread, and so forth out of leather.
Hats, waistbands, meditation belts, and all impure, loathsome leather or leather articles must not be kept; however, [the use of certain items] is permitted.
One should carry a water skin. If there is dust at one's dwelling place, one must not use leather as a ground-covering.
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding leather sandals in one's hands; this is how one should train. (63)

Exegesis: Regarding the origin of the rule, whether an offense has been committed therein or not, and for all other members of the fourfold assembly, it is entirely as previously stated (since it was previously forbidden to enter there wearing [shoes], and furthermore, because one might grasp and carry them while proceeding, leather sandals were prohibited; as they are objects for treading upon and may be defiled by impurities, it is likewise forbidden to carry them into the stupa).
One must not wear leather sandals while circumambulating a stūpa; this is how one should train.

(64) *Explanation of the Meaning:* Regarding the setting where this was promulgated, what constitutes an offense and what does not, and its application to the other four assemblies—all are exactly as previously stated.

(There are two kinds of circumambulation: first, circumambulating because the path passes by the side of the stūpa; second, circumambulating to express reverence. What is referred to here as "circumambulating" refers to passing by the side of the path.)
Appendix: Examination of the Rites of Reverence in India The Vinaya Master Yijing states: Regarding the original rites of paying homage in the Western Heavens (India), there are many varieties;

some employ prostration as a mark of respect, while others employ circumambulation. As for prostrations, they are categorized into nine grades. As for circumambulation, it is divided according to the left or right side;
circumambulating to the right is auspicious, while circumambulating to the left is inauspicious. The number of circuits begins with one or two.

From three up to one hundred thousand times, each according to what it symbolizes. For instance, the common practice of circumambulating three times symbolizes making offerings to the Three Jewels, ceasing the three poisons, and purifying the three types of karma.
However, whatever is symbolized must not fall outside the categories of the Dharma; it is acceptable provided it accords with the holy teachings.
As for the mention of "nine" and so forth: first is the verbal expression of greeting, and second is the bowing of the head to show respect.
1. Raising the hands high in a formal salutation; 2. Joining the palms with hands level and hollowed; 3. Bending the knees; 4. Kneeling upright; 5. Placing the hands and knees on the ground; 6.
Bending all five limbs (the two feet, two knees, and two elbows) together; 7. Prostrating the entire body to the ground. These nine grades constitute the utmost form of a single prostration.
To kneel and praise the virtues is called "exhausting respect. At a distance, one bows the head to the ground and raises the hands; when near, one licks the feet.

They rub the other's heels. Whenever they deliver a message or receive instructions, they lift their robes and kneel for a long time. When honoring the worthy or receiving a prostration, there must be words of consolation;
they may rub the person’s head or pat their back, using kind words to instruct and guide them as a sign of intimacy and affection.

Once a renunciant śramaṇa has received such respectful greetings, he merely offers virtuous wishes and does not accept further kneeling or prostrations. These local customs have long been established.
This is improper. The wise should follow the instructions; do not comply with worldly sentiments and thereby impair the sacred regulations.
One must not wear boots when entering a Buddhist stūpa; this is how one should train. (65)
Exegesis: Regarding the setting and the origin of the rule, as well as what constitutes an offense and what does not, along with the other four assemblies, all are identical to the previous cases.
