The Sanskrit term is *pura*; this is translated here as "short-calf boots."
Regarding the wearing of boots, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Boots should not have high heels; they are permitted to reach only above the ankles.
They must not be like boots, and the front should be open."
Appendix: Examination. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states:

According to the holy teachings, when facing an image or in the presence of a venerable teacher, it is the proper etiquette—unless one is ill—to go barefoot; there is no allowance for wearing shoes or sandals.

One should leave the right shoulder exposed while the garment covers the left arm, and the head should be bare without a turban or cloth wrap; this is the constant custom. When traveling elsewhere, it is permissible to do so, and there is no fault in it. If...
This is a cold country; it is permitted to wear short boots. Other types of footwear may be used as appropriate according to the circumstances.
However, since distant lands and foreign regions differ in their climates—some being cold and others warm—there are many instances where local practices deviate from the sacred teachings.

In principle, during the months of deep winter, one may temporarily adopt such measures for the sake of maintaining physical health. Yet during the spring and summer, one must strictly follow the regulations of the Vinaya: footwear must not be used to circumambulate Buddhist stupas.
The instructions have already been clearly explained. The *pūrala* incense burner must not be advanced onto the altar; this has been decreed for a long time.
Nevertheless, there are those who contravene these teachings, thereby acting with arrogance toward the golden words [of the Buddha].
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding a *puṭa* (foot-wiping cloth) in one’s hand; this is how one should train. (The sixty-sixth rule.

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting where this was promulgated, the offenses and non-offenses therein, and its application to the other four assemblies, all are the same as previously [stated].
(Whereas the previous prohibition concerned wearing [the cloth] while entering, this regulation forbids holding it while entering.)
One must not sit and eat beneath a stūpa, leaving grass or food that defiles the ground; this is how one should train. (67) The Origin Story:

There were two regulations for this. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the group of six monks sat and ate beneath a stūpa, and having finished, they left behind leftover food and grass, defiling the ground before departing. At that time, there was a monk who possessed proper conduct...

They censured [the practice] and informed the Buddha, who then established a precept. After the precept had been established, the bhikṣus offered food after completing the construction of a stūpa, and offered food after completing the construction of a vihāra.
When the assembly gathered, the seating area was so cramped that they did not dare sit and eat beneath the stūpa. The Buddha said:

"Listen: you shall eat while seated. You must not leave grass behind, nor defile the ground with food scraps. At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu who did not dare to leave leftover food or grass to defile the ground.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to gather them and place them by your side; when you depart, take them away and discard them.
This was the second regulation established.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies as previously stated.

There is no offense in cases such as when one has such an illness, or when one gathers [excrement] in one place to carry it out for disposal, or during the initial period before the precept was established.
One must not carry a corpse past the base of a stūpa; this is how one should train. (68) The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus carried a corpse [past a stūpa].
As they passed beneath the stupa, the deity who protected it became enraged. Among the bhikṣus, there were those who delighted in training in the precepts and possessed a sense of shame;

they censured the group of six, reported the matter to the Buddha, and [the Buddha] established the precept. (The term "dead" (*shi*) means the exhaustion of all [vitality]; that is, the cessation of breath and the end of life. "Corpse" (*shi*) refers to the former physical form. When it is on a bed, it is called a corpse; when it is in a coffin, it is called a bier.)
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein by the four assemblies are all identical to what was stated previously.
There is no offense in cases such as passing along this path, being led away by those using force, or when the precept had not yet been established.

Appendix: Examination of the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas). It states that at the time of death and mourning, monks and nuns often establish elaborate rituals;
some even share the same expressions of grief as the laity, claiming to be filial sons. Some set up spirit-tablets within their quarters to serve as objects of veneration.
Some wear coarse, dark-colored cloth, deviating from the norm; others let their hair grow long, violating established rules. Some lean on staffs while wailing, or sleep upon mats of reeds.
These practices are all contrary to the ritual protocols of the teachings; their non-observance carries no fault.

In principle, one should prepare a chamber for the deceased with pure adornments, or perhaps provisionally provide a canopy, recite the sutras and the Buddha’s name, and fully offer incense and flowers.

This is intended to ensure that the departed soul may be reborn in a favorable realm; only then does one become a filial son and truly repay their kindness. How could it be appropriate to weep blood for three years?

If one intends to perform a *śrāddha* (ancestral offering) but does not eat for seven days, would this truly be in accord with repaying the debt of gratitude? This is merely to further bind oneself to the afflictions of saṃsāra and again entangle oneself in shackles;
it is to enter from darkness into darkness, failing to awaken to the three stages of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

How could such a person, driven by their own impulses, ever realize the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Vehicle? Nevertheless, according to the Buddhist teachings, when a bhikṣu passes away, one should observe and understand [the following]:
Having resolved to die, he was carried on a litter to the cremation site that very day and immediately burned with fire.

At the time of the cremation, his relatives and friends all gathered and sat to one side; some made seats by tying grass together, others formed platforms by piling up earth, and still others placed bricks or stones to serve as seating.
They had a capable person recite half a page or a full page of the *Anityatā-sūtra* (Sutra on Impermanence), but [they were not to...]
After they have been fatigued for a long time, each should contemplate impermanence and return to their quarters. At the pool outside the monastery, they shall wash together with their robes on;
where there is no pool, they shall bathe at the well. In all cases, they must use old clothes and not damage new garments;
they shall put on dry clothes separately before returning to the floor of their rooms, which they should smear with cow dung. All other matters shall be as previously described regarding old clothes.
Regarding the ritual for wearing [the robe]: there has never been even a fragment of a distinction [in this regard].

Some, however, collect the *śarīra* (śarīra here meaning "relics" or "bones") and construct a stūpa for the deceased, calling it a *kūṭāgāra*. Its shape is like a small pagoda, but it lacks the wheel and canopy on top.
How can one possibly discard the holy teachings of the Father of Śākya and instead follow the secular rites of the Duke of Zhou, wailing for several months and wearing plain cloth for three years?
[This is] indeed [the case] (from the *Anityatā-sūtra*, found in the Northern Canon, Case Xio; Southern Canon, Case Dang).
One must not bury a corpse beneath a stupa. This should be studied. (Sixty-ninth).
Exegesis: Regarding the origin of the setting, what constitutes an offense and what does not, and the other four assemblies—all are exactly as previously stated.

[The term] "burying" means interring. Whenever a bhikṣu passes away, one should follow the four methods of burial prescribed by the Buddha: namely, cremation, water burial, earth burial, and abandonment in the forest. These four methods must necessarily depend upon the appropriate location.
One must not act rashly; otherwise, it will contradict the holy teachings. One must be cautious. Appendix:
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "When a bhikṣu dies, he should be cremated. Upāli said to the Buddha:
"As the Buddha has taught, there are eighty thousand worms within this body. How can [this be done]?"
When cremating [the body], the Buddha said: "These various classes of insects are born together with the person and die together with the person.
If there are sores on the body, one should observe that there are no insects [inside] before proceeding to cremate or bury it. If firewood cannot be obtained, it may be discarded in a river;

if there is no river, dig a hole in the ground and bury it. Since the ground abounds in insects and ants, one should place the body in a deep thicket or dense bush, ensuring the head points toward the north."
He should lie on his right side, supporting his head with a bundle of grass, and cover his body with grass or leaves.
The bhikṣu escorting the funeral should have a capable person recite the *Triskandhaka* Sūtra on Impermanence and chant gāthās to offer prayers for the deceased.
Once the task is completed, he should return to the monastery and wash his body; if he has touched the corpse, he must bathe along with his robes. As for those who did not...
Regarding "touching": having merely washed one's hands and feet, one should return to the monastery and pay homage to the caitya.
One must not burn corpses beneath a stūpa; this is how one should train. (Seventieth)

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting where [the offense] was initiated, what constitutes an infraction therein and what does not, as well as the remaining four assemblies, all are identical to the previous cases.
The *sūtras* and *vinayas* refer to this as *chāpī* (荼毗) or *shájí* (闍維); this translates as "cremation."
One must not burn a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is what one should learn (71). Explanation of the Meaning:
Regarding the setting where the rule was established, the nature of the offense and its non-offense, and the application to the other four assemblies, all are identical to what preceded.
(*Xiang* here means that one must not burn [a corpse] directly facing the front of the stūpa.)
One must not burn corpses within four paces of a Buddha-stūpa so that foul odors enter it; this is a training rule (the seventy-second). Explanation of the Meaning:
Regarding the setting where this was established, the nature of the offense and its non-offense, and the application to the other four assemblies, all are the same as previously stated.

[The previous prohibition concerned the front directly facing the stūpa; this regulation concerns all four sides. One should circumambulate the Tathāgata’s stūpa with incense and flowers, observing its features with reverence; how could one allow the impurity of corpse-odors to permeate from all four directions? One must seek [a place for cremation elsewhere].
(In a secluded place, it is appropriate to cremate them). Appendix:
Examination. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana consumed various fragrant oils."

He burned his body and arms as an offering to the Buddha to repay the profound kindness of the Dharma-milk. His radiance shone universally throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty billion Ganges Rivers.
Within them, all the Buddhas praised him with one voice. For the Sage perceives the Way and realizes the emptiness of nature;
his three karmas are purely immaculate and free from all defilement. Although he burned his physical flesh, this is called the True Dharma.
To offer [such things] would constitute an impurity for ordinary people; therefore, it is prohibited.
One must not carry a deceased person’s clothing or bed past a stūpa, except when they have been washed, dyed, or perfumed with incense.
This is a training rule (the seventy-third).
The Origin: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The group of six monks carried a corpse’s shroud and a bier as they passed beneath a stūpa.
The deity residing there became enraged. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them with disapproval and informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.
At that time, the bhikṣus who wore rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika) were uncertain and did not dare to pass beneath a stūpa carrying a corpse’s shroud.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to wash, dye, and perfume it, and then carry it across. This is therefore an exception; this is the second regulation.
Regarding the offense incurred therein, for all members of the fourfold assembly, it is entirely the same as before. As for those who do not commit an offense: [as stated previously].
If at any time there is such an illness, or if [the robe] has been washed, dyed, or perfumed, as well as in cases prior to the initial formulation of the precepts,
the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one obtains a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) that has been long submerged in water, because it is purely..."
Wash it clean with ash and smear it with kṛṣṇāgaru incense; only then may one wear it and enter the stūpa. (To wear robes made of discarded rags is the dhūta practice of shame and modesty.

That these may be washed, dyed, and perfumed until they are pure, clean, and free of impurity—this is what the Sage’s compassion permits for entry into the stūpa. This has a profound purpose: first, to cause those who crave finery to feel self-reproach; second, to cause the assembly of dhūta practitioners to increase their cultivation.
The intent behind this is deep.)
Appendix: An Examination of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When ill, one should not consume garlic. If the illness does not subside, its consumption is permitted.
Once it has been consumed, one should not circumambulate a stūpa. If the stūpa is located in the open air, one may perform prostrations from a distance downwind."
The Fifteenth Volume of the Compendium on the Cessation and Maintenance of the Vinaya:
Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings. *Tángtū* means to collide or to push forward impetuously.
The character for "gingiva" (齦) is pronounced yín; it refers to the flesh at the base of the teeth.
It is a phonetic loan from "to augment" (益).
"Yawning" (欠) refers to the act of stretching one's limbs while yawning; it is synonymous with "frowning and stretching" (顰伸).
*Lángbèi* (lower tone for *bèi*): The *láng* has long forelegs and short hind legs; the *bèi* has short forelegs and long hind legs.
A *láng* cannot stand without a *bèi*, and a *bèi* cannot walk without a *láng*. If they are separated, they can neither advance nor retreat.
This is now used as a metaphor for young bhikṣus who do not separate from their elders when entering or leaving.
The first character, 嚅 (ruó), has the upper radical pronounced as bó and the lower radical pronounced as jí.
The character 嗗 (wò) is pronounced wā; it denotes the sound of drinking.
The character 啜 (chuò) is pronounced chuān with a final stop; it is synonymous with 歠 (chuò).
Zhuan (專): the pronunciation is zhuan; it refers to the calf muscle.
Nie (齧): the pronunciation is nie; it refers to a boil. Zuo (痤):
pronounced with the level tone (ping sheng); it refers to a small swelling.
*Jiá* (頰): the sound is *jié*; it refers to the sides of the face.
*Kǎi* (摡): the sound is *xì*; it can also be pronounced *gài*; it means to take up.
*Fèi* (屝): the sound is *fèi*.
*Jiè* (屩) is pronounced *jué*.
*Yì* (瘞) is pronounced *yì*; it means to bury or to conceal.
Tuṣita Heaven is the same as Dōushuītā Heaven, which translates here as "Contentment. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

Because this heaven is the most supreme within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*caramabhavika*) all manifest birth therein for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
*Chān* (襜) [is pronounced with a level tone]; it refers to a garment that covers the front.
*Qiáng* (strong) means forceful; it signifies violence.
The *Shǒulóngnà Gēnběn Lǜ* (The Fundamental Vinaya of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa) states: "Śroṇakoṭī" is translated here as "two hundred koṭis.
In the city of Campā, there was a wealthy and noble elder who obtained an heir late in life. Whenever someone reported this news, he would immediately bestow two hundred gold coins as a reward.
He was named Erhuibiyi (Two Hundred Billion) after his father, who, upon hearing [of his birth], was filled with joy and bestowed two hundred billion gold coins upon him.

It is said that Erhuibiyi’s physical appearance was so upright and majestic that it was rarely seen by others; the hair on the soles of his feet was four finger-widths long and the color of pure gold.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that he was courageous and diligent, capable of enduring ascetic practices.
This refers to the twenty billion bhikṣus.
They were actually raccoons and foxes.
"Fox" (hú) is the name of a beast; its nose is pointed and its tail is large. It excels at manifesting as a malevolent spirit; it is lustful by nature and full of suspicion. This is its name.
The *Shanji* (Records of the Mountains) states: The fox was once a lewd woman of antiquity named Zi; she transformed into a fox and frequently referred to herself as "Zi.
*Tatan* (獺灘) is a rhyming word; it is the name of a beast whose form resembles a small dog. It dwells in water and feeds on fish. On the first month of the year, it sacrifices to the fish.
The otter does not sacrifice fish; consequently, the state has many thieves and bandits.
*Ōng* (written with the radical for leather) means "boot" or "leather footwear.
*Cǎn* (pronounced as in "miserable") refers to a light blue-black color.
"Sāi" (賽) is pronounced with the third tone; it means "to report.
"The three sections of non-awakening to dependent origination" refers to the statement that ignorance and non-awakening give rise to the three subtle states.
These—the karmic, the evolving, and the manifesting—arise in succession; hence they are called the "three sections."
*Cuì* (pronounced *cuì*) means "to gather.
*Táo* (pronounced *táo*) refers to the sound of wailing and weeping.

Seventy-fourth Training Rule: One must not defecate or urinate beneath a Buddha stūpa; this should be studied.

Exegesis: The setting for the origin of this rule is as stated above. Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as the other four assemblies, all are identical to the preceding [rules].
(Whenever one defecates or urinates, one should stay far from a stūpa and remain in a designated place; one must not relieve oneself haphazardly everywhere.)
Citation from the *Utpalaka-rāja-sūtra*: "If one performs even a small act of walking upon the ground of the Gaṇa-dharmadhātu, one shall fall into the Bāba hell for five hundred lifetimes.

Thereafter, for twenty minor kalpas, one shall be constantly forced to embrace one's own elbows and hands in that foul and filthy place of excrement and urine, all the way down to the Yellow Springs."
One must not defecate or urinate toward a Buddha-stūpa; this is how one should train. (Seventy-fifth). Explanation of the Meaning:
The setting and the origin of the rule are as above. Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as the remaining four assemblies, it is the same.

All these points are identical to what was stated previously. (The previous rule prohibited [this] beneath a stūpa; here, although one is at a distance from the stūpa, one still must not face it directly.

One must understand that the circular shadow of a stūpa is where the Tathāgata’s manifold virtues are gathered, where devas and humans gaze upon it in reverence, and where benevolent deities provide protection; one ought to show even deeper respect. How could a bhikṣu ever act with such arrogance?)
One must not defecate or urinate around the four sides of a stūpa, allowing the foul odor to enter. This is how one should train.
(Seventy-sixth). Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and origin are as above. Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not, this applies equally to the other four assemblies.

All is as previously stated. (The previous regulations restricted the four cardinal directions; here, the four intermediate corners are also included, hence the term "encircling. Thus, throughout the entire perimeter of the stūpa, regardless of distance, one must not defile it by allowing impure vapors to pollute it.)
One must not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecation or urination; this is how one should train (the seventy-seventh precept).

[Commentary: Following the example set by the rule for Buddha images, one must likewise not carry images of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, or any other holy sages, nor the Dharma-treasure of the Tripiṭaka, to or from impure locations.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies as previously stated.
There is no offense in cases where one passes through by way of the road, or is taken away by forceful persons, or when the precept has not yet been established.
One should train oneself: "I shall not chew a tooth-stick beneath a Buddha stūpa.
(78) One should train oneself: "I shall not chew a tooth-stick facing a Buddha stūpa. (79)
One must not chew tooth-sticks within four cubits of a Buddha stūpa; this is a training rule (the eightieth).
Explanation of the Meaning: The origin and setting for these three preceding precepts are the same. Regarding the offenses therein, they apply equally to all four assemblies.
All [the preceding details] are the same as before. There is no offense in cases such as: a large bird has carried it and placed it near a stūpa; it was blown away by the wind;

or it occurred before the precept had been established. (The Vinaya states: there are five benefits to chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*): first, the mouth has no foul odor; second, one can distinguish flavors;

third, it does not increase internal heat and *dhātu*; fourth, it promotes the intake of food; fifth, the eyes become clear. If one does not chew it, there are five disadvantages, which should be understood as the reverse of the above).
Regarding the practice of chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

One must not chew a tooth-stick in the presence of the Buddha, before one’s *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, before any senior monks (*sthavira*), before a Buddha stūpa, or before a stūpa of a *śrāvaka*. To do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, it is not an offense to do so before a fellow monk of the same seniority.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Chew about an inch of the tip to make it soft, and then slowly rub the teeth, the gums, and the molars, ensuring that all areas are thoroughly covered.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If willow twigs are difficult to obtain, one should cut off the portion used for chewing and discard it; once washed, [the remainder may be used]."
As for what remains, it may be used again the following day.

The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "Every morning, one must first chew a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) to clean the teeth and scrape the tongue, ensuring that the practice is performed according to the Dharma.
Only after washing and rinsing until completely pure should one perform acts of reverence. If one does not do so, both receiving and offering salutations will be entirely [defiled]."
One commits an offense.
One must not spit or expectorate beneath a Buddha-stūpa; this is how one should train.
(81) One must not spit or expectorate toward a Buddha-stūpa; this is how one should train. (82)
One must not spit on the four sides of a stūpa; this is how one should train.

(Eighty-third) *Exegesis:* The origin of these three preceding precepts and the circumstances for their promulgation are as follows: the Buddha established these rules as previously described. Regarding "spitting" (*tì-tuò*): it refers to the impure fluids flowing from within the body.

That which issues from the nose is called *tì* (mucus); that which issues from the mouth is called *tuò* (saliva). Whenever one spits or salivates, one should do so in a secluded place, and furthermore, one must snap one's fingers or clear one's throat before discarding it. For those who are elderly or infirm, the use of a spittoon is permitted.
Nevertheless, one must refrain from defiling the monastic quarters. As for reciting mantras at a Buddha stūpa, one must be strictly careful.
Regarding the offenses committed therein, they apply equally to all four assemblies and are identical to those mentioned above. There is no offense in the following cases:
There may be such illnesses; or a large bird may carry [the patient] and place him beside a stūpa; or he may be blown away by the wind;
as well as cases prior to the initial establishment of the precepts.
According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*: "In each of the four corners of the monastery, a spittoon shall be placed beneath the pillars (although it was permitted..."
One should place them there for various uses; however, they must be covered and should not be left constantly exposed).
One must not sit with one's legs extended toward a stūpa; this is how one should train. (84)

Exegesis: The setting for the origin of this rule is as previously described. The Buddha established the precept [stating that] those who stretch out their feet act with emotional indulgence and negligence, greatly violating dignified decorum.
[He was] entirely devoid of fear or respect; therefore, he prohibited it).
Regarding the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein by the fourfold assembly are all identical to those previously mentioned. As for non-offenses: [as stated before].
At times there may be such illnesses; or if there is an interval [between people], or if one is held by a powerful person, or during the initial period before the precepts were established.
The *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* states: "If the stūpas within the monastery grounds are full, it is permitted to sit with legs extended in the space between them" (Xicheng).

Whenever a bhikṣu attains the fruit of the path and enters nirvāṇa, his sacred relics (śarīra) are all collected to construct a stūpa, which is enshrined within a monastery for veneration; thus, the monasteries and stūpas are filled.
One must not occupy an upper room while placing a Buddha-stūpa in a lower room; this is how one should train. (85) The Origin Story:

While the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala toward the brahmin village of Tumbavana, the group of six bhikṣus placed a Buddha-stūpa in a lower room and occupied an upper room themselves. The other bhikṣus heard of this.

The Buddha censured the group of six monks and, having been informed [of the matter], established a precept: (There are two kinds of upper rooms: first, those that are high and prominent in location; second, those that are exquisite and beautifully adorned.

There are also two kinds of lower rooms: first, those that are low in location; second, those that are coarse and dilapidated. Furthermore, one may also designate a multi-storied building as an upper room.)
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies. As for those who do not commit an offense:
it may be when one has such an illness that one carries a stūpa of the Tathāgata while staying in a lower room and resides oneself in an upper room;
or when there is danger to life, danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), or when the precept has not yet been established.
The fourth section states: The group of six [monks] placed the Tathāgata’s stūpa in an inferior room while they themselves stayed overnight in a superior room.

The Buddha said, "This should not be done. One should place the Tathāgata’s stūpa in a superior room and stay overnight in an inferior room" (this refers to a room that is exquisite and magnificent as being "superior"). They then placed the Tathāgata’s stūpa in a lower room.
He stayed in the upper room (this refers to the multi-storied building being the upper room), while the Buddha said, "It should not be so.
You should place the Tathāgata’s stūpa in the upper room and stay overnight in the lower room. He then stayed in the same room as the Tathāgata’s stūpa.
The Buddha said, "It should not be so. However, there was a bhikṣu who, for the sake of guarding it securely, was apprehensive and did not dare to stay together with it.
[The monks] stayed overnight. The Buddha said, "I allow you to sleep with a wooden peg [for support], or to sleep at the head of the bed.

They walked while clutching a stūpa of the Tathāgata under their armpits, with their robes tucked back over the shoulders, wrapped around the neck and covering the head, wearing leather sandals, and carrying the stūpa of the Tathāgata on their shoulders.
The Buddha said, "You should not do so. You should bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, and carry it either on the head or on the shoulder."
Carrying the Tathāgata’s stūpa on his shoulder while walking.
Examination: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when establishing a monastery, one must first survey a suitable site. The location for the stūpa should be in the east or in the north.
The grounds for the Saṃgha and the grounds for the Buddha must not encroach upon one another, nor should the flow [of water] from the Saṃgha’s grounds be diverted [to the Buddha’s grounds].
Water that has entered the Buddha-ground may flow into the Sangha-ground and the stūpa. It should be made at a high and prominent place.
One must not wash, dye, or dry clothes within the stūpa courtyard. One must not wear leather sandals, cover the head, or cover the shoulders there.
One must not spit on the ground. One must not wash clothes or bathe in the stūpa pond; however, one may wash hands, face, or the alms bowl, provided the water flows out from the lower end.
Water. One may use it as one wishes.
When another person is seated and oneself is standing, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in cases of illness. This is how you should train.
(The eighty-sixth rule. Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and origin are as above. After the Buddha had established the precept, at that time the bhikṣus were doubtful.
"I venture to preach the Dharma for the sake of the sick. Thus, the exemption for illness was established; this is the second regulation.

All subsequent cases are to be judged according to this principle. (Regarding those who preach: they honor the Dharma above all else and do not seek gain or sustenance as they propagate the teachings. Regarding those who listen: they believe with utmost sincerity, and through hearing and understanding the meaning, they enter into the principle.

In this way, both parties obtain benefit. If both the speaker and the listener fail in their proper conduct, then both will incur transgression. Therefore, out of great compassion, the Buddha prohibited each of these instances one by one.)
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies. As for those who do not commit an offense:
this includes cases where one has such an illness, or is taken away by a king, a royal minister, or others, as well as cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precepts.

Regarding the practice of gathering, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one indulges the sense faculties while claiming to be free from illness, and a seated person speaks [of this], it is a transgression of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, for the sake of stūpa affairs or monastic affairs, goes before a king or a local lord...
He said: "Do not speak the Dharma to me; let it be so that fear may arise and doubt be produced.
If there is someone standing nearby, he should direct his attention toward speaking for that person. Even if the king listens, the bhikṣu incurs no offense.
One must not preach the Dharma to a person who is lying down while one is sitting, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (the eighty-seventh).

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting where this was promulgated, the nature of what constitutes an offense and what does not, and its application to the other four assemblies, all are identical to what preceded.
(Lying down refers to reclining on one's back. Because such a person stretches out their body with arrogance and lacks any faith or respect, one must not preach the Dharma for them.)
One who is seated while oneself is not seated shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train. (Eighty-eighth) Explanation of the Meaning:
Regarding the setting, the origin, the offense, and the non-offense, as well as the other four assemblies, all are the same as before.

"Seated" refers to being on a formal seat; "not seated" refers to not being on a formal seat. This includes everything from wooden stumps and earthen mounds to the ground itself—all are subsumed under "not seated."
When another person is seated on a high seat and one is seated on a low seat, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.

This is a training rule that should be observed (the eighty-ninth). Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting where this was established, what constitutes an offense and what does not, and its application to the other four assemblies—all are as previously stated.

As for "a high seat," the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of 'high': that which is tall in stature is called high, and that which is exquisite in quality is also called high. By extension of this principle, "low seats" may likewise be divided into two types: those that are small in size are called low, while those that are coarse and inferior are also considered low.
...is also called "low" (below).

Quotation from evidence: The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: The World-Honored One rebuked the group of six monks, saying, "How can you, being superior, preach the Dharma while standing above those who are inferior?
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "In the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was one..."
There was a householder named Cāpaka whose wife became pregnant and longed for mangoes (*āmra-phala*). Her husband said, "This is not a mango.
She thought again, "It exists only in the king's garden. At night, her husband entered the king's garden and stole one.
Before the appearance of dawn, he was not permitted to leave the park; thus, he hid himself within a tree.
At that time, the king and a brahmin entered the park, intending to eat mangoes. The brahmin sat on the ground while the king sat upon a high seat, and the brahmin preached the Dharma to the king.
The person stealing the fruit remained in the tree, thinking to himself: "I am now stealing..."
"Regarding this matter, I ought to have been put to death. Yet now I have escaped; I am without fault, the King is without fault, and the Brahmin is likewise without fault.
Why is this? It was for the sake of a woman that I stole the King's fruit, yet the King remains arrogant."
Therefore, while the teacher remains below, one may sit upon a high seat to listen to the Dharma.

Yet, because the Brahmin was greedy for gain and offerings, he sat on a low seat while preaching the Dharma to the king. "I have no connection with the Dharma shared between the king and this Brahmin;
I am now liberated. Having said this, he descended from the tree and spoke a verse to the king:
One person does not know the Dharma; one person does not see the Dharma. The teacher does not rely on the Dharma, and the listener does not understand the Dharma.
It is for the sake of eating fine rice and various other delicacies—that is, for the sake of food—that I say this is "without Dharma," because it is done for the sake of fame and profit.
"You have destroyed the laws of your own family. When I was still an ordinary man, I saw someone preaching the Dharma from above while another spoke from below, claiming it was not the Dharma.
How much more so now, when you, my disciples, preach the Dharma from high while remaining yourselves below?
As for the one who stole the fruit, he was none other than the Tathāgata."
When walking on a path, one should not preach the Dharma to a person who is ahead while one is behind, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train.

(Ninety. Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting, the origin, what constitutes an offense and what does not, and the inclusion of the other four assemblies, all are identical to the preceding [rules].

If one is walking on a path with another person ahead and oneself behind, the exception for illness here—based on the underlying principle—should apply to the preacher. This refers to those whose vision has failed or who have physical ailments in their feet, such that they must be supported by another.
"You were supposed to preach the Dharma later. However, some powerful person took you away. While on the way, they instructed the bhikṣu who was to preach the Dharma to remain behind instead."

Regarding the practice of preaching [the Dharma]: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if a bhikṣu has an eye ailment and another person holds a staff to lead him forward while preaching for him, there is no offense.
However, if a person is on a high walking path (*caṅkrama*) and one is on a lower walking path, one should not preach the Dharma for them unless they are ill. One should...

One should train [in this] (Ninety-first). Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and the origin. Regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not among these, as well as for the other four assemblies, all are identical to the preceding [cases].

(Within this, there are two kinds of "high": first, naturally high; second, having piled stones to form a foundation, which serves to manifest height). As for the "place for walking meditation" (*caṅkrama*): it is as when the Buddha permitted the construction of a hall for walking meditation.

There are five benefits: first, one is well-suited for long journeys; second, one is capable of reflection; third, one has few ailments; fourth, one digests food well; and fifth, one attains and abides in meditative concentration for a long duration.
When a person is on the path and oneself is off the path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train.
(Ninety-second). Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting where this was promulgated, what constitutes an offense and what does not, and the other four assemblies—all are the same as before.
(The "path" refers to the correct road; the "non-path" refers to the side paths to the left and right.)
One must not walk along a road holding hands; this is how one should train. (93) The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. A group of six bhikṣus walked along a road holding hands, and they even obstructed men and women.
When the laypeople saw them, they all reviled and disparaged them, saying, "They walk along the road holding hands."

Just as kings, royal ministers, and wealthy elders were heard by the bhikṣus to reprove the group of six for their fondness for violating the precepts, they reported this to the Buddha, who then established the rule:
(Regarding "holding hands," this refers to joining hands; it is not appropriate for bhikṣus, according to their decorum, to walk side-by-side along a road holding hands.)
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein by the remaining four assemblies are all identical to those previously mentioned.
There is no offense in cases such as when one has such an illness, or when a bhikṣu suffers from eye disease and requires assistance, or during the initial period before the precept was established.
One should not climb a tree higher than the height of a person, except for a specific reason;
this is a training rule (the ninety-fourth). The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
There was a bhikṣu who was observing the summer retreat atop a large tree. He voided excrement and urine while on the tree. A tree deity became angry. [The monks...]
[The monks] heard that there were those who felt shame and reproached [the practice], reporting it to the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not observe the rains retreat in trees, nor may you defecate or urinate around a tree.

If defecation or urination has already occurred [there], there is no offense in using such places. This is established as a precept. At that time, there were many bhikṣus traveling toward the country of Kośala.
While traveling, he encountered a fierce beast on the road. Terrified, he climbed a tree; others were unable to climb higher than his level, and he was consequently killed by the beast.
Therefore, the words regarding the causal conditions for the removal [of the robe] were added; this was the second enactment.
Regarding the determination of the offense: the transgressions committed therein are all identical to those previously stated for the other four assemblies.

There is no offense in cases such as when there is danger to life, danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or when the precept has not yet been promulgated (here, the minor assemblies are also governed by this rule as there is no provision for exemption;
however, if one takes willow branches, flowers, fruits, and so forth on behalf of the Great Sangha, or if a *śrāmaṇera* or *śrāmaṇerī* climbs a tree, there is no offense).
The *Varṣā-vastu* states: "If one wishes to take dry firewood from a tree, it is permitted to use a hook to retrieve it, or to use a ladder to retrieve it, or to retrieve it by means of a rope.
If the entire body of the tree is dry, it is permitted to climb it (for when a tree is dry, no deity dwells within it; therefore, this is allowed)."
One must not carry a bowl placed in a net-bag, suspended from the head of a staff, over one’s shoulder while walking; this is how one should train.
(Ninety-fifth) The Origin Story: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Upananda carried a bowl placed in a net-bag, suspended from the head of a staff, over his shoulder. When the lay devotees saw him, they thought he was an official and all stepped off the path.
He avoided him and watched from a secluded place; thus he learned it was Baddhananda and felt revulsion and disdain.
Those who possessed contentment heard of this and informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein, they are all identical to those of the other four assemblies.

There is no offense in cases such as being coerced by forceful persons, being bound, facing the two perils of life or the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), or when the precept has not yet been established at the outset.
The fourth section states: "One should not travel carrying objects on one's back, except within the monastery.

If there is an elderly bhikṣu who requires a staff and a shoulder-sling (kambala), it is permitted to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for him" (this procedure is explained in the section on "Performing and Carrying").
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a staff who lacks respect, except in the case of illness; this is the ninety-sixth training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
Explanation of the Meaning: The setting and origin are as before. The Buddha established the precept.

At that time, the bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to preach the Dharma to those holding a staff who were ill. Thus, he again made an exception for the case of illness; this was the second formulation of the rule.
Regarding the determination of the offense: whatever transgressions are committed therein by the other four assemblies are all identical to those previously described.
There is no offense in cases such as acting for the sake of a king or a royal minister, or when the precepts have not yet been established.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu is on a dangerous road in a state of fear, and a person providing protection says, "Venerable sir, preach the Dharma for me," there is no offense in preaching to them even though they are holding a staff.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a sword, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (the ninety-seventh). Explanation of the Meaning:
Regarding the setting, the origin, what constitutes an offense and what does not, and the application to the other four assemblies—all are identical to the preceding [rules].

[Commentary on "Sword"]: A sword is for the purpose of restraint (*saṃvara*). It is used to guard against the extraordinary (*asādhāraṇa*). If there is someone whose mind is disturbed by illness or whose spirit is depleted with fear, and who uses a sword to protect their body, one may preach the Dharma to them to provide guidance and consolation; in such a case, there is no offense.
The same applies to the latter two precepts).
One who carries a spear should not be taught the Dharma, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train. (Ninety-eighth).
Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the place where the rule was established, the offenses and non-offenses therein, and the remaining four assemblies, all are likewise.
As before (a *ho* is a type of weapon; like a spear, it has three edges).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a sword unless they are ill. This is how one should train. (Ninety-ninth.)

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding the setting, the origin, and so forth, each point is identical to what preceded [in the previous section]. (As for the "knife," it has various forms and is also a defensive weapon.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a parasol, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train. (One hundred rules.)
**Explanation of Terms:** Regarding the setting, the origin, and so forth, all are identical to the above. (*Gai* refers to a parasol.
**Synthesis:** The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Whatever can effectively shield one from rain or sun is all termed a 'parasol' (*chattrā*)."

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of stūpa affairs or monastic affairs, approaches a king or a local lord, and that person says, "Bhikṣu, preach the Dharma to me," he must not allow the sunshade to be withdrawn, fearing it might give rise to suspicion.
If there is an attendant nearby, he should intentionally speak to the attendant for their benefit;
although the king permits it, there is no offense. This also applies when rain or wind occurs during the time of a Dharma master or a Vinaya master.

During times of cold, snow, or great heat, one may hold a parasol while preaching; there is no offense. (This provision for the masters of the Dharma is established so that, in their extensive work of propagating the teachings, they may be free from transgression when encountering such cold or heat.)

If one were to seek distinction for the sake of fame or plot for gain and sustenance, how could they be compared to this precedent? Therefore, it is only when there is benefit that permission is granted; if there is no merit, it is not permitted. This is not a matter of uniform approval.
The fourth fascicle says: While walking on the road, Upananda carried a fine, large, round parasol.
When the lay devotees saw him, they thought he was a king or a royal minister, and all cleared the way for him. Not far away, they looked closely and realized he was a bhikṣu of the Buddha.
Because of this censure and suspicion, it was therefore prohibited that one should carry [an extra robe], nor should one store one.

There were some bhikṣus who, when it rained, went to the places for the morning or midday meal, or during the uposatha ceremony, and their robes were ruined by being soaked by the rain. Therefore, for the purpose of protecting their robes, [the Buddha] permitted [the carrying of an extra robe].
Within the monastery, one should carry [a fan] made of tree bark, leaves, or bamboo. One must not hold a large, round royal fan.
If one obtains such an already-made fan, it is permitted to accept it and offer it to a stūpa.

If one suffers from heat, it is permitted to make a fan from tree leaves, branches, grass, or cloth (cloth refers to textile materials, namely woven fabrics). If the hair in the nostrils grows long, it is permitted to remove it with tweezers.
If the nails are extremely long, like a grain of barley, they should be clipped; one should not dye the nails with colors.
One should not trim the beard and hair with scissors; rather, the beard and hair should be shaved off entirely. If the hair is extremely long, it may reach two finger-widths.
If one shaves once every two months, one should not comb the beard and hair, nor should one apply oil to the hair.
One should not paint one's eyes; if suffering from eye pain, the application of medicinal ointment is permitted.

One should not look at one's face in a mirror or in water. If the face has sores, the application of medicinal ointment is permitted. One may stay alone in a single room and look at oneself with water or a mirror (*The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:

"If it is for the purpose of examining a sore, or for observing one's former appearance as young or old, there is no fault in looking into a mirror"). One should not wear earrings, ear-rings, or necklaces.
One should not make necklaces, armlets, anklets, rings, or finger-seals; nor should one make a waistband of lead or tin.
One must not use threads of five colors to bind around the armpits, the waist, or the arms.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "It is permitted to ride in a cart drawn by a *gaṇḍa* ox, provided that another person drives it; one must not drive it oneself."
Combing or brushing the hair: *duṣkṛta*. Leaving a small tuft of hair on the crown: *duṣkṛta*. Keeping the hair long: *duṣkṛta*.
However, for a forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣu, there is no offense if the hair grows to two inches in length.
If there is a sore on the head, one should trim it with scissors. Rubbing the beard and hair with the hands: *duṣkṛta*. When washing the feet, [if one does not...]

[Having completed] the seven rules of training concerning speaking with others (the Seven Rules of Training for the Eightfold Assembly), [we come to] the eight rules for the settlement of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).

Regarding "disputes," the Buddha stated in the third *khaṇḍa* that there are four kinds of disputes: first, disputes concerning speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*); second, disputes concerning accusations (*anuvāda-adhikaraṇa*); third...
Disputes concerning offenses; disputes concerning the four matters. What is a dispute concerning speech? If a bhikṣu disputes with another bhikṣu, citing the eighteen grounds for dispute:

whether it is Dharma or non-Dharma, Vinaya or non-Vinaya, an offense or no offense, light or heavy, with remainder or without remainder, grave or not grave, customary practice or not customary practice, prescribed or not prescribed, taught or not taught.

If, by means of such characteristics, they engage in mutual verbal dispute and subsequently fight with one another, this is called a *vāda-vivāda* (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* calls it *lakṣaṇa-vivāda*;

the *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* calls it *anuvāda-vivāda*). What is a *anveṣaṇa-vivāda*? If a bhikṣu seeks out the offenses of another bhikṣu by means of the three grounds for accusation—namely, transgression of the precepts, transgression of views, or transgression of deportment—based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected, and seeks out the offense through such characteristics, this is [an *anveṣaṇa-vivāda*].

This is what constitutes a dispute over searching (*vitandā-vivāda*; in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* it is called a dispute over slander; in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, a dispute over instruction; in the *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha*, a dispute over non-discourse). What is a dispute over offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*)?

The commission of the seven types of offenses—*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, *sthūlātyaya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita*—constitutes a dispute concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*).

What is a dispute concerning matters (*vatthu-adhikaraṇa*)? That which constitutes a matter within a dispute concerning speech (*bhāṣā-adhikaraṇa*), that which constitutes a matter within a dispute concerning searching (*mārga-adhikaraṇa*), and that which constitutes a matter within a dispute concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*)—this is called a dispute concerning matters.

Regarding the settling of disputes concerning the destruction of the Dharma (*dharmaviniścaya-vivāda*): it is settled by two *vinayas*, namely, *sammukhavinaya* (decision in the presence of) and *yadbhūyaḥkaraṇīya* (the majority decision), or by one *vinaya*, namely, *sammukhavinaya*.

Regarding the settling of disputes concerning searching (*anveṣaṇa-vivāda*): it is settled by all four *vinayas*, namely, *sammukhavinaya*, *smṛtivinaya* (decision based on memory), *amūḍhavinaya* (decision for one who is not deluded), and *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (decision by investigating the nature of the offense;

"the place of the offense" refers to the investigation of the characteristics of the offense). Regarding the settling of disputes concerning transgressions (*āpatti-vivāda*): it is settled by three *vinayas*.
"Extinction" (*nirodha*) means being present before one. It refers to confession (*pratideśanā*), reconciliation (*sāmīcī-kṛtya*), or "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).
Disputes concerning matters (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*) are settled by all methods of discipline (*sarva-vinaya*) according to the offense committed. ("All" refers to the seven methods of settlement;

"according to the offense committed" means that among the three types of disputes, whichever dispute is acted upon—namely, the matter itself—is matched with the corresponding rule). Now, the four types of disputes that arise are combined with the seven methods capable of settling them.

It is given this name; thus, it is called the "Seven Methods for Settling Disputes. If categorized according to the commission of an offense and its resulting transgression, it is properly subsumed under the fifth *pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation).
However, in order to conform to the characteristics of the precepts, it is listed as the eighth.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: There are six roots of dispute (the "roots" being the causes). First, harboring resentment and remaining silent; second, an evil nature with a desire to harm;
third, greed and envy; fourth, contentious crookedness; fifth, lack of shame and remorse; sixth, evil desires and false views. These constitute the six.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu who accomplishes five qualities is able to extinguish disputes: (1) knowing what is factual and what is not factual;
(2) knowing what is beneficial and what is not beneficial; (3) having companions and not lacking companions;
(4) having impartial companions and not having partial companions; (5) acting at the proper time and not acting at the improper time."
The First Method for Settling Disputes:
*Saṃmukhavinaya* (Settlement in the Presence). One should grant *saṃmukhavinaya*; one must grant *saṃmukhavinaya*. The Origin Story:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Kālodāyin and the group of six [monks] were there...
They bathed in the river. Having finished bathing, they first stepped onto the bank and put on the robes of the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika), thinking them to be their own;
they departed without checking. When the group of six stepped onto the bank, they did not see their robes and immediately claimed that the others had stolen them.

Since those monks were not present, they performed the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against them. Having heard this, Kālodāyin became doubtful and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha [instructed him as follows].
The question was asked: "With what intention did you take it? He replied: "I thought it was my own robe; I did not take it with the intent of a thief. The Buddha said:

"If there was no intent to steal, there is no offense. However, one should not wear a robe without inspecting it, nor should one perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) in the absence of the person concerned.
From this day forward, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) as a means to extinguish disputes."
**Exegesis:** The Vinaya states: "That which is present" refers to the presence of the Dharma, the Vinaya, the person, the Saṃgha, and the boundary (*sīmā*).

What is the presence of the Dharma? It refers to those dharmas upheld for the settling of disputes—that is, at the time of settling a dispute, there are the seven methods for settling disputes (*sattarasa adhikaraṇasamatha*) that are maintained and can be relied upon.

What is the presence of the Vinaya? It refers to those Vinayas upheld for the settling of disputes—that is, there is the Vinaya Piṭaka of training that is maintained and present [at the time of settling].

A dispute is not settled by abandoning the correct meaning, but rather by employing other means of cessation. What is "in the presence of persons"? It refers to the disputant and the one who has ceased the dispute being present, engaging in the exchange of words, asking and answering questions back and forth.
What is "in the presence of the Saṃgha" through a formal act (*karmavācanā*)? It is when they have assembled together in one place;

those who did not come have given their authorization (*anujñā*), and while it is permissible to reprove those present, they do not reprove [the offender]. What is [the opposite]? It is the reverse of this, which is "not in the presence [of the Saṃgha]. What is...?

The boundary is manifested. Regarding those who establish restrictions for the *karmavācanā* within the boundary (that is, after the four directions have been proclaimed and the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* performed, the limits for the monks' residence, Dharma, food, and movement are established):

"That which should be granted" means it is appropriate; "that which ought to be granted" means it is logically fitting. If one clearly understands what is to be ceased and what is to be performed, and exercises authority according to the occasion, one must first deliberate upon what is appropriate, and only then apply the ritual according to the matter at hand.

If one grants what should not be granted, it is entirely due to being ignorant of the *vinaya* and failing to exercise prior discernment. Even if one exerts effort by force, it is of no benefit and incurs blame. This is not merely a matter of extinguishing disputes...
The Dharma should be given and shall be given to all practitioners; it is the same for all who perform and uphold [the precepts].
If one bhikṣu, before another bhikṣu, speaks with kind words, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha, saying:
"This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what was taught by the Buddha," then he— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content up to that point.)

Regarding those who persist in a dispute and say, "This is the Dharma," etc., they believe their verbal instructions and desire to abandon [the matter]. Then [the mediator] speaks again, saying: "You should accept this; this is what is acceptable. (This sentence is precisely for one who is skillfully able to extinguish disputes.
It is an admonition to cease the dispute and an exhortation to harmonize with the Sangha. If such a dispute is thus extinguished, this is called a dispute concerning speech (*vāda-vivāda*).
By means of the *tatsvabhāvaniruddha* (extinction by its own nature) and the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of), the majority decision (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*) is not required.
Regarding the determination of the offense: if a dispute among monks has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, yet one should raise it again, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu who has received the precepts recently, regarding what was a first dispute, should initiate it again, he commits a pāyattika offense.
It is the same if one bhikṣu [does so] on behalf of two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or even on behalf of the Saṃgha.
If two bhikṣus [act] for one bhikṣu, for three bhikṣus, or for the Saṃgha, it is likewise.
If three bhikṣus [act] for two bhikṣus, for one bhikṣu, or for the Saṃgha, it is likewise.
If the Saṃgha acts for one bhikṣu, for two bhikṣus, for three bhikṣus, or likewise for the Saṃgha—this is the meaning of "being present before" (sammukha).

If [the dispute] can be settled [in this manner], then when there are four or more people, the method is the *vinaya* of the Saṃgha. Regarding the five types—person, Saṃgha, boundary, and so forth—if it is not present before [all these], it is not called *sammukhavinaya*. If it can be settled [in this manner]:

Or, in the case of only two or three bhikṣus, where one bhikṣu [is present] solely through the presence of the Dharma and the Vinaya, and the person is present in three ways, while the Saṃgha and the boundary (*sīmā*) are not present in two ways—this is also called *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence). This is what has been explained above.

This explains the method for settling legal disputes within a single monastic residence (*sīmā*). Below, it further clarifies the method for settling them among monks residing in different locations. Furthermore, when traveling to another location, there is the method for reducing the number of participants en route, as well as the method for settling the dispute upon arrival at that place.
Because verbal disputes are difficult to settle and the matters involved are complex, this has been recorded in detail according to the Vinaya.
If the disputing bhikṣus cannot endure it, the Saṃgha shall settle the dispute in this manner.
Hearing that there are virtuous monks, excellent elders, and wise persons at another residence, those bhikṣus should go to that residence because of this dispute.
If, while on the road, they are able to settle the dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, this is [the method].

Regarding verbal disputes, they are settled by a single method of resolution: the *pratyakṣavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the accused). One does not employ the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (majority decision).
If it is impossible to settle the matter according to the Dharma while on the road, one should go before the elder monks who possess wisdom in that monastery and speak as follows:
"This dispute of mine arose in such a manner; it is such a fact; because of this, the Saṃgha has been stirred."
"It was done; it has been settled in this way. We do not approve of it. Therefore, we have come to you, Venerable Sir. Excellent, Venerable Sir!
Please settle this dispute for us in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
If you, Venerable Sir, can settle this dispute for us, we shall relinquish this dispute before you."

If the Elder is unable to settle this dispute according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s instruction, I shall personally cause the dispute to continue and further increase its gravity, so that the bhikṣus will dwell in discomfort.
Those disputing bhikṣus should thus relinquish the dispute before the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha should say to them: "Elder..."

Regarding the matter of an old dispute: if it arises in such a manner, as it truly is, according to its cause, and if the Saṃgha can settle that dispute—if one can speak of it truthfully, we shall weigh whether it is appropriate to settle this dispute.
If one does not speak of this dispute truthfully, the matter will become even more grave; it will be contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to what was taught by the Buddha.
It must not be suppressed. The bhikṣus will not be able to dwell in peace and happiness. That saṃgha should receive [the matter] in this manner:
once the dispute has arisen, it should be adjudicated. If those bhikṣus who are disputing are junior (navaka), they should be told: "Step aside for a moment;
we shall settle this matter together according to the teachings of the Dharma and Vinaya. If the bhikṣu is a senior (sthavira), the saṃgha should...
Having withdrawn to another place, they collectively adjudicated the matter for the Saṃgha, thinking:
"If we settle this matter before the Saṃgha, we fear that other matters may arise, causing the verbal accounts of both sides—good and bad—to remain unresolved.
We would rather assemble separately in one place with those who possess wisdom to collectively adjudicate this matter. Thereupon, they should make a formal announcement (*jñapti*).

To adjudicate this matter (this is a simple *jñapti-karman* within the category of formal acts; it is the method for assembling wise persons as listed in the *Gangmu*, wherein, after performing the preliminary procedures, one makes the formal announcement).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha now assemble those who possess wisdom to collectively and impartially adjudicate this matter.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Once the announcement has been made, the case is adjudicated. If a bhikṣu possesses ten qualities, he should adjudicate the case through differentiation:

first, he is fully endowed with the precepts; second, he is widely learned; third, he is extremely proficient in reciting both divisions of the Vinaya; fourth, he extensively understands their meaning.
Fifth, if one is skillful in speech, possessing clear eloquence and the capacity for dialogue, thereby causing others to rejoice;

sixth, if one is able to extinguish disputes when they arise; seventh, being without attachment; eighth, being without anger; ninth, being without fear; and tenth, being without delusion when adjudicating matters.
Among the bhikṣus, there may be those who do not recite the precepts and do not know the Vinaya; they then abandon the true meaning and act as follows:

Regarding one who speaks improperly: the Saṃgha should formally announce and dismiss this bhikṣu. The announcement for his dismissal should be made as follows (this is the formal announcement for the dismissal of one who does not recite the Prātimokṣa from among those who hold the duties).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. That bhikṣu so-and-so does not recite the precepts and does not know the precepts;
he abandons the correct meaning and utters what is contrary to the Dharma. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha now expel this bhikṣu.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Having made the motion, he is expelled."
Among the monks presiding over the legal proceedings at that assembly, there may be one who recites the *Prātimokṣa* but does not recite the *Vinaya*.

If such a person abandons the correct meaning and speaks only a few words of the text, the Saṃgha should make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to have him removed. The announcement should be made as follows: (This is the procedure for the single announcement for removing one who does not recite the *Vinaya* from among those performing the formal acts).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. That bhikṣu so-and-so recites the *Prātimokṣa* but does not recite the *Vinaya*.
He abandons the correct meaning and speaks only a few words of the text. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the Saṃgha now expels this bhikṣu.
The motion is made as follows. Having made the motion, he is to be sent out.

If, among the monks presiding over the legal proceeding, there is a Dharma-master seated who abandons the correct meaning and speaks with forceful rhetoric, the Saṃgha should make a formal motion to send him out.
The motion is made as follows: (This refers to the dismissal of one who abandons the correct meaning during the performance of the formal act.)
The formal motion for expulsion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu Dharma-master [Name] has abandoned the meaning of the True Dharma and speaks with forceful rhetoric.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now expel this bhikṣu. This is the motion."
Having made this announcement, they should dismiss him.

If, while the monks presiding over the legal proceeding are reciting the *Prātimokṣa* or the *Vinaya*, they speak in accordance with what is right and just and in conformity with the Dharma, the Saṃgha should assist them.
If those monks do not settle the dispute according to the rules and teachings of the Dharma (this refers to the monks of the original location), [the procedure continues].
Now the Saṃgha should settle this dispute according to the instructions of the Dharma and Vinaya (this refers to the monks of the later separate residence).

If that Saṃgha settles it according to the instructions of the Dharma and Vinaya, then this present Saṃgha shall also accept this matter (this is what is meant by "the Vinaya has no dual regulations" and being in accordance with the method of settling).
The Saṃgha should say to those quarreling bhikṣus: "If that Saṃgha settles this disputed matter according to the Dharma and Vinaya, we too shall accept it."
This matter may be settled according to the Dharma. We should now likewise settle this dispute.

If it can be settled in this way, it is a case of verbal dispute (*vāda-vivāda*) which is settled by means of the "present" method (*sammukha-vinaya*), and not by means of the "majority decision" (*yadbhūyaśikṣā*).
Regarding the offense: if a monk, after a legal dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, subsequently re-ignites it, he commits a *pāyattika*.
If a monk who arrived later and is newly ordained claims that this was the original dispute and re-ignites it, [he likewise commits an offense].

*Pāyattika*: One who, having already granted consent (*chanda*), later regrets it, commits a *pāyattika*. (In this context, because there is the formal procedure for the single-announcement *jñapti-karman* regarding the selection of a person, those residing within the same boundary must necessarily grant consent in accordance with the Vinaya.)
If those disputing bhikṣus cannot endure it, the second Saṃgha should effect its settlement in this manner.
Hearing that there are many bhikṣus at another residence who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkā (the commentaries), one should go to that place.
If they are able to settle it while on the way, this is a dispute over speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*) settled by a single means: the presence of the parties (*sammukha-vinaya*).
One should use the language of many people.
If it cannot be settled according to the Dharma midway, one should go to where those bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya, the Dharma, and the Mātr̥kās reside, and say:
"Venerable sirs, this dispute of mine arose because of such [causes]; it is such in its reality; it arose because of this. The Saṃgha has acted..."
"It is settled in this manner. The second *saṃgha* has also settled it in this same way. I do not approve of this; therefore, I have come among you, Venerable Sirs.
It would be well if you, Venerable Sirs, could settle this dispute according to the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya.
I shall relinquish this matter among you. If you, Venerable Sirs, cannot settle it according to the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya, then we..."
If one arbitrarily instigates a dispute, it causes the offense to become even more grave and heavy, and the bhikṣus dwelling there find no peace or comfort.
Those bhikṣus who have instigated the dispute should, before a community of many bhikṣus, relinquish this matter. The many bhikṣus should say to those bhikṣus who have instigated the dispute:
"Venerable sirs, regarding this matter of dispute, if it has arisen from its true cause, as in the case of a second saṃgha..."
"Extinguished. [The disputant] speaks according to reality. Having spoken thus, they abandon the dispute. We should consider whether we are capable of extinguishing it.
If one does not speak according to reality, this matter of dispute remains unresolved; the offense committed becomes even more grave, and the bhikṣus will dwell in discomfort.
A great number of bhikṣus should accept the dispute in this manner; having accepted it, they shall adjudicate that dispute. The bhikṣus...
If he is a junior monk (*navaka*), one should say to him: "Please move aside for a moment; we wish to settle this matter impartially.

If he is a senior monk (*sthavira*), one should move elsewhere oneself and settle it together with others. If that community does not resolve the matter in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, [it must be corrected].
If the second *saṃgha* also does not settle the dispute according to the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya, the many monks should settle it according to the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya.
If that *saṃgha* and the second *saṃgha* settle the dispute according to the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya, the many monks should also accept this matter.
They should say to the quarreling monks: "Just as that *saṃgha* has settled the dispute, we also accept it."
It is acceptable. Now, one should settle this dispute in this manner. This is a dispute by speech; it is settled by a single means: the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
It does not require the method of "many voices. In this context, "presence" refers to the presence of the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the persons, as described above.
**The Offense:** If a dispute among monks has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, and a monk should initiate it again, he commits a *pāyattika*.
If a monk who arrived later and is newly ordained should consider this to be a new dispute and should initiate it again, [he likewise commits a *pāyattika*].
It is a *pāyattika*.
If one goes to the dwelling of a single bhikṣu who maintains the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, and even upon reaching the halfway point, it is as stated above.
If one goes to the dwelling of two bhikṣus who maintain the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, and even upon reaching the halfway point, it is also as stated above.
Regarding the bhikṣuṇīs who study together:
the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are two kinds of illegal *pratyakṣavinaya*.
If it is illegal, one should admonish the illegal party to submit; if it is illegal, one should admonish the legal party to [submit].

There are two ways of subduing that are in accordance with the Dharma: if one is acting in accordance with the Dharma, one should command those who are in accordance with the Dharma to subdue [the offender];
if one is acting in accordance with the Dharma, one should command those who are not in accordance with the Dharma to subdue [the offender].
Mahāyāna bhikṣus who study together should skillfully reconcile disputes.
Examination based on the *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā*: it states that there are ten types of *karmavācanā* performed without the assembly being present (*asammukha*).

1. Covering the bowl (pātra-praticchādana). 2. Abandoning the covering of the bowl (pātra-praticchādana-parityāga)—meaning that when laypeople revile or slander monks, the Sangha should perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā) against them, ceasing all social interaction; subsequently, [the layperson] must recognize their own transgression.

1. Following the mind’s request for the Saṃgha to grant a formal release (the Saṃgha should perform a *karmavācanā* to grant the release and relinquishment; this constitutes the release). 2. The three types of learned families (*śaikṣakula*). 3. Relinquishing the learned families (as explained in the section on the method of confession). 4.

Building a dwelling (this refers to using the site of an old, abandoned monastery and, through a *karmavācanā*, granting it to a layperson to manage, who then builds a residence for the Saṃgha). 5. Śrāmaṇeras (referring to those who have been expelled for holding wrong views;

all those mentioned above have not yet received the full ordination and are thus not permitted to hear the *karmavācanā* methods, so they need not be present. Regarding the two types of releases and the building of a dwelling, as well as the expulsion of a śrāmaṇera, they should be placed where they are within sight but beyond hearing).
7. Insanity (meaning that because of ignorance, it is not necessary for [the accused] to appear in person). 8. Not prostrating. 9. Not conversing together. 10.

Not making offerings (meaning that when a bhikṣu unlawfully harasses a bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣuṇī may not deal with him face-to-face before the Great Saṃgha; she must instead follow the Buddha’s regulations and perform these three kinds of *karmavācanā* from a distance. Excluding these ten matters, it is clear that all other procedures require the accused to appear in person;
this is explained in detail within the section on "Performing and Maintaining").
The fourth section states: A bhikṣu should be known as a person capable of adjudicating legal cases through twenty-two types of conduct:
first, being fully endowed with the observance of the two hundred and fifty precepts; second, being widely learned; third, being well-versed in the Abhidharma and the Vinaya.
